en: May Gaṇapati, the first chapter, grant you auspicious things— he at whose displeasure even Brahmā falters in attempting to accomplish even the most trivial task.
Once that rise of fortune and good luck, easily attained by prostrating at his feet, has occurred, even the sovereignty of the Lord of the Gods enters the stage without restraint. || 1 ||
May this very goddess of speech, who eternally occupies the lion-throne of the nectar of Puṇyahiraṇyagarbha, bestow upon you abundant blessings—
she by whom [the ocean] was made to overflow with the moonlight from the nails of her pure, tender toes and fingers.
The ocean of the nectar of the Word-Brahman sports unrestrainedly within the mind that has dispelled all confusion. || 2 ||
O Śubharatā, this news of a fresh bouquet of *rāga* flowers is truly heart-stirring; O charming girl, you have displayed such cleverness as I have done.
O beloved Śubharatā, she knows exactly what you do, for whatever you perform, she understands it.
Thus addressed, the Conqueror of Madhu, his face rendered speechless, embraced his beloved; may he protect you. || 3 ||
Attached to the ground of the Lord of Mountains, sporting with a multitude of moon-faced women, and possessing the renown of a lion through his association with virtues, he shone forth. || 4 ||
Now, first, generosity and tranquility are being described. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, among the four castes and the four stages of life within the system of the four varṇas, I shall proclaim the duty of giving just as it was spoken by the Lord."
In the Nandipurāṇa: They praise giving as supreme; giving alone is the ultimate refuge. Giving is the kinsman of human beings, for giving is indeed the unsurpassed treasury.
Charity is the supreme substance, the very life-force; charity is like a mother and a father.
Without charity, no desired fruit whatsoever can be attained.
Even for a mere tip of a hair, no scale can be found to weigh it; there is no equal to those who possess the virtue of giving. Therefore, one should take refuge in generosity.
The supreme palace was filled with the resonant sound of necklaces and anklets;
indeed, the perfection of the quality of beauty is obtained through generosity alone.
In the Saura Purāṇa: Nothing greater than charity is seen in the three worlds;
by charity heaven is attained, and by charity alone prosperity is obtained.
Through giving one conquers enemies; through giving, disease is destroyed.
Through giving, knowledge is obtained; through giving, one gains the company of young women.
It is remembered as the supreme means for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Uśanas said:
There is no other way for a wealthy person to show favor than through giving;
for that which is being given increases for him even further.
The seer Vedavyasa said:
"Whatever you give to distinguished persons and whatever you eat day by day—that, I consider, is your wealth; the remainder belongs to someone else who guards it."
Whatever one gives and whatever one eats—that alone is the wealth of the wealthy;
others play with even the wife and the riches of the deceased.
[6] Bṛhaspati said: In the Kṛta age, austerity is the duty; in the Tretā age, knowledge is traditionally taught;
in the Dvāpara age, sacrifices are proclaimed; and in the Kali age, charity, compassion, and self-restraint [are the duties].
Regarding this matter, there is the Śatapatha Śruti:
"One should practice these three: self-restraint (dama), generosity (dāna), and compassion (dayā).
Through generosity one becomes an enjoyer of wealth; through service to the elders, one becomes wise."
The wise have said that through non-violence one attains long life. Yama says: For ascetics, however, the duty is tranquility; for forest-dwellers, it is fasting.
For householders, charity alone is the duty; for students, service is the duty.
But a single gift given to a brahmin who is a worthy recipient saves a man who is joined with evil deeds and falling into hell.
Likewise, it is taught in all the scriptures that wealth should be acquired by righteous means, increased, and protected, and then bestowed upon worthy recipients.
The Kūrma Purāṇa:
No duty superior to the duty of giving exists here for living beings;
therefore, gifts should be given by the twice-born to a learned Brahmin who is well-versed in the Vedas.
The phrase "by the twice-born" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), because the act of giving is common to all. As stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"For wealth acquired through hundreds of labors and dearer even than life, there is but one true destination: giving; all other uses lead to ruin."
Whoever gives wealth to a worthy Brahmin who asks for it,
places a desired treasure for himself in the world beyond.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Indeed, it is my conviction that there is nothing superior to giving;
for one who possesses wealth and grain, there is nothing that cannot be seized by kings or thieves."
In the Vahni Purāṇa: "O brahmin-sage, after penances, sacred fords, vows, and observances have been duly performed, one should subsequently practice charity."
[7] The wealth of that embodied being which is not for giving, nor for enjoyment,
nor for fame, nor for dharma— that wealth is utterly useless.
Therefore, having obtained wealth through fate or through human effort,
one should properly give it to the twice-born and cause monuments of merit to be erected.
Vyāsa says:
I consider him who performs his cleansing day after day to be like a teacher who is constantly entreating for gifts.
What will embodied beings, whose refuge is fragile, do with wealth?
That body for the sake of which they desire wealth is impermanent.
If indeed wealth must be abandoned when departing— whether for the sake of dharma, pleasure, or fame— why then is it not given away?
When will such a manifestation of power ever belong to anyone that it accords with their desires?
A man who does not give is a renouncer only in name; he merely departs after abandoning his wealth.
I consider a donor to be a miser, for even in death he does not relinquish his wealth.
Manu says:
One should constantly practice the duty of giving, both that which pertains to sacrifices and that which pertains to public works.
With a state of complete satisfaction, having encountered a worthy recipient, [one should give] according to one's ability.
That which is given at a sacrifice, such as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and so forth, is called *aiṣṭika*;
and that gift which is given outside the sacrificial altar (*bahirvedi*) is called *pūrtika*.
Whatever may be asked for should be given without malice;
for a worthy recipient will surely arise who can deliver one from all [suffering].
Desiring heaven, long life, and prosperity, as well as for the pacification of sins,
and likewise desiring liberation, one should give to the Brahmins every day.
Because of the nature of Viṇdu,
he does not give gifts, and thus his acquisition of wealth is in vain.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having risen again and again, one should give to the Brāhmaṇas.
In the Vahnipurāṇa: "O you whose wealth is austerity, by giving food, roots, fruits, vegetables, and vessels of water according to their means, righteous men go to heaven."
Likewise: "Those fools who here perform sacrifices, give gifts, and constantly enjoy pleasures dedicated to me— they are happy only in this world, not in the next."
Yājñavalkya says: A gift should be given every day to a worthy recipient, especially on specific occasions;
even by one who is distressed, it should be given according to one's ability, purified by faith.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "A gift endowed with all the aforementioned qualities and free from the aforementioned defects yields its desired fruit, like a wish-fulfilling cow."
In this world, one gains fame known as generosity; in the third heaven, abundant enjoyments; and even in a future birth, the power of supreme excellence through giving with faith.
A liberal giver is one who bestows much.
Generosity alone is the supreme dharma; generosity alone is the supreme austerity.
Indeed, there is nothing higher than generosity, both in this world and in the next.
Through giving one obtains enjoyments; through giving one finds long life;
and through giving alone a person attains both heaven and liberation.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "Even by causing distress to one's family, food should be given to a high-souled brahmin mendicant by one who desires his own welfare."
Devala said: Birth in the land of Bhārata is difficult to obtain; more difficult than that is human status;
and the state of being a Brāhmaṇa is considered even more difficult to attain than human status.
Being a brahmin, it is difficult to attain the possession of qualities such as knowledge;
therein, the acquisition of wealth earned through righteous means is desired, and from that, the attainment of devotion is sought.
Having obtained this conjunction of qualities— a sacred ford, a worthy recipient, and an auspicious occasion—
those men who bestow gifts have fulfilled their purpose on earth.
Agastya said:
The earth is sustained by seven [supports]: by cows, by Brahmins, by the Vedas, by virtuous women, by those who speak the truth, by those free from greed, and by those whose nature is generosity.
Those by whom nothing has been eaten [in charity], nor offered in sacrifice, nor death met at a sacred ford (tīrtha),
and who have not honored Brahmins with gold, food, or water— [for them there is no liberation].
For indeed, O Great King, those who are born again and again are seen to be wretched, naked, emaciated, and with hands marked by skull-bowls.
From the Viṣṇudharma:
"The evil-minded person who, despite having the means, does not give to a preeminent twice-born man who comes as a petitioner, falls into hell."
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"But he who, having acquired wealth, does not worship the Brahmins and the gods—
the king should confiscate all his property and banish him from the kingdom."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Those who are of good conduct, of noble birth, handsome, sweet-spoken,
highly learned, and knowers of dharma— when they come as supplicants from another's house..."
O Sage, all living beings are seen to be suffering at all times;
those who live off the fortune of others are born so because they failed to give gifts in the past.
Vyāsa said:
Those two syllables— "nāsti," "nāsti"— which were practiced in the past,
have now appeared in their opposite form as "dehi," "dehī."
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"People do not wake others and beg piteously, saying 'Give!
May you never come to such a state as this through failing to give."
[10] By saying "Give," the petitioner seems to awaken the person;
for this painful state of begging is indeed the fruit of not having given in the past.
With one standing below and the other standing above,
the distinction between the giver and the beggar was indicated by their very hands.
But that sinful-souled person who, out of delusion, prevents gifts from being given to cows, Brahmins, fire, or deities, shall go to the womb of an animal.

‘Being given’ means being relinquished for its sake; such is the meaning. Śātātapa says: “He who says ‘Do not give’ regarding a cow, fire, or Brahmins, having passed through a hundred births as an animal, is born among the Cāṇḍālas.”
Yama said:
"He who creates an obstacle during the giving away of a daughter, at a sacrifice, or in any situation involving a crisis of dharma,
him they call a slayer of a Brahmin."
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should create obstacles to non-giving;
one should give day after day to a worthy recipient out of a desire to conquer both worlds.
In the Mahābhārata: "For those who are worthy and deserving, there is indeed nothing that should not be given;
even the horse Uccaiḥśravas is known by the virtuous as something to be bestowed."
Having gratified him according to his desire, that Brahmin, true to his word and firm in his great vows, went to heaven after protecting the life of another with his own life.
And Rantideva, the son of Saṅkṛti, having offered cool water to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, departed from here for the back of the celestial vault.
Having duly bestowed wealth upon the Arhats Ātreya, Candra, and Damaya,
that wise lord of the earth went to infinite worlds.
Having offered his limbs, his wife Śivirī, and his beloved biological son for the sake of a Brahmin, Śīna ascended to the highest heaven.
[11] Pratardana, the lord of Kāśī, having given away his own two eyes to a brahmin, enjoys incomparable fame both in this world and in the next.
Having given that divine, golden parasol of supreme splendor with its polished ribs to Devamṛdu, he, together with his kingdom, ascended to heaven.
With polished staff and radiant frame,
Saṅkṛti and likewise Ātreya, having instructed their disciples in the attributeless Brahman,
departed for the unsurpassed worlds, endowed with great splendor.
Having given eleven billion cows to the Brahmins, the powerful Ambarīṣa, together with his kingdom, ascended to heaven.
Having given the divine earrings to Sāvitra and his beautiful residence to Janamejaya, he departed for that world.
Having renounced everything for the sake of the Brahmins, they went to the highest world:
all their jewels, the bull, the Darbha grass, the young horses, and the three beloved ones.
Having given a beautiful dwelling, Nimi, the King of Videha, ascended to that world; and the son of Jamadagni gave the earth to the kingdom of Nimi.
Gaya also gave the earth, along with its cities, to the Brahmins;
and when there was no rain during a drought, he repeatedly provided for all living beings.
And King Mitrasaha, having given his beloved Madayantī to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, ascended to heaven together with her.
And the highly illustrious royal sage Sahasrajit,
having renounced his dear life-breaths for the sake of a brahmin, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
Having given a golden mansion filled with all desirable things to Mudgala,
the high-minded Śatadyumna went to heaven.
[12] And there was a powerful king of Śālva named Dyutimat;
having given his kingdom to Ṛcīka, he went to the unsurpassed worlds.
And the royal seer Madirāśva, having given his slender-waisted daughter to Suvarṇahasta, departed for those worlds praised by the gods.
And the royal sage Lomapāda, having given that daughter to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga,
was gratified by all his great desires.
Having given away a hundred thousand cows along with their calves, King Prasenajit,
possessed of great majesty, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
These and many others— high-souled men of disciplined mind who had conquered their senses— went to heaven through the practice of charity along with austerity.
Their fame shall be firmly established for as long as the earth shall endure;
for some indeed attain heaven through acts of giving, sacrifice, and the procreation of offspring.

"By generosity beings are brought under control; by generosity even enmities come to an end. Even a stranger attains the status of a kinsman through generosity; for generosity destroys all calamities.

Thus [ends the section] in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by the illustrious Hemādri, who is the sovereign of all learned men, a master of all branches of knowledge, and the illustrious Mahādeva, the supreme king of great kings.
Chapter Two: The Section on the Praise of Giving, within the Section on Giving [13].

Now, the true nature of giving is described by one who follows the path of the ancient masters of right conduct, through whom the world attains its foundation because of their pure and distinguished acts of sacrifice and public works, which have rendered the multitude of the virtuous worthy of battle.

Now, the master Hemādri, free from all faults, speaks this chapter on the nature of various gifts— a purifier through manifold, wondrous, and friendly compassion that delights the minds of diverse scholars.
In this regard, Devala says:
"The offering of wealth with faith to a worthy recipient when [the recipient] has appeared is designated as 'giving' (dāna); its explanation is now being told."

When [the time] has arisen as determined by the scriptures, the presentation of objects—defined as a relinquishment extending to the point of establishing the relationship of master and servant toward the recipient—is called *dāna* (giving).
It is said to have two causes, six bases, six limbs, and six results;
it is fourfold, threefold, and characterized by three types of destruction.
The explanation of this was stated by that very same author: "In that regard, regarding 'having two causes':
neither the smallness nor the greatness of a gift brings about prosperity;
rather, faith and devotion are recorded as the factors that cause the increase or decrease of gifts."

Faith (*śraddhā*) is the conviction that [the teachings] are true. Devotion (*bhakti*) is contemplation preceded by affection. If the reading is *śakti*, it means tranquility (*śānti*) or generosity (*audārya*). "Having six bases" (*ṣaḍ-adhiṣṭhāna*) means that which has six bases—that is, six supports—as its causes. He states these:
"Virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), pleasure (*kāma*), as well as shame (*vrīḍā*), joy (*harṣa*), and fear (*bhaya*);
these six are declared to be the bases of gifts."
[14] He distinguishes these:
that which is given from alms-bowls constantly, without regard for any purpose,
but solely with the intention of renunciation— that is called the gift of Dharma.

"Without regard for purpose" means without seeking after visible results. They say that what is given incidentally, only with regard to a specific purpose, is "gift for the sake of gain," which has its cause in worldly fruit.
That which is given out of attachment to women, drinking, hunting, and gambling,
or to unworthy recipients out of passion, is called "the gift of desire."
When a teacher is requested by supplicants in an assembly out of a sense of shame,
and that gift is then bestowed, it is known as a "gift out of shame."
When a gift is given with joy after seeing or hearing pleasant things,
those who contemplate Dharma call that gift "joy-giving."
That which is given to those who cause suffering for the sake of countering abuse,
misfortune, and violence is called the gift of fearlessness.
Regarding the "sixfold [gift]":
the donor, the recipient, faith, the object to be given, and the merit (dharma),
as well as the place and the time— these they know to be the six factors of gifts.
He explains these [qualities]:
"Free from disease, virtuous in nature, desirous of giving, free from vices, pure,
and having blameless livelihood and actions— the giver who possesses these six qualities is praised."
Free from diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣmā),

possessing the three types of *śukta*, living by means of gleaning (*kṛśavṛtti*), compassionate, with all his senses intact, and liberated from defects of birth— such a Brāhmaṇa is called a worthy recipient (*pātra*).

"Triśukta" means one for whom the three—knowledge (*vidyā*), lineage (*anvaya*), and conduct (*vṛtta*)—are "śukta," that is, pure. "Ghṛṇālu" means compassionate. "Sakalendriya" means having unimpaired faculties.

[15] Always having great joy upon seeing those who seek [help], characterized by a pleasant countenance and so forth, as well as hospitality and freedom from envy—that is proclaimed as "faith" (*śraddhā*).
Acquisition through effort that causes no harm to others and involves no distress—
whether the gift be small or large— is what is designated as "that which ought to be given."
Whatever auspicious thing is difficult to obtain, and whatever time it may be—
those two, the place and the time, would be most excellent for giving, unlike others.
Depending on the excellence of the circumstances, place, time, recipient, and donor,
even an inferior gift may become superior, or a superior gift may otherwise become inferior.
He speaks of the sixfold ripening: "Bad fruit, fruitless, inferior, equal, vast, and inexhaustible—these six are taught as the pairs of ripenings according to their maturation."
He explains those [verses]:
"That which is given to an atheist, a thief, one who is violent, a paramour, an outcast, a slanderer, or a killer of an embryo, shall yield evil fruit."
A gift devoid of faith, though great, is fruitless; it yields a bad fruit, like a fruit that has been vomited out. A gift that causes harm to others, even if vast, shall lead to diminution.

"Fruitless" means having inferior fruit; however, if it were to mean being entirely without fruit, then the statement that "whatever one performs with faith becomes more powerful" would be inconsistent with the meaning of the other [passage], and there would be a contradiction with the words "fruit" (*phala*) and "ripening" (*vipāka*). "Supreme" means most excellent. "Inferiority" implies being slightly less; otherwise, there would be the consequence of redundancy with what preceded.
As it has been said: "But that which is given with a defiled mind, through the fault of its intention, shall have a fruit equal to [that of] mere giving."
A gift given with all six constituent factors is of vast fruition;
a gift given out of compassion attains imperishability.
*Anukrośa* means compassion. He states that it is of four kinds:
*dhruva*, *ājaśrika*, *kāmya*, and *naimittika*, in that order.
This Vedic path of giving is described by the twice-born as being fourfold.
Water-stations, groves, ponds, and so forth, which yield all desired fruits, are certainly constant;
they say that such [merit] is perpetual when it is given day after day.
Whatever is desired for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty, women, or children—
that gift which is established upon desire is designated as "kāmya" (motivated by specific wishes).
It is recorded as being dependent on time, dependent on action, and dependent on purpose;
thus the occasional rite (naimittika) is said to be threefold: that accompanied by oblation and that devoid of oblation.
He states the threefold nature:
"Nine are superior, four are middling according to their method, and the remaining are inferior; they know this to be the threefold nature."
He explains that very point:
sour curds, honey, a protective garment, a cow, land, gold, a horse, and an elephant—
these are the supreme gifts, because they consist of supreme objects.
The gift of knowledge, dwellings, enjoyments, and medicines—
these are the middling gifts here, due to the giving of middling objects.
"Use" refers to the implements for use, such as beds and seats; namely, sandals,
swings, vehicles, umbrellas, drinking vessels, and seats,
as well as items made of wood or fruit, the last of which lasts for many years.
Because the varieties of objects are so numerous, no numerical limit is prescribed for the remaining gifts;
therefore, the wise know all other gifts to be inferior.

"Bahuvārṣika" means that which has been obtained for many years; that is to say, ancient. By this it is shown that even excellent things, such as elephants and horses, become inferior when they have reached a state of decay. [17] He speaks of the nature of destruction: "That which is sacrificed, given, or studied perishes through being repeatedly mentioned;
and through praising and grieving, one whose splendor is broken comes to ruin."
Therefore, one should not boast in vain of the merit one has performed;
they say that only he who has actually experienced [the result] is a speaker of truth regarding his deeds.
*Ślāghā* means praise; *vṛthā* means without a purpose such as protection and so forth. From the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"It is said to be of four kinds: obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), optional (*kāmya*), and pure (*vimala*).
That which is given day after day to one who does not provide a return favor [is the pure gift]."
That which is given daily to a Brāhmaṇa without aiming for a specific fruit belongs to that category;
however, that which is placed in the hands of the learned for the sake of pacifying sin is of a different nature.

That gift which is performed by the virtuous for the sake of pacifying evil is designated as *naimittika* (occasional), signifying its specific, determined cause. That which is bestowed for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty, or heaven [is likewise occasional].
That gift is declared by the seers who contemplate dharma to be "desirable" (kāmya).
That gift which is bestowed upon those who know Brahman for the sake of pleasing the Lord,
with a mind intent on enjoyment, is pure and auspicious.
Manu says: "For with whatever disposition one bestows any gift,
with that very same disposition one receives it in return, being honored."
“By whatever state of being”—namely, by that which is characterized as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and so forth. This has been stated in the Bhagavadgītā:

“That gift which is given with the thought ‘it ought to be given,’ to one who does not return the favor, at the proper place and time, and to a worthy recipient—that gift is remembered as *sāttvika*.”
But that gift which is given for the sake of a return favor, or with a view toward a fruit, or again,
which is given with distress, is considered to be of the nature of passion (rājasa).
[18] That gift which is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients,
being unrefined and contemptuous, is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
From the Viṣṇudharmottara:
Actions performed devoid of prescribed rules, for the purpose of deceiving another,
and by one overcome by anger and greed— these should be designated as tāmasa (of the nature of darkness).
A human being always experiences the fruits of *sāttvika* actions even in the state of an animal,
or else in old age, through the influence of their caste and sacraments.
Whether in childhood or in the state of servitude, there is no need for deliberation on this point;
otherwise, in human existence, the fruit belongs to those of a rajasic nature.
One enjoys the fruit of those characterized by sattva in the state of divinity; of this there is no doubt.
From the Matsya Purāṇa:
O best of men, for some whose previously performed karma is characterized by sattva,
the fruit is seen even without human effort.
In this world, the fruit of rajasic action is obtained through [ordinary] action;
know that the fruit of tamasic action is obtained through arduous action.
From the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"Giving is considered to be threefold: bodily, vocal, and mental.
That which is the gift of gold and other such things to an Arhat is considered bodily."
"‘I grant fearlessness to those who are distressed’—this indeed is remembered as the verbal [gift].
O twice-born ones, that gift which is mental is that by which a yogi [is perfected] through knowledge."
Hārīta says:

The giving of an improper substance does not lead to heaven. That which one regrets after having given is, in effect, no gift at all and yields no fruit. That which one gives to a benefactor is merely a repayment for services rendered. That which one gives with guile or when solicited yields little fruit. That which one gives to an unworthy recipient is an undesirable gift that leaks away. That which one gives while boasting of it, or that which is given with a smirk, is demonic (*āsura*). That which one gives without faith or out of anger is rakshasa-like. That which one gives after reviling the recipient, or reviles them after giving, is unrefined and belongs to the *piśācas*. That which one gives with contempt, or treats the recipient with contempt after giving, is dark (*tāmasa*) and intended for those on the verge of death. And that which one gives who is not of natural disposition—these are the defects of giving, by which a gift is rendered unsuccessful, disconnected, non-heavenly, disgraceful, unstable, or fruitless.

In that context, "non-giving" (*adāna*) refers to the failure to offer the substance being given at the very moment of intention; the meaning is: with the desire for a reciprocal favor from a benefactor. "Only that much" (*tanmātraṃ*) means as much as has been given. "With a pretext" (*sopadhaṃ*) means accompanied by a condition such as affection. "Solicited" (*abhyācitaṃ*) means made known for the sake of public perception. "Giving what is undesirable" (*aniṣṭadānaṃ*) is giving to an enemy. "Proud giving" (*smayadānaṃ*) is a gift characterized by a specific mental state of pride (*smaya*), such as thinking, "There is no other donor like me. "Uncommon" (*aprākṛtaḥ*) refers to one who is intoxicated and so forth. [1] *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
One should indeed always know the great gifts and the supreme gifts;
one should diligently distinguish between merit-bestowing, desirable, and futile giving.

The great gifts (*mahādāna*) are the sixteen [rites] to be described, beginning with the *tulāpuruṣa*. Indeed, the ten great gifts are: gold, a horse, sesame seeds, an elephant, a female slave, a chariot, land, a house, a maiden, and a tawny cow.
In the Sāmavedopaniṣad:
They say there are three supreme gifts—the cow, the earth, and Sarasvatī;
for by means of recitation, sowing, and milking, they indeed deliver one from hell.
Śaṅkha says: "He who sacrifices with *iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices (*paśubandhas*), and the four-monthly rites (*cāturmāsya*),
and who performs sacrifices such as the *agnihotra* and others— he indeed has sacrificed."
The Agnihotra sacrifice, austerity, truthfulness, the preservation of the Vedas,
hospitality, and the Vaiśvadeva offering— this is designated as *iṣṭa*.
Whatever rite is performed in the single-fire ritual and so forth, whatever is offered in the three fires,
and whatever gift is given within the sacrificial altar— that is designated as *iṣṭa*.
Śaṅkha says:
"And the nursing of the sick should be designated as *pūrta*."
Vyāsa says:
"Ponds, tanks,
temples, the gift of food, and groves— this is designated as *pūrta* (meritorious works)."
Nārada said:
That gift which is given during an eclipse of the planets, at the sun's transits (saṃkrānti),
and on the twelfth lunar day and so forth— this is called *pūrta*.

Thus ends the second chapter, on the Nature of Giving, in the *Dānakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the sovereign over all kings, the illustrious Mahādeva, lord of all faculties, and master of all branches of knowledge.
[21] The Third Chapter:
Now follows the determination of the factors of giving.

And these are known as substance, time, faith, and designation. As it is said in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "The recipient, the substance, the time, the place, and pure faith—these should be known as the five constituent factors of gifts."
In that regard, the examination of the recipient is as follows. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, Lord Śiva speaks to the Goddess:
"These Brahmins are indeed mines of the Vedas, like the oceans are of jewels; therefore, they should be honored with great effort by one who is the foremost among the wise."

"Candraviprādhipā" means she whose face is like the moon, the lord of the brahmins; this is an address to the Goddess. "O Goddess of gods, wherever the brahmins who know the Vedas do not consume the supreme oblation, there the gods never eat the oblation."

And so says the Taittirīya Śruti: "As many deities as there are on earth, all of them dwell in the Brāhmaṇa who knows the Veda," and so forth. The word *viyat* refers to the sky (*vyoman*); the root *vi* is traditionally recorded in the sense of "leading" (*prāpaṇe*). Since these [Brāhmaṇas] lead the givers to heaven (*divam*), they are therefore remembered as *vipras*.
Even Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, Brahmā, Skanda, Anila,
and Śikhī do not rejoice in that knowledge wherein Brahmins are not honored.
A wise person should honor those brahmins for whom life, dharma, happiness, wealth, prosperity, fame, and residence in heaven are easily obtained through their grace.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, the Blessed One said:
"When Brāhmaṇas are constantly honored, I am honored; of this there is no doubt. And when they are reviled, I too am reviled in all my activities."
O King Yudhiṣṭhira, the Brahmins are my supreme refuge; he who honors them, I behold in my own true form.
Those who are one-eyed, crippled, eunuchs, poor, and diseased—
whatever brahmins are of such a form, behold them as my very own form.

This [verse], however, is intended merely as a praise of the Brāhmaṇa caste. Yājñavalkya says: "Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Vedas, for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods, and for the preservation of dharma."
Matsya said:
There is no god equal to a Brahmin; there is no teacher equal to a Brahmin.
There is no enemy greater than a Brahmin; there is no destiny greater than a Brahmin.
From the Vahni Purāṇa:
"Neither birth, nor lineage, O King, nor study of the Vedas, nor sacred learning—these are not the causes of being twice-born; conduct alone is the cause."
What will noble birth avail a wicked soul devoid of virtuous conduct?
Do not worms arise even within fragrant flowers?
Indeed, recitation is not understood as being exclusively for the purpose of grasping;
rather, let the meter be sought therein—for what is not recited by the Rākṣasas?
What is the use of much study for one who is evil-minded, like that of an actor? Only he has truly studied or heard the scriptures who puts their practice into action.
Just as water held in a skull-cup and even milk do not taste right due to the defect of their container, so too sacred learning becomes contemptible when its possessor lacks proper conduct.
Therefore, O Great King, know that conduct is the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa;
even one who has mastered the four Vedas, if he is of evil conduct, is considered inferior to a Śūdra.
[23] Truth, self-restraint, austerity, charity, non-violence, and control of the senses—
wherever these are seen, O King of Kings, he is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa.
Vasiṣṭha says: He whom no one knows as existing or non-existing, as unlearned or widely learned, as well-behaved or ill-behaved— that man is a Brāhmaṇa.
"Existent" means distinguished; "non-existent" is the opposite of that. The intended meaning here is that he who does not manifest self-exaltation is a worthy recipient (*pātra*). Yama says:
"One who is constantly devoted to non-violence, who offers oblations into the sacred fire, who is devoted to his own wife, and who is a giver—he is called a Brāhmaṇa."
He whose learning follows wisdom, and whose wisdom follows learning,
who does not transgress the noble boundaries— he indeed is called a Brāhmaṇa.
O King, they know him as a brahmin who does not perform blessings or worship for the sake of wealth or gain, and who has turned away from greed and delusion.

Blessings are benedictions; for the sake of wealth means for the acquisition of riches. Attachment is excessive intimacy. Generosity, forgiveness, good character, kindness, compassion, and pity—wherever these are seen in this world, O Lord, they know him to be a Brāhmaṇa.
Yama and Śātātapa state:
"Austerity, righteousness, compassion, charity, truthfulness, purity, learning,
discernment, and faith— this is the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa."
Baudhāyana says:
Knowledge, austerity, and birth—this is the definition of a Brāhmaṇa.
He who is devoid of knowledge and austerity is merely a Brāhmaṇa by birth.
Vasiṣṭha said: Those who are patient and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with sacred learning, who have conquered their senses, who abstain from the killing of living beings,
and whose hands and minds are turned away from accepting gifts— those Brāhmaṇas are capable of delivering others across [the ocean of saṃsāra].
[24] Yama said: Those Brahmins who possess knowledge, who are observant of excellent vows, who practice austerities,
who are endowed with truth and self-restraint, who are devoted to meditation, and who have conquered their senses;
Those who have attained the vision purify [others]; how much more so those who have entered into association with them?
By giving to them and by eating with them, one shall attain the supreme goal.
Having given to a pure twice-born man, the donor goes to an auspicious state.
And that man who possesses knowledge, austerity, and virtuous conduct, he too delivers others across.

In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "One should give to those best of the twice-born who are devoted to Vedic study, who possess knowledge, who have conquered their senses, and who are endowed with truthfulness and self-restraint."
To one learned in the Vedas, of noble birth, humble, ascetic,
observant of vows, and poor, a gift should be given according to one's ability.
Saṃvarta says:
That gift which is given to a learned Vedic scholar who is poor and especially in need,
that gift brings about auspicious results.
As for the definition of a *śrotriya* stated by Yama:
"He who learns the three *Sāvitrī* verses preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*,
and has practiced the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*), he is called a *śrotriya*."
The phrase "preceded by the syllable *oṃ*" refers to the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛtis*). Yājñavalkya says: "Brahmins who are distinguished by their learning and study are the source of all;
those devoted to ritual action are superior to them, and those who possess the highest knowledge of the inner self are superior even to them."
In the Padma Purāṇa: "Just as the Grandfather (Brahmā) is the eldest and most excellent among all the gods,
so too is the man of knowledge— who is free from the sense of 'mine' and possesses no worldly attachments— always worthy of worship."
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "Character is to be known by living together; purity by one's conduct in worldly affairs;
wisdom by conversation; thus a person is examined through these three."
In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa: "Patience, lack of longing, compassion, truthfulness, generosity, good conduct, austerity, and learning—
these eight limbs are declared to be the supreme characteristics of a worthy recipient."
Vasiṣṭha said: [One should choose] one who is rich in Vedic study, of noble birth, tranquil, established in the sacrificial rites, fearful of sin, and possessed of great knowledge.
One who is patient toward women, righteous, a refuge for cows, and exhausted by vows— such a person they call a worthy recipient.

One who possesses a [proper] lineage, born of a praiseworthy family; established in the sacrificial rites (*vaitāna*), devoted to the *agnihotra* and other rituals; patient toward women, meaning patient regarding women; one who seeks refuge in cows, meaning intent on serving cows; self-restrained (*yama*). One endowed with learning, virtuous in character, tranquil, patient, self-controlled, truthful, and grateful.
One who is devoted to his livelihood, who is intent on the welfare of cattle, who provides refuge for cows, who is a donor, and who performs sacrifices— such a Brāhmaṇa they call a worthy recipient.
A Brahmin who is devoted to sacred study, observant of the rules, ascetic, skilled in meditation, patient, self-controlled, and truthful is said here to have attained [the goal].

In the Mahābhārata: "O bull among the twice-born, the sages know that he who has studied the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, and who has not desisted from the six duties, is a worthy recipient."
"A worthy recipient" means the most excellent recipient. Vasiṣṭha says:
"One worthy recipient consists of the Veda, another worthy recipient consists of austerity;
but among all worthy recipients, that one is the most worthy whose belly has never held the food of a Śūdra."
Bṛhaspati said:
One vessel consists of the Veda, and another vessel consists of austerity;
whichever vessel arrives [as a guest], that vessel shall deliver [the giver].

One who observes celibacy is a worthy recipient; one who has mastered the Vedas is a worthy recipient; but the most excellent of all recipients is he in whose stomach no food from a Śūdra has ever entered.
Vyāsa said:
One vessel consists of the Veda, and another vessel consists of austerity;
but that vessel which is unmixed [with worldly taints] will deliver one across [the ocean of existence].
"Unmixed," meaning free from the confusion of birth and other such factors. Yājñavalkya says:
"One does not become a worthy recipient through learning alone, nor even through austerity alone.
That person in whom both of these, as well as right conduct, reside is indeed proclaimed to be a worthy recipient."
Devala says:
First is the *mātra*, then the *brāhmaṇa*, and beyond that the *śrotriya*;
likewise the *anūcāna*, the *bhrūṇa*, the *ṛṣikalpa*, the *ṛṣi*, and the *muni*.
Thus these eight types of Brāhmaṇas have been described first in this praise;
among them, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding by virtue of the excellence of their learning and conduct.
When one who is born into a family of Brahmins is merely so by birth,
being uninitiated and devoid of ritual action, he is designated as a *mātra*.
One who is uninitiated— that is, devoid of the sacred thread ceremony—
but who has mastered a portion of the Veda,
is upright, restrained, truthful in speech, and compassionate; he is declared to be a Brāhmaṇa.

The "transgression of a portion" is the study of the Veda with some part deficient. "Nibhṛtaḥ" means tranquil. Having studied one branch together with its ritual manuals (kalpa) or with the six auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), the Brahmin who is devoted to the six duties is called a *śrotriya*, a knower of dharma.
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, whose soul is pure and who is free from sin,
and who has acquired the remainder [of the qualities] like a *śrotriya*, is traditionally known as an *anūcāna*.
One who is endowed with the qualities of a learned Vedic scholar, consecrated by sacrifice and Vedic study,
who eats only the remnants of the meal and has conquered his senses, is called a *bhrūṇa* by the wise.
He who, having acquired all knowledge— both Vedic and worldly—
remains constantly self-controlled while established in his stage of life (āśrama), is remembered as being equal to a seer (ṛṣi).
Worldly knowledge consists of the knowledge of acquiring wealth and so forth.
One whose semen is drawn upward, who is intent on austerity at the outset, who is restrained in diet, and free from doubt;
capable of both cursing and blessing, such a one shall be a seer (ṛṣi) true to his word. [27]
Withdrawn from worldly life, knowing all principles, and free from desire and anger,
the sage remains established in meditation, actionless, self-controlled, and regards a clod of earth and gold as equal.

"Abstinent" means having desisted from prohibited and desire-driven actions; "inactive" means devoid of activities such as the acquisition of wealth. Thus, these lords of Brahmins, endowed with [proper] lineage, knowledge, and conduct, are known as the "Triśukta" and are honored at the Soma-pressings and other rites.
At sacrifices such as the *savana* and other rites,
even a Brahmin who is capable of receiving gifts, by accepting them according to the rule,
delivers both the donor and himself through his own spiritual power.
The meaning is that even one who is capable remains truly capable.
In the world, there is nothing more purifying or meritorious than Brahmins;
and for those twice-born leaders who live according to their prescribed conduct, there is nothing impossible to achieve.
A Brāhmaṇa who has undergone the triple purification (triśukta) may be employed by the twice-born for offerings to the gods and ancestors;
however, one who is overcome by the aforementioned defects or tainted by them is not desired.
"Overpowered" means degraded by the aforementioned family traditions, learning, and conduct, as well as by faults such as minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and the like. Manu says:
"Indeed, according to the excellence of the recipient and likewise according to one's faith, whether it be small or great, the fruit of a gift is obtained after death."
Dakṣa says:
"The distinction in the fruit of giving is respectively equal, double, a thousandfold, and infinite; for it is exactly the same regarding the time [of death]."

A gift given to a non-Brahmin yields a hundredfold merit; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, it yields a twofold merit; to a teacher, it yields a thousandfold merit; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, it yields infinite merit.
[28] A non-Brahmin (*abrāhmaṇa*) refers to those such as royal servants and the like. As Śātātapa said:
"Six types of non-Brahmins have been declared; so the sage Śātātapa spoke. Of these, the first is the royal servant, and the second is the buyer and seller."
The third is one who has many patrons for sacrifices; the fourth is a village priest.
He who has many patrons is a "bahuyājya.
But the fifth is one who is supported by them [the patrons] of a village or a city.

The grammatical construction is "he is a hireling of the village or the city. That twice-born man who does not perform the morning twilight devotion when its time has arrived, nor the evening twilight devotion when it has commenced, is declared to be the sixth type of non-Brāhmaṇa.
The term *brahmaṇabruva*, however, will be explained later in the context of unworthy recipients (*apātra*). Regarding the teacher (*ācārya*), it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"O best of the Bharatas, that twice-born man who teaches a disciple who has undergone the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) the entire Veda along with its secret doctrines (*rahasya*)."
O great-souled one, the wise declare such a person to be an Ācārya,
whether he has taught a single portion of the Veda or even the Vedāṅgas.
O best of kings, he who teaches for the sake of his livelihood is called an *upādhyāya*; he who performs the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* is [called a *guru*].
That brahmin who honors him with food is called his guru,
just as one performs the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), and the Agniṣṭoma and other rites.
The twice-born who performs [the rite] when duly chosen shall indeed truly be a sacrificial priest (ṛtvij).
[29] Yama says: A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin yields equal merit; to one who merely claims to be a Brahmin, it yields double;
to one who has studied the Vedas, it yields a hundred-thousandfold; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, it yields infinite merit.
One who has commenced his studies is called *prādhīta*.
He who knows the origin and dissolution of beings, as well as their coming and going,
and who understands both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), he would be one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas (*vedapāraga*).
Bṛhaspati says: A gift to a Śūdra is considered equal [in merit]; to a Vaiśya, it is remembered as twofold;
they say it is threefold for a Kṣatriya, and for a Brāhmaṇa, it is remembered as sixfold.
For a *śrotriya*, the fine is one thousand; for a teacher (*ācārya*), double that;
for one who knows the Self (*ātmajña*), sixty thousand; but for an *agnihotrī*, it is infinite.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"A gift given to a non-human being is known to yield fruit equal [to that of a human];
likewise, it is said to be double that when given to one of mixed caste among the three [twice-born] classes."
For a Śūdra, it is declared to be fourfold; for a Vaiśya, it shall be eightfold;
for a Kṣatriya, sixteenfold; and for a mere Brahmin (brahmabandhu), it is exactly that same amount.

That [gift] is declared to be a hundredfold when given to one who has studied [the Veda]; it is commensurate with a hundred thousand when given to one who is highly learned; and it is said to be infinite when given to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.

Regarding these [unworthy recipients], such as those who are non-Brāhmaṇas yet claim to be Brāhmaṇas (*brāhmaṇabruva*) and others who are unworthy vessels, the determination of their worthiness as vessels applies only to gifts other than the giving of cows and so forth accompanied by mantras. For there is a statement of Śātātapa: "A gift preceded by mantras that is given to an unworthy recipient cuts off the hand of the giver and severs the tongue of the consumer; a cow, a horse, gold, or land destroy the giver when they see the hand of a Brāhmaṇa who is not a *śrotriya* and has been excluded."

And because of this statement by Vasiṣṭha, since there is a prohibition against bestowing gifts of cows and the like upon unworthy recipients even when preceded by mantras, the determination of Śūdras and others as worthy recipients refers specifically to the giving of food. This is because of Gautama’s statement, "Cooked food [may be given] to others," and because it will be stated later that "food should be given everywhere. Dakṣa says: "If one begs for the sake of calamity, misfortune, debt, or for the sake of the family, one should give after having investigated [the case]; this is the rule for all gifts."
*Vyasana* refers to calamities such as those caused by kings or thieves; *āpad* refers to afflictions such as famine and the like. The first word, *artha*, signifies cessation [of debt]. Manu says:
"One who seeks offspring, one about to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, and one who has given away all his wealth..."
For the sake of the teacher, for the sake of parents, for the sake of Vedic study, or for one who is afflicted by illness.

One should know these nine types of Brāhmaṇas as *snātakas* who are beggars for the sake of dharma: the *sāntānika*, meaning one who seeks marriage for the purpose of procreation; the *adhvaga*, here meaning one who has set out on a journey for the sake of dharma; the *sārvavedasa*, one who has performed a sacrifice in which his entire property is given as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); the *upatāpa*, one afflicted by disease; and [the others]. Gifts should be given to these indigent persons, with special regard to their specific learning.
To these foremost of the twice-born, food together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given;
however, for others, cooked food is prescribed to be offered outside the sacrificial altar.

"According to the distinction of learning" means that one should give little to one of little learning and much to one of great learning. Baudhāyana says: For those who are well-versed in the Brāhmaṇas, learned in the Vedas, and masters of the Vedas; for those whose wealth has been consumed by the needs of their teacher, medicine, or livelihood; for those who are about to sacrifice, those engaged in study, or those traveling on a journey; and for those who have won all [the stakes]—for these, when they beg outside the sacrificial enclosure, a distribution of goods should be made according to one's ability. To others, cooked food should be given.

*Niveśa* means marriage. A *vaiśvajita* is one who has performed the Viśvajit sacrifice with the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvasva-dakṣiṇā*). Because of the mention of "outside the sacrificial ground" (*bahirvedi*), wealth must necessarily be given to these [categories of persons] even outside the sacrificial ground; however, for others, the rule regarding the giving of wealth applies only within the sacrificial ground. But outside the sacrificial ground, it applies only to cooked food (*kṛtānna*). — Āpastamba.

When begging, the occasions for doing so are: a teacher, a marriage, a sacrifice, the desire to support one's parents, and the risk of violating the observances (*niyama*) of an *arhat*. Having considered the merits in these cases, one should give accordingly. However, one should not show such regard for one who begs for the sake of gratifying the senses, as that is without a valid occasion. "The desire to support" (*bubhūrṣā*) means the desire to prevent death. Regarding "the risk of violating the observances of an *arhat*": it refers to the danger of a qualified person (*adhikārī*) failing to perform mandatory rites. Yama says:
"An offering made into the fires of the Vedas, which are like blazing fuel, and into the mouths of Brahmins, is truly offered."
It delivers the donor even from great sin.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "One who, endowed with faith, feeds a single Brahmin who has mastered the Vedānta, indeed eats for ten million Brahmins; there is no doubt about this."
Śātātapa says:
One should feed even a Brahmin who is devoted but ignorant of the Vedas, provided he has his mouth full of Vedic knowledge; however, one should not feed a fool who has fasted for six nights.
Vyāsa says: Whatever grain-particle a pure knower of the Vedas, devoted to the six duties, consumes, the fruit for the donor is incalculable; that remains inexhaustible birth after birth.
When a learned Śrotriya, who has completed his Vedic studies and vows with the ceremonial bath, arrives at one's house, all medicinal herbs rejoice, thinking: "We shall go to the highest state."

Herbs and grains. From the *Mahābhārata*: "O King, those who are devoted to them, whose wealth is theirs, who dwell in their houses, and who depend upon them—when such seekers come for their sake, a gift given to them yields great fruit."

(In this context), by the word "that" (*tat*), the ancestors and deities mentioned previously are referred to. Alternatively, it refers to those for whom that very food being given is their sustenance; the same applies to words such as "their wealth" (*taddhana*) and so forth. O Yudhiṣṭhira, what is given to those who are afflicted by fear from thieves or enemies, or to those seekers who desire to eat, yields great fruit.
[32] For those Brahmins who, when their country is in turmoil, have been robbed of their wealth and their wives and approach for the sake of property— the gift given to them yields great fruit.
O King, that which is given to those who are disciplined in conduct, who are emaciated, whose livelihoods are meager,
and who approach you as supplicants, yields great fruit.
Those who have not strayed from their own duties nor into the doctrines of heretics,
whose hands are withered and whose food is meager— for them, a gift given yields great fruit.
Whatever is given to ascetics devoted to austerity, as well as to those who wander for alms and seekers who desire it, yields great fruit.
From the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Those who are free from anger, devoted to dharma, tranquil, and delighting in self-restraint—
gifts given to such virtuous Brahmins yield great fruit."
Those who have been stripped of all their possessions by powerful men, though they themselves are innocent, long for those who are truly devoted; what is given to them yields great fruit.
Now, Śātātapa and Parāśara [state]:
"He who bypasses a nearby Brāhmaṇa who is studying,
whether at a meal or at a gift-giving, burns his family down to the seventh generation."
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "That fool who, bypassing a Brahmin standing nearby— provided he is not an outcast— should instead feed one who is far away though rich in virtues, shall go to hell."
Therefore, a wise man should not neglect his Brahmin neighbors—
those whose houses are situated not far from his own—
as well as all his relatives, his daughter's son, and his brother-in-law.
Especially your sister's son, as well as your kinsmen, O lord of the house.
A man must not transgress these [rules], O Lord of the Earth, even if they are very foolish;
for by transgressing them, he shall go to the most terrible Raurava hell.

The term *viṭpati* refers to a son-in-law. The rule that one should not bypass even those who are very foolish applies specifically to the giving of food; however, in the case of gifts such as gold and the like, there is no fault in bypassing a fool who is present. As stated by Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, Baudhāyana, Śātātapa, and Pārāśara:
"If in someone's house there is one fool and elsewhere a man of great learning, the gift should be given to the man of great learning; there is no fault in bypassing the fool."
There is no transgression against a Brahmin who is devoid of the Vedas;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire.
In the Mahābhārata: "If there should be a brahmin who is superior, though he be far away, and endowed with good conduct and other virtues,
one should strive to give to him, even by bypassing those who are nearby."
Viṣṇu states: "The family priest is a worthy recipient for oneself alone; so too are one's own sister, daughter, son, and son-in-law.
For whomsoever these—the priest and the others—are related, they are worthy recipients by virtue of being a priest and so forth, even if they lack other [general] qualities.
Vyāsa says:
Whatever is given to one's mother and father, to brothers and sisters,
and to one's wife and children— that is blameless and leads to well-being.
A gift to a father is said to be a hundredfold, and to a mother, a thousandfold;
a gift to a daughter is infinite, and what is given to a uterine sister is inexhaustible.
From the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"One's own self indeed shall be the recipient, and no one else shall be the domestic priest (purohita).
A gift given to one's own domestic priest is said to be inexhaustible."
Human beings should not observe a waiting period of a year toward their preceptor, officiating priest, or teacher, nor toward their mother or father.
One should not take account of caste with respect to one's mother or father.
The preceptor and the others have already been explained. Likewise:
"The mother's sister, the [own] sister, and likewise the father's sister;
the maternal grandmother, the sister's daughter, and likewise the sister's son."
A gift given to a daughter’s son, to a husband of a Vaiśya woman,
and to those who have fallen from prosperity— such a gift is said to be inexhaustible.
One who desires prosperity should give to one's mother and father, to a teacher, a friend, a humble person, and a benefactor, as well as to the poor, the helpless, and those who are distinguished.
From taking what is not given, those who subsist on the fortune of others are born.
"Beneficent" means intent on helping others. "Distinguished" means endowed with an excellence of virtues. In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:

"Whatever gift, worship, or adoration a father may perform toward his daughters—one should know that whatever meritorious deed is performed toward them, when given to them, that becomes inexhaustible."
Whatever is given to those maidens, that gift is indeed meritorious.
From the Kālikā Purāṇa:

That which is given to a brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, that which is given to a celibate student (brahmacārin), that which is given to one who is a treasure-house of austerity, and that which is always given out of compassion; [all these yield great fruit].
Having rendered all that gift inexhaustible through its stainless purity.
From the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"O twice-born one, one who desires merit should not consider even the slightest worthiness of the recipient when giving food;
indeed, food should be given everywhere."
Even when [the recipient] is full of faults, it is faultless; even when [the recipient] possesses qualities, it brings further qualities.
Therefore, food should always be given with every possible effort.
The gift of food to those devoted to the study of sacred knowledge yields great fruit.
Likewise,
it is said that for those who give wealth to the wealthy who are afraid of kings,
and to those who are afraid of thieves, the fruit is inexhaustible.
It is proclaimed that what is given to those desiring to sacrifice, to those wishing to cross over calamity,
and to the miserable who are beset by suffering, becomes inexhaustible.
Whatever is given during ceremonies such as marriage, the tying of the girdle, and consecrations,
when [the recipient] is in distress, that is declared to be inexhaustible.
Saṃvarta said:
These gifts and others of all kinds should be given in every way by a wise person who desires their own welfare, to the wretched, the blind, the miserable, and those who beg.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"Toward the wretched, the blind, the miserable, the helpless, and those deprived of speech; likewise toward the disabled and others—the dull-witted, the dwarfs, and the lame."
And that wealth which is given to those afflicted by disease shall yield great fruit.
Now follows the examination of those who are unworthy vessels.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Cowherds, merchants, as well as artisans and actors..."
One should treat messengers and usurers as Śūdras, even if they are Brāhmaṇas.
Those who have fallen away from their own duties, who subsist on the food of others,
and yet desire the status of the twice-born— one should treat them as Śūdras.
A Brahmin does not become a non-Vedic reciter, nor a merchant, nor an actor;
he does not become one who performs service for a Śūdra, nor a thief, nor a physician.
For that village where twice-born men wander for alms while being neither observant of vows nor learned in the Vedas, the king should punish; for it is a provider of sustenance for thieves.
Vasiṣṭha says: Those who cohabit with a menstruating woman, those who maintain no sacred fires,
and those whose family lacks Vedic learning— all these follow the dharma of Śūdras.
Viṣṇu says:
One should not give food for the sake of fame, nor out of fear, nor to a benefactor; nor to those habituated to dancing and singing—this is the settled rule for the sake of dharma. [36]

"Towards one who has been helpful and intent on helping oneself" means with the desire for a return favor. In the *Mahābhārata*: "But that fool who employs beloved twice-born men in the offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*), shall not obtain the fruit thereof; such is the Vedic revelation."
Yama says:
To those who observe no vows, who know no mantras, and who subsist by their birth alone—to these, no gift should be given; a stone does not save a stone.
Wealth must never be given to one who has abandoned the Agnihotra fire, who acts against the wishes of his guru, and who is constantly engaged in sinful deeds.
Twice-born men who teach the low-born (vṛṣala) do not deserve to receive gifts;
by teaching a Śūdra, a Brahmin falls—of this there is no doubt.
Likewise: "The royal capital is as empty as a well without water;
and just as an oblation poured into what is not fire, so is a gift given to a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas."
Vasiṣṭha says: As is an elephant made of wood, as is a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three are merely bearers of names.
In those kingdoms where ignorant people eat foods fit for the wise,
they invite drought or a great danger arises.
Vyāsa and Śātātapa state:
"When food is given to a Brahmin who has lost his ritual purity, who has fallen from his vows, and who is devoid of Vedic knowledge, the food weeps: 'What evil deed have I committed?'"
But those Brahmins who are devoid of purity and do not wear the sacred thread—their oblations, gifts, and ascetic penance perish; of this there is no doubt.
[37] A seed sown in saline soil, that which is offered as an oblation into ashes,
and that which is given to those devoid of ritual action— in these three cases, destruction is ordained.
A seed sown upon a rocky wasteland, milking from a broken vessel,
or an offering poured into ashes— such is a gift given to the unworthy.
Although the qualities of a worthy recipient were already described previously, the mention of faults once again is for the purpose of prohibiting people who possess such defects.
Manu says: "For that Brahmin who, though being a worthy recipient, accepts a gift..."
If one employs them in improper tasks, nothing at all should be given to him.
One who accumulates wealth by accepting gifts from all sides,
yet does not employ it for the sake of Dharma— one should not honor such a person as a thief.
Regarding forbidden things such as gambling and the like: Dakṣa says,
"If one gives a gift to an unworthy recipient or in a manner devoid of ritual injunctions,
not only does that gift go to waste, but even the remainder of his merit perishes."
Manu says: That which one gives to the undeserving and does not give to the deserving,
one loses both wealth and merit through the failure to distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy.
Yama said:
"But he who bestows upon those devoid of marks a livelihood that belongs to those possessing marks, is cooked in the terrible sin of killing a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt."
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "Wealth should not be given to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, nor should it be given to a Brāhmaṇa who performs no rites;
nor indeed to one who merely calls himself a Brāhmaṇa, nor to a base Brāhmaṇa."
Vyāsa says: One born from the seed of a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the purificatory rites of mantra,
and whose seed is merely his birth, is truly no Brāhmaṇa at all.
One who is endowed with the rites beginning with conception and likewise with the initiation ceremony,
yet neither performs the ritual acts nor studies, shall be a Brāhmaṇa devoid of action.

In the *Vārāha Purāṇa*: "A Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya who do not observe vows, the three castes beginning with the Śūdra who are not Brāhmaṇas, and a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of Vedic study and vows— these are called 'pseudo-Brāhmaṇas' (*brāhmaṇabruva*)."
Yama says:
He whose Veda and sacrificial altar are lost for three generations is called a *durbrāhmaṇa*, as is he who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī*.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "A knower of dharma should not give even water to an atheist, nor to a rationalist, nor to any heretic, nor to one who does not know the Veda."

An *nāstika* is one devoid of the impression (*vāsanā*) of a future world; a *haituka* is one who seeks to deny the next world through logical arguments—such as Manu and Viṣṇu [who are cited as examples].
One should not accept even water from a twice-born man who observes the "cat-vow" (*baiḍālavratika*).
A knower of the Dharma should not give to one who follows the "heron-vow" (the hypocrite), nor to a sinner, nor to one ignorant of the Vedas.
For wealth acquired according to the rules and given to any of these three results in misfortune for the giver and for the recipient in the next world. (MDh 4.192–193)
Misfortune is a transgression. Just as one who attempts to cross water with a stone raft sinks, even so both the giver and the receiver sink headlong. (MDh 4.194)
Yama:
He who, having set aside the true cause, practices the observance of vows merely to conceal his sin under the guise of a vow— that is known as the "cat-vow" (*baiḍāla-vrata*).
Having taken great wealth and given it away, one should abandon the *liṅga*;
that vow which protects [only] the next stage of life is called the "cat-vow" (*baiḍāla*).
But he who, having gone to the hermitage of ascetics, returns again [to worldly life], [is fallen].
That vow which involves the violation of the duties of an ascetic is called "cat-like."
Viṣṇu says: One who abandons dharma, who is always greedy, a Śūdra-like person, a deceiver of the world,
violent, and a betrayer of all— such a person should be known as one who observes the "cat-vow" (baiḍālavratika).
And he who always raises the banner of righteousness like the banner of the gods,
yet whose sins are concealed— that is called the "cat-vow" (baiḍālavratam).
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own ends,
crafty, and falsely humble, is one who practices the "heron-vow."
Those Brahmins who practice the vow of the heron (*bakavratin*) and those who bear the marks of a cat (*mārjāraliṅgin*),
fall into the *andhatāmisra* hell because of that sinful deed.
[From the Caturviṃśatimata]
The food being given weeps, crying, "What evil deed have I committed,
that I see the hand of this unworthy Brahmin who has neglected his Vedic studies?"

Kātyāyana, however, has stated otherwise: "He who is devoid of Vedic study and the sacred fire, and who has not worshipped the gods and others with these [offerings], and who rejects the gods and so forth— he is to be known as a *nirākṛti* (an outcaste)."
Śātātapa says: What is given to a temple-priest (devlaka) is not desired; what is given to a usurer is unstable;
and what is given to a merchant—neither here nor after death does it bear fruit.
Dakṣa says: What is given to a rogue, a bard, a wrestler, a quack physician, a gambler, a cheat, a flatterer,
a wandering minstrel, or a thief becomes fruitless.

In the Skanda Purāṇa: That which is given to one who is devoid of gods and ancestors, as well as to the lords (Īśvaras), and that which is proclaimed after being given to one who has abandoned the Vedas and the sacred fires; |||

That which is given with wealth acquired by unjust means, or that which is given to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, to a teacher who speaks falsehood, to a thief, or to an outcast— [that gift is fruitless].
And that which is given to an ungrateful person, to one who always hates the knowers of Brahman,
to a priest for hire, and likewise to the husband of a Śūdra woman;
[40] To a servant, to an employee, to everyone who is malicious—
these, O Indra among kings, are the sixteen futile gifts.
Even as an ignorant child dwelling in the womb, one experiences [the results of karma], not in youth but in old age;
therefore, O destroyer of enemies, there is no destruction whatsoever of what has been given here in this world.
The phrase "its fruit" is to be understood as the ellipsis. From the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"A gift given in vain at an improper place is proclaimed to be faulty;
so too is that which is given by one who has fallen from his high estate, or through unjust means, or with wealth belonging to others."
For a gift given to a fallen Brahmin, to a thief,
to one who causes displeasure to his teacher, to an ungrateful person, or to a village priest is indeed in vain.
Likewise, [what is given] to a seller of the Vedas, to one in whose house a paramour resides,
to those who are dominated by women, and similarly to a snake-catcher;
That which is given to a Brahmin in name only, that which is given to the husband of a low-caste woman,
and that which is given to a servant— these sixteen kinds of gifts are in vain.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Those who are lame, blind, deaf, mute, or afflicted by disease— these, O Great King, must be supported, but no gift should be given to them."
Thus concludes the determination of the recipient.
Now, the element of giving known as the "object" (dravya) is described in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
Whatever is desired, whatever is excellent, and whatever may be rightfully obtained—all that should be given to one possessed of virtue; this is the definition of giving.
In the Vahni Purāṇa: Whatever a man performs with even a small amount of merit acquired through auspicious means,
he obtains infinite fruit, just as Mudgala did in ancient times.
"By means of what is auspiciously acquired and earned through righteous means. The remainder [of the sense] is: "by means of a small amount, that is, by very little wealth.
In the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"O best of kings, even if they are merely potherbs obtained through righteous means..."
These should always be given to goddesses, virgins, and women.
And while those Brahmins and others were constantly eating it, [the following occurred].
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is dear to one in one's home—
that very thing should be given to a virtuous person by one who desires that it become inexhaustible.
In the Mahābhārata: "O Great King, there is no end to that which is acquired by righteous means and given with faith, according to the rules, to a worthy recipient."

Gautama states: “One becomes the owner through inheritance, purchase, partition, acquisition, and finding; for a Brāhmaṇa, what is obtained is the primary means; for a Kṣatriya, what is conquered; and for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, what is earned through service. Inheritance (*ṛktha*) is property acquired without obstruction. Partition (*saṃvibhāga*) is property acquired with obstruction. Acquisition (*parigraha*) is the appropriation of water, grass, wood, and so forth, which previously belonged to no one. Finding (*adhigama*) is the discovery of buried treasure and the like. Through these causes, one becomes the owner. “Primary” (*adhika*) means exclusive or unique. “Earned” (*nirviṣṭa*) refers to that which is obtained through agriculture and the like, or through service to the twice-born. This is according to the traditional authority (Smṛti) which states: “*Nirveśa* denotes wages and enjoyment” (Amara 3.3.801). Thus says Manu.
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, professional labor, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous.
The application of wealth is for the purpose of increasing one's resources. The application of ritual action is the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*). Nārada says:
"All activities have wealth as their root; therefore, effort is prescribed for its acquisition.
Its regulation consists, in due order, of protection, increase, and enjoyment."

Furthermore, that [action] should be known as threefold: white, variegated, and black; moreover, its division is to be understood as sevenfold. [NSm 1.30–40] [42] The meaning is that for each of the [types] beginning with the white, there are seven subdivisions.

Wealth acquired through learning, heroism, austerity, a daughter, officiating at sacrifices, a disciple, or inheritance is of seven kinds and is "white" (śukla); its increase is likewise of that same nature. [NSm 1.41] The word *āgata* ("acquired") is connected with each of the preceding terms, beginning with *śruta*. Wealth "acquired through a daughter" refers to the pair of cattle and so forth received from the bridegroom in the *ārṣa* form of marriage. Wealth "acquired through officiating at sacrifices" is that obtained from performing priestly duties (*ārtvijya*) and the like. Wealth "acquired through a disciple" refers to the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*) and so forth. In these cases, one should understand their "whiteness" according to the specific circumstances. "Increase" means the fruit; the sense is that this too is pure for him.
That which is acquired through usury, agriculture, trade, crafts, tolls, or following a profession,
as well as that obtained from one who has rendered a service, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala).

The investment of capital for the purpose of increasing profit is usury (*kuśīda*). Craftsmanship is the work of artisans and the like. Revenue from mines and such sources is toll (*śulka*). Service is attendance. That which is acquired through side-bets, gambling, theft, distress, forgery, violence, or deceit is called "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) for all [these means].

What is acquired through side-ventures refers to what is obtained by means of bribes and the like; what is acquired through distress refers to what is obtained by inflicting pain upon others; forgery refers to the counterfeiting of gems, gold, and so forth; violence refers to acts such as "stealing before one's eyes" while accepting the risk to one's own life; and fraud refers to hypocrisy in the form of asceticism and the like. Through these, buying and selling, giving and receiving, as well as various other activities and even sexual enjoyment, proceed.
Whatever a person performs with a particular kind of material substance,
he obtains a corresponding result, both here and after death.

In whatever manner one performs acts such as giving—whether by means of that which is white, black, or variegated—one obtains a corresponding fruit. "White" means pure and free from suffering; "variegated" means mixed; "black" results in the arising of unhappiness. As stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Merit performed with white wealth shall yield abundant fruit."
The variegated yields middling fruit; the black yields inferior fruit.
As proclaimed by Brahmā: "He who, endowed with faith, performs a religious duty with white wealth (śuklavitta),
having encountered a sacred ford (tīrtha) and a worthy recipient (pātra), enjoys that merit in the state of divinity."
One should give gifts to guests with a passionate disposition and with variegated wealth; that one enjoys while in the human state.
But that lowest of men who, being characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas), gives with black wealth,
enjoys the fruit of that action after death in the state of an animal.
Nārada says: That [adultery] is further recorded as being of twelve kinds based on the respective castes;
three are common to all, and the remainder is recorded as being of nine kinds.

The word "lawful" (*dharmyam*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. The meaning is that there are twelve kinds [of property]: nine kinds based on the individual castes (*varṇa*), and three kinds common to all; thus, they total twelve.

The three kinds of wealth for all castes without distinction are: that which has come down by succession, that which is given out of affection (*prītidāya*), and that which is acquired together with the wife.
The specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as having three characteristics:
that acquired through receiving gifts, from a patron for whom he performs sacrifices, and likewise from a pupil.
They say that there are also three specific kinds of wealth for a Kṣatriya:
that acquired in battle, from imprisonment, and from fines and legal proceedings.
Labor, such as offering oblations and so forth,
is to be known as the specific wealth of a Vaiśya, which likewise possesses three characteristics;
that of a Śūdra consists of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade, while [the duty] toward these [higher castes] is through service.
From these, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas: [44] For all social classes (varṇas), this is the lawful means of acquiring wealth;
through its opposite, it would be unlawful, unless there is a grave emergency.
Having thus defined the substance that constitutes the means for accomplishing Dharma, and in response to the inquiry as to how much and what kind of thing should be given,
Yājñavalkya states: "One's own property may be given without detriment to one's family, with the exception of one's wife and sons."
Nor [is it theft] when there is a lineage, nor that which has been promised to another as one's entire property.
"In the lineage" means in the family line. "Promised" means agreed upon. Bṛhaspati has explained non-contradiction regarding family obligations as follows:
"That which remains after providing for the food and clothing of the family must be given;
otherwise, the giver’s duty becomes like poison with a taste of honey that turns bitter later."
Food means grain; clothing means garments. (The meaning is that one should give what exceeds the amount of wealth required for the family's food and clothing, but the remainder should not be given.
Manu says: "One who is capable of giving to strangers while his own kin live in misery..."
That which is like drinking poison while tasting honey is a counterfeit of the Dharma.
Kātyāyana states: "One's entire property, with the exception of the house and whatever is necessary for the maintenance of the family, is what may be given; any other property would be ungivable."
Likewise:
whatever field is acquired from a house or field within seven nights—
whether obtained by the father or acquired by oneself— that which is intended should be given.
(The meaning is that what is accumulated beyond seven nights and so forth— that which becomes excessive— is intended to be given away), according to the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Therefore, one should set aside one-third of one's wealth for the purpose of living."
Two parts, however, are for the sake of dharma, since life is impermanent.
