[45] (The meaning is that one should divide one's entire wealth into five parts, preserve three parts for one's livelihood, and allocate two parts for the sake of Dharma. In the *Mahābhārata*: "One who possesses ten cows should give one cow; one who possesses a hundred cows should give ten; one who possesses a thousand cows should give a hundred. All these are recorded as yielding equal fruit."

(* Now, since the two words *vitta* (wealth) and *go* (cow) mentioned in these two statements function as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) and thus refer to "whatever is to be given" in general, the allocation of unequal shares would be contradictory. If, however, there were no contradiction because they refer specifically to "cows and wealth" exactly as heard [in the text], then by the statement "one who possesses ten cows should give one cow," even a wealthy person possessing fewer than ten cows would lack the qualification to give a cow. On the other hand, if [the terms] refer to wealth sufficient for the acquisition of ten cows, then because the position of them being indicators is accepted, the contradiction remains as it was. Therefore, it is well-established that the two arrangements—of fewer or more [shares]—are determined solely by the status of the qualified persons as being either stingy or generous.)

(It has been stated that one should give without causing hardship to one's family. Vyāsa states an exception to this rule: "One who desires his own welfare should give food even to a high-souled Brāhmaṇa or to a mendicant, even by causing distress to his family."
(*This refers to the subject of hospitality for guests and so forth. Kātyāyana states:

That which is obtained by oneself may be given away at one's own will; likewise, a pledge given according to the custom of lending, and that which has come down through the lineage of marriage—there is no restriction on giving these away at any time.

A pledge (*bandhaka*) or deposit (*ādhi*) must be returned in its very form, according to the practice regarding pledges. That which was obtained at the time of marriage must not be given away at all while that wife is still living. Furthermore, that which has descended through the lineage of the grandfather and others must not be given while the son is alive.

Whatever may be *saudāyika* (received as a gift from a relative), inherited by succession, or acquired through valor, if it is given with the permission of the wife, the kinsmen, or the owner, it attains validity.

*Saundāyika* means that which was obtained at the time of marriage; it is permitted by the wife. *Kramāyāta* means inherited from one's ancestors; it is permitted by the kinsmen who have not divided the property. *Bhṛtaka* means obtained through battle while being a hired servant; the meaning is that it is permitted by the master. Yājñavalkya says:
"What has been promised must indeed be given, and having given it, one must not take it back again. Yama says:
Whatever has been promised by word but not fulfilled by deed,
that wealth remains bound by debt both in this world and in the next.
"Connected with debt" means being connected with the fault arising from the non-payment of a debt. "A man, by not giving what has been promised, destroys seven unborn [beings], seven present ones,
and seven who have passed away."
By failing to give what was promised and by misappropriating what has been given,
all the merit accumulated since birth is utterly destroyed.
In the Mahābhārata:
"One who, having personally summoned a Brahmin living in poverty for the sake of alms,
later says 'there is nothing,' should be known as a slayer of a Brahmin."
Likewise:
"He who, having promised, does not wish to give, and he to whom one gives after having asked—both of these are liars;
they incur sin through falsehood."
Likewise: "He who, having made a promise, does not give— whether it be little or much—
his every hope is destroyed, like the fruit of offspring for a eunuch."

O King Yudhiṣṭhira, if one looks upon another with anger born of former expectations, he would burn away his own welfare, just as the Kaṅka bird that eats its own offspring does; therefore, once a promise has been made here, it must certainly be fulfilled.
Nārada:
If there is no one belonging to the lineage of a Brāhmaṇa to whom a gift should be given, one should deliver it to his *sakulya*;
in the absence of that, to his kinsmen.

[47] But when there is no kinsman of the same lineage, nor any relatives or blood-kinsmen, one should give it to disciples of the same caste; in the absence of these, one should cast it into the water.

Gautama says: "Even if one has given a promise, one should not give to one who is associated with unrighteousness. Kātyāyana says: "Even if it is said, 'I shall give you my entire property at the end [of my life] if you rescue me from this danger to my life,' it should not be so."

Now, for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the fruit, [the text describes] specific gifts according to the specific recipient. In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "One should constantly and without sloth give cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth; likewise, one should give specific objects according to the specific recipient."
The gift of food to those in distress, the gift of cattle to householders,
and likewise the gift of land to those lacking a stable dwelling, are highly praised.
The highest goal is attained by those who give a bride of equal caste to officiating priests, sacred knowledge to those of perpetual celibacy, and a daughter to those who are childless.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O best of the twice-born, goods that are implements for war belong to the Kṣatriya;
those useful for trade belong to the Vaiśya; and those useful for crafts belong to the Śūdra."
Whatever object is useful to someone, that should belong to him alone;
and by whatever vessel a person's livelihood is said to be sustained, that vessel belongs to him.
A wise person desiring merit should give each of those very things to him:
a staff, a black antelope skin, and likewise, O Brahmins, a water-pot.
By giving these to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin)—
namely clothing, bedding, a seat, grain, a house, and household furnishings— one obtains steadfast merit.
It should always be understood that what is given to a householder yields great fruit;
[this includes] wild rice, bark garments, vegetables, fruits, roots, and cow's milk products.
[48] That which is given to one who has retired to the forest is proclaimed to be infinite;
likewise, the gift of alms to an ascetic and the gift of a begging bowl are considered beneficial.
Perfumes, auspicious items, betel, red garments, and so forth—these should be given to women;
however, the gift to women must be delivered into the hand of their husband, and not otherwise.
Indeed, this is declared to be a secret means of gathering [support]:
providing food and shelter to a traveler yields great fruit for one who offers it to his master.
He who, knowing the Dharma, provides the means for the successful completion of rites such as marriage at the time they are performed, shall obtain the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
By giving wealth to those who are afflicted, a gift becomes of great fruit;
likewise, by giving toys for children and delicious food as well.
A man who gives delicious food to those desiring delicious foods obtains a captivating fruit, or indeed the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O best of the twice-born, by giving food to one who is destitute of fortune, one obtains inexhaustible fruit and goes to the heavenly world.
O Brahmins, even those men fallen from prosperity who have donned pure white garments and taken refuge in great merit are objects of supreme compassion for one who knows the Dharma.
Compassion for him must be shown by those who abide on the path of the virtuous;
having made a firm resolve for truth, one should act when others approach.
One obtains inexhaustible fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point—by the gift of barley to twice-born men who possess cows.
O knowers of dharma, one enjoys inexhaustible fruit from [gifts] of salt;
likewise for that which is given during childbirth, or in times of calamity, distress, and fear.
That gift is declared to be inexhaustible for a wise man,
O tiger among Brahmins, when he gives a water-vessel to one who asks for it.
One attains imperishable fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Aṅgiras:
Merit should be diligently bestowed upon the gods, upon teachers, and likewise upon one’s mother and father; demerit is never enjoined to be given.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*: "A man who gives what is evil always receives evil multiplied a hundred-thousandfold;
one who gives merit receives merit by the hundreds and thousands."
Likewise, a gift becomes increasingly superior according to the excellence of the recipient;
for that which is given to one's father, mother, teacher, or a knower of Brahman is of the highest merit.
One should know that such merit or indeed such evil is multiplied a hundred thousandfold.
In the Vahni Purāṇa: "These two persons in the world pierce the solar orb:
one who gives food during a famine, and one who gives gold and clothing during times of plenty."

Now follows the determination of what should not be given. Devala says: Even if one were to give away the entire earth acquired through unjust means to an unworthy recipient while devoid of faith, one would not attain any prosperity whatsoever.
From the Vahni Purāṇa:
"Indeed, that unwise man who, desiring merit, performs a sacrifice after taking wealth acquired through unjust means, does not enjoy the fruit of dharma."
But that evil-souled man who is a hypocrite regarding the Dharma gives gifts to the Brahmins for the purpose of gaining the world's trust.
A Brahmin who, having acquired wealth through sinful deeds,
is deprived of his inheritance and possesses a mind filled with passion and delusion, shall attain a defiled womb.
For one whose mind is intent on the accumulation of wealth, fallen under the sway of greed and delusion,
and possessed of a sinful disposition, causes distress to living beings through violence.
Thus, having acquired wealth through greed, he who performs sacrifices and gives gifts does not attain success by that evil deed, according to the ancient tradition.
Likewise: "With these and many other riches acquired through unjust means, whatever rites are undertaken, there the *piśācas* are the presiding deities."
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
He who performs funeral rites for the deceased with wealth acquired by unjust means does not obtain the fruit thereof, because of the improper acquisition of that wealth.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The property of the gods, the property of the guru, and the property of Caṇḍeśvara—
these three types of downfall are seen to result from giving it away, violating its use, or consuming it."
Yama said:
But that donor who, having stolen the wealth of another, bestows it as a gift, goes to hell; the fruit of that act belongs to the one whose wealth it was.
Likewise:
that which is already consumed, treated with contempt, insufficient, or unrefined—
whatever one gives to Brahmins, that remains as ashes.
"Used" refers to items such as clothing that have already been put to practical use. "Inadequate" refers to things incapable of performing their intended function, such as an old ox. Śātātapa says:
"Wealth designated for the sale of the Vedas, that which is acquired from women, and that which has come from a eunuch—these are not to be given to the ancestors or the gods."

"Vedavikraya" (the sale of the Veda) is pointed out or designated; if the reading is "nirviṣṭam," it means that which was obtained from the sale of the Veda. "And that which is acquired from women" means that which was obtained by living off the occupation of women; some say this refers to women who have been sold.
Dakṣa says:
"Common property, what is borrowed, a deposit, a pledge, and one's wife—these are [considered] her wealth."
A loan for use, a deposit, and one's entire property [are not lost] when there is a descendant.
Even in times of distress, nine things must not be given away by the wise;
he who gives them is a foolish soul and that man incurs the need for expiation.

[51] *Sāmānyam* (common property) is that which has multiple owners. *Yācitam* (borrowed goods) refers to items such as clothing or ornaments brought back after being requested for the purpose of social interaction. *Nyāsaḥ* (a deposit) is property placed in the hands of a householder’s kinsman with the instruction that it must be returned to the owner without showing it to him, but rather in his absence. *Ādhiḥ* (a pledge) is well known. *Dārāḥ* means wife; *taddhanam* means the wealth belonging to the wife. That has been explained by Manu: “[Property] received before the nuptial fire, the *adhyāvāhanika* (gift from the groom), what is given out of affection (*prītikarma*), and what is received from brothers, mother, or father—this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman. [MDh 9.194]

*Adhyagni* is that which is given to a woman in the presence of the fire. *Adhyāvāhanika* is that which is given by the father or others at the time of marriage. That given by the husband as an act of affection due to the relationship between the man and woman is [also included]. Furthermore, that obtained from brothers and others even after the marriage is [included].
Yājñavalkya also says:
"That obtained from brothers, mother, father, or husband is *adhyagni*."
And that which is received upon taking a second wife is also proclaimed as "woman's property" (strīdhana).

That which is given by a husband desiring another wife is the *ādhivedanika* (gift for supersession); such a form of woman's property (*strīdhana*) should not be given. *Anvāhita* is that wealth which was placed in the hand of one person and subsequently deposited in the hand of another with the instruction, "Give this back to the owner. *Nikṣepa* is wealth deposited in the presence of the house-owner. Kātyāyana says: "Wives, sons, and even one's entire property should not be made over [in gift or sale] against their will; however, one may employ them oneself."
In times of distress, however, giving away or even selling [the sacred objects] must be performed;
otherwise they do not function—such is the certainty of the scripture.
(However, the statement that "in times of distress one may perform giving or even selling" refers to the wife and other [possessions] regarding which one has the desire to give or sell.)

[52] As for the statement by Dakṣa that wives must not be given away even in times of distress—that is intended for those wives who do not desire to be given away or sold. Vasiṣṭha says: “A person is produced from semen and blood, having parents as his cause; in the giving, selling, or abandoning of him, the parents have authority. However, one should not give away or receive in adoption an only son, except with the permission of the husband” (VaDh 15.1–5). Bṛhaspati says: “Whatever has been given to someone who asks for it may be for the sake of dharma.”
And later, when it would no longer be so, that [gift] should not have been given to him.

(*The meaning is: if something is given to one who asks to perform a religious duty (*dharma*), and that person does not subsequently perform the duty, then it should not have been given to him. Aṅgiras:
Cows, houses, beds, and women should not be given to many [people at once];
for when these sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are distributed individually, they indeed deliver the giver.
A single [cow] should be given to one person, never to many;
having fallen into the state of being sold, she burns the family up to the seventh generation.
(*This demonstration of faults applies only to the seller, not to the donor under discussion*)—so says Aupakāyana:
"The maiden’s bedchamber, as well as whatever cattle, women, and so forth are to be given, should be bestowed upon a single person; by no means should they be given to many."
Vyāsa says: A man should not give to a Brahmin a cow that is crippled, barren, emaciated, one whose calves have died, a dwarf, or one that miscarries.
A *vehat* is a cow that destroys its own fetus. Devala says:
"By giving away a cow that is without a calf, diseased, emaciated, old, terrifying with its horns, or one whose body and limbs are devoid of milk, one incurs sin."
Kātyāyana says: One should never, under any circumstances, give land that is saline, nor land that has been scorched by fire,
nor land surrounded by a cremation ground, nor land frequented by evildoers.
"Evil creatures" refers to predatory animals such as tigers and the like. In the *Viṣṇudharmottara* it is said:
"An excellent twice-born man should not give land that contains fragrant grass (*uśīra*), is infested with thieves, or likewise abounds in venomous serpents, nor land situated at crossroads."
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "A man who gives evil always incurs evil a hundred-thousandfold;
therefore, a wise person should never give a sin to anyone."
In the Mahābhārata: For what compassionate person would wish to inflict further suffering upon beings already distressed by death, disease, old age, and the like?
Whoever inflicts suffering upon another will certainly experience suffering himself;
therefore, one who fears suffering should never inflict suffering on anyone.
Now, the gift according to the specific vessel is stated. Yama says:
"He who bestows gold, silver, or copper upon ascetics does not obtain the fruit thereof; it remains right there."

*Parivarta* means reversal; the word *eva* has the sense of "even" (*api*). Therefore, even in that case—toward such a recipient—he undergoes a reversal; the meaning is that he produces a result contrary to the Dharma. And so it has been said: "By giving gold to an ascetic, even the donor shall go to hell. Thus says Devala.

One who desires merit should not give cooked food to a householder, nor milk products to a forest-dweller; furthermore, one should not provide for their livelihood by means of the alms-gathering practices of mendicants.
Livelihood (*vṛtti*) means subsistence other than by begging. Likewise:
"One should not give sacrificial oblations (*havis*), blessings (*svasti*), milk, sesame seeds, or honey to a Śūdra;
one should not accept gifts from a Śūdra, but may offer them other things."
Cow's milk, gold, a field, cows, sesame seeds, honey, clarified butter,
and likewise all other flavorful substances— these are not to be given to Caṇḍālas.

[54] "May he grant us well-being" (*svasti na dadyāt*): the meaning is that one should not say "well-being" (*svasti*) to a Śūdra without first performing a salutation. "Of those": the meaning is that for the purpose of purchasing milk and other such items, one should offer some other substance. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not give to Śūdras *kṛśara*, *pāyasa*, barley-gruel (*yāva*), curd, honey, black antelope skins, nor anything that has been consecrated (*upākṛta*). From the Viṣṇudharmottara: "One should not give land, a cow, a horse, gems, gold, sesame seeds, or an elephant without having ascertained their merits and defects."
Now, that which may be accepted is stated. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"One may accept what is unsolicited from a virtuous Śūdra for the sake of one's family;
however, for the sake of one's own livelihood, one should never solicit anything at all."
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "When a terrible famine has arrived and the family is perishing from hunger, one may,
without lethargy, accept a gift even from an unrighteous person."
The best of the twice-born may accept gifts for the purpose of discharging debts,
with the desire to perform a sacrifice, and likewise for the sake of their mother and father.
One should always receive [food] from a Brāhmaṇa who abides by proper conduct;
when it is given with faith and is pure, in that way one's dharma does not decline.
Even from a gift given by one who is not a Brahmin, though it be entirely pure,
it should be accepted by a Brahmin who knows it to be forbidden.

Even that which is prohibited—such as the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and so forth—is not forbidden when there is no distress. From the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "A Brahmin who accepts gifts from a patron or a pupil according to the rules during times of distress does not fall away from dharma."
For the sake of dharma, one should undertake [the practice] for six months, one month, one day, six days, three days, or even a single fire-offering, each subsequent being superior to the former.
[55] From the Garuḍa Purāṇa: "One should indeed accept only so much as is sufficient to enable one to perform and complete the five great sacrifices for oneself and for one's family."
Whatever has been received from blameless persons and whatever may be purified by faith—
even a heap of material goods— is superior for those who accept from the blameless.
Even a mere fragment of a censurable object results only in misfortune.
Bṛhaspati said:
Even from kings who have committed evil deeds, the virtuous accept gifts;
for they desire nothing else, as this is indeed the supreme means of purification.
From the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
For the sake of one's father, mother, or guru, for the purpose of marriage, and for the sake of sacrifice, a learned man should always accept wealth in accordance with dharma.
When accepting cows, land, gold, and so forth, one should not investigate them in such a manner;
however, prepared food should be accepted only after it has been thoroughly examined many times.
Saṃvarta says: A householder, ever disciplined, should contemplate only the Dharma;
for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of those dependent upon him, the wise man should desire wealth.
Likewise:
"Even from one of evil deeds, food brought unasked may be accepted,
except from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, and likewise from an enemy."
Yājñavalkya says:
One who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from a king, a pupil, or one for whom he performs sacrifices;
however, he should avoid those who are hypocritical, those who rely on fallacious reasoning, heretics, and those who act like herons.
Likewise:
"For the sake of worshipping the gods, for the maintenance of teachers, servants, and others,
and solely for the purpose of his own livelihood, he may accept gifts from anyone."

"From all [sources], even from a Śūdra and others. "Self-sustenance" (ātmavṛtti) means merely the maintenance of the body, not complete satiation. Thus Viṣṇu says: "Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from anyone; however, he himself should not become satiated by them."
[56] Aṅgiras:
One should not accept gifts from a Śūdra for the sake of one's teacher, guests, or especially dependents; nor should one consume anything oneself that has come from him.
Manu says:
Prajāpati considered that alms which are offered when called for, or brought forward, or even unsolicited beforehand, may be accepted even from one of evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblations, for him who treats her with contempt.
Yājñavalkya: Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers, curd, earth, meat, a bed, a seat, parched grain, and water— these should not be refused.
Manu says: One should not take away a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, land, curd, fish, parched grain, milk, meat, or even vegetables.
Likewise:
"One may accept from anyone fuel, water, roots, fruits, food that is offered,
honey, and the gift of safety."

Fuel is wood. That which is offered spontaneously and arrived unasked; the grain found in a threshing floor or field; water found in a pond or well; and milk found in a cow-pen—these may be taken even from those who do not give them. *Aṅgiras* says: "Fuel is wood. That which is offered spontaneously and arrived unasked; the grain found in a threshing floor or field; water found in a pond or well;
and milk found in a cow-pen—these may be taken even from those who do not give them."
One may receive from a Brahmin cooked food, excluding grains; from a Kṣatriya, cow-peas;
from a Vaiśya, all kinds of grain; but from a Śūdra, nothing at all should be accepted.
(This refers to the case of Brahmins whose food is otherwise unfit to be eaten:
"But grain situated in a field, or in a threshing floor, or outside the house—
Aṅgiras maintains that this may be taken at all times even from Śūdras."
[57] For this grain is purified by ritual preparations; therefore, it is traditionally held to be pure.
Consequently, a gift may be accepted even during periods of death or childbirth.
The rule "even during [the periods of] death or birth" refers to times of distress (*āpad*).
Raw meat, honey, clarified butter, parched grain, milk, molasses, and buttermilk may be accepted; there is no prohibition against receiving these from a Śūdra.
Vegetables, fish, sour gruel, fried grains, roasted flour, sesame seeds, sugarcane, fruits, and oil-cake may be accepted from anyone.
*Kantukāḥ* means patched garments. *Bṛhaspati*:

"In marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, however, even if an internal impurity (*amṛta-sūtaka*) occurs in the interim, everything that has been previously resolved upon should be accepted; no fault is proclaimed [in this case]."

Śaṅkha says: "At the birth of a son, there is no fault in accepting gifts of molasses, sesame, gold, clothing, goats, or grain while the umbilical cord is still uncut; some say this applies only on that very day. Pracetās says: "For all kinsmen, there is no fault in accepting two-footed or four-footed animals, grain, dwellings, water, or sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). From the Viṣṇudharmottara: "One should accept even from a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa the gift of saving one's life; for by living, one obtains everything, and by living, one performs dharma."
The body, which is the very essence of all dharma, must be protected with diligent effort.
Now, that which is not to be accepted is stated in the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"A Brāhmaṇa may always accept gifts from a virtuous person for the sake of his livelihood;
however, he should avoid [gifts of] sheep, horses, gems, elephants, sesame seeds, and iron."
One who accepts a black antelope skin or sesame seeds shall not become a man again;
nor one who accepts the bed, ornaments, or garments of the deceased.
One shall not return from hell by giving a cow, sesame seeds, or land;
likewise, one shall cross over even the theft of the wealth of Brahmins many times over.
But how will that which has been taken from the sick man be delivered?
From the *Vahni Purāṇa*:

"A twice-born man who has gone abroad during times of distress may take the beds, seats, and so forth belonging to the dead, as well as elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles, and even a black antelope skin, from one who is ill and about to die."
Likewise, O twice-born one, [the merit of] giving to both types of persons, to the earth including its mountains even when it is terrible,
and the gift given at Kurukṣetra from a Caṇḍāla or likewise from an outcaste— [all these are equal].
Even at the monthly *navaśrāddha*, one who eats shall attain the state of a *preta*.
In the *Skandapurāṇa*:
"A deerskin, a bed for the deceased, and a horned cow with two faces..."
And by receiving [it] at Kurukṣetra, a person shall not be born again.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "The gift of the Brahmāṇḍa and the gift of the earth must not be accepted by one person alone;
by accepting them, he incurs sin, there is no doubt—it is the same as the murder of a Brahmin."

"Gift of land" refers here to the subject of the gift of golden earth, which is included among the sixteen great gifts (*mahādāna*). Vasiṣṭha states: "Weapons, poison, or liquor are not to be accepted by a Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding the acceptance of alms, Manu says:
[One should avoid accepting alms] from physicians, ungrateful persons, surgeons, and usurers.
One should avoid even the advances of a eunuch and an unchaste woman.
(The word *bhikṣām* [alms] is to be understood as the ellipsis. Here, a "physician" refers to a quack; a *ṣaṇḍa* is a eunuch; a *kulaṭā* is an unchaste woman. Regarding Yama:
"One should avoid the alms offered by a physician, a hunter, a prostitute, a gambler, a eunuch, and a dancer."
[59] A hunter is one who kills deer. Vasiṣṭha says: "The property of a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a snarer, a eunuch, and an unchaste woman is not seized, even if it has been forfeited."
Some maintain that the two qualifiers, "of the physician" and "of the hunter with a snare," should be applied respectively to the "surgeon" (*śalyakartṛ*) and the "hunter" (*mṛgayu*). Viṣṇu states:
"Even in these matters, though one may be capable, [one should not accept gifts] regarding the acceptance of alms."
One should not accept [gifts] from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, or one who has fallen, nor from an enemy.

"In these" means in those previously mentioned activities, such as the worship of the guru, the deity, and guests. Manu says: "One should not seek wealth through worldly attachment nor by prohibited actions; one should not seek it from here and there when wealth already exists, nor even in times of distress."

Yājñavalkya says: One should not strive for wealth that conflicts with Vedic study, nor from improper sources; one should never be addicted to forbidden things and should always remain contented. [YDh 1.129]
Likewise:
"In the case of receiving gifts, the butcher, the oil-presser, the liquor-seller, the prostitute, and the king are considered evil;
each one is ten times more [evil] than the preceding one. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.141)

A *sūnā* is the slaughter of living beings; one who possesses such a slaughter-ground is a *sūnī*, one devoted to the killing of living beings. A *cakrī* is an oil-presser. A *dhvajī* is a maker of liquor. Saṃvarta says:
"Accepting gifts from kings is terrible; its taste while being consumed is like that of poison."
It is better to eat the flesh of one's own son than to accept the patronage of a king.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "One who, deluded by greed for wealth, abandons a Brāhmaṇa, is consumed by the acceptance of gifts from a king and does not attain rebirth."
But one who, greedy for the bait of sensory objects, accepts gifts from a king,
will certainly fall here into the terrible Raurava hell.
Trees scorched by a forest fire sprout again at the arrival of the rainy season;
but those burnt by accepting gifts from kings never sprout again at any time.
Likewise: "The acceptance of gifts from a king is terrible, fierce, sinful, and fearsome;
who would have the power to endure the horrific torments in hell?"
Likewise,
the Brahmarṣi Gālava, who formerly resided at Kurukṣetra,
fell short because of accepting horses and consequently entered the womb of a horse.
One who is burned by a forest fire grows again from water;
but one who is consumed by the fire of receiving gifts does not grow once he is burnt.
Manu says: A mendicant should never beg wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
for by begging and sacrificing with such wealth, he is born as a Caṇḍāla after death.
Those who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice—
all such Brāhmaṇas are blameworthy and censured among the exponents of the Veda.
Likewise: "One who, lacking knowledge, accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter, is reduced to ashes like wood."
But a twice-born man who is unrefined, blind, and delights in accepting gifts,
sinks along with that very gift, like one using a stone as a raft in the water.
Therefore, an ignorant man should fear accepting gifts from whomever;
for even by a very small gift, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud.
Yājñavalkya says:
One who is devoid of learning and austerity must not accept a gift;
by accepting one, he leads both the giver and himself downward.

Therefore, it is understood from the *Viṣṇudharmottara* that even one who is destitute and lacks knowledge and austerity should accept only a small amount of wealth sufficient for the maintenance of his family—provided there is an abundance of gold and other assets—and he must not be overly intent upon such acceptance: "Even if one is capable of receiving gifts, one should avoid attachment to them;
through the acceptance of gifts, the spiritual luster (*brahmatejas*) of Brahmins perishes."
Without knowing the righteous rule for the acceptance of material gifts,
a wise man should not accept them, even if he is perishing from hunger.
*Vidhi* is defined as the manner of performing a ritual through mantras and the prescribed procedure. Yājñavalkya says:
"Even though he is capable of receiving gifts, he who does not accept them attains those eternal worlds that belong to those whose nature is to give."
Thus concludes the determination of the substance.
Now, the limb of giving known as time (kāla) is described.
Among these, first is the auspicious time (puṇyakāla). In the Devīpurāṇa:
Time is eternal, all-pervading, and constant; its states are born of causes.
Through specific conditions and other factors, it bestows the fruits of merit in the world.
In the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: Ten nimeṣas make one kāṣṭhā, and eight [kāṣṭhās] make one kalā;
thirty kalās, measured by thirty kāṣṭhās, constitute one muhūrta.
A day and night for humans is traditionally reckoned as consisting of thirty muhūrtas;
thirty such days and nights constitute two fortnights, which is called a month.
By those six [months], a year consists of two [halves]: the southern and the northern.
That is a day and night of the gods; among them, the northern course is the day.
"With eight, ten, or eighteen" means with eighteen. Dakṣa says:
"Rites for the gods should be performed in the forenoon, those for humans at midday, and those for the ancestors in the afternoon; this is the settled rule."

Here, the time of the lunar days (*tithi*) is first described. In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "Because it was proclaimed by Brahmā as the foremost of the lunar days, and because it establishes one in the primary state (*pūrva-pada*), it is called *pratipad*."
Bathing and giving gifts on whichever lunar day occurs in the month of Kārttika yield a hundredfold merit.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "When the month of Āśvina has arrived, on the second lunar day— whether of the bright or the dark fortnight—
it is said that whatever gift is given on that day yields infinite fruit."
In the Padma Purāṇa: "The meritorious third lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha bestows infinite fruit upon the donor for acts such as ritual bathing and giving."
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "O King, Śivā, Śāntā, and Sakhā—thus the fourth lunar day is remembered as being of three kinds;
that which is bright in the month of Bhādrapada is honored in the worlds of Śiva."
O King, by the grace of the Elephant, bathing, giving gifts, fasting, and likewise recitation performed at that place shall become multiplied a thousandfold.
O Lord of the Earth, that fourth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha is eternally peaceful and bestows peace; it indeed always brings about tranquility.
All acts such as bathing and giving charity performed on this day are said to be inexhaustible;
this is especially so when the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight coincides with a Tuesday.
Then that [day] is to be known as the bestower of happiness; it is celebrated as the foremost among all sources of joy.
It is said that all acts such as bathing and giving gifts performed on this day become inexhaustible.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "The fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and that which occurs in Śrāvaṇa, when white (i.e., falling on a weekday),
yield great fruit through bathing and giving gifts, and bestow the world of the Nāgas."

In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "O bull among the Bharatas, whatever bathing, giving of gifts, and other such acts are performed on this sixth lunar day in the month of Bhādrapada, it is said that all of them become inexhaustible."
[63] Likewise: If the seventh day of the bright fortnight should fall on a Sunday, that seventh day is named Vijayā; what is given on that day yields great fruit.
When the constellation consisting of five stars occurs on the seventh day of the bright fortnight,
then that seventh day is to be known as Jayā.
O Lord, bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts performed on that day shall yield a hundredfold merit.
The five stars are Rohiṇī, Āśleṣā, Maghā, and Hasta.
O Hero, that seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is called Nandā; it is remembered as the bringer of all joy.
All acts such as bathing and giving gifts performed on this [day] are said to be inexhaustible.
In the Ādipurāṇa: "The Sun-god has declared that a gift given on a seventh lunar day (saptamī) falling on a Sunday when it coincides with the asterism Revatī yields a hundred-thousandfold merit."
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"O Goddess, when Mercury falls on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Pauṣa,
then that [day] is highly meritorious and is celebrated as Mahārudā."
O Goddess, bathing in that river, making great gifts, offering libations, and feeding Brahmins performed for my pleasure shall become equivalent to a hundred thousandfold merit.
In the Mahābhārata,
it is declared that whatever is given on the Aṣṭakā days becomes infinite.

Āśvalāyana states: "The Aṣṭakā rites are on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. Likewise, the Śatapatha Śruti says: "There are twelve full-moon days, twelve Aṣṭakās, and twelve new-moon days. This means that all twelve refer to the eighth days of the dark fortnights. In the Devīpurāṇa: "O King, a gift given on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina becomes multiplied ten-millionfold."

In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*: "The tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha is remembered as the 'mouth of the year' (*saṃvatsaramukhī*). On that day, one should perform ritual bathing and especially give gifts."
O best of beings, when the eleventh day of the bright fortnight coincides with the Puṣya asterism,
that day is declared by Viṣṇu to be the destroyer of sins.
Whatever gift is given with Janārdana in view,
even if no fire-offering (homa) is performed on that [day], its fruit is said to be inexhaustible.
The twelfth lunar day in the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, is to be known as the Great Twelfth; it yields great fruit for one who observes a fast.
And the fruit of offerings made there shall be a hundred thousandfold.
From the Viṣṇudharmottara:
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the month of Caitra, when conjoined with the asterism of Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī), yields great fruit.
The asterism of fortune is Pūrvaphalgunī;
it is joined with Hasta in Vaiśākha, joined with Svāti in Jyeṣṭha,
likewise with Jyeṣṭhā in Āṣāḍha, and joined with Mūla during the Vaiplava.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa during the Vaiplava [intercalary] period,
as well as in the month of Bhādrapada conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism,
the twelfth day (dvādaśī) in Āśvina becomes meritorious when conjoined with the Ārdrā asterism.
The Āja constellation is Pūrvabhādrapadā.
In Kārttika, it is conjoined with Revatī; likewise, in Saumya (Mārgaśīrṣa), it is conjoined with Kṛttikā.
Saumya is Mārgaśīrṣa.
In Pauṣa, the twelfth lunar day conjoined with Mṛgaśiras; in Māgha, it is conjoined with Āditya—Āditya being Punarvasu;
and in Phālguna, it is conjoined with Puṣya—this supreme twelfth day is purifying.
On these [days] conjoined with the lunar mansions, bathing, giving gifts, and fasting [are meritorious].
[65] That which is performed even once by humans yields inexhaustible fruit.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "He who performs ritual bathing and charity on the thirteenth day of the month of Caitra..."
That man obtains a hundredfold fruit for that deed.
In the science of astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra):
"When the moon is in the constellation Maghā on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight and the sun is in Hasta,
then the 'Elephant's Shadow' (Gajacchāyā) occurs, which is attained through the merits of performing a Śrāddha."
The fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādrapada,
as well as that which falls in the dark fortnight of Māgha— these indeed yield great fruit for the giving of gifts.
From the Viṣṇudharmottara:
The full moon days of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and Māgha yield great fruit;
likewise, all full moon days that coincide with the lunar mansions of their respective months.
In this [occasion], the fruit of baths and gifts shall be tenfold,
when the mighty Jīva enters into conjunction with the full moon.
O best of the twice-born, that full-moon day is to be known as "Mahā" (Great);
bathing, giving gifts, and likewise the recitation of prayers on that occasion are remembered as being inexhaustible in merit.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "When the lunar mansion Āgneya (Kṛttikā) coincides with the full moon day of Kārttika,
that lunar day should be known as 'Great' (Mahatī), and it is most excellent for ritual bathing and giving gifts."
The lunar mansion Kṛttikā belongs to Agni.
When the lunar mansion belonging to Yama occurs on that same lunar day at any time,
that lunar day is proclaimed by the sages to be exceedingly meritorious.
O lord of men, when the lunar mansion Bharaṇī,
belonging to Yama, coincides with that lunar day,
it is called Mahākārtikī; it is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
The constellation Ṛkṣa (Ursa Major) is presided over by Prajāpati; Rohiṇī is likewise. Vyāsa says:
"The new moon day (Amāvāsyā) on a Monday, and the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) on a Sunday."
The fourth [tithi] on Tuesday yields fruit equal to that of the equinox.
Śaṅkha also says:
"But the new moon day with the Moon, the seventh with the Sun,
the fourth with the Son of Earth (Mars), and the eighth with the Son of the Moon (Mercury)."
These four lunar days are equal to the times of eclipses and the like;
herein, all acts such as bathing, giving gifts, and recitation are said to be inexhaustible.
In the Mahābhārata: "When it falls on a New Moon, a Monday, or a Thursday, that lunar day is called Puṣkara; it is superior to a hundred solar festivals."
Śātātapa says: [The conjunction of] the new moon with Monday, the seventh lunar day with Sunday,
or the fourth or fourteenth lunar day when Tuesday occurs [is highly auspicious].
In that place, whoever performs an action, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
the doer experiences its fruit for sixty thousand years.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "O Maitreya, when the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is conjoined with the Viśākhā asterism,
the host of ancestors obtains satisfaction for eight years from that śrāddha."
When the new moon occurs under the asterism Puṣya, Raudra (Ārdrā),
or Punarvasu, the ancestors, when honored, attain satisfaction for twelve years.
The constellation Ārdrā belongs to Rudra;
one desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors [should offer] during the constellations of Dhaniṣṭhā or Ajaikapād.
During the constellations of Śatabhiṣaj or Pūrvabhādrapadā, it is difficult even for the gods to obtain.

Vāsava is Dhaniṣṭhā; Ajaikapād is Pūrvābhādrapadā; Vāruṇa is Śatatārakā; and Āpya is Pūrvāṣāḍhā. Sometimes, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, there occurs a conjunction with the lunar mansion Vāruṇa.
That time is supreme for the ancestors, O King, and it is not obtained by those of little merit.
[67] The constellation Śatatārā belongs to Varuṇa. Now, regarding the beginnings of the Yugas and so forth, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Kṛta age emerged."
It indeed occurs on the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha.
The Dvāpara Yuga commenced on the new moon day of the month of Māgha;
the Kali Yuga began on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
These are indeed remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas (Yugādis), which cause whatever is given to be inexhaustible.

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "The lunar days that mark the beginnings of the ages are celebrated as the 'Yuga-beginnings' (yugādyas). On those days, the fruit of gifts given and oblations offered is proclaimed to be infinite."
Likewise: These four lunar days are the beginnings of the Yugas; what is given or offered in sacrifice on them becomes inexhaustible and is swiftly attained.
Whatever merit is gained through austerity over a hundred years in each Yuga, that same merit is obtained in a single day at the time of a Yuga-beginning.
Likewise:
at the sun's transit into Capricorn (saṃhasaṃkrānti), there is the end of the Kṛta Yuga;
and likewise, at the sun's transit into Scorpio (vṛścikasaṃkrānti), there is the end of the Tretā Yuga.
But the period to be known [as Dvāpara] ends with the transit of the Sun into Virgo by way of its numerical count;
likewise, the end of the Kali Yuga occurs at the transit into Aquarius.
In the Ādityapurāṇa: "Know that day to be the end of the Yuga when the sun’s asterism is Revatī, when its movement occurs among the zodiacal signs; a gift given there is infinite."
During an eclipse of the planets, at the equinoxes, during a solar halo,
on the seventh day of either the bright or dark fortnight, they know these to be days like the end of a Yuga.
The conjunction of the Sun with the Moon is called *mihitopadi*. Manu says:

"A gift given on the anniversaries of the beginnings of the Yugas (*yugādi*) becomes multiplied a thousandfold; likewise, rites such as the *śrāddha* performed on the anniversaries of the beginnings of the Manvantaras yield the same result. [68]
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the twelfth of Kārttika,
the third of Caitra, and likewise that of Bhādrapada."
The new moon of Phālguna, the eleventh of Pauṣa,
the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise the full moon of Āṣāḍha.
The tenth day of Āṣāḍha, the seventh of the month of Māgha,
the full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Caitra, as well as the fifteenth day of Jyeṣṭha.
These [lunar days] at the beginning of the Manvantaras and other such times cause what is given to be inexhaustible;
likewise, bathing, giving, recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors [performed then yield eternal results].
One should know that everything performed during the Manvantaras and other such periods is indeed inexhaustible.

(Here, with the exception of the new moon and the eighth day, all [days] are indeed bright fortnights. However, according to another Purāṇa, it is established that the new moon of Śrāvaṇa and the dark eighth day of Bhādrapada are the beginnings of Manvantaras. For example: "The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, likewise the twelfth of Kārttika, the third of the month of Caitra, and likewise of Bhādrapada."
Likewise, the new moon of Śrāvaṇa, the eleventh day of Pauṣa,
the tenth day of Āṣāḍha, and the seventh day of the month of Māgha.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya, as well as the full moon of Āṣāḍha;
the full moons of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha, as well as the fifth day [of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha].
These, including the beginnings of the Manvantaras, cause what is given to be inexhaustible.
Now, regarding times such as the Vyatīpāta: Yājñavalkya says:
A gift of a hundredfold at the waning of the moon, but a thousandfold at the end of the day;
a hundred-thousandfold at the equinox, and indeed infinite at the *vyatīpāta* conjunction.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
A gift on the new moon day yields a hundredfold merit;
that same gift on the day of the sun’s passage (saṃkrānti) yields a hundred times that; on the equinox (viṣuva), it yields a hundred times the latter.
At the beginning of a Yuga, it is multiplied by one hundred; at a solstice, it is multiplied by one hundred times that;
during a lunar eclipse, it is multiplied by one hundred times that; and during a solar eclipse, it is multiplied by one hundred times that.
Those who know the Vedas understand that a gift given during the Vyatīpāta yoga yields incalculable merit.

"Śataghna" means a hundredfold. Likewise, at the time of its arising it is a hundred-thousandfold (lakṣaguṇa), and during the period of its revolution it is ten-millionfold (koṭiguṇa). The measurements for its arising and so forth are stated in the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra).
At the fall [of the breath], there are ten nāḍīs; at the great fall, seven nāḍīs.

(Vyatīpāta is the seventeenth yoga among the Viṣkumbha and other yogas. However, Vṛddhamanu has demonstrated vyatīpāta in another manner: "When Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, or Mūla are conjoined with Saturday, that is called vyatīpāta."

The *nāgadaivata* is Aśleṣā; its head consists of the first quarters [of the three constellations]. (The term "head" is connected individually with Śravaṇa and the others). (In another treatise, another *vyatīpāta* is mentioned): If Jupiter and Mars are situated in Leo and the Sun is in Aries during the bright fortnight, the lunar day joined with Rohiṇī and called "noose" (*pāśa*) is here the *yoga* known as *vyatīpāta*.
For by giving gifts of cows, land, gold, and clothing in this [place], a person, having abandoned all sin,
attains heroism, the status of Indra, freedom from disease, and sovereignty like that of Manu.

The five-faced one is the lion (*siṃha*). Jupiter and Mars are *gurubhūmiputrau*. The twelfth lunar day is named *pāśā*. The "camel" (*karabha*) refers to the asterism *hasta*. (In the *Jyotiḥśāstra*, however, the subtle *vaidhṛta* and *vyatīpāta* yogas are shown to occur when the transits of the sun and moon coincide. Regarding this, Gālava says:
"A most fierce person, whose form arises from the gaze of the eyes of the moon and sun, resembling the brilliance of the fire of time (*kālānala*)."
Falling from the sky toward the earth while looking down with the thought,
"I shall kill the heron," is the *vyatipāta* yoga.
Bhṛgu said:
"O lords of sages, the time of the equality of the solstices is declared to be similar to a solar eclipse;
at that time, Bhārgava says that whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, muttered as prayer, or worshipped, gains a merit multiplied by millions upon millions."

(This means that when the longitudinal movements [krānti] of the sun and moon are equal, two auspicious times occur: one is called *vyatīpāta*, and the other is called *vaidhṛta*. Among these, the *vyatīpāta* characterized by the equality of transits occurs during three and a half conjunctions starting from the latter half of *gaṇḍa*; what is given during *vaidhṛta* or *vyatīpāta* becomes inexhaustible. Bharadvāja says: "There is no end to what is given during *vyatīpāta* and *vaidhṛta*;
it is especially so during *vyatīpāta*, for that is proclaimed to be subtle."
(But in the gross manner, the twenty-seventh yoga is well known as Vaidhṛta.
[71] Now, the time of eclipses.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "When there is a conjunction of the moon or the sun with Rāhu, it is known as an eclipse (uparāma); therein, infinite fruit is recorded."
The merit at the moon [festival] is a hundred thousandfold, and at the sun [festival] it is tenfold;
but when one has reached the bank of the Gaṅgā, the merit of the moon is ten millionfold and that of the sun is one hundred millionfold.

"Ten times that of the Sun" means ten times the [merit] of a hundred thousand [times]. The same applies to the subsequent cases as well. Likewise: "On Sunday there is an eclipse of the Sun; on Monday, an eclipse of the Moon.
This is known as the Cūḍāmaṇi [eclipse], and its fruit is remembered as infinite."
Bharadvāja said:
Now that which must be done during an eclipse of the moon or the sun is being declared:
every gift shall consist of gold, and all twice-born men shall be equal to Brahmā.
All the water of the Gaṅgā [becomes equal] when the sun is seized by Rāhu.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said: When the sun is seized by Rāhu, whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony,
by that very act the entire earth is indeed placed into the hand of the brāhmaṇa.
Śātātapa says: At the solstices, one should always give that which is especially excellent in one's own home,
as well as at the commencement of the Ṣaḍaśīti periods and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.

The meaning is that [the auspicious time] occurs while the liberation (*vimokṣa*) is taking place, but not when the two [planets] are already liberated; for so it is remembered in the traditional law: "But during an eclipse, that [time] is auspicious. And likewise Vasiṣṭha says: "Sixteen nāḍīs before and after the transit—by the mere sight of Rāhu, this is proclaimed as the meritorious time."
Jābāli also says:
"At the time of the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), the period of merit consists of sixteen kalās on either side;
however, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, it lasts as long as the event remains within the range of vision."
Now, regarding the times of the transits (*saṃkrānti*):
Śātātapa said:
"Whatever offerings to the gods (*havya*) and ancestors (*kavya*) are given by donors at the time of a transit,"
The Sun bestows these constantly, birth after birth.
Indeed, that man who does not bathe during the meritorious transit of the sun will remain a partaker of suffering for seven future births, even if he be a yogi.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says: Two solstices, two equinoxes, the eighties-six (ṣaḍaśīti) [periods] which are four,
and the four Viṣṇupadas— these are recorded as the twelve transits (saṃkrāntis).
The transits of Pisces and Cancer are the two solstices, northward and southward respectively;
the transits of Libra and Aries are the two equinoxes; those following them are within the [northern and southern] hemispheres.

The *jhaṣa* is the crocodile; the *gola* is the zodiacal circle. The Sun’s transit through Virgo, Gemini, Pisces, and Sagittarius is declared to be the *ṣaḍaśītimukha*, which possesses sixty-fourfold fruits.
When the sun is in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, or Leo, this is called Viṣṇupada; its fruit is superior even to that of the equinoxes.
Gālava said: A gift given at the equinox, at Viṣṇupada, at the beginning of the southern solstice,
when the six-aśīti period has passed, and likewise during the northern solstice, yields abundant fruit.
(And this has been stated for the purpose of demonstrating the superiority of the fruit:
"The time of the lunar festival (parvakāla), however, may occur both before and after the transit (saṃkrānti).
Regarding that, Devala says:
The moment of transition is subtle and difficult to perceive through the instants of flesh;
its conjunction likewise purifies thirty channels, both below and above.
When the sun’s transit occurs during the day, the merit of bathing and giving gifts lasts for half a day;
when the transit occurs at night, that merit lasts for the entire day, as does the merit of the equinoxes and solstices.
Those nāḍīs which are proximate [to the moment of transition] are remembered as most meritorious.

[The meaning of this is: in all transitions (*saṃkrānti*), disregarding whether it has already passed or is yet to come, if the transition—whether past or future—is proximate during this half-day, one should perform bathing, giving, and other such rites there. Vasiṣṭha, however, states a specific distinction:
"In the case of Cancer, thirty nāḍīs are remembered; in Capricorn, twenty."
In the current [solar transits] of Libra and Aries, there are ten nāḍīs on both sides.
(Here, the terms "present" and "on both sides" are connected with all [the periods] beginning with Karkaṭaka.
When the Ṣaḍaśīti has passed, eighty nāḍikās are said to be meritorious;
sixteen are called Puṇya on both sides of the Viṣṇupadī, both before and after it.

Eighty is sixteen [more than sixty-four]. The phrase "when the six eighty-period has passed" is intended to indicate an abundance of merit (for it has been established that the time for merit exists even at the beginning of the six eighty-period). This is stated in another Smṛti:
"When the sun’s transit occurs during the night while the sun is in Sagittarius, Pisces, Aries, or Virgo, and is moving from the former [half] to the latter [half], that is Viṣṇupadī."
In the case of rites prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti, five *nāḍīs* in the forenoon are auspicious.

(By this it is meant that when the *Ṣaḍaśīti* has passed during the night, the five *nāḍīs* in the forenoon of the following day are auspicious; and when it occurs on the previous day, the five *nāḍīs* in the afternoon are said to be auspicious. *Nṛyuk* is the sign of Gemini (*mithuna*). When the sun's transit (*saṃkramaṇa*) occurs during the day, the entire day is proclaimed to be auspicious.
If the transit occurs at night, the merit for bathing and giving gifts lasts for half a day;
and if the transit occurs after sunrise, it lasts for two praharas.
If the sun enters [a new sign] at the exact moment of midnight,
they say that both days are meritorious, with the exception of Capricorn and Cancer.

This is the meaning: when the transit occurs during the first watch of the night (*pūrvarātra*), the ritual of giving and so forth should be performed in the latter half of the preceding day; however, when the transit occurs during the last watch of the night (*apararātra*), the ritual of giving and so forth should be performed in the forenoon of the following day. When the transit occurs at the solstice (*ayana*), the ritual of giving and so forth should be performed in the forenoon of the following day. But when the transit occurs at midnight (*madhyarātra*), both days are meritorious, because bathing, giving, and other such acts are prohibited at night. As for the traditional teaching that one should perform bathing, giving, and so forth even at night on the occasion of a transit (*saṃkrānti*) and similar events, that refers specifically to the southern and northern transits (*dakṣiṇottarāyaṇa*). For this very reason it is said: "excepting Capricorn (*makara*) and Cancer (*karkaṭa*). Consequently, regarding the favor of bathing and giving even at night during Capricorn and Cancer, one should understand that they apply to whichever *nāḍīs* (moments) are proximate [to the transit]. The prohibition against bathing, giving, and so forth at night, however, remains in force for all other transits.
Gālava speaks of the subtle periods of merit at the equinoxes and other times:
"The sages know that at the equinox (viṣuva) there are six muhūrtas of merit; at the commencement of the Ṣaḍaśīti, two; and likewise at Viṣṇupada, three."
Bharadvāja stated the result:
"Whatever gift is given during the six-aśīti period, and whatever gift is given during the two equinoxes—
the end of the ocean may be seen, but no end to that [merit] exists."
Gālava describes the most subtle auspicious times, beginning with Viṣṇupada:
"Viṣṇupada occurs when the Sun is in a fixed sign; Ḍaḍaśītimukha in a dual sign; the equinoxes (Viṣuvat) in Libra and Aries; Dakṣāyana in Capricorn; and Saubhyaka when the Sun is in Taurus."
[75] This has been explained by the preceding verses:
"This becomes manifest in a time equal to the degrees of the solstice (ayanāṃśaka);
for all the distinctions and so forth mentioned regarding Viṣṇupada and the others occur otherwise during the solstice."
When the sun is in the signs of Capricorn, Cancer, and so forth, and is in its southern or northern course,
then the transits (saṃkrānti) are known as Viṣṇupada and the others, which are meritorious for giving gifts.

This is the meaning: there are thirty degrees for each zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), and the Sun traverses one degree per day. In this regard, by as many degrees as the solstitial shift (*ayanacyuti*) occurs, by that much of the Sun’s future time yet to be traversed (*bhogyakāla*), the shift of the *Viṣṇupada* and other such points occurs. Consequently, when the solstitial shift occurs after twelve [degrees], then twelve days prior to the upcoming transit (*saṃkrānti*) is the meritorious time (*puṇyakāla*). And during that time, acts such as giving gifts (*dāna*) should be performed for the sake of pacifying that [shift]. This should be understood to apply similarly even when [the shift] is less or more than that. Not only at the time of the Sun’s transit is there a meritorious time, but rather, at the transit of all planets into a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or a zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), there is a meritorious time. Thus it is said in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:

At the transit of the sun into a new zodiacal sign (*saṃkrānti*), the six and thirty *nāḍīs* (forty-two minutes) before and after it are meritorious; likewise, for the moon, the four *yugas* (four minutes) and one *nāḍī* are declared auspicious by the sages.
Four nāḍīs and one pala belong to Mars; for Mercury, three nāḍīs joined with thirteen palas;
for Jupiter, one and a half nāḍīs joined with seven palas; and for Venus, four nāḍīs and one pala.

The two *nāḍīs* of the serpent [constellation] joined with seven *palas* are declared by Śanaiścara to be most meritorious; performing recitation, giving, and fire-offerings during the first or the middle [period], one attains the abode of the Lord of the Gods.

The meaning of this is as follows: during the transit of the Sun through a zodiac sign or a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the period of merit (*puṇyakāla*) extends sixteen *ghaṭikās* both before and after that transit. Likewise, for the Moon’s transit through a zodiac sign or a lunar mansion, the period of merit is one *ghaṭikā* and thirteen *palas* both before and after. Similarly, for Mars, the period of merit is four *ghaṭikās* and one *pala*. For Mercury, it is three *ghaṭikās* and fourteen *palas*. For Jupiter, it is four and a half *ghaṭikās* and seven *palas*. For Venus, it is four *ghaṭikās* and one *pala*. And for Saturn, it is eighty-two *ghaṭikās* and seven *palas*.
Now, the miscellaneous times.
Viṣṇu says:
"The new moon day, the vyatīpāta yoga, and the eclipses of the moon and the sun."
The beginning of the Yugas such as that of Manu, the solar transits (saṃkrānti), and likewise the Vaidhṛti yoga;
The end of the day, the gap in the day, and likewise the intercalary day;
the two solstices, the equinoxes, and the six *aśītimukhas*.
The four Viṣṇupadas, the birth of a son and other such occasions,
and the conjunctions of the planets beginning with the Sun with the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
This should be recognized as a time for merit by those who have investigated it with the help of astrologers;
one should perform acts such as giving there for the increase of one's own merit.
The new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and others are well known. Regarding the "loss of a day" (*dinakṣaya*), it is stated in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"When two lunar terminuses (*tithyanta*) fall on the same weekday, that shall be a loss of a day.
Vasiṣṭha also said:
When three *tithis* occur within a single *sāvana* day, that is declared to be a "day of loss" (*dinakṣaya*); the fruit [of an action] performed then is said to be a thousandfold.

Bhṛgu states the definition of a "day-break" (divasachidra): Bhārgava has declared that the "day-breaks" are similar to the lunar eclipses (parvan) occurring at the junction of two lunar days (tithi), at the half-tithi, at the conjunction of planets, and at the junction of asterisms (nakṣatra).

(The meaning is this: the half-tithi is the *karaṇa*; at the end and the beginning of the *karaṇas*, the lunar days (*tithis*), yogas, and asterisms (*nakṣatras*), there is a time of transition (*parvakāla*) equal to a lunar eclipse, and that is designated as a "day-interruption" (*dinachidra*). The measure of that time has also been stated by that same author:

"The time of the interruption and so forth is said to be two *ghaṭīs* of the lunar day and its *karaṇa*, augmented by eight hundred and thirty-three *pala*s; for the asterism, it is joined with twenty-five *pala*s. )
Two nāḍīs joined with sixteen palas from the moment of conjunction is declared the time for "cutting" (cheda) and so forth; giving [gifts] at this time yields infinite fruit.

*Kṛti* means eight; *nāga* means eight; *vahni* means three; *bha* means a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*); *tattva* means twenty-five; and *yuti* means conjunction (*yoga*). Thus, the following meaning is established: (for the *tithi* and *karaṇa*, the auspicious time consists of two *ghaṭikās* and thirty-eight *palas* at their beginning and end);
(for the *nakṣatra*, however, it is two *ghaṭikās* joined with twenty-five *palas*);
and for the *yoga* as well, it is two *ghaṭikās* joined with sixteen *palas*.
Viṣṇu states the definition of an *avamadina*:
"When a single weekday touches three lunar days (*tithi*), that is indeed an *avama*.
Where a lunar day touches three weekdays and also touches [the next] day, that is so designated."
(In this regard, there is this much difference between *dinakṣaya* and *avamadina*): where the end of the weekday occurs at the conclusion of two lunar days (*tithi*), that is a *dinakṣaya*;
where, even at the conclusion of two lunar days, the weekday continues, that is an *avama*.
As declared by Brahmā:
"The eleventh lunar day, the new moon, the full moon, the birth of a son, the Vaidhṛti yoga, the Vyatīpāta yoga, the Bhadrā tithi, and the day of the waning moon."
The *nyāda* and other such conjunctions would occur at the same time as the *indraparvan*;
likewise, there would be equality of declination (*krāntisāmya*), the "gap of the day" (*dinachidra*), and the planetary revolution (*bhaga*).
[78] *Bhaga* is movement among the zodiacal signs and lunar mansions. In the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"The *vyatīpāta*, *viṣṇupada*, likewise the *ṣaḍaśītimukha*, the equality of the solstices (*krāntisāmya*), the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), an eclipse, and that which is the *aidhṛti*."
And so forth; such is the auspicious time for rites such as fire-offerings and giving.
In the Skandapurāṇa: "An eclipse of the moon or sun, the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa),
the equinox (viṣuva), the vyatīpāta yoga, and likewise the ṣaḍaśītimukha [yoga]— these are the most excellent [times for giving]."
The "day-intervals" (dinacchidra), the "transits" (saṃkrānti), and furthermore the "steps of Viṣṇu" (viṣṇupada) should be known;
thus has time been fully described as that which increases the merit of men.
Gifts given here, as well as ritual baths, fire offerings, and austerities,
shall yield infinite fruit and even bestow heaven and liberation.

Cyavana said: "The new moon, the sun's passage into a zodiac sign (*saṃkrānti*), the *vyatīpāta* yoga, the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), the solstices (*ayana*), the six *aśītimukha* periods, the *viṣṇupada*, the *vaidhṛti* yoga, and up until an eclipse—these alone are meritorious times.
"What is given at the solstices, during the six *aśītimukha* periods, likewise during lunar and solar eclipses, at the beginning of the Yugas, and during the *vaidhṛti* yoga, becomes inexhaustible."
Śātātapa said: "Whatever is given during the solstices (ayanāni), at the beginnings of the six periods of eighty days (ṣaḍaśītimukhāni),
and during lunar and solar eclipses, that gift becomes inexhaustible."
Nārada said:
When the sun is in Viśākhā and the moon is in Kṛttikā, that conjunction is named Padmaka; it is difficult to find even at Puṣkara.
Now, the prohibited times. On this point, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One should avoid food, sexual intercourse, sleep, ritual action, study, as well as giving and receiving gifts during the time of the two twilights."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "A gift should never be given by anyone at night;
because Rākṣasas seize it, it brings fear to the donor."
Especially at midnight, inauspicious action leads to misfortune;
therefore, a wise person should avoid the great night during the periods beginning with the *dāda*.
Likewise, one should not perform ritual bathing, great acts of charity, Vedic study,
or libations during the first year following the death of a primary guru.

Jyotiḥparāśara said: One should avoid the establishment of the sacred fires, the consecration of images, sacrifices, gifts, and the undertaking of vows, as well as auspicious ceremonies and royal ablutions, during an intercalary month (malamāsa).
When performing the consecration of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, if one acts while the sun faces north,
or facing the southern direction, one shall not obtain the fruit thereof.
Whether during childhood or old age, or when Venus has set,
one should diligently avoid these [rites] during an intercalary month.
The intercalary month (*malamāsa*) is the *adhikamāsa*. Regarding its definition, Pracetas says:

"When two new moon days (*darśa*) occur while the sun remains in a single zodiac sign (*rāśi*), that [month] should be known as an intercalary month (*adhikamāsaka*), which destroys the performance of rites for the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*)."
Paiṭhīnasi says:
A sinful month occurring within the year destroys the fruit of sacrifices;
it is called *malimluca*, lacking a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), and devoid of the sun's passage into a zodiacal sign.
One should recognize the intercalary month as censured for all ritual acts.
[80] Likewise: "All rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti are declared to be performed in the twelfth month;
however, in the thirteenth month, all of them are designated as fruitless."
Therefore, one should by no means perform those [rites] in the thirteenth month;
for by performing them, one would quickly bring about misfortune and even one's own destruction.
Hārīta says:
That month is proclaimed as the beginning of the month in which Indra and Agni are offered oblations;
Agni and Soma are situated in the middle, and Pitṛ and Soma at its conclusion.
But when the sun ever passes beyond that [lunar month],
the first is to be known as the *malimluca* (intercalary), and the second is recorded as the *prākṛta* (ordinary).
In that ordinary month, one should perform the śrāddha according to the prescribed rule;
likewise, the auspicious rite (abhyudaya) should always be performed as a single, constant duty.
Vyāsa says: A month that has been traversed by the sun is indeed unfit for all ritual acts;
Vādarāyaṇa has stated that a month consists of sixty days.
Having abandoned the first half of the month, the latter half is praised for the Upākarma rite,
as well as for offerings to the gods (havya), offerings to the ancestors (kavya), and festive ceremonies on the lunar nodes (parvan).
If one performs the northern rite first, that [southern rite] performed later would become fruitless.
Pārāśara states: "The Upākarma, the Utsarga, the birth-anniversary (prasava), the full moon, and the Aṣṭakās—
these should be performed on the later [tithi] when there is an increase in the month, except for those rites pertaining to the ancestors."
Likewise, in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): "When the sun has entered Libra, Virgo, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, or Aquarius, an intercalary month (adhimāsa) is not ordained."
Māṇḍavya says:

For rites performed for one still in the womb, for a creditor, for one who has died, for a spirit, for daily rites, for monthly rites, and for the first annual rite, an intercalary month (adhimāsa) is not prescribed.
Now, it is stated that even for that which is prohibited, there is the status of being a time for merit (*puṇyakāla*) due to specific circumstances. Devala says:

"During an eclipse, at the sun's passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*), at weddings, at times of calamity or prosperity (*atyayavṛddhi*), and during optional vows (*kāmyavrata*), one should perform bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts even at night."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
"During eclipses, weddings, transits [of the sun], journeys, and childbirth, giving is to be known as occasional (naimittika); it is desired even at night."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The honoring of guests and the honoring of travelers should likewise be understood as taking place at night; and the honoring of cows has also been declared [to be done then]."
In the Mahābhārata: "O best of the twice-born, they praise the giving of gifts at night, with the exception of the gift of fearlessness,
knowledge, a maiden, a lamp, food, and shelter."
In the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"The 'great night' (mahāniśā) should be understood as the two middle praharas;
one should not perform a bath during that time, except for optional (kāmya) or occasional (naimittika) rites."
Viśvāmitra says:
The two *ghaṭikās* of the middle watch of the night constitute the "great night" (*mahāniśā*);
one should perform occasional rites (*naimittika*) at that time, but not even slightly the obligatory rites (*nitya*).
Furthermore, according to the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, all times are always auspicious for merit:
"Every time is prescribed and every recipient is declared suitable;
there should be no hesitation regarding the granting of fearlessness."
That indeed is the time for giving when danger has arisen.
Likewise:
"No restriction of time is seen regarding the giving of shelter;
its gift is said to be at that very moment when the arrival of a traveler occurs."
For one should not wait for the right time to give water to one who is thirsty;
"Food and water should always be given," so said the Blessed Manu.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "One should give a cow that has recently calved, without considering the time or other factors;
for the very moment when that cow is two-faced (giving milk from both udders) is the auspicious time for its acceptance."
Vyāsa says:
A cow with her calf should be given by one whose death is imminent, as previously described;
in the absence of that, a cow alone is indeed for the sake of deliverance from hell.
If at that time one is unable to give the Vaitaraṇī cow,
another capable person, having given it himself, should bring about the welfare of the deceased.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "The Vyatīpāta yoga, the Saṃkrānti, and likewise an eclipse of the sun—
all these auspicious times [become so] when death has arrived."
Then, gifts such as cows, land, gold, and so forth, shall become inexhaustible.
Likewise:
"O King, as long as the umbilical cord is not severed after a son is born,
they say that period is equal to an eclipse of the moon or the sun."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O best of the twice-born, whatever is given when the umbilical cord has not yet been severed upon the birth of a son,
and during the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) of that son, is proclaimed to be inexhaustible."
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"Whenever wealth arises accompanied by a mind endowed with faith,
at that very moment it should be the time for giving, for life is indeed impermanent."
Thus concludes the determination of time.
Now, the factor of giving known as "place" (deśa) is described.
Regarding this, the Devīpurāṇa states:
"All hermitages of Śiva are meritorious; all rivers bestow auspiciousness."
They constantly bestow upon men the fruits of charity, ritual bathing, fasting, and other such acts.
Viṣṇu said: "That country in which the established order of the four castes does not exist should be known as a Mleccha country; beyond that is the Ārya country."
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "O twice-born one, that land where Dharma remains complete in all four quarters is my supreme and eternal realm, most meritorious of all."
O best of Brahmins, that region where one who is served by those possessing such qualities resides, and where the conduct prescribed in the scriptures prevails, is considered supreme.
Yājñavalkya: Learn the laws in that region where the black antelope roams.
In the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "Indeed, that region where the river Godāvarī flows is the most sacred place on the entire earth."
Vyāsa said:
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, at Avimukta, at Puṣkara,
at the city of Aṭṭahāsa, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
What is given at Kurukṣetra, at Gayā, or at the holy site of Amarakaṇṭaka,
and at other such sacred places, attains imperishability.
The Gaṅgā embodies all sacred fords; a gift given there yields great fruit.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, and the Pañcakrośīs;
the Gaṅgā-Sāgara confluence, Naimiṣa, and Amarakaṇṭaka.
Śrīparvata, Mahākāla, Gokarṇa, Vedaparvata—
these and other such regions are celebrated as being frequented by gods and siddhas.
All sacred mountains, all rivers together with the oceans, and those regions inhabited by cows, perfected beings, and sages are proclaimed to be meritorious.
Whatever is given at these sacred fords shall produce infinite fruit.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "O observer of noble vows, wherever the Gaṅgā flows toward the north and the Sarasvatī toward the east,
there the merit of bathing and giving gifts is equal to that of a hundred sacrifices."
Wherever a linga or even an image is seen,
all that becomes meritorious, and there is great fruit in gifts given there.

It is said that what is given at a place proclaimed by Brahmā, on a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or in the house of Brahmins, yields a hundredfold merit; however, in the presence of the Sun, it yields a hundred thousandfold.
That which is given in the presence of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Agni becomes inexhaustible.
Likewise: "Whatever is given, even in a small measure, at an Agnihotra sacrifice, in a cow-pen purified by the sound of the Vedas, or in a sanctuary of Śiva,"
That should be known as having infinite fruit, due to the power of the sacred field of Śiva.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "O Earth, wherever a stone originating from Śālagrāma and adorned with the marks of discs remains, that area is a sacred field for three yojanas."
O Goddess, the stone of Dvāravatī is sealed with my seal;
wherever it may be taken, that place shall become a sacred pilgrimage site extending for twelve yojanas.
Likewise,
by giving at sacred fords such as Prayāga, in holy shrines,
and in meritorious rivers and forests, one obtains inexhaustible merit.
"In a sacred site (*āyatana*), such as a field of Śaṅkara and others. This has been stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"The field of Śiva, the Supreme Self, shall extend for the distance of one *krośa*;
the death (*pañcatva*) of living beings therein is the cause of attaining union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*)."

The fruit of offerings made to a Liṅga installed by human beings in a sacred field (kṣetra) is proclaimed to be infinite; this is the standard measure remembered for such cases. At a self-manifested (svayambhu) Liṅga, the merit is a thousandfold, and at one established by a Ṛṣi, it is half of that.
Now, the section on faith (*śraddhā*) as a constituent element of giving (*dāna*) is described in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"One should give a gift with effort, purified by faith and free from sloth."
Even a very small gift, when given with faith, attains infinity.
[85] Even if one gives away one's entire possessions out of a lack of faith, O best of beings, it does not lead to fruit; therefore, one should rely upon faith.
Devala says:
By giving even a handful of vegetables, offered with faith and devotion,
to a great person who is a worthy recipient, one shall attain all prosperity.
In the Mahābhārata: Dharma is accomplished through faith, not by vast heaps of wealth;
indeed, the munis, though possessing nothing, have gone to heaven because they were full of faith.
Faith is the supreme cause of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
for those devoid of faith, there is neither virtue nor its fruit.
From the Vahni Purāṇa:
All dharmas are preceded by faith; they abide in the middle and at the end within faith;
