they have faith as their culmination and faith as their foundation; indeed, faith alone is proclaimed as dharma.
Subtle and consisting solely of the essence of what is heard, Pradhāna, Puruṣa,
and Īśvara are grasped through faith alone, neither by verbal testimony nor by the eye.
The subtle Dharma is not attained through many bodily austerities nor by heaps of wealth, even by the gods if they are devoid of faith.
Faith is the supreme, subtle Dharma; faith is knowledge, sacrifice, and austerity;
faith is heaven and liberation; faith is this entire world.
If one were to give away all one's possessions and even one's very life without faith, one would not obtain anything at all; therefore, one should be full of faith.
Vedavyāsa said: O King, Śraddhā is indeed the goddess of the Sāttvika nature, the daughter of the Sun;
she is the mother, the progenitress, and likewise the one who inspires confidence in living beings.
Faith protects one who is superior in speech, and it also protects one who is superior in mind, O Bhārata.
In the Mahābhārata: "One who is active in ritual action, full of faith, generous, wise, free from malice,
and a knower of the distinctions between dharma and adharma— such a person crosses over all that is difficult to cross."
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Faith is like a mother, the progenitor of both knowledge and merit;
therefore, having generated faith, one should acquire knowledge and merit."
Manu says: One should always perform sacrifices and works of public utility with effort and faith;
for when performed with faith using wealth acquired through righteous means, those two become inexhaustible.
Yājñavalkya says: One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on specific occasions;
even when solicited, one should give with faith and according to one's ability.
Bṛhaspati says:

Through defects in the mantra or the clarified butter, there may be deficiency in the oblation; through defects in austerity or the senses, there may be deficiency in the penance; but when accompanied by faith, there shall never be any deficiency in the gift.

This determination of the place has already been explained in detail in the *Vratakhaṇḍa* and other sections; here, however, only a mere indication is provided for the purpose of fulfilling the promise to determine the constituent factors of the gift, such as the recipient (*pātra*). Nor should it be suspected that, while the fivefold constituents of the gift are being determined according to the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*, the donor—who is himself a constituent of the gift—is not mentioned separately. This is because a gift cannot occur without a donor, and thus the donor is necessarily implied by the act itself. [Objection: If that were so, then place, time, and the other factors would also not be mentioned.

Now, even if that [the agent] is implied by the general [injunction], it is defined for the purpose of obtaining specific details such as Brahmāvarta and so forth; however, in that case, the giver too would have to be defined for the purpose of obtaining specific qualities such as purity and so forth. It is replied: its non-definition is due precisely to the fact that it is conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*) contained within the respective prescriptive sentence, and not because of implication; furthermore, the acquisition of specific qualities like purity comes from another sentence. But in the view that the agent is not denoted (*kartranabhidhāna-pakṣa*), since that [agent] is implied specifically by the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) conveyed by the suffix itself, there is no parity with the place and other factors. Considering such difficulties, Devala—who speaks of "giving with six limbs" (*ṣaḍaṅga-dāna*)—indeed does define [the giver]. For instance: [Devala says: "The giver should be born of a good family, pure, self-controlled, truthful, and free from envy; he should be intent on giving, learned in the Vedas, and devoted to his own duty. Thus it is.

"The giver, the recipient, faith, the object to be given, the place, and the time—these six are known as the constituent factors of gifts. [87] (Since their characteristics have already been explained previously, we do not concern ourselves with them again. However, unlike faith and the other factors, the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not a constituent factor of the gift; therefore, it must be performed in every instance. As Yājñavalkya said:
"That which is given to a worthy recipient (pātra), accompanied by faith, with regard to place, time, and means—that is the complete definition of dharma.

Here, "means" (upāya) refers to the procedure (itikartavyatā). Regarding this, it is said: "The specific procedures will be explained in the sections on specific types of giving, as they cannot be fully set forth here; however, the general procedure must necessarily be stated, and for that purpose this section is commenced. Thus concludes the determination of faith (śraddhā).
Now, the general procedure for giving is stated. Among those, the duties of the donor are as follows;
in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"The qualified person must perform the ritual action with the complete collection of necessary means."
O Great Hero, [this is taught] by one free from desire and by one possessed of desire for the sake of desired objects.
One who is endowed with right conduct, possessed of faith, wise, and the foremost among those who know the inner self,
as well as one whose wealth is acquired through righteous means, attains the fruit of his actions.

"Properly" means by means of the first ritual procedure (*kalpa*) and so forth. "Accomplishment" (*saṃsādhana*) refers to the performance of the rite exactly as prescribed. The "qualified person" (*adhikārin*) is one who is desirous, capable, and learned. One who possesses the highest knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātmavittama*) is one who has firm conviction regarding the self, which partakes in the fruits of the world beyond. "Wealth acquired through righteous means" (*nyāyārjitadhana*) means wealth acquired through one's own lawful occupation. Āpastamba says: "The instigator, the consenter, and the doer are sharers in the fruits of heaven and hell; whichever of these exerts himself more, to him belongs the greater portion of the fruit. Yājñavalkya says: "But he who performs an action prescribed by rule in a manner contrary to the rule..."
[88] He obtains no fruit at all; for that [action] of his is merely affliction.
Manu says: For that person of evil intellect who, though capable of following the primary rule, conducts himself according to a secondary rule, there exists no fruit pertaining to the next world.

It pertains to the future life and the world beyond. Yogi-Yājñavalkya says: Whatever action is performed by men, joined with faith and according to the prescribed rule, and with a perfectly pure disposition, that conduces to infinity.
Whatever is performed devoid of prescribed rules, corrupted by intention, and done without faith—
that is seized by the Asuras from that deluded person of undisciplined soul.

In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "O Pārtha, the ritual procedure for giving gifts performed according to the rules for specific desires has been proclaimed by the sages to lead to fruit; when performed otherwise, it brings fear."
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"That which is given at an auspicious place and time to a worthy recipient becomes inexhaustible;
the sin accumulated over ten million births perishes for one who gives it."
Even one who possesses all his limbs, if he becomes a burden during the performance of the act of giving—
even if he were a most wicked person— he is desired to attain immediate liberation.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "By one who is pure, purified in disposition, and observant of patience, truth, vows, and so forth,
even a gift as small as a mustard seed shall deliver the donor in this world."
The skillful one [should act thus]: "And a gift should be given according to the rule, at the proper time, to a worthy recipient endowed with virtues."
Yama says: A gift accompanied by virtuous qualities is remembered as meritorious in all circumstances— even when given to those such as dog-cookers (outcastes)—
but it is especially so when given to a worthy recipient at the proper place and time according to the prescribed rule.
That which possesses qualities yields the highest fruit. Likewise:
"For he who, out of great respect, bestows a gift upon those who possess virtues, shall, after passing away, obtain wealth and enjoy it together with his sons and grandsons."
Furthermore, by giving a gift here without causing harm,
the wise man indeed obtains wealth after death that results in happiness and culminates in happiness.
"Without causing injury or producing pain; resulting in happiness, that is, having a happy ultimate fruit. In the *Rāmāyaṇa*:
"Nothing whatsoever should ever be given by anyone to anyone with contempt;
for whatever is given with contempt brings that fault upon the giver."
Śātātapa says:
A gift given after having approached [the recipient] and a gift given unasked—
there may be an end to the ocean, but there is no end to those.
Secret gifts, knowledge free from egoism,
and well-performed austerities— the fruit of these is infinite.
As proclaimed by Brahmā: "One who studies in secret, gives in secret, performs worship in secret, and honors the fire in secret,
is honored in all worlds by all the gods, like Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices."
Vyāsa says: That gift which is given to a worthy recipient with devotion after having been personally carried there, returns to the donor having become a thousandfold.
Bṛhaspati said:
In the Kṛta age, the gift is given after going [to the recipient]; in the Tretā, it is given at home;
in the Dvāpara, the recipient asks for it; and in the Kali, it is given when followed by a servant.
(* That which is given after going to the house of the recipient is [considered] given in the Kṛta Yuga.

That which is given after having summoned the recipient to one's own home, that is "given" in the Tretā Yuga; this is the meaning. The same applies to the subsequent cases as well. [As stated] in the Vahnipurāṇa:
But that gift which one shrouded in darkness gives out of fear or likewise out of anger, O King— all of that he experiences while still in the womb.
He who gives to the twice-born out of envy, with a mind full of pride, for the sake of hypocrisy, or for the sake of wealth, experiences the fruit of that gift in his childhood.
He who gives to the twice-born at the proper place, time, and to a worthy recipient,
with a well-pleased mind, enjoys the fruit of that gift in his youth.
Whatever gift is given devoid of the Vaiśvadeva rite and lacking the performance of the Sandhyā prayers,
one enjoys the fruit of that gift only in old age.
Manu said:
One should not be proud of one's asceticism; having sacrificed, one should not speak untruth;
one should not speak ill of Brahmins when distressed; and having given a gift, one should not boast of it.
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride;
life-span perishes through reviling Brahmins; and a gift perishes through boasting.
Yama said:
"One who creates hope for a non-giver and makes a request at the time of giving,
yet feels remorse after having given, him they call a slayer of a Brahmin."
Hārīta says: Charity, knowledge, austerity, renunciation, the performance of mantra-rites and rituals,
auspicious customs, and observances— all these are fruitless for one who has fallen away from purity.
Pracetas said:
One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors,
as well as for the recitation of purifiers, for giving, and for whatever is enjoined by rule.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "If an atheist performs a ritual act here out of delusion without having sipped water (ācamana), all his rites do not become effective in that manner; of this there is no doubt."
Śāṭyāyana says: One should perform giving, sipping water, fire-oblations, eating, worship of the deities, Vedic study,
and libations to the ancestors with the feet firmly planted on the ground.
One who has placed his feet upon a seat, or likewise upon his knees or shanks,
and who has crossed his legs, is called *prauḍhapāda*.
Vasiṣṭha says: Whatever recitation, fire-offering, or gift is performed with a dry garment in water, or with a wet garment on land, all of that shall be fruitless.

In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "One should not engage in rites such as the fire-oblation (homa) and the worship of deities, nor in sipping water (ācamana), nor in the recitation of the Vedas by Brahmins, nor in silent prayer (japa), while wearing only a single garment."
Regarding the recitation by the twice-born (*dvijavācanaka*) and the like, such as the *svastivācana* performed by the twice-born, Śātātapa states:

"One should know him to be 'wearing only a single garment' (*ekavastra*) whose cloth has slipped from the left shoulder and remains only around the waist; he should be excluded from rites for the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*)."
Ślokagautama says:
During bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, and rites for the gods or ancestors, one should not wear the sacred thread around the neck; at other times, it may be worn as one pleases.
Yājñavalkya:
A garment with the waist-knot tied outside is indeed demonic;
therefore, those who know the law should avoid it with great effort in the performance of religious rites.

"Outside the enclosure" (*bahiḥ kakṣā*) means an enclosure that has gone outside. Manu says: "One should not cause pain to anyone by deed, thought, or speech, even while performing the ritual ablution (*abhiṣeka*), though one may be acting otherwise in other matters."
During the two twilights, while reciting prayers, when eating, when cleansing the teeth,
during rites for the ancestors or the gods, and likewise after voiding urine or excrement;
By maintaining silence especially in the presence of gurus, during acts of giving, and while practicing yoga, a person attains heaven.
Parāśara says:
During bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, and rites pertaining to the gods and ancestors,
the hands of the twice-born must be provided with the sacred grass (pavitra) and used with the right hand uppermost (savya) and the left hand uppermost (apasavya).
Laghuhārīta states:
During recitation, burnt offerings, giving gifts, Vedic study, and the libation to the ancestors,
one should ensure that the hand is not empty, using gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass.
A twilight devotion performed without darbha grass, a gift given without water,
and that which is recited without counting— all of that is rendered useless.
Hārīta says:

The gods and the ancestors indeed preside over asceticism, sacrifice, and charity; they are the directors of all means for accomplishing one's tasks and become protectors from affliction, fear, and calamity. The deities of the mantras act in such a way that one who possesses perfected mantras acts as if he were a god: whatever he gives, he gives through the deities themselves; whatever he receives, he receives through the deities themselves. Therefore, one should not receive [a gift] without mantras. For if the deities were presented with [gifts] without mantras, they would receive them silently and would become deceitful. Therefore, having sprinkled [the object] with water accompanied by mantras, or having touched it, one should give it.

"Having sprinkled" means having performed the ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). "Having touched" means having made contact with the hand that has been moistened with water. Āpastamba states: "All gifts are preceded by water; in the sacrificial enclosure (*vihāra*), however, it is according to the scriptural injunction. The meaning is that in the *vihāra*—that is, at a sacrifice during the giving of the *anvāhārya* rice and so forth—one should do exactly as much as is prescribed by the scripture, and there is no restrictive rule requiring the gift to be preceded by water. In the *Varāha Purāṇa*: "One should give water into the hand of the twice-born; this is remembered as the rule for giving."
With hands thoroughly cleansed with water, one should likewise say, "I give."
Gautama says: Having placed his hand between his knees, and having prepared water with sesame seeds and kuśa grass,
as well as fruits, he should offer them endowed with faith.
(Regarding the absence of a vessel, however, a specific rule is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa): Having mentally designated a recipient, one should pour water upon the ground;
there may be an end to the ocean, but there is no end to [the merit of] this gift.
Dhaumya said:
"When the time for giving has arrived but the recipient is not present,
the gift is placed upon the recipient by pouring water into the hand of another Brahmin."
From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
Having mentally visualized the recipient as one who is active in ritual and endowed with virtues,
when the proper place and time have arrived, one should cast the gift into the water.
(But regarding the case where neither is present, the distinction has been stated in that very same place:
"If, while the substance and the vessel are being drawn apart, one intends to give [the gift] out of sight,
then the vessel shall go to the earth and the substance shall have the Sun as its deity."
[93] Dhaumya said: Even if a gift is given in the absence of the recipient, at a sacred ford (tīrtha) during a ritual bath, even if it lacks water,
they say that such a gift is "with water" and bestows infinite fruit.
If a gift is intended for one who is absent and no worthy recipient is available, how should it be disposed of?
One should give it to members of the same lineage; in their absence, to one's own kinsmen.
Furthermore, that gift which is given in the absence [of the recipient], with a mind full of devotion,
to teachers, friends, and the twice-born— that gift is indeed infinite.
Indeed, that which is given in secret and devoid of the word "svasti"—
its end may be seen, but the end of the ocean is never seen at all.
Āpastamba says:
Therefore, having uttered "Om," the practitioners of the Veda always perform the acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity as prescribed by the rules.
The practitioner of Brahman should always employ [the syllable Om] with three measures;
however, those who contemplate the meaning of reality should perform it with three and a half measures.
At the time of meditating upon the deity, one must not make it protracted (pluta); of this there is no doubt.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:

"In the giving of a daughter, they bestow the object to be given while pronouncing the name and lineage of the recipient and of oneself; however, in the case of a son, three [generations] are mentioned."
(*The phrase "three males" means the three ancestors beginning with the great-grandfather. As it has been said:
"In the *nāndīmukha* rite and at a wedding, a learned man should pronounce the name beginning with the great-grandfather; in other [ancestral rites], he should begin with the father."
Likewise, a man sitting on a bed of kuśa grass facing the east while performing acts of giving, fire-offerings, and recitation,
obtains infinite fruit from these.
From another Smṛti:
Having pronounced the name and lineage, one should give [the gift] endowed with perfect faith,
having announced the place, time, and so forth, saying, "I bestow this upon you."
One should also proclaim the cessation of one's own sense of ownership with the words "not mine," according to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"But when the fire has been well-kindled, one should offer the three *vyāhṛtis*."
Upon the tips of the upward-pointing darbha grass, one should place the vessel.

Having himself stood upon the tips of the grass blades pointing eastward, and having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the donor should bestow the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) while dedicating it toward his own merit.
Having offered all the *vyāhṛtis*, one should complete the rite thereupon;
then, having honored the Brahmin, one should dismiss the vessel.
According to this procedure, the gift should be given preceded by a fire-oblation (homa).
That ritual action does not deserve [to be performed] without the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and without the fire-oblation.

And this [passage] has been shown to refer to the injunction of specific qualities (*guṇavidhi*) by way of restating the oblations (*homānuvāda*) in those cases where the oblation is an integral part of the rite; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would apply even to the giving of betel leaves and the like, which are not seen to be practiced by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) as such.
Now, the duties of the recipient (*pratigrahītṛdharma*).
In the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*:
Pure, with his hands holding purifiers, facing north,
meditating upon his chosen deity, and having conquered his senses, he should receive [the gift] mentally.
Always wearing his upper garment, with his hands between his knees,
and contemplating the desired object of the donor, he should offer [the gift] with self-restraint and purity.
Āpastamba says: "If one should perform japa, fire-offerings, or accept gifts while wearing wet clothes,
or whatever is done with the knee outside [the garment], all that becomes Rākṣasa."
Baudhāyana says: "If one who wears saffron robes performs recitations, burnt offerings, or accepts gifts,
that oblation to the gods, the offering to ancestors, the *svadhā* call, and the sacrificial food become fit for the gods."
Chagaleya says:
The Brahma-tīrtha is in the middle of the hand, but not for the purpose of receiving gifts.
Pracetā said: “The *tīrtha* of Agni is on the middle of the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa; one should accept [gifts] with the [thumb] of Agni. [95] In the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:
Having bathed, having properly sipped water, and wearing two washed garments...
And with his hand holding the purifier (pavitra), the knower of dharma should accept it.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O Brahmins, during a period of impurity due to death or birth, no gift should be accepted;
yet even in such cases, men may accept the 'gift of fearlessness' (*abhayadakṣiṇā*)."
That alone is the proper time for receiving [gifts] when danger has arisen;
likewise, O twice-born ones, other gifts should not be accepted by one who is impure.
O knowers of dharma, having properly sipped water after bathing, being restrained and pure, one should receive [the guest] while anointed and with the topknot loosened.
The recipient should always recite the name of the progenitor;
thereafter, he should recite the name of the deity of the substance together with the substance itself.
Thereafter, one should conclude with the *kāmastuti* for the acceptance; at its end, one should recite "svasti. This is the procedure for the acceptance (*pratigraha*).

The *sāvitrī* is the well-known verse dedicated to the deity Savitṛ, beginning with "devasya tvā... and so forth. The *dravyadevatā* (the deity of the substance) is that which will be mentioned later as "abhayaṃ sarvadaivatyam" (fearlessness, whose deity is all [gods]) and so forth. The *kāmastuti* (praise of desire) is the mantra "ko 'dāt kamā adāt" and so forth; however, in another recension (*śākhā*), it is the well-known "kāmaḥ kāmāya" and so forth. In the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"Uttering the syllable *oṃ*, the wise man should take the water with *kuśa* grass and wealth in his right hand; at its conclusion, he should proclaim 'svasti'."
Likewise:
"Having accepted gifts from the best of the twice-born, one should recite the formula aloud;
but for a Kṣatriya and likewise for a Vaiśya, one should recite the mantra in a low voice."
One should perform the recitation of the *svasti* formula mentally for a Śūdra;
for a Brāhmaṇa, one should utter it with the syllable *oṃ*, while for a king (Kṣatriya), one should do so without the syllable *oṃ*.
[96] For a Vaiśya, one should likewise recite it in a whisper; for one born of a Śūdra, one should say "svasti" mentally.

Regarding the acceptance of each gift, the mantra should be recited in a medium tone. When a Brāhmaṇa is the donor, one should perform the *svastivācana* (invocation of well-being) accompanied by the syllable *oṃ*. It is the same for Kṣatriyas and others. In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Fearlessness has all the gods as its deity; the earth indeed has Viṣṇu as its deity."
A maiden, a male slave, and likewise a female slave are declared to be of the Prājāpatya type.
And likewise, it is said that the entire one-hoofed animal has Yama as its presiding deity;
the buffalo is likewise of Yama, while the camel belongs to Nirṛti.
Raudrī is declared to be the cow; one should designate the goat as belonging to Agni;
one should know the ram to belong to Varuṇa, and likewise the boar to Viṣṇu.
All wild animals are said to have Vāyu as their presiding deity;
likewise, all reservoirs of water, water-vessels, and water-pots [have the same deity].
Understand that the water-pot (kumbha) and the small pitcher (karaka) belong to Varuṇa;
O best of the twice-born, gems produced from the ocean are also the properties of Varuṇa.
Gold is said to belong to Agni, as do all metals;
and all cooked food, O twice-born ones, belongs to Prajāpati.
All fragrances should be known as belonging to the Gandharvas by the wise;
clothing is remembered as belonging to Bṛhaspati, and likewise, flavors are to be known as belonging to Soma.
All birds are likewise proclaimed to belong to Vāyu;
Brāhmī learning is specified, as well as the implements of learning.
Scholars should know that books and such items belong to Sarasvatī;
for all vessels made of rice-husks, Viśvakarman is the presiding deity.
Furthermore, among trees, flowers, leafy vegetables along with greens,
and likewise among all fruits, it should be known that there is a "lord of the forest" (vanaspati).
Fish and meat are likewise prescribed for the Prājāpatya penance;
as are an umbrella, a black antelope skin, a bed, a chariot, and a seat.
Likewise, sandals, a vehicle, and whatever else is devoid of living beings—
a person may accept those as a gift according to the tradition of Aṅgiras.
Everything that is useful for a hero— be it the banner of the scriptures and dharma or any other equipment for battle— should be understood as being sacred to all the deities.

O best of the twice-born, that which has not been mentioned should be understood as having Śakra as its deity; or, O most excellent of the twice-born, everything may be understood as having Viṣṇu as its deity.
Then, having taken water in his hand, the man should recite [the mantra] for all the substances while they are being offered to the deity, and then accept the gift.
In this ritual, at the conclusion of the application, one should indeed say: "Oṃ, I accept this for such-and-such a deity"; at the end of that, one should proclaim "Svasti."
For example: "I accept the gold for Agni.
Having touched the items so that they do not waver from their place, the Brahmin should recite these;
however, in the case of giving a maiden in marriage, he should not recite them individually for each item.
Likewise, those best of the twice-born who do not know the righteous rule regarding the acceptance of gifts are considered to be included within that [category].
One who is joined with the theft of property goes to hell;
however, a Brahmin, having understood the righteous rule regarding the acceptance of gifts, [is not so affected].
Together with the giver, he certainly crosses over even great difficulties;
therefore, it has been said that a Brahmin should perform the prescribed rite when accepting a gift.
One should practice the means for one's own spiritual welfare as well as the giving of gifts;
therefore, with every effort, the rule regarding the acceptance of gifts should be understood.
Likewise:
"The best of the twice-born should accept land by circumambulating it clockwise; but for a daughter, a male slave, or a female slave, he should do so while taking them by the hand."
Having placed it upon the hand, one should accept it according to the Dharma;
"acceptance" here means taking possession.
It is prescribed for an elephant by mounting it, and for a horse by touching its ear.
And likewise, one should accept all single-hoofed animals, especially those, as well as their horns and tails, and similarly a black antelope skin.

(Generally, the acceptance of one-hoofed animals by the ear has been stated; however, the meaning here is that those one-hoofed animals which possess horns should be accepted specifically by the horn.
All hornless animals are to be accepted by the tail by the wise;
one should accept the buffalo by the horn and the donkey indeed by the region of the back.
From the acceptance of gifts, from mounting camels and vehicles,
from taking a handful of seeds, and from taking jewels from all quarters.
One should take up a garment from its hem, or having put it on again; likewise, one should mount upon sandals, or indeed mount upon a couch or wooden shoes.
O twice-born ones, having touched the two dharmadhvaja pillars and likewise entered the house,
one should descend into all the water-reservoirs.
A twice-born man should accept a chariot by its pole, as well as an umbrella and a staff;
he should accept trees while placing his hands upon their roots.
Having taken up his weapons and likewise put on his ornaments, [he set forth].
"At the pole" means at the tip of the shaft; "having fastened it to the bride," is the meaning. In the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
"One should seize a cow by the tail, or an elephant by the ear;
a female slave by the head, a goat likewise, and a mule or a donkey on the back."
One should hold a horse by the ear or even by the mane, aiming for its end;
likewise, having touched a bed, a seat, a house, or a field, one should take up gold.
Having touched the hump of a camel and wild animals such as buffaloes and others,
and having touched birds on their tails according to the ritual prescribed for the lizard.
This same rule is prescribed for fanged animals, those wearing armor, as well as small wild beasts,
and for creatures such as goats and the like.
Having respectfully taken up the parasol at its handle and the fruit at the root of the tree,
and having likewise fastened the sandals, he should cause [the preceptor] to recite.

Then, having taken a garment, he should accept a wife who has previously belonged to another, provided she is in her fertile season and her virginity remains intact, either by placing it on her head or in her hand.
Place the son upon your lap and accept him as a *dattaka*;
having touched the front of the chariot, accept him at the pole.
The *kūvara* is the wooden pole that supports the yoke.
There is no acceptance of yoked animals, gold, or garments from one who lacks limbs.
Now, regarding the duties pertaining to both [gods and ancestors], the *Garuḍapurāṇa* states:
"Whether it be a rite for the gods (*daiva*) or one for the ancestors (*pitrya*), you ought not to perform it while impure;
indeed, bathing alone is recorded as the supreme means of purification for the twice-born."
Therefore, one who has bathed is fit for the Arhats in both giving and receiving;
an action performed by one who has not bathed leads to the state of a Rākṣasa.
[100] In ancient times, Prajāpati created this purifier for the protection of ritual action;
it is the supreme destroyer of demons, ordained by the sages at the sacrifice.
Therefore, it should be held in the hands by one who gives or receives,
and especially by one performing ritual bathing, fire-oblations, silent recitation, and so forth.
Having abandoned the Vaiṣṇava path that has emerged from the Brahman-path,
one who performs a single circumambulation is called "purified."
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, eating, and even the offering of oblations—these must always be performed with the thumb; otherwise, they belong to the Asuras."

"With the thumb" means with the thumb joined to the fingers. These very same acts, especially giving and so forth, as well as the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), O King, should be performed with the hands between the knees.
Baudhāyana says:

Eating, offering oblations, giving gifts, presenting offerings, and receiving gifts—these acts, as well as sipping water (ācamana), should not be performed with the knees outside [the hands]. Thus it is remembered.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
One who has loosened his lower garment or likewise loosened his top-knot is not qualified for giving,
receiving gifts, performing sacrifices, or rites such as the Brahma-yajña.
For the gods, having assembled together, fashioned that garment for men;
therefore, they declare one who is devoid of clothing to be incomplete.
Then, one who is about to perform any ritual act should wear an upper garment;
however, one should not put on two unwashed garments, nor those that have been "pecked at by crows."
While giving and receiving, one should wear only an unwashed garment.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "Having bathed well, having properly sipped water (ācamana), having performed the rites such as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and so forth,
being free from desire and anger, and avoiding contact with heretics (pāṣaṇḍa)."
One who has conquered the senses, speaks the truth, and is a worthy recipient is praised as a donor.
[101] Likewise:
When a person of the same lineage has died, or during a period of birth-impurity,
one is unfit for ten nights to perform acts of giving or receiving gifts.
It is appropriate to offer the funeral rice-ball, water, and other oblations to the deceased during the period of impurity;
likewise, once the umbilical cord has been severed, one becomes worthy of giving gifts during the birth-impurity.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Whether pure or impure, one should give the gift of fearlessness;
whether by a pure person or an impure one, both [the giver and the gift] are to be accepted when presented."

The *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "That which is given or received by one seated upon *kuśa* grass and wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*) is fruitful; otherwise, it is indeed fruitless."
Jātūkarṇya said: "One should give and receive with the syllable *oṃ*. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The *praṇava* is the seed of the worlds and indeed the beginning of the Vedas."
This alone is the supreme Brahman, this is the most excellent purity.
Therefore, having uttered the Praṇava, the acts of giving and receiving should be performed.
Yama said: He who accepts what has been honored and he who gives after having honored it—both of them go to heaven; in the opposite case, the reverse occurs.
In the Liṅgapurāṇa: One should give a gift according to one's ability, preceded by constant worship;
and the Brāhmaṇa, in turn, should accept the gift given with devotion.
Śātātapa says:
He who first asks for a gift from a Brāhmaṇa goes to hell first, and the Brāhmaṇa follows immediately after.

"Preceded by a question" means: having said, "If you recite this chapter or this section without stumbling, then I shall give this much to you," and [the gift] being given when that has been done—that is what is "preceded by a question. Vyāsa says:
He who gives with contempt and he who accepts a gift [with contempt], both of them shall dwell submerged in hell for a hundred autumns.
[102] Śātātapa says: He who, out of greed for gain, might give a gift, or he who might accept a gift—
first the giver goes to hell, and immediately after him, the Brāhmaṇa.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "A gift that has been bestowed according to the prescribed rule, and a gift that has been accepted according to the prescribed rule."
Of these two, the application of the latter should be performed; thus one attains the highest good, of this there is no doubt.
Now, the mixed dharmas. In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"One who does not know the procedure for giving ought not to give;
and one who is ignorant of receiving, by accepting [a gift], experiences hell."
The recipient who accepts with contempt falls downward;
a Brāhmaṇa should never be asked by the donor, "Do you know [this]?"

When questioned by him [the donor], he too should not proclaim himself for the sake of giving. Direct testing—such as saying, "If you recite this, then I shall give this to you"—is prohibited here; however, testing by other means for the purpose of recognizing his worthiness as a recipient is indeed permitted.
Thus it was said by Yama:
"Character is to be known from living together; purity from one's conduct in dealings;
wisdom from conversation. By these three, a worthy recipient is examined."
Discourse [on the teachings] with a pure disposition constitutes the discourse on Vidyā. In the *Vārāha Purāṇa* it is said:
"One should not give even as much as a mustard seed to one who is skeptical;
nor indeed should one accept anything if it has not been mentally authorized."
Whether giving or receiving, if one acts out of greed, fear, or other such motives,
one fails to attain union with the highest good and instead goes to hell.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
A gift devoid of the proper place, time, and ritual procedures brings fear to both the giver and the recipient; it is always harmful when accepted from one who is unworthy.
From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
Having pronounced the name and lineage, and having announced the object to be given while facing east,
one should cause a *svasti* (benediction) to be recited at the end after giving to a Brahmin facing north.
(*Regarding "after announcing the gift": the meaning is that it is after the time of announcing the gift, i.e., having given.
In a marriage ceremony, the giver and the receiver stand facing east or west;
one facing east should give the object—this is the rule that always applies.

As for what they cite—"One should receive [the gift] facing east, but during the day it is the reverse"—if its basis in an authoritative source is established, there is an option regarding the performance; even so, because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) that specifies facing north when giving, that alone should be performed.
Thus it is said in another Smṛti:
"One should give while facing east; one should receive while facing north."
The lifespan of the giver increases, while that of the receiver is diminished.

Thus ends the section on the constituent elements of gifts in the *Dānakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, who is the sovereign over all sciences and the lord of all functions, under the patronage of the illustrious Mahādeva, the great king of kings.
Now, as for the technical definitions:
when the moon is curved like the deadly Kālakūṭa poison, what doubt could there be regarding the nectar-like essence of the sweet lip-juice of beloved women? It is perfectly certain.
The union with Rāhu’s tongue was censurable, followed by their separation; now, however, the words of Hemādri Sūri are an infinite treasury of nectar.
By this, the surface of the earth is understood in a general sense;
by this, the technical terminology here is explained in a general sense.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"The seer, the meter, the deity, and likewise the ritual application—
these must be known with effort, especially by a Brāhmaṇa."
But he who performs officiating at sacrifices, teaching, recitation, burnt offerings, or rites such as those performed within water without knowing [the rules], his fruit shall be meager.
Likewise:
"And he who knows in accordance with reality the seer, the meter, the deity,
the application, the Brāhmaṇa, the meaning of the mantra, and the ritual action."
He too should indeed be honored like a guest by each individual seer;
he attains union with the deity here, of this there is no doubt.
The twice-born who knows the seers and the other [components] in the manner previously described shall be qualified for the secret rites and the like.
Likewise:
"That mantra by which a particular seer perceived [the truth] and by which he indeed attained accomplishment—that was proclaimed by the seers as his; that is its 'seer-nature' (ārṣaka)."
In ancient times, the gods, fearing death, covered their own selves with the *chandas* as if with two garments that had not yet been fashioned. Thus was the *chada* taught through the *chandas*.
The Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras—by them indeed those Vedic meters [are defined];
and for whichever mantra there is a deity specified, that deity belongs to it.
Its form shall become that [of the deity]; its divinity is called "divinity.
In a former aeon, mantras and their ritual purposes arose for the sake of action alone.
That which must be performed by means of this [mantra] is called its *viniyoga* (application);
and the etymological meaning of the mantra is the purpose of that application.
The installation and the praise—this is what is called here as the Brāhmaṇa.
Thus, one should practice this fivefold yoga while grasping it for the sake of victory.
Likewise, when at home, within water, in yoga, during private study, or while performing a sacrifice.
The *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states:
"The wise have declared that there are three kinds of non-performance for those who act out of desire:
non-performance (*akriyā*), performance by another (*paroktā*), and thirdly, improper performance (*ayathākriyā*)."
That foolish person who, having abandoned what remains in his own branch of the Veda, desires to perform rites based on another's branch, finds that whatever fruit he obtains is in vain.
That which is not prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, provided it is not contradictory,
should be performed by the learned, just like the Agnihotra and other such rites.

The Agnihotra is prescribed in the branches of the Yajurveda, as it is performed by the Chandogas and others. Regarding this, the author of the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa states: "Whether extensive or brief, whatever rite has been proclaimed for one's own Gṛhya-sūtra..."
When that much of the meaning of the treatise has been accomplished by him, everything will have been accomplished.
If one should somehow perform what has begun otherwise due to delusion,
one should complete it from the very point at which it became otherwise.
"Commenced" means begun. "Otherwise become" refers to that which has reached a state of reversal through a change in its sequence and so forth.

When it is completed, if one should realize, "This was performed by me incorrectly," then one should do it again at that very moment; there is no requirement for the repetition of every single action.
(*This, however, concerns the case of performing otherwise when the ritual action has already been completed.

Where there is non-performance of the principal rite, that rite together with its subsidiaries must be performed again; but when a subsidiary has been performed, there is no repetition, nor is that [principal] rite performed again.

Where the primary rite (*pradhānakarma*) is not performed, that must be performed again together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*). However, if only a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is omitted, there is neither a repetition of the primary rite along with its subsidiaries, nor is there a performance of merely that specific subsidiary; rather, only an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed. As stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"Darbha grass, the black antelope skin, the mantras, the Brāhmaṇas, the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), and the fires..."
These, being unfaded, may be employed again and again.
Marīci: On the new moon day of the month of Nabhasya, the gathering of darbha grass is prescribed;
those darbha blades, having not lost their potency, may be employed again and again.
The *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* by Kātyāyana:
Green *darbha* grass is fit for sacrifices; yellow *darbha* is for the five daily sacrifices (*pañcayajña*).
Those with roots are for the ancestors (*pitṛdaivata*); speckled *darbha* is for the Viśvedevas (*vaiśvadevika*).
The *kuśa* grasses that are short are for the *pravaraṇī* (the act of choosing or performing), while those that are long are for the *barhis* (sacrificial grass).
Those fit for the five sacrifices are suitable for the five great sacrifices. *Pravaraṇa* means performance; those suitable for that are *pravaraṇīya*.
— Thus says Laghu-Hārīta.
One should avoid six types of *kuśa* grass: those on a funeral pyre, those on a path, those from sacrificial grounds, and those used for spreading, as seats, or for funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
The darbha grass used for the purpose of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa), those by which the libation to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) was performed,
and those held during the discharge of urine or while one is impure from food remnants— their disposal is prescribed.
One should know those Darbha grasses which are placed within the folds of the lower garment and those which are made into the Brahmasūtra as sacred; as is the body, so are the Kuśa blades.
A sacred thread (*pavitra*) made of *kauśa* grass, containing an infinite number of fibers, with its tip intact, consisting of two strands,
and measuring one span (*prādeśa*), is to be known as appropriate for any occasion whatsoever.
That very same characteristic which was declared for the tuft of darbha grass is also exactly the same for the purpose of purifying the clarified butter.
Āpastamba says: [One should not study] in a temple, at a Śrāddha ceremony, in a cow-pen, at a sacrifice,
during the two twilights, in the company of virtuous men, or in the presence of a teacher.
In the fire-sanctuary, at weddings, during Vedic study, and likewise while eating—
at these points in the ritual path of Brahmins, one should raise the right hand.
(* "He should lift up his right hand" means that having placed the cloth on the left shoulder, he should bring the right arm out from under the upper garment. Yājñavalkya:

Having recited mantras dedicated to Rudra, the Pitṛs, or Asuras, as well as those for the gods or for malevolent rites, and having touched himself and then water, one should perform other [ritual] acts.

The *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* by Kātyāyana: During the recitation of mantras for the ancestors (*pitṛ*), the choosing of the lineage (*pravaraṇa*), looking at oneself or water, the discharge of downward wind (*adhovāyu*), laughing, or speaking untruths; [these occasions require purification].
Upon touching a cat or a mouse, when reviled, or when anger arises—
in all such circumstances while performing ritual acts— one should touch water.

In the case of "touching oneself," which refers to the touching of the heart as prescribed for sacrifices and similar rites, "looking" must also be understood as that which is specifically prescribed for sacrifices and the like.
Yājñavalkya states: "If, in any way, there should be a lapse in the restraint of speech during recitations (japa) and other such acts..."
One should either recite a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Whatever may fall away during sacrifices through ignorance or delusion, that becomes complete through the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu; such is the Vedic revelation.

Likewise, the *Śatapatha-śruti* states: "Since he speaks while restraining his speech, this sacrifice indeed turns away; therefore, one should mutter there either a *ṛc* or a *yajus* addressed to Viṣṇu," and so forth. From the *Chandoga-pariśiṣṭa* by Kātyāyana:
"Where a ritual action is prescribed but the limb of the performer is not indicated, the right hand is to be understood as the one that brings the rituals to completion."

In those rites such as recitation and fire-offerings where no restriction of direction exists, three directions are prescribed: the eastern (aindrī), the northern (saumyā), and the unconquered (aparājitā).

The eastern direction belongs to Indra; the northern to Soma; the northeast is Aparājita (the unconquered). Regarding the posture—whether sitting, standing, or even lying down—where no such rule is specified, it should be performed while sitting, and not while bowing or standing.
Brahmā [is described] with knees bent in prostration; [one should be] bowed down, deeply humbled; standing upright; [and] Vasiṣṭha [is described].
In recitations, fire-offerings, and fasts, one should wear clean garments;
adorned, pure, silent, full of faith, and having conquered the senses.
Kātyāyana says: One should always wear the sacred thread and always have one's topknot tied;
whatever one performs without the topknot or without the sacred thread is as if it were not done at all.

In the *Nigama-pariśiṣṭa*: "The sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is on the left shoulder for rites pertaining to the gods (*daiva*); it is worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) in the reverse manner for ancestral sacrifices (*pitṛyajña*); it is suspended from the navel with two ends hanging around the neck during the *utsarga* ceremony; and during sexual intercourse (*grāmyadharma*), it hangs down from the back. Sexual intercourse refers to union with a woman. Baudhāyana states: "One engaged in ritual action should avoid touching anything below the navel. Manu says: "A Caṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, a dog, as well as a menstruating woman and a eunuch—these six should not look at twice-born men while they are eating."
Whatever is looked upon by these at the giving of a house or at a meal—
whether it be an offering to the gods or one for the ancestors— that becomes ineffective.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "Heretics, the fallen, and those people who are nihilists— no proximity to them is ever desired during a meritorious rite."
Now, from the *Vijñānalalita*:
"The mandalas of earth, water, fire, and air are in sequence;
he declares the earthly one to be yellow, four-cornered, and having Indra as its deity."
The Tārtha [mantra] is to be obtained; Padmāka is dedicated to Varuṇa.
The Asra, joined with the Svastika, is fiery (taijasa) and has Agni as its deity.
The square is presided over by Vindu; the wind-deity is black and belongs to the air.
In the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:
"Two parts of musk, four of sandalwood,
three of saffron, and one of camphor— this is the 'fourfold' (catuḥsama) [perfume]."
Camphor, sandalwood, darbha grass, and saffron in equal parts are declared to be "all-fragrance" (sarvagandha), which is beloved by all the gods.
Likewise: camphor, agallochum, musk, sandalwood,
and kakkola— by means of these five, yakṣakardama is produced.
In the Śivadharmottara: "The five nectars (pañcāmṛta), O King, are curd, milk, sugar, honey, and ghee."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with Kuśa grass—
this is declared to be the Pañcagavya, which destroys all sins.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "The tender leaves of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, Cūta, and Nyagrodha are declared to be the 'five-fold bhaṅga,' auspicious for all ritual acts."
In the *Pañcarātra*: "One should indeed have the five-colored powders prepared for the sake of the mandala;
[these may be] from the powder of *śāli* rice or from barley."
Red [pigment] arises from safflower, vermilion, red ochre, and so forth;
yellow arises from orpiment, and sometimes from turmeric.
[110] With black substances, it becomes green; when mixed with yellow and black, it becomes variegated.
*Rajanī* is turmeric. In the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
"In the absence of all gems, one should employ gold everywhere."
The seed-syllable of Rudra is supremely pure, because it belongs to him alone at all times.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "O King, for an image of a deity whose specific material and number have not been mentioned, it may be made of gold, silver, copper, wood, or likewise of clay."
Whether made from colored powders or produced by applying a paste of flour, it should be fashioned according to one's own means,
ranging from the size of a raw bean up to a *pala*, by those free from deceit.
Gold, silver, copper, and likewise brass,
iron, tin, and lead— these are proclaimed to be the metals (dhātavaḥ).
Likewise: water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, curd, unbroken rice,
sesame seeds, barley, and white mustard— thus the eightfold *argha* offering is proclaimed.
Likewise: dūrvā grass, barley sprouts, bālaka, mango shoots,
the two types of turmeric, white mustard, peacock feathers, and snake-skin.
These nine medicinal herbs known as the *kaṅkaṇa* are remembered as the *kautuka*.
In the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"Kuṣṭha, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, surā, śaileya, candana, vacā, campaka, and musta— these are remembered as the ten universal herbs (*sarvauṣadhyaḥ*)."
The invitation, the seat, the arghya, the water for the feet, the water for sipping, the honey-mixture, and the waters for the bath.

"Clothing, ornaments, perfumes, fine flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, circumambulation, and prostration— these they call the sixteen modes of service (*upacāra*)," as stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
"They may be made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, provided they possess the proper characteristics."
In processions, marriages, consecrations, and other such rites, there should be water-pots for the ceremonial sprinkling.
It should be fifty finger-breadths in width and sixteen finger-breadths in height;
the base should be twelve finger-breadths, and the opening eight finger-breadths.

Regarding the term *pañcāśāṅgula*: *āśā* means directions (*diśaḥ*), and these are well known in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* and other sciences as denoting the number ten. Thus, *pañcāśāḥ* means five directions. Those [lines] whose width consists of that many finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) are so described; the meaning is that they measure fifteen finger-breadths in transverse measurement at the middle part. Alternatively, when guided by a cord in the shape of a circle along the outer part, they measure fifty finger-breadths at the central point. In this latter case, the form *pañcāśāṅgulā* is a Vedic usage (*chāndasaḥ prayogaḥ*); such is the rule for mixed cases.
Now follows the determination of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth.

Regarding this, the *Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa* states: “That sacrifice, being un-sacrificed (*ahata*), did not prosper. The gods made it prosper through sacrificial fees; because they made it prosper through sacrificial fees, therefore they are called *dakṣiṇās*. In the *Bhaviṣya-Purāṇa*:
“O best of kings, a gift and even a vow that lacks a sacrificial fee [is ineffective].”
One should know that to be fruitless, like an oblation poured into ashes.
From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"One who is endowed with faith, pure, and self-controlled should give a gift accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
But that gift which is without a sacrificial fee is 'left-handed' (*savya*) and becomes fruitless."

The *Maitrāyaṇīyapariśiṣṭa* states: "If a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is obtained, one gives roots and edible foods; however, one should not perform the sacrifice in this manner [without such a fee]. Likewise, the *Śatapatha-śruti* says: "Therefore, there should be no oblation (*havis*) that is without a sacrificial fee. In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"Whatever is given for the sake of a specific desire (*kāmya*) brings complete happiness;
however, if it is incomplete, it leads to harm both in this world and the next."
Therefore, O Great King, one who desires the complete fruit should not give a gift that is devoid of a priestly fee (*dakṣiṇā*) or deficient in its prescribed ritual procedure.
Otherwise, that which is given leads only to harm;
for it is evident that there is a loss of wealth, and it will not yield any fruit.
The Blessed Vyāsa said:
Gold is the supreme gift; gold is the highest sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Among all gifts indeed, gold is desired as the sacrificial fee.

And this [rule] applies to those gifts where a general fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed, with the exception of specific gifts such as a cow or a garment for which particular fees have been ordained. Even there, the phrase "the most excellent of all" indicates its high praise; it does not, however, exclude other fees, because the purpose of a fee is to provide inexhaustible merit, and since gold is preeminent, the meaning of the statement is that gold serves as the fee in all gifts. Other items as well—such as rice and the like—that are useful for a person’s sustenance may also be employed for the purpose of a fee. As it is heard in scripture: "And for other gifts, gold is traditionally prescribed as the fee."
When gold is being given, however, silver is prescribed as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Thus, having fully understood this which has been heard from tradition, it should be believed:
gold, silver, copper, rice, and grain as well—
the daily *śrāddha* and the worship of the gods— all of this must indeed be accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "One should determine the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as one-third of the substance to be given;
however, in a gift where no fee is specified, it may be one-tenth or according to one's capacity."
Regarding gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa* and others, the *Liṅgapurāṇa* states:
"One should cause a hundred, or fifty, or even twenty-five [gold pieces] to be given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
and for all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), one should cause ten *niṣkas* to be given."
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"O Pārtha, one hundred niṣkas should be known as the supreme rule regarding gifts;
the middling is half of that, and the lowest is remembered as half of that."
And likewise in the case of a ewe, a black man, or other great beings;
similarly in the case of a tree, a fire, a cow, and a black antelope skin.
This rite of five gold pieces has been prescribed even for one who is incapable;
therefore, that lowest of men who gives a great gift with even less than this [is truly base].
Or if he accepts it, it will bring him suffering and grief.
Having described the victory-consecration (jayābhiṣeka) in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"One should indeed give a gift of sixty-eight palas to the preceptor,
and for all the officiating priests (hotṛ), thirty palas is prescribed."
The teachers shall receive half of that, and the gatekeepers half of that.

By this, the distribution of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) elsewhere should also be understood as follows: half for the preceptor and the senior officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), half of that for the reciters (*jāpaka*), and half of that for the gatekeepers. In the *Brahmavaivarta*, Subāhu said:
"O Brahmin, having taken an image of the gods, a Brāhmaṇa himself uses it for his own benefit, either by selling it or by dividing it."
[114] Furthermore, how can things such as the sesame-cow be eaten by one who possesses discernment?
Since it is a cow, is its consumption praiseworthy or not? Such is the doubt.
Viśvāmitra said:
Those who know the Vedas declare that Dharma has the Śruti as its primary root;
the Śruti, however, is the root of the Smṛtis, along with the Purāṇas and Itihāsas.
That which is proclaimed as having its root in the Śruti must not be disturbed;
indeed, at the time of the gift, the divinity of the images is fully extolled.
The status of being a "cow" for even those who are not cows is declared by the Śruti through their connection with the act of giving;
indeed, at the time of the gift, they are proclaimed as "cows" for the donor.
It is certain that at the time of the Brahmin’s expenditure, that wealth belongs to him;
for the wealth has come into the house by means of a Brahmin associated with the act of giving.
O Lord, all that may be sold at his own will by that learned man;
he must provide for the maintenance of his family and perform all religious duties in every respect.
"Otherwise, one goes to hell"—thus spoke the Grandfather (Brahmā).
How can sesame seeds possess the nature of a cow, and how can there be divinity in images?
One should learn of both the status as a cow and likewise the deity from the scripture;
for it is an established principle that scripture is the supreme authority among all authorities.
The world's conviction arises from scripture alone, and not from anything else; for what reason [should it be otherwise]?
The Purāṇas, the Dharma of Manu, the Veda with its auxiliary limbs, and medical science [are all based on scripture].
These four established by authoritative command are not to be refuted by logical arguments.
Now, the gift of substances. In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:

"Those designations for the purpose of measurement which have been recorded by the sages in the treatises on Dharma—all of them must be understood according to tradition for the sake of legal practice."
[115] Manu says: I shall declare in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold which are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions.
That subtle particle of dust which is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is called the *trasareṇu*, the most minute among atoms.
One should know that eight *trasareṇus* from the *paramāṇu* constitute one *likṣā*;
three of those [likṣās] are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those are a *gaurasarṣapa*.
Six mustard seeds make one medium barley grain; three barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*.
Four suvarṇas make one pala; ten palas make one dharaṇa.
Two kṛṣṇalas weighed together are to be known as one silver māṣaka.
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* constitute one *purāṇa*;
furthermore, a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa*, also called a *paṇa*.
Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one *śatamāna* of silver;
furthermore, a *niṣka* should be understood by its standard measure to consist of four *sauvarṇikas*.
Yājñavalkya says: A mote of dust seen in a sunbeam through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*. Eight of those are a *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*.
Three *gauras* make one *tuttha*, six of those make one *yava*, three of those make one *madhya*,
five of those make one *kṛṣṇala*, five of those make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*.
Four or five suvarṇas are proclaimed to be one pala;
two kṛṣṇalas are a silver māṣa, and sixteen of those are a dharaṇa.
A *śatamāna* consists of ten *dharaṇas*, as does a *phala*. A *niṣka* is four *suvarṇas*; a *kārṣika* is a copper coin known as a *paṇa*.

Viṣṇu says: A particle of dust that enters a sunbeam through a lattice window is called a *trasareṇu*. Eight of those make a *likṣā*; three of those make a *rājasarṣapa*; three of those make a *gaurasarṣapa*; six of those make a *yava*; three of those make a *kṛṣṇala*; five of those make a *māṣa*; twelve of those make half an *akṣa*; four *māṣas* make a *suvarṇa*; four *suvarṇas* make a *niṣka*. Two *kṛṣṇalas* make a silver *māṣaka*; sixteen of those make a *dharaṇa*. A copper coin is a *kārṣāpaṇa*. [Thus says] Kātyāyana.
A māṣa should be known as the twentieth part of a kārṣāpaṇa;
a kākiṇī, however, is the fourth part of both a māṣa and a paṇa.
In the region of the Five Rivers, this is the conventional designation;
the measure of a kārṣāpaṇa is that which is fixed right here.
One [māṣaka] is to be known as a kārṣāpaṇa; four of those make a dhānaka.
Twelve of those make a suvarṇa, while three are traditionally recorded as a dīnāra.
Nārada says:
In the southern direction, the silver kārṣāpaṇa circulates;
in the eastern direction, it is fixed at sixteen paṇas for each kārṣāpaṇa.
Also in the work proclaimed by Agasti:
"Six mustard seeds shall make one barleycorn (*yava*); three barleycorns shall make one *guñjā*;
and five *guñjās* are declared to be one *māṣaka*."
Sixteen māṣas are said to be one suvarṇa;
four of those [suvarṇas] are known as one pala, and ten palas they understand to be a dharaṇa.
Eight distinct white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*) constitute one *taṇḍula*;
that is said to be a *yava* of bamboo-measure, though others have declared it to be a *godhūma*.
Viṣṇugupta says:
Five guñjās make one māṣa, and four times that [māṣa] makes a śāṇa;
those expert in the measurement of gems call a kaṇaja a dharaṇa.
They know that one *majjāṭikā* is a specific variety of *kaṇaja*, equal in weight to two *guñjās*;
twenty *majjāṭikās* are considered by those who know the subject to be one *dharaṇa*.
It is recorded that for rubies (padmarāga) and for sapphires (indranīla) and other gems, the weights— whether large, medium, very fine, or even extremely fine— are measured in māṣakas.
In what case should that [measure] be employed where no specific measure has been stated?
A dīnāra is proclaimed to be equal to twenty-eight rūpakas.
A seventieth part of gold is considered a *ropaka*.
He has also stated it in another way:

when grains such as *māṣa* beans are produced in a good field at the proper time of ripening, ten of them equal one *suvarṇamāṣa*; five *guñjās* constitute a *suvarṇamāṣaka*, and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*. The second designation for that which is established by this measure is *karṣa*. Four *karṣas* make a *pala*; a hundred *palas* make a *tulā*; twenty *tulās* make a *bhāra*, and the second designation for this very *bhāra* is *udataulika*. Thus it is declared in the *Brahmaprokta*.
Twenty palas are considered a vīśa; five vīśas are a tulā.
That same [tulā] is called an udataulika, and twenty tulās are a bhāra.

Viṣṇugupta states: The distinct measurement for silver is now described. Eighty-eight white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*) constitute one silver *māṣaka*. Sixteen of those make a *dharaṇa*, or twenty *niṣpāva* grains; this is also called a silver *pala*. Ten *dharaṇas* make a *pala*, and one hundred of those *palas* make a *tulā*. Twenty of those *tulās* make a *bhāra*. It is said that when twenty grains of rice (*vrīhitaṇḍula*) are weighed on a scale, they equal one *dharaṇa* of the gemstone known as *vajra*. Some maintain that one should calculate a grain of rice using eight white mustard seeds. Thus it is stated in the *Nirghaṇṭu*.
Weight is measured by scales, finger-breadths, and *prastha*s; five *guñjā*s and so forth constitute one *māṣaka*.
Sixteen of those make one *akṣa*, which is also called a *karṣa*; four *karṣas* make one *pala*, which is not feminine.
A *suvarṇa* is a *vistā*; a *hemnokṣa* is the same; a *kuruvista*, however, is one *pala*. A *tulā* (feminine) is one hundred *palas*, and twenty *tulās* make a *bhāra*.
Ten bhāras would constitute an ācita; a cartload is an ācita bhāra.
A kārṣāpaṇa is equivalent to a kārṣika, and a kārṣika is a copper paṇa.
In the Ādityapurāṇa: "One, ten, a hundred, and a thousand— O best of beings—
as each subsequent term is ten times the preceding, ten thousands make an ayuta."
A hundred times a thousand is called a *niyuta* by the wise;
likewise, ten hundred thousands are called a *prayuta*.
One hundred times one hundred thousand is called a *koṭi*;
ten *koṭis* are an *arbuda*, and they know a hundred *koṭis* to be a *vṛnda*.
Those who know these [numerical] designations say that ten thousand koṭis is a kharva;
ten thousand times ten thousand koṭis is called a śaṅku.
They know that a thousand times ten million is indeed a *padma*;
and a thousand times a thousand such millions, multiplied tenfold again, is [the next number].
Those who know calculation indeed say that the ocean is mathematics itself.
Now, regarding the measurement of grain: in the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa it is stated that those seeds known as domestic and wild were sacrificed;
they are recorded as one hundred and seventeen types of plants that end with the ripening of their fruit.
Rice, barley, wheat, millet, sesame, panic seeds,
kovidāra, koradūṣa, and cīnaka.
Māṣas, mudgas, masūras, niṣpāvas, sakulotthakas,
āṭakyas, and caṇakas, as well as śaṇa— these are recorded as the seventeen [grains].
Thus, these are recorded as the varieties of cultivated plants;
fourteen types of medicinal plants, both cultivated and wild, are to be known as fit for sacrifice.
Rice, barley, wheat, millet,
mustard, beans, mung beans as the seventh, and lentils as the eighth.
Śyāmāka, nīvāra, jartila, gavedhuka,
along with kovidāra, as well as those that are bamboo-seeds—
these are recorded as the fourteen plants, both cultivated and wild.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Barley, wheat, grains, sesame, millet, and kulothika;
black gram, mung beans, lentils, flat beans, and dark mustard.
Gavedhuka, nīvāra, āḍhakī, and satīnaka;
caṇaka and cīnaka—these indeed are the eighteen grains.
Grains (*dhānya*) are rice (*vrīhi*). Gavedhukas are *kasakas*. Nīvāras are wild rice. Satīnakas are round peas. Cīnakas are a specific variety of sixty-day rice. According to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Barley, wheat, grains, sesame, as well as *kaṅgu*, śyāmāka, and cīnaka—these are declared to be the seven grains (*saptadhānya*)."
In the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*: "Two *pala*s make a *prasṛta*; twice that is considered a *kuḍava*. Four *kuḍava*s make a *prastha*, and four *prastha*s make an *āḍhaka*."
Four of those *āḍhaka*s are said by the wise to be one *droṇa*;
two *droṇa*s are a *kumbha*; a *sūrpa* is a *khārī*; and sixteen *droṇa*s are a *khārī*.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "A *pala*, a *kuḍava*, a *prastha*, an *āḍhaka*, and a *droṇa*—
these should be understood as increasing fourfold in sequence when measuring grain."
Sixteen *droṇas* are said to be one *khārī*, and twenty [of those] are called a *kumbha*. Ten *kumbhas* constitute a *vāha*; thus the measurements of grain are proclaimed.
In the *Vārāha Purāṇa*: "Two palas are a *prasṛta*; one *muṣṭi* is said to be one *pala*.
Eight *muṣṭis* make a *kuñci*, and eight *kuñcis* make a *puṣkala*."
Four *puṣkala*s are proclaimed to be one *āḍhaka*;
four *āḍhaka*s constitute a *droṇa*. This is the definition of measurement.

Four *setikās* are proclaimed as one *prastha* (some say this is the *muṣṭi*, or handful, of the sacrificer). It is stated [in the *Pādmapurāṇa*]: “One *muṣṭi* is remembered as one *pala*; a *setikā* is called a *kuḍava*.
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*: [the same].
Four *kuḍavas* make one *prastha*; four *prasthas* make one *āḍhaka*;
four *āḍhakas* make one *droṇa*: such is the definition of these measures.
Now, in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa:
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; sixty-four of those make one *pala*.
Thirty-two *palas* make one *prastha*, and four *āḍhakas* make one *droṇa*.
Regarding liquid substances, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"Two palas are considered a *prasṛta*; double that is a *kuḍava*.
Four *kuḍavas* make a *prastha*, and an *āḍhaka* consists of four times those."
Four guṇas make one droṇa; this is the calculation for liquids.

Now, regarding the magnitude [of the atom]: in the *Ādityapurāṇa* it is said: "The subtle particle of dust that is seen when the sun's rays pass through a lattice opening—that is declared to be the first among measurements, the *trasareṇu*."
Eight atoms (paramāṇu) should be known as one mote of dust in a sunbeam (trasareṇu); eight such motes of dust in a sunbeam are traditionally said to be one chariot-dust (rathareṇu).
Eight of those chariot-dust particles are known by the wise as one hair-tip;
eight hair-tips are one nit, and eight nits are known by the wise as one louse-egg.
They say eight *yūkās* make one barleycorn (*yava*), and eight barleycorns make one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
A span (*vitasti*) is proclaimed to be exactly twelve finger-breadths in measure.
The placement [of the hand] with the thumb and the index finger is called a *prādeśa*; a *tāla* is traditionally defined by the middle finger, and a *lokārṇa* by the ring finger;
a *vitasti*, however, is traditionally known as twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) when measured with the little finger.
A *ratni* should be known as twenty-one finger-joints;
a *hasta*, however, consists of twenty-four fingers.
A *kiṣku* is traditionally held to be two *aratnis*, or forty-two *aṅgulas*;
and a bow-staff (*dhanurdaṇḍa*) is proclaimed to consist of ninety-six *aṅgulas*.
A pair of bow-staves is to be known as a *nāli*, for these [are the measures] of the barley-corn and the finger-breadth;
those who know calculation say that thirty *dhanus* make a *nalva*.
Two thousand bows are taught to be one *gavyūti*,
while eight thousand bows are proclaimed to be one *yojana*.

In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: the atom (paramāṇu), the subtle particle (paraṃ sūkṣmaṃ), the mote in a sunbeam (trasareṇu), the dust of the earth (mahīrajaḥ), the tip of a hair (vālāgra), the nit (likṣā), the louse-egg (yūkā), then the barley-corn (yava), and finally the finger-breadth (aṅgula).
They say that eight *yavas* successively make one *aṅgula*; eight of those make one *aṅgula*.
They say that six *aṅgulas* make a *pada*, and twice that is remembered as a *vitasti*.
Two *vitastis* make one *hasta*; the *brahmatīrtha* [measurement] consists of two *ceṣṭanas*.
Four *hastas* make a *dhanus*, a *daṇḍa*, or a *nālikā*; and a pair of those [two *nālikās*] makes one [unit].
Two thousand *dhanus* make one *kośa*, and four times that is a *gavyūti*;
from that, a *yojana* is said to be double, according to those skilled in calculation.
Bṛhaspati says: A *nivartana* consists of thirty *daṇḍas*, each *daṇḍa* being ten *hastas* long;
he who gives ten such *gocarmas* to Brahmins [attains great merit].
Vasiṣṭha says:
One should give ten bamboo poles on each side, with five additional ones; this is called a *gocarma* (cow-hide).
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"If a twice-born man eats whatever is produced [as food] for the duration of a year,
it is declared by the wise to be equivalent to one *gocarma* of land."
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "Thirty daṇḍas of seven cubits each constitute a nivartana;
Prajāpati has declared that three-quarters of this is the measure of a gocarma."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
Where a hundred cows and one bull may stand unconfined,
those who know the Vedas call that area "gocarma" (the measure of a cow-hide).

Now, the characteristics of the pavilion and other structures. Baudhāyana states: "The standard cubit (*prāmāṇika-kara*) is the distance between the middle finger and the elbow. In the Chandogapariśiṣṭa:
"Wherever the measurement of a thumb-breadth (*aṅguṣṭhāṅgula*) is prescribed, there the wise man should measure by means of the knots at the joints of the large fingers."
Now, regarding the five-night rite:
one should construct pavilions with four doors for the Vaiṣṇava sacrifices;
the pillars should be made of heartwood, firm, straight, and equal.
One should erect twelve pillars for the pavilion, raised to a height appropriate for it, provided with finials, and resembling the Vedas [in number], with a decorative molding at their tops.
On the exterior, according to the measurement of the pedestal, there is a platform there by means of the division of the lines;
therein, for the medium and superior [altars], there is a platform by means of the division of the lines.
Its height should be one-fourth [of its width], or three, seven, or five [parts];
or one may construct it with bricks having nine or eleven courses.
[123] The smallest pavilion should be ten cubits, the medium twelve cubits,
and the best one here should be sixteen cubits.

"Veda-saṃkhyān" means "having the number four. *Cūḍā* refers to a crest; it is fashioned on the top of a pillar for the purpose of inserting the upper groove of the joint (*sandhi-valikā*). "External" (*bāhya*) means being outside in relation to the four pillars set within. This is the meaning: having first set up the four central pillars, one should then set up twelve pillars on the outer perimeter; thus, the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) comes to consist of sixteen pillars. Regarding "by the division of the cord" (*sūtra-vibhāgataḥ*): the meaning is that the pillars should be placed leaving an interval measuring one-third of the cord of the site, whether that cord runs east-west or north-south. Regarding "in the smallest [pavilion] it is two cubits": in the smallest pavilion, the door should be made with a width of two cubits; however, for the medium and largest [pavilions], it should be increased by four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each.
In the Viśvakarmavāstuśāstra:
"Having left a space between the pavilions, two pavilions should be constructed;
having abandoned the space between one temple and another, the sacrificial pavilion should be placed in front of the temple."

Whether ten, twelve, or sixteen cubits (*kalāhasta*) [in size], when two pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) are constructed, one should build the second pavilion after leaving aside a space equal to the measurement of the first pavilion. However, when a pavilion is built in front of the temple (*dhāma*), the meaning is that one should build the pavilion beyond a space equal to the measurement of that temple. A *kalāhasta* is sixteen cubits.
The pavilions, such as the Vijaya and others, should be covered with six cubits [of cloth].
But those made from the branches of the aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, and vaṭa trees, however, [are forbidden].
One should cause these doors to be made for the pavilion in every direction;
they should be five cubits in measure in height and two cubits in width.
But in the highest [grade], they increase by six finger-breadths up to seven cubits.

Regarding "five cubits": in the smallest pavilion, the door-frames should be made five cubits; in the medium, six cubits; and in the largest, seven cubits. Furthermore, the width should be increased by six *aṅgulas* starting from one cubit.
On the top, one should place the conch, discus, mace, and lotus with their twelve parts, made of wood, arranged in the sequence beginning with the east.
One should place a fifth part upon the ground; this is the rule common to all.
Regarding that, in the *Saṃgraha*:
"For each pit, banners are prescribed by those learned in the meaning of the scriptures;
the banners should be seven cubits long and one-seventh as wide."
The six banners of Himaprabhā are described as having the colors of the world-protectors;
they are known to have yellow, red, and other colors, and each has five hands.
They are considered to be joined with those bamboo poles, each measuring ten cubits in length.
With banners five or ten cubits [in length], according to the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*: "Banners should be made five cubits [long] and two cubits in width;
the flags should be seven cubits [long] and twenty finger-breadths in width."
The staffs of the banners were ten cubits long and fifty were set up;
they were vermilion, variegated, smoky, grey, and resembling clouds.
O Pākaśāsana, auspicious banners of these colors— green, pale yellow, and white— should be made in sequence starting from the east.
In the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa: Having left a space between the altar and the feet [of the image], there should be nine or five sacrificial pits;
they should be square like the Vedas, or sometimes equal to the balance-beam (tulā).
The weapons of the Vedas are square. In the secret tradition (āmnāya), the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be square, or shaped like a circle or a lotus stalk;
they should be made nine, five, or even one, provided they possess the defining characteristics.
In the ritual procedure for nine fire-pits, when eight pits are situated in the cardinal directions,
one should cause the ninth pit to be made in the intermediate space between the east and the northeast.
In the procedure for five fire-pits, the fifth shall be located in the northeast.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "The squares in the directions [number] four, five, and nine; but the fifth is in the region of Īśa.
Also in the *Nāradīya*:
In whatever ritual where a set of four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is prescribed, they are respectively:
a square, a semi-circle, a circle, and one resembling a lotus.
The wise practitioner should construct four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the directions beginning with the east.
The distance between the pit and the altar should be one and a quarter cubits (sapādakarasaṃmita).
