The pit should be well-rounded, properly proportioned, and constructed like a pedestal.
In the *Bahvṛca-pariśiṣṭa*: "For eating, for liberation, as well as for nourishment, especially for the restoration of what is decayed,
always for the fire-oblation (*homa*), and likewise for pacification (*śānti*), the [sacrificial] ground should be oriented toward the direction of Varuṇa (the west)."

In the Kāmika [Tantra], however, the description of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) for the sake of various results in their respective directions is as follows: for paralyzing (stambhana), a square pit in the east; for enjoyment (bhoga), a vulva-shaped one in the southeast;
for killing (māraṇa), a half-moon in the south; and in the southwest, a double or triple triangle.
In the west, for pacification, the wheel is prescribed; in the six directions, for eradication, it is in the southeast;
in the north, for nourishment, it is the lotus; and in the northeast, the eight-spoked [wheel] grants liberation.
In all these cases, the area of the site should be prepared according to the fire oblation (*homa*), measuring one cubit (*hasta*) and so forth. This has been stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"For fifty [oblations], the measure is a fist; for a hundred, it is the span of an elbow (*aratni*);
but when a thousand are to be offered, one should make the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) the size of a cubit."
For ten thousand oblations, that [pit] should be two cubits; for a hundred thousand oblations, four cubits;
and for ten million oblations, the pit should consist of eight cubits, but not more.

"Measuring a fist" means the size of a hand with the fist closed. Now, the procedure for the construction of square and other types of fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) is described. Regarding the square pit first, Viśvakarman says:

"Having laid a cord from east to west at half the [total] length, and having placed cords between the two 'fish' (intersection points) in the south and north, one then [obtains] a square by means of the marked corners."

Having determined the east by means of the previously mentioned method, one should draw a line from east to west and mark its midpoint. Then, by laying down another thread over that [first] thread, one should form two "fish" figures (*matsya*) for the south and north directions; in the treatises on architecture (*śilpa-śāstra*), the shape formed at the intersection of threads is called a "fish. The production of the two fish figures should be performed as follows: placing the end of a thread equal in length to the previously drawn line at the base of that very line, one should rotate it to form a circle. Then, placing the same end of that thread at the other extremity of the line, one should rotate it again to form a second circle. When these two circles are made, the two fish figures for the south and north directions are produced. Next, having laid a single thread through the two fish figures and the previously marked midpoint, one should draw a line extending from south to north. Once the cardinal directions have been established in this way, one should mark the corners to determine the intermediate directions (*vidiś*). The procedure for this is as follows: at each of the four ends of the previously drawn lines, place half of the desired measurement on both sides and make marks for the corners at those junctions. Then, by laying down four threads through those corner marks, one should construct a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) facing east or north. As for the extraction of the *yoni*-shaped and other forms, they are derived from the square as their primary basis according to the *Kāmika-śāstra*.
Having set aside one-fifth at the front, [one should draw] from the center with a measurement of four parts;
by means of a circular rotation, the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha) is thus described.

Having set aside one-fifth part of the field toward the eastern direction of the city—[the remainder being] in the middle of the diagonal line—it means that by means of rotation, through the revolving of the end of the cord, one should fashion a pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the shape of an *aśvattha* leaf in the south-eastern direction. The method of its construction is as follows: having made the previously mentioned field a perfect square, one should draw a central line (*garbharekhā*) from the center of the western side to the center of the eastern side, exceeding the diagonal line of the field by one-fifth part. Then, having marked a point at one-fourth part of the diagonal line in the south-western corner, and having fixed the beginning of a cord upon that mark with its end placed at the base of the aforementioned central line, one should rotate it to produce a semicircle outside; likewise, one should fashion a semicircle in the north-western corner. Then, having dropped two cords from the ends of the central line so that they touch the ends of the two semicircles, one should construct a *yonikuṇḍa* in the shape of a *pippala* leaf in the south-eastern direction, with its opening facing north. "In a square divided by the planets (nine), having discarded the first and last parts, a pit shaped like a crescent moon is formed by the measure of the seven middle parts. When the square field is divided by nine, having discarded the first and last [parts], one should make a pit resembling a crescent moon by rotating a cord according to the measure of the remaining seven parts. The procedure here is this: having divided the square field into nine parts and having removed the first and last two parts, one should place the beginning of a cord at the center of the first of the remaining seven parts, and the end of that same cord at the center of the last line of those seven parts. By rotating that cord, one should fashion a resting semicircle equal to the first line. Then, having joined both ends of the first line to the semicircle, one should create a "half-moon" (*khaṇḍacandra*) situated in the southern direction with its opening facing north. "By increasing by one-third and using three 'fish' (triangles), there shall be a *naiśācara* (south-western) pit. By increasing by three parts of three in three places, using three 'fish', one should make a *naiśācara* pit related to the south-western direction. Here is the tradition: having constructed a square field as before, one should draw a central line from the middle of the horizontal western side to the middle of the horizontal eastern side, exceeding the diagonal line of the field by one-third. One should also make the two ends of the previously mentioned western line exceed the diagonal line by one-third. Then, having dropped two cords from the ends of the central line so that they touch the two ends of the previously mentioned western line, one should produce a triangular pit in the south-western direction with its opening facing east. And when this is performed, the increase of three parts of three in three places, and the production of three 'fish' therein, is accomplished. "A circular pit is taught here by the addition of one-eighth of half the working cord. By the correct placement of one-eighth part of half the working cord, a circular pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*) is formed. The method of its arrangement is this: having divided the cord that goes from corner to corner in the square field—which is called "half-corner"—into eight parts, one should place outside in the four directions a portion equal to the eighth part. Then, having placed the beginning of a cord at the center of the field and having rotated the end of that same cord around the eighth part placed outside, one should make a circular pit in the western direction with its opening facing east. "A six-sided pit shall be formed by increasing by one-sixth and using four 'fish'. Having increased each of the two sides of the field by one-sixth, and having produced four 'fish' in the remaining directions, the six-sided pit is produced by the falling of six cords. Here is the tradition: having divided the square field into six parts, one should extend the field on the right and left sides by the measure of one-sixth part, thereby making that very field a rectangle. Then, one should draw a central line running north-south that touches the two lines of the sides just mentioned. Then, having dropped one cord each from the center of the field and from the middle of the northern side-line, measuring half of the previously mentioned central line, one should produce a 'fish' in the interval between the east and northeast; by that same method, one should make a 'fish' in the interval between the west and northwest. Then, again, one should drop four cords from the center of the field and from the middle of the southern side-line, touching four marks starting from the two ends of the previously mentioned central line. Thus, by the application of six cords together with the two cords situated between the marks, one should make a six-cornered pit (*ṣaṭkoṇakuṇḍa*) in the northwest direction with its opening facing east.
The pericarp should be made by dividing the square into eight parts;
outside of that, one should fashion the filaments using one part.
In the third [circle], the middle parts of the petals; in the fourth, the tips of the petals. Through this rotation, there shall be a lotus petal, showing the tip of the petal outside.

In the center of a square divided into eight parts, the pericarp (*karṇikā*) should be formed by the eighth part. Outside the pericarp, on the second eighth-part placement situated along the circumference, the filaments (*kesara*) should be placed. Outside the filaments, on the third eighth-part situated along the circumference, the filaments should be placed. Outside the filaments, on the third eighth-part placement situated along the circumference, one should fashion the centers of the petals; then, having fashioned the tips of the petals on the fourth [part], one should cause the tips of the petals to touch the exterior of the square. Here too, the phrase "by the eighth part" is to be connected. "Respectively" (*vibhāgaśaḥ*) means in each division, that is, in all directional divisions. The words "by the turning of the thread" are to be supplied as the remainder. And this [procedure] is to be applied everywhere.

This is the meaning: Having divided a square field into eight parts by means of lines running eastward and northward, and having marked the center, one should place another eighth part all around outside the field in the four directions. When this is done, there will be five lines in each direction reaching up to the fifth-eighth part from the mark. Then, by rotating a cord whose starting point is placed upon the previously mentioned mark and whose ends are fixed upon those respective lines, one should produce five circles and erase the lines that exceed the circles. Then, having designated the first circle as the pericarp (*karṇikā*), the second as the filaments (*kesara*), the third as the centers of the petals, the fourth as the tips of the petals, and the fifth as the outer edges of the petals, one should construct an eight-petaled lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) facing east with its opening (*yoni*) toward the north.
Now, O King, this circular pit (kuṇḍa) is described by another method:
"The circular pit is equal [to the square], or else it is of another kind;
having first made the circular pit, one should divide the girdle (mekhalā) into four parts."
Having likewise made the height, that pericarp (karṇikā) shall be one and a half [units];
the remaining portion shall be for the petals, either four petals or eight petals.

Just as the circular pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*) was described in the western direction, here too one should construct it in exactly that same manner; then, in its center, one should fashion a lotus-pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) according to the divisions. Now, by the words "or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth, the third method is stated. The meaning is that first, taking the circular pit itself—along with its girdle (*mekhalā*)—as the limit, one should perform the division of the fourth field by constructing three circles. Then, in the middle of that field, a pericarp (*karṇikā*) should be made with an extent of one and a half parts. And having likewise made the height, that is to say, having made the elevation of the pericarp also one and a half parts, one should fashion the petals themselves—excluding the filaments—with the remaining two and a half parts. In this way, one should make a four-petaled or an eight-petaled lotus-pit.
Having set aside the twelfth part of the field on all four sides within its interior,
one should lead out another quarter-measure of that same dimension.
One should mark its sides according to the measurement of the ear;
there, by the conjunction of eight lines, it is called an octagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

Having laid out in the four directions a portion equal in measure to the twelfth part of the field divided into twelve parts, one should—within that [space], meaning in the outer region of that field (the word *antara* here signifies "outside," according to the rule *antara* being used for both "inside" and "outside" in the context of yoga and clothing)—lead forth, that is, construct, another second square by the same measurement as that previously laid out outside, namely the twelfth part. Regarding the term *turyāsra*, the suffix here is pleonastic (*svārthika*). Regarding "by the measurement of its diagonal" (*karṇapramāṇena*): in the Śilpa-śāstras, a cord touching from corner to corner is well known as a *karṇa* (diagonal). However, in this context, with the intention that there are four distinct diagonals extending from the center of the field to each of the four corners, even half a diagonal is referred to by the word *karṇa*. Thus, the meaning is as follows:

One should mark [the corners] on its arms—that is, on the arms of that diagonal—by a measurement equal to the length of the diagonal extending from the outer square to the center of the interior. Here, the term "arms" refers to the lines of the outer square itself, which, situated on both sides of the diagonal, take the form of their own arms. This is the intended meaning: having placed the beginning of a cord measuring half the diagonal at one corner related to the outer square, one should extend that cord over the line of the square and mark the end of the cord. Likewise, having placed the beginning of the cord at each corner, by extending the cord in both directions (both forward and backward) and marking the respective ends, one makes two marks for each direction; thus, by laying down eight cords upon the marks in the four cardinal directions, one should construct an eight-cornered (*aṣṭāsra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
This is the manner of transformation here.

As before, having set aside the twelfth part on each of the four sides outside of the square field, one should construct another square of that same measurement. Then, by placing the starting point of a cord measuring half the diagonal of that [square] at each corner and extending it over the lines of the square, one marks the respective ends; thus, having made eight marks in the four directions, one should construct an eight-cornered (*aṣṭāśri*) fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with its opening facing east in the northeast direction by laying down eight cords upon those marks. Now, without regard for the fixed directions, two types of fire-pits taught in the *Vijñānalalita* for their utility in various rites are described.
Having set aside one-seventh part on the outside and drawn a circle here by means of rotation,
[one should mark] with measurements equal to the eastern field minus one-fourth.
A five-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) marked by five lines in the shape of a bowstring is recommended for oblations intended to subdue spirits, śākinīs, and planetary influences.

In the external region of the square field, one should lay out a seventh part of the field in each of the four directions. Then, by rotating a thread everywhere around the perimeter—starting from the center of the field and ending above the seventh part situated outside—one should produce a circle. Regarding the phrase "by means of the previous field," the term "previous field" refers specifically to the inner square field in relation to the circle situated outside.

The meaning of this is as follows: Having reduced the length of the inner square by one-fourth of its own measure, one should prepare a cord of that resulting measurement. By laying five such cords inside the outer circle, one should form the corners at the junctions of the cords. Since each of those five cords touches the circle at two ends, they take the shape of bowstrings—resembling the string mounted upon a bow. Then, having wiped away everything except for the five cords, one should construct the five-cornered (*pañcāsra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). And that is to be employed in fire-offerings (*homa*) such as those for the subjugation of planets (*graha-nigraha*).
Having placed the tenth part outside and drawn a circle here by rotation,
one should divide the field of the mandala into sixty-four parts, and then further into thirty-three parts.
The Samāya-sūtra is derived from that [central] axis; from seven threads, a seven-sided [mandala] is formed, which is known as the homa-pit for the purpose of pacifying malevolent magic.

Here too, having set aside a tenth part of the square field on the outside in the four directions, one should draw a circle as before. Then, having divided the original field into sixty-four parts, and having made a cord measured by thirty-three of those sixty-four parts, one should place seven such cords along the circumference of the circle and construct a seven-sided *kuṇḍa*. In this case as well, it should be understood that the cords take the form of bowstrings, the corners are formed at the junctions of the cords, and the excess beyond the seven cords is to be removed, exactly as previously described. This *kuṇḍa* is to be employed in fire-offerings (*homa*) for the pacification of the defects resulting from malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). Thus says Viśvakarman:
Whatever the extent of the width of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has been stated, that same measure is prescribed for its excavation; likewise,
whatever shape the pit is prescribed to have, [that same shape applies to the excavation].
One should fashion the girdle in such a form.
For the installation of all sacrificial pits, the banner bestows all accomplishments.

In all these cases, having adjusted the fingers, barley grains, and so forth, by making them either less or more than the prescribed measure, the *dhvaja* (flag) should be determined. When the width multiplied by the length is divided by eight, if one remains as a remainder, then it is a *dhvaja*. If the pit is too large, there will be disease; if too small, a loss of cattle and wealth.
In a curved pit, there is suffering; in one with a broken rim, death.

If the girdle is omitted, there will be excessive grief; if the wealth is diminished, there is loss of property. It is declared that the destruction of the wife occurs if the *kuṇḍa* is made without a vulva-shaped cavity.
That which is devoid of a neck is declared to be a *kuṇḍa* that destroys one's offspring.

Since it has been shown that a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) devoid of the characteristics of its excavation (*khāta*) and other features yields undesirable results—by such statements as "there shall be disease in one whose pit is deficient in excavation"—the characteristics of the excavation and so forth are now being described. As follows, in the *Mohacūḍottara-śāstra*:
"Having calculated a twenty-fourth part as a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), one should calculate the cubit (*hasta*) of the sacrificial pits as twenty-four finger-breadths."
One should dig a pit one cubit deep horizontally, together with the girdle at the top.

The measurement of the *kuṇḍa* has been stated in accordance with the common usage of hands and fingers—such as "half a hundred [fingers] is the measure of a fist" (*muṣṭimānaṃ śatārdham*)—following the requirements of the fire-oblation (*homa*). However, this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is now established for the purpose of specifying the measurements of the excavation (*khāta*) and other parts. One should divide the area of the intended *kuṇḍa* into twenty-four parts and, having determined that the twenty-fourth part constitutes one *aṅgula*, one should define a *hasta* as twenty-four *aṅgulas*. Then, using that *hasta* as the standard, one should determine the horizontal and vertical measurement of all *kuṇḍas*. Furthermore, one should determine the vertical measurement of the excavation—including its girdles (*mekhalā*)—using that same *hasta*. Regarding the first [type of *kuṇḍa*], it was said: "The *kuṇḍa* is twenty-four *aṅgulas* (jināṅgula) in width and height, together with the girdles. Here, "twenty-four *aṅgulas*" (*jināṅgula*) means twenty-four *aṅgulas*. This is also stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*:
Having ascertained that the height of the three girdles is five [parts], one should dig the remainder below.
It has also been stated by Viśvakarman:
"The trench is said to be equal in width to the [structure], but its depth is fifteen finger-breadths."

The depth of the excavation is fifteen finger-breadths (*tithyaṅgula*), while its elevation is nine finger-breadths; since this will be explained later, in the case of three girdles (*mekhalā*), the height of the first girdle is nine finger-breadths, so that both together total twenty-four finger-breadths. The measurement of the neck (*kaṇṭha*) is stated in the *Kālottara*:
"Outside the excavation, the neck is one finger-breadth; this is the rule for all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*).

One should fashion the neck—also known by the synonym "lip" (*oṣṭha*)—with a measurement of one finger-breadth in the space between the excavation and the girdle. This is stated in the *Sārasamuccaya*.
The neck is one external finger from the edge of the pit; outside of that, the girdle follows in sequence.
The characteristics of the girdle are stated in the *Kāmika*:
its lip should be one-twelfth of the field, and that [lip] should be one-sixteenth of it.
The girdle should have a broad height and be shaped like a bowl;
however, for the sake of simplicity, only a single girdle should be fashioned for all of them.

The lip, which is designated by the term *kaṇṭha*, shall be one-twelfth part of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). The width of the girdle (*mekhalā*) shall be one-fourth of that, being a quarter-part of the pit. Likewise, the height of the girdle should be made one-sixth part, being a sixth-part [of the pit]. This is also stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Leaving aside one finger-breadth from the excavation, there should be the placement of the girdles;
there may be one girdle, or three, or five, O Dear One."
The "number of elements" refers to the number five. And it was stated in the first [chapter]:
"Outside the finger-breadth of the neck, a single girdle should be made six finger-breadths wide;
or else three [girdles] of four, three, and two finger-breadths [respectively] are beautiful in all cases."
When there is one girdle, it should be made six finger-breadths in both width and height;

for it is stated by Piṅgala: "One girdle is considered to have a height and width of six finger-breadths. However, when there is the position of three girdles, they should be made in sequence with measurements of four, three, and two finger-breadths, according to the *Mohaśūrottara*.
Three girdles (mekhalā) should be made, consisting of four corners, three [units], and two [units] in finger-breadths (aṅgula).

Here, "corners" (koṇa) are four; "Rāmas" (rāma) are three; and "Yamas" (yama) are two. Among them, the outermost [girdle] is two finger-breadths wide, the middle ones are three finger-breadths, and the one adjacent to the rim of the pit (kuṇḍakaṇṭha) is four finger-breadths. This being the case, the height (utsedha) of the first girdle, starting from the rim of the pit, would be nine finger-breadths. Also, in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*:
"The first [girdle] is eight finger-breadths in width, and it is raised nine finger-breadths."
From the middle, however, it is three finger-breadths on the outside; the third, moreover, is two and a half finger-breadths.
Or five girdles should be made, [measuring] five, six, five, three, and two-and-a-half cubits respectively.

Situated near the first *kuṇḍa*, it is nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in internal height, while externally it is four finger-breadths; [the other dimensions are] eight finger-breadths and four finger-breadths. There are four seasons (*abda*) and two fortnights (*pakṣa*). The characteristics of the *yoni* have been stated in the *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*:
"The *yoni* is in the middle of the girdles (*mekhalā*); it is half the size of the *kuṇḍa* and three parts wide.
It should be made with a thumb for its lip and neck, and shaped like a leaf of the *śvattha* tree."
The yoni of the fire-pits located in the east, south, and southeast is said to face north;
the remaining ones are recorded as facing east, arranged according to what is aesthetically pleasing.

In the interior region of the *mekhalā*, a *yoni* should be made, half as long as the *kuṇḍa* and one-third as wide as the *kuṇḍa*. Here, the word "lip" (*oṣṭha*) refers to the tip of the *yoni*, and the word "neck" (*kaṇṭha*) refers to the rim of the *yoni*. The word "thumb" (*aṅguṣṭha*) is a synonym for "finger" (*aṅgula*). The meaning is that one should fashion the tip and the rim of the *yoni* with a measurement of one finger-breadth; for it is stated by Piṅgala: "The width of the *yoni* is eight fingers, and its tip is measured at one finger. Thus it is said in the *Nāradīya*.
The *yoni* should have a width equal to one-third of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) and a height of one finger-breadth;
it should be as long as half the pit and shaped like a leaf of the Bodhi tree, with lips corresponding to the rim of the pit.

"Kuṇḍoṣṭhī" means that just as the rim (*oṣṭha*) is prescribed for the *kuṇḍa* by means of a twelfth part, so too the rim of the *yoni* should be made by means of a twelfth part; the meaning is: "that whose rim has entered into the *kuṇḍa*. "Bodhipatra" refers to the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree. In the *Trailokyasāra*:
"From the long [line], the navel is twelve finger-breadths in length, but reduced by one-third in width;
it is one finger-breadth in height, and likewise enters within."
It is considered to be joined with two jars and like the leaves of the aśvattha tree;
it is provided with a girdle one finger-breadth wide, and likewise has a vessel for clarified butter in the middle.
The [fire-]pit situated to the south-east is for the eastern [quarter], while that situated in the north-west is for the western [quarter];
even for the nine-month [consecration], the *yoni* of the pit is located on the southern petal.

"Sūryāṅgulāḥ" means twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas). "Tryaṃśonā" means its width is less by one-third of its length. "Ekenāṅguleno-cchritā" means it is raised by one aṅgula; likewise, it enters into the center of the pit by one aṅgula. "Kumbhadvayasamāyuktā" refers to two circles located at the base of the *yoni*—which has the same shape as the previously mentioned Āgneya pit—and these are called "pots" (*kumbha*) because they have the form of an elephant's frontal globes (*kumbha*). Therefore, it should be understood here that the shape of the pot-base consists of either two jars or two lumps of clay to be placed there. "Aṅguṣṭhamekhalena" means it is encircled by a girdle (*mekhalā*) measuring one aṅgula in size. Regarding "in the middle," the intention is that just as an offering (*bali*) is made into the ladle (*sruva*) to hold the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), so too a cavity should be made in the middle of the *yoni*. Regarding "in the south," in the eastern, Āgneya, and southern pits, the *yoni* should be made facing north with its tip toward the southern part; however, in the Nairṛtya and other pits, it should be made facing east in the western part. Regarding "the ninth," having thus arranged the pits in the eight directions, the meaning is that the *yoni* should also be made on the southern side of both that which is the ninth pit in the interval between the east and northeast, or that which is the fifth pit in the northeast when four pits are made in the four cardinal directions. [This is stated] in the *Bahvṛca-Pariśiṣṭa*.
Furthermore, the Śruti declares: "The ignorant man who offers oblations into the fire with smoke [as its sign] shall become blind, along with his sons."
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"An offering made with the hand consists of twelve finger-joints; if made with a leaf such as a plantain leaf, it should fill the ladle up to the joints."
The oblation is offered with the divine sacred formula and at the proper time into the fire that has auspicious embers and clear flames.
The man who offers oblations into a fire that lacks flames or whose embers have been extinguished is born with weak digestion, prone to disease, and indeed destitute.
Therefore, one who desires health, long life, and ultimate prosperity should offer oblations only when the fire is well-kindled, and never when it is not kindled.
One should offer oblations both before and after the pouring with the hands, winnowing baskets, ladles, and so forth;
one should not blow on the fire, but should fan it with a fan or similar means.

"One should indeed blow upon the fire with the mouth, for it was born from the mouth"; however, that which people apply to the case of ordinary fire—that one should not blow upon it with the mouth—is [a rule] restricted to that specific context.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "O tiger among men, that which is offered while the vessel rests on the ground and the left hand supports it is not considered an offering made into the intermediate space."
The Soma-tīrtha is located in the middle of the lines for wealth, longevity, and wife;
with it, one should perform the offering of parched grain and other oblations, as well as the shaving of the head.
*Vapana* refers to the pouring out of rice and other grains. In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Pounding, grinding, and likewise winnowing should always be done only once for the ancestors; for the gods, it is said that these should be performed three times."

Marīci says: "In rites for desired objects, such as those for subjugation and the like, sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) should be taken with their tips pointing eastward, being neither too short nor split at the ends; if they are the opposite, one intends to strike [the practitioner]."

"In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, following the recurrence of the word 'fuel-stick' (*samit*), it is stated: 'arising from the *śamī*, *palāśa*, *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, or *vaikaṅkata* trees; shattered, split, short, crooked, with many nodes, or thin.'"
The Aśvattha, Udumbara, Bilva, Candana, and likewise Sarala trees.
The *śāla*, the *devadāru*, and the *khadira*—these are the [woods] fit for sacrifice, according to the ritualists.
Kātyāyana, in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*, states:
"The fuel-stick should never be thicker than the thumb;
it must not be devoid of straightness, nor infested with insects, nor split."

The sacrificial fuel-sticks used in fire-offering rituals should not be longer or shorter than a span; they should not have forked tips, nor should they have leaves attached, according to one who knows the rules.
Likewise:
"When the object as described is not available, that which resembles it should be accepted,
just as wheat [is accepted] in place of barley, or rice in place of paddy."
When no specific substance is prescribed for oblations, clarified butter (ājya) is ordained as the material;
and when no mantra or deity is specified, Prajāpati is the established rule.

"In the absence of instruction" means in the absence of a specific prescription. When there is no instruction regarding either the deity or the mantra, Prajāpati is the deity and the mantra belongs to Prajāpati; this applies to the *vyāhṛtis* taken as a whole. However, where a deity is mentioned but no mantra exists, there the "root-mantra" (*mūlamantra*) should be understood.
And that has been stated in the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:
"O best of beings, it begins with the *praṇava*, ends with 'namas', and is in the dative case."
The deity's own name is proclaimed to be the root mantra.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"In the absence of curd, milk should be used; likewise, in the absence of honey, jaggery.
O King, one may substitute either milk or curd for clarified butter."

Paiṭhīnasi states: "One should provide a substitute based on similarity in regard to stalks, roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, sprouts, juices, fragrances, and so forth; in the absence of all these, barley becomes the substitute. [This is found] in the Maitrāyaṇīyapariśiṣṭa.

In the absence of *darbha* grass, *kāśa* grass is the substitute. For sacrificial fuel (*idhma*), the wood of *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, *khadira*, *rohitaka*, and *udumbara* is used; in their absence, the wood of all forest trees may be used, with the exception of *tilaka*, *nīpa*, *nimba*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *śālmali*, *nyagrodha*, *lūka*, *kapittha*, *kovidāra*, *vibhītaka*, *śleṣmātaka*, and all thorny trees. Ghee is the substitute for other [clarified] substances; in its absence, curd or milk may be used.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the pavilion and so forth.
Now, regarding the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*:
Śātātapa says,
"One should not perform any Vedic rite without having first performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛ-yajña*)."
Even there, the mothers must first be worshipped with diligent effort.
If one performs the Vedic rite without first performing the Mātṛ-yāga,
the Mothers, possessed by wrath, will surely seek to cause him harm.
The groups of Mothers (Mātṛgaṇas) are described in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa as follows:
Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā, Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā, Mātā, and the other Lokamātṛkās.
Hṛṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi, along with Ātmadevatā,
should be worshipped in a painting or in an image, bestowing boons, fearlessness, and life.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "At the marriages of daughters and sons, upon entering a new house, during auspicious rites for children such as the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākarma), and so forth."
At the parting of the hair ceremony and upon seeing the face of a son or other offspring,
the self-restrained householder should first gratify the Nāndīmukha ancestors.
Jābāla says:

One should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* on occasions of sacrifice, marriage, consecration, the binding and unbinding of the lock of hair (*mekhalā*), the birth of a son, and the ritual release of a bull.

Therefore, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* should be performed in connection with Vedic *homa*-subsidiaries such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and others, as well as in those final rites (*antyeṣṭi*) specified by particular scriptural injunctions. Likewise, even for the *tulāpuruṣa* and similar rites, because they are designated as sacrifices (*yāga*), and because in all the mantras for the invocation of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) there is the use of expressions such as "protect my *adhvara*" and "guard the sacrifice," these must be permeated by the characteristics of a sacrifice despite their being essentially gifts; thus, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* must be performed there as well. In this very same way, it should be understood to apply to rites involving oblations (*sahomaka*), such as the *dhānyaparvata* and others.
Kātyāyana states the procedure for that.

In rites for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), the ritual procedure is performed from left to right (*pradakṣiṇa*); it takes place in the forenoon; the recitation of mantras is omitted except at the joints of the year (*parvan*); the *darbha* grass is straight; barley serves the purpose of sesame seeds; the question regarding satisfaction is "Is it well-prepared?"; being permitted with "It is very well-prepared," the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) are mixed with curd, jujube fruits, and unbroken rice; he asks, "I shall cause the Nāndīmukha ancestors to pronounce [the benediction]," and being permitted with "Let it be pronounced," he asks, "I shall invoke the Nāndīmukha ancestors," and being permitted with "Invoke them," he says, "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased," substituting this for the formula "May they find inexhaustible [satisfaction]" (*akṣayya-sthāne*). He should say, "May the Nāndīmukha fathers, grandfathers, mothers, and maternal grandfathers be pleased. He should not employ the word *svadhā*. He should feed an even number of guests. Thus it is said.

[142] This has been explained by the preceding statement. In the *Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "A wise man should perform the rite of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water-libations for the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors through the *Prājāpatya* *tīrtha*, and whatever else may be produced [thereby]."
Now, regarding the honey-mixture (madhuparka),
Jābāla says:
[It should be offered] to one who has come to the house for a wedding, to a sacrificial priest, and to a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya).
One should honor a *snātaka* with the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) upon his arrival at the house.
Viśvāmitra says:
One should have the officiating priests perform the ritual after honoring them with the honey-mixture (madhuparka);
if one has them perform the ritual without honoring them, one is joined with nothing but sin.

The procedure for this is found in the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*: "There are six persons worthy of the *arghya* offering: the teacher (*ācārya*), the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the bridegroom (*vaivāhya*), the king, a dear friend, and one who has completed his Vedic studies (*snātaka*). They should honor them every year; the officiating priests are those who perform the sacrifice. Having had a seat brought forward, he says: 'I shall honor you, O venerable ones, because of your virtuous nature. They bring forth a seat (*viṣṭara*), water for washing the feet (*pādya*), water for the feet (*pādārghya*), water for the *arghya* offering (*udakam argham*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) consisting of curds, honey, and ghee in a bronze vessel. Another person, using a bronze ladle, announces three times each the items beginning with the seat. He accepts the seat, saying: 'I am the roof of my peers, rising like the sun.'"

"I step upon this [seat] so that no one may harm me. With these words, he sits down upon it. Another person, sitting on a seat of grass (*viṣṭara*), washes his left foot; then, for one who is seated, he washes the right foot. If he is a Brāhmaṇa, he washes the right foot first. "I partake in the milking of Virāj; may I obtain the milking of Virāj through the water for the feet (*pādya*). With these words, he accepts the *arghya* offering. "O Waters, through you may I attain all desires"—with these words, while pouring them out, he consecrates them. "I send you to the ocean; go to your own source."

"May our heroes be unharmed; may the waters flow toward us with milk"—with these words he sips water. "O Āma, come to me with rawness; unite me with cooked food and with luster; make me dear to my subjects, a lord of cattle, and unharmed in my limbs"—with this mantra, [saying] "By the power of thee," he awaits the *madhuparka*. With "By the power of the god," he receives it. Having placed it in his joined hands, he stirs it three times with the ring finger of his right hand, saying: "Homage to Syāvāśva, the son of Aśvya! Whatever has been pierced by the stone, that I remove from thee. And with the ring finger and thumb, he sprinkles it out three times. He eats of it three times, saying: "That which is the honeyed, supreme form of honey, the essence of food—with that honeyed, supreme form, the essence of food, may I become supreme, honeyed, and an eater of food. Or, having recited verses containing the word "honey" for each, he should give the remains to his son or a resident pupil sitting nearby. Or he may eat it all. Or, before the movement [of the guests], he should lead it away. Having sipped water, he touches his vital organs: "Speech in my mouth; breath in my nostrils; sight in my eyes; hearing in my ears; strength in my arms; vigor in my thighs; may my limbs be unharmed; may my body be firm. To one who has sipped water, he says: "We shall praise this gift-cow. He replies three times: "She is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, the navel of immortality. I have declared this to the wise person: do not strike me, O sinless one; let the sin of such-and-such a person be struck down. If he intends to sacrifice her, he says: "The sin of both me and such-and-such a person is struck down; release her to eat grass. But he should never let her go if she is barren. Regarding the *dadhiyajña* (curd-sacrifice) at a wedding, he should simply say: "Perform the sacrifice. Even if he does not sacrifice with *soma* throughout the year, they should perform the sacrifice for him only after the *arghya* reception has been performed, according to the *śruti*: "They should sacrifice for him only when the *arghya* has been offered, not when it has not been offered."

The meaning of this is as follows: the section ending with "the seat should be brought" is easy to understand. "May you be gracious," and so forth, is the formal invitation (*adhyeṣaṇa*) regarding the *arghya* offering. They bring the *arghya* related to the ancestors; the plural number is used with reference to the male ancestors. It is made from twenty-five *kuśa* blades, with the tips cut off and arranged in the form of a seat (*viṣṭara*).
Thus it is stated in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
"With how many [blades] is the *brahman* [seat] formed, and with how many is the *viṣṭara* considered to be?"
A *brahmāsana* consists of five or six [seats], while a *viṣṭara* consists of half that number.
[144] Brahmā has upward-pointing hair, while Viṣṭara has hanging hair;
Brahmā has a clockwise curl, while Viṣṭara has a counter-clockwise curl.

The first *viṣṭara* (seat-grass) is for the purpose of sitting. Regarding "the foot-water" (*pādya*), this refers to the second *viṣṭara*, which is the water for washing the feet (*pādārghya*). The water for the feet (*pādārgha*) should be pleasantly warm. The term *argha* has already been explained. The water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) is likewise water; the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) consists of curd, honey, and ghee, placed in a bronze vessel and covered by that same [vessel]. Except for the one who offers the *argha* and the one who receives it from the paternal uncle, another person recites the words for the *viṣṭara* and so forth three times each: "The *viṣṭara*, the *viṣṭara*, the *viṣṭara*—let it be accepted. As for the *argha*, however, having silently accepted the *viṣṭara*, he sits upon it with the mantra, "I am the height" (*varṣma asmi*). Regarding "another for the two feet," this is superseded by the water for the feet (*pādārgha*).

And then, after the washing of the feet, there is the offering of a second seat (*viṣṭara*). Accordingly, the subsequent sūtra states: "Having sat upon the seat, having washed the left foot, he washes the right foot. Thus, the washing of the feet for one sitting on a single seat is taught. If the guest is a Brāhmaṇa, then he should wash the right foot first. Taking water with the mantra, "Thou art the milking of Virāj," he washes [the feet] while he himself is the recipient of the *arghya*. He accepts the *arghya* with the mantra, "O Waters, you are..."; while pouring out the *arghya* water, he mutters, "Thee as the ocean..."; he sips water with the mantra, "Sipping for Mitra..."; and he looks at the *madhuparka* with the mantra, "For the sake of Mitra...". He accepts the *madhuparka* with the mantra, "Thee for the sake of the god...". In all these cases, another person announces each of these substances three times and says, "May it be accepted."

Then the *arghya* priest, holding the vessel of *madhuparka* in his right hand, stirs the *madhuparka* three times with the ring finger of that same hand while reciting the mantra "namaḥ syāva. The meaning is that he mixes it. [145] And with the ring finger and thumb, he silently sprinkles it three times; the meaning is that he pours it out. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), he also stirs it. Consequently, for each guest, the sprinkling is performed in this manner; and since the sprinkling intervenes, it is established that the stirring must be performed three times accompanied by the mantra.

One should consume the *madhuparka* three times with verses containing the word "madhu," such as "yan madhunaḥ. For there is a traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating, "In the case of the *madhuparka* and in the case of *soma*, one does not become impure by leavings"; thus, the recitation of the mantra occurs while one is still in a state of having leavings. Then, having sipped water (*ācamya*), while touching the seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇāyatana*) with the mantras beginning with "vāṅ ma āsyè," the word "asti" (it exists) is supplied here because of the syntactic expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*). And the word "saḥ" (he/that) is to be supplied as an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) everywhere.

"May my limbs and body be unharmed"—the word "be" (*santu*) is to be supplied here. Having taken up water for rinsing and having taken the sacrificial knife (*śāsa*), he says three times, "A cow! Some say that because of the mention of "having taken up water for rinsing," there must be a further rinsing of the mouth. Others, however, say: "He by whom water has been sipped is 'one who has taken up water for rinsing' (*ācāntodaka*); the taking up of the weapon is for his sake. And this purposefulness belongs to the immolation of the animal, since it is for that purpose; and this must be spoken by the one offering the *arghya*. Thereupon, the recipient of the *arghya* should respond with the mantra: "The mother of the Rudras... and so forth.

And the name of the person being honored (*arghyayitṛ*) is to be mentioned with the word *amuṣyai*. If one were to seize [the victim], the formula is: "I cause the evil of such-and-such a person to be slain. Now, if one wishes to release it, one should say: "Release the evil of both me and such-and-such a person; let it eat grass! Here too, there is the mention of the name of the person being honored. One should say: "Om, release it; let it eat grass! This is a *nigada* (liturgical recitation). However, that honor (*argha*) should not be for oneself alone; one should say, "He performs this for the sake of the sacrifice and for the sake of the marriage," and the rest is easy to understand. Now follows the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*). Thus says the *Vedanyāsa*.

Having honored them with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, one should cause the Brahmins to pronounce auspicious blessings during rites of dharma, on auspicious occasions, in battle, or upon witnessing a marvel.
Yama: The recitation for the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in rites for the gods;
one should perform this very same rite without the syllable *oṃ* for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.

Kaśyapa says: "In worldly rites for prosperity (*bhūtikarma*), there should indeed be such sentences as 'May it be an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and well-prosperous'. By "rites for prosperity" is meant those acts that bring about success, such as the recitation of benedictions (*svastivācana*) and so forth. These [sentences] begin with the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). The recitation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) is described in the *Bahvṛcapariśiṣṭa*.

Having placed his joined palms, resembling lotus buds, upon his head with the knees touching the ground, and holding a golden pitcher filled with water in his right hand, he should say: "By this measure of longevity—the long-lived Nagas, rivers, mountains, and the three steps of Viṣṇu—may there be a holy day; may there be long life! May the waters be auspicious! May there be well-being! May there be safety and freedom from misfortune! May the perfumes protect you; may there be auspiciousness! May the flowers protect you; may there be prosperity! May the unbroken grains (akṣata) protect you; may there be longevity! May the betel-leaves protect you; may there be sovereignty! May the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) protect you; may there be health! May there be long life, peace, nourishment, contentment, fame, glory, learning, humility, wealth, many sons, and a long lifespan! I, having been authorized by you who have granted permission, shall recite the auspicious benedictions of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, beginning with the syllable *Oṃ* and following the tradition of many sages, for the sake of this meritorious and holy day (*puṇyāha*). Let it be recited! 'May the Giver of Wealth grant wealth! 'Savitṛ is behind him. 'He becomes ever new as he is born. 'Those who give sacrificial fees stand high in heaven. These verses one should recite on a holy day. Let the minds of all the Brāhmaṇas, distinguished by their vows, observances, austerities, Vedic study, self-restraint, and charity, be composed. [147] Our minds are composed. May you be gracious; we are pleased. May there be peace! May there be nourishment! May there be contentment! May there be growth! May there be no obstacle! May there be longevity! May there be health! May the rite be auspicious! May there be success in the rite! May there be abundance of sons! May there be abundance of wealth and grain! May there be the attainment of what is desired! May there be the removal of what is undesired! May whatever is evil be warded off! May whatever is good prevail! May there be no obstacle in the subsequent rites! May there be daily increase in prosperity higher and higher! May the subsequent actions be successful and auspicious! May there be the excellence of the lunar day, the *karana*, the hour (*muhūrta*), and the asterism (*nakṣatra*)! May the presiding deities of the lunar day, the *karana*, the hour, the asterism, the planets, and the ascendant be pleased! May the lunar day, the *karana*, the hour, the asterism, along with its planet and deity, be pleased! May Durgā and Pāñcālī be pleased! May the Viśvedevas, led by Agni, be pleased! May the hosts of Maruts, led by Indra, be pleased! May the hosts of sages, led by Vasiṣṭha, be pleased! May the Mothers, led by Maheśvara and Umā, be pleased! May the faithful wives, led by Arundhatī, be pleased! May all the gods, led by Viṣṇu, be pleased! May all the Vedas, led by Brahmā, be pleased!"

May Brahmā and the Brāhmaṇas be pleased; may the Sarasvatīs be pleased; may Faith and Intelligence be pleased; may the Blessed Kātyāyanī be pleased; may the Blessed Māheśvarī be pleased; may the Blessed Ṛddhikarī be pleased; may the Blessed Vṛddhikarī be pleased; may the Blessed Puṣṭikarī be pleased; may the Blessed Tuṣṭikarī be pleased; may the two Lords Vighna and Vināyaka be pleased; may all the family deities be pleased; may all the village deities be pleased; and may those who hate the Vedas be destroyed.

Slain are the enemies; slain are the adversaries; slain are those who create obstacles; slain are those who cause impediments. May our foes meet with defeat. May the terrible things be pacified; may sins be pacified; may calamities be pacified. May auspicious things increase. May the waters be auspicious; may the seasons be auspicious; may the fires be auspicious; may the oblations be auspicious; may the trees be auspicious; may the waters be auspicious. May day and night be auspicious for us. At our desire, at our desire, may Parjanya rain down upon us. May our plants bear fruit and ripen; may our security and prosperity be established. May all the planets—Venus, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—along with the Moon and preceded by the Sun, be pleased. May the Blessed Nārāyaṇa be pleased; may the Blessed Parjanya be pleased; may the Blessed Lord Mahāsena be pleased. I shall proclaim the hour of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). Let it be proclaimed! Like a Udgātṛ priest, O Śakuni, you sing the Sāman; he sacrifices with the *Yājyā*. Speak of whichever asterism is auspicious. One should perform [the rite] when the sun rises until the last star has vanished from sight. As far as the sun travels there where one can still see the final star, so far should one act. Whatever one intends to do, if one acts thus on an auspicious day, it is accomplished. Those which are the Yama-asterisms are indeed the Deva-asterisms; one should perform [the rite] under them. Whatever one intends to do, if one acts thus on an auspicious day, it is accomplished. "May you, sirs, declare the auspicious day! "Om, the auspicious day! We invoke Vāyu for well-being; we invoke the risen Āditya. May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya of unbroken wheel grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.

The eight divine Vasus are worthy of Soma; the four goddesses are most renowned through the dustless realm. May they protect the sacrifice from the east of the mid-region, [granting] the year-long immortality and well-being.

"May you say 'Svasti'! May there be well-being for the long-lived one! May we prosper through the *stoma*; may we prosper through all prosperity; may we prosper through oblations. Having approached the divine Mitra with the *nabhas* [offering], and increasing our friendship through the *anūrādhā* oblation, may we live a hundred autumns, united with our kin. Indeed, there are three prosperities of the gods: the three meters, the three pressings, and these three worlds. Through this very power, he becomes firmly established in these worlds. May you say 'Prosperity'! May there be prosperity! Born for glory, may he go toward glory—he in whom the Brahman won all this, both that world and this one. May that constellation Abhijit, having conquered all, bestow glory upon us. Protect my mantra, which has its root in the dawn and its foundation in the unassailable—the Yajus, the Riks, and the Samans, which the seers who know the triple Veda know. For that is the immortal glory. 'May there be glory,' let the venerable ones say; 'May there be glory! May there be the prosperity of an auspicious day! May the Blessed Lord Prajapati be pleased!"

Thus ends the section on technical definitions (*paribhāṣā-prakaraṇa*) in the *Dānakhaṇḍa* (Section on Gifts) of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the sovereign over all faculties, a master of all branches of knowledge, and the illustrious Great King of Kings, the venerable Mahādeva.
[150] The Fourth Chapter: Now, the Fruits of Giving.
By means of his conduct, he brought his twice-born lineage to a state of enviable excellence;
by various collections of virtues, he established the fame of his family as pervading all paths;
and by means of Mīmāṃsā and prosody, he manifested that certain supreme splendor.
By which [the donor] is made to appear like oneself in the greatness of giving that bestows lofty fruits.
He who, such as Hemādri, always praises Śiva as proclaimed in the scriptures on all forms of giving,
has today declared the fruit of giving as proclaimed in the scriptures on all forms of giving.

In that regard, the Sāmaveda Upaniṣad states: "Through giving, one obtains all desires; through celibacy, one attains long life, beauty, and non-violence; through eating leaves, one reaches heaven; by eating only fallen fruit, one becomes twice-born; by the vīrāsana posture, one gains wealth; and through service to father, mother, and teacher, as well as meditation, one becomes fit for heaven; and by the gift of gold, one likewise attains heaven. Thus says the Blessed Ṛgveda.
"High in heaven abide those who give sacrificial fees; those who give horses dwell with the sun.
Those who give gold partake in immortality; those who give clothing, O Soma, prolong their lives. Thus says Hārīta.

By giving water, one conquers thirst and redeems oneself. By the gift of food, one redeems the vital breaths (*asūn*); one becomes possessed of food, an eater of food, and a lord of food. By the gift of clothing, one redeems speech; one becomes handsome, unclothed no longer, and a possessor of garments. By the gift of gold, one redeems splendor; one becomes radiant, illustrious, and a possessor of gold. By the gift of a cow, one redeems speech; one becomes eloquent, free from sin, and a possessor of cattle. By the gift of an ox, one redeems the vital breaths (*prāṇān*); one becomes free from disease, strong, and a possessor of draft-animals. By the gift of a chariot, one redeems the body; one becomes a possessor of servants and various celestial vehicles (*vimāna*). By the gift of a bed, one redeems happiness; one becomes a possessor of the various pleasures of travel, sleep, and seating, as well as prosperity. By the gift of an immeasurable amount, one nourishes immeasurable satisfaction and attains immeasurable desires.

That gift is of two kinds: the unknown gift (*avijñāta-dāna*) and the known gift (*vijñāta-dāna*). That which one gives to an ignorant person is the unknown gift. Now, that which one gives and receives from a learned fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*) who is receiving the *vaiśvānara* [initiation] is the known gift. This is also stated in the *Yajus*: "To whom has this been given? The meaning is that one ransoms oneself; one gives nothing but oneself. In this manner, the giving of water and so forth is indeed praised. Viṣṇu:

By the gift of vessels made of refined metal (*taijasa*), one becomes a recipient of all desires; by the gift of honey, ghee, and oil, as well as by the gift of medicine, one attains health; by the gift of grain, as well as by the gift of crops, one attains contentment; by the gift of fuel, one’s fire becomes radiant and one achieves readiness in battle; by the gift of a seat, one obtains a high station; by the gift of a bed, a wife; by the gift of sandals, a chariot yoked with mules; by the gift of land, heaven; by the gift of fans with handles of *lātā* wood, freedom from suffering; by the gift of flowers, one becomes superior; and by the gift of unguents, one becomes possessed of fame. [ViDh 92.15–30]
Manu said:
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision.
The giver of land obtains everything; the giver of gold, long life;
the giver of a house, excellent dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.
The giver of clothing attains the world of the Candas; the giver of horses, the world of the Aśvins;
the giver of an ox, abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow, the realm of the Sun.
The giver of a vehicle and a bed obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty;
the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahman.
"Brahmasārṣṭitā" means having a state equal to that of Brahmā; "brahmasamānagati" means having a destiny identical to that of Brahmā. Yājñavalkya says:
"By giving land, lamps, horses, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, clarified butter, shelter, a wedding gift, gold, and draft-animals, one is glorified in heaven."
By giving a house, grain, fearlessness, sandals, an umbrella,
garlands, ointments, a vehicle, a tree, prosperity, or a bed, one shall become supremely happy.

Providing shelter for travelers, providing a dwelling, and providing materials for the purpose of marriage; likewise, massaging those who are weary, attending to the sick, worshiping the gods, washing the feet of others, and clearing away the remnants of food from twice-born men— these are equal to the gift of a cow.
Yama said: Having given shelter in this world, and likewise having granted fearlessness,
as well as having given land to a Brahmin, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
The giver of an umbrella obtains a house; likewise, the giver of a house obtains a city. Similarly, by the gift of sandals, one obtains an unsurpassed chariot.
By the offering of fuel, a fire blazes forth upon the earth;
by the gift of a cow-station, one is liberated from all sins.
The giver of gold obtains everything; the giver of silver, supreme beauty; the giver of clothing, the same world as the moon; and the giver of a horse, the same world as the sun.
Having given royal regalia and various jewels,
and likewise having given a city, one becomes a king upon the earth.
Likewise:
removing the garlands from the deity, sweeping the temple,
performing worship, and clearing away the remnants of the food eaten by the Brahmins.
Having provided the washing of the feet and rendered service,
she likewise offered anointing of the feet and massaged him when he was weary.
Scratching the cows, giving them fodder, and saluting them;
likewise, the offering of alms and lamps, as well as the honoring of guests.
Yama declares that the fruit of each one of these is equal to the gift of a cow for him who,
having gathered together the necessary materials, bestows them upon the Brahmins.
I am not able to describe his worlds earned through merit.

The "provision" refers to the materials required for sacrifices, marriages, and other such rites. One should always remain filled with joy after giving fruits, roots, drinks, various kinds of vegetables, and vehicles to the Brahmins.
Likewise: One who gives grain and water, and one who gives clarified butter, enjoys happiness;
and one should give sandals, beds, and seats to the Brahmins.
And having bestowed various kinds of gifts, one shall become a king.
Likewise: "One who gives food shall become prosperous, well-satisfied, and also renowned;
so too one who gives oil, *āmalaka* fruit, and likewise foot-massage."
A man becomes well-satisfied, radiant, and indeed possessed of happiness.
Likewise:
by giving earth, cow dung, darbha grass, and an upper garment to a virtuous brahmin, one will be born into an excellent family.
He who provides a pleasant dwelling and even a tooth-stick shall become pure, of noble birth, eloquent, and always happy.
He who provides the washing of the feet, as well as a vehicle, and the cleansing of the anus and genitals to a Brahmin, shall always remain pure and purified.
He who gives fragrant herbs, anointing oil, honey, and likewise salt to a Brahmin truly obtains good fortune.
Atri says:
One who gives food during a famine, one who gives gold when there is plenty,
and one who gives water in the wilderness, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Devala says: One who gives food to the weary ascends to heaven by means of a celestial chariot;
one who provides medical treatment for the sick obtains the merit of ten gifts of cows.
By washing the feet of a Brahmin, one obtains the merit arising from the gift of a cow;
likewise by offering sandalwood paste, a palm-leaf fan, fruits, and flowers.
By giving betel, a seat, and a bed, one becomes exceedingly happy.
Kātyāyana says: They should be especially honored by the best of the twice-born with massages for the feet and head, with gifts, honors, worship, and the like, and particularly with pleasant words.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Those who give gifts of sandalwood, conch shells,
and pearls rescue even their ancestors who have committed sins, according to the sacred revelation."
In the Mahābhārata:
By giving a female slave, a male slave, ornaments, fields, houses,
and a daughter as a *brahmadeya* (a gift to a Brahmin), one attains heaven without doubt.
And the man who offers oblations and flowers attains the auspicious state.
Likewise,
by the gift of draft-oxen, as well as by horses—
A man attains the worlds of the Vasus by the gift of an umbrella;
likewise, by the gift of sandals, he obtains an excellent house and a vehicle.
By the gift of clothing, the fruit is a beautiful form; by the gift of perfume, a man shall become fragrant. One who gives alms-food, drink, and flavorful substances [attains these fruits].
And he obtains all flavors to his heart's content.
The giver of shelter and clothing obtains those very things; there is no doubt in this matter—
[as well as] garlands, incense, perfumes, and ointments.
The man who [offers] baths and garlands...
He who gives [these] to the twice-born shall become free from disease and likewise endowed with a beautiful form in the world of kings.
Likewise:
"The man who bestows sandalwood, agallochum, and incense upon Brahmins,
as well as betel and garlands, shall proceed to heaven."
Giving sesame seeds, water, lamps, food, and shelter, as well as these pleasant and truthful words— these are the deeds of the virtuous who desire heaven.
One who bestows consolation attains everything and is liberated from all sorrows;
by the gift of objects for sight, one finds memory and intelligence.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Those who are givers of the treatises on Dharma, those who are devoted to the giving of sacrificial sessions (satra),
and those who provide gifts such as sacred fords, ponds, wells, boats, and bridges;"
He who carries others on his shoulders across [a river], he who gives water to those afflicted by thirst,
he who bestows irrigated fields, and he who gives fruit-bearing trees;
Sixty thousand crores and three arbudas of them indeed sport in the city of heaven; this, O best of the twice-born, has been told.
Likewise:
"He who, being well-restrained, gives as a gift to Brahmins either a horse, or a draft animal, or even beautiful sandals."
For him, there shall be divine vehicles— chariots adorned with banners and flags—
and no difficult path whatsoever shall exist here for him in any way.
[156] Food, drink, horses, cattle, clothing, umbrellas, beds, and seats—
these eight gifts are especially praised in the world of the pretas.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"By giving clothing, water, and a sacred thread to a Śiva-yogin,
one attains great enjoyment and, in the end, eternal yoga."
He who gives a seat, a bed, or a vehicle to one who is illustrious,
and who is equal toward all beings— for him no suffering exists.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "One should daily offer, for his sake, anointing oil, fuel, water, as well as a bed and a seat, and even the daily fodder for a cow."
One should offer food to the embodied beings for their sake;
or rather, what is the use of much talk? Whatever good deed is performed on this earth [is for them].
Performing it even as a mere play, one attains that auspicious state by aiming for Śiva.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "Wealth such as land, gold, cows, grain, sesame, clothing, ghee,
and so forth [is attained] through ritual procedure, fasting, and eating only a single meal at night."
One who gives, being pure, purified in heart, patient, and observant of vows of truth and so forth,
shall deliver even the giver of a gift as small as a mustard seed.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Furthermore, Keśava becomes pleased by the gift of food and the gift of land;
the Moon becomes pleased by molasses, milk, ghee, and garments."
Through the gift of water, Varuṇa shall always be well-pleased;
and through the gift of silver, Maheśvara shall be gratified.
By the gift of gold, Agni is eternally pleased;
likewise, Maghavan is pleased by gifts of elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, and seats.
Yama [is honored] with beds and dwellings, the Sun with the thread of dharma, Yama with sandals, the Cow with cattle, and the Tressed One (Śiva) with matted locks.
By the gift of two sandals, Padmayoni is highly pleased;
likewise, Pārvatī, the Mother of the World, is pleased by ornaments and marks of honor.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who gives a milch cow, along with a buffalo, both adorned and provided with vessels of bell-metal,
clothing, and other gifts, obtains all his desires."
In the Saura Purāṇa:
"A black antelope skin, a buffalo, a ram, and ten cows,
as well as the Tulāpuruṣa [gift], bestow the world of Brahmā."
In the Vahni Purāṇa:
"O Sage, those who are always devoted to what is sinless give vehicles, horses, oxen, gold, silver, gems, and sesame seeds."
For them, a terrifying path never arises at any time.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, Haṃsa said:
"O best of Brahmins, by the gift of a seat, a man avoids being censured everywhere; and by the gift of a bed, he obtains a wife."
By giving a well-spread bed with an upper cover to a twice-born man,
one attains birth in a great family, endowed with beauty and wealth.
Likewise, one obtains a wife who has brothers and is submissive;
by this very gift of food, a wife may obtain a husband.
By the gift of a canopy, one is liberated from all sins;
likewise, O Brahmin, by the gift of an umbrella—of this there is no need for deliberation.
Having given an umbrella with a hundred ribs to ward off rain and sun,
one who is liberated from all sins is honored in the heavenly world.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born,
by giving a pair of sandals provided with smooth oil, one proceeds happily along the southern path.
He ascends to the third heaven in a chariot yoked with mules;
liberated from all evil, he shall travel happily along the path of Yama.
By the gift of a palm-leaf fan, one is liberated from all sins;
likewise, by the gift of a chowrie, one is released from all sufferings.
By the gift of sandals, one attains an auspicious state;
by the gift of a footstool, one finds a place everywhere.
By giving a staff to a twice-born man, one obtains the very same merit as bathing;
by the gift of a sacred thread, one obtains the fruit of the gift of clothing.
Thus has this fruit of the gift of an *uṣṇīṣa* been proclaimed;
by the gift of a tooth-stick, one shall obtain great good fortune.
By the gift of clay, one becomes pure in all circumstances;
by giving water for ritual bathing and purification, one is born free from disease.
One who always provides oil for anointing attains the destruction of disease;
likewise, through the gift of medicine, one experiences the destruction of disease.
By giving fragrant bathing powders, one enjoys good fortune;
by the gift of ointments, one is born handsome.
He who bestows upon a Brahmin the supreme brilliance of bodily radiance and the splendor of his limbs for the sake of accomplishing [his goals], [attains great merit].
He attains the same world as Agni and achieves the destruction of his enemies,
by giving metallic vessels along with salt.
For one who offers vessels made of refined metal filled with oil,
supreme health is proclaimed, as well as supreme beauty.
Likewise: One who gives conch shells and other items produced from the ocean becomes a vessel for all desires and for glory; of this there is no doubt.
By the gift of a comb, one releases oneself from supreme affliction;
likewise, the gift of a bed is the supreme means for bathing in the worlds.
By giving unguents and garlands, one attains supreme prosperity.
Likewise: "O best of the twice-born, it is said that for that man who properly presents a palanquin for human transport to a brahmin, he obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice."
By the gift of a palanquin, one obtains the fruit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice;
he who provides a warrior goes to the same world as Śakra.
But for him who bestows a female slave who performs manual labor upon a Brāhmaṇa,
the worlds of the Vasus are said to be easily attained.
But he who gives away a young maidservant endowed with beauty sports and rejoices in the forest, filled with joy, together with the Apsarases.
O twice-born ones, he who gives even a camel or a donkey reaches Alakā and rejoices together with the lords of the Yakṣas.
The gift of a horse is declared to be the best among all gifts;
likewise, the gift of a mare is remembered as yielding abundant fruit.
Those who bestow horses go to the world of the Sun for as many hundreds of years as there are hairs upon them.
By giving a white horse, the fruit shall be tenfold.
Just as a tawny cow is most excellent, so too is a white horse.
For one who gives a well-bred horse adorned with ornaments, [the merit is immense].
It is declared to have the merit of a white lotus; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
It is yoked with four horses and provided with all necessary equipment.
By giving a chariot to a twice-born man, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
by properly bestowing a female elephant, O Lord, one obtains this same fruit.
By the gift of an elephant, a man who has descended from heaven becomes a king in this world,
endowed with fame and valor.
O twice-born ones, by giving a golden-girthed elephant to a Brahmin,
one undoubtedly obtains the fruit of both the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
By giving a chariot yoked with four elephants to a twice-born man,
one undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a gift of the entire earth.
Likewise: "A man who, having purchased a tawny cow according to the prescribed rite, gives it away,
becomes enriched with all his desires and enjoys the fruit of sacrifice."
One attains the world of the cows and uplifts one's own lineage;
furthermore, by giving a buffalo, one attains the world of Varuṇa.
By giving away that adorned goat, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow;
by giving away an adorned she-goat, one is glorified in the world of Vahni.
By giving a goat according to the prescribed rite, a man attains that very world;
by the gift of a buffalo, he is glorified in the world of Yama.
O best of kings, by giving a jewel one attains the world of Varuṇa;
likewise, by the gift of a grindstone, one enjoys that very same fruit.
By the gift of wild animals, one is glorified in the world of Vāyu;
this very fruit has been declared for the giving of birds as well.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Whatever is most excellent in the world and whatever is dear to oneself—
all that should be given to the ancestors by one who desires for them imperishable [merit]."
The giver of food obtains an imperishable, divine celestial chariot, resplendent like the sun, filled with divine apsarases, and made of the sound of singing and dancing.
He who gives a new, unwashed garment during the performance of a śrāddha rite obtains long life, radiance, sovereignty, and auspicious beauty.
He who gives a sacred thread and sandals during the performance of a śrāddha rite obtains a splendid vehicle as well as comfort for his feet.
By giving a fan and a palm-leaf whisk to a Brahmin with due honor,
one shall obtain a comfortable bed provided with a couch.
By always giving sandals to Brahmins during Śrāddha ceremonies on the ground,
he obtains divine vision as well as a chariot yoked with horses.
An excellent, stainless parasol, adorned with garlands of flowers,
having become a supreme palace, follows after him as he goes.
Having given a shelter filled with jewels, along with beds, seats, and vessels,
to the ancestors during a śrāddha ceremony, one is glorified in the vault of heaven.
He who gives at a Śrāddha vessels filled with pearls, lapis lazuli, garments, and various kinds of gems, as well as with salts;
The flavors, as well as longevity and good fortune,
attend upon him who gives a pleasing vessel made of metal during the performance of a śrāddha rite.
A vessel made of silver or gold becomes a receptacle for desires, sacred knowledges, and wealth; one should indeed give such vessels at the performance of a śrāddha rite.

The donor who gives a cow at the ancestral rites (śrāddha)— one that has calved for the first time and yields a jar of milk at each milking— obtains abundance, as well as the power of irresistible will and wealth.
Cows attend upon him, as do the prosperity of cattle;
likewise, there are fragrant, diverse, and sweet-smelling unguents for bathing.
Having honored the vessels at the śrāddha, one should respectfully cause them to be given;
[thereby one obtains] rivers that carry fragrances, great rivers, and various pleasures.
Those who are devoted to their husbands purify the giver;
beds, seats, vehicles, grounds, and carriages attend upon him.
Givers attend upon him, and thus he is glorified in heaven;
he who gives these things at śrāddha ceremonies shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having honored vessels filled with clarified butter at a Śrāddha ceremony, one should cause them to be given;
[the donor] obtains the merit of a thousand cows that yield milk from jars.
By giving beautiful dwellings, one partakes in half the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
likewise, by giving [a bed] fully adorned with ornaments, provided with pillows, and well-decorated.
By giving various kinds of beds, a twice-born man becomes a partaker of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
likewise, by giving female and male slaves, as well as camels, goats, and sheep.
By constantly providing elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles at the performance of faithful rites,
and by giving various kinds of sesame seeds, one obtains imperishable fruit.
One who is intent on the rites for the ancestors, performing meritorious deeds with auspicious rice,
and having offered thick flowers along with fruit, attains a beautiful state.
Having given wells, groves, tanks, fields, wives, and houses,
one rejoices in heaven eternally as long as the moon and stars endure.
By giving a well-spread bed adorned with jewels at a Śrāddha ceremony,
his ancestors are pleased, and he enjoys infinite bliss in heaven.
Likewise, there is cloth made of silk, woven cotton, and a woolen blanket;
also a deerskin from the Ruru deer, which is purifying and made from the hair of wild animals.
Having given these to the Brahmins and having fed them according to the rule,
the faithful man obtains the fruit that belongs to the horse sacrifice.
[163] He who gives these at the *śrāddha* ceremonies— silk, linen, fine cotton cloth, and likewise unwashed cloth— attains unsurpassed desires.
He who offers cooked foods, rice-mash, sweetmeats, clarified butter, sugar, *kuśarā*, honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), milk, milk-porridge (*pāyasa*),
and smooth, warm food, shall obtain the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
In the Mahābhārata: "Those men who give clothing and ornaments, as well as those who provide food, drink, and alms, and those who provide sustenance for their families, go to heaven."
Those men who provide for a thousand, likewise those who give to a thousand,
and those who are protectors of thousands, go to heaven.
O bull of the Bharatas, those men who are givers of gold and cows,
and who are bestowers of vehicles, go to heaven.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those men who provide wedding swings, spectacles,
and garments are destined for heaven.
Those men who provide monasteries, dwellings, gardens, wells, parks, and excellent gifts, as well as those who establish water-stations, go to heaven.
Those men by whose act [others] are delivered from falling, as well as from affliction, poverty, and the assault of disease, go to heaven.
O Bhārata, those men who take what has been earned through service and austerities,
and who are free from attachment to receiving gifts, go to heaven.
Those men who have desisted from all violence, who are patient with everything,
and who have become a refuge for all, go to heaven.
O Bhārata, those men who are wealthy, powerful, and in the prime of youth,
yet remain wise and have conquered their senses— they are the ones who go to heaven.
In the *Nārasiṃha Purāṇa*:
"These twenty-one heavens are situated upon the summit of Meru;
they belong to those who practice non-violence and give gifts, as well as to performers of sacrifices and austerities."
In these dwell people who are free from anger.
