Immediately following [the heavens of the gods] are the twenty-one heavens that will be described, beginning with Ānanda; among them, one enters the water at Ānanda, and joy at Pramoda, while at Vahnisāhasa...
There is bliss in leaping from a mountain precipice, and indeed, there is supreme purity in battle.
Furthermore, one who dies through fasting or renunciation shall go to the triple heaven;
a performer of sacrifices goes to the vault of the sky, and an observer of the Agnihotra fire attains liberation.
O twice-born one, the performer of the *kratuyajña* and the sacrificer of the *somayāga*, as well as the maker of tanks and wells, obtains nourishment;
the giver of gold attains good fortune, and the one of great austerity attains heaven.
The person who kindles a great fire during the cold season for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings shall attain heaven and the company of apsarases.
Through the gift of gold, cattle, and land, one attains freedom from egoism;
through the pure gift of land, however, one obtains the state of peace.
By the gift of a cow, a man attains the stainless heaven;
by the gift of a horse, an auspicious day; and by the gift of a maiden, prosperity.
Having offered libations to the twice-born and having given garments with devotion,
one attains the white heaven, reaching which one does not grieve.
By the gift of a tawny cow, one is glorified in the ultimate truth;
so too is that mortal who always eats only once a day or observes the practice of eating only at night.
Observing fasts for three nights and so forth, one shall obtain the happiness of heaven at the end;
eating only once a day, observing the vow of a single meal,
bathing in rivers, having conquered anger, practicing celibacy, and being firm in one's vows.
One who is stainless attains happiness; likewise, so does one who is devoted to the welfare of beings.
Through the gift of knowledge, the wise one shall attain freedom from egoism.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"By giving camphor, agallochum, musk, and sandalwood to a twice-born man,
one duly obtains the auspicious enjoyment of the apsarases."
By giving jewels, ornaments, garments, beds, seats, and vessels,
a man becomes highly fortunate and happy.
He who gives great beings, horses, chariots, and elephants,
shall ascend an excellent celestial palace and go to the city of Prajāpati.
The highly illustrious person who gives a camel, a sheep,
a goat, or a buffalo never encounters residence in hell at any time.
In the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa:
"He who bestows all kinds of gifts upon Brāhmaṇas shall attain the peaceful and healthy God and shall not return [to worldly existence]."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O lords of brahmins, having gone to the world of the brahmins through their own acts of worship, what indeed [is the fate] of a brahmin?"
Being honored by gods and brahmins, one shall be happy;
therefore, that which is requested should be given to the brahmins.

Thus ends the section on the fruits of giving in the *Dānakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the sovereign over all sciences, lord of all instruments [of state], and illustrious Great God (*Mahādeva*), the supreme king of great kings.
[166] Chapter Five: Now, the acts of giving are set forth.
Among those, first, by way of distinction, are the sixteen great gifts (*mahādāna*), such as the *tulāpuruṣa* and others.
Many men have been born and exist who are prodigal in giving;
yet, are people capable of praising them even by comparison with the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) and the cow of plenty (*kāmadhenu*)?
Who would not silently nourish that cow and that tree as they bestow from the great gift-hall of the earth,
providing objects of comparison for the Golden Mountain (Meru)?
He has described the procedure for the gifts beginning with the *tulāpuruṣa*, which are both those that may and may not be performed together with [other rites].

In this regard, the gift of the *tulāpuruṣa* (the man of gold) is first described. Sūta said in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the glorification of the great gifts (*mahādāna*), as it was also declared in the *Dānadharmma* by the powerful Viṣṇu."
That which was proclaimed on earth by Vāsudeva in sixteen forms brings about the destruction of all sins for men and the eradication of suffering.
It is meritorious, purifying, life-prolonging, auspicious, and the remover of all sins;
it is honored by the deities, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others.
The gift of water for the feet (pādya) is indeed superior to all gifts, as is the gift known as the Tulāpuruṣa;
next after that is the Hiraṇyagarbha gift, and immediately following that is the Brahmāṇḍa.
The gift of the wish-fulfilling tree, the fifth being the gift of a thousand cows;
likewise the gift of a golden cow of plenty and the gift of a golden horse.
Likewise, the Hiraṇyāśvaratha, the Hemahastiratha,
the Pañcanāṅgalaka, and similarly the Varādāna.
The twelfth is the Viśvacakra, followed by the Kalpalatā;
then the gift of the seven oceans and likewise the Ratnadhenu.
In the same way, the sixteenth is proclaimed to be the jar of the great elements;
the slayer of Śambara fashioned all of these in the past.
And the Blessed Vāsudeva, King Ambarīṣa,
he named Kārtavīryārjuna, Prahlāda, and Pṛthu as well.
Other rulers of the earth, such as Bharata and others,
always performed great acts of giving despite thousands of obstacles.
All the deities protect even a single person on this earth;
one may accomplish any one of these through the grace of Vāsudeva.
It cannot be made otherwise even by Śakra on the surface of the earth;
therefore, having propitiated Govinda, Umāpati, and Vināyaka, [one should proceed].
One should perform the great sacrifice of giving (mahādānamakha), approved by the Brahmins.
Janārdana, being well-pleased, spoke this very thing to Manu;
I shall recite it as it was told, so listen, O best of sages.
Manu said:
O Acyuta, tell me of those great gifts which are purifying and auspicious in this world, and which, being secret, are to be bestowed.
[168] Matsya said:
I shall duly declare to you, in proper sequence, those sixteen great gifts which have not been mentioned as secrets.
This is the yoga of the "man on the scale" (tulāpuruṣa), which is declared to be the first for those [practitioners].

The first is the primordial nature. On the solstices, the equinoxes, auspicious occasions, the *vyatīpāta* yoga, the end of a day [of Brahmā], on the beginnings of the Yugas, during eclipses, and likewise on the beginnings of the Manvantaras.
On the day of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), on the day of Vaidhṛti yoga, on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days,
on the full moon of the bright fortnight, on festival days (parvan), on the twelfth lunar days, and on the Aṣṭakā days.
At sacrifices, festivals, and weddings; upon seeing a bad dream or a marvel;
upon obtaining wealth or a Brahmin; or wherever faith arises.
At a sacred ford, in a temple, in a cow-pen, or by wells, gardens, and rivers;
or likewise in a house, in a forest, or in a beautiful pond.
One who fears the cycle of existence should give great gifts,
because life is impermanent and wealth is exceedingly fickle.
One should practice dharma as if already seized by the hair by Death;
having reached an auspicious lunar day, one should perform the recitation of the Veda.

The syntactical connection is that one should have the pavilion and so forth constructed as will be described hereafter. The mention of the "lunar day" (tithi) is illustrative; it should be understood to include the forenoon, auspicious moments (muhūrta), and so on. The "recitation by Brahmins" (brāhmaṇavācana) refers to the recitation of words such as "auspicious day" (puṇyāha) by the Brahmins; the procedure for that has already been stated previously in the section on technical definitions (paribhāṣā).

And here is the sequence of the ritual procedure (*prayoga-krama*). On the day prior to the day of performing the gift on any one of the aforementioned times, the patron (*yajamāna*), having bathed well in the morning, should form the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "On the morrow, I shall bestow such-and-such a gift. Then, having worshipped Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Vināyaka to ward off all obstacles, and being authorized by the Brahmins, he should commence the rite. Next, having performed the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and immediately thereafter the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij-varaṇa*), and having honored them according to the *madhuparka* ritual, he should enter the western gate-pavilion and perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) in the afternoon. The characteristics of the *madhuparka* ritual, the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilions (*maṇḍapa*), and so forth, are to be found in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*); however, the specific details will be stated below.
A wise and learned man should have a pavilion constructed measuring sixteen *aratnis*, or ten or twelve *karas*, with four auspicious entrances.

The *yajamāna* (the sacrificer’s span) is twenty-one finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the *aratni* is twenty-four finger-breadths, and the *kara* [is likewise]. These three measures are to be understood according to the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior. "Having four auspicious faces" means that it is one whose faces—meaning doors—are endowed with the four auspicious qualities. As Viśvakarman said concerning the hall of charity (*dānasabhā*):
"That which is adorned with four doors opening outwards, possessing a beautiful form and appearance."
"She is said to be born from jewels; indeed, her auspicious, blameless, and indestructible [form] must be fashioned. Thus, in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
The altar in the center should be seven cubits high, or alternatively five cubits;
in its middle, one should construct an auspicious archway made of solid wood.

In the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the altar (*vedī*) should be seven cubits for the superior [type], while for the other two it is five cubits; such is the established option. That altar should be made of earth or wood, raised by one-fourth [of its width].

In its center, there is a *toraṇa* (arched gateway) because of its arched form, intended for supporting the balance-beam (*tulā*); it should be made of heartwood trees such as *śāka*, *iṅgudī*, and so forth, which will be described later.
A wise person should construct four sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) in the four directions.
Likewise, there were great seats joined with pedestals having beautiful girdles, filled with full jars,
and provided with two copper vessels.
Together with the sacrificial vessels and the ritual seats.
The offerings of sesame, clarified butter, incense, and flowers should be very beautiful, measuring one cubit in size.

The phrase "on the four sides" implies that there are altars (*vedi*). The distance between the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the altar should be measured at one and a quarter cubits (*sapādahasta*). A full pitcher (*pūrṇakumbha*) is a water-filled jar. Two copper vessels serve as the receptacles for the oblations to be offered in the fire. The sacrificial implements (*yajñapātra*) include the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and others. A *viṣṭara* is made of twenty-five blades of *kuśa* grass with their tips cut off. Incense (*dhūpa*) consists of substances such as *guggulu*. An offering (*upahāra*) includes fruits, cooked rice, and so forth.
Furthermore, an altar measuring one cubit in size should be placed in the northeast for the worship of the lords of the gods, beginning with the planets (*graha*).
The worship and adoration of Brahmā, Śiva, and Acyuta should likewise be performed with fruits, garlands, and garments.

In the north-eastern quarter, that of Īśāna, an altar (*vedi*) should be constructed, measuring one cubit in length and breadth, and one span (*vitasti*) in height. In its center, one should place the Sun (*sūrya*). To the south-east, Soma; to the south, Bhauma; to the north-east, Budha; to the north, Guru; to the east, Bhārgava; to the west, Śani; to the south-west, Rāhu; and to the north-west, the Ketus. These are also included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*): Īśvara, Gaurī, Skanda, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śakra, Yama, Kāla, and Citragupta are the presiding deities (*adhidevatās*).

Fire, Water, Earth, Viṣṇu, Śakra, Śacī, Prajāpati, the Serpent, and Brahmā—these are the secondary deities (*pratyadhidevatās*), and they should be installed in proximity to their respective presiding planets.

Likewise, Vināyaka, Durgā, Vāyu, Ākāśa, and the two Aśvins are to be installed to the north of Saturn and the Sun, and to the south of Rāhu and Ketu; this is the installation of Durgā and the others. Furthermore, the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) and so forth are also to be installed here, because they will be mentioned later as deities.
As it is said in another Smṛti:
Indra should be established in the east, likewise Yama in the south;
Varuṇa in the western part, and Kubera one should place in the north.
Indra is yellow, Yama is dark, Varuṇa has the luster of crystal,
Kubera is golden-hued, and Agni is also golden-colored.
In the same way, Nirṛti is dark blue and Vāyu is praised as smoky;
Īśāna, however, should be red—one should meditate on these in this sequence.
On the right side of Indra, the wise one should invoke the Vasus:
Dhruva, Dhvara, Soma, Āpa, Anila, and Anala.
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus; between Deveśa and Īśāna is likewise the path of the Ādityas.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśu, Bhaga,
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu, the non-inferior one born of no inferior [mother]—
thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names.
In the western portion of Agni, they know to be the abode of the Rudras:
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, and the highly illustrious Girīśa.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and the unconquered Aparājita; Bhuvanādhīśvara, Kapālin, and Viśāmpati.
Sthāṇu and the lordly Bhaga are recorded as the eleven Rudras;
one should designate the station of the Mothers between Preteśa and Rakṣas.
The names of the Mothers, such as Gaurī, Padmā, and others, have been shown in the section on terminology.
They know that the abode of Gaṇeśa is to the north of Nirṛti;
the location of the Maruts is said to be between Kubera and the Maruts.
O God, those groups of yours are indeed named Maruts, consisting of seven in each;
namely Āvaha, Pravaha, Udvaha, and likewise Saṃvaha.
"Vivaha, Pravaha, and likewise Parivaha, the wind.

These [deities], beginning with the Sun, should be worshipped according to the procedure prescribed for the sacrifice to the planets (*grahayajña*). However, for those whose mantras have not been specified, the rites of installation and so forth should be performed using their names preceded by the *praṇava* (OM), in the dative case, and ending with "namaḥ. Furthermore, in that very context, the worship of Brahmā, Śiva, and Acyuta, as well as the consecration of their images, must be performed. Their characteristics will be described in the section on the gift of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍadāna*) in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
Banners of the colors of Lokeśvara should be placed all around,
and in the center there should be a flagstaff equipped with small bells; furthermore, archways should be constructed at the gates.
There are also four [types] of milk-yielding trees.
At the doors, two jars should be placed here,
provided with garlands, perfumes, incense, garments, and jewels.

They have the colors of the world-protectors (*lokeśa*); that is, they possess colors identical to those of the world-protectors mentioned immediately above, such as Indra being yellow and Yama being dark blue (*śyāma*). "On all sides" means in all directions, starting from the east, of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). "Bells" (*kiṅkiṇikā*) refers to small bells. Regarding "of the milk-exuding trees" (*kṣīravanaspati*), one should construct arches (*toraṇa*) marked with the signs of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus made of wood upon the tops of the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *nyagrodha* trees, respectively, at the eastern, southern, western, and northern gates. [173] "Jewels" (*ratna*) refers to gold and so forth, as described in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). [The wood of] *śāka*, *iṅgudī*, *candana*, and *devadāru*—
Having firmly established two pillars made of *śrīparṇī*, *bilva*, *priyaka*,
or *kāñjana* wood, five cubits in height and dug into the ground at a distance of two cubits [from each other].
Immediately following that, there should be four cubits for the northern part, which is likewise square.

*Śāka* is a specific type of tree, well-known in Mahārāṣṭra as *sādha*. *Śrīparṇī* is the *bhadraparṇī* tree. *Priyaka* is the *bījaka*. Having made two pillars square, they are to be placed on the eastern and western sides in the middle of the altar. The *uttarāṅga* (upper beam) is the wooden timber above the two pillars. And that [beam] is to be placed four cubits above the two pillars which are five cubits high. Now, regarding the reading "and the *uttarāṅga* is indeed its member" (*tadaṅgam eva*), the meaning is that it is made of wood of the same species as the pillars. Furthermore, it should be of the same species as the balance-beam (*tulā*).
It should be joined with a golden man in the center;
its length should be four cubits,
and its width ten finger-breadths.
She should be fashioned with auspicious golden ornaments, joined with two iron nooses and chains,
and adorned with a jeweled necklace of gold.
Adorned with garlands and unguents, they possess a radiant luster.

Of the same kind as the archway, it should be suspended twelve finger-breadths below the middle of the upper beam of the balance, with its tips pointing upward. It is to be suspended by a man—namely Viṣṇu—by means of a golden chain. The characteristics of that image are stated in the *Pañcarātra*:
"In the two lower hands, a discus and a mace respectively;
in the two upper hands, a conch and a lotus; [this is] Govinda, whose body is tawny."
The fire [altar] should be understood as being four cubits long, excluding the six circular sections situated at the two ends where the iron chains are fixed.

Since the entire balance is measured at one hundred and eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas), its width should be made equal to a cord measuring ten finger-breadths and shaped like a ring; this is the meaning. Furthermore, it should be joined with chains attached to the two iron chains, meaning it should be constructed so that it is equipped with chains suspended from the two iron chains which support the planks for holding gold. As stated in the Vahni Purāṇa:
[One should prepare] a staff made from the Aśvattha, Khadira, or Palāśa tree, born of a fine tree,
measuring four cubits at most, very smooth, very firm, and new.
Likewise, it should be perfectly round, level, smooth, and provided with three apertures;
it should be equipped with two loops made of muñja grass and tied to a sacrificial post.
Nārada said:
The balance-beam should be made square, and its two feet likewise;
on all four sides, the measurement should be four finger-breadths.
Having first removed the rings, the wise man should place them at both ends;
the lower balance-beam below shall measure four cubits and be provided with chains in the middle.
"One should make the loop three cubits long and the ring four finger-breadths wide. Thus it is said.
As Viśvakarman stated:
"The specific gift [consisting of] the balance and so forth has been described."
Therefore, the characteristics of the balance (tulā) are stated first:
the measurement of the balance is traditionally held to be sixty-nine finger-breadths in length for the solid parts.
It is stated that there are six finger-breadths at each of the two ends,
one hundred and eight finger-breadths for the scale,
and twenty-five metal joints.
One should cause the presiding deities to enter into the bonds.
Īśa, Śaśin, Māruta, Rudra, Sūrya, Viśvakarman, Guru, Aṅgiras,
Agni, Prajāpati, and the Ordainer of the entire universe.
And Parjanya, Śambhu, and the Pitṛ-devatās.
And Saumya, Dharma, the King of the Immortals (Indra), Agni, Varuṇa, Mitra, Varuṇa, the hosts of Maruts,
Dhaneśa, Gandharva, Jaleśa, and Viṣṇu— [175].
These are indeed the twenty-four deities.
There may be one great-souled man who, when weighed upon a scale, would equal twenty-five [others];
these [others] are to be placed within gold.
Those forms of the deities are adorned with jewels.
The square pedestal should be six finger-breadths [in height], with Viṣṇu, known by the name Ananta, on both sides;
on the upper portion of the base, there should be two pitchers.
Likewise, there is a pair of hooks at the lower end of the balance-beam.
The ring, arising from six finger-breadths, has a thickness of one finger-breadth; it is Viṣṇu, known by the name Ananta,
and its two sides should each be four finger-breadths.
Thus have I declared to you the authoritative means of knowledge.
In the middle joint of the ring finger, there are exactly fifty-two finger-joints in length;
its circumference here is one finger-breadth.
In that regard, Vāsuki is indeed said to be the presiding deity.
Each individual rope measures seventy-three finger-breadths when taken as a total,
and the pair of cloths likewise measures finger-breadths.
Likewise, there would be thirty plus fifteen more.
Attached to that, one should apply a pair of finger-breadths at the junction of the auspicious wooden block; above this,
the presiding deity of the [first] zero should be established.
"The lord of the earth should be placed within the balance.

Thus [it is said]. "Īśa, Śaśin," and so forth. Here, the characteristics for the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa (Cosmic Egg) involving Īśvara, Candra, Maruta, Sūrya, Devarāja, and Jaleśa will be described. Regarding Rudra, [his form] is in the Viśvacakra; the construction of the form of Viśvakarman is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Viśvakarman, however, should be made with a beard, a broad chest, and a protruding lower lip."
Holding tongs in his hand, two-armed, he is the great one who bears a form of radiant energy.
The true forms of Guru (Jupiter) and Saumya (Mercury) will be described in the section on the offering of the nine planets. Viśvakarman said that Aṅgiras has the form of Agni:
"They bear at the tips of their hands, in sequence from all sides, a water-pot, a sacrificial ladle, a spear, and also *darbha* grass; these are known by the name Aṅgiras. [176]
And their hands likewise hold fire;
they also carry a rosary for recitation, a spear, a book, and in due order, a water-pot.
When these two are joined together, they constitute the deity. The nature of Prajāpati is described in the *Siddhāntasaṃhitā*:
"Wearing a sacred thread, with one face and four arms, Prajāpati holds a rosary, a *śruc* ladle, a *sruva* ladle, and a water-pot."

The characteristics of Viśvadeva will be described in the section on the gift of Viśvambhara. His form is identical to that of Prajāpati, the Creator; however, he is to be fashioned with four manifestations. The characteristics of Parjanya are stated in the Siddhārthasaṃhitā:
"He who is known by the name Parjanya should be understood as being endowed with three elephant faces;
he who, as the soul of all living beings, holds the boon, the seed, and the conch."
The exceedingly pure one holds in his ten hands an axe, a lotus, a wish-fulfilling gem,
a noose, a discus, a sprout, and a water-pot.
Śambhu is as before; these two together also possess the status of a deity. The definition of the ancestors (*pitṛ*) is stated in the *Mayadīpikā*:
"The ancestors, seated upon lotuses made of *kuśa* grass and flour, hold the vessels for the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
The form of Dharma is described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The wise practitioner should depict Dharma as having four faces, four feet, and four arms, clad in white garments, adorned with all ornaments, and white in complexion.
In his right hand is a rosary, and in his left is a book.
The characteristics of the two Aśvins will be described in the section on the gift of the golden horse-chariot. Viśvakarman describes the form of Mitra:
"Mitra has a lotus in his hand and is seated upon a lotus throne."
He has two arms, possesses a white form, and is devoted to the welfare of all beings.

Varuṇa, however, is as described previously; here too, the two together constitute the deity. The form of the Marut-gaṇa is to be understood from the section on the gift of the Marut-mountain. The characteristics of Dhaneśa are found in the section on the gift of the grain-mountain (dhānyācala). Regarding the form of the Gandharva, Yama says:
"The Gandharva should be made beautiful in form, granting boons to the world of devotees, wearing a crown and earrings, holding a mace, and likewise devoted to playing the lute."

Viśvakarman describes the characteristics of Viṣṇu: "Viṣṇu, adorned with the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, the conch, and the discus, should always be [depicted] starting from the lower right hand and proceeding clockwise."
Two nooses made of iron and two pieces of cloth should be suspended from the ground at a height of one *pāda* (foot-measure). Now, in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"One should draw a wheel containing a lotus in its center upon the ground, strewn with various powders and flowers."
And one should place a five-colored canopy above, adorned with flowers and fruits.

The wheel has twelve spokes and is joined with the interior of a lotus and water; in its center is a lotus. On the ground, in the middle of the altar, [it is drawn] with various powders such as white, yellow, and so forth.
Now, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should be appointed—those who know the Vedas, and who are endowed with handsome appearance, dress, lineage, and character.
Those eminent twice-born ones who are skilled in ritual procedures, eloquent, well-disposed, and born in the noble land (Āryadeśa).
And the Guru should be one who knows the meaning of the Vedas, born in a noble land, endowed with virtue, noble lineage, and beauty;
he should be devoted to the ancient traditions, exceedingly skillful, and possess speech that is clear, profound, and elegant.
Clad in white garments, he was made beautiful by earrings, golden necklaces, armlets, and throat ornaments.

The learned ones are free from passion. The "Land of the Aryas" has been explained. Therein, eight officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), eight gatekeepers, eight reciters (*jāpaka*), and the preceptor (*guru*) are to be chosen. Thus it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"In that [rite], there should be eight auspicious hotṛ-priests and likewise eight gatekeepers;
eight reciters should be appointed, Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas."
Twenty-five brahmins adorned with golden ornaments should indeed be appointed.

The procedure for this is as follows: "Today, by means of the sacrifice of such-and-such a gift, I shall perform a sacrifice; for that purpose, in order to perform the rites such as the *homa* which are constituent parts thereof, I choose you, of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), named such-and-such (*śarmā*), a student of such-and-such Veda, to be my officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Similarly, one should understand the formula to be: "Today, by means of the sacrifice of such-and-such a great gift (*mahādāna*), I shall perform a sacrifice; for that purpose, in order to perform and cause to be performed all the constituent rites, I choose you, of such-and-such lineage, named such-and-such, a student of such-and-such Veda, to be my preceptor (*ācārya*)," and so forth. In every case, the response is: "I am chosen. And its specific application is shown in that very same place.
Having adorned the gatekeepers on all sides with perfumes and flowers, the preceptor, while making offerings to them, should say to them: "Recite!"
And he should say "Sacrifice! to the officiating priests even before [the sacrifice].
"Remain with the recitation of the supreme mantra," [he says] to the chanters.
To the east there should be two knowers of the Ṛgveda, and two knowers of the Yajurveda should be stationed to the south.
The two Sāmaveda Brahmins should be stationed at the back,
and the two Atharvaveda Brahmins should be placed to the north.
Of the Vināyakas and other planetary deities, the world-protectors, the Vasus, the Aṣṭakas, and the hosts of divine Maruts;
of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, the Sun, and the Lord of the Forest (Śiva).
From the *samantra* [mantra], there should be four oblations (*homa*).
Likewise, their hymns to be recited should be chanted in their proper sequence and according to their true form.

And this restriction regarding the directions, such as the east and so forth, is to be understood as applying to the officiating priests who are learned in the Ṛgveda and other Vedas, as well as to the gatekeepers.

By the word "Vināyakādi" (beginning with Vināyaka), [it refers to] the eleven Rudras, the presiding deities (adhidevatās) and secondary deities (pratyadhidevatās) of the nine planets, as well as Durgā, Vāyu, Ākāśa, and the Aśvins. According to their respective mantras—that is, by the mantras of their own Vedas—there is a fourfold oblation (homa). Because of the connection with the four Vedas, there are four types of oblations. Then, once the Guru has performed the installation of the fires, two priests each, in their respective fire-pits (kuṇḍas), should offer twelve oblations of sesame and clarified butter for each deity beginning with Vināyaka, using the mantras prescribed in their own Vedic branches.

In this context, first of all, since it is impossible to maintain the rule of twenty-one oblations per *kuṇḍa* for eighty-five deities— namely, the thirty-two Vināyakas and other gods, the ten world-protectors (*lokapāla*), the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, the seven groups of seven Maruts, and the five beginning with Brahmā— that has been demonstrated in the *Paribhāṣā*:
"At the conclusion of the *homa*, the Guru, accompanied by the sound of trumpets, takes the offerings of food, flowers, and incense."
Accompanied by the sacrificer, he should invoke the lords of the worlds in sequence with these mantras.
Come, come, O Vajradhara, Lord of the Immortals, praised by all the gods, Siddhas, and Sādhyas,
being fanned by the breeze from the courtyard of the Apsarases!
O Blessed One, protect our sacrifice; homage be to you!
Oṃ, homage to Indra.
Come, come, O bearer of oblations for all the immortals,
you who are praised on every side by the foremost of sages,
together with the radiant host of worlds!
May he protect my sacrifice; may his impetuous force be yours.
Oṃ, homage to Agni! Come, come, Vaivasvata, Dharmarāja,
embodiment of Dharma worshipped by all the immortals!
O Lord of auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, joy, and sorrow, protect our sacrifice for our welfare; salutations unto You!
Oṃ, homage to Yama!
Come, come, O leader of the hosts of Rākṣasas, together with your retinues of Viśāla, Vetālas, and Piśācas!
Protect my sacrifice, O Lord of the Auspicious Mind;
you are the Lord of the World, O Blessed One—homage to you!
Oṃ, homage to Nirṛti!
Come, come, together with the hosts of aquatic creatures, the oceans, the clouds, and the Apsarases!
O Blessed One, praised by the lords of the Vidyādharas and the gods, protect us; homage be to you!
Oṃ, salutation to Varuṇa!
Come, come, O Lord of Sacrifice, mounted upon your deer and accompanied by hosts of Siddhas, for the sake of protection!
O Lord of the vital breath, companion of Kālakavi, accept our worship; homage be to you!
Oṃ, salutation to Vāyu!
Come, come, O Lord of Sacrifice; perform the protection of the sacrifice together with the host of constellations.
O Blessed One, together with all the medicinal herbs and the ancestors, accept this worship; salutations to you!
Oṃ, homage to Soma!
Come, come, O Lord of the Universe, together with the bearer of the trident, skull-topped staff, and khaṭvāṅga!
O Lord of Beings, for the successful completion of the sacrifice by the world, accept this worship; O Blessed One, salutations to you!
Oṃ, homage to Īśāna! Come, come, O Lord of the Universe, Sovereign of the Gods, together with the world and the ancestral deities!
O Sustainer of all, possessed of immeasurable power,
may you constantly grant us prosperity by making our sacrifice successful.
Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā.
Whatever beings there are in the three worlds, both stationary and moving,
may they, together with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, grant me protection.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas;
sages, seers, cows, and the divine mothers as well.
"May these [deities], filled with joy, perform protection for me in this sacrifice.
Having thus invoked the gods, he should give golden ornaments to the officiating priests.
And earrings, golden threads, and bracelets;
then variegated rings, garments, and beds.
One should give double the amount of ornaments, clothing, and so forth to the preceptor;
the reciters should chant the Śāntika chapter in every direction.
Then, having fasted and performed this consecration (adhivāsana),
one should have the Brahmins recite blessings at the beginning, the middle, and the end.

The chapter on pacification (*śāntikādhyāya*) begins with "May Indra and Agni be auspicious for us with their blessings," and so forth. Regarding the inability to fast, the *Padmapurāṇa* states: "There must indeed be a fast; in case of incapacity, eating at night (*nakta*) is prescribed.

Thus, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the preceding day, everyone should remain right there. Then, on the following day, near the time for the gift-giving, one should perform the recitation by Brahmins (*brāhmaṇavācana*) and complete the ritual procedures beginning with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). In the event of an urgent matter, the procedure for consecration may be performed immediately. This has been stated:
"Or else, a man who is incapacitated may perform the formal acceptance immediately. Thus it is said. Now, in the *Atharvaṇa-gopatha-brāhmaṇa*:

The officiating priest and the sacrificer, having had their hair, beards, and nails shaved, and having prepared the ritual materials and the necessary substances, perform the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings. Then, having brought together the remnants of the oblations with the *saṃpāta* water using the verses "This is our Agni," the *Mahāvyāhṛtis*, "Brahma-yajñāna," "O Agni, [come] with the cows," "O Agni, return," "O Agni, born from the womb," and "What they bound," he should pour them into the *snātaka* jars. He should then pour [the water] over [the person] with the verses "Idam āpaḥ" and "Āpo hi ṣṭhā," and sprinkle him with his two arms as prescribed. Having caused him to apply collyrium, ointment, and unguents, and having placed upon him garments, perfumes, and a garland during the *Abhijit* moment, he should weigh him on a scale. During the *Abhijit* moment, having sprinkled the scale with gold-colored purifying waters, having honored it with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and having presented offerings, he should summon the king, give him half [of the fee], and cause him to ascend the scale.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
Then, having been put to sleep with auspicious sounds by the foremost of Veda-knowers,
he circumambulated [the image] three times and took handfuls of flowers in his joined palms.
Wearing white garlands and garments, he should consecrate that scale with mantras.

They should perform the ritual ablution with water from the jars situated near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). The mantras for the ablution are to be understood as those recited in the *grahayajña* (sacrifice to the planets), beginning with "May the gods sprinkle you" (*surās tvām abhiṣiñcantu*).
"Homage to you! You are the power (*śakti*) of all the gods; you are the refuge of all.
You are the witness, the sustainer of the world, created by the Source of the Universe."
O beloved of the world, you have been placed in the midst of all truths on one side and hundreds of falsehoods on the other, by those who perform righteous and unrighteous deeds.
O Tula, you are proclaimed here as the standard of measure for all beings;
weighing me, lift me up from saṃsāra—homage be to you!
He who is that god, the Lord of Reality, the Puruṣa consisting of twenty-five principles—he, O Goddess, is established within you; therefore, salutations, salutations!
Salutations, salutations to you, O Govinda, who are known as Tulāpuruṣa!
O Hari, protect us from this ocean of saṃsāra.
Having reached an auspicious time and performed this consecration (adhivāsana),
the wise man, having again circumambulated it, should ascend that scale.
Equipped with sword, shield, and armor, and adorned with all ornaments,
he took up Dharmarāja, who was joined with a golden sun.
With his two hands clenched into fists, he remains gazing at the face of Hari.

The King of Dharma (Yama), however, should be depicted mounted upon a buffalo, four-armed, and holding a staff and a noose in his hands. The Sun (Sūrya) also should be made of gold, seated on a lotus throne, and holding a lotus. Having placed those two [deities] with their fists clenched at the right and left [sides], they should look toward the face of Hari situated in the middle of the scale; this is the meaning.
Then, on the other side of the scale, the eminent brahmins should place gold that is exceedingly pure, equal to or even exceeding [the weight of the donor].
But one who desires prosperity, O lord of men, should perform it upon the ground.

The phrase "one desiring prosperity" (*puṣṭikāma*) indicates a connection between a quality and its fruit, such as [the injunction] "one desiring cattle should fetch water with a *godohana* vessel"; this is how it should be understood. Here, first of all, it was stated that the king’s mounting of the scales occurs first, followed by the placement of the gold. However, in the *Gopatha Brāhmaṇa*, it is said: "Equipped with a sword, wearing a helmet, and adorned with all ornaments, having placed refined gold (*tapanīya*) in front, the lord of men should afterwards be weighed.
O lord of men, the gold should be on the right side, and the [king] on the left."

Therefore, the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* are considered the fifth Veda. If they possess equal authority, there is an option regarding their performance. However, for those who consider the *Purāṇas* to be like the *Smṛtis*, according to their view, the placing of gold comes first, followed by the placing of the king.
Having remained thus for a moment, he should then utter this:
"Salutations to you, O eternal one, who have become the witness of all beings."
O Goddess, you were created by the Grandfather, the Supreme Lord;
by you the entire world, including all that is mobile and immobile, is sustained.
Salutations to you, the sustainer of the universe, who dwells within all beings as their very self.
In the Vahni Purāṇa: Having performed the fire-oblation according to the rules, having bathed well in the waters of a sacred ford,
and having worshipped the scale according to the prescribed rite with Brahmanical and Vedic mantras.
Having well nourished [the deity], one should worship Lord Hari, who wears yellow garments;
thereafter, one should ascend that swing, facing either eastward or northward.
Having filled a scale separately with pure Jāmbūnada gold,
[the donor], his body adorned with all ornaments and provided with garments and a seat, [should offer it].
Having remained there for a moment, he should stand upon a substance that brings about elevation;
he should then recite the mantra or the three verses beginning with "punantu."
Just as the incomparable purifier is the offspring of Jātavedas,
so may gold indeed purify me by its own purity.
The exceedingly great splendor of Rudra and the birth of Kārttikeya—
may gold, by its own purity, indeed purify me.
Just as Agni is the essence of all deities and gold is of that same nature,
so may gold indeed purify me by its own purity.
Whatever evil deed has been committed by me through my own body, mind, or speech— may supreme, auspicious liberation, residing within the golden [relic], protect that.
Having said this, the disciple should indeed give that very [object] to the officiating priest;
then, having emerged, he should take up another [object] from the Aṅgadaṇṭa.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Then, having descended [from the altar], one should first present half [of the offering] to the preceptor;
one should give the other half to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), preceded by the pouring of water."
One should present the gems of the musical modes to the preceptor and the sacrificial priests.

In this regard, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) is as follows: *Oṃ! Today, in such-and-such a place, at such-and-such a time, I, [Name] of such-and-such a lineage, for the sake of [Name] Śarman of such-and-such a lineage, a Brāhmaṇa, give this half of the gold of the *tulāpuruṣa* gift, desiring such-and-such a goal; [this is] equal [to my weight]; salutations! For the sake of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of this gift, I give this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), which is equal [to my weight]; salutations!* Having preceded this with water, one should give the first half to the Guru; likewise, the other half to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). However, whatever gift is given without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*), all that becomes fruitless.

From this statement, it follows that when looking toward the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) here, village lands, jewels, and so forth, as well as sacred learning (*śruta*), are connected as the fee for the teacher.

Now, in the *Gopatha Brāhmaṇa*: "With the four verses beginning with 'acyutā dyauḥ,' one should cause [the person] to descend. Having consecrated that scale, having offered clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *mahāvyāhṛti*, *sāvitrī*, and peace-mantras (*śānti*), and with the *ahomuya* formulas, and having turned clockwise with the formula 'sarvasyāvṛtam,' one should give the self-ornament to the performer, and a thousand [coins] as the fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and an excellent village. Thus it is said.
To the performer, the teacher, and the officiating priest.

In that regard, since it is stated that "half belongs to the teacher and half to the officiating priests" regarding "a thousand as the sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇā*), and because no specific number of items to be counted is mentioned for the word "thousand," and because no specific number is provided for the term "jewels" (*ratna*) in the *Matsya Purāṇa*, and because other Vedic branches (*śākhā*) prescribe excellent jewels as the place for the sacrificial fee, it is logical that there should indeed be a "thousand jewels. However, according to the principle of the section on sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇādhikaraṇa*), just as with cows, this number must relate to items of the same kind; thus, it is understood that there should be a thousand of one among pearls and so forth, according to one's capacity and availability.
"An excellent village" means the best of villages.

However, some explain that in the phrase "village-jewels for the teacher," the word *ratna* (jewel) also denotes excellence. According to their view, because of the statement "gold is remembered as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for all gifts," in the passage "a thousand [is] the sacrificial fee," it should be understood that gold alone constitutes the fee. Furthermore, the determination of the number one thousand—starting from a *kṛṣṇala* and so forth—should be accomplished according to one's capacity.
Having obtained their permission, he should likewise cause these to be given to these [others] as well.
One should honor the poor, the helpless, and those distinguished by their suffering, together with the Brahmins.

Here, by the word "others" (*anya*), the reciters (*jāpaka*) are meant; these are distinguished individuals who, though not Brahmins, are endowed with qualities such as service to their parents. In this matter, one view is that half of the substance for the *tulāpuruṣa* rite should be given to the teacher (*guru*) and half to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); in this view, a separate sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be given to the reciters. Another view is that, with the permission of the teacher and others, one may give [the remainder] to other [reciters] as well.

In that regard, when the quantity of the substance to be given to the preceptor and others is not specified, it is logical to follow the rule regarding the number of items to be given as heard in the section on the gift of the earth and other elements—which are modifications [of primordial matter]—namely, "one should offer a fourth part of the *dharā* to the preceptor.

Alternatively, one should practice what is taught in general terms, such as "that by which the preceptor is satisfied," and likewise give to the poor, the helpless, and distinguished persons; this is the third position.

[187] Although there is no word here explicitly expressing an alternative, nevertheless, by resorting to another position, an alternative is established by implication. In the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "A wise man should not keep consecrated gold in his house for long, because it remains a source of fear and causes grief and disease for men."
By quickly taking possession of another's property, one attains abundant prosperity.

Then, as before, having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* (declaration of an auspicious day), the patron (*yajamāna*) should go near the altar of the deities (*devatāvedi*) and perform the worship and other rites for the deities in the eastern direction. The preceptor (*ācārya*), however, should say:
"May all the hosts of gods depart, taking their worship from the king, for the sake of granting desired boons and for the purpose of returning again."
With this mantra, one should perform the dismissal of the deities.
Whoever performs the *tulāpuruṣa* rite according to this procedure shall dwell in the station of a world-protector during each *manvantara*.
Being honored by apsarases, he shall then go to the city of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot, sun-colored and garlanded with networks of tinkling bells;
for as long as a hundred koṭis of kalpas, he is glorified in that world.
Through the exhaustion of his karma, he is once again born here on earth as a king of kings,
whose footstool is adorned by the crest-jewels of sovereigns;
endowed with faith, he becomes a performer of a thousand sacrifices.
He had conquered the entire world of kings by means of his blazing majesty.
He who, filled with devotion, beholds [the Lord] even while being given [gifts],
remembers Him at another time, or requests Him here in this world;
or he who hears or recites [this account] with a mind as humble as Indra’s— [he attains the supreme goal].
He attains that abode cherished by the god Purandara.
In the Vahnipurāṇa:
"Having thus given gold, a person destroys even such sins as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa and, having been freed from those evils, goes to the heavenly world."
O King, having remained there for a long time,
he who is the illustrious Lord of the lords of kings returns to the surface of the earth, free from sorrow and free from disease.
Endowed with beauty and good fortune, and always devoted to dharma,
he goes again to the abode of Viṣṇu, having reached which he does not grieve.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the person on the scale (*tulāpuruṣadānavidhi*).
Sanatkumāra said: "O Nandin, the sixteen gifts for kings have been declared."
For the sake of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation, the great-souled ones act through action alone.
Listen now to those rites, such as the ascension of the scales (tulādhirohaṇa) and others, exactly as they are:
[to be performed] during auspicious times such as eclipses, in a beautiful and most splendid location.
One should construct a pavilion or even a peaked roof measuring twenty cubits,
or alternatively eighteen cubits, or again sixteen cubits.
Having thus prepared the altar in the center, one should make it nine cubits in measurement,
or eight cubits, or again seven cubits.
The altar (vedikā) should be very beautiful, measuring either two cubits or one and a half cubits;
it should be joined with twelve pillars and possess an excellent, lovely top.
One should have nine square pits constructed all around;
O son of Brahmā, the principal pit is located between Indra and Īśāna.
Alternatively, O best of Brahmins, one should have fire-pits for women constructed as quadrangular, as well as in the shape of a womb (yoni), or in other shapes beyond these.
The fire-pit (kuṇḍa) is excellent when it is semicircular, triangular,
circular, hexagonal, or even on all sides triangular and resembling a lotus.
An eight-cornered sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be prepared on all paths, or simply one alone,
provided with four doors and adorned with four arches (toraṇas).
It is joined by the eight elephants of the quarters, adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass,
endowed with the eight auspicious symbols, and beautified by a canopy above.
Furthermore, trees such as the *tulā*, the *drama*, and especially the *bilva* and others—
including the *bilva*, *aśvattha*, *palāśa*, and so forth— or even the *khadira* alone [are suitable].
Thus, whatever supports have been fashioned by him, he should cause all [the rest] to be made accordingly;
or else, he may arrange them according to a mixed method or by means of bamboo.
The width of the pillar of the scale-beam should be eight cubits in measure and two cubits in length;
its circumference is considered to be three times that [width].
It should be well-rounded, free of blemishes, and two finger-breadths less [in circumference];
furthermore, O King, the distance between the two [ends] is traditionally recorded as six cubits.
The distance between two pillars made four cubits apart,
or even six cubits apart, should be known as that which is situated above them.
The width of the lintel should be one *vitasti*, and its thickness should be that many finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
the cross-beam, however, should be equal in measure to the two pillars and commensurate with the door.
The span [of the beam] should be thirty-six finger-breadths (mātrās) in length and equal in weight;
its width, however, should be eight finger-breadths and five barley-corns (yavas).
The navel should be thirty-six *mātras* in measure, free from blemishes, circular, and auspicious.

Regarding "twenty cubits" and so forth: a *kūṭa* is a specific type of pavilion. With sixteen cubits (*kalāhasta*), for the three mandalas measuring twenty cubits and so on, the height of the three altars (*vedī*)—which have a width of nine cubits and so forth respectively—should be made two cubits, one and a half cubits, and one cubit.
Having constructed the pavilion, one should lead the altars there into its center.
With nine, eight, or seven cubits, or with two cubits, or one and a half cubits.
It was twelve cubits in both width and height, and was provided with twelve pillars.

Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*. "The top and the summit are beautiful and pleasing" means that the upper portion must be made both perfectly square and level. Alternatively, the term "square" (*caturasra*) implies that the nine types of arrangements—beginning with the square for the eastern and other directions—should be established in sequence; however, for women, since they act as the sacrificers (*yajamāna*), the shapes should be exclusively in the form of a *yoni* (womb). Or else, according to the aforementioned forms, whether as an altar (*sthaṇḍila*) or otherwise, the area of one cubit (*hasta*) everywhere must be made such that the area-measurement (*kṣetraphala*) is equal, and this has been demonstrated in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). The four arches (*toraṇa*) are made from *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa* wood. There is the group of eight elephants of the directions, along with banners of the colors corresponding to their respective directions and times. The eight auspicious signs (*aṣṭamaṅgala*) will be described in the section on the gift of the Universal Wheel (*viśvacakra*). The length of the two pillars of the balance (*tulāstambha*) is eight cubits; "length" (*āyāma*) here means longitudinal measurement. The width (*viṣkambha*) of the two balance-pillars is two cubits; this is the grammatical connection. Three times that is the circumference (*parimāṇa*). "Reduced by two finger-breadths" refers to that same circumference; by gradual reduction, it should be made two finger-breadths less at the front. However, in the *Kāmika*:
The height of the side pillars is considered to be seven, six, or five cubits;
starting from eight cubits, it may then increase by two, five, or two finger-breadths.
The width of the base of the balance-pillar is considered to be three times its height;
it should be well-rounded, free from blemishes, and reduced by two finger-breadths [in diameter at the top].

Thus, the width (*viṣkambha*) is ten finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), being two finger-breadths less than twice five; the circumference (*pariṇāha*) is thirty finger-breadths. And that [circumference] decreases gradually so that at the tip it is twenty-eight finger-breadths—this is the meaning. Immediately following the two pillars, a space of six or four cubits (*hasta*) should be constructed, in accordance with the height of the visible pillars. The interval between the two six-cubit pillars is an illustration for the length of the crossbeam (*guṇa*). The lintel (*uttara*) should be twelve finger-breadths in both width and height. Having inserted that into the upper tips of the pillars at the ends of the openings, the archway (*toraṇa*) is to be completed.

Now he states the measurement of the beam of the balance (*tulādaṇḍa*): "The measure is thirty-six," and so forth. *Vyāyāma* is defined as the distance between the two hands when both arms are extended sideways with the palms joined; this is according to the definition: "the *vyāyāma* is the lateral interval between the two [hands] when the arms are extended. Therefore, the length of the balance-beam is exactly one *vyāyāma*, consisting of thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). As for the width, it is "eight measures" (*aṣṭamātra*); that is, the projection at both ends of the balance-beam is eight finger-breadths and five barley-corns (*yava*).

In that context, by implication, the circumference at the base is thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Regarding the phrase "the measure is thirty-six," this means the circumference in the middle of the balance-beam (*tulā-daṇḍa*) is thirty-six finger-breadths. By implication, the width at the bottom is twelve finger-breadths.
However, the width at the top is eight finger-breadths plus one barley-corn (*yava*).
But the circumference of thirty-six finger-breadths is prescribed for the middle part.
Thus it is stated in the Kāmika:
"One should bind [the staff] at the top, the base, and the middle with a golden band;
three suspension-threads should be made within the band."
One should have it made of copper, silver, or even iron;
in the center, a very beautiful support should be fashioned facing upwards.
One should also bind it to the top of the archway with cords according to the prescribed rule;
a single tongue is placed in the middle of the balance, and the archway is likewise ordained.
Then, in the middle of the northern [side], one should properly fix two excellent stakes, firmly securing them by covering them from above with a canopy.
The measurement of the middle of the scale must be very firm according to the standard of finger-breadths (aṅgula),
while the width of the cloth itself should be exactly five [finger-breadths].
The wise man should fasten the wheel-noose, well-situated by means of a support,
and have it made firm with a binding of strong cord.
The two loops should be made below, five spans in width;
they should be made with a cord of one thousand [threads], five spans in width.
The support and the lover should be made with a thousand *pala*s,
or one may make them with eight hundred *pala*s, or even with six hundred *pala*s.
A width of four tālas is proclaimed as the middle [measurement],
and a width of three and a half tālas is prescribed as the rule.
The fruit is said to be five measures, four measures, or three measures;
it is endowed with four gates, or the gate is [measured] by a finger-breadth.
It should be provided with earrings that are smooth and clear;
for each pair of earrings, there should be a circular chain.
One should attach the ring supporting the chain by means of a suspension;
leaving a space of one span or four finger-breadths on the ground, one should cause it to hang down.
The two pillars should be made beautiful and each one man’s height;
there, one should place two stone slabs filled with two cubits of sand.
[193] Two pits measuring two cubits each should be established with effort;
the wise man should fill the remainder on all sides with sand. He should cause it to be done in such a manner that it attains stability.

Regarding "at the front, at the base," and so forth: the binding of the cloth-strip with gold or other materials should be performed on the scale in such a way that the scale does not break due to the pressure exerted when inserting the supporting pegs, piercing, or striking.

The support (*avalambana*) should be made in the shape of a raised beak with a ring-base attached to a chain and so forth, hanging from the tip. Alternatively, having placed an upward-facing nail of copper or similar material at the point of suspension on the balance-beam, one should fashion an archway (*toraṇa*) made of copper or similar material that rests upon two side-posts fixed across a horizontal nail threaded through the hole at its base; this archway should be joined to a ring suspended above and below by cords tied to its rings. Regarding "one tongue": this refers to the aforementioned upward-facing nail called a "ring" located in the middle of the balance-beam; the "tongue-archway" has already been described previously, and this is seen in small balances used by goldsmiths and others. Regarding "of the north," however: at the base of the upward-facing iron peg whose ring-tip is suspended in the middle of the north [beam], one should place an iron plate spread out and extended over the north; then, having spread it out horizontally, one should join it so that its base is divided into two parts above that.

Regarding the phrase "the peg (*śaṅku*) is provided with a hollow": when the ends are coiled and suspended from above and below, one should fix a ring as thick as a thumb upon the downward-facing peg; for it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "The peg provided with a hollow is equipped with a ring. Regarding the phrase "of the cloth-belt (*paṭṭa*)," this is a statement of measurement for the aforementioned belt: "one should bind it at five *mātrās*, a *yava*-finger (*yavāṅgula*). One should attach the ring called the "wheel-noose" (*cakrapāśa*), which serves as the support for the chains of the respective scales, to the two ends suspended from the extremities of the balance-beam. "Copper" (*śulva*) means bronze. Regarding the phrase "the two supports (*ādhārau*)," the two supports—which hold the stream of the sacrificer’s materials—should be made respectively of eighteen, sixteen, and twelve *palas* of copper, with widths of five *prādeśas* and so forth, and heights of five, four, and three finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) at their edges. They should be provided with four rings threaded through four holes each, one finger-breadth apart. One should attach the four chains called "scales" (*śikya*), which are joined to the four sets of those rings and have two rings fashioned at the top, as suspenders hanging down from the end of the beam. The four holes of the supports known as the "balance-stand" (*dhaṭa*) should be joined together with beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*), and the two supports should be placed above the ground. Regarding the phrase "four finger-breadths," they should be suspended in the air at a distance of one *prādeśa*. The two pits, however, are for the purpose of digging in the southern and northern pillars. Here, one should note that the pillars are south and north, while the balance-beam extends east to west, because it will be stated later: "One should place the gold to be weighed there in the eastern quarter. Having placed the two stone slabs known as "cloth-stones" (*paṭṭaśilā*) there in a pit filled with two cubits (*dvihasta*) of sand, one should fill it with sand and make it firm.
Listen to this supreme secret: the mandala upon the altar, endowed with the eight auspicious symbols and adorned with a finger-shaped goad.
In the center of the altar— which is strewn with fruits and flowers, provided with incense and lamps, and resembles the surface of a mirror— one should perform [the rite].
One should first draw the mandala, provided with four gates,
endowed with primary and secondary ornaments, and furnished with a pericarp and filaments.
One should have it fashioned with a small knob at its base, endowed with five colors,
and with a vajra in the northern portion and a blazing spear in the southeast.
One should draw a staff in the south, and a sword in the southwest;
a noose is to be drawn in the west, and a banner in the region of the wind (the northwest).
One should draw a mace in the north and a trident in the northeast;
moreover, a discus should be placed to the left of the trident and a lotus to its right.
Having written thus, one should thereafter commence the rite of fire-offering (homakarma):
the principal offering with the Gāyatrī mantra, "Svāhā to Śakra and to Agni."
To Yama, the king of the gods, to Varuṇa, and to Vāyu;
likewise to Kubera, to Īśa, to Viṣṇu, and again to Brahmā.
The oblation should be offered according to the prescribed ritual, ending with *svāhā* and preceded by the *praṇava*,
through the mouth of the fire of one's own Vedic school (*sva-śākhā*), and joined with the *jayā*-offerings and others.
The one most learned in the Vedas should cause all rites to be performed up to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering;
regarding all oblations and the initial oblation, the fuel-stick of the *pālāśa* tree is now described.
One should perform twenty-one oblations with this mantra.

"O Jātavedas, this fuel is not your self; with that [self], grow strong. And if you do grow strong, cause us to prosper with offspring, cattle, spiritual luster, and the enjoyment of food—Svāhā! Bhūḥ Svāhā! Bhuvaḥ Svāhā! Svaḥ Svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ Svāhā!
The fire-oblation of the kindled wood, the sacrificial porridges (caru), and the clarified butter are performed in their proper order.
It is traditionally taught that the sacrificial porridges consist of *śukra* rice, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and mung-bean porridge.

A thousand times, or half of that, or a hundred and eight; "O Agni, you purify our lives; bring us food swiftly; grant us wealth from the pressers. Agni is the seer, the purifying one, the domestic priest of the five peoples. For the sake of greatness, O Agni, purify yourself, the great one; O skillful one, bestowing upon us luster and heroic vigor, grant us wealth and nourishment. O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings. With whatever desire we sacrifice to you, may that be ours. May this man be the father of that one, and that one the father of this one; may we be masters of riches. *Svāhā!*
All of that is common to every oblation, performed according to the prescribed rule;
likewise, there is the offering of fuel-sticks for the principal deity with the Gāyatrī mantra.
One should likewise offer oblations of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and clarified butter (*ājya*) for Śakra and the others;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-offerings (*homa*) for the vajra and the other implements, beginning with a thousand [repetitions] in successive order.
To Brahmā and Viṣṇu, salutations without a mantra for the Brahmayajña.
We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva.
May that Viṣṇu inspire us.
This most auspicious path of fire-offerings (homa) has been described as a distinction:
twenty-five [offerings] each, separately, with dūrvā grass sprinkled with milk.
We sacrifice to Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity. Like a cucumber from its stem, may I be liberated from death, not from immortality. Svāhā!
This offering of *dūrvā* grass is praised, as is the *vāstu-homa* in every respect;
likewise, the expiation with the *aghora* mantra and the *vāstu-homa* are always recommended.
The expiation is performed one hundred times each with the Aghora mantra and with clarified butter.

"Listen," and so forth: within the previously mentioned altar (*vedi*), the mandala named Sarvatobhadra should be drawn; and by the terms "ornament" (*śobhā*) and "subsidiary ornament" (*upaśobhā*), the initiation mandala (*dīkṣāmaṇḍala*) described in the *Pañcasāra* is to be understood, the characteristics of which two have been detailed in the *Paribhāṣā*. Regarding the word "thunderbolt" (*vajra*): outside the mandala, the weapons of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) should be drawn in their respective quarters. The oblation (*homa*) for Gāyatrī-Audryā is performed in the principal fire-pit (*pradhānakuṇḍa*); the Rudra-Gāyatrī is: "We know that Tatpuruṣa, we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra inspire us."

The oblation (*homa*) should be performed in the eight fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) of the East and other directions using the names of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), such as Śakra and others, preceded by the *praṇava* (OM), in the dative case, and ending with *svāhā*. The oblation for Brahmā and Viṣṇu should be performed in the *apośāna* pit. Once the fire has been kindled according to the ritual face of one’s own Vedic school (*śākhā*), the subsidiary oblations (*upahoma*) beginning with the *jaya* offerings should be performed with clarified butter (*ājya*) after the principal oblations (*pradhānahoma*). For Āpastamba has stated: "Having offered the principal oblations in their respective places, he offers the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, *rāṣṭrabhṛt*, and *prājāpatya* offerings, followed by the *vyāhṛti* and the *sauviṣṭakṛta*. This mention of the *jaya* and other offerings is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those [rituals] prescribed in one's own respective *gṛhya-sūtra* that follow thereafter.

[197] The *sarvahoma* (all-encompassing oblation) is the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*). In that regard, the fuel-stick (*samit*) is made of *pālāśa* wood. Here, "oblation" (*homa*) refers to the form consisting of the preparatory rites (*anvādhāna*), the fuel-wood (*idhma*), and so forth. Regarding both the *sarvahoma* and the initial oblation (*agrahoma*), the *pālāśa* fuel-stick is prescribed; furthermore, the phrase "numbering twenty-one" constitutes a separate statement. In that context, during the preparatory rite (*anvādhāna*) with the *vyāhṛti* formulas, four fuel-sticks are to be offered. With the mantra "This is for you" (*ayaṃ te*), the remaining fuel-wood—previously employed for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the *ārā*, the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), etc.—is to be placed in the fire. This also serves as an illustration of the preceding ritual system (*pūrvatantro*) as stated in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. Next, the oblation of fuel-sticks and other materials must be performed. In this regard, the sacrificial substances (*homya*) such as the five items beginning with the fuel-sticks—including *caru* (cooked rice) and pure food—are to be used. Prior to the principal oblation, an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*) is to be performed with the four mantras beginning with "O Agni, [grant] long life" (*agne āyūṃṣi*). In the central sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the principal oblation of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and *caru* is to be performed using the *Rudra-gāyatrī* itself. In the respective pits for the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) such as Indra and others, an oblation of clarified butter numbering one thousand or five hundred is to be offered according to their individual mantras. Furthermore, in each pit, an oblation of twenty-five *dūrvā* grasses is to be performed with the *ambaka* mantra, and an oblation of the site (*vastuhoma*) with the mantra "O Lord of the Site" (*vāstoṣpate*). The site-oblation may also be performed using the names of the various deities such as Śikhin and Parjanya; these will be explained in the section on the gift of a house. An expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*) numbering one hundred is to be performed with clarified butter. All of these oblations are to be performed after the worship of the Lord together with his retinue (*saparivāreśvara-pūjana*). For it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "Having described the worship of the deity with the words 'In the center, the Lord of Gods; on the left, accompanied by Gaurī,' and so forth, the oblation is then to be performed."
On the right [he placed] Brahmā, on the left Viṣṇu, and Śiva, the teacher of the universe;
in the center of the altar was Mahādeva, surrounded by the hosts of Indra and the other gods.
Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Ravi, the god Divākara;
likewise Ūṣā, Prabhā, Prajñā, Sandhyā, and Sāvitrī.
To the Great-Souled One described in the Śākhā— Chāyā, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi,
Vistarā, Śubhagā, and Bodhanī— one should circumambulate [the tree] clockwise.
Having fully worshipped the Sun-god, who nourishes all, seated upon his lotus throne,
one should first prepare the Prabhūta vessel in the east and likewise the Vimala vessel in the south.
One should worship Sāra in the western part and Ārādhya in the north;
one should know that Sukha is in the center, and [the others] in the filaments in due order.
Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, Vimalā in sequence,
Āmoghā, and Vidyutā, with Sarvatomukhī in the center.
Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha, Jīva in due order,
as well as Bhārgava, Manda, Rāhu, and Ketu on all sides.
One should worship, perform fire oblations, and especially offer water for the guest (arghya);
one should feed there the Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.

Having thus completed this extensive ritual procedure for those perfected in the study of the sciences, while the fire-oblation (homa) is being performed, [one should act] in the central location situated in the eastern direction.
One should cause the king to ascend according to the prescribed rite with the Rudrādhyāya;
there, one should maintain the sacrificer for the duration of one ghaṭikā according to the rule.
The sacrificer should mutter the mantra known as the Rudra-gāyatrī for half a ghaṭikā or half of that; at that very spot, he should begin his seated posture.
Having looked at his garment, the wise king— equipped with ornaments, bearing a sword and a shield, and composed in mind— struck [the image] with his beard.
At the beginning and especially at the end, accompanied by blessings, prosperity, and other auspicious rites,
the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences should perform the *puṇyāha* ceremony.
With the most beautiful sounds of the Vedas, such as the words "Victory" and "Auspiciousness," accompanied by dances,
instrumental music, songs, and all manner of splendors;
One should place gold there in the direction of Indra (the east);
when the two scales are equal and balanced, then the weight on the scale is equal.

"Having worshipped Brahmā," and so forth: having fully worshipped Īśvara, who is surrounded in the center by the deities beginning with Brahmā, one should then worship the Sun. Within the pericarp (karṇikā) previously conceived within the mandala, *Ūṣa* and *Āditya* are to be worshipped; then *Prabhā* and *Bhāskara*, as well as the four pairs of deities beginning with *Prajñā* and *Bhānu*, are to be worshipped in the corners starting from the southeast (*āgneya*). The four powers (*śakti*) beginning with *Chāyā* are to be worshipped in the directions starting from the east; however, *Vistārā* and the others are on the legs of the seat in the southeast and other corners, while *Prabhūtā* and the others are on the parts of the seat in the east and other directions. *Paramasukhā* is to be established in the center as the sun's rug; upon that, one should worship the aforementioned Sun, named *Āditya*, atop a lotus. The powers (*śakti*) beginning with *Dīptā* reside in the filaments (*kesara*), and among them, *Sarvatomukhī* is to be worshipped in the pericarp. Then, outside of that, on the tips of the petals, those headed by *Soma* are to be worshipped. Having thus propitiated Śiva and Sūrya, and having performed the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) as prescribed in the Śaiva tradition in the Śiva-fire, one should offer an oblation (*argha*) to the Sun, commence the fire-sacrifice (*homa*), feed the Brāhmaṇas, and after reciting the "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāha*) formula—which is a limb of the weighing ceremony—before the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should cause the weighing to take place.
The best [type] is said to exceed one hundred niṣkas; the middling is considered to be half of that;
and the lowest shall be half of that as well—thus it is prescribed there as being of three kinds.
A pair of garments, as well as a turban, earrings, a neck ornament,
a finger-ring, and an ornament for the wrist.
And all these very items, at the commencement of a religious rite,
one should first give to the domestic priest and then cause them to be presented to the officiating priests.
The wise one should give all the previously mentioned ornaments, together with the turban and the garment, as well as the covering for the earrings, to those who perform the rite.
One should cause a hundred and fifty *dakṣiṇās* to be given to a Brahmin,
and one should cause ten *niṣkas* to be given to each of all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
One should cause the materials used for the sacrifice to be given to the preceptor;
however, one should cause the desired gifts for the other twice-born ones to be given separately.
He himself should cause sacrificial fees to be given to the domestic priests and the twice-born;
they should especially be bestowed upon the teachers and those learned in the Vedas.
He should release those who have been made captives and those confined in prisons;
he should bathe the Supreme Lord with water from a thousand jars.
One may worship the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, with pure ghee alone,
or with milk, or with curd, or even with all [other] substances.
It should be given either with the Brahmakūrca or again with the Pañcagavya;
the cow-urine with the Gāyatrī and the cow-dung with the Praṇava.
With the mantra "May you swell" (āpyāyasva), he should offer milk; with "O Dadhikrāvan" (dadhikrāvṇo), curd;
and with "You are brilliance" (tejo 'si), clarified butter; then he should perform the consecration with the Īśāna mantra.
With the mantra "devasya tvā," one should bathe the Supreme Lord, the Lord of Gods and Master of All, with fresh jars of kusha-water while reciting the Rudrādhyāya.
O Nandin, [this was done] with the thousand pitchers of Śambhu and with the thousands of names,
whether those spoken by Viṣṇu or those belonging to Nandin himself.
Whether it has been proclaimed by Dakṣa, the foremost of sages, or by a wise man,
the Great Worship of Mahādeva must be performed with devotion.
An auspicious gift consisting of half [of the fee] should be given to the teacher who worships Śiva;
and gifts should likewise be given in due order to all those who worship the deities.

One should feed the poor, the blind, the wretched, the helpless, children, the elderly, the emaciated, and the sick according to the prescribed rule, and one should also cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given.

"Two garments," and so forth: the pair of garments, the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), earrings, and other such items should be given at the very beginning, immediately after the selection [of the officiants] and the performance of the *madhuparka* offering, to the domestic priest (*purohita*), the Brahman, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and the assembly members (*sadasya*). To the Preceptor (*ācārya*), double [the amount] should be given; one should give double the amount of ornaments, clothing, and so forth to the Guru. This is because of the statement of the *Matsya-purāṇa*: "One should give to these performers the aforementioned ornaments made of a hundred *niṣkas* or more. Regarding the phrase "and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," having given a fee of a hundred *niṣkas* or more to the Preceptor, one should give ten *niṣkas* to the officiating priests, while for the other attendants, it is merely one *niṣka*.

"Where there are laborers, one should cause a *niṣka* to be given to them separately," according to the statement in the *Kāmika*. The opinion of the *Kāmika* is that the wealth placed upon the scale should be given only to others; [it states]:
"One should cause the wealth mounted on the scale to be bestowed upon the Brahmins."
"One should especially prepare [offerings] for my devotees, or even for my sake; one should give them with faith, especially to the teachers.

Now, it is said that the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka), its worship, and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for its performer must be performed, beginning with the words "with a thousand jars" and so forth. "With all substances" refers to gold, fruits, water containing gems, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and others. "Half the sacrificial fee" means half the amount prescribed as the fee for the teacher of the weighing ceremony (tulārohaṇa). This refers to the giving of the sacrificial fee to the worshippers of Śiva and others. However, in the *Kāmika* [Tantra], the weighing ceremony is mentioned after the great consecration and worship.
Having invoked all the deities worshipped in the mandala, one should perform the fire offering (homa);
one should likewise complete the ritual here with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and so forth.
Having bathed the Supreme Lord with a thousand jars and other vessels,
a great worship should be performed, accompanied by abundant offerings of meat and liquor.
One should perform an ablution with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), milk, and so forth;
thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins and proceed with the ritual of ascending the scale (tulārohaṇa).

[202] Now, following the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it is established that the completion of the subsequent ritual manual (*uttaratantra*)—beginning with the *pūrṇāhuti* offering—and the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) must be performed. It was stated that one should bathe Īśāna with a thousand jars while reciting the thousand names; this has been declared exactly as taught in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*. The Thousand Names are now written out.
The Sages said:
"O Nandin, the thousand names of Rudra were [revealed] by Brahmā."
O Sūta of noble vows, you have related everything for the sake of the god Brahmā.
"You ought to recite the auspicious thousand names of the Brahmins.
Sūta said:
"Of Hara, who is the self of all beings and possesses immeasurable splendor..."
O observer of noble vows, there are indeed one thousand and eight names for everyone.
I shall now fully declare that mantra which, when recited, enables even the best of sages to attain the status of Gaṇapati and which destroys all sins.
Oṃ! You are the steadfast one, the pillar, the Lord, the radiant one, the source, the giver of boons, the most excellent;
