you are the soul of all, renowned everywhere, the performer of all actions, and the progenitor.
He has matted hair, wears a deer skin, and bears a topknot; he is all-pervading and the creator of all beings.
He is Hari, he is known as Dakṣiṇa, and he is the Lord who withdraws all living creatures.
He is both engagement and withdrawal; the restrainer born from the mouth;
the Lord who wanders in the cremation ground, moves through the sky, and makes the earth weep.
He is to be saluted; he is of great deeds, an ascetic, and the sustainer of all beings; disguised in the garb of a madman, he is the Lord of Progeny for all the worlds.
He is of great form and great body, possessing all forms and great fame;
he is the Great Self and the being of all beings, yet deformed, dwarfed, and unassuming.
Lokapāla, Antarhitātman, Prābhāsa,
Bhavana, Ruci, Pavitra, Mahas, Niyama, and Niyamāśrita.
[203] He is the beginning of all actions and primary rites, the primordial source and treasure-trove;
he is the thousand-eyed one, the large-eyed one, Soma, Dakṣa, and the maker of nectar.
He whose seat is the moon and sun, the comet, the planet, the lord of planets, and the intellect;
the first king, the creator of fear, the one who fixed the arrow upon the deer, and the sinless one.
One of great austerity and terrible penance, a mirror, a performer of many rites; the mantra practiced for a year is the supreme measure of austerity.
The teacher of yoga, the great image, the one of great semen, the one of great strength;
he whose semen is gold, the omniscient one, the excellent seed, whose vehicle is the bull.
He has ten arms, is unblinking, blue-throated, and the lord of Umā;
he is the universal form, the best of ascetics, powerful and heroic, and the leader of the strong.
The creator of the host, the Lord of the Host, the sky-clad one, and the one who is desired;
the knower of mantras, the supreme mantra, the performer of all states of being, Hara.

Carrying a water-pot, armed with a bow, possessing many hands and bearing a skull-cup, he is the lord of the thunderbolt and the lord of the śataghnī weapon; great, he has swords and arrows as his weapons.
Aja, Mṛgarūpa, Tejas, Tejaḥkara,

having taken hold of one's chosen deity and bathed it with ghee and other substances.
This procedure for all types of gift-weighing (tulādāna) has been proclaimed;

Through honey one obtains good fortune; through oil, many offspring;

From salt comes beauty, and from jaggery, freedom from disease;
through sugar one gains a husband with no rival wife, and through sandalwood, a beautiful form.
She shall never be separated from her husband, as the scales and the saffron are inseparable;
and there shall never be any distress in her heart, as with milk and the scale.

Having consecrated a single tulā-measure of lead with a mantra, he should give it to the twice-born;

A person does not experience the prolongation of sorrow.

Having descended from the scale, he should present it to his preceptor;
he who, free from envy, should give this gift of the scale according to this rite.
He goes to the world of Pārvatī, served by hosts of apsarases;

Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the *tulāpuruṣa* consisting of ghee and other substances, as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"By this very same procedure, some [perform it] again with silver."
Likewise, some eminent Brahmins desire [the offering] with camphor.
"By this" means by that which was described as the primary gift of the *tulāpuruṣa*.
Likewise, on the third day of the bright fortnight, women proud of their good fortune offer [gifts] with saffron, or with salt, or with molasses.
In that case, one should cause the mantras or the fire-oblations to be offered in exactly this manner.
Viśvāmitra said:
When the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, one should weigh one's body against gold;
when there is an eclipse of the moon, however, it is with silver—listen now to how the gift should be made.
Yoked at the commencement of the Pravargya rite, arising from the body of the vessel, I give this for the removal of all sins; may the Moon be pleased.
Having uttered this, the best of the twice-born should pour water into the waters;
the ancestors are pleased by [offerings] in bell-metal, and the grandfathers likewise by those in copper.
Lakṣmī is pleased by salt produced from the ocean, and Pārvatī by jaggery;
jaggery is favored for its fragrance, while clothing brings good fortune, and salt is excellent for bestowing conjugal bliss.
"May the one who is the delight of the universe be pleased"—this is declared to be the mantra for the gift.
O King, by means of the Tulāpuruṣa rite, go to that supreme state.
With their souls purified of all evil, they attain liberation from which there is no rebirth;
yet having killed a Brahmin, one must once again weigh out a body for oneself.
By giving gold equal to one's own weight, one expiates the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thus ends the section on the Tulāpuruṣa rite involving silver and other materials.
Now, in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa,
Sanatkumāra said:
Now listen to the Tulāpuruṣa-dāna arising from the conqueror of death (Mṛtyuñjaya):
eight types of metal are to be offered for the pacification of all diseases.
Bell-metal should be given for consumption (yakṣman), tin for hemorrhoids (arśas),
lead for epilepsy (apasmāra), and copper for severe leprosy (kuṣṭha).
One should administer copper in cases of internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), silver in cases of menorrhagia and urinary disorders (pradara-meha),
and gold in all diseases, along with cooked rice mixed with the fruit of the *mṛt* plant.
Likewise, one should give an offering produced from fruit during a long and terrible eclipse;
molasses (*gauḍa*) during diseases caused by *bhasmaka*, and a medicinal preparation (*yoga*) during *gaṇḍamālā*.

When there is sluggishness of the digestive fires, one should use *jāṅgala* [ghee]; when there is horripilation, *pauṣyaka*; and when there is cough, asthma, or dropsy, *madhūdbhava* should likewise be administered.
*Jāṅgala* refers to that which is produced from wood.
Similarly, that which originates from honey should be given.
Likewise, ghee derived from milk should be administered for the pacification of vomiting;
milk for the destruction of bile (pitta); and curd for the opening of abscesses.
Salt is for the destruction of strength; flour-based food is for the destruction of ringworm;
and grain is likewise traditionally held to be for the destruction of all diseases.
With respect to the deities, Mahābhairava is said to reside in iron; Pūṣan and the Aśvins are in bell-metal, and Vāyu is traditionally held to be in lead.
In copper, the Sun is said to reside; likewise, in bell-metal, Mars;
in silver, the ancestors are to be known; and in gold, all the deities.
Soma resides in fruit, Apsarases in molasses, and Vināyaka in betel leaf; the Gandharvas reside in flowers, and Agni is likewise remembered to dwell in the forest.
In honey, the Yakṣas are said to reside with effort; in ghee, Mṛtyuñjaya is remembered;
in milk, all the hosts of stars (Tārāgaṇas) dwell; and in curd, the serpents are proclaimed to abide.
In the flour is the god Prajāpati, and in the cooked food are all the deities;
when one is afflicted, one should obtain a vessel from a meritorious place.
Whatever is given here according to the rite for attaining the Conqueror of Death over death, that alone serves for the sake of all pacification; of this there is no doubt.
The meaning is that one should worship Mṛtyuñjaya according to the procedure for attaining Mṛtyuñjaya.
And the procedure for the worship of Mṛtyuñjaya is found in the Devīpurāṇa:
"By means of the mantra *oṃ juṃ saḥ*, this four-armed, three-eyed deity [is worshipped]."
The Lord, wearing a rosary of beads, holds it with his right hand.
In his left hand he holds a vessel of nectar filled with ambrosia;
his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and he is adorned with divine ornaments.
White in color and wearing blue garments, he is seated upon a lotus;
his seed-syllable (bīja) is known as *jātī*, and his crest (*śikhā*) is remembered as *javaṃvāśva*.
"Vauṣaṭ" is proclaimed as the armor (*kavaca*) and the eye (*netra*);
"Jaḥ phaṭ" shall always be the weapon (*astra*); and the syllable *Oṃ* is the mantra for invocation (*āvāhana*).
The syllable *oṃ* indeed belongs to the rite of dismissal; there are eight powers measured by five syllables:
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā.
Bhadrakālī, Kapālī, Kṣemyā, Amṛtā, and Parājitā;
by the application of the mantra *oṃ juṃ saḥ*, Śiva, the Conqueror of Death (*mṛtyuṃjaya*), is to be worshipped.
Just as the worship of a Brāhmaṇa is performed with perfumes and other offerings according to the rule,
so too is the procedure prescribed for all the gifts mentioned in the Mṛtyuñjaya [Tantra].
It should be recited: *oṃ jūṃ saḥ*. Indeed, one should always accomplish the fulfillment of the donor's desires.
Then, one should implant this mantra into the heart of the recipient within the metal.

Accompanied by sandals, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, and a throne,
[this should be offered] during the auspicious solstices, equinoxes, and on festival days such as Vyatīpāta.
[218] Endowed with faith, in a pure place— especially during the northern course of the sun—
one should bathe the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Then, one should bathe the Lord Dhūrjaṭi first with pure ghee alone,
and thereafter with fragrant sandalwood water.
Having anointed the Supreme Lord with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, kaṅkola, and musk, one should then worship Him with flowers.
Having offered the food offering with devotion and a faultless mind,
one should then bow down to the Lord of the worlds and pray as follows.
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, compassionate Supreme Lord,
deliver me, who am distressed by the constriction of the mire of saṃsāra.
Having thus prayed, the man who gives iron equal to his own weight goes to the same world as Śiva for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Then, having returned here once more, he shall become the sole sovereign on earth.

In all of these, gold is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), because it is prescribed according to one's capacity for those gifts where no specific fee is mentioned. Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Iron *Tulāpuruṣa* as declared in the *Skanda Purāṇa*. Now, the second great gift (*mahādāna*), called the *Hiraṇyagarbha*, is described. In the *Matsya Purāṇa*, Matsya said:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the unsurpassed great gift."
Through gold, one attains that which is called Hiraṇyagarbha, the destroyer of great sins.
Then, having reached an auspicious day, as in the case of the Tulāpuruṣa gift,
one should provide for the officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, ornaments, coverings, and so forth.
Having fasted, one should likewise perform the invocation of Lokeśa;
having performed the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), one should likewise perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).

In this rite, everything— including the selection of the place and time, the increase of prosperity, the *śrāddha*, the worship of Śiva and other deities, the recitation by Brahmins, the formal invitation (*varaṇa*) of the preceptor and officiating priests, the offering of the *madhuparka*, the preparation of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and the altar (*vedi*), as well as the collection of materials, the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*)— should be understood as being prescribed according to the *Tulāpuruṣadāna* described in the *Matsyapurāṇa*, which serves as the archetype for the fifteen great gifts beginning with the *Hiraṇyagarbha*. One should have a beautiful sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) brought, made of refined gold, measuring twenty-seven finger-breadths in height, and containing a golden lotus within it.
Its width should be reduced by one-third, and it is praised when shaped like a drum (muraja).

"Kunda" refers to the vessel known as *hiraṇyagarbha*. This is made of refined gold (*tapanīya*), consisting of a golden eight-petaled lotus; that very [lotus] is what is designated by the term "navel. "With a width reduced by one-third" means a width of forty-eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). "In the shape of a *muraja*" means in the shape of a drum (*mṛdaṅga*). Regarding the reading "filled with clarified butter and milk" found in some versions: there, the quantities of ghee and milk are equal. Although it is said to be "overflowing," nevertheless, it should be filled in such a way that, upon the entry of the sacrificer, it does not spill over the outside.
The ten entrails along with the gems, the sickle, and likewise the needle; the golden stalk with the crystal, joined externally with the sun.
In the same manner, one should likewise place a golden waist-band, a sacred thread,
and similarly a golden staff and a water-pot by the side.

There is a reading in some places: *daśāntrāṇi*, *daśakhaṇḍāni*, *abhrāṇi* ("ten intestines," "ten pieces," "clouds"). These are golden, and they are called "clouds" because of their cloud-like shape. Some say that *abhra* means a spade (*khanitram*). The five well-known jewels, along with the casket (*sapīṭakam*) and accompanied by the *majjupā* (a type of vessel), are to be placed "outside"—this connects with the phrase "one should place them on the sides in the outer region of the golden basin (*hemakuṇḍa*). There is an alternative reading: *vahnir ādityasaṃyutam*. The characteristics of the fire-god (*vahni*) and the sun-god (*bhāskara*) will be described in the section on the gift of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍadāna*). Regarding the reading *vahnim apyayasaṃyutam*, in that case *apyaya* refers to Varuṇa; its characteristics are also described in that same place. "A covering for the navel" means a golden cloth intended to cover the navel; the sacrificial knife (*dātra*) and other implements should also be made entirely of gold.
The arrangement should be lotus-shaped, exceeding [the base] by one finger on all sides,
provided with a string of pearls and endowed with petals of ruby.
Then one should worship it, having placed it upon a mound of a drona-measure of sesame seeds in the center of the altar.
Droṇa has been explained in the section on technical definitions (paribhāṣā).

In this matter, since no specific measurement of gold for the creation of the *Hiraṇyagarbha* is prescribed, the vessel should be fashioned to such a size as is suitable for the sacrificer’s entry and maintenance; and having placed a *droṇa* of sesame seeds upon a drawn wheel in the center of the altar, one should install it thereon and worship it. Then, on the day following the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the *Tulāpuruṣa* gift, one should perform the recitation by the Brahmins and complete the remainder of the ritual, beginning with the *pūrṇāhuti*. Thereafter, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is performed as before with the waters from the jars situated near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Thus it is said:
Then, amidst auspicious sounds and the resonance of Vedic chants,
he was bathed with water containing all medicinal herbs by the preeminent masters of the Vedas.
All medicinal herbs have been explained.
Wearing white garlands and garments, adorned with all ornaments,
and holding a handful of flowers, one should recite this mantra:
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha and to Hiraṇyakavaca;
homage again and again to the Lord of the gods of the seven worlds, the sustainer of the universe.
The worlds, headed by the Bhūrloka, are situated within your womb;
likewise, O God, Brahmā and the other deities are there—salutations to you, the sustainer of the universe.
Salutations to you, O support of the worlds; salutations to you, O refuge of the worlds.
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, within whose womb resides the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Since you alone are the self of all beings, established within the elements and the living beings,
therefore deliver me from the entire ocean of saṃsāra and its suffering.
Having addressed him thus, he entered into their midst and sat facing north.
Grasping the faces of Dharmarāja and Caturmukha with both fists and placing his head between his knees, he remained there for five breaths.

In this [image], Dharmarāja is made of gold; his characteristics have been described in the context of the *tulāpuruṣa* rite. Furthermore, Caturmukha is also golden; his characteristics will be explained in the section on the *brahmāṇḍa-dāna*. In that [image], Dharmarāja is in the right fist and Caturmukha is in the left fist.
Then those eminent twice-born ones should perform for Hiraṇyagarbha the rites of conception (*garbhādāna*), the male-impregnation (*puṃsavana*), and the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*).

In these rites to be described, beginning with the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) and including the birth-rites (*jātakarma*) and so forth, one should understand that there is also "non-coveting" (*anavalobhana*); here, one should merely perform meditation accompanied by mantras.
Then, one should satisfy the preceptor with the sound of singing and auspicious proclamations, and thereafter perform the sixteen other rites, beginning with the birth-rite.

And these are enumerated as follows: (1) the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), (2) the naming-rite (*nāmakaraṇa*), (3) the first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*), (4) the first feeding (*annaprāśana*), (5) the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), (6) the initiation (*upanayana*), (7) the *prājāpatya*, (8) the *aindra*, (9) the *āgneya*, and (10) the *saumya*. There are four *vedavrata*s, namely the *godāna* and the *keśānta*; thus, including the four preceding ones, there are sixteen among both [categories]. Having given the needle and other items to the teacher, he should mutter this mantra:
"Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha; homage to you who are the womb of the universe."
Salutations indeed to the one who has become the abode of the world of moving and unmoving beings!
Formerly, I was born as a mantra, an excellent twice-born man subject to mortal conditions.
"Because of being born from your womb, I shall possess this divine body. Then, O best of the twice-born, those four jars [were filled] once again for you.
They should perform their ablutions, being cheerful and adorned with all their ornaments.
With the water-pots situated near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), they should perform the bathing of the patron; this is the implied meaning.
With the mantra "devasya tvā," while [the patron] is seated upon a golden throne:
"Today, we shall sprinkle the limbs of you who have just been born."
"Live long and be happy with this divine body.
Then, the wise man should give that Hiraṇyagarbha to them.

In this matter, the employment of the words of dedication (*dānavākya*) and so forth, as well as the distribution of materials among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the preceptor (*ācārya*), should be understood to be the same as in the *Tulāpuruṣa* rite.
They are to be honored with one's whole being, or many may be appointed at their command.
There, one should present all the ritual implements to the preceptor.
Sandals, shoes, umbrellas, chowries, seats, vessels,
or even a village or a district, or whatever else may be available.

A *viṣaya* is a collection of villages; "other" refers to gems and so forth. Here too, one should give oneself as an ornament to the teacher, and villages and the like are connected specifically as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), because that is how it is seen in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Then, as before, once the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) has been performed, the worship of the deities, their dismissal (*visarjana*), and so on, should be carried out.

Now we shall explain the ritual procedure for Hiraṇyagarbha. For the removal of all sins, during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, on an auspicious day under a favorable lunar mansion, both the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should have their beards, hair, and nails trimmed. Then, before sunset, the priest takes wood from an *aśvattha* tree grown in the wilderness and consecrates the fire being churned with two verses beginning, "Be born, O Agni, from the *aśvattha*. With the third verse he consecrates the fire once it is born, and with the fourth he places fuel upon it. Having clothed him in a pure garment and caused him to perform the application of collyrium, ointment, and unguents as prescribed, and having fastened garments, perfumes, and golden garlands upon him, he should kindle the fire, take hold of the clarified butter (*ājya*), and offer oblations: "To Hiraṇyagarbha, Svāhā! To Brahmā, Svāhā! To Viṣṇu, Svāhā! To Prajāpati, Svāhā! To Parameṣṭhin, Svāhā! To Ka, Svāhā! Having made these proclamations, he should worship with those same verses. Having tied a golden garland around the fire with the verse, "The gold which was born from Agni, when they bound it," and having performed protection with the four verses beginning, "May the fires protect you," he should spread *darbha* grass and both should sleep and sit upon the ground below. On the following day, at the *abhijit* moment, having placed a golden vessel shaped like a circle reaching up to the navel, along with a lid, a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), a vessel for clarified butter, water vessels, and ornaments for himself—all made of gold—he should bathe the King with golden jars using the *payaḥ-ṛcas*, the two *payaḥ-śrīs*, the *homuca*, the *śānta-toya*, and the *Hiraṇyagarbha-sūtra*, as well as the five names. Having poured the remnants of the offerings (*saṃpāta*) into that vessel, he should cause the King to be addressed by the priest: "The King desires the state of Hiraṇyagarbha; may the venerable ones grant him dominion over men. Once permitted by them, he should cause him to enter with the two verses beginning, "Go forth, O steed," and cover him with the verse, "Thirty-three gods. Without uncovering him, he instructs him: "Restraint of speech, withdrawal of the senses, and with the mind, meditating on the specific [deities], remain meditating upon the venerable Hiraṇyagarbha Parameṣṭhin. He remains thus for seventeen measures of time, for Prajāpati is seventeenfold; this is the turn of Prajāpati. Having been permitted by them with the words, "Lift him up with wealth," he should lift him up. Likewise, having been permitted by the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*), he should lift him up. Uncovering him with the verse, "With a golden wheel," he should lift him up with "In my breath" (*mate prāṇa*). Having lifted him up, he should fasten him with the name of gold and approach him with "Thy death is not... He should gaze at him while being gazed at with "Beholding... Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce blessings, he should pay homage with the verses beginning, "To Hiraṇyagarbha. These indeed are the ones who please Hiraṇyagarbha. The Brahmins should say to him, "Arise, you are favored by Hiraṇyagarbha. Having offered oblations with the *Apratiratha* hymn and concluded the rite, he should go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the verse, "In the waters, O Varuṇa, is your king," and after bathing, sprinkling himself with purifiers, and adorning himself, he should worship the Sun.
"Since you are gold as an embryo and are born from the womb of gold, you are Hiraṇyagarbha; therefore, protect me from great fear. Thus [he said].

Having turned clockwise with the words "The turning of the sun," and having approached the planets with the words "Homage to the planets," and having worshipped Agni with the verse "O Agni, you are the diminisher," he should release [the bull] and give a hundred thousand [cows] as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the twice-born, along with a choice village, a *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a vessel for clarified butter, a water-pot, and ornaments; or he should give to the members of the assembly (*sadasya*) as much as they may desire, or as much as they might be satisfied with, and he should serve the Brahmins with food according to his wish. On this matter there are these verses:
Where there are those who have reached the further shore of the four Vedas and are the best among the knowers of Brahman...
If they are pleased, whatever blessings they may utter shall become a complete sacrifice for him.
By the grace of the brahmins, the sun shines in the sky;
even Indra, by their grace, outshines the gods.
"The fruit of the gift of gold is immortality," so says the Śruti;
for it is heard that he who is its donor attains immortality.
Those stainless royal sages of old, beginning with Ikṣvāku,
having given gold to the brahmins, became light and abide in heaven.
That king who has been thus consecrated according to the ritual prescribed by the expounder of the Veda attains here sovereignty over his subjects, as well as preeminence and excellence.
Having indeed experienced bliss together with Brahmā in that Satyaloka, which consists of light, one does not return here again.
Thus says the Brāhmaṇa. In the Matsya Purāṇa: "He who, according to this rite, should present the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha on an auspicious day, is ordained to dwell in the world of Brahmā."
In the pure realms of the world-protectors, he shall dwell for the duration of each Manvantara;
for as long as a hundred crores of Kalpas, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Freed from the impurities of the Kali age, worshipped by both the accomplished and the unaccomplished,
he is fanned with rows of beautiful garlands by celestial nymphs.
Indeed, even a single person may rescue a hundred ancestors, as well as kinsmen— sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons— even if they are submerged in hell.
Whoever thus recites this, or whoever hears it correctly here,
shall be honored by the Siddhas in the world of the Enemy of Madhupura; and he who gives even a thought to people for their benefit, [attains the same].
He shall be the leader of the people who have been divided, and his [efforts] shall be unfailing.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha.
The Blessed One said:
Listen to that gift among the duties of giving which is the most excellent of all gifts.
By performing which, living beings are always liberated from all sins.
For him who gives [this] to the Brahmins, even heaven is not far off;
he should fashion that Hiraṇyagarbha out of eight *tulās* of gold.
On one side of the scale, there is an increase of seven, six, five, or four [units];
having fashioned a sacrificial pit made of gold, three cubits in height.
One should draw a golden lotus in a clean and level place; it should be auspicious, two finger-breadths in diameter, circular, and adorned with various jewels.
The mandala should be square, four cubits in size, and have four gates;
having drawn a lotus in the center, one should cause it to be strewn with jewels.
The sacrificial pit established upon a lotus is known as Hemagarbha;
it is two spans in width and four spans in length.
Having fashioned a beautiful golden navel encircled with a golden thread,
if it is made to the proper measure within the interior of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), [it is auspicious].
One should fill that pit with milk and worship it with fragrant flowers;
and upon the pit, on its sides, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
A man, having bathed and being pure, should properly fashion images of the Sun, the planets, and the world-protectors out of gold, and worship all the deities.
There one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and the twice-born should perform the fire oblation (homa).
Having performed the ritual entry for the sacrifice, one should encircle that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Everything should be surrounded with garments until the rite is completed,
including the *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, and so forth.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], he should afterwards go forth, concealing that within the interior of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
and place a golden thread upon the navel and the region of the neck.
Having taken hold [of the vessel], he should draw the Brahmins toward him; the donor shall go from heaven to the earth.
Raising the sun [the vessel] aloft, he should cause the loud sound of conchs and trumpets to resound.
[227] Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha!
One should recite this mantra while performing the sixteen purificatory rites, beginning with the birth ceremony (jātakarman).
One who knows the mantras should have the twice-born perform the Vedic rites as prescribed;
then, one should feed the officiating priests that prepared milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should apply that very remainder of what was eaten by the best of the twice-born to oneself;
and [one should offer] the beautiful Hiraṇyagarbha together with a golden navel.
A man or a woman should give all of that—along with their sacrifices and charitable works—to a Brahmin priest; thus they attain the state of being born from the Self of Brahman.
Listen also to the fruit that belongs to him who performs this great merit:
upon death, he attains the state of Brahmā, with a swan as his vehicle, radiant like the sun.
Served by the daughters of Brahmā, he goes to the world of Brahmā;
there he sports like Brahmā for three Brahmā-years.
Having descended from the Brahma-world, he is honored in the world of Indra;
and after delighting in the world of Indra for three hundred million years, he remains there.
Then, having sported for ten million years each in the delightful city of Brahmā, as well as in the cities of the Vidyādharas and the Gandharvas, he likewise enjoyed himself.
When this world has been attained, the Lord, the supreme king of kings,
[reigns] over a mandala three times as large, extending for a hundred yojanas.
Indeed, a hero endowed with beauty and good fortune is born; for a hundred years, his reign shall be prosperous and free from thorns—of this there is no doubt.
He is radiant, always partaking of happiness, righteous, and one who has conquered his senses.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Indeed, one scale has been described for these [deities], having first employed the primordial Form."
[228] I shall now describe the second [mantra], Hiraṇyagarbha, which bestows all accomplishments.
The lower vessel is prescribed with a thousand pieces of gold;
the upper vessel is made with half that amount, being just large enough to fit over the mouth.
One should thus fashion a beautiful fruit, adorned with all ornaments;
one should meditate upon the two wives below in the vessel, endowed with the three qualities.
One should worship the Goddess Caturviṃśatikā, who embodies Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Agni,
in the upper vessel which transcends the qualities (guṇas), and the Lord of Umā (Śiva) as the thirty-sixth principle.
One should meditate upon the Self as the twenty-fifth Puruṣa, the lotus-born,
in the previously mentioned location, specifically within the mandala upon the altar.
Having led [the image] there and wrapped it in new cloths, one should place it in the midst of śāli rice,
smear it with a paste of black gram, and fill [the vessel] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should worship with the five [deities] beginning with Īśāna according to the rule;
and the worship as well as the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed in due order, just as before.

The first [rite], consisting of the acts prescribed for the *tulāpuruṣa*, serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for the gifts beginning with the *hiraṇyagarbha*; therefore, it does not take another form. The meaning is that, together with the specific particulars of the *hiraṇyagarbha* and other rites, there is a general conjunction (*samuccaya*) of everything stated for the *tulāpuruṣa*, from the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) up to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). It should be noted that "one should perform the plowing with a thousand [gold pieces]. One should make the lower vessel out of gold by means of a thousand [pieces]; the upper vessel should be made with half of that, or both may be made with a thousand.
It should be made two-thirds, three-quarters, one-and-a-quarter, or even one-and-a-half [of the standard size],
or it may be made double, or according to what is available.
Or, having fashioned it from a noble tree, one should wrap it with gold bands.
Thus it is stated in the Kāmika-tantra. [229] And this refers to the subject of one who is qualified for a small gift; however, regarding the case of the wealthy, it is as stated in the Tulā-tantra:
"The best [liṅga] has forty-six thousand [units], while the middling is declared to have twenty-five thousand."

"One should remember the Goddess and the Consort"—it should be understood that this means having fashioned their images. Also in the *Vātula*: "The serene form of Umā should be made in the lower vessel, while the embodiment of Maheśa should be made in the upper vessel."
Alternatively, one should indeed fashion Lakṣmī upon the portion representing Śakti;
however, the supreme and auspicious form of Viṣṇu should be fashioned upon the upper vessel.

The characteristics of these will be described in the section on the gift of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍadāna*). Regarding the phrase "himself" (*ātmānam*): one should contemplate the sacrificer, infused by the Lord while in the womb, as being the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*). Then, one should place the lotus situated within the mandala, together with the fruit known as Hiraṇyagarbha, in the center of the pericarp upon a heap of grain. The paste of black gram (*māṣakalka*) is intended for the purpose of making the iron plate seamless. The filling with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is stated in the *Vātula*: "Cow's urine is twice the amount of milk; curd is said to be half the amount of milk; cow dung should be known as half of that; and ghee should be equal to the cow dung."
One should pour cow urine there with the verse beginning "hiṃ kṛṇvatī," and one should apply cow dung there with the verse beginning "śakamayam."
One should prepare milk there with the mantra "āpyāyasva," and one should employ curd there with the mantra "dadhi krāvṇa."
One should mix ghee with the mantra and stir the ghee therein;
thus, the preceptor should diligently fill it up to the height of the knees.
"The wise man should indeed completely fill [the vessel] with the *brahmajajñāna* mantra;
having entered facing east, the wise man should sit down after entering facing north.
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, the mantras beginning with *Īśāna* are found in the Taittirīya Śruti.

Īśāna, lord of all sciences, lord of all beings, sovereign of Brahman, supreme lord of Brahman—may Śiva be my Brahman, may he be Sadāśiva. I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta. In existence, in non-existence, and beyond existence, favor me; salutations to Bhavodbhava. Salutations to Vāmadeva; salutations to Jyeṣṭha; salutations to Śreṣṭha; salutations to Balavikaraṇa; salutations to Balapramathana; salutations to Sarvabhūtadamana; salutations to Manonmana. To the non-terrible ones, and to the terrible ones, and to those more terrible than the terrible, from every side, to all you who are all the gods, let there be salutation to you in your forms as Rudras. We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra inspire us.
"As before" means as in the case of the Tulāpuruṣa gift mentioned in the Liṅga Purāṇa.
Having recited the Gāyatrī of Gaurī, he himself should enter facing the east:
"We know her who is auspicious; we meditate upon her who is garlanded with glory."
"May Gaurī impel us.
This is the Gaurī-gāyatrī.
Thereafter, according to the prescribed rule, the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* (the conception ceremony) should be performed.
Having performed [the rite] according to the ritual procedure on the sixteenth day, the best of Brahmins,
The sprinkling should be performed with the juice of dūrvā grass into the right nostril,
along with twenty-one kuśa blades and udumbara fruits.
Then, according to one's means, one should perform the *sīmantonnayana* rite at that very time;
having given away the maiden in marriage with thirty *niṣkas*, he should make it beautiful.
Having thus adorned [the child] and offered oblations, he should present him to Śiva;
at the rite of the first feeding of solid food, the wise man should feed [the child] with milk-rice and other such foods.
In this manner, the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the Viśvajit sacrifice must be performed by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas, using the seed-syllable of Śakti.
One should perform all the remaining rites according to the prescribed rule, as in the case of the gift of a balance (tulādāna).

"According to the prescribed rite," and so forth: there are sixteen rites, namely—conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), birth rites (*jātakarma*), naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first outing (*upaniṣkramaṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the four Vedic vows (*vedavratacatuṣka*), the gift of a cow (*godāna*), the return home (*samāvartana*), and marriage (*vivāha*). Among these, during the rites of conception and the rite for a male child, the officiant brings a couple who stand in the place of the sacrificer’s parents; then, having placed [the substances] into two apertures—the upper vessel and the nostril of either the man or the woman—the preceptor should sprinkle the juice of *dūrvā* grass into the right nostril.
[He should bring] the performer, accompanied by his wife and adorned with all ornaments.
Having brought [the disciple] there, one should perform for him the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) while he remains situated therein.
"One should perform the sprinkling of dūrvā juice into the wife's joined palms," according to the statement in the Kāmika-tantra.
Thereafter, one should perform the sprinkling with the two mantras *prajāvat* and *jīvaputra*, using dūrvā juice; and an oblation of ghee should be offered with the *vyāhṛti*s.

And because of this statement from the *Vātula*: "One should perform the parting of the hair (*sīmantakarma*) with twenty-one *kuśa* blades together with *udumbara* fruits, using the seed-syllable of Śakti called *hṛdayollekhā*. [These] are twenty-one in number and accompanied by *udumbara* fruits."

"Having brought *kuśa* grass, one should perform the *sīmantonnayana* rite according to one's capacity," as stated in the *Kāmika*. Furthermore, the triad beginning with *niṣeka* (conception) is to be performed while the fetus is still within the womb, whereas the others are to be performed once it has emerged. Thus, these are the sixteen rites (*ṣoḍaśakriyā*). Beyond those, there are twenty-four duties consisting of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) ending with *aryamā*. In this way, the forty sacramental acts (*saṃskārakarma*) prescribed in the *Smṛtis* of Gautama and others are to be performed together with the *Viśvajit* sacrifice; such is the meaning. Regarding "the remainder": the sacrificial fees for the officiating priests and the teacher, the gift of the substance of Hiraṇyagarbha to all, and the giving of gifts to other learned Brahmins (*śrotriya*) and so forth with their permission—all this is to be followed according to the *Tulāpuruṣa* gift described in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha) as declared in the Śrī Liṅga Purāṇa.
Now, the third great gift (mahādāna), known as the Brahmāṇḍa, is described. In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Brahmāṇḍa according to the prescribed ritual."
That which is the most excellent among all beings and the destroyer of great sins.
Then, having reached an auspicious day, as in the case of the Tulāpuruṣa gift,
one should prepare the officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, the ornaments, the coverings, and so forth.
Likewise, there is the invocation of Lokeśa, and similarly the rite of consecration (adhivāsana).

The phrase "like the Tulāpuruṣa gift" means that everything— such as the timing and location, the increase of the *śrāddha*, the worship of Śiva and others, the recitation by Brahmins, the selection of the preceptor (*guru*) and officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the offering of the *madhuparka*, the preparation of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the altar (*vedikā*), the ritual materials, the invocation of the world-protectors (*lokeśa*), and the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*)— should be understood as prescribed for the Tulāpuruṣa gift described in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.
"A wise man should fashion a golden cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) joined with two hemispheres, weighing from twenty *palas* upwards up to a thousand, according to his capacity."
"Two fragments" means two pieces. Their definition is given in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"The form of the cosmic egg is such that the shadow of the jar [of the moon] appears when the moon has risen in the western direction at the beginning of the bright fortnight. Thus it is said.

Regarding "the shadow of the pitcher" (kumbhacchāyā), it should be understood that the shadow of the pitcher extends from the neckless pitcher. It is joined with the eight elephants of the quarters, endowed with the six limbs,
accompanied by the eight guardians of the world, and has the four-faced one situated in its center.
It has Śiva, Acyuta, and Arka as its peaks; it is endowed with Umā and Lakṣmī;
it contains the Vasus, Ādityas, and Maruts within its womb; and it is filled with great jewels.
Now, the characteristics of these [elephants], beginning with the elephants of the directions, are stated in sequence in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"The glorious elephant Airāvata has white clouds as his appearance and four tusks;
Puṣpadanta has large clouds as his appearance and possesses six tusks."
The remaining elephants of the quarters are traditionally held to have the general form of an elephant.
Their names are found in another treatise:
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda,
Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka are the elephants of the directions.
The auxiliary sciences of the Vedas (*vedāṅga*) are mentioned in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), etymology (*nirukta*), astronomy (*jyotiṣa*), and metrics (*chandas*);
these six are declared to be the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas."
In this world, those auspicious-faced forms of Brahmā, complete with rosaries,
dwell among the twice-born, carrying water-pots.

And these should be placed in the western direction near the Veda; for, since no specific direction is prescribed, by the maxim that "the principal [element] being led [to a place] draws its subsidiaries there with it," and as it will be stated later: "the four Vedas in the west. Viśvakarman describes their forms as those of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*):
"Purandara, the lord of the East, should be fashioned mounted upon a four-tusked elephant, holding a thunderbolt in his hand, and adorned with various ornaments."
[234] With tawny eyebrows, beard, hair, and eyes, with stout limbs, belly, and thighs,
seated upon a goat, holding a rosary and the seven-flamed fire, and bearing a spear;
Yama should be depicted as slightly corpulent, holding a staff in his hand, and wise;
Nirṛti is red-eyed, wrathful, holding a noose, and having a distorted face.
Seated upon a man, holding a sword in his hand, surrounded by spirits and Rākṣasas,
Varuṇa, gentle and bearing a noose, resides in the west, seated upon a crocodile.
The Wind-god, bearing a banner, runs mounted upon the back of a deer;
Soma, the bestower of boons, rides a chariot drawn by ten horses and holds a mace in his hand.
According to another tradition, he is borne by a hare.
In the northeast is the Supreme Lord, three-eyed, seated upon a bull, bearing a trident,
holding a skull-cup in his hand, and adorned with the crescent moon.
Regarding the four-faced form, according to the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Brahmā, seated upon a lotus-leaf throne, should be made four-faced,
bearing a rosary, a garland, a book, and a water-pot."
His garment was a black antelope skin, and likewise, a swan was by his side.

The characteristics of Śiva are described in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "Sadāśiva has five faces, is mounted upon a bull, possesses three eyes in each face, carries a skull, a trident, and a *khaṭvāṅga*, and has the moon as his crest-ornament."
The characteristics of Viṣṇu have been described in the *Tulāpuruṣadāna*. The characteristics of the Sun are described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The Sun should be depicted with handsome moustaches, possessing a beautiful luster red as vermilion;
seated upon a lotus, holding a lotus in his hand, adorned, and wearing a girdle."

"Endowed with Umā and Lakṣmī" refers to Śiva and Acyuta being present there, accompanied by Umā and Lakṣmī, who are free from the body (videhyau). The characteristics of Umā are described in the Devīpurāṇa:
"Gaurī, possessing the luster of the color of a conch or the moon, attended by the night (Śarvarī), seated in the lotus posture (vṛtta-padmāsana), holding a rosary and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu)."

[She is] rich in a form raised to grant boons, fond of all garlands and fruits; that is to say, she is endowed with a form raised to grant boons, with hands [displaying] the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. The characteristics of Lakṣmī are stated in the Pañcarātra:
"One should represent Śrī, the mother of the three worlds, seated upon a lotus throne."
She was fair-complexioned, beautiful, and adorned with every ornament.
With her right hand she holds a golden lotus and bestows boons;
the forms of the Vasus and others are described in the Nāradīya:
"They have serene faces, are gentle, grant boons, and hold spears in their hands."
The Vasus should always be depicted seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) with two arms.
Seated upon thrones, they have two arms and possess a splendor like the interior of a lotus;
they hold a lotus stalk with its stem extending from their hands up to their shoulders.
Below are situated the zodiac signs beginning with Aries, their feet covered;
there are the twelve Ādityas, Indra and the others, standing in the midst of a circle of light.

Likewise: "The deities named Maruts are to be fashioned with forms resembling wind"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. The names of the Vasus and others are to be understood as those mentioned in the *Tulāpuruṣa* [chapter]. Regarding the phrase "endowed with great jewels," the "great jewels" are those defined in the technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*). As for the reading found in some versions, "accompanied by the infinite couple" (*anantamithunānvitam*): Ananta is accompanied by seven hoods, and Pṛthvī assumes her own form; thus they constitute the "infinite couple. Now, the subject at hand is stated:
One should place [the image], measuring one hundred finger-breadths in length and width, wrapped in silk cloth, upon a drona-measure of sesame seeds;
likewise, one should arrange eighteen kinds of grain all around it.

"One *vitasti* is one hundred *aṅgulas*" means that, starting from twelve *aṅgulas*, it should be performed according to one's capacity up to one hundred *aṅgulas*. The measure of a *droṇa* and the eighteen grains should be understood from the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*); and that *tila-droṇa* (measure of sesame) should be placed upon the wheel drawn on the altar (*vedikā*).
To the east is Anantaśayana; Pradyumna is to the southeast;
Prakṛti is in the southern region; and after that is Saṃkarṣaṇa.
To the west, the four Vedas; beyond that, Aniruddha;
to the north, Agni; and beyond that, Vāsudeva made of gold.
The wise man should worship ten golden images of those seated upon pedestals of virtues on all sides;
he should also place ten full water-jars wrapped in cloth.

"Towards the east," and so forth: one should place the Lord resting upon the couch of Śeṣa (Anantaśayana) on the seat of qualities (guṇapīṭha) in the eastern region of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa); such is the characteristic of that image. From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The God of gods should be fashioned as sleeping upon Śeṣa with four arms;
one foot of this Lord should be made resting upon the lap of Lakṣmī."
Likewise, another [hand] should be made, positioned on the mark of the remaining enjoyment;
one arm of this [deity] should be made extended there at the knee.
Another hand of his should likewise be placed at the region of the navel;
in the same manner, another hand of the deity should be made to rest upon the neck.
Likewise, his other hand holds a cluster of blossoms from the lineage;
and the Grandfather (Brahmā) sits comfortably upon the lotus born from his navel.
"However, Madhu and Kaiṭabha should be depicted attached to the stalks, situated upon lotuses;
thereafter, one should place the conch, discus, mace, and other [weapons] in their embodied forms.
Thus [it is said]. The characteristics of Pradyumna are found in the Pañcarātra and other [scriptures].
"One should place a lotus in the upper right hand and a conch in the lower right hand;
then, O twice-born, one should place a discus in the upper left hand and likewise a mace in the lower left.
Alternatively, Pradyumna may hold a bow and quiver; he is handsome and the deluder of the universe."

In this context, although it is impossible to fashion the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) because of its unmanifest form, nevertheless, it is possible to fashion that form which is designated by such terms as *lakṣmī* and so forth; therefore, it is logical to create one of those very forms. This has been stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"The primordial Mahālakṣmī of all things is the Supreme Goddess endowed with the three qualities (*triguṇā*), bearing a citron, a mace, a shield, and a drinking vessel."
"And bearing the form of a Naga and a *liṅga* upon their heads, O King.
Thus [is described] the form of Saṃkarṣaṇa in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa should be fashioned with the form of Vāsudeva."
That best of the Yadus should be made with a white body and blue garments.
"And in the place of the mace, a pestle; and in the place of the discus, a plow.
The forms of the Vedas will be described in the Bhūtaṣṭaka. The form of Aniruddha is described in the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]:
"Kṛṣṇa has four arms; in his right [hands] he holds an arrow and a sword, and in those to the north..."
They declare the hero Aniruddha to be bearing a bow and a shield.

[238] The characteristics of Agni have been described. The form of Vāsudeva is also given in the Nāradīya: "Vāsudeva is Śiva, peaceful, with a white lotus, four-armed, performing yoga, holding a conch aloft, and placing his hand upon the region of the heart."
"One should hold the discus in the upper hand and the mace indeed in the right hand. Thus it is said.

And these specific deities must be fashioned from gold distinct from the gold used for the construction of the *brahmāṇḍa* (the golden cosmic egg). For there is a rule here that the *brahmāṇḍa* ranges from twenty *palas* up to a thousand *palas*, as seen in the Purāṇas; therefore, when the gold is subtracted from that [total], because the number would be deficient, it would fail to fulfill the prescribed requirement. Nor should it be argued that—on account of the statement "endowed with the eight world-elephants (*diggajas*) and accompanied by the guardians of the quarters (*lokapālas*)" and so forth—the principal deity (*aṅgin*) is produced with all those limbs at once, and thus there is no contradiction in fashioning the images of the world-elephants and others from the very same gold used for the *brahmāṇḍa*. This is because the further injunction "he should have them made of gold" would otherwise become redundant. As for the images whose dimensions are not explicitly heard, their size should be determined according to one's capacity, ranging from the joint of the thumb up to a span (*vitasti*). In the instruction "he should place full jars," the word "evenly" (*samantāt*) is to be supplied.
Ten cows indeed should be given,
together with gold, garments, and milking vessels, along with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, a lotus-seat, and a mirror.
With foods, edibles, grains, lamps, sugarcane, fruits, garlands, and ointments,
and at the conclusion of the fire-oblation and consecration, he was installed by the preeminent Veda-knowers.
Thus, one should recite the mantra three times and then perform a circumambulation from left to right.

Regarding the phrase "with golden garments and milking vessels": cows with golden horns and copper milking vessels, provided with cloths, should be prepared on the side for the sake of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Among them, two cows are to be given to the *ācārya*, and others to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); for the reciters (*jāpaka*) and others, a separate fee according to one's capacity should be given. However, in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, it is stated that "O Pārtha, a hundred *niṣkas*" and so forth, meaning that gold alone should be prepared for the sake of the sacrificial fee. On the day following the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the *śrāddha*, once the remainder of the ritual—beginning with the instruction of the officiating priests at the fire-pits—is completed, as in the case of the *tulāpuruṣa* gift, the patron (*yajamāna*), having been bathed as before, wearing white garlands and white garments, holding a handful of flowers, and having circumambulated the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) three times, should recite the mantra. The mantra is as follows:
Homage be to you, O Lord of the Universe, the abode of all, the progenitor of the world; O Blessed One, homage to you!
Grant us prosperity together with the womb of the seven worlds, including the gods and the earth.
May those who suffer become happy; may the sins of all beings, both moving and stationary, depart.
May the defects of the cosmic egg perish for those whose transgressions have been struck down by the weapon of your gift.
Having thus paid homage to the Embryo of the Universe (Viṣṇu), one should give [the gift] to the twice-born after dividing it tenfold.

Having assigned two parts therein to the preceptor, one should distribute the remainder equally in due order. The formula for the act of giving should be understood as being the same as that for the *tulāpuruṣa* rite. That [gift] is to be divided tenfold; having assigned two parts to the preceptor, one should divide each of the remaining eight equal parts into three, and distribute them equally among twenty-four persons, such as the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others, and with his permission, one may also give to other Brahmins.
The Guru alone should perform the very brief fire-oblation according to the method of the single-fire rite;
he is the most worthy of worship by those of meager means with the aforementioned materials, ornaments, and so forth.

Regarding substances ranging from twenty *palas* up to a thousand *palas* within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), when one conceives of three grades—superior, middling, and so forth—starting from a thousand and its half, it should be noted that the "smaller portion" refers to the smallest part; some say that only that which is made of twenty *palas* is considered small. Others state that "smallness" is to be understood as performing the rite according to one's capacity for less than twenty *palas*. As for the "single-fire rite" (*ekāgni-vidhāna*), it means performing the oblation (*homa*) in a single sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

[240] The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) situated in the direction of Varuṇa (the west) should also be made circular; this has been established in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). Then, when the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) has been performed, having gone near the altar of the deities (*devatāvedī*), and once the worship of the deities has been conducted by the patron (*yajamāna*) as prescribed, the preceptor (*ācārya*) should perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
Thus, the person who performs all of this here, having obtained the gift of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍadāna*), attains a great celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
With a body purified by the removal of all impurities, he attains the abode of Murāri, which brings joy, together with the celestial nymphs.

He who, by means of the gift of the universe which shatters the mass of his sins, shall deliver eight hundred kinsmen— fathers, grandfathers, sons, grandsons, relatives, paternal ancestors, guests, and wives; [he is truly a donor].
And he shall bring joy to his mother’s entire lineage without exception.
Whoever recites or hears this in the celestial abodes or in the homes of the righteous,
and even forms an intention toward it, shall rejoice.
In the abode of the Lord of the Dead, together with the Apsarases and the Apsarases.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.
The King said:
"By performing this rite of the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa, one shall become a partaker of liberation."
Tell me all of this: the time, the place, the twice-born, and the sacred ford.
By performing that through which I may become a partaker of the fruit of everything,
may there be for me soon liberation from this contemptible state of existence.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this, O King, the Brahmin priest of that monarch then had a golden cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) fashioned out of all kinds of metals.
One should fashion a pedestal with a thousand niṣkas and arrange a lotus there;
in its center, one should place Brahmā, adorned with rubies.
Together with Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī, along with the ṛṣis and munis,
all his sons beginning with Nārada, and likewise with the gods beginning with Indra.
All those with golden forms were the precursors of Brahmā;
and the eternal Lord, in the form of the Boar, was there together with Lakṣmī.
One should have blue emeralds set in his ornaments;
one should have the body of Rudra fashioned from pure silver.
In this matter, the wise man who would seek to produce the splendor of the moon with pearls,
or the splendor of the sun with tree-bark, [would act in vain].
Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī, however, should be placed at the sides of Brahmā. Regarding this, Nārada says:
"Sāvitrī on the right side and the one named Gāyatrī on the left, both gazing upon Brahmā, who holds a rosary and a water-pot."

The seven sages are Gautama and the others. As it is said in the Āditya Purāṇa: "Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Kāśyapa, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, and Atri—these are the seven in the Vaivasvata interval."
Yama describes the characteristics of the Seven Sages:
"The Seven Sages have matted hair and carry water-pots and rosaries; they are devoted to meditation. Vasiṣṭha, however, should be depicted together with his wife."
The "sages" are those in the forest-dwelling stage (*vānaprastha*); "by Nārada and others" is their qualification. Regarding them, Manu says:
"Desiring to create progeny, I performed most difficult austerities;
then, in the beginning, I created ten great sages, the lords of progeny."
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada.

Viśvakarman describes their characteristics: "The sages should always be depicted with two arms, wearing matted hair and beards, peaceful, with veins visible on their ten limbs, and holding saffron flowers and rosaries."
Among them was Nārada, seated calmly with his left arm resting [on the shoulder],
his body as white as camphor, and holding a rosary and a water-pot.

The forms of Indra and others have also been described previously. Regarding the form of the Boar (*vārāha*), the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states: "The Lord should be depicted in the form of a boar, situated upon Śeṣa. And Śeṣa should be made four-armed, endowed with beautiful jewel-adorned hoods."
O Yādava, his two hands should be fashioned as a pestle and a mortar;
likewise, he should be made in the form of a serpent with his palms joined in reverence.
The Blessed One should be situated in the ālīṭa posture upon his back;
Vasundharā, in the form of a woman, is positioned to his left.
One should perform auspicious salutations to him with two arms;
on that arm where the goddess Earth is held, there should be a conch in the hand.
His other hands should be made to hold a lotus, a discus, and a mace;
one should depict Śrī, the mother of the three worlds, seated upon a lotus throne.
She is fair-complexioned and beautiful, adorned with all ornaments,
her left hand occupied with a golden lotus, while her right hand grants boons.

The form of Rudra has been described previously; the characteristics and colors of the planets will be explained in the section on the gift of the nine planets (*navagraha-dāna*). The meaning is that one should cause gems of all colors—colors corresponding to those of the planets—to be given for the purpose of ornamentation. It was stated that the Brahmāṇḍa should be made from all metals (*sarva-dhātu*); having first specified the application of gold for the construction of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and so forth, what is now to be done with the other metals is being stated. O King, silver should be seven times the weight of the pedestal, copper likewise seven times that of the silver, and bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) should be made seven times the weight of the copper.
Beyond the tin, one should likewise fashion the boundary and the iron [ring];
[therein are represented] the seven continents, the seven oceans, and the seven principal mountain ranges.
Having understood this number, they were fashioned by skillful artisans.

The meaning is that it should be of such a kind as to possess seven qualities; "seven islands" and so forth means that one should fashion each island, ocean, and principal mountain from each of these respective elements. Furthermore, one should have the wild animals made of silver, and the forest-dwelling creatures made of gold.

Having prepared all things here according to the rules—the trees, the forest lords (vanaspatis), the grasses, creepers, and shrubs; whatever grows in water; trees that bear both flowers and fruit; forest lords that bear fruit without flowers; and shrubs such as clusters and bushes—all this should be offered at the sacred bathing place by the wise.
At Kurukṣetra, at Gayā, at Prayāga, and at Amarakaṇṭaka;
At Dvāravatī, at Prabhāsa, at Gaṅgādvāra, and at Puṣkara— at these sacred fords, indeed, gifts should be given during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
In all the gaps of the day, during the southern and northern solstices,
at the vyatīpāta conjunction, and especially at the equinoxes, [the merit] is manifold.
O Indra among kings, this must be given; one should not entertain any hesitation regarding a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fire from childhood, who is handsome and endowed with virtuous qualities.
Having honored him along with his wife and adorned them with ornaments,
he appointed the preeminent domestic priest as well as the other officiating priests.
They invited those endowed with the twenty-four qualities, together with their wives,
who were dressed in unwashed garments, well-covered, wearing garlands, and beautifully adorned.
One should cause finger-rings, gems, and ear-ornaments to be given;
having thus honored them in this manner, one should stand before them oneself.
Having prostrated again and again with the eight-limbed salutation,
he placed his hands together in the gesture of reverence before the priest.
Indeed, you Brahmins are favored by the Creator through your very nature of friendliness;
by your gracious countenance here, a man himself becomes purified.
Through the joy associated with you, the Grandfather himself was delighted;
and by the gift of the Cosmic Egg, Janārdana became pleased with them.
The Lord whose hand holds the Pināka bow and Śakra, the lord of the thirty-three gods—
these indeed attain satisfaction when meditated upon by the best of the twice-born.
Having praised them thus, the king then gave the Brahmāṇḍa to his preceptor, who was a master of the Vedas, along with the prescribed ritual offerings, again and again.
Then, having performed austerities with all his desires, that lord of men went to heaven;
and that [wealth] was also divided by him, his elder brother, together with the Brahmins.
O lord of men, that portion of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) which was given by them has been given to others as well;
therefore, the gift of the earth (bhūmidāna), which is the cosmic egg itself, must not be accepted by only one person.
By accepting it, he incurs the fault of killing a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
O lord of men, that [gift] must be given in the presence of everyone.
And those who see it being given indeed become purified;
by the mere sight of it they would become purified—of this there is no doubt.
The Bhīmadvādaśī has been described here; [as well as] Svarṇanābhi and Mṛgājina.
Having gone to these, one should behold them; for when these are seen, the fruit of the ritual act is attained.
"One shall obtain, without effort, the very same world as the maker [of the gift].
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa in the Padmapurāṇa.
Now begins the fourth great gift, known as the Kalpapādapa (the Wish-fulfilling Tree).
Matsya said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the unsurpassed great gift known as the Kalpapādapa-dāna, which destroys all sins.

Then, having reached an auspicious day, one should perform the *puṇyāhavācana* ceremony as in the rite of the gift of the *tulāpuruṣa*, and likewise perform the invocation of the world-protectors (*lokeśa*).
The officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, the ornaments, the coverings, and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), one should understand—as in the case of the Tulāpuruṣa gift described in the *Matsya Purāṇa*—the [observances of] time and place, the performance of the *vṛddhiśrāddha*, the worship of Śiva and others, the selection of the four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the preceptor (*guru*), the offering of the *madhuparka*, the fire-oblation (*homa*), the drawing of a wheel upon the altar (*vedī*), and the five-colored canopy, banners, and arches (*toraṇa*).
One should have golden trees fashioned, complete with various fruits;
one should also have various seats, garments, and ornaments made.
Various fruits— women, men, cows, elephants, horses, jewels, diamonds, gold, silver, foodstuffs, fruits, and so forth—
one should prepare according to one's capacity, from three *palas* upwards to a thousand.
One should have a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpapādapa*) fashioned from half of the gold thus prepared.
And upon a prastha of jaggery, it is covered with a pair of white cloths;
it is accompanied by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, along with five conch shells and the Sun.
And one should fashion Kāmadeva below him, together with his wife.

Regarding the phrase "half of the gold prepared": one should fashion a *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree) together with images of Brahmā and the other deities using half of the gold prepared for the gift according to one's capacity. One should also divide the second half into four parts and, with each single portion, construct the *santāna* and other trees mentioned below, together with their respective presiding deities. Here, a *prastha* of molasses is measured at thirty-two *palas*; as it has been stated: "A *prastha* of thirty-two *palas* is proclaimed in the *Purāṇa*. The characteristics of Brahmā and the others have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*, while the form of Kāmadeva is taken from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Kāmadeva, however, should be fashioned as peerless in beauty on earth;
he should be made with eight arms, adorned with a conch and a lotus.
Holding a bow and arrows in his hand, with eyes rolling from intoxication, he had these resplendent wives: Rati, Prīti, and Śakti.
Four wives, enchanting in form, should be made for him;
and four hands should be made for him, reaching toward his wives' breasts.
"And the great Ketu should be made as a makara with five arrow-like faces.

The word "below" (adhastāt) is connected to Brahmā and the others as well. Now, since there is no fixed measurement in the primordial archetype (prakṛti), the determination of the size of the image and so forth is according to the will of the person [commissioning it]. One should fashion the continuity as before; likewise, one should calculate it by means of a fourth part.

"By a fourth part" means by a fourth part of the second half. "In that manner" means like the *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree); one should fashion it with five branches, placed upon a vessel of molasses, and endowed with images of Brahmā and the other deities—this is the meaning. Some, however, apply the instruction "one should fashion Kāmadeva below" to the *santānavṛkṣa* (progeny tree); according to their view, only an image of him should be made.
On the right side, one should place the *mandāra* tree together with Śrī atop a vessel of ghee;
on the west, the *paribhadra* tree together with Sāvitrī atop cumin seeds.
In the same way, having smeared it with yellow sandalwood mixed with fragrant substances,
one should prepare it with a fourth part of white sandalwood combined with fruits.
The characteristics of Śrī have been described in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa; Nārada states the characteristics of Sāvitrī:
"Sāvitrī is seated upon a lotus, holding a rosary and a water-pot."
The characteristics of the *surabhi* are described in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "A *surabhi* is a cow with her calf; she is a cow who has come forward, yielding milk.

[The direction is] by the north, which is auspicious. Since there is a statement that "it is the same" when there is a requirement for the measurement of ghee and other substances, and because of their proximity, it should be understood that the measurement is one *prastha*.
[They should be] joined with silken garments and provided with sugarcane, garlands, and fruits.
Likewise, [he should offer] eight full jars, sandals, a seat, and a vessel.
It should be provided with a lamp, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, and a seat;
likewise, Vināyaka should be placed above it, accompanied by fruit and garlands.
In that manner, one should arrange eighteen kinds of grain all around:

a vessel for solid food, a vessel containing soft foods, and a five-colored canopy. Then, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the previous day as before, on the following day one should complete the remainder of the ritual from the recitation by the Brahmins up to the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation.
At the conclusion of the fire-offering (*homa*) and the consecration, the [initiate], having been bathed by the preeminent Vedic scholars, [is prepared].
Having circumambulated three times clockwise, one should utter this mantra.
Homage to you, the wish-fulfilling tree, who bestows desired objects;
homage to you, the divine sustainer of the universe, whose form is the universe itself.
Since you alone are the soul of the universe, Brahman, the Immovable One, and the Sun; since you are the supreme seed, both manifest and unmanifest, therefore protect me, O Eternal One.
You alone are the entirety of the nectar of immortality, the infinite and imperishable Person; being endowed with the lineage and other virtues, protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra.
The gods are immortal; their everything is the "everything-of-ambrosia" (*amṛta-sarvasva*).

Having thus addressed him, one should give that wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpa-pādapa*) to the guru, and one should likewise assign the lineage [of the tree] and so forth to the four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

The formula for the gift-offering (*dānavākya*) here is to be inferred from what is stated regarding the *tulāpuruṣa* rite. The phrase "he should allot to four" means that he should give to each one individually; from the mention of "to four," it is understood that only four priests (*ṛtvij*) are to be chosen here. In the cases where there is a group of eight priests, the term "to the priests" means "to the pairs of priests. And in this case, a different sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be given to the chanters (*jāpaka*) and others. Some maintain that this number four of the priests is based on the four Vedas. It should be understood that after obtaining their permission, he should likewise cause gifts to be given to others as well. The determination of the sacrificial fees is as before. In minor rites, he may act like those who maintain only a single sacred fire (*ekāgni*); or he may perform the worship of the Guru alone. He should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, nor should he be filled with pride. The explanation of what constitutes a "minor" rite is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. Then, when the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) has been performed, the sacrificer, having gone near the altar (*vedi*) and performed the worship of the deities, should perform the dismissal of the deities (*devatāvisarjana*) just as before.
Whoever offers a great gift according to this rite,
being liberated from all sins, shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Surrounded by Apsarases, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Pannagas,
he shall deliver as many men of the past and future as there are hairs on his body.
Being praised upon the back of heaven, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu by means of a sun-colored celestial chariot, accompanied by his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons.
He shall remain in heaven for a hundred kalpas and thereafter become a king of kings,
endowed with the power of Nārāyaṇa and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
One who is devoted to the stories of Nārāyaṇa shall go to the city of Nārāyaṇa.
Whether a man of little wealth should recite this entire *Kalpataru*, or listen to it, or even merely remember it, he too,
having reached the world of Indra, shall dwell there with the Apsarases.
With his body liberated from sin, he dwells for the duration of a manvantara.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the Kalpataru (Wish-fulfilling Tree) as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa. In the Liṅga Purāṇa, Sanatkumāra said:
"Now I shall further describe another supreme Kalpapādapa (Wish-fulfilling Tree)."
It should be performed with a hundred niṣkas and be endowed with all the Vedic branches.
All branches, with branches extending to the ends of all directions,
should be fashioned according to the ritual rule; having suspended strings of pearls from each branch, one should then arrange divine emerald sprouts upon them.
"Divyaiḥ" means with excellent [materials].

"The wise man should cause the tree to be adorned with coral" (pravālena drumasya ca) means that he should cause the coral to be adorned with coral; by "with trees," the meaning is that he should cause the sprouts to be made of [artificial] snakes.
The fruits were made of rubies, the beautiful trunk of the *pārijāta* tree was of sapphire, and its excellent shoulder was of diamond.
The top of the tree with lapis lazuli, the head with topaz;
the portion above the shoulder is the head, and above that is the top of the tree.
With agate indeed the shoulder, and with sun-crystal, O observer of good vows.
Or a pedestal for the tree made of moonstone or crystal.
The length of the tree is proclaimed to be one *vitasti*,
and its width and height likewise equal to eight branches.

The height of the tree, distinct from its branches, should be made one *vitasti*; likewise, the ninth branch, which is the central one facing upward from the trunk, should also have a height of one *vitasti*. "The width equal to the eight branches" means that one should make the lateral extent of the eight branches facing the eight directions exactly one *vitasti*. One should place the *liṅga* at its base, surrounded by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*s). Having placed the tree within the mandala in the center of the previously mentioned altar: [One should place the tree] in the center of the previously mentioned altar, within the mandala.
One should worship the Lord Īśāna and the world-protectors with diligence;
as before, one should perform the recitation, fire-oblations, and other rites according to the procedure for the scales and the loads.
O King, one should then offer the tree to Śambhu, or to a Brāhmaṇa;
or else, by offering it to Brāhmaṇas, the king shall become a sovereign ruler of the whole earth.

Regarding the instruction "one should act like one carrying a load on a scale," the meaning is that one should perform the ritual procedure prescribed for the *tulāpuruṣa* gift-offering as described in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*. As stated in the *Kālottara*: "One should fashion a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpapādapa*) with a thousand *palas*."
Together with its roots, stalks, and leaves, and provided with fruits and flowers.
Having visualized the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), the wise one should establish them for the five [deities];
with the Sadyojāta mantra, [the substance] should be given and received in the presence of Śiva.
At the end of his body, he is glorified in the world of Śiva by means of divine celestial chariots;
his ancestors, O lord of the earth, rejoice in the world of truth.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift from the Śaiva-kalpataru.
Now, the fifth great gift (mahādāna), known as the Thousand Cows, is described.
Matsya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift known as the "Bestowal of a Thousand Cows," which is supreme and removes all sins.
Having reached an auspicious lunar day (tithi) such as the beginning of a Yuga or Manvantara,
one should observe a milk-vow (payovrata) for three nights or even for a single night.
One should perform the invocation of Lokeśa as in the ritual of the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa;
one should likewise perform the recitation of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) and the fire oblation (homa).
One should consecrate the officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, the ornaments, the coverings, and so forth,
as well as a bull endowed with the auspicious marks, in the center of the sacrificial altar.
Having emerged from a thousand cows, there were indeed ten cows.

[252] “One who observes the milk-vow for three nights” means that for three nights prior to the day of the gift, one should observe the milk-vow. Here, by the word “etcetera,” the following items prescribed in the *Matsyapurāṇa* for the *tulāpuruṣa* gift are included: the selection of the place and time, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the worship of Śiva and others, the choosing of the preceptor and officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the offering of the *madhuparka*, the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and altar (*vedikā*), the canopy (*vitāna*), the drawing of the mystic diagram (*cakra*), the banners (*patākā*), and so forth. Regarding “a bull endowed with auspicious marks,” the characteristics of a bull—such as having a high hump and shoulders, and bright, long hair—are to be understood exactly as stated in the section on the ritual release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
