As for the phrase “having extracted from a thousand cows,” it should be understood as being from ten thousand cows, because later on the employment of a thousand cows plus ten is seen; even though in the passage “a group of ten cows” there is only the perception of cows in general, nevertheless, because of the specific designation of “milch-cows” (*dhenu*) in the subsequent passage, “one should present one milch-cow from each group of ten to the officiating priests,” and because of this in another *Purāṇa*.

Based on the scriptural injunction, "Having brought forth ten cows with their calves from among a thousand cows," one should indeed consecrate ten milch-cows (*dhenus*). However, in the case of other [types of gifts], there is no necessary regard for them being of the form of milch-cows. One should lead outside a thousand cows adorned with garments and garlands.
Adorned with golden horns and provided with silver feet.
Therefore, having caused it to enter, one should worship the set of ten with garments and garlands—
equipped with a small golden bell and provided with flowers and perfumes.
It was adorned with peaks joined by gold and jewels, as well as chowries,
and was provided with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, vessels, and seats.

[253] For a horn weighing ten *suvarṇas*, the hooves weigh five *palas*. The milking vessel weighs fifty *palas*; otherwise, it is so designated because the word *suvarṇa* here—referring to the gold for the bells and other parts—denotes a quantity of sixteen *māṣas*, since it is illogical to abandon the specific measure understood from the word *suvarṇa* when it is uttered only once. Regarding the two sandals (*pāduke*), they are made of wood; the distinction is that *upānahau* (shoes) are made of leather.
In the midst of a herd of ten cows, there should be a golden image of Nandikeśvara, clothed in silk garments and adorned with various ornaments.
On the peak of the Lavaṇadroṇa mountain, provided with garlands, sugarcane, and fruits,
one should perform all of this in its entirety, starting from four hundred palas.
According to one's devotion, one should arrange all of this up to three thousand *palas*, or even for a hundred cows, by calculating a tenth part of that amount.
"On the peak of Lavaṇadroṇa" means "above Lavaṇadroṇa. The characteristics of Nandikeśvara are from the *Lalitavijaya*:
"Nandikeśvara has three eyes, two arms, and a gentle face;
he holds a trident in his left hand and is endowed with a rosary in his right."

"Standing upright" (*ūrdhva*) means not lying down, but remaining seated. "From one hundred *pala*s upwards to three thousand *pala*s" refers specifically to the case of Nandikeśvara with his ornaments, due to the immediate context. Regarding the phrase "in the case of a hundred cows, by a tenth part," the meaning is that when a hundred cows are to be given, one should consecrate (*adhivāsayet*) one cow and one bull in the middle of the altar; from ten *pala*s upwards to three hundred *pala*s, one should perform the arrangement of Nandikeśvara with his ornaments and so forth.
Then, having reached an auspicious moment with the sounds of songs and auspicious music...
He was bathed with water infused with all medicinal herbs by the most eminent of Vedic scholars.
[254] Holding a handful of flowers, one should recite this mantra.

In this case as well, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the previous day as before, on the second day, after the recitation by the Brahmins, the preceptor (*guru*) shall complete the remainder of the ritual—from the seating of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at the fire-pits (*agnikuṇḍa*) up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, having secured an auspicious time characterized by a favorable *lagna* and *muhūrta* for himself, the patron (*yajamāna*), bathed by the Brahmins with water from the jar situated near the fire-pits and wearing white garlands and garments, shall utter the following mantras:
"Salutations to you who possess universal forms and who are the mothers of the universe."
And salutations again and again to the Rohiṇīs who dwell in the worlds.
The twenty-one worlds abide within the limbs of the cows;
likewise, O God, may Brahmā and the other deities, as well as the mother Rohiṇīs, protect us.
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me;
may cows always be upon my head; I dwell in the midst of cows.
"Since you, in the form of a bull, are indeed the eternal Dharma"—
having addressed him thus, one who should give Nandikeśvara to the preceptor.
A wise man should present to the officiating priests a pair of oxen equipped with all necessary implements, and from among the ten, he should assign one cow to each priest.
A hundred cows, or even one each, or half of that, or twenty;
Or fifty plus ten more, by his permission.

The formula for the gift (*dānavākya*) here should be understood as being like that for the *tulāpuruṣa* rite. These options, ranging from one hundred down to five, refer to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because they follow immediately after [the mention of the teacher]. From this, the following meaning is established: from among ten cows, one should present a pair of cows accompanied by Nandikeśvara to the teacher (*guru*), and give one cow each from the remaining eight to each of the officiating priests; or likewise, having given two hundred from among a thousand cows to the teacher, one should give one hundred each to the officiating priests. Alternatively, one hundred to the teacher and fifty to the officiating priests; or forty to the teacher and twenty each to the officiating priests; or twenty to the teacher and ten each to the officiating priests; or ten to the teacher and five each to the officiating priests. The remaining cows may be given to others with his permission. And here, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given exactly as before. Since it is stated that "where no fee is mentioned, gold is the fee," one may give gold according to one's capacity. Then, as before, one should perform the recitation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship and dismissal of the deities, and so forth.
One cow should not be given to many, for it would cause harm;
rather, many cows should be given to one for the increase of prosperity and health. Furthermore, one who has given a thousand cows should observe the milk-vow (payovrata) for one day.
And this observance of the milk-vow is dependent upon one's capacity, for there is a scriptural statement that "in case of incapacity, eating at night is permitted.
One should either recite or listen to the glorification of the great gifts;
on that day, one should observe celibacy if one desires abundant prosperity.
In the Ātharvaṇa-Gopatha-Brāhmaṇa.

Now, therefore, follows the procedure for the thousand cows (*gosahasra-vidhi*). Having kindled a fuel-pile (*idhma*) facing east in a cow-pen near water in a pure place, and having touched it, he should then offer oblations. He should first offer with the *Āgāvasūkta*. Having cooked a sacrificial pap (*caru*) of large-grained rice (*mahāvrīhi*) for Indra and one for Soma in the milk of that thousandth cow, he should offer them with the hymn beginning "The cows... and "Thus both... After the fire, having placed a jar filled with water from a sacred bathing-place (*tīrtha*), he should have ten cows bathed with the hymn "In the union with the serpent..."; having quickly sprinkled those [others], he should bathe the thousandth cow with its bathing water while reciting: "O Indra, increase this Kṣatriya; these waters... Having consecrated the king with the six verses beginning "These waters...", and having performed the anointing, smearing, and unguents as prescribed, he should first adorn the thousandth cow and cause all the cows to lie down together with the verse: "O cows, stand near me, rich in offspring, on good pasture... Having given them their favorite food, he should touch the thousandth cow with the verse "O inviolable ones, three-fold... and mutter the mantra: "By me, accompanied by the cows, it has been increased. Having offered the guest-offering (*argha*) with this mantra, and having again taken hold of the thousandth cow, he should mutter: "May she, standing on the ground, accept [the gift]. Walking behind the thousand cows, circumambulating them all, bowing, and pronouncing a blessing, he should announce [the completion] to the Brahmins. Ten cows are the fee for the officiant, and the thousandth cow along with a pair of garments is also for him.
Verses:
A man who gives a cow shall, by this prescribed rite, instantly destroy the sin committed by seven men over the course of seven lifetimes.
A man who bestows a thousand cows upon Brahmins obtains that fruit which has been proclaimed here as the result of all gifts.
They say that he who performs an Aśvamedha sacrifice, the rite of releasing a bull, or gives away three thousand cows— taking [the merit of these], they indeed satisfy him on all sides.
"Therefore, that man who, according to this rite, bestows a thousand cows, being purified in soul, goes to that supreme state. Thus it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
Whoever becomes a giver of a thousand cows according to this rite shall be liberated from all sins and attended by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
By means of a celestial chariot, sun-colored and garlanded with networks of tiny bells,
he is honored in the world by all the guardians of the quarters.
He shall remain for the duration of a manvantara and become a king of kings once again;
devoted to the meditation on Śiva, he shall perform a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Having attained the world of Viṣṇu, one is then released from bondage;
and the ancestors rejoice in the auspicious giver of a thousand cows.
"May there be born in our family a son or even a grandson who, having become a giver of a thousand cows, shall deliver us from hell."
Therefore, he may be a laborer or even a mere spectator;
yet he is the one who will ferry us across this ocean of saṃsāra.
Whoever recites this gift of a thousand cows, or remembers it, or even beholds it, shall go to the world of the gods;
or, while being recited, he shall experience happiness to his heart's content.
With his body cleansed of all impurities, he too goes to the world of Indra.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a thousand cows.
Sanatkumāra said: I shall now speak of the merit of giving a thousand cows; listen for the sake of spiritual success.
Having taken a thousand auspicious cows, together with their calves and possessing all excellent qualities.
Having worshipped those eight [vases] properly and with great effort according to the scriptures,
one should then bind their horns with gold at each respective horn-base.
One should fasten the bells around the neck with silver;
how else could they be made beautiful by means of a single niṣka?

"Taking a thousand cows" means one should understand it as a thousand and eight cows, according to the statement in the *Vātula*: "O fortunate one, having carefully gathered those and other eight. "One should bind them by the neck" implies that they are to be bound where the calf is.
Having tied a cloth around the neck [of the image], one should cause cows to be given to the Brahmins in succession;
having fashioned a gold *niṣka*, one should fasten a silk ribbon around its neck.
Thus it is stated in the Kāmika:
"One should cause cows and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to be given to the Brahmins individually;
[the fee] should be ten niṣkas, or half of that, or even half of that again."
According to the extent of one's means, or even just a single *niṣka*,
a pair of beautiful garments should be given separately to each of the Brahmins.
Cows that are most beautiful should be given after being carefully propitiated;
having thus given them according to the prescribed rite and having worshipped Śiva, the auspicious Śaṅkara.
One should recite, according to the rule, this unsurpassed hymn of praise to cows at the outset:
"May cows always be before me; may cows be behind me."
"May cows always dwell in our hearts; I myself reside in the midst of cows.
Having praised them thus and having given those cows along with sacrificial fees to the foremost of the twice-born, [he attained his goal].
For as many years as there are hairs on his body, he is glorified in the heavenly world.

As before, having performed the consecration of the auspicious [liṅga] and the ablution with a thousand jars and other rites, one should recite the *Gostava* and perform the gift of a cow for each [of the thousand]. The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the preceptor and others is as previously described.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a thousand cows as taught in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*.
Hereafter follows the gift remembered [in the Smṛtis], by which embodied beings do not fall back into rebirth.
That supreme abode is difficult to attain, yet they are completely satiated by all their desires.
He who, for the sake of Śiva, duly gives a thousand cows with their calves for the purpose of bathing, he too shall attain that state.
Having bathed Śaṅkara with the milk of a thousand cows, as well as with curd and a full measure of clarified butter, accompanied by auspicious sounds such as musical instruments,
one should diligently worship and offer a golden lotus and a linga.
It should be made of gold;
at its edge, it should be beautifully adorned down to the base with *vātapuṣpa* flowers.
One should also offer a canopy, golden bells, and other such items in pairs.
The remaining portion [of the vessel] should be filled with flowers up to the base; this is the sense.

Having gratified the fire with clarified butter by means of a mantra, the knower of mantras, together with a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), should present the lamp, mirror, food offering (naivedya), golden-handled fly-whisk, and [other offerings].
Indeed, by a twice-born man adorned with a pair of golden garments.

"With clarified butter," and so forth; the meaning is that one should satisfy [the officiant] with the substance of clarified butter by means of a learned *śrotriya* priest accompanied by his assistants. "With gold and a pair of garments" means with gold and a pair of beautiful garments.
Then, with the sound of the Veda (*brahmarava*), a white and auspicious cow should be led there;
one should raise a canopy over her and proceed toward the southeast.
And he should cause all those other cows belonging to Hara to be led forth,
adorned with gold, garments, and the like, accompanied by the sounds of great musical instruments.
Then, having performed a circumambulation of the deity, the sacrificer should place all those cows in front of him and perform a circumambulation himself.
And one should first perform all that for the preeminent Surabhī with the great Brahma-sound, indeed, as if it were a thousand cows.
Then, taking hold of the tail with both hands holding flowers and water, one should offer it to Śaṅkara along with sesame oblations and unbroken grains of barley.
With barley and unbroken grains (akṣatayava);
then, having reflected upon what should be given to them, one should likewise present other cows together with their calves to eleven Brāhmaṇas.
There, one should feed those who observe no vows as well as those of good vows— especially Brahmins— and the poor and the deeply distressed, without restriction.
Those who, with devotion, perform the Svarjita and Gosava sacrifices according to this rite,
dedicating them to the god Śaṅkara, are liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.

The *svarjit* and *gosava* sacrifices serve as the illustrative examples. Alternatively, one may give another supreme gift of a hundred cows. The word "hundred" (*śata*) here signifies a large number, and in this context it refers to a thousand, since a thousand is seen to be employed later on.
To Rudra, to the Power of Consciousness (*Cicchakti*), and to Mitra, one should offer eleven more.
Having first completed the worship of the Lord of Consciousness (*Cidhi*) with diligence according to the previous procedure, [one should proceed].
One should offer [the gift] to Śambhu right there, accompanied by fire-oblations, worship, and so forth;
indeed, having brought together one hundred initiated persons to the temple of Śiva.
Then, having worshipped them according to the rule, he should give to them as follows; listen: ten [coins] for each one, individually.
Having meditated upon Śambhu within one's heart and likewise among the cows, one should offer them to Him;
for where there is this additional group of ten, [it is] in the case of Nīlakaṇṭha, whose crest is the moon.
One should give cows together with their calves according to the previously described ritual procedure.

"Of a hundred initiated ones," and so forth; the meaning is that one should give [the gift] for the pleasure of Śambhu, having meditated upon Śambhu, to those initiated ones who have become the recipients (*saṃpradāna*). According to the previous injunction, by means of the method of ritual bathing (*sravaṇa*). Alternatively: "Or else, having invited learned Brahmins (*śrotriya*) who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, the wise man should give five [gifts] each to them, doubled."
Having performed this rite, a living being shall never be an object of grief;
he shall never again wander through the fever of the womb-chamber.
"In the fever of the womb, in the suffering of dwelling within the womb.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a thousand cows in three ways as taught in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*.
Agastya said:
I shall proclaim the supreme gift-mantra known as the "Thousand Cows," by performing which on the banks of the Narmadā one is liberated from the bonds of existence.
Likewise, one should feed a thousand Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas,
and then a thousand milch-cows that are white in color.
Mixed with a pregnant cow and accompanied by ten bulls,
it should be honored with perfumes, flowers, and the like, and adorned with golden ornaments and garments.
Having commenced the circumambulation with devotion, using this mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Vāsudeva"— this is the mantra.
In a beautiful temple of Viṣṇu crowded with those who know the Vedas,
one should approach the waters of the Narmadā and arrange a row of lamps.
Cows are always before me, and cows are indeed behind me;
cows are also in my heart, and I dwell in the midst of cows.
Having recited the mantra for the cows, one should stand before them and mutter it,
holding a copper vessel filled with scented water and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having bathed with water from the tails of cows, clad in white garments,
he is then liberated from all impurities, pure, and of a clean mind.
Having bathed those cows and the brahmins there in the waters of the Narmadā on the fifteenth day, when the full moon was in conjunction with Rāhu, [he gave them away].
Together with those very lords of brahmins, having offered worship, one should remember Hari,
accompanied by servants, sons, wife, and so forth, as well as kinsmen and relatives.
Endowed with faith, one should offer [the oblation] to the Brahmins with the mantra during a Śrāddha,
a gift-giving ceremony, a fire-sacrifice (homa), a marriage, or likewise on an auspicious occasion.
These cows, who always reside in the world of Viṣṇu and are dear to Śiva,
have been given by me to Śiva and to the high-souled Viṣṇu.
Thus, one who gives well-adorned cows for the sake of a sacrifice to a Brahmin,
having first offered a thousand well-adorned cows to Śarva;
He attains the supreme state, from which having gone he does not return,
having delivered thirty generations of his kin, servants, and relatives from hell.
He shall indeed be established in the world of Viṣṇu and that of the high-souled Śiva;
he is omniscient, perfect, pure, omnipresent, and the Lord.
Liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra, he becomes equal to Hari;
by this very method, householders may attain liberation.
Even without the yoga of knowledge, by the gift of a thousand cows;
therefore, O Indra among kings, you too become a giver of a thousand cows.
[263] "By this, the ancestors always rejoice like gods in heaven.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a thousand cows as stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*. In the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
Then, O great sage, one should bestow a thousand cows upon the Brahmins;
one should honor them with perfumes and flowers, and adorn them all with silk cloths.
With cloths and garments;
all those cows should have golden horns and all should be adorned with silver hooves. One should not give cows that are deficient in limbs, nor those that are emaciated, aged, or diseased.
One should worship one [of these] limbs; now hear the procedure for the remaining ones.
One should indeed give a hundred sesame seeds as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.

Having likewise gratified the twice-born according to the rite for offering water for the feet (*pādya*), [giving] a hundred *tilas*— meaning a hundred *droṇas* of sesame seeds— and having become pure with a cleansed mind, he who should worship Janārdana.
Having bowed his head to the God and swiftly given cows,
all of them will undoubtedly be honored by him.
Those twice-born ones who know the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, who teach the Samhitas,
who are devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, and who are dedicated to the private recitation of the Veda;
O great sage, one should examine these Brahmins when giving a cow;
that which is given to such as these is said to be infinite in this world.
"Then, O Great Sage, it is true that the gift of Ananta [is inexhaustible] for one who has observed the fast according to the rules, with a serene mind and all the senses under control."
Having approached, he should quickly give cows to the Brahmins;
having touched those cows, he should be well-disposed and perfectly composed.
Having touched and given [these],
one should not strike them with sticks, nor with the hand, nor with a clod of earth;
for that twice-born man who bestows a thousand cows as prescribed, [attains great merit].
Having abandoned all afflictions, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Likewise:
"But he who gives a hundred sesame seeds without [the gift of] cows,"
A single *pala* of gold is superior to a thousand cows;
for it has been said that one should indeed bestow a thousand cows upon the twice-born.
The donor obtains that fruit and is immediately liberated from evil;
even the evil-minded person who beholds it is likewise liberated from evil.
Having extracted twenty-one [verses], those men who are established in the preceding [sections] quickly deliver one hundred and one generations of their kin.
If a thousand cows cannot be obtained, one ought to give gold to the twice-born— either five hundred,
a hundred, or even less— along with sesame seeds.
And thus, O best of the twice-born, that person constantly obtains the full fruit of thousands of worshipped [deities].
O Brahmin, a thousand cows with complete sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) is proclaimed;
indeed, one hundred measures of sesame seeds are equal to the gift of those cows.
"Half a thousand of gold"—the remainder being that it is measured by sixteen *māṣas*. In the *Mahābhārata*:
"O lord of men, he also obtains victory everywhere;
one who gives ten thousand cows constantly rejoices with Śakra."
A man obtains inexhaustible worlds by the hundreds of thousands.
Furthermore, the giver of a thousand cows adorned with golden horns attains the merit of the world of Śakra in heaven.
Thus have the assemblies of sages and Vedic seers spoken.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a thousand cows.
Now, the sixth great gift, known as the Golden Wish-Fulfilling Cow (Hiraṇyakāmadhenu), is described.
The Fish [Purāṇa] said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme ritual of the Kāmadhenu,
which grants all desires to men and destroys even the greatest sins.
Likewise, the invocation of Lokeśa, the fire offering, and the consecration should be performed;
one should construct the sacrificial pit, the pavilion, and the altar-platform just as in the Tulāpuruṣa rite.
In small-scale rites, the preceptor alone, being composed, should perform them as in the *ekāgni* (single-fire) ritual.

The mention of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and altar (*vedikā*) is illustrative. For here, all that was prescribed for the *tulāpuruṣa* gift in the *Matsyapurāṇa*—namely, the place and time, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the worship of Śiva and others, the recitation by Brahmins, the selection of the preceptor and officiants, the offering of the *madhuparka*, the drawing of the wheel upon the altar, and the five-colored canopy, arches, banners, and so forth—is to be understood as applicable. Regarding the phrase "in small-scale rites, as in the *ekāgni*," the performance according to the *ekāgni* model has been explained.
One should have a cow and a calf fashioned from highly purified gold.
The superior [measure] is in thousands of palas, while the middling is half of that.
The Kāmadhenu is proclaimed to be half the size of the smallest [image];
one may have it made according to one's ability, from three palas upwards, even if one is incapable [of making a larger one].

[266] Here, although the measurement of the calf (*vatsa*) is not explicitly stated, nevertheless, as in the procedure for the *Kāmadhenu*, the calf should be fashioned from one-fourth of the quantity of refined gold. This is determined because, in all cases, the construction of the calf is observed to be derived from a portion of the substance equal to the measure of the cow; since there is no distinction here regarding the nature of the gift of the cow, it is concluded in the same way. Accordingly, it will be stated in various places that in the case of the *Guḍadhenu* (sugar-cow) and others, the calf should consist of one-fourth of that [quantity]. Upon the altar, one should place a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) provided with a *prastha* measure of sugar, and upon that, one should set down the cow, adorned with great jewels.
It should be provided with eight water-pots and endowed with various kinds of fruits.

The *prastha* measure has been explained in the context of the gift of the *kalpataru*. "Great jewels" refers to rubies (*padmarāga*) and so forth. There is a reading in some texts: "one should place a calf on the right. "Various fruits" refers to cows, elephants, horses, women, men, and so forth; these should be made of gold as described in the gift of the *kalpataru*.
Likewise, one should arrange eighteen kinds of grain all around.
Similarly, there should be eight stalks of sugarcane provided with various fruits.
Likewise, a vessel, a seat, and similarly a copper milking-pot.
The eighteen kinds of grain should be understood from the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). There are various fruits, such as the *mātuluṅga* and others.
It is joined with a pair of silken garments and is delightful with lamps, parasols, and ornaments.
And she held a chowrie, was adorned with earrings, carried a bell, and wore a rosary, sandals, and silver foot-ornaments.
It was surrounded on all sides by all kinds of flavors, with turmeric, many flowers and fruits,
cumin, coriander, and sugar.
And above it, a canopy of five colors.
Then, having bathed amidst the auspicious sounds of Vedic chanting and having circumambulated [the image] with flowers in his hand,
he should invoke that Guḍadhenu with its mantras.
Then, with darbha grass in hand, he should give it to the twice-born.

Regarding the phrase *aghaṇṭāgaṇatrikā* and so forth: the analysis of the compound is as follows: that which exists together with a bell (*ghaṇṭā*), a rosary (*gaṇatrikā*), and sandals (*pādukā*) is "with-bell-rosary-sandal" (*saghaṇṭāgaṇatrikāpādukā*); this [image] is both that and has silver feet (*raupyapādā*). It is called *gaṇatrikā* because it is a means of counting; in some places the reading is *akṣamālāgaṇatrikā*. In that regard, some say the *gaṇatrikā* is a neck ornament, while others, reading *galantikā*, explain it as a water-jar (*karkarī*) filled with water. The "flavors" (*rasāḥ*) have been mentioned in the technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*): cumin (*ajājīrakam*) and coriander (*dhānyakam*). Having thus prepared the necessary materials and performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) as before, on the following morning, the patron—having had the *puṇyāhavācana* recited, having completed the remainder of the ritual in the fire-pits from the seating of the officiants up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), having bathed in water infused with all medicinal herbs, wearing white garlands and garments, and holding a handful of flowers—should circumambulate [the image] three times and invoke it with the mantras for the "molasses-cow" (*guḍadhenu*). The mantras for the molasses-cow, beginning with "The Lakṣmī who is in all beings," etc., are to be found in that specific section. After the invocation, one should address [the deity] with the mantra to be stated hereafter.
You are the embodiment of the assembly of temples for all the hosts of gods;
you are the Lord of the Universe, the triple-pathed river, and the ocean and mountains. By the weapon of your gift, the entire mass of sins has been severed into pieces.
I have attained the most supreme nirvāṇa; I bow down to you.

Having encountered you, who bestows the fruits and riches desired in this world, what mortal indeed would undergo the suffering of existence? Strive as you wish for the pacification of the suffering of saṃsāra.
The hosts of gods call you the "Wish-fulfilling Cow."
Having invited a Brahmin endowed with virtue, noble lineage, beauty, and good qualities, he who should bestow this golden cow upon him.
He attains the abode cherished by the gods led by Purandara, a station surrounded by throngs of celestial maidens belonging to the Moon-crested Lord.

In this regard, the formula for the gift should be inferred from that prescribed for the *tulāpuruṣa* (weighing-gift). The singular form "to the Brahmin" (*viprāya*) applies to the case where the rite is performed with a single fire. However, in the case of multiple fires, the arrangement of the distribution among the preceptor and others should follow the model of the *tulāpuruṣa* gift. Immediately thereafter, one should perform the recitation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship and dismissal of the deities stationed upon the altar, and the deliberation regarding the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) as before.
This concludes the procedure for the gift of the Golden Wish-Cow (*hiraṇyakāmadhenu*) as declared in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
Vyāsa said:
O King, one should give even a single wish-fulfilling cow here, dedicated to you, Keśava,
to a brahmin endowed with all virtuous qualities.
Having performed the Kṛcchra vow with captivating [deeds],...
But the fruit that a person obtains at the end of time by giving thousands of cows properly, together with their calves, clothing, and gold—
And nothing is equal to the wish-fulfilling cow for the sake of the twice-born.
By means of hundreds and thousands of horses thus duly bestowed, as well as great elephants,
or chariots for maidens yoked with mules and horses;
Constantly [giving] by the hundreds and thousands to the twice-born.
The fruit that a person obtains from gifts given on the banks of the Jāhnavī in the Himalayas is equal to that which one receives from the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), and not otherwise.
He indeed always performs intense ascetic penance.
Desirous of attaining the state of Brahmā, that lord of the twice-born thought:
"This is not the fruit of the wish-fulfilling cow, nor can it be achieved through Cāndrāyaṇa fasts, Kṛcchra penances, or Mahāparāka rites."
A person joined with evil is completely purified by human beings.
In the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, a man with a restrained mind,
having fasted on the eleventh day, should then observe a fast for four days.
One should bathe Viṣṇu with clarified butter or with cow’s milk;
eating only at night, one should worship Madhusūdana with offerings of cow-products.
With perfumes and flowers, with excellent food offerings, and with garments, ornaments, and earrings.
I offer half [of this] to Janārdana, whose arms are raised with the conch, sword, and discus, and who holds the mace and the Śārṅga bow in his hands.
Even of the mountain (Dharādhara) who was endowed with splendor (Śrī).
I bow to the Lord of Śrī, the bearer of Śrī, the sole beloved,
the friend of Śrī, who is ever-favorable to Śrī,
and whose abode is Śrīdhara.
Being duly honored by me, may he grant my desires.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite with names associated with Śrī,
one should perform a separate vigil for the Lord of the World together with Śrī.
May that Goddess Nandā, who chose the Bhārgava lineage and is honored everywhere, come to my home well-pleased and grant me boons.
The goddess Sunandā, who is ever-present for the descendant of Aṅgiras,
may she come to my house, well-pleased, true, and bestowing boons.
May that fragrant wish-fulfilling cow, the bestower of all desires who [sustained] Bharadvāja,
always come here to my home, honored by the gods.
May she who was Suśīlā, who devoted herself to Kaśyapa and granted all desires everywhere—
may she, the wish-fulfilling cow, be ever well-pleased with me in my home.
May that auspicious Sumanā, who rejoiced upon reaching Vasiṣṭha,
be ever well-pleased with me as the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) in my home.
May she, the granter of desires who is honored with boons, always come to my home.
Having thus performed the worship according to the prescribed rite, at the clear and auspicious dawn,
he— having bathed, wearing white garments, and adorned with white garlands and unguents— [should proceed].
Having performed his daily rites, joyful and adorned with earrings and armlets,
he stood upon the surface of the earth, which was anointed and well-covered with a black antelope skin.
It was strewn with a prastha of sesame seeds, adorned by the four castes,
provided with white linen garments, and joined with vessels of honey and clarified butter.
Having covered her with fine cloths and adorned her with all kinds of jewels,
she was beautiful to behold, possessing four horns of gold, complete with hooves, and capable of drawing four plows.
One should worship the cow, who is endowed with the waters of the Ocean of Milk, using the mantras dedicated to the cow;
she who belongs to all the gods and to the sages of purified soul.
May she who emerged from the Ocean of Milk remain firmly established for me;
and having diligently performed the consecration of Viṣṇu with ghee and milk, [may she abide].
Having worshipped them duly with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in the proper sequence, one should recite:
"May cows be before me; may cows be at my sides and behind me."
Cows are ever in my heart, and I dwell in the midst of cows;
[I meditate on her] facing either the east or the north, wearing a white sacred thread.
"O God, O God, Lord of the World, please accept these;
may Govinda be pleased with this cow together with her calf and her ornaments."
O lord of men, having performed a circumambulation, one should give those [gifts] to the Brahmin,
and follow him for eight steps as he departs.
He who bestows the wish-fulfilling cow according to this rite goes to the heavenly world for the sake of the fulfillment of all desires.
O King, the fruit that is obtained by giving away the entire earth when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu is undoubtedly attained through the gift of a wish-fulfilling cow.
O King, the wish-fulfilling gem, the cow of plenty, and the auspicious jar—
these three gifts, the best of sages say, yield equal fruits.
O Lord of the Earth, such a person liberates seven descendants, seven ancestors, and himself from the sins committed throughout a hundred births.
At every step, a person obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
this is proclaimed as the most excellent of all gifts.
It bestows all desires, destroys sin, grants everything, and is auspicious;
it [removes] even the great sins that have arisen for all beings, however high-minded they may be.
"O King, this expiation is praised and has been declared by Brahmā;
it must be performed with diligence by Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Śūdras, O King."
This wish-fulfilling cow belongs to the virtuous for the sake of obtaining the fruits of all desires;
one should diligently worship the wish-fulfilling cow with oblations of ghee and sesame seeds offered by means of a bull.
Having bestowed this entire [text] here, one becomes a donor of the whole earth.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the Kāmadhenu as described in the Vahnipurāṇa.
Now, in the Liṅgapurāṇa,
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, therefore, I shall duly explain the ritual for the golden cow in its proper sequence;
it pacifies all sins and destroys famine in the land.
It destroys calamities and wards off all diseases;
one should have it fashioned from a thousand niṣkas of gold.
Or even with half of that, or again with half of that half,
or with a hundred— thus should it be properly performed in all undertakings by one of firm vows.

"In all matters that are unmanifest and not specifically mentioned, regarding the gift of gold, the quantity to be given shall range from one thousand down to one hundred. This statement is incidental; however, another measure is stated in the *Vātula*: "One should fashion a cow out of gold weighing from three *palas* up to one thousand. "O Mahāsena, he who gives a wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*) before Śiva when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, [using] five hundred *palas* of gold..."
By him everything would be given, even unto the realm of Brahmā.
Thus is the doctrine of the Kālottara:
one should place a divine form of a cow, complete with hooves and endowed with all auspicious marks;
a vajra should be placed on the tips of her hooves, and a ruby (padmarāga) indeed upon her horns.
O best of sages, one should place a divine pearl between the eyebrows;
one should fashion the breasts from lapis lazuli and the tail from sapphire.
It should be fashioned at the place of the teeth, adorned with all kinds of jewels;
having made it like a beast, one should fashion a very beautiful calf.
It should be made with one-tenth [of the materials] and adorned with all kinds of jewels.
In the Kāmika, however, it is said: "O child, [the altar] should be one-fourth [of the previous size]. One should fashion a maṇḍala in the center of the previously mentioned altar;
having placed the Surabhi cow in its center, she who contains all jewels in every respect.
There, one should wrap the cow Surabhi, together with her calf, in a pair of garments;
furthermore, one should worship the cow Surabhi and her calf with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Then, one should perform the oblation according to the rite of the single fire (ekāgni) as prescribed;
having offered the fuel-stick with the portion of clarified butter as before, one should perform the remaining rites in the same manner.
The worship of Śiva should be performed by bathing the Liṅga with ghee and other substances; having touched a cow while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra, one should cause it to be given to the Brahmins.
And a sacrificial fee of thirty niṣkas must be given, O Mahāmati.

The meaning is: "by means of the Gāyatrī, that is, by the hymn-mantra known as the Gosāvitrī. This is because it is stated in the Vātula: "And the wise one should recite with the mantra called Gosāvitrī. However, in the Kāmika [it says]:
One should worship the deity with clarified butter and other offerings, as well as with a thousand jars and so forth;
having propitiated the cow with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should cause her to be given to the Brahmins.
One should first honor the teacher with armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments;
having offered a pair of garments, one should then make a formal request according to the prescribed ritual.
But as a sacrificial fee, O one of great asceticism, thirty niṣkas should be given.

The gift of thirty *niṣkas* as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), however, pertains to the ritual procedure involving a single fire (*ekāgni*). In the case of multiple fires (*anekāgni*), the fee is like that for the *tulāpuruṣa* rite. This has been stated in the *Śaiva* tradition:
"Alternatively, according to the single-fire procedure, fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and oblations of sacrificial food should be offered;
in the single-fire ritual, a gift of at least thirty *niṣkas* is to be given to the preceptor."

The option of using a single fire pertains to one who possesses very little wealth. "The rest is as before" means that whatever remains unmentioned should be performed entirely according to the procedure for the *tulāpuruṣa* sacrifice prescribed in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*. In the *Kālottara*:
"He who is the giver of this [gift], by him the entire world of moving and non-moving things is given;
accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage, he travels in celestial chariots of divine splendor."
One attains the world of Śiva for as long as the fourteen Indras endure;
at the end of that time, one becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) and, possessing knowledge, shall go to Śiva.
Thus concludes the gift of the Kāmadhenu according to various treatises.
Now, the seventh great gift (mahādāna), known as the Golden Horse, is described.
Matsya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme rite of the golden horse,
by the grace of which one enjoys a world of infinite fruit.
Then, having reached an auspicious lunar day and performed the recitation by Brahmins,
one should perform the invocation of the world-protectors (lokeśa) as in the rite of the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa.

A wise person should perform the sacrifice of the golden horse (Hemavājimakha) even with very few resources, like the single-fire rite (Ekāgni), provided it is adorned with the necessary equipment for the pavilion of the Ṛti-rite, including decorations and coverings.

Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is included everything prescribed in the *Matsyapurāṇa* for the Tulāpuruṣa gift, beginning with the selection of the place and time, the performance of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the worship of Śiva and other deities, the invitation of the preceptor and officiating priests, the offering of the *madhuparka*, the drawing of the mystic diagram (*cakra*) upon the altar (*vedi*), and the consecration of the canopy, arches, and banners; this is explained as being performed with a single fire when the rites are small. One should place [the image] in the middle of the altar upon black antelope skin and sesame seeds—that is, upon a quantity of sesame seeds measuring one *droṇa* placed on the black antelope skin. The wise man should have a golden horse fashioned, covered with silk cloth, weighing from three *palas* upwards to a thousand *palas* according to his capacity.
[The image] is accompanied by wooden sandals, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, and vessels,
together with eight full jars, and provided with garlands, sugarcane, and fruits.

The bedding-appurtenances consist of various types of rugs, pillows, cloths, fruits, flowers, saffron, camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, betel, mirrors, combs, chowries, fans, and seats; as well as these items placed in front: vessels, swords, signet rings, a pair of sandals, copper water-cups, water-vessels, lamps, canopies, and so forth. "Joined with Mārtaṇḍa" means that one should fashion a golden horse of the Sun mounted upon it. [276] The characteristics of the Sun are described in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*.
Then, having been bathed with all medicinal herbs by the most eminent of Veda-knowers:
One should recite this mantra while holding a handful of flowers in cupped hands.

Here too, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the previous day, on the second day the preceptor (*guru*) should complete the ritual—from the recitation of the *puṇyāha* formula up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*)—just as before.
Then, the patron (*yajamāna*), having bathed in water containing all medicinal herbs and wearing white garments, should circumambulate [the deity] three times and utter the mantra to be described:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of all gods, you who are intent upon seizing the deities!"
In the form of a horse, protect me from this ocean of saṃsāra.
Since you yourself, having become sevenfold in the form of the Vedic meters,
cause the sun to revolve through the worlds, protect us as the eternal one.
Having recited this, one should present that horse to the preceptor;
by giving it, through the destruction of sins, one attains the eternal world of the Sun.
One should honor all the officiating priests with gifts of cattle;
one should present all kinds of grain and ritual implements to the preceptor.
Having prepared everything, including the bedding, he should indeed eat without using oil;
likewise, he should cause the recitation of the Purāṇas to take place after the meal.

Regarding the *dānavas*, one should follow the previous procedure; since no specific sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is mentioned, gold is the fee. Thus, there is a gift of gold according to one's capacity. Those with wealth should honor all the members of the assembly (*sadasya*) and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) with cows, in accordance with their own means. Because of the application of the phrase "all grains and implements," the placing of the grain is understood to occur prior [to the distribution]. Regarding the instruction "he should announce it to the Guru," in the case of giving a small amount of material, it refers to the Teacher alone; having given the horse, he should give gold and so forth to the officiating priests according to his capacity. However, in the case of giving a large amount of material such as a thousand *palas* and more, the arrangement is according to the archetype (*prakṛti*). This should also be observed in the case of very small amounts and even when following the single-fire (*ekāgni*) rite. Thereafter, as before, he should perform the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the deities, and the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
He who performs this ritual of the golden horse,
being honored in heaven by the lords of the gods,
is freed from sin and enters the city of Murāri.
He attains [this] while being honored by the perfected ones (siddhas).
The king who recites this gift of a golden horse, freed from all impurities, goes to the world of the Sun by means of a golden celestial chariot as if by the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Furthermore, one who sees that which is worshipped by the wives of the Lord of the Thirty-three [gods] shall behold it.
Or whatever man of little wealth hears of it, or remembers the gift of the golden horse, or rejoices in it here in this world—
he too goes forth with his body purified and his defilements destroyed.
This bath is frequented by the gods Purandara and Maheśvara.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a golden horse as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: I shall now describe the gift of a golden horse, which brings about victory.
O observer of noble vows, listen to this secret, which is superior to ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
Having prepared a horse endowed with auspicious marks and adorned with all ornaments, [one should perform the rite] one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times.
The words "hundred" and "thousand" are intended as indicators for whatever has been prescribed.
From three palas upwards, up to even a thousand palas,
according to one's capacity, a wise person should perform the Hemavājimakha sacrifice like the Ekāgni rite when the means are small.
Thus it is stated in the Vātula-tantra:
"One should properly have the Pañcakalyāṇaka made of silver;
with white [markings] on the four feet and the face, the horse is called Pañcakalyāṇaka."
Endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed of all limbs,
equipped with every weapon, the imperishable vehicle of Indra.
Having stationed that horse, endowed with excellent qualities and equal to Uccaiḥśravas, in the Middle Country, and having recognized him as such, one should bring him back and worship him.

"Having established it in the Middle Country": having placed that horse upon the sesame seeds in the center of the maṇḍala-altar prescribed for the Tulāpuruṣa gift in the Liṅgapurāṇa—the archetype of this type of gift—one should worship it while meditating upon Uccaiḥśravas. To the east of it, one should worship a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas with the thought that he is Indra, the Lord of the Gods, and cause five niṣkas to be given to him.
Having honored that horse, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa according to the prescribed rite;
indeed, one should give a golden horse and then worship the teacher.
According to the extent of one's wealth— whether with five niṣkas or even more—
one should satisfy the poor, the blind, the wretched, the helpless, children, the elderly, the emaciated, and the sick with gifts of food, and especially the Brahmins.
One should bathe the deity—the Liṅga, the Great Lord in embodied form—with ghee;
likewise, one should bathe it with milk in the same manner, using exactly one hundred palas.
Having established [the deity] with the *brahmakūrca* mixture and smeared [the image] with agallochum and sandalwood,
one should worship, prostrate, and then ask forgiveness from the God of gods.
The man who performs this gift with devotion,
having enjoyed the worlds of Indra for a long time, shall become a lord of kings upon the earth.

Having given five *niṣkas* to the Brahmin who has been propitiated with the thought that he is Indra, and having given the golden horse to the *śrotriya*s and others, one should honor the *ācārya* and give him five *niṣkas*. The entire subsequent ritual procedure, beginning with the bathing of Śiva, is as before. However, in the *Matsyapurāṇa* and other texts, the gift of the horse is said to be for the *ācārya* alone. But in the *Kāmika*:
"Having honored him with perfumes and other offerings, one should present [the horse] to the Brahmins;
having worshipped him with the thought that he is Surendra (Indra), one should bestow five *niṣkas*."
One should perform the worship of the mandala, the fire sacrifice (homa), the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa),
and likewise the offering of fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and others, in the same manner as the Tulābhāra rite.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a golden horse as declared in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*.
Now begins the eighth great gift (*mahādāna*), named the Golden Horse, according to the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
The Fish [incarnation] said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift known as the "Horse-chariot," which is meritorious and the destroyer of great sins.
Then, having reached an auspicious day and performed the recitation by Brahmins,
one should perform the invocation of the world-protectors (lokeśa) as in the ritual for the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa.
The officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, the ornaments, the coverings, and so forth.
"Like the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa": it should be understood as being like the Tulāpuruṣa described in the *Matsyapurāṇa*; the word "etc. (*ādi*) is also to be explained as before.
Having placed sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, one should have a golden chariot fashioned—having eight horses or four horses, with four wheels and well-adorned.
[280] It is joined with a sapphire pitcher in the form of a banner,
accompanied by the eight world-protectors, and endowed with petals of ruby.

In this context, regarding the requirement for the quantity of sesame seeds and the chariot, there is no fixed rule based on human preference, as no specific measure is mentioned in the original injunction (*prakṛti*). However, some authorities maintain that, due to proximity, the sesame seeds here should be measured by a *droṇa*, as is established in the case of gifts such as gold, elephants, and chariots. The *kūvara* is the wooden pin at the front of the yoke. The *dhvaja* is the staff; since the chariot is made of gold, this staff must also be golden, and it should be provided with a pitcher made of sapphire (*indranīla*) placed upon it. The characteristics of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*.
Four full jars, eight or ten grains of grain,
and a canopy above joined with silken cloth.

One who is devoted to a particular deity should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) with the "Hundred Names" using a garland joined with blades of kusha grass and accompanied by a person.
A canopy of five colors should be provided here; a man in the form of one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) should be placed upon a golden chariot, along with his own wife, sandals, and wooden shoes.
One should give cows according to one’s means, as well as beds and seats.
A wise person should have [the image] made according to their ability, weighing more than three palas of gold.

The weight is two thousand *palas*. This measurement of gold is to be understood as including the flag-man (*dhvajapuruṣa*), the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), the horse, and the wheel-guardians. One should give it joined with eight chariots, or joined with four chariot-horses, or even joined with two, provided it is equipped with a golden lion-banner.

In the case of eight horses, the banner should be equipped with a golden lion; in the case of four horses, a pinnacle made of sapphire (*indranīla*) should be placed on the banner; and in the case of two horses, a golden lion—such is the established rule. Then, both his wheel-protectors, the Aśvins, mounted upon horses, arrived at an auspicious time; he was then bathed by the twice-born as before.
Wearing white garlands and garments, one should give and recite this mantra:
The two protectors of the wheel (cakrarakṣau), the Aśvinī-kumāras, should be depicted mounted on horses near the wheel. Gobhila states their characteristics:
"The two divine physicians should be made with two arms, riding upon horses;
in their right hands, celestial medicinal herbs should be depicted."
"O twice-born one, two beautiful books should likewise be placed in the two left hands. [Thus it is said.

Regarding the auspicious time—the *lagna*, *muhūrta*, and so forth, which is favorable to the patron (*yajamāna*)—here too, as before, on the day following the day of preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), upon the completion of all rites such as the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the patron, having bathed with water containing all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*) and having taken handfuls of flowers, should circumambulate [the image] three times and recite the mantra to be spoken hereafter:
"Salutations, salutations to the Destroyer of Sin (*pāpavināśana*)."
O soul of the universe, whose vehicle is the Veda-steed, sovereign lord of all abodes, source of both existence and non-existence,
O forest fire to the thickets of sin— grant me peace!
You alone are the creator and the supreme treasure-house of the Vasus, Aṣṭakas, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts;
therefore, may my heart go forth toward you.
The state of being stretched toward the Dharma arises from the destruction of the flood of evil.

Here too, the preliminary procedures—such as the preparation for the gift, the offering of gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the distribution of materials among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the preceptor (*ācārya*), and the performance of the rites with a single fire according to the prescribed rules—should be understood as being the same as before. Thereafter, one should perform the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the deities, their dismissal (*visarjana*), and so forth.
Now, in the *Atharvaṇīya-pathabrāhmaṇa*:

Oṃ. Now, therefore, we shall set forth the ritual procedure for the horse-chariot. During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, on an auspicious lunar mansion, impelled by faith and joined with the planets—or at the time of a planetary conjunction—one should have the officiant bring a golden chariot from the time of its dedication. Having sprinkled everything with water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*), having caused the prescribed rubbing, anointing, and smearing to be performed, and having fastened garments, perfumes, and garlands, one should kindle the fire, take hold of it, and then offer oblations with the two verses beginning "Come forth, O steed" (*ud ehi vājin*). Having cooked a sacrificial pap (*caru*) for Sūrya and consecrated it with the mantra "The overcomer, the victorious" (*viṣāsahiṃ sahamānam*), one should take hold of it and then offer the oblation.

Having sprinkled the chariot, the yoke-strap, the yoke, and both horses with water consecrated for peace (*śāntyudaka*), one should offer oblations from the *sthālīpāka* upon the heads of the two horses with the verse beginning "O swift horse" (*turaṅga vājine*). Having paid homage with the nine mantras beginning "Salutation to him who rises" (*udayate namaḥ*), one should satisfy the twice-born at the conclusion.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"Whatever fruit is proclaimed for all gifts whatsoever..."
By giving a horse-chariot to Brahmins according to the prescribed rite, one obtains all of that.
Having attained the stainless state, which is inviolable by the gods, well-earned, and golden, he,
possessing the splendor of gold, is liberated from sin.
Moving in chariots, he traverses the world of the sun.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Thus, he who performs here this gift of horses and chariots, which destroys the fear of worldly existence,"
With his body liberated from the cloth-bags of all impurities,
he attains the supreme state of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
With his body blazing so brightly that he surpassed the splendor of the sun, the fierce-rayed lord of the gods,
he entered the celestial sphere while being drunk in by the bee-like eyes of the Siddha maidens.
He dwells for a long time together with the one born from the lotus of his lotus-like mouth.
Whoever thus recites or hears this account of the gift of the golden-horsed chariot shall never go to the city of hell.
He goes again to the abode of the enemy of Naraka.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a chariot drawn by golden horses.
Now begins the ninth great gift (mahādāna), known as the Golden Elephant Chariot, as described in the Matsya Purāṇa.
The Fish [Incarnation] said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the auspicious golden elephant-chariot,
by the gift of which a human being goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.

Then, having reached an auspicious lunar day, the wise man should perform the invocation of the deities (āvāhana) in the world, as in the ritual of the gift of one's weight in gold (tulāpuruṣa), by reciting the words of the Brahmins.
The officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, the ornaments, the coverings, and so forth;
likewise, one should fast here as well, and partake of a meal together with the Brahmins.

Here too, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), all that was not mentioned—such as the place, time, the increase [of merit], and the *śrāddha*—is to be understood as being established according to the *Tulāpuruṣa* rite described in the *Matsyapurāṇa*. Regarding the phrase "having fasted," it should be understood that even eating only at night (*nakta*) is permitted in the event of an inability to fast.
One should have a golden chariot made in the form of a flower-cart (*puṣparatha*), adorned with jewels, featuring various *valabhī* (pinnacles) and equipped with four wheels.
Endowed with the eight guardians of the world (lokapālas), joined by Śiva, the Sun, and Brahmā;
in the center, accompanied by Nārāyaṇa and attended by Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi.

The *puṣparatha* is a chariot for the purpose of play. It is covered on top in the shape of a four-sided pavilion (*catuṣkikā*), and from its rings [proceed] the supports for the World-Guardians (*lokapāla*). The characteristics of the World-Guardians, Brahmā, Śiva, and Arka (the Sun) are described in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. The word "middle" is connected with both the preceding and the following [terms], since the requirement for a location for Śiva and the others is satisfied by that very [term]. The characteristics of Nārāyaṇa and the others are derived from the *Pañcarātra*: "Nārāyaṇa has four arms; likewise, he holds a conch and a discus in his left hands, while in his right hands he holds a great lotus and a bow resembling a closed lotus."
"On the left [should be] Śrī with a lute in her hand, and another [goddess] with a fist and a lotus in her hand.
Having placed these upon a black antelope skin over a drona-measure of sesame seeds, one should establish the chariot,
as well as the eighteen grains, along with vessels, seats, and sandalwood.
One should place a lamp, sandals, an umbrella, wooden shoes, and a mirror [on the flagstaff];
on the banner, one should depict Garuḍa, and at the tip of the pole, Vināyaka.
Above it was a canopy adorned with various fruits,
made of five-colored silk and decorated with unfading flowers.
It was accompanied by four water-jars and eight cows,
and by four horses and elephants adorned with strings of pearls.
Having fashioned [the image] according to its true form and yoked with two elephants, one should present it;
one should make it from five palas upwards, even up to a bhāra, according to one's capacity.
"One should place Garuḍa upon the banner," and so forth; here, "banner" refers to the staff (*daṇḍa*). The characteristics of Garuḍa are described in the *Nāradīya*:
"Oṃ! In front of Indra stands the bird Guḍākeśa with palms joined in reverence.
His left knee rests upon the ground, and his head is adorned by a hooded serpent."
The son of Vinatā should be depicted with the shanks of a bird, a human neck, a prominent nose, and a human body; he has two arms and is endowed with wings.
Now, regarding Vināyaka: here, the elephant-faced one should be depicted with four arms and three eyes,
wearing a snake as a sacred thread and having the moon as his crest-ornament.
One should place a tusk in the right hand, a rosary in the second,
an axe in the third, and likewise a sweetmeat in the fourth.

"Teeth and so forth [should be placed] on the upper and lower hands; this is what is to be given. *Kūvara* has been explained. *Amlānakusuma* is a specific type of flower, according to the maxim that "conventional usage overrides etymological derivation. By the term *mahāsahā*, the well-known [plant] is understood; *bhāra* has been explained. Furthermore, the deities residing upon the banner must be fashioned from gold of the same proportions as the chariot, measured at five *palas* and so forth. Having thus prepared the materials and performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) as before, and having completed the entire ritual procedure—including the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*)—on the appointed days, the preceptor (*ācārya*) shall perform the ceremonial bathing of the patron with water containing all medicinal herbs.
Then, bathed with auspicious sounds by the foremost of Veda-knowers,
he circumambulated [the deity] three times and took handfuls of flowers in his joined palms.
One should recite this mantra and announce it to the Brahmins.

Homage, homage to you, O God, who are served by Śaṅkara, Padmaja, Arka, the Lords of the World, Vidyādharas, and Vāsudeva; protect us, O you who are the movement consisting of the splendor of the ancient sacrifice!

That most secret state of the Enemy of the Gods, which consists of bliss and whose nature is composed of qualities, is perceived within in meditative absorption by sages whose minds are focused solely on yoga; O Lord, you who are mounted upon the chariot are that very reality—*tattvam asi*.
For you alone are the refuge for those who have taken shelter in the ocean of worldly existence.
It is a vessel for the drinking of sacrifice, filled with the treasure of bliss;
therefore, show favor by quelling the flood of my sins through the gift of a chariot drawn by a thousand golden elephants.

Having prostrated with this mantra and prepared a gold *dakṣiṇā* according to one’s capacity, one should perform the ritual procedure as before and present that elephant-chariot—equipped with a living elephant—to the Brahmins. The distribution of the remaining portions, such as half or a fourth, to the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others, as well as giving to others by his permission, and the relief of the poor and helpless, should be carried out as prescribed for the original rite. Then, when the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) has been performed, the patron (*yajamāna*), having approached the altar, should perform the worship of the deities; the preceptor, however, should dismiss them. Thus it is stated in the *Ātharvaṇagopathabrāhmaṇa*.
Now, therefore, I shall describe the ritual for the gift of an elephant-chariot.
Having fashioned a chariot made of gold, beautifully adorned with wheels,
and yoked to seven elephants, one should worship it according to the prescribed rule.
Alternatively, it may be made of gold or silver, joined with four [components],
or even made of wood, provided it is untouched [by impurities] and filled with all the necessary materials.
Clad in a pair of elephants or a pair of bulls,
he enjoys the earth with its seven continents for exactly seven lifetimes.

When the moon is in conjunction with the asterism Hasta—on either the full moon or the new moon day, or on another auspicious lunar day—one should perform the *tantra* rite during the day in a pure place. Having kindled the fire with fuel placed toward the east and having touched it, one should offer oblations, saying: "To Savitṛ, svāhā! To Pataṅga, svāhā! To Pāvaka, svāhā! To the thousand-rayed one, svāhā! To Mārtaṇḍa, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Parameṣṭhin, svāhā! Having offered these, and having poured the remnants of the oblations into a water-jar while reciting, "May the splendor of the elephant extend; may great fame increase," one should sprinkle the yoke, the thong, and the chariot—all of them—with the formula: "I yoke you with the wagon of the sacrifice. Then he should yoke it with: "I yoke you with the wagon of the unwearied and the foremost; you are the bearer of the spoken word. Be a carrier for those who run. He should present the guest-offering (*argha*) to the yoked horse with the verse: "Yoked with dark steeds, his chariot is white-hued and golden, which rolls along auspicious paths. May the peaceful Agni, the finder of wealth, the maker of gold, the golden-handed Savitṛ, protect us."
He who, with his hand, strikes the interior of a large elephant-chariot yoked [to horses],
attains the auspicious station of Savitṛ, which possesses divine, desire-swift speed.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "He who,
having thus prostrated, causes the gift of a golden chariot to be made,
shall have his body liberated from all sins."
He attains that state beyond the senses of the moon-crested Lord, which is frequented by hosts of Vidyādharas, gods, and lords of sages.

And he leads all his kinsmen— fathers and grandsons— even those who, though tormented by the distress of being burned amidst the mass of blazing fire-flames arising from the expansion of their committed evils, are drawn away from Raurava itself.
Having bestowed gifts of elephants and chariots, he attained the eternal abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the golden elephant chariot.
Now, the tenth great gift, known as the Pañcalāṅgala, is set forth.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift known as Pañcalāṅgalaka, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
Having reached an auspicious lunar day, such as the beginning of a Yuga or an eclipse,
a man should bestow a gift of land accompanied by five furrows.
[288] A mountain fort, a hamlet, or even a village rich in crops;
or a hundred nivartanas, or even half of that, according to one's capacity.
Having fashioned five ploughs out of heartwood,
the wise one likewise prepared another five made of gold, equipped with all necessary implements.
The nature of a *karvaṭa* and similar settlements is described in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "A city has high ramparts and walls, is surrounded on all sides by moats,
measures half a *yojana* in width, and is twice that length."
A *kheṭa* should be half that size, and a *karvaṭa* a quarter of it;
likewise, there should be villages consisting mostly of pure people and well-to-do cultivators.
"It dwells in the midst of the soil that constitutes the field's share, known as a village.

He will later state, "measuring back with a staff of seven cubits," and so forth. "Hard woods" refers to *śāka*, *iṅgudī*, *candana*, and the like; "implements" refers to the yoke, the thong, the plowshare, the rope, the goad, and so on.
"And ten bulls, endowed with auspicious marks, capable of bearing the yoke."
Adorned with golden horns and decorated with pearl-tipped tails.
One should consecrate in the hall those [images] which have silver feet and forehead-marks, are adorned with red silk garments, and are provided with garlands and sandalwood paste.

The characteristics of a *vṛṣala* include good character, youthfulness, possession of the senses, freedom from disease, and endurance of hardships, among others. The "forehead" (*agra*) refers to the region of the forehead; therefore, they should have feet made of silver and silver *tilaka*-marks on their foreheads.
One should offer a *caru* oblation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to Parjanya, Āditya, and the Rudras;
one should present this *caru* to him in a single sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Likewise, one should offer fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, clarified butter, and black sesame seeds.

Here too, having performed the preliminary rites such as the formal acceptance (*adhivāsana*) as before, and having performed the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) on the following day, one should complete the remainder of the ritual, beginning with the seating of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at the fire-pits (*agnikuṇḍa*). However, there is this further distinction: from among the priests prescribed for the *tulāpuruṣa* sacrifice, the Guru should designate one particular priest; that single priest alone, at a single fire-pit, should offer one thousand and eight oblations of materials such as milk-rice (*pāyasa-caru*) and so forth, using mantras bearing the characteristics of Parjanya, Āditya, and the Rudras.
A wise person should perform the invocation of the world-protectors (*lokeśāvāhana*) just as in the *tulāpuruṣa* rite.
Then, amidst auspicious sounds, the wise one, wearing white garlands and garments, [proceeded].
Having summoned a brahmin couple, one should adorn them with golden threads, rings,
silken garments, bracelets, and jewels.
One should give a bed with its furnishings and a single milch cow;
likewise, one should place eighteen kinds of grain all around it.
Then, having circumambulated [the deity] and holding a handful of flowers,
one should recite this mantra and then offer everything as an oblation.

The phrase "invoking Lokeśa" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). For here, the ritual procedures prescribed in the *Matsyapurāṇa* for the *Tulāpuruṣa* sacrifice are to be understood, including: the invocation of the place and time, the ancestral offering (*śrāddha*), the worship of Śiva and other deities, the recitation by Brahmins, the selection of the preceptor (*guru*) and officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the offering of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the altar (*vedikā*), the canopy (*vitāna*), the drawing of the mystic diagram (*cakralekhana*), and the arches and banners (*toraṇapatākā*). Regarding the word "then" (*tataḥ*): the syntactic connection is that immediately after the fire-oblation (*homa*), having bathed in water infused with all medicinal herbs and wearing white garments, one should give. As for the phrase "having invited a Brahmin couple": since no other fee for the preceptor—who is appointed to oversee the entire rite—is perceived, and because there is no reason to abandon what is at hand, and because the term "Brahmin" is not contradictory in this context, it is understood that the gift should be given to the preceptor himself along with his wife. Furthermore, by his permission, it may also be given to others. It should be understood that even in minor rites, the rule of using a single fire (*ekāgni*) applies. The items such as the bed and its furnishings (*śayyopaskara*) have already been explained in the section on the gift of gold and horses. Now follows the mantra: [Mantra omitted per instructions] *Note: The provided text ends with the instruction to provide only the translation; thus, the final sentence regarding the mantra is left untranslated.*
Since all the hosts of gods, and all things both stationary and moving,
abide upon the body of Dhūrjaṭi, may my devotion be fixed upon Śiva.
Since other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of land,
may my devotion to this very dharma remain firm.

Having recited this mantra and prepared a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his capacity, he should present it according to the previously mentioned procedure; thereafter follow the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), the worship of the deities, and their dismissal. Prajāpati states that thirty daṇḍas of seven cubits each constitute a *nivartana*, and that three-quarters of that is the measure of a *gocarma*.
O wise one, for that person who gives a hundred nivartanas according to this measure and by this rite,
the entire mass of their sins is swiftly destroyed.
Or he may give even half of that, or even a mere *gocarma* (cow-hide) area, or even just enough space for a dwelling; such a person is also liberated from sins.
For as many plow-path openings on the surface of the earth as there are hair-pores born from the body of the Daughter of the Lord of Speech (Sarasvatī),
for that many years shall he remain in the city of Śaṅkara.
The man who makes a gift of land here in this world.
Having approached a great celestial mansion with its fly-whisks being waved by hosts of gandharvas, kinnaras, asuras, suras, and siddhas,
he is honored together with his fathers, grandfathers, and kinsmen.
And becoming a leader of the immortals, he goes to the city of Śambhu.
Even the status of Indra, once attained, comes to an end through the gift of cattle, land, or the plowshare;
therefore, [one should give] that which destroys the mass of sins arising from the earth.
Generosity should be practiced even for the sake of the arising of great supernatural power.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the five-ploughed field as declared in the glorious Matsya Purāṇa.
The Blessed Lord said:
Hereafter, I shall describe to you another most wonderful gift.
O Indra among kings, by means of which gift one becomes a giver of all gifts.
The gift known as the "ploughed furrow" (saṃyuktahalapaṅkti), which pacifies all sins, bestows all happiness, and grants all fruits.
A row is said to consist of ten plows, and a plow consists of four yokes;
the wise say that the ten blades are made of solid wood.
Bound with golden bands, adorned with jewels, auspicious,
young, strong, noble, free from physical defects, and well-adorned.
A man should yoke to those plows bulls with auspicious limbs, their heads anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with flowers of cloth and gold.
One should have halters made that are joined in pairs along with the bulls,
as well as goads, pins, fastenings, and all other necessary implements.
With such ploughs, one should construct a continuous row of fields,
whether it be a small hamlet, a market town, or even a village abounding in grain.
One should arrange for a hundred circumambulations, or even half of that;
with a disciplined mind, one should offer such a thing during the time of a festival.
One should cause [the gift] to be given on the full moon of Kārttika or Vaiśākha, during the northern solstice, at the time of one's birth, during an eclipse, or at the equinoxes.
He should invite an even number of Brahmins who are perfected in the Vedas, whose limbs are unimpaired, well-adorned, skilled in the Śrauta rituals, and disciplined.
A wise person should have a pavilion constructed measuring ten cubits;
and on the preceding day, he should prepare one auspicious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit.
There, those best of the twice-born should perform an oblation with the *vyāhṛtis*;
they should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to Parjanya, Āditya, and the Rudras.
Likewise, having offered sacrificial fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, clarified butter, and black sesame seeds,
he should then cause the auspicious row of guests to sit down amidst the grain.
Then, having bathed in the vicinity of the Sārma [river], pure and clad in white garments,
the sacrificer, with a concentrated mind, yoked the row of ploughs.
Amidst the sounds of conchs and drums and the abundant chanting of the Vedas,
one who has taken handfuls of flowers should recite this mantra.
Since all the hosts of gods always stand upon the plow,
stationed upon the shoulders of the bull, may my devotion be fixed upon Śiva.
And because other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of the [spiritual] ground,
may my devotion to the Dharma always remain firm.
When this has been said, that best of the twice-born should then cause a row to be sown with seeds,
all kinds of gems, gold, and likewise silver.
Having himself subsequently attached it to the neck, he should offer it into the hands of the Brahmins;
the wise man should continue this until the time of returning, and then he should desist.
Then, having performed a circumambulation and having presented gifts to the Brahmins according to the rules for giving sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), one should prostrate and bid them farewell.
Whoever bestows this gift according to this rule is honored in the heavenly world, together with twenty-one generations of his lineage.
For seven births, one shall not experience poverty, misfortune, or diseases;
likewise, one shall become a sovereign of the earth.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, by merely seeing a gift being given, one is liberated from the sins committed since birth; of this there is no doubt.
In former times, this gift was bestowed by Dilīpa,
Yayāti, Śibi, Nimi, and the wise Bharata.
Even today they rejoice in heaven by the power of this gift;
therefore, O protector of the earth, O best of kings, one should give this gift with great effort.
It should be given by a woman or a man endowed with devotion,
O King, even if there is no assembly of five or four;
even a single ploughshare should be given according to the prescribed rule by the wise.

For as many atoms of dust as there are in the earth turned up by the tip of a plow, and for as many hairs as there are on the body of a well-bred bull, for that many eons shall he remain in the city of Śaṅkhapura.
The man who here performs the offering of a row [of guests],...
Those virtuous ones who, on an auspicious day, desire to provide this row of ploughs yoked with exceedingly powerful bulls, together with provisions, for the foremost of the twice-born,
shall obtain the earth.
Having approached the presence of the king, they become worthy of honor.
