Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the plough and the furrow as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
Now, the great gift known as the "Bestowal of the Eleven Earths" (*ekādaśadharādhāna*) is described. In the *Śrī Matsyapurāṇa*, the Fish [Incarnation] said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed gift of land,
which causes the destruction of the sins of men and the eradication of inauspiciousness.
One should have fashioned a golden earth resembling Jambudvīpa,
complete with its boundary mountains and Mount Meru in its center.
Endowed with the eight world-protectors, consisting of nine continents,
provided with hundreds of rivers and streams, and surrounded on the outside by the ocean.

"Anukāriṇīm" means "similar. For here, when it is said that one should make [the model] similar to Jambudvīpa, since the similarity to the entire earth—including its mountains, cities, lakes, forests, and so forth—would otherwise be implied, the phrase "possessing the boundary-mountains (*maryādāparvata*) and so on" is used to indicate that the imitation of the earth consists only of those specific features. Otherwise, if that were understood through the general term alone, the specific qualifications would be rendered useless. Thus, the meaning is as follows: when it is said "one should make a golden earth," there is the possibility of referring to the earth consisting of seven continents; therefore, it is specified as "imitating Jambudvīpa. Even then, there is the possibility of imitating [Jambudvīpa] as being endowed with various mountains; therefore, it is specified as "possessing the boundary-mountains. When that is the case, there is the possibility of imitating Meru; therefore, it is specified as "having Meru in the center. To exclude the presence of various hosts of gods, it is specified as "endowed with the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Furthermore, by adopting this perspective of enumerating [specific features], the suspicion that one might adopt alternative views such as the four regions (*varṣa*) shown in other Purāṇas is removed; thus, it is stated as "endowed with nine regions (*navavarṣa*). In that regard, Jambudvīpa is described in the Viṣṇupurāṇa.
O Maitreya, I have thus briefly described to you this Jambudvīpa, which is nine thousand yojanas in extent and one hundred thousand yojanas in width.
Encompassing Jambudvīpa, the Ocean of Milk stands outside, a hundred thousand yojanas in extent, Maitreya, shaped like a circular ring.
Jambudvīpa stands in the center of all the continents;
even in its center, Maitreya, is Mount Meru, the mountain of gold.
Its height is eighty-four thousand yojanas;
its base is sixteen cubits wide, and it is thirty-two cubits wide at the summit.
At its base, its extent is sixteen thousand [yojanas] on all sides;
however, in another Purāṇa, it is stated that its height is sixty-eight yojanas. Likewise:
"There, extending nine thousand [yojanas], it lies in the four directions of Meru."
O illustrious one, there is Ilāvṛta and four surrounding mountain ranges.
To the east is the mountain named Mandara, to the south Gandhamādana;
Vaibhrāja is known to be on the western side, and Supārśva on the north.
The boundary mountains within the cosmic egg are shown in the Purāṇas:
Jāṭhara and Devakūṭa are two mountains in the eastern direction;
they extend from south to north, reaching as far as the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains.
[296] Kailāsa and Himavat are the two excellent mountain ranges in the south;
these two extend from east to west, reaching as far as the ocean.
Triśṛṅga and Jārudhi are the two northern excellent mountains;
these two extend five yojanas toward the east and are situated at the edge of the ocean.
Niṣadha and Pārijāta are the two excellent mountain ranges in the west;
they extend from south to north, reaching as far as Nīla and Niṣadha.

The mountains Nīla and Niṣadha will be described further on. Regarding the phrase "endowed with the eight world-protectors" (lokapālāṣṭakopetām): the eight world-protectors are Indra and the others; their characteristics were previously mentioned in the section on the gift of Brahmāṇḍa. Their locations should be established above Mount Meru, proceeding clockwise in the directions starting from the east. Regarding the phrase "endowed with nine regions" (navavarṣasamanvitām): the description of these regions is found in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "That which lies north of the ocean and south of the Snowy Mountain (Himādri) is indeed named Bhārata, where the lineage of Bharata resides."
O twice-born one, Bhārata is the first region; beyond that is remembered Kimpuruṣa, and likewise Harivarṣa is another to the south of Meru.
To the north is the region of Ramyaka, and following that is Hiraṇmaya.
The Uttarakurus are indeed just like Bhārata;
to the east of Meru are the Bhadrās, and to the west is Ketumāla.
Two regions are declared to be on either side of them, with Ilāvṛta in their midst;
each of these, O best of the twice-born, measures nine thousand [yojanas].
Likewise: Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha are on the south;
Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin are the mountain ranges on the north.
They are two thousand yojanas in height and as many in width;
two in the middle are one hundred thousand yojanas in measure, while the others are ten less than that.

"Measuring one hundred thousand [yojanas]," and so forth: the two mountains Nīla and Niṣadha, situated on both sides of Ilāvṛta, are to be understood as being one hundred thousand-fold in length. The two mountains Śveta and Hemakūṭa, situated outside of those, are to be understood as measuring ninety thousand yojanas. Likewise, the two mountains Śṛṅgin and Himavat, situated further outside, measure eighty thousand yojanas; this is the meaning. The reasoning for this is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Because each island forms a circle, a decrease and increase [in size] is proclaimed. [This is also stated] in the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*.
To my west, extending for nine thousand [yojanas],
lies the Gandhamādana mountain, measuring thirty-four thousand [yojanas].
Increasing forty thousand [yojanas] from the surface of the earth,
and being twice as wide at its depth of one thousand [yojanas],
the Mālyavat mountain is proclaimed to be of that same measure in the east.

In this context, since it is impossible to construct the earth and other elements with dimensions of a hundred thousand *yojanas* and so forth, one should assume a measurement such as half a finger-breadth (*ardhāṅgula*) in place of a thousand *yojanas*, and thus carry out the gradations of number as described. Regarding the phrase "endowed with hundreds of rivers and streams": the rivers are those such as the Bhāgīrathī, and the streams are those such as the Śoṇa; since it is impossible to arrange them in their entirety, a representation should be made to the extent possible. Finally, regarding "encircled by the ocean": although the ocean is exactly the same size as the earth, nevertheless, because this is merely an instruction for a representation, one should perform only what can be represented.
[298] Adorned with great jewels and joined with the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas,
it should be made with a thousand palas of gold, or half of that, or according to one's capacity.
One may fashion it with three hundred [palas], or with two hundred, or even with one hundred;
a wise person, even if incapable, should fashion it with at least five palas.
The wise man should perform the invocation of Lokeśvara as in the Tulāpuruṣa rite,
as well as the preparation of the sacrificial priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, the ornaments, the coverings, and so forth.
Having spread a black antelope skin upon the sacrificial altar, one should place sesame seeds upon it,
as well as the eighteen kinds of grain and liquids such as salt and the like.
Likewise, one should arrange eight full vases all around,
as well as a silk canopy and various kinds of fruits.
Having thus prepared beautiful garments and pieces of sandalwood for her, preceded by the rite of consecration (adhivāsana), he performed the ceremony.
Wearing white garlands and garments, adorned with white ornaments,
he then performed a circumambulation while holding a handful of flowers.

Regarding "great jewels" (*mahāratna*) and so forth: great jewels such as rubies (*māṇikya*) and others have been shown in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). The forms of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas are mentioned in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*. Regarding "clothing and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), everything mentioned in the *Tulāpuruṣa* rite is to be performed—this includes the place and time, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the worship of Śiva and others, the recitation for the Brahmins (*brāhmaṇavācanā*), the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), and so on. It should be noted that the full jars (*pūrṇakalaśa*) are to be provided with garlands, perfumes, five gems, sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, and mango shoots. "A canopy of five colors" (*pañcavarṇa vitāna*) is the description. "Having circumambulated" (*pradakṣiṇaṃ kṛtvā*) means having turned three times to the right (*triḥ pradakṣiṇam āvṛtya*). Furthermore, the circumambulation and subsequent rites are to be performed on the second day, after the completion of the remainder of the ritual up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), following the bath with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhisnāna*).
Then, having reached an auspicious time, one should recite these mantras:
"Salutations to you, since you alone are the abode of all the gods;
and since you are the nurse of all beings, therefore protect us, O Vasundharā!"
Because you sustain the Vasus and possess exceedingly pure wealth, you are therefore born as Vasundharā; for that reason, protect us thoroughly from fear.
Even the Four-faced One cannot reach the end of you, O Immoveable One;
therefore, salutations to the Infinite One—protect me from the mire of saṃsāra!
You alone are Lakṣmī in Govinda, and as Gaurī you abide in Śiva;
you are Gāyatrī at the side of Brahmā, Jyotsnā in the moon, and Prabhā in the sun.
Intellect (buddhi) is renowned in Bṛhaspati, while wisdom (medhā) resides among the sages;
because she stands pervading the universe, she is therefore considered Viśvaṃbhara (the Sustainer of the Universe).
O Goddess, protect us from the ocean of saṃsāra through these forms: Dhṛti, Kṣiti, Kṣamā, Kṣauṇī, Pṛthvī, Vasumatī, and Rasā.
Having thus addressed that goddess, one should present her to the Brahmins;
or else, one should bestow half of the land, or a fourth part, upon the preceptor.
And having prostrated before the officiating priests, he should dismiss them with the remainder.

Here too, having uttered the formula of giving as before, one should perform the gift preceded by water with the permission of the preceptor; the giving to others is for the fulfillment of the needs of the poor and the helpless. However, in the case of a minor rite, the rule of a single fire (*ekāgni*) applies. It should be understood that in rites to be performed by a sovereign, the gift of villages and so forth constitutes the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), whereas in rites performed by those who are incapable, the gift of gold according to one's ability serves as the fee. Then, after the recitation by the Brahmins, one should perform the worship and dismissal of the deities. [This is stated] in the *Ātharvaṇa-Gopatha-Brāhmaṇa*.

Then, having fasted entirely on the day of Rohiṇī, the donor—having prepared a water-pot filled with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) scattered with seeds, juices, gems, and perfumes according to the Vedic injunctions—sprinkles himself with the consecration mantras as prescribed. He enters upon the vow with the formula: "O Lord of Vows, through this vow... Both [the donor and his wife] eat only what is unasked for and sleep on the ground. Having observed the ritual service of the vow for one night, five nights, or twelve nights according to their ability, on the following day, having performed the ritual procedure up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, and having taken hold of the fire, he should offer oblations of clarified butter with the *Kāmasūkta*, the *Kāsasūkta*, and the *Puruṣasūkta*. Then, having fashioned a golden representation of the earth the size of a cow-hide (*gocarma*) and brought it forward, he places it on the northern side of the altar with the words: "Upon this altar. He establishes the mountains with the verse: "Those mountains, the hills... and adorns them with gold, silver, gems, pearls, coral, and so forth. Having fashioned the rivers with the verses: "On the day they flow together" and "With pleasant voices," he fills them with liquids. He represents the oceans with the verse: "Thou art the further shore; I release thee unto the ocean," and the trees with: "The Lord of the Forest with the gods has come to us," and "Bṛhaspati has led us. He should mentally intend other things for the sacrifice, for here everything becomes realized by mental intention. Having caused a salutation to be made with the verse: "She supports the treasure," he should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited with the *Satya-bṛhaspatyanuvāka* and the hymn: "The gods who are eleven in heaven... He should conclude the rite and, having consecrated it with the mantra: "Neither from heaven nor from the gods' knowledge," he should give it to the Brahmins. This gift fulfills every desire or wish of the donor, even if it be difficult to attain.
Just as seeds sprout upon the surface of the earth when ploughed by a plow,
even so do desires always sprout in the mind after death.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for all gifts whatsoever,
that one obtains by giving land to Brahmins according to the prescribed rule.
Now, in the Matsya Purāṇa: "He who, when an auspicious time has arrived, gives a beautiful golden earth according to this rite, goes indeed to the station of Viṣṇu."
Having gone to the city of Nārāyaṇa by means of a celestial chariot, sun-colored and garlanded with networks of tinkling bells, one shall dwell there for three kalpas.
"He shall deliver twenty-one generations—sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons.
Thus, whoever recites this or even hears it incidentally, being liberated from their body on all sides by means of celestial chariots freed from impurity; |||
He goes to heaven, being entreated by the wives of the immortals,
to the abode of the moon-crested Lord that is frequented by thousands of gods.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of land.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa,
Sanatkumāra said:
I shall now briefly describe the gift of the golden earth;
one should perform it at the previously mentioned place and time, together with sages.
According to the prescribed characteristics, as before, one should cause a divine ground to be prepared either in a well or in a pavilion, or even again with a thousand [bricks].
It should be made with one hand, square and very beautiful,
and endowed with the seven islands, oceans, and mountains.
It is endowed with all the holy fords (tīrthas) and mountains, and in its center is Mount Meru;
or else, one should arrange the central island into nine divisions.
Having performed everything as previously described within the mandala in the center of the altar,
one should [perform the rite] according to the rules from a thousand [grains], using one-seventh part.
The sacrificial fee previously prescribed should be given to the Brahmins;
and one should worship Śiva, who is auspicious, with a thousand jars and other offerings.
The golden earth is said to be within this linga; it is considered to be a mountain.

"By the sages" means together with Brahmins who have restrained their selves. "With a thousand" should be understood as a *pala* of gold; for the *Matsya Purāṇa* states that one should fashion [the earth] from five *palas* upwards, up to a thousand *palas*. And that [earth] should be made one cubit in measure, square, and representing the seven continents (*saptadvīpavatī*). Alternatively—this refers to the case of those with limited wealth—the text says: "by a single part out of seven parts"; that is, by the seventh part of a thousand, one should fashion [the earth] consisting of nine divisions, the size of Jambudvīpa alone. "To the Brahmins"—the plural number refers to the option of multiple sacrificial fires (*anekāgni-pakṣa*). "As before" means as in the *Tulāpuruṣa* gift described in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*. [This is stated] in the *Kālottara*.
Listen now briefly, O Ṣaṇmukha, to the gift of earth:
earth is considered to be of three kinds—superior, middling, and inferior.
The supreme [mandala] is proclaimed to have an extent of fifty million [yojanas],
while the middling one is declared to extend as far as the seven continents.
O maiden, one should conceive of Jambudvīpa as having three forms;
the best [image] should be fashioned from five *bhāras* of gold.
With exactly two thousand [units], one should designate the twelve mountains;
with half of that, the tortoise made of pearls, and likewise the lotus.

The twelve mountains, however, are to be seen as described in the *Kālottara* in the offering of the jewel-meru (*ratnameru*); [the base] is made of silver (*tāraja*). The best earth is said to be made of three parts, while the middling is considered to be one-third [of that];
here, the inferior is one-third less, in the case of the tortoise and the lotus.
One should entrust the chanting of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas to those devoted to Śiva,
as well as to one who recites the Saṃhitās containing the four quarters and the six categories of meaning.
A quarter [of the fine] should be assigned for offenses against Pṛthī, tortoises, and goats;
and in the case of the remaining [animals], one should report it after ascertaining the facts according to the rule.
During a solar eclipse, one should offer a calf before Śiva;
there, one should arrange thirteen mountains like Mount Meru.
One should fashion Mount Meru there with a thousand palas;
likewise, the twelve mountains should be fashioned with two thousand [palas].
Each of the planets is traditionally held to be composed of four hundred [parts];
likewise, the zodiac signs should be conceived in the same way, and the lunar mansions as half of that.
Then, the continents known as Jambū and so forth should be conceived like planets;
likewise, the seven oceans beginning with the salt ocean, and the eight classes of divine beings.
Just as the animals and others [occupy] the earth, so too do Brahmā and the others;
one should conceive of the seven netherworlds (pātāla) and the seven heavens beginning with Bhūrloka.
Having thus visualized the tortoise as having a thousand fragments and the lotus-born Brahmā as having nine fragments,
one should cause them to be given before Śiva to the Śiva-brahmins.
The earth should be given to those who are firm in their vows, whose bodies are unhurt, and who are knowers of the Vedic Siddhāntas; thus one should remember the manifold form [of the gift].

He who possesses many forms that are both non-terrible and most heroic is the multiform Aghora-mantra: "To those who are non-terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those who are more terrible than the terrible;
to all you Rudra-forms, O Śarva, let there be salutation from every side."
When the solar disc is being seized by Rāhu, one should perform the oblation;
having thus made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should cause it to be offered according to the rules in the presence of Śiva.
Indeed, for as many atoms as there are in the universe,
for that many thousands of kalpas one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
His ancestors rejoice and move about at their pleasure;
until the end of Rudra’s lifespan, they dwell in the world of Rudra.
[304] At the conclusion of that, however, they indeed become devotees of Śiva through their devotion to Śiva;
for them, liberation arises by virtue of the initiation into the state of Śiva.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the golden earth.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, hereafter I shall proclaim [the rite] unto you.
The gift known as the "Gift of Jambudvīpa" is the most excellent among all gifts.
By the gift of which a person indeed attains the world of Viṣṇu,
which causes the destruction of all sins and brings about all auspiciousness.
Thus, it bestows the glory of health, is the supreme increaser of lifespan,
grants enjoyment and liberation to men, and is auspicious, yielding all desired fruits.
O best of sages, just as the Blessed Lord Śambhu spoke when questioned by the Daughter of the Mountain, so shall I relate this to you.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World as he sat in a secluded spot on Kailāsa, the daughter of Himavat respectfully questioned Īśa.
O Blessed One, what must men do to ward off all suffering,
O Lord of Gods, without effort and as a bringer of all auspiciousness?
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose banner is the bull, [replied].
Just as your lordship told the Goddess, I shall relate all of that to you.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to that great gift called Jambudvīpa,
just as the Blessed One Janārdana, born from the lotus, has spoken it today.
On an auspicious day, under an auspicious constellation, and at an auspicious time in every respect;
likewise during the equinoxes, the solstices, and at the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
[305] Or one should perform it during a *vyatīpāta* yoga, or especially on one's birth asterism;
or one should practice the giving of gifts regularly on the eighth or fifteenth lunar day.
Gifts should be given in all meritorious places, such as by rivers or at temples, or in one's own home, or wherever faith arises.
Having diligently honored a Brahmin who is a knower of the Vedas as his preceptor,
he should have the Brahmin perform all the necessary tasks, such as the smearing of the ground with cow dung and so forth.
One should smear the entire ground with cow dung mixed with water;
there, one should smear a circular area measuring twenty cubits.
O Pārvatī, one should then imagine an ocean of salt all around that [mandala],
measuring one span in width and consisting of eight droṇas.
There, one should scatter unbroken grains all around with white flowers;
in the center of that, one should indeed construct Mount Meru with three *bhāras* of grain.
In the center, Meru should consist of great rice and be joined with golden wish-fulfilling trees; to the east, it should be joined with pearls and diamonds.
To the south, with gomedaka and puṣparāga gems.
And afterwards, with emeralds and sapphires,
with gentle lapis lazuli and ruby lotuses, and with pieces of sandalwood on all sides and coral—
It should be provided with creepers and have surfaces of mother-of-pearl stone.
There should be a row of clouds with white garments in the east, yellow ones in the south,
and then variegated garments in the west.
And the two thick clouds to the north are indeed red.
But Brahmā, seated upon a lotus throne in the center, with four faces and a body fashioned of gold,
should be installed here with four arms.
And there he held both a sacrificial ladle and a water-pot.
Likewise, holding a rosary for the practice of recitation and a black antelope skin over his shoulder,
he placed the four branches of the Ganges that had fallen [there].
And [he sees] the four directions filled with water.
Then, having installed the eight world-protectors beginning with Mahendra in their proper order,
[he placed] silver images of various multitudes of birds.
And deer should be settled everywhere.
To the east is Mount Mandara, its interior surrounded on all sides by barley, rice, and white cloth,
and likewise by a golden *plakṣa* tree and a bull.
It should be fashioned from silver, adorned with trees, deer, and birds.
It is resplendent with a golden jambu tree to the south,
with golden mung-bean trees,
and with the Lord of Yakṣas made of gold.
And he was completely surrounded by one wearing yellow garments.
Thereafter, one should fashion a mountain of sesame seeds, variegated in appearance on top, covered with a garment, and joined with *pippala* fruits, gold, and a swan;
it should be vast, deep-sounding, and adorned with fragrant flowers.
Resplendent with a spear fashioned from silver.
Having established that vast mountain, and to the north of it,
the Supārśva mountain made of mung beans and fine cloth,
as well as a banyan tree made of gold and a magnificent cow.
And having fashioned an auspicious [image] out of silver and [other materials] fashioned with spears...
One should fashion a flower-ornament for Meru,
and [place] springs of ghee and water in the cardinal directions; likewise,
lakes of milk, clarified butter, curd, and honey.
And for those [deities], starting from the east and so forth, in their respective order.
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha,
along with Nīla and Śveta, are situated respectively on the southern and northern sides;
they extend outward for the measure of a span.
For all [the pillars] extend eastward and are covered with cloth above.
The wise maintain that the quantity of grain here is equal to the weight of each of the rain-shielding mountains individually;
and all of them are endowed with wings made of silver according to their capacity.
Fragrant flowers, fruits, and pairs of garments should be provided.
These are Ānīla, Niṣadha, Mālyavat, and Gandhamādana;
Meru stands in their midst, and those two [peaks] are composed of grain.
Niṣadha and Pārijāta are these two boundary mountains;
like Gandhamādana and [Mālyavān], they are each one-fifth the size of Meru.
[308] This Gandhamādana mountain is situated to the east and west according to its proper form;
it stands to the south and north, fashioned from white rice.
All those beginning with Sitānta are in the south,
while those beginning with Śaṅkhakūṭa are proclaimed to be in the north.
Having fashioned those three Kesara mountains out of auspicious grain,
one should wrap the lord of mountains, Meru, as well as the others, with cloths.
The southern region is Bhāratavarṣa, which is surrounded by Kiṃpuruṣavarṣa;
beyond that, to the south of Meru, is said to be Harivarṣa.
Ilāvṛta surrounds Meru; likewise, there are the fourth, Vṛṣabha, as well as Ramya, Hiraṇmaya, and the Northern Kurus.
Bhadrāśva and Ketumāla are situated in the east and west respectively;
thus the nine regions (varṣas) have been described by name within Jambudvīpa.
One should install the Lord of Gods and Śrī in the middle of the Himālaya;
these two, fashioned from gold, should face the temple.
[He saw] Acyuta, holding a conch and a discus in his hands, clad in yellow garments,
wearing a crown and armlets, with his chest marked by the Śrīvatsa.
One should place the goddess to his right, seated upon a lotus throne, holding a lotus in her hand, with beautiful eyes and a serene countenance.
One should install both me and you in the center of Kailāsa—
me, named Śaṅkara, and you, O fair-faced one, as Gaurī.

One should place me as four-armed, seated upon a bull, with matted hair and the moon upon my crest, holding a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a trident, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
And you, seated upon my lap with the goddess Dīrghā by your side,
and the Blessed Lord Hari in the form of a horse-headed being upon the auspicious throne.
One should install the golden deity in the form of Kūrma in Bhārata;
likewise, Vārāha in Ketumāla, and Matsya in the northern Kurus.
Then, one should place vessels made of gold or silver in due order;
thus, having fashioned the island called Jambūdvīpa according to the prescribed rite.
The half-water for the feet, the seat, the bath, and the installation in due order;
likewise Brahmā and the other gods, the mountains, and the wish-fulfilling trees.
They are worthy of worship with their own name-mantras, illuminated by the addition of "namas" at the end,
as well as with perfumes, flowers, prostrations, incense, lamps, and fruits.
Likewise, having worshipped with effort through offerings and other rites,
one should perform a fire-oblation with clarified butter in the region of Bhadrāśva.
One should offer oblations with the mantras of one's own names, joined with the utterance of "svāhā.
Having offered one hundred and ten oblations to Brahmā and likewise to Meru, [one should proceed].
And for all the others, one hundred and eight oblations should be offered;
for the purpose of bathing the patron, one should place a water-pot in front of him.
One should place one's own beard, wrapped in cloth and filled with an *āḍhaka* measure, along with perfumes and flowers; then, one should insert the tips of *kuśa* grass into it.
Then, one should invoke here all those who will bestow prosperity,
as well as all rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, the oceans, and the lakes.
"May they come, bringing about the destruction of the sacrificer's misfortunes.
Having thus invoked them, he [should then place] a jar of pure water for him.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should install [the image] with affection;
there, one should bathe the donor, facing eastward, with water from the ritual jars.
When the time for giving has arrived, whether it be a woman or a man, the giver [should recite] the Ṛg-verses dedicated to Varuṇa and those belonging to the Pāvamānī hymns.
Having been bathed by that preceptor, one should perform an act of giving together with him;
having circumambulated three times and holding a handful of flowers.
Having prostrated before each and every joint while moving forward,
one should give the middle joint to the Guru and utter this mantra:
Or it may be given to another, provided you have obtained his permission;
and just as all the worlds, beginning with the earth, are eternally situated within you, O King of Mountains.
These gods, asuras, lords of the world, and hosts of deities such as Brahmā and others, are eternal.
O King of Mountains, grant me such a blessing that through your gift I too may become entirely liberated from all sins.
Act, O Lord, together with the best of gods.
Having said this, one should present Meru together with gold and a pair of silver garments to each of the eminent brahmins individually.
One should offer the others in sequence, beginning with the east.
O Mount Mandara, you have truly fulfilled the purpose of providing nectar for the gods and asuras;
likewise, protect me from all sides.
Through your grace, may I likewise be free from old age.
O Lord of Mountains, celebrated as Gandhamādana,
salutations to you even in the Veda as Garuḍa;
may all my faults and sins be destroyed by the gift of you.
And you, O best of mountains, protect me constantly with your shade.
Salutations to the vast abode of the gods, to the immovable one,
to the swan, and to the Person of the Vedas; salutations to the infallible one,
by whose gift the entire heap of your sins has been destroyed.
Together with Haṃsa, O Amarācala, protect me!

I pay homage to Supārśva, the immeasurable mountain of the immortals; I am eternally prostrate before the divine cow Surabhi. Through the virtuous practice joined with devotion to your gift, may I today—
I go to you alone for refuge; know me.

I go for refuge to Nārāyaṇa, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, who is beginningless and unborn, the sovereign of all worlds, the cause of everything, and the infallible one, together with the lords of the mountains.
Together with Śrī, I praise the primordial abiding of Himavat.
To the God Bhava, whose pair of lotus feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods, who destroys the suffering of his devotees,
and whose eternal abode is Mount Kailāsa; [to him] forever...
Salutations to Śiva, the beloved of Gaurī, the bestower of boons.

But the Lord Hari, the Discus-bearer, who is without beginning or end, has gone to the realm named Bhadrāśva; O Protector, that Acyuta remains there with a body for the yogis such as Sanaka and others, having come to me who have sought refuge.
He was endowed with ancient fame that was celebrated by the multitudes.

Seated in the form of a tortoise between the great ocean and the Himalayas, I go for refuge to him who eternally upholds the churned nectar of the further and the near shores, for the sake of liberation from worldly existence.
I bow to you, who are immeasurable and worshipped by the gods.
I bow to the one in the form of a boar, the infinite one whose banner is infinite,
who embodies the nature of the world, possessing many heads, eyes, and feet;
the upholder of the earth, immeasurable, and of boundless fame.
I go for refuge to Hara, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Sovereign.
O God, likewise, that Fish whose lotus feet are worshipped by the hosts of the lords of the gods dwells eternally even among the Uttarakurus;
may that infallible Lord of all the worlds protect us.
I have come to you for refuge, shaken by the sufferings of saṃsāra.
Having recited for each of the preeminent brahmins the mantra for the gift that destroys sin,
he partakes of food and then desires whatever auspicious things his mind wishes for.
And one should go to that place from which a mortal does not return here.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, as well as gold and two garments;
one should present all the implements used in the sacrifice to the preceptor.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, delighted by Pārvatī;
and I too have related all of this to you, O best of sages.
[313] Thus ends the procedure for the gift of Jambudvīpa as declared in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
Listen, O divine sage, to that gift called the "Seven Islands";
by performing it, one enjoys the entire fruit of the gift of the earth.
On all auspicious occasions, such as lunar and solar eclipses,
and in sacred places such as temples and holy shrines.
One should first choose there a Brahmin who is a learned preceptor, a knower of the Vedas, skillful, and a bestower of knowledge;
he shall cause the performance of the rites pertaining to Śiva and its ancillaries.
Except for this gift from the Guru, everything [is subordinate].
One should smear a level ground with cow dung mixed with water so that it is pure; there, in the center,
one should duly fashion an island known as Jambudvīpa.
And outside of that, the one named Plakṣa is situated.
The island called Ambupaḷkṣa, and likewise the other, Śālmala;
Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara as the seventh.
These continents are surrounded by seven seas,
respectively consisting of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water.
Jambudvīpa is considered the center of all these;
and in its center, O divine sage, is Mount Meru, the golden mountain.
The extent of Plakṣadvīpa is held to be sixteen finger-breadths; it is said that for each subsequent island, the size increases by one-quarter more than the preceding one.
One should fashion Plakṣadvīpa with sixteen droṇas of grain;
thereafter, it is said that for each subsequent [continent], the size increases by one-quarter.
This is the full extent of the continents and the oceans in every respect.
In each of the five islands, beginning with Plakṣa, there are seven mountain ranges and seven rivers that form the regions; these are all composed of white rice.
O Sage, hear now the names of the other two regions: in Puṣkara, there is one mountain named Bhūdhara in the center, shaped like a ring.
In Plakṣa, the year consists of the seasons Śāntamaya, Śiśira, and likewise Sukhada;
it brings joy, auspiciousness, security, and indeed happiness.
Gomedaparvata, Candra, Nārada, Dundubhi,
Somaka, Sumanas, and Vaibhrāja— these are the seven mountains.
Anutaptā, Śivā, Ambikā, Tridivī, Amṛtā, and Sukṛtā— these seven rivers flow there in succession.
In the first year, however, one should place a Plakṣa tree in the center,
fashioned from a pala of gold or according to one's ability, or even half of that.
Beside that, one should install Hari, the Lord of the gods of gods and the teacher of all the worlds— the deity who assumes the form of the moon— made of gold.
Śveta, Harita, Rohita, Vaidyuta,
Narmada, and Suprabha— these are the seven mountains that form the boundaries of the regions.
Kumuda, Codana, and the third, Valāhaka;
Kaṅka, Mahiṣa, and Kakudmān is the seventh mountain.
Yoni, Toyā, Vitṛṣṇā, Candrā, Śuklā, Mocanī,
and Vivṛtti— these seven rivers are proclaimed to exist in Śālmala.
Udbhid, Veṇumān, Suratna, Lavaṇa, Dhṛti,
Prabhākara, and Kapila— listen to these mountains, O Nārada.
Maṇidruma, Haimaśaila, Dyutimān, Puṣpavān,
Kuśodgama, Harita, and Mandara as the seventh.
Dhūtapāpā, Śivā, Pavitrā, and likewise Śamitā;
Dyudambhā, Mahiṣī, and likewise Sarvapāpaharā.
Learn from me these regions and mountain ranges in Kuśadvīpa and Krauñcadvīpa: Kuśastamba, Viṣṇu, and Para.
Andhakāra and Muni, and likewise Dandubhi as the seventh;
Krauñca and Vāmana, and then Andhakāra as the fifth.
Puṇḍarīka and Dundubhi—these seven shall be the immovable ones here;
Gaurī, Kumārī, Saṃdhyā, Rātri, and Manojava.
The Yakṣas and others, as well as Puṇḍarīka, are said to be seven each;
in Śāka there is the Śākavṛkṣa tree, and in Varṣaplakṣa there are rivers.
O divine sage, listen as I speak of those seven and seven:
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, and Maṇīcaka;
Kusumottamamoda, the seventh, Mahādruma, Udaya,
Jaladhāra, and Raivata are the secondary mountains.
The fifth is the mountain Abhragiri; likewise Ambikā, Kesari, Sukumārī, Kumārī, Nalinī, and Veṇukā.
Induka, Reṇukā, and likewise Gabhasti as the seventh;
at Puṣkara, however, they are proclaimed as Mahāpadma and Dhātakī.
In the middle, they are ring-shaped, and here there are mental mountains;
in the eastern [quarter] is the Nyagrodha tree, which is said to be the abode of Brahmā.
The seventh is Puṣkaradvīpa, surrounded in exactly the same way;
thus the continents and oceans are each surrounded by seven of their own kind.
Equal to the continents and oceans, and each subsequent one twice the size of the preceding,
he should cause all the trees of the size of those continents to be fashioned out of silver and installed.
Likewise, one should cast birds, wild animals, and fish into the mountains and oceans,
and there one should also establish Viṣṇu, the lord of Jambudvīpa.
In Plakṣa he is Soma; in Śālmala he is the form of Vāyu; in Kuśadvīpa he is the ancient form of Brahmā;
in Krauñca he is Rudra; and in the one named Śāka, he is the Sun.
The divine god in the lotus possesses a Brahmanic form.
Having manifested the primordial Lord of the worlds, born of gold, who possesses a beautiful form capable of appearing as one and as many,
and having washed him with pure water consecrated by mantras;
Having sprinkled [the area] with *darbha* grass and having established the deities,
Having wrapped the lords of mountains with cloths,
one should scatter a rain of flowers all around them,
along with handfuls of offerings such as the *argha* and other oblations.
Having fully honored Meru and all the Pramathas.
The fire-offering mantra is performed as before with one's own name-mantras joined with "namaḥ" and joined with "svāhā";
one should act there exactly as was done previously.
Thus [it is] for the lords of mountains and forest trees.
Having completed [the rite] according to the rule on the very previous day,
the Guru should perform the consecration (adhivāsa) there during the night;
likewise, he should remain in the nights, authorized by the Vedas.
And thereafter, the gift of clothing and so forth follows in due order.
Then, at the clear dawn during that time of giving, he was bathed and dressed in clean garments,
just as it had previously been told regarding the one named Jambu.
Likewise, having caused the gift to be performed with reverence.
Then, having honored the Brahmins, he should cause her to be given to them in due order according to the prescribed mantras;
[to those representing] Soma, Vāyu, the form of Brahmā, and Candra.
Likewise, the sun is the primordial form of Brahman.
Since you are the unborn source of the lords of creepers, herbs, trees, wild animals, and the entire world,
therefore protect me always.
Pervading all that is within and without, you remain joined to it;
O you of immeasurable self, whose movement is eternal, protect me, for you have been invoked by me.
He who is the creator and protector of the worlds, the Grandfather of the realm of Brahmā—
O Lord of Gods, through your gift, may there always be prosperity for me.
O Śaṅkara, for the sake of protecting the gods of gods and the worlds as well, the triple city was burnt by you; may you therefore always be gracious toward me.
May he who rises, sets, and eternally protects the three worlds,
and who is manifest before the eyes of all people, be gracious toward me.
May the blessed Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the worlds, be forever gracious to me.
In this very manner, O best of the twice-born,
one should give a gift to each of the preceptors individually and in due order, and then likewise offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the principal teacher.
Clothing is more precious than gold; gold itself is more precious [than that].
Having prepared the earth extending to the limits of the seven continents and having fashioned deities out of gold in due order,
one should give the remainder of the gift to that preceptor.
All [this], including the primary limbs, the secondary limbs, grain, clothing, and so forth.
At the beginning and at the end, the five eminent brahmins should pronounce the auspicious day, well-being, and success;
one should give them a sacrificial fee consisting of gold.
And one should feed the Brahmins with clothing and grain.
O Nārada, having thus performed this gift of the seven islands,
whether a woman or a man, shall attain the world of Brahmā.
The Blessed One, the creator of the worlds, spoke thus to Nārada;
and all that has been told by me as well, O best of sages.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the seven islands as declared in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
Pulastya said:
There, the sages headed by Śaunaka were seated.

Then, at the conclusion of the sacrificial rites during a long-duration sacrifice (*satrayāga*) in the Naimiṣa forest, those wandering ascetics (*cāraṇa*) approached the son of Sūta as he sat comfortably and questioned him.
Ugraśrava, we ask you:
having done what does that person, whether man or woman, obtain a full lifespan and remain free from diseases?
He is liberated and attains the highest prosperity.
It brings about the destruction of suffering and the removal of fear from malevolent planets,
as well as the pacification of the three kinds of portents or other fears and defects.
It bestows the accomplishment of the desired goal upon the practitioner.
What gift, vow, or worship of the deities must one perform so that they become fulfilled?
And what is it that those who desire to hear your word [should do]?
O most learned one, tell us about the gift of a charioteer.
Thus addressed by the sages at that time, Ugraśravas then replied to them:
"Listen, I shall relate that to you."
Such indeed was that gift of the earth-lotus.
One should perform it in a temple, on the bank of a river or a stream, in another house, or in a meritorious place;
or one may perform it by a pond or in the Nandana grove.
Or one delights in whatever grove the mind finds pleasing.
Having respectfully engaged a Brahmin preceptor who is expert in the Vedas and Purāṇas, one should then give that preceptor a garment according to the ritual sequence.
A pair of auspicious golden ornaments.
Adorned in this way, he performs everything; indeed,
there is no task here whatsoever that can be accomplished except by means of cow products— be it dung, water, or earth.
And one should apply [the ointment] over an area measuring twenty cubits.
One should first prepare a roof-structure for the protection against rain and sun, either level or sloping toward the east,
measuring sixteen aratnis and square in shape.
One may indeed act there as desired and construct pillars;
it should be provided with four gates and adorned with four archways.
Encircled by a garland of darbha grass and adorned with auspicious sprouts,
it was covered above by a beautiful canopy of white appearance.
One should arrange banners for the world-protectors on all sides;
the wise practitioner should wrap the pillars with cloths in the four directions.
One should hang flower garlands on all sides at the joints of the pillars;
one should smear the ground, which slopes toward the east and north, with cow dung.
In this manner, one should likewise prepare a water-trough, a waterfall, or a cloth-painting;
in the center, one should fashion Mount Meru out of rice.
The middle [mountain] was made with ten bhāras, and the others with a fourth part each;
having placed Mandara in front, Gandhamādana was on the south.
To the west is the vast mountain Śaila, and to the north is the immovable Supārśva;
there are two supporting mountains, one in the eastern region and one in the western region.
And within the surrounding regions, the mountain ranges of the continents (*varṣaparvata*) are mentioned;
specifically, *Viṣkambha* and *Vārdhava* are intended, as well as *Mandara* and *Gandhamādana*. However, the other *varṣaparvatas* should be understood as those taught in the *Dharādāna*.
There are the two islands named Jambu and Plakṣa, and another, Śālmala.
Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara as the seventh.
Salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and water—
thus the continents are surrounded by seven oceans, each being sevenfold.
In this manner, one should likewise have mountains made of rice and birds as well;
or otherwise, one may fashion other mountains weighing half a bhāra.
"The others" means the mountain ranges of the world-enclosures (*varṣaparvata*).
Having enveloped all the mountains with garments and all the great oceans,
he should settle into each of the four vessels with its respective substance.
One should place golden Mandāra, Pārijāta, Santāna, and Haricandana trees upon Mount Meru, situated in the four directions.
In the center of that, one should place a golden wish-fulfilling tree and a golden lotus-seat,
upon which the two-armed deity Brahmā is seated, facing the east.
One should fashion four silver peaks for Meru;
one should place the golden Mādana and Plakṣa trees upon Mandara.
One should fashion a golden Garuḍa on Mount Jambū and Gandhamādana,
and a golden swan and a holy fig tree in front.
One should place a golden Surabhī on Supārśva and a Nyagrodha tree; furthermore, all the animals, birds, and trees should be made of silver.
One should place pieces of sugarcane and sandalwood in all [the vessels].
At the doors, there are two *mumba* fruits joined with water and cloth,
provided with fruits and pieces of sandalwood;
likewise, at the corners, there is a full pitcher.
Having placed sugarcane juice in the four directions.
Having thus honored the gods, the foremost among the Madris, with sandalwood, flowers, and incense,
they propitiated them with their own names in mantras ending with "namas."
Then, having honored all those foremost of brahmins.
Together with the Guru and those five [disciples],
they should recite the auspicious day, the benediction, and the success;
then the Guru alone should perform the fire oblation (*homa*) there.
In the north-eastern direction of the mountains.
Having established the fire, he offers oblations of ghee and curd while uttering the names of the deities;
likewise, [he offers] with the name-mantras of the mountains as well.
Thus, there are ten oblations and one additional one.
On the preceding day, the preceptor himself should perform this rite, and likewise keep a vigil through the night;
he remains there reciting the mantras that destroy demons.
Then, at the clear dawn, he shall perform [the rite].
When the auspicious time for giving has arrived,
the wise donor, having bathed with water mixed with kusha grass and sesame seeds and being purified, is sprinkled by the preceptor.
Likewise, with Vāruṇa and Pāvamāna mantras.
Having performed a circumambulation of Meru, one should offer a handful of flowers there;
having worshipped, one should give [the gift] to a Brahmin or to a preceptor who maintains the sacred fires.
Since you are the abode of the world-protectors, of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, and of all the gods, therefore protect me from every side.
Since you, O mountain, are the pericarp of the lotus that is the earth,
therefore you must indeed always bestow prosperity upon us.
Thus, one should then give the Great Meru to a learned Brahmin;
thereafter, one should bestow upon the Brahmins the regions starting from the east and ending with the north.
One should arrange one [seat] for each of the four wise ones;
and having performed a circumambulation, one should also offer a handful of flowers.
Since you, O mountain, are the abode of Madana even for the gods,
may the blessed Mandara, the best of mountains, be well-pleased with me.
Since you are the abode of Garuḍa and an immovable mountain that is always a dwelling for the gods,
may the Blessed Lord Gandhamādana Mountain be pleased with me.
May that Vipula, the best of mountains, be well-pleased with me, for it is there that the one in the form of a swan always dwells within the Aśvattha tree.
A fragrant banyan tree stands eternally upon your summit;
you are the pleasure grove of the deities—O Supārśva, may you be full of joy.
Thus, having given this supreme gift of the earth-lotus, which is likewise the highest of gifts,
one enjoys superior pleasures and attains the same world as Brahmā.
Together with the preceptor, he should cause the proclamation of "an auspicious day," "well-being," and "success";
he should then give sacrificial fees to those five learned Brahmins.
One should present a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the teacher who has given the instruction on the gift.

Here, the "instructor" (*upadeṣṭṛ*) is intended as the sixth; furthermore, by the rule stating that "one should give a sacrificial fee to the teacher of the Vaitānika rites and to those [others]," one should likewise give the fee to them.
This is because of the accomplishment of the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). According to the prescribed rule, a *niṣka* of gold, equal in value to the honorarium,
[should be given], as well as a seat, a bed, clothing, a vessel, and implements for eating.
One should present a bronze vessel for holding water to the preceptor.
All this is also applicable to the act of giving; one should present that entire collection of garments to the preceptor.
He himself eats the ghee, as stated by Pāṇini.
One should feed the gurus, the brahmins, and one's circle of kinsmen.
Thus, in ancient times, the lotus-born Creator spoke to the sage Nārada;
and by me has this gift of the earth-lotus been described.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, what more shall I say?
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Earth-lotus as declared in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
Śaunaka said:
A mortal who has sexual intercourse with an outcaste woman is born pale and afflicted by disease.
I shall explain its remedy through such rites as giving gifts and performing fire-oblations.
One should fashion the earth out of three palas of silver, or one may do so with half that amount; however, one must not practice stinginess regarding the wealth expended.
Having placed all the nine jewels within the entire earth, including its mountains and forests and encircled by the oceans, one should wrap it with a white cloth.
Having placed [the vessel] in a bell-metal bowl fashioned from eight *palas* of *palāśa* wood,
one should invoke there the Goddess, the support of all, the beloved of Hari.
Come, come, O Goddess Dhātrī; enter perfectly into this form.
Together with the mountains, islands, and oceans, be well-disposed.
The invocation mantra:
Having thus invoked the Goddess, the preceptor, who is learned in all the scriptures, should worship her with perfumes, garlands, and the sixteen types of ritual services.
One should also perform a fire offering (homa) with sacrificial fuel sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds;
the oblation of fuel sticks is prescribed to be performed with the mantra "bhūmir bhūmi."

Likewise: "The earth has gone to the earth; the measurer to the measurer; the mother to the mother"—this mantra is proclaimed, and one should offer oblations of sesame and clarified butter into the fire.
To the north of the fire, one should also place a flawless, bright water-pot wrapped in a cloth, along with earth from a horse-stable and other such sites.
Then, once it has been filled with pure water,
one should perform the consecration while reciting the *pavamāna* and other mantras.
One should also perform the propitiation with the *śan no devī* hymn and the *anuvāka*;
and one should wipe the limbs of the consecrated person with a cloth.
With the *Anuvāka* beginning with "Akṣobhya," according to the respective characteristics of the mantras and accompanied by *darbha* grass,
the sick person, being composed in mind, should offer that earth to the preceptor.
Facing east, one facing north should duly offer [the earth] with this mantra:
"The nurse of all beings, the supporter, the beloved, was raised up by Varāha."
Wearing the ocean containing a treasure of jewels as her sole garment, she who is all-beautiful—
being well-pleased by this gift, may she dispel the disease of jaundice.
The mantra for the gift:
Having diligently bestowed the gift of the earth according to this rite,
whatever gift is indeed made by a mortal through the path of the *antyajas*, [326] it becomes [meritorious].
All that, including great ailments such as jaundice, comes to destruction;
for the sake of pacification, one should perform the Puṇyāhavācana rite together with Brahmins.

Thus ends the ritual for the gift of earth as taught in the *Padmapurāṇa* for the removal of jaundice (*pāṇḍuroga*). Now, the twelfth great gift (*mahādāna*), known as the Viśvacakra, is described. In the *Matsyapurāṇa*, Matsya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift known as the Viśvacakra, which destroys all sins.
One should have it fashioned from pure refined gold during the equinoxes and other auspicious times;
the superior [image] with a thousand *palas*, and the middling with half of that.
The smallest universal wheel (viśvacakra) is said to be half of that;
another may offer it even if unable to afford more than twenty palas.
Then, one should visualize a sixteen-spoked wheel revolving, encircled by eight rims;
in the center of its hub stands Viṣṇu, established in yoga, four-armed,
with a conch and discus at his sides, surrounded by the eight goddesses.

The *nābhi* (navel) is a specific part [of the wheel] shaped like a rod that extends from the center to the rim. The *nemayaḥ* (felloes) are the spokes, which revolve and are situated in a circular form. It is surrounded by, or encircled by, eight of these with equal intervals; that is, it rests upon the *nābhi-padma* (navel-lotus). The *nābhi* has the form of an eight-petaled lotus, and upon its pericarp (*karṇikā*) is the one mounted in yoga. Having visualized Viṣṇu—whose two hands are placed at the region of the heart, and who has the conch and discus situated at his sides—one should install the eight Śaktis upon the eight petals in the sequence starting from the east. Their characteristics are described in the *Nāradīya*:
Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and likewise another, Yoga; then Prajñā, Satyā, Īśānā, and the ninth is Anugrahā.
All of them shine with their right hands in the gesture of granting boons;
with their left hands they hold wheels; they are in female form and adorned with beautiful ornaments.
In this context, because of the statement "surrounded by the eight goddesses," there is no application for a ninth [deity].
Likewise, in the second enclosure, starting from the east, are Jalaśāyin, Atri, Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, Brahmā, and Kaśyapa.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, then the Man-lion, the Dwarf, Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki— these are [the incarnations] in sequence.
The characteristics of [the incarnations] beginning with Jalaśāyin (the Water-Sleeper) are described in the two Brahmāṇḍadāna texts; those of Matya (the Fish) and the others are in the Pañcarātra:
"In the left [hand] a conch, in the right a mace, possessing two arms, bearing the form of a fish;
or having human feet while in the form of a fish; or Janārdana in the form of a fish."
This very same description of the tortoise applies when the term "tortoise" is used in place of "fish.
[The deity] has a honey-yellow complexion, is endowed with four arms and weapons,
possesses a human body with the face of a boar, is somewhat stout, and is very formidable.
Śrī resides on the left elbow, while Dharā and Ananta follow at his feet;
this is the Lord Varāha, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, bearing this very form.
Having a form like a blazing fire, with the face of a lion and the body of a man,
his mouth was formidable with fangs and his tongue was lolling, making him most terrifying.
He has rounded eyes, matted hair, and is enraged; he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture with a broad chest, possessing impenetrable and fierce claws, and he mimics the Dānava in his left hand.
And he [saw] Narasiṃha, the Lord of the World, tearing open that [demon’s] chest with his two hands and his claws, while holding a mace and a discus with his other two.
Carrying a water-pot and a parasol, Vāmana is celebrated as being twice as tall;
he bore in his hand a terrible battle-axe that brought about the end of the Kṣatriyas.
Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, must be depicted with eyes reddened by rage;
he is youthful, with a serene countenance, lion-like shoulders, and great strength.
Rāma should be depicted with arms reaching down to his knees, holding an arrow and a bow;
he should be made to hold a conch and a discus, with the complexion of a blue lotus petal.
Kṛṣṇa, with his two long arms, the destroyer of all the Daityas,
was clothed in saffron robes with his outer garment draped over his shoulder.
The Buddha is proclaimed as being seated upon a lotus, two-armed, and meditative;
[Avalokiteśvara], however, is wrathful, with hand raised holding a sword, mounted upon a horse, and possessed of great strength.
"The one who effects the destruction of the Mlecchas is proclaimed as the two-armed Kalpī.
Thus [it is said]. In the third enclosure, Gaurī is joined by the Mothers and the Vasus.
The characteristics of Gaurī are stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa. The seven Mothers, beginning with Brahmāṇī, are described;
their characteristics are also stated in the Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha.
Gaurī is four-faced and heroic, holding a rosary and a sacrificial ladle;
on the left, Brahmāṇī is seated upon a swan, holding a fire-pit and a vessel of clarified butter.
This is the specific description of Gaurī, Nairṛtavarṇā, and Brahmāṇī: she has three eyes, holds a trident in her hand, is adorned with matted hair and a crescent moon,
wears a garland of skulls, is white in color, and Rudrāṇī is seated upon a bull.
The goddess Kaumārī, who has the form of Skanda, is red in color, holds a spear, is adorned with red garlands and garments, and is mounted upon the back of a peacock.
The goddess Vaiṣṇavī is dark-complexioned and four-armed; she rides upon Tārkṣya, wears a garland of forest flowers, and holds in her hands the conch, discus, mace, bow Śārṅga, and sword.
Dark-complexioned, with a full belly and a cruel nature, she resembled a sow;
clothed, yet bursting with youth, she was a woman adorned with ornaments.
Vārāhī, however, stands upon a buffalo; she holds wine and a staff, is equipped with a sword and a shield, or else possesses four arms.
The thousand-eyed Indrāṇī, mounted upon an elephant, golden-hued and wielding a thunderbolt,
has all her aims accomplished and is adorned with every ornament.
With eyes like pits, her body emaciated, and her sunken belly terrifying,
she stands upon Śiva or Kauśika with mouth agape and fierce fangs.
Licking [her lips], with eyes wide open, adorned with blazing hair like snakes,
wearing a garment of tiger skin, furious, Cāmuṇḍā wears a garland of severed heads.
"Having matted hair, being circular, and having three eyes, she holds [objects] in her four arms:
a skull and a curved knife in the right hands, and a noose and a trident in the left.
Thus is described the characteristic of the eight Vasus in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*.
In the fourth [layer] are the twelve Ādityas and the four Vedas;
in the fifth are the five elements and the eleven Rudras.
In the sixth [enclosure], one should place the eight world-protectors (lokapāla) and likewise the elephants of the directions;
in the seventh, one should have all weapons and auspicious objects fashioned;
and furthermore, in the eighth, one should arrange the deities at regular intervals.

[230] The characteristics of the elephants of the Sun, the World-Protectors, and others have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*. The forms of the Vedas will be described in the *Mahābhūtaghaṭadāna*. The five elements, beginning with earth, are as follows; their characteristics are stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The Earth should be fashioned of auspicious color, adorned with divine ornaments, four-armed, of gentle form, and clothed in garments resembling the rays of the moon."
O delighter of the Yadavas, a jewel vessel, a vessel of grain, and a vessel containing medicinal herbs should be placed in his hand, as well as a lotus.
She should likewise be depicted on the backs of the four world-elephants;
the goddess is remembered as being white in color and endowed with all medicinal herbs.
The form of the waters is described in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"While he was previously engaged in meditation, the waters became manifest to him in the form of women, fair-complexioned, two-armed, and clad in white garments."

Seated upon a crocodile (*makara*), she holds a noose and a jar in her two hands. Regarding fire (*tejas*), its form has been described in the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa* (in the section on the gift of the Cosmic Egg).
And regarding wind (*vāyu*) and space (*ākāśa*), their forms have been described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The sky should be depicted with the luster of a blue lotus, wearing garments of that same color;
it should have two arms, holding the moon and sun in its hands, and possess a serene appearance.
Having the appearance of one sixteen years of age, and devoid of the sexual characteristics of both male and female.
The characteristics of Rudra have been described by Viśvakarman:
"The Rudras should be fashioned as red-colored, three-eyed, two-armed, and moon-crested; they should have matted hair and hold arrows and bows."

Regarding the seventh [verse], "the weapons, all of them": although the word "all" (*sarva*) is present here, because they are intended for placement within the sixteen squares, it is logical to include only these—namely, eight auspicious weapons and eight auspicious [objects]. The weapons have been described in the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:
"The sword, trident, mace, spear, lance, goad, bow, and the axe—these are the weapons; among them, the bow is praised."
Parāśara has declared auspicious objects: right-spiraling conch shells, yellow pigment (rocanā), sandalwood, as well as pearls, gold, an umbrella, and a fly-whisk.
And the mirror should be known as auspicious and the bringer of good fortune.

The phrase "in each interval" (*antarāntara*) refers to what was stated previously; it connects with all [the deities], meaning the innermost middle region among the intervals. Regarding the eighth enclosure, however, the author of the *Dānaviveka* states that one should install the sixteen deities previously mentioned, beginning with Brahmā. Some say that one should install one's chosen deities (*abhīṣṭadeva*). Furthermore, these specific deities are to be fashioned mounted upon the wheel from the very center of the gold already prepared for the construction of the Universal Wheel (*viśvacakra*), and not from separate gold, because of the instruction that the wheel must be made of precisely such [material].
One should arrange everything else on all sides according to the procedure for the Tulāpuruṣa rite,
including the officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, ornaments, coverings, and so forth.
Then one should fashion a universal wheel (viśvacakra) upon a black antelope skin and sesame seeds,
as well as the eighteen types of grain and the flavors such as salt and others.
One should also cause eight full jars, various garments,
garlands, sugarcane, fruits, jewels, and even a canopy to be prepared.

Here, by the word "etcetera," the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the worship of Śiva and others, the recitation by Brahmins (*brāhmaṇavācana*), the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), and so forth are included.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"Then, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsya*) of the wheel, one should subsequently perform the fire-oblation (*homa*)."
The Sūtras and Brāhmaṇas of the four Vedas consist of four or eight [sections].
With self-restraint, adorned with garments and ornaments, and equipped with the materials for the oblation,
they should perform the *homa* using sacrificial ladles (*sruk* and *sruva*) and copper vessels.
For deities who are established upon a wheel, a fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed;
one should offer oblations with mantras possessing their characteristic marks for the pacification of all calamities.

In the Matsya Purāṇa: Then, having bathed to the sound of auspicious chants, the householder, clad in white garments and holding a handful of flowers, [should proceed] at the conclusion of the fire-oblation and the preliminary consecration.
One should recite this mantra three times while performing a circumambulation:
"Homage to the one whose nature is universal illusion; homage to the soul of the universal wheel."
You, whose nature is supreme bliss, protect me from the mire of saṃsāra;
for yogis always behold this world as consisting of light.
In my heart, I bow to the reality that transcends the qualities (guṇas), the wheel of the universe;
the wheel resides in Vāsudeva, and Mādhava resides in the center of the wheel.
I prostrate to these two as they abide here in a state of mutual support,
for this Universal Wheel is supreme and the remover of all sins.
"Uproot me from this existence, which is the weapon of latent predispositions";
having thus addressed [the teacher], one who is free from envy should offer the Viśvacakra.
Liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
having reached the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, four-armed and eternal,
he is served by throngs of apsarases and shall remain there for three hundred kalpas.

Here too, having uttered the formula for giving as before, one should perform the formal transfer of the water-filled vessel accompanied by a gold *dakṣiṇā* according to one's capacity to the preceptor and the officiating priests; with their permission, one may also give to others, provide for the satisfaction of the poor and the helpless, and—though in a small-scale rite only a single limb is prescribed—arrange the distribution of shares among the officiating priests and the preceptor. All this should be carried out according to the standard model (*prakṛti*). Then, one should perform the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the deities, and their dismissal. Or, having performed it oneself, one should daily pay obeisance to the Viśvacakra.
His lifespan increases constantly, and his prosperity shall become vast.
Thus, having arrived at the abode of Hari along with the perfected ones (siddhas), he bestows that golden sixteen-spoked realm which is the dwelling place of the gods of the entire world.
Having approached for a long time, they pay homage with their heads bowed.
He becomes difficult for his enemies to behold,
yet easy for passionate women to look upon;
he is like Keśava, who possesses the Sudarśana [discus].
His sins were burnt away by the gift of the beautiful golden discus.
Having cast off the heavy sins committed, and having pierced through the abode of the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu), which is protected by the excellent Sudarśana disc with its sixteen spokes, he proceeds.
Having transcended existence and having existed in the world, [he] does not exist again.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the Universal Wheel as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.
[334] Now, the thirteenth great gift, known as the Kalpalatā, is described.
Matsya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift known as Mahākalpalatā, which destroys even the most heinous sins.
Then, having reached an auspicious lunar day and performed the recitation by Brahmins,

one should carry out the rites for the officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, the ornaments, the coverings, and so forth; and like the Tulāpuruṣa rite, one should perform the invocation of the world-protectors (lokeśas) and other ceremonies.
The explanation of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is as before.
One should fashion ten auspicious wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpalatā*) made of gold,
endowed with various flowers and fruits, and adorned with various garments.
They were graced by pairs of Vidyādharas and Suparṇas,
and by Siddhas and birds who desired to offer fruits to Hara.

Various fruits, such as men, women, cows, elephants, horses, and so forth, are appropriate because they serve to illustrate the comparison with the flowers and fruits of their own nature. *Aṃśukāni* means garments. *Suparṇāḥ* means birds. Having thus arranged the ten *kalpalatās*, one should place two in the center upon the drawn wheel on the altar, and eight in the directions starting from the east.
The deities within them should be fashioned according to the world-protectors (*lokapālas*).
One should place Brāhmī and Anantaśakti upon the salt.
And below those two, in their midst, are the auspicious [goddesses] Padmā and Śaṅkhakarā.

The goddesses who follow the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) mean the powers (*śakti*) of the world-protectors. "And below those two" means that beneath the two wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpalatā*) placed in the middle, one should establish Brāhmī in the form of a lotus and Anantaśakti holding a conch. Regarding the measurement of the salt and so forth, since no specific measurement is prescribed, it is determined by the desire of the practitioner. There is a reading in some places stating, "one should place salt upon the two *stūpas*"; in that context, *stūpa* means a heap, and the dual number refers to the two heaps.
Seated upon an elephant-throne on the east, however, is she whose weapon is the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*), situated in molasses (*guḍa*).
The one born of the night stands in the southeast; then, with a rosary of *tuhi* seeds in hand, [he stands] in the fire.
Mounted upon a buffalo, bearing a mace and standing upon rice grains, she should be placed in the southwest (Nairṛti) with clarified butter; she is accompanied by a sword in the south-west.
In the western quarter, Vāruṇī is seated upon a fish in milk, holding a noose for serpents;
and in the northwestern quarter, Patākinī is seated upon a deer on a mound of sugar.
Śaṅkhinī, established among gentle winds, is situated in a treasure;
Māheśvarī is mounted upon a bull, while Triśūlinī has the hand of Īśa.

The elephant is the *ibha*, and it should be depicted with four tusks. The *kuliśa* is the thunderbolt (*vajra*). Regarding the phrase "standing upon a goat at night" (*rajanyajasthitā*): *rajani* is turmeric and *aja* is a goat; thus, the meaning is that she stands upon turmeric, having a goat as her vehicle. In *anala*, the southeastern quarter, and in the southwestern quarter (*dakṣiṇāpara*), one should note that Nairṛtī has a corpse as her vehicle (*pretavāhanā*)—the meaning is that she has a crocodile (*makara*) as her vehicle, stationed on a corpse. "Established upon a treasure" (*nidhisaṃsthitā*) means she is situated upon a jar resembling a treasure-vessel.
Their crowns and gestures of granting boons (*varada*) should likewise be fashioned, and they should be provided with locks of hair.
One should fashion [these] with a spear (*śakti*) weighing from five palas upwards up to a thousand.
And above all of them is a five-colored canopy,
as well as cows, ten water-pots, and pairs of garments.

[336] “Wearing crowns” means they wear diadems; “granting boons” (varadāḥ) means that with one hand other than the one holding the aforementioned weapons, they are endowed with the boon-granting gesture (*varadamudrā*). “With locks of hair” (*vālikā*) refers to an ear ornament; however, some read *vālakānvitāḥ*. In that case, it is explained as “having children seated on their left laps. Furthermore, all of this should be fashioned by dividing the gold prepared for the construction of the *kalpalatā*—measured at five *pala*s and so forth—since there is no instruction to use separate materials.
As for the middle two [images], they are for the preceptor (*guru*) and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and the others likewise.
Then, having bathed to the sound of auspicious proclamations and wearing white garments, the wise one should circumambulate three times to the right and recite these mantras.

The word "tataḥ" (then) indicates the immediate succession following the previously mentioned collection of rites, such as the fire-oblation (*homa*), the consecration (*adhivāsana*), and the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*). "Bathed" (*snāta*) means he has been bathed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) with water containing all medicinal herbs situated in a jar near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); it should also be understood that he has taken handfuls of flowers (*kusumāñjali*). Now follows the mantra:
"Salutations, salutations to those who destroy sin, the protectors of the lords of the worlds within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)."
From the quarters, which bestow fruits exceeding all expectations, and likewise from the celestial kalpa-creeper brides;

Then, having recited the ritual application (*prayoga*) as before, one should present the two middle *kalpalatās* together with the deities and other components to the preceptor (*guru*). One should then present the remaining ones to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). By his permission, one may also give them to others; this includes the giving of gifts to the poor and the needy, while it should be understood from what was previously stated that if the rite is small, the procedure for a single fire (*ekāgni*) applies. Thereafter, one should perform the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the deities, and their dismissal (*visarjana*).
Thus, whoever performs this gift of the "Ladies of All Directions" (*sakaladigaṅganāpradāna*), which brings about the destruction of the fear of worldly existence (*bhava*).
In the celestial realm that bestows desired fruits, his father does not dwell for thirty years like the Grandfather Brahmā.
In this [state] which bestows desired fruits— that is, which grants the wished-for results—
one may cause a hundred ancestors to cross over the ocean of existence;
it is a place purified by the destruction of the flood of misdeeds.
Surrounded by thousands of the wives of the lords of the gods, he is one to be saluted by the assembly of lotuses.
Thus, whoever here recites, remembers, or beholds this ritual for the offering of the golden wish-fulfilling vine to the lady of the quarters, [attains his desire].
He attains the station served by Purandara.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Kalpalatā as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Now, the fourteenth great gift (mahādāna), known as the Seven Oceans, is described.
The Fish [Incarnation] said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme great gift (mahādāna) named Saptasāgaraka, which destroys even the greatest sins.
Then, having reached an auspicious day and performed the recitation by Brahmins,
the wise man should perform the invocation of the Lords of the World (lokeśa) as in the Tulāpuruṣa rite.
The wise man should cause the officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, ornaments, coverings, and so forth—

by the word "and so forth" (ādi) is meant the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*), and other such rites— to be prepared; he should also have seven golden sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) constructed.
Furthermore, they may be a span in measure, or even a cubit in measure.
One should perform [the rite] with seven palas as the minimum up to a thousand, according to one's capacity;
and all [the vessels] should be placed upon a black antelope skin and sesame seeds.

The sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and vessels (*bhāṇḍa*), as well as measurements such as the *prādeśa* and others, are to be understood according to their horizontal and vertical dimensions. An *aratni* is measured by twenty-one finger-joints (*aṅguṣṭhaparva*); half of that is a *prādeśa*. The *tila* seeds are measured by a *droṇa*; they are to be offered in gold because of the observed pervasion of those [seeds] belonging to the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*).
A wise man should first fill the pit with salt;
likewise, the second with milk, and the third again with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*).
The fourth [offering] is with jaggery alone, and the fifth likewise with curd;
the sixth is with sugar, and similarly the seventh with water from a sacred ford.
One should place an auspicious golden image of Brahmā at the edge of the salt,
Keśava in the midst of the milk, and Maheśvara in the midst of the ghee.
One should place Bhāskara in the midst of molasses, Surādhipa in the midst of curd,
Lakṣmī in sugar, and Pārvatī in the midst of water.
In all [these gifts], all kinds of gems and grains are to be provided on all sides.

The characteristics of the images of Brahmā and the others have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*. All the gems and all the grains are mentioned in the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). As in the *Tulāpuruṣa* [gift], one should arrange the remainder here as well.
Then, at the conclusion of the Vāruṇa oblation, having been bathed by the preeminent among the knowers of the Vedas,
he should circumambulate three times to the right and recite these mantras:

By the word "remainder" (śeṣa), one should understand the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the giving of water and the aforementioned gifts to the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others, and by his permission, the giving of gifts to others as well, the satiation of the poor and the helpless, and the performance of the single-fire rite (*ekāgnividhāna*) in cases of minor rites; these and other such matters are to be kept in mind. This is the specific detail: on the second day, upon the completion of the remainder of the ritual actions prescribed for the *tulāpuruṣa*, a *vāruṇahoma* numbering one thousand oblations must be performed with clarified butter and sesame seeds using mantras containing words indicative of that [deity], prior to the *pūrṇāhuti*.
[The mantra is: "Obeisance to you, the eternal foundations of all rivers."
Salutations again and again to the Prāṇada mountains and to the oceans.
Since you gladden the multitudes of living beings in the three worlds with milk, water, clarified butter, curd, honey, salt, the essence of sugarcane, nectar, and wealth;
Therefore, grant me also the complete destruction of my sins.
For in all the worlds, you alone possess a vast expanse of jewels consisting of holy fords, gods, and asuras,
for the sake of destroying sins and for clothing, ointment, and ornamentation.
