May that prosperity which the world sustains be mine as well.

Then, at the conclusion of the formal gift accompanied by the appropriate sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should perform, as before, the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the deities, and their dismissal. Thus,
filled with long-standing wonder, people here give oceans joined with the six flavors.
Possessing the color of pure gold, he,
surrounded by immortals, attains the station of Hari.
Resplendent with the destruction of all sins, he was fully capable of [rescuing] his father, grandfather, son, and wife,
even though they were crowded within the world of hell.
Saying "Ṛk," he ascends to the abode of Śiva.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the seven oceans as declared in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
[340] Now, the fifteenth great rite (mahādana), known as the Jewel-Cow (*ratnadhenu*), is set forth in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
Matsya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift known as the Jewel-Cow (Ratnadhenu), which yields for men the fruit of Goloka.
Then, having reached an auspicious lunar day, as in the case of the Tulāpuruṣa gift,
one should perform the invocation of the world-protectors (lokeśas) and thereafter prepare the cow.
Having spread a black antelope skin upon the ground and placed a drona-measure of salt upon it,
one should fashion a cow made of jewels, having performed the formal ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the prescribed rules.

The phrase "invoking Lokeśa" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). For here, all that is prescribed in the *Matsya Purāṇa* for the *Tulāpuruṣa* rite is included: the invocation of the deities, the determination of place and time, the ancestral offering (*vṛddhi-śrāddha*), the worship of Śiva and others, the recitation by Brahmins, the selection of the preceptor and officiating priests, the offering of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), the construction of the sacrificial pit, the pavilion, the altar, the drawing of the mandala, the canopy, the archways, and the banners. Regarding the instruction "one should fashion a cow": the meaning is that one should construct the form of a cow with her calf, facing east, upon a *droṇa* measure of salt using lines drawn by a woman who has not recently given birth (*udakyā*).
"A wise man should place eighty-one rubies in its mouth."
In the same way, one should place a hundred topazes on the nose;
a golden tilaka on the forehead, and a hundred pearls on the two eyes.

It is understood from the principle that there is a distinction in the fruit according to the quality and the quantity [of the materials used]—such as on the nose (ghoṇā), meaning the tip of the nose, or in the case of golden *tilaka* marks and so forth—that the practice should be performed according to one's capacity. A hundred pearls should be placed by dividing them between the two eyes;
a hundred corals on the pair of eyebrows; two mother-of-pearl shells situated on the two ears; golden horns; and the head consisting of a hundred diamonds.
The plural "horns" is used in reference to the horns of calves.
[341] On the neck is a silken eye-band consisting of a hundred *gomeda* gems;
on the back is a hundred *indranīla*s, and on each side is a hundred *vaidūrya*s.
Likewise, its belly should be made of crystal, its hips from a hundred *saugandhika* gems;
its hooves should be made of gold, and its tail from strings of pearls.

In this context, because of the association with *sphaṭika* (crystal) and the statement "in that same manner," it should be understood that there are one hundred [of each]; the same applies to the *saugandhika* (a specific ruby), and it should also be understood that there are one hundred pearls.

One should cause the sun-stone (*sūryakānta*) and the moon-stone (*indukānta*) to be made for the nostrils, camphor and sandalwood for the sense of smell, saffron for the body hairs, and silver for the navel.
In the same way, one should visualize a hundred *gārutmata* gems in the *apāna*;
likewise, one should place other jewels in all the joints.

One should place other gems, such as rubies and the like, according to one's ability and availability. One should fashion the tongue from sugar, cow-dung from molasses, cow-urine from clarified butter, and likewise curd and milk in their natural forms.
One should place a chowrie at the tip of the tail and a copper milking vessel nearby;
one should also provide golden earrings and ornaments according to one's means,
and likewise fashion the calf using one-fourth of that [amount].
"In this very manner" means by means of these very substances mentioned for the cow, such as jewels and so forth.
Likewise, all grains are prescribed, and the feet are made of sugarcane;
there are all kinds of various fruits and a canopy of five colors.
Having performed the arrangement in this manner, and likewise the fire-oblation and the consecration,
the wise man, having given the sacrificial fee to the officiating priests, should address the cow.
Having addressed [the recipient] as in the case of the jaggery-cow (guḍadhenu), one should then recite this [verse].

[342] "In that same manner" means as in the *Matsya Purāṇa*’s description of the gift of the *tulāpuruṣa*. The bathing with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*) and so forth should also be understood in that very same way. Regarding the phrase "having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," the sequence is not intended here; the fee in this case is gold according to one's capacity, whereas in a gift performed by a king, it consists of villages, jewels, and so on. This is like the "molasses-cow" (*guḍadhenu*), performed with mantras such as "O Lakṣmī... and "Since they recite you as the abode of all the hosts of gods... [and] Rudra, Indra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Vāsudeva..."
Therefore, O Goddess, together with all the deities of the three worlds, protect me who am being tormented by the ocean of worldly existence.
Having addressed her thus and circumambulated her from all sides with devotion,
one who has observed a fast on this meritorious day should give her to the twice-born preceptor preceded by water.
With his body liberated from sins, he attains the state of Murāri.

It should also be understood that [the donor] should circumambulate [the image], perform a right-hand circuit, and hold a handful of flowers. Having observed a fast on the day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), or if unable to do so, having taken a single meal at night, one should give [the gift] to the Guru; this refers to the case where there is only a single sacred fire (*ekāgni*). In the case of multiple fires (*anekāgni*), however, the procedure is established as in the *tulāpuruṣa* rite. Immediately after the giving, one should perform, as before, the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the deities, and their dismissal (*visarjana*).
Thus, the knower of all rituals who bestows the gift of the Jewel-Cow, having attained a brilliantly shining celestial chariot (*vimāna*), shines forth.
Freed from all impurities, endowed with beauty through the grace of Madana, and accompanied by his kinsmen, sons, and grandsons, he attains the abode of Śambhu.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Jewel-Cow as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Now, the sixteenth great gift (mahādāna), known as the Jar of the Great Elements (Mahābhūtaghaṭa), is described here.
The Fish (Matsya) said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed Great Offering,
known as the Jar of the Great Elements, which destroys even the most heinous sins.
Then, having reached an auspicious lunar day and performed the recitation by Brahmins,

one should perform the rites beginning with the invocation of the world-protectors (lokeśa), just as in the Tulāpuruṣa rite, including the selection of officiating priests, the preparation of the pavilion, and the gathering of ornaments and coverings.
The word "etcetera" (ādi) should be explained as before.
A wise person should have a golden pitcher made, adorned with great jewels;
he should make it according to the proper measure, from one span up to a hundred finger-breadths.
Likewise, [the vessel] should be filled with milk and clarified butter (*ājya*) and provided with a *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree).

The cow's milk and clarified butter should be placed in equal quantities; the characteristics of the *kalpavṛkṣa*—such as having five branches—are to be understood from the section on the gift of the *kalpataru*.
Similarly, one should place Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara seated upon lotus-thrones.
In the same manner, one should fashion the earth, complete with lotuses, as if it were lifted up by a horse.
And Varuṇa seated upon a golden crocodile,
Hutāśana (Agni) seated upon a ram, and Vāyu with a deer as his seat.
Likewise, one should fashion Vināyaka as the lord of space, seated upon a mouse;
these, joined with the five Vedas, one should place within the center of the jar.

The characteristics of Brahmā and others, as well as those of Varuṇa and others, are to be understood as prescribed in the *Matsyapurāṇa* for the gift of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍadāna*). However, the characteristics of the Boar (*varāha*) are found in the *Brahmāṇḍa* section of the *Padmapurāṇa*. The form of Vināyaka is "the elephant-chariot.
The rosary (*akṣasūtra*) belongs to the *Ṛgveda*, while the lotus belongs to the *Yajurveda*.
The lute (*vīṇā*) belongs to the *Sāmaveda*; one should place the lute to the right.
Furthermore, the Atharvaveda has a *sruk* and a *sruva* ladle and a lotus in his hand;
the Purāṇaveda is the bestower of boons, holding a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
On all sides, there were all kinds of grains, yak-tail whisks, thrones, mirrors,
wooden sandals, leather shoes, umbrellas, lamps, and ornaments.
Having bathed at the conclusion of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), one should utter this mantra while [preparing] the bed, the water jars, and the five-colored canopy:

The sandals are made of wood, and there are sixteen water-jars, as such is seen in the original ritual manual (*prakṛti*). Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the previous day, and having completed the remainder of the rite—from the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*)—on the second day, the patron (*yajamāna*), bathed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) with waters containing all medicinal herbs as before, should circumambulate three times from left to right and, holding a handful of flowers, recite the mantra to be stated hereafter:
"Salutation to you, the supports of all the gods, both moving and unmoving!"
May there be peace from the presiding deities of the great elements; may there be auspiciousness for me.
Since there is nothing whatsoever within the cosmic egg or among all living beings that is created without the great elements, may there be prosperity and protection for me.
Having uttered this, whoever offers a vessel of the great elements (mahābhūtaghaṭa) shall be liberated from all sins and proceed to the supreme goal.
Accompanied by his paternal kinsmen, he goes to the realm of Viṣṇu in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, being praised by the women of the immortals.

In this case, water should first be offered to the Brahmins for the purpose of distribution. Once it has been bestowed according to the rules of partition as in the *tulāpuruṣa* rite, one should—by their permission—give gifts to others as well and provide for the poor and the destitute, because a ritual performed without a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is fruitless. According to one's capacity, land, gold, and so forth should be given to the preceptor and others as the fee; however, in the case of a small-scale rite, it should be understood that the single-fire procedure (*ekāgnividhāna*) may also be employed. Immediately thereafter, as before, the recitation of the "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the deities, and the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*) are to be performed. The man who performs these sixteen great gifts (*mahādāna*)...
For him there is no returning again to birth in this world.
Whoever thus recites this, or listens to it correctly here in the presence of Vāsudeva, together with his children, parents, and wife—
whether in the abode of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva) or in a temple of the Sun or Lakṣmī— [attains the highest state].
He too rejoices with the wives of the immortals for a full kalpa.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the jar of the great elements as declared in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.

Thus ends [the section] in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrī Hemādri, the illustrious sovereign of kings (*mahārājādhirāja*), the lord of all faculties, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
In the section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), the procedure for the sixteen kinds of gifts [346];
now begins the sixth chapter.
Now, the procedure for the offering of mountains: This Lokāloka mountain is the supreme Himavat, eternally rising,
possessing the glory of the Supārśva range, and beautiful with its vast, expansive expanse.

Thus, even though it is directly perceived, this mountain, with the full majesty of the lord of mountains manifest before us, reveals itself as the supreme Hemādri (the Golden Mountain), where the gods have found their rest.
Now, in this work, the venerable Hemādri undertakes an introductory exposition on the diverse and extensive ritual procedures for the gifts of mountains of grain and other such offerings.
In that regard, the gift of the mountain of grain is first described. That very [account] is found in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
Bhīṣma said, "O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the supreme majesty of giving."
That which is inexhaustible in the other world and honored by the hosts of celestial sages.
Pulastya said:
O best of sages, I shall describe the tenfold gift of Meru,
by the grace of which a man attains worlds honored by the gods.
Neither among the Purāṇas, nor among the gods, nor in sacrifices, nor in sacred shrines, does one obtain here that fruit which one enjoys through what has been studied and performed.
The connection is that the fruit [obtained] from the Purāṇas, the Vedas, sacrifices, and sacred shrines is not attained when these [rites] have been performed.
Therefore, I shall describe the unsurpassed ritual for mountains:
first there should be the mountain of grain (dhānya-śaila), and second the mountain of salt (lavana-acala).
The third is Guḍācala, while the fourth is Hemaparvata;
the fifth should be Tilashaila, and the sixth is Kārpāsaparvata.
The seventh is the mountain of ghee, and the eighth is the mountain of jewels;
likewise, the ninth is of silver, and the tenth is the mountain of sugar.
I shall describe their ritual procedure correctly and in due order:
during the solstices, the equinoxes, the vyatīpāta yoga, and on the day of the sun's turning.
On the third day of the bright fortnight, during an eclipse, at the waning of the moon,
or on the twelfth day during a wedding, a festival, or a sacrifice.
On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, or under an auspicious constellation, according to the prescribed rite,
the mountain of grain and other such offerings should be given according to one's faith and according to the injunctions.
At a sacred ford, in a temple, in a cow-pen, or even in the courtyard of one's home,
one should devoutly have a square pavilion constructed, facing the north.
Likewise, it should be sloping toward the east or the north, or one should face the east according to the injunction.

The characteristics of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) have been explained in the section on technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). Here, the sequence of the procedure is as follows: On the day prior to the day of the gift, during the forenoon, the donor—having performed his ablutions and other rites and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), "I shall perform the gift of such-and-such a mountain tomorrow"—should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* (the ancestral rite for prosperity) and the *ābhyudayika* (rite for auspicious occasions), and then perform the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) as previously described. Immediately thereafter, he should say: "Today, in this place, at this time, I shall sacrifice with the gift of such-and-such a mountain; for that purpose, in the fire-oblation and other constituent parts thereof, I choose you, O [Name] Śarman, student of such-and-such Veda, as my officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)."

The selection of four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are knowers of the *Purāṇas* and the Vedas, as well as the selection of the preceptor (*ācārya*), should be performed with the formula: "Om! Today, in such-and-such a place, at such-and-such a time, I, [name], shall perform the gift of such-and-such a mountain; for that purpose, I choose you, of such-and-such a lineage, named such-and-such, a student of such-and-such a Veda, as my preceptor to perform and cause these constituent rites to be performed. In every case, the response is "I am chosen. Therein, one should first honor him with the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*); this is the procedure common to all mountain-gifts.
Having spread kuśa grass upon a ground smeared with cow dung,
one should fashion a mountain in its center, accompanied by the surrounding foothills.
In this world, the best mountain [of grain] would consist of a thousand *droṇas* of grain;
the middling, five hundred; and the smallest would be three hundred.

The definition of a *droṇa* has been stated in the technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*). For a man of standard height with normal hands and feet, twelve *prasṛtis* constitute a *kuḍava*. By this *kuḍava*, the *prastha*, *āḍhaka*, and *droṇa* follow in a fourfold progression; thus, it is explained by the Kalpataru that a *droṇa* consists of sixty-four *kuḍavas*.
In the center [of the world], however, Mount Meru is composed of great rice (*mahāvrīhi*).
It should be joined with three golden trees: on the east, it is joined with pearls and diamonds;
on the south, with gomedaka and topaz.
And afterwards, with emeralds and sapphires,
with gentle lapis lazuli and ruby lotuses, and with pieces of sandalwood on all sides— [348] — with coral...
It should be provided with creepers and have surfaces of mother-of-pearl stone.
Then Brahmā, the Lord Viṣṇu, the enemy of Mura, and even the Sun-god should be golden here;
this arrangement of their heads was established by one free from envy.
Likewise, multitudes of twice-born ones should be fashioned out of gold.
Its four peaks are made of silver,
and its slopes are likewise silver;
its caves are covered with moist sugarcane and bamboo.
And the Praśravaṇa mountain, with its waters of clarified butter, is situated in the cardinal directions.
There should be a row of clouds with white garments in the east, yellow ones in the south,
and then variegated garments in the west.
And on the north, there is a thick row of red [flowers].
Then, having installed the eight world-protectors, headed by Mahendra, in their proper order made of silver,
there should be a row of various fruits all around.
And delightful garlands and ointments.
And above it is a canopy of five colors,
adorned with unfading flowers, and white.

"Meru," and so forth, refers to the great grains: *rājānna-śāli* rice. "Endowed with trees and creepers" means that one should fashion three trees: the *mandāra* to the south, the *pārijāta* to the north, and the *kalpataru* in the center; likewise, the *haricandana* to the east and the *santāna* to the west—these two trees. Since it will be stated later regarding the sugar-mountain (*śarkarācala*) that "all these must be made for all [mountains]," it should be noted that all of them possess five branches. *Vajra* is diamond; *gārutmata* is emerald; *sarojarāga* is ruby (*padmarāga*). The pearl and other gems are to be placed on the silver peaks as they will be described according to their respective directions. *Murāri* is Maheśvara. The characteristics of Brahmā and the others have been explained in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*. "Established at the head" means situated in the upper region. "By one free from envy" means by one devoid of stinginess regarding wealth. "Multitudes of twice-born" refers to flocks of birds. In some readings, the term is *divīśāḥ* (lords of heaven).

In that regard, the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the lords of heaven are situated therein; their characteristics have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*, and the characteristic of Rudra in the *Viśvacakra*. Sugarcane itself is the bamboo staff, clarified butter is the water, and garments are the variegated masses of clouds. The characteristics of the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*.
Having thus arranged the preeminent mountain of the gods and the supporting mountains (*viṣkambhagirīs*) of Meru in due order—
One should establish flowers, ointments, and dances in the four directions with one-fourth of the portion.
To the east of Mount Mandara, it was endowed with many fruits, frequented by hosts of attendants, marked by golden *bhadrakadamba* trees,
and resplendent with a golden embodiment of Desire.
One should cause flowers, garments, ointments, and dance to be performed.
Then, it should shine with the Kṣīra and Aruṇoda lakes, as well as the forest;
and to the south, it should be adorned by the Gandhamādana mountain fashioned from precious gems.
It may be made of a heap of wheat or of silver.
It should be joined with the golden Yakṣapati, with Ghṛtātmāna, and with Vastrā and Rājatavana;
thereafter, the mountain of sesame seeds [should be adorned] with many fragrant flowers.
It was joined with golden pippala trees and made of gold swans.
One should cause it to be adorned with a grove of silver flowers;
likewise, in front of that, one should place a great mountain consisting of curds, white substances, and liquids, endowed with wealth. Then, to the north of that, one should establish it.
Also a mountain made of mung beans, well-proportioned, along with cloth.
One should cause it to be fashioned with flowers, topped by a golden *vaṭa* tree, shining with a golden cow,
and likewise accompanied by the Sākṣīka, Bhadra, and Sarasa forests.
Having fashioned it joined with silver and adorned with a sun symbol.

"Having thus established," and so forth: having thus established Meru, one should construct each of the supporting mountains (*viṣkambhagiri*) from a separate material measuring a fourth part of that [Meru], but not by taking a fourth part of each of the four [mountains] together. And so he will say regarding the Salt Mountain (*lavaṇācala*): "One should have the supporting mountains made with a fourth part; separately. Because of its proximity, Mandara also is made of rice (*vrīhi*). "Endowed with hosts" means accompanied by three hosts in human form. There is a reading in some places: "endowed with many rows of fruits, with barley. If it possesses a *bhūlatā*, the performance with barley must also be carried out. It is marked by a golden tree named Bhadrakadamba.
