"Kāma, the beloved of Rati, slender-waisted, bearing a bow and arrows;

Ālīḍha, Nandana, Rājī, handsome, the delighter of the universe. Thus it is said. The connection is that [the mountain] shines with a lake filled with milk, known as Aruṇoda, and also with a forest made of silver. Regarding "to the south," and so forth: Gandhamadanī refers to Gandhamādana. "Kaladhautajāmba" means by a golden jambu tree. The form of the Lord of Yakṣas is described in the *Śrīpraśna*.

"One should always meditate upon the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), the friend of Śiva, who is short-statured, has reddish-brown eyes, holds a mace, possesses a yellow body, and is seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot.

Regarding the phrase "by the Ghṛtamānasa": this refers to a lake named Mānasa made of silver and filled with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Regarding "behind" (*paścāt*): in the western region, there is a lake made of silver, filled with curds, called Sitoda. Regarding "the Vipula mountain": this means the mountain named Vipula, which is joined by the Bhadrasaras lake made of honey (*mākṣika*), that is, filled with honey.

In this context, it should be understood that for all mountains dedicated to deities, the westward-facing orientation of Kāmadeva, the eastward-facing orientation of the swan, and the southward-facing orientation of the golden cow depend upon their respective positions within the cardinal directions established on the sugar-mountain (śarkarācala). This arrangement of the skins [and so forth] is determined by some scriptural authority. Furthermore, these figures—Kāmadeva and the others—are to be placed beneath the specific trees native to each mountain, such as the *kadamba* and others. Then, four oblations (*homa*) should be performed by eminent Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas and Purāṇas, self-controlled, and of irreproachable conduct and appearance.
Having constructed a sacrificial pit here measuring one cubit to the east,
the rite should be performed with sesame seeds, barley, ghee, fuel-sticks, and *kuśa* grass.
And at night, with wakefulness accompanied by songs and musical instruments played without agitation,
I shall describe the invocation of the mountain peaks.

"Towards the east," and so forth: having constructed a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*) on the eastern side of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and having prepared a divine altar (*devatāvedi*) in the north-eastern quarter of that pit according to the characteristics described for the *tulāpuruṣa* rite, one should perform worship there for Vināyaka and the other deities as previously prescribed. Subsequently, at the conclusion of the installation of the fire (*agnisthāpana*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with sesame seeds and other materials using the specific mantras associated with the deities to be mentioned hereafter, such as the planets (*graha*) and the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Regarding the statement, "When a thousand [oblations] are to be offered, one should make the pit one cubit in size," the author of the *Dānaviveka* maintains that because a pit of one cubit is prescribed here, a thousand oblations (*āhuti*) must be offered.

In this context, there are thirty-two deities beginning with Vināyaka, the twelve Ādityas, the eleven Rudras, the ten Lokapālas, the eight Vasus, the four—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Sūrya—and the four—Kāma, Dhanada, Haṃsa, and Kāmadhenu. Thus, for these eighty-one deities, when thirteen oblations are offered to each deity, the total number of oblations amounts to one thousand fifty-three. However, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* will state that "one hundred and eight [oblations] should be offered," and that the sacrificial materials are only the four beginning with sesame seeds. It should be understood that these sacrificial substances are smeared with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). As for the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), because they are common to all, those of the *udumbara* tree are used. After the other offerings, one should take flower-offerings and invoke the mountains in their proper order with the mantras to be mentioned; among them, the mantra for invoking Meru is as follows:
O you who are the treasury of the abode of all the hosts of gods, quickly destroy this mountain of the immortals which has become hostile even in our home;
grant us security and perform for us unsurpassed peace.
Indeed, he was fully honored by me with supreme devotion.
You alone are the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun; you are the manifest, the unmanifest, and the supreme seed. Therefore, protect me, O Eternal One!
Since you are the abode of the world-protectors, of Viśvamūrti,
and of the Rudras, Ādityas, and Vasus, therefore grant me peace.
"Since it is not devoid of immortals and likewise filled with women,
therefore deliver me from this essence of saṃsāra, which consists of endless suffering.
Having thus worshipped that Meru, one should also honor Mandara.
Now, regarding Mandara:
Since you are adorned by the Caitraratha and Bhadrāśva regions,
O Mandara, may you quickly become a source of abundant nourishment.
Now, regarding Gandhamādana:
"Therefore, O Gandhamādana, you are the crest-jewel of Jambudvīpa;
since you possess the splendor of the Gandharvas, may my fame be firm."
Now, for Vipulaparvan: Since you have a golden Aśvattha tree as your crest, and because of Ketumāla and the Vaibhrāja forest, may there be constant prosperity for me.
Now, regarding Supārśva:
Since you always shine with the Northern Kurus and the Sāvitra forest,
O Supārśva, may my prosperity be imperishable.
Having thus addressed them all, at the clear dawn,
he should bathe and then give the middle of the best of mountains to the guru.
O King, one should give the Viṣkambha mountains to the officiating priests in due order;
furthermore, O Ruler of the Earth, one should give twenty-four cows, or otherwise ten.
According to one's capacity, one should give seven or eight, or if lacking the means, five;
or one may give even a single tawny cow that yields milk to the preceptor.

Having thus addressed [the deities], on the day prior to the day of giving, one should perform all these rites beginning with the address; then, having passed the night with songs, instrumental music, and so forth, at dawn the preceptor and the others, having performed the rites of bathing and so on, and having completed the remainder of the entire ritual up to the *pūrṇāhuti* offering, should bathe the patron as before with the water from the jar placed near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). The patron also, dressed in white garments, having circumambulated [the mountain], should present it from the mountain in due order with the mantra to be recited below. The procedure for that is as follows:

Oṃ. Today, at this time, I, [Name], belonging to the [Gotra] lineage, desiring [this specific desire], give this mountain, together with its appurtenances, to you, the Brāhmaṇa [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage; salutations. For the sake of establishing this gift of the mountain to the Brāhmaṇa [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage, I give this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to you. And here, since there is a requirement for a sacrificial fee and the postulation of another fee not mentioned in the scripture is untenable, it is connected as the fee precisely because of the scriptural statement "one should give cows. Some maintain that even without the explicit designation "sacrificial fee," the status of being a fee exists; however, it is more appropriate to accept the fee as stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, such as "having given a thousand-fold fee," and so forth.
This very same rule is prescribed for all mountains without exception;
the same mantras are prescribed for their worship, and the same ritual implements are prescribed.

For all the planets, the world-protectors, and those beginning with Brahmā, the fire-oblation (homa) in all cases on the mountains is prescribed to be performed with their own respective mantras. One should always observe a fast; however, for one who is unable, eating only at night is permitted.

Since it will be stated later that "one should eat food free from pungent substances and salt everywhere," it should be understood that the meal at night is likewise free from pungent substances and salt.
O King, listen now to the procedure for all the mountains in due order,
as well as the mantras to be used at the time of giving and the fruit obtained from the mountains.
Now the mantra:
"Food is Brahman, for it has been declared; in food the vital breaths are established.
From food all beings arise; by food the world subsists."
Since food itself is Lakṣmī and food itself is Janārdana, protect me in the form of this mountain of grain; therefore, salutations, salutations!

Having thus honored the preceptor and the others, one should give [the remainder] to others as well with their permission. Then the patron (yajamāna), having worshipped the deities on the altar as before, should pay obeisance. The preceptor should dismiss them. Then, according to one's capacity, a meal for the Brahmins is provided; on the day of the gift, the patron who has observed the fast must avoid alkaline salts and pungent flavors. All the mountain-appurtenances and furnishings are to be delivered to the house of the Brahmin; this is to be understood everywhere as prescribed in the case of the "Mountain of Sugar" (śarkarācala). Whoever gives a mountain made of grain according to this rite—
He is honored in the world of the gods for one hundred and fifty manvantaras.
Surrounded by hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas,
he travels to the heights of heaven in a celestial chariot, honored by the gods.
Through the exhaustion of karma, one attains the sovereignty of a king in this world; of this there is no doubt.
Now, from the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa:
[357] The Blessed One said: "Henceforth I shall describe the supreme mountain of grain."
By giving which, a human being obtains the fruit of all possible gifts.
Having caused a pavilion to be constructed on the bank of a river, or in a house, or likewise in a temple, one should perform the ritual procedure according to the rules.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, at the solstice, or during an eclipse in its entirety,
as well as on other occasions whenever faith arises.
One should construct a mountain of auspicious characteristics that produces great joy;
the best is one thousand [units] in size, while the middling is half of that.
O best of kings, the smallest [size] consists of three hundred droṇas;
however, if these cannot be obtained, one should have it made according to one's ability, endowed with faith.
In the center, one should fashion the auspicious Mount Meru made of large rice grains;
and one should make the supporting mountains out of barley, starting from the east.
Then, one should fashion mountains with wheat on the south, likewise with sesame seeds on the west,
and with beans on the north, each being one-fourth the size [of the central mountain].
The wise man should have all of them constructed with golden peaks,
their bodies variegated with every kind of jewel, and adorned with banner-trees.
Having covered those [trees] endowed with various trees and creepers, fragrant and adorned,
with cloths, one should worship them with perfumes and garlands.
Having fashioned such a mountain, one should worship it on all sides with various kinds of food, as well as with fruits, roots, and diverse flavors.
One should likewise fill [the area] on all sides with grains from both cultivated fields and the forest;
there, one should place golden images of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
To the east, one should have a very beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) made, measuring one cubit;
there, eight or four Brahmins shall be the officiating priests (hotṛs).
The householders were virtuous and self-controlled, with all their limbs complete;
they wore washed garments and were adorned with bracelets and other ornaments.
With their bodies anointed with sandalwood and likewise adorned with flowers,
the Brahmins, being thus prepared, should perform the fire-oblation without weariness.
And for Indra and the other guardians of the world, a fire-oblation is prescribed,
performed with their respective characteristic mantras, using sacrificial fuel-sticks or else with sesame seeds.
The offering for Brahmā and the others is prescribed with the Pauruṣa Sūkta;
likewise, the oblation is indeed performed with the Vyāhṛtis, along with sesame seeds and clarified butter.
One hundred and eight oblations should be offered for the fulfillment of all desires;
thereafter, the sacrificer, with a serene mind, should worship the mountain.
Having bathed and put on white garments, free from desire and anger,
[one should reflect that] food is indeed the life-breath of beings, as well as their strength and splendor.
The entire world, both moving and unmoving, is established upon food;
from food beings come into existence, and by food they indeed grow.
And that food, by virtue of its being grain, shall be of many kinds;
therefore, may Meru, as it exists within the grain, accomplish my desire.
Homage to you, the support of all worlds, worshipped by the gods!
Let there be no one at all in my family here who is destitute of wealth.
In this very way, may food be never cut off for me in birth after birth;
and may that which is being given day and night never come to exhaustion.
Having thus performed the worship on the preceding day, one should hold a great festival during the night,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and trumpets and by singers reciting auspicious verses.
Then, in the presence of everyone, he should present it to a Brahmin,
having provided a thousand-fold sacrificial fee according to his ability and his means.
A sacrifice devoid of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) arises as an enemy;
therefore, whatever is designated as a gift should be given accompanied by a sacrificial fee.
O wise ones, one who possesses the Viṣkambha yoga should give gifts to those who serve as the Hotṛ priests there;
afterwards, he should honor the preceptor with cows, horses, and likewise with elephants.
One should worship that preceptor with principal ornaments, garments, flowers, and unguents, and having fed him according to the prescribed rite.
O King, cows that are adorned, yielding much milk, endowed with good qualities,
beautiful, and young, should be given by those performing the oblations for the sake of satisfaction.
Whoever, according to this rite, should give a mountain made of grain,
having raised it up together with himself, shall ascend to the highest heaven.
Whether it be a woman or even a man, having ascended a divine celestial chariot, they rejoice with the gods for twenty-six manvantaras.
Upon the exhaustion of his merit, even after returning here, he shall become the lord of the seven islands;
O Indra among kings, he is born for ten lifetimes during the Dvāpara age.
He who, with a concentrated mind, listens to this gift being proclaimed, shall have a lifespan of ten thousand years, accompanied by sons and grandsons.
Even that poor person shall attain a happy rebirth through supreme devotion.
From the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: Hereafter I shall describe the excellent mountain of grain. One should have it made of rice, or else of wheat or barley.
One should construct the best [image] with a thousand [gold pieces], the middling with half of that,
and the smallest with half of that again, according to the extent of one's wealth.
One should perform everything for them in due order according to the rules for the lunar festivals;
or else, O King, one enjoys that very fruit beforehand.

O Brahmin, those of noble intellect who, having prostrated, bestow the Mountain of Grain— which shines with golden trees, is joined by the supporting mountains, and is frequented by gods and siddhas— [attain great merit].
They attain the pair of supreme lotus feet of Parameṣṭhin.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the gift of the mountain of grain.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the gift of the mountain of salt.
Pulastya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme Mount Lavana,
by the gift of which a person attains union with Śiva in this world.
The best mountain for reaping should be made of sixteen droṇas;
the middling should be half of that, and the lowest is recorded as being four [droṇas].
One who is destitute of wealth should have half of a *droṇa* made according to his capacity;
he should have the supporting mountains made separately with a quarter-measure each.

The characteristics of the *droṇa* have been stated. By "with a fourth part" (*caturthāṃśena*), it is meant that from the primary mountain-salt, salt measured at a fourth part of each [other ingredient] should be added separately.
The ritual procedure for Brahmā and the others should always be performed as before.
Likewise, one should fashion all the golden trees and the abode of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*).
One should likewise place the lakes, Kāmadeva, and the others here.
"In that same manner" means as with the mountain of grain.
One should perform even a mere vigil; now learn the mantras for the gift:
"Since the essence of salt is produced from the essence of good fortune..."
And since you are identical with that [salt], protect me from sin, O best of mountains;
for all savory juices are not intense without salt.
Since it is eternally dear to Śiva and Śivā, and since it arises from the body of Viṣṇu and increases health, therefore grant me peace.
Therefore, protect [us] from the ocean of saṃsāra in the form of a mountain.
Whoever should give a mountain of salt according to this rite, [attains great merit].
One may dwell in the world of Umā for an eon, and from there one attains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the mountain of salt as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the excellent mountain of jaggery.
By the giving of which a man attains heaven, which is honored by the gods.
The best [type of recipient] is considered to be capable of ten burdens; the middling, five;
the lowest, three; and one with little wealth, half of that.
The term *bhāra* has been explained in the commentary.
Likewise, one should [worship] the invocation, the honor, the fire-oblation, the sacrificial tree, and the worship of the gods;
likewise the supporting mountains, the lakes, and the forest deities.
One should perform the fire offering (homa), the ritual vigil (jāgaraṇa), and likewise the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for the world-protectors (lokapāla);
one should act as in the case of the mountain of grain (dhānyaparvata) and recite this mantra:
Just as this Janārdana is the supreme Soul of all among the gods,
so too is the Sāmaveda among the Vedas and Mahādeva among the yogins.
Just as the syllable Om is among all mantras and Pārvatī is among women,
so too is sugarcane juice always considered the most excellent among all liquids.
Therefore, O Guḍaparvata, grant me supreme fortune,
since you, O Guḍaparvata, are the brother of Saubhāgyadāyinī.
"And since it is also the dwelling place of Pārvatī, protect me always from that [sin].
He who gives a mountain made of jaggery according to this rite—"
Being honored by the Gandharvas, he is glorified in the world of Gaurī;
then, at the end of a hundred kalpas, he becomes the sovereign of the seven continents.
Endowed with long life and good health, he shall be unconquered by his enemies.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a mountain of jaggery as described in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
The Blessed Lord said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the supreme mountain of jaggery.
It removes all sins, is meritorious, and is the supreme producer of good fortune.
It bestows nourishment, peace, happiness, and the enjoyment of the two kinds of wealth;
one should construct it with ten parts, or according to one's ability.

Having constructed a pavilion as before, and all the necessary implements as before— the phrase "as before" means as described for the mountain of grain in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*— it should be provided with the guardians of the quarters (*lokapāla*) and likewise possess golden peaks.
His body was variegated with pearls, his form adorned with garments and ornaments;
he was endowed with coral sprouts and held a stalk of sugarcane and a bamboo flute.
One should fashion its silver buttocks, refined with the form of a girdle,
and its copper shoulder adorned with various minerals.
Having fashioned such a mountain, covered with all kinds of grain,
endowed with all medicinal herbs, possessing peaks and great trees.
Having constructed a canopy according to the prescribed rite by those who are skillful,
one should then prepare a single sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is quadrangular and well-adorned.
In that rite, learned Brahmins of praised vows should be appointed;
honored according to the rules, they should perform the oblation without weariness.

The best of the twice-born should perform the fire-oblation for the world-protectors, the planets, and Brahmā and the others, according to the prescribed rules and with the mantras specified for their respective symbols.
And with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the preceptor, being well-composed, should perform ten thousand oblations there together with those Brahmins, according to the prescribed measure.
Having caused a great festival to be held there with the chanting of the Veda (*brahmaghoṣa*),
and having thus performed the ritual on the preceding day, he was filled with faith.
One should give it especially on the third day of the month of Māgha,
or one should cause it to be given according to the prescribed rite on the third day of Caitra.
One should also cause [the ritual] to be performed at other times, such as during eclipses;
for you are eternally the best of all flavors and always beloved by the gods.
Grant me happiness always; salutations to you, O best of mountains!
[364] As long as the earth, the oceans, and the rivers endure, and as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars remain, so long may you grant me happiness as well as incomparable good fortune.
Having thus performed the worship, one should announce it to the brahmins;
afterwards, one should honor the preceptor and also those who are poor, blind, and miserable.
Having dismissed those Brahmins and performed a circumambulation,
one should eat sweet food, free from salt, on that day.
A man who applies this unguent becomes truly fulfilled;
therefore, one who desires the highest fruit should give this gift.
For the sake of an eternal destination in the world, as well as good fortune and beauty,
a mountain of molasses should be given according to this very rite.
It should be made to weigh twenty bhāras; one should perform the remainder as previously described.
O King, this gift is especially recommended for women.
This is prescribed for anyone who desires royal sovereignty;
having attained the previously mentioned fruit, one indeed becomes one who has fulfilled all duties.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a mountain of jaggery as declared in the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*.
Pulastya said:
Now I shall describe the supreme mountain of gold, which removes all sins.
By the giving of which a human being goes to the abode of Viriñci.
The best [stūpa] consists of a thousand palas, the middling of five hundred;
the lowest is half of that, and likewise one who possesses little wealth may do so according to his ability.
Free from envy, one should give more than one *pala* according to one's ability;
O best of kings, one should perform everything just as in the case of the mountain of grain.
In the same manner, one should present the supporting mountains with the officiating priests, saying:
"Homage to you, the seed of Brahman; homage indeed to you, who contain the Brahman within."
Since you bestow infinite fruit, therefore protect Śiloccaya;
since you are the essence of Agni, therefore grant merit, O Lord of the World!
Therefore, O best of mountains, protect [us] in the form of the Golden Mountain;
whoever should give a mountain of gold according to this rite, [attains great merit].
He goes to the supreme world of Brahmā, which causes bliss;
there he shall remain for a hundred kalpas, and from there he attains the highest goal.

In this regard, although it is stated that one should give the central mountain to the preceptor (*guru*) and the supporting mountains to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and furthermore, no such rule is heard as in the case of the *tulāpuruṣa* sacrifice, nevertheless—since a single person capable of giving gold measured by thousands of *palas* and so forth is rarely found, and because we observe the practice of giving among many recipients even in other rites involving much gold—it is understood that there too, having given three-quarters (or a portion) to the preceptor as in the *tulāpuruṣa*, one should give the remainder to others with his permission. If it is argued that this cannot be so because it is not seen in the archetype (*prakṛti*), we reply: let it not be so in the archetype; however, what contradiction is there in accepting exactly what is established in the *tulāpuruṣa* and similar rites? And if it is argued that since there is only one ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*), it is impossible for one rite to have two archetypes, we say: in the archetype itself, the arrangement is exactly like this. If it is asked how the *dhānyaparvata* (mountain of grain), which serves as the archetype for all mountain-gifts such as the *lavaṇācala* (salt mountain), can incorporate the characteristics of another rite, we reply: no, because even the archetype depends on its own constituent parts and the principal act; thus, we observe that even in the *dhānyaparvata*, there is the adoption of the characteristics of the *tulāpuruṣa*, such as the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the characteristics of the preceptor, and so forth.

Consequently, it is established that when there is a large quantity of material, the gift should be given to many; when the quantity of material is small, it should be given to five Brahmins; and when one's own wealth is very meager, it should be given to the teacher alone.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Golden Mountain as declared in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
Now follows the procedure for the gift of the sesame-mountain (*tilaśailadāna*). From the *Padma Purāṇa*, Pulastya said:
"Therefore, I shall now fully explain the rite of the sesame-mountain according to the prescribed rules."
By the giving of which a person goes to the unsurpassed world of Viṣṇu.
O best of Brahmins, a mountain of sesame seeds weighing ten *droṇas* is considered the highest; five *droṇas* is regarded as the middling; and three *droṇas* is proclaimed as the lowest.
O best of kings, I shall now duly proclaim all the subsequent mantras for the gift of the tree-supporting pillars and so forth, as well as those for the preceding ones.
Since sesame seeds, kusha grass, and masha beans originated from the sweat of Vishnu's body in Madhuvana, may they grant us prosperity here.
O Lord of Mountains, since offerings to gods and ancestors are characterized by the sesame seeds within you, deliver us from worldly existence; O Sesame-Mountain, salutations be to you!
Having thus addressed [the deity], whoever should give this unsurpassed mountain of sesame seeds attains the station of Viṣṇu, from which a return to worldly existence is difficult to find.
A person attains long life both in this world and the next;
honored by the ancestors, gods, and gandharvas, he shall go to heaven.
Then, from the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, the Blessed One said:
"Henceforth I shall describe the most excellent mountain of sesame seeds."
That gift which, among all gifts, yields fruit in the world beyond.
Sesame seeds are an incomparable purifier and the most sanctifying among all purifiers;
since they have originated from the body of Viṣṇu, they have attained the state of being supreme.
Sesame seeds serve for the protection of all three worlds;
he who offers water with sesame seeds to the gods during the bright fortnight [attains great merit].
During the dark fortnight, having bathed and being endowed with faith, one should offer a handful of sesame seeds— either seven or eight— in conjunction with water for the ancestors.
The gods, together with the ancestors, grant him a hundredfold speech when he is satisfied;
however, that which has been defiled by dogs, crows, or even by outcasts and the like [is not so].
Everything sprinkled with sesame seeds becomes pure; of this there is no doubt.
He who, according to this rule, has fashioned an excellent mountain out of sesame seeds—
One should bestow it upon a preeminent brahmin; his merit shall become inexhaustible.
I shall describe its ritual procedure as well as its supreme majesty.
During a Vyatīpāta yoga, during an Ayana, during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
on one's birth star, during the equinoxes, and especially in the month of Māgha, [a gift] should be given.
Whatever gift, fire-oblation, or even libation is performed with sesame seeds during the month of Māgha,
that shall become inexhaustible in this world.
Likewise, having constructed an excellent pavilion either by a river or in a house,
one should perform everything in its entirety according to the previously described procedure.
"By what was previously stated" means by that which is prescribed for the Mountain of Grain in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
One may fashion it with three hundred *droṇas* according to one's capacity;
one should fashion it with a fourth part of the mountain [of grain].
[368] The wise man should likewise fashion the quarters as petals, Mount Mandara and the other mountains out of sesame seeds, and the world-protectors, beginning with Brahmā, out of gold.
One should decorate the sacrificial pavilion on all sides with stalks of sugarcane;
the wise practitioner should have a single square fire-pit constructed to the east.
One should establish there pure twice-born men belonging to the four Vedic schools, together with a navel and a girdle measuring one cubit in size.
The fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed there according to the previously mentioned procedure;
one should also worship Parvata with garlands, garments, and ornaments.
On the first day, with great effort, you were caused by me to be fashioned from gems, jewels, and corals, as well as from sesame seeds produced from the body of Viṣṇu.
O Great Meru, abode of the gods, salutations to you, the best of mountains!
Whatever sin has been committed by me throughout seven lifetimes—
"O best of mountains, by your grace may all that go to destruction.
Having thus worshipped him and received auspicious blessings, [he departed].
Having held a great festival at night near the mountain, he,
being composed, duly honored the twice-born along with their preceptors.
One should give a thousand as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or cause it to be given according to one’s capacity;
here too, eight or even four cows should be given.
Then, having performed a circumambulation of the mountain as well as the Brahmins,
and having prostrated with his head, he should follow Śrāddhāvāsu.
Whoever bestows this gift according to this rite shall go,
together with his ancestors, to the incomparable world of Viṣṇu.
Having ascended a supreme celestial chariot adorned with a network of tinkling bells,
surrounded by hosts of apsarases, and exceedingly beautified by gandharvas;
For ten crores of years, he enjoys pleasures as he desires;
when his merit is exhausted, he returns here and becomes a righteous king.
His wife or his consort shall be fortunate and endowed with beauty;
she will be skillful, the upholder of the lineage, and possessed of sons and grandsons.
One may be born in the Kṛta Yuga and afterwards attain liberation,
as was the case with Sagara, Kakutstha, and Dhundhumāra in ancient times.
Indeed, this gift was given in the past by Māndhātṛ, Yavaneśva, and Kārttavīrya, as well as by their wives.
Incomparable sovereignty has been attained, as well as eternal fame in the world;
therefore, O best among the foremost of kings, this gift should always be given.
Having heard this injunction, a poor person endowed with faith shall obtain a fruit equal to the merit of the gift of a tawny cow.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the gift of the mountain of sesame seeds.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme mountain of sesame seeds.
Having performed [the rites] at the previously mentioned place and time, one should then worship [it].
In this context, by the word "previous," the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa as described in the Liṅga Purāṇa is to be understood:
"O Sage, having established a staff measuring ten tālas upon a level, delightful ground free from anthills and the like."
Having sprinkled [the vessel] thoroughly with water, one should subsequently cast sesame seeds into it.
[370] “The *tāla* is prescribed for the middle [finger], and the *gokarṇa* for the ring finger,” and so forth; thus the measurement of a *tāla* is stated in the technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*).
The best of Brahmins should sprinkle that ground with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and the wise man, being well-composed, should fashion the mandala as before.
Having established [the image] with new garments and having scattered *droṇa* flowers,
one should especially fashion a mountain there out of loads of sesame seeds.
The height at the top is proclaimed to be one span (prādeśa) from the staff;
however, that which is four finger-breadths less than this is proclaimed for the middle [type].
It should be equal in length to a staff when placed on the little finger; one should have it made even if slightly less than a staff.
Having wrapped it all around with new cloths, one should worship it in due order.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Sadyojāta and the others, one should worship according to the prescribed rite;
furthermore, the forms of the deities should be established in the eight directions in their proper sequence.
Then, one should have each of them fashioned from three niṣkas of gold.

The *sadya* and other mantras refer to those beginning with *Sadyojāta*. For the gods, that is, the world-protectors (*lokapālas*), the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be offered according to the prescribed rule, as in the case of the gift of the *tulāpuruṣa*.
And the fire-oblation (*homa*) has been declared previously, O best of sages, exactly as it was described.
It should be understood that the *tulāpuruṣa* rite mentioned here is precisely that described in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"One should worship the Lord of the gods, who is surrounded by the world-protectors,
situated in the midst of a mountain of sesame seeds, and having the form of a mountain of sesame seeds."
And the worship of Śiva should be performed with a thousand jars and other offerings;
one should show the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, situated in the midst of sesame seeds.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rules and in the proper sequence, one should perform the ritual dismissal;
one should cause a mountain of sesame seeds to be given to a poor Vedic scholar.
[371] Thus has been described the gift consisting of sesame seeds, which is the most excellent and supreme of all;
by performing it, a human being certainly attains both heaven and liberation.

The procedure here is as follows: having sprinkled the previously described pavilion, altar, and mandala with products of the cow (*gavya*), having scattered *darbha* grass, *droṇa* flowers, and so forth, and having covered them with cloths, the patron (*yajamāna*) should place a staff (*daṇḍa*) measuring ten *tāla*s. Covering the staff with barley, unbroken rice, and pure sesame seeds, he should fashion the form of a mountain. In the best case, it should exceed the staff by one *prādeśa*; in the middling case, by eight fingers; but in the lowest option, it should be equal to the staff—this refers to the heap of sesame seeds. Then, having covered it with cloths and meditated upon it as the form of Meru, one should place Śiva upon it, fashioned from gold weighing no less than three *pala*s, and install the [faces] beginning with Sadyojāta. There, in the first enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), are the five Brahmās; outside that, having installed the universal form (*sarvādimūrti*); outside that, the forms beginning with Earth (*bhūmyādimūrti*); and outside that, the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). All these should be fashioned from gold weighing three *niṣka*s and worshipped with their respective mantras. Among them, the characteristics of Śiva have been stated in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*.
The characteristics of Sadyojāta and the others are stated in the Mayadīpikā:
"One should represent Sadyojāta as white, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness."
He is gentle, adorned with the crescent moon upon his crown, having the form of a youth and three eyes;
he is Vāmadeva, with limbs deeply red, wearing garlands, garments, and a sacred thread.

He had a prominent nose and carried a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga); his hands held a sword and a shield; he had tawny eyebrows, tearful eyes, and a moon-like face with protruding fangs and a long, distorted mouth.
In the four [hands] holding nooses and clubs, one should provide a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and a body;
in the right hands, one should place a trident, a staff, an axe, and a sword.
One should depict a man wearing yellow garments, very gentle, resembling saffron in color,
adorned with a crown-moon, and holding a noose and a trident in his two hands.

"One should fashion Īśāna as the fifth [face], resembling crystal, the cause of the universe, with three eyes, the moon upon his crest, and holding a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands.
Thus Viśvakarman states the characteristics of all [the faces] beginning with that one.
Sarva, Bhūma, Mahādeva, Rudra, Paśupati, Bhava, Ugra,
and Īśāna— these eight forms are indeed like Śiva himself.
"Those who have the moon as their crest-jewel, adorned with circles of matted hair, three-eyed, and holding excellent khaṭvāṅgas and tridents in their hands. Thus it is said.

Among the eight forms (*mūrtyaṣṭaka*), the forms of earth, water, fire, air, and ether have been described in the context of the gift of the jar of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūtaghaṭadāna*); those of the moon and sun, however, will be explained in the section on the granting of boons (*varadānaprakaraṇa*). Since no specific distinction is mentioned, the form of the patron (*yajamānamūrti*) should be understood as being identical to that of any other person. The characteristics of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) have been stated in the *Brāhmāṇḍadāna*. Thereafter, following the worship, one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and so forth with their respective mantras; then, having performed the consecration with a thousand jars (*sahasrakalaśābhiṣeka*) for Śiva who is stationed separately, and having worshipped Śiva and the others for the sake of the patron, one should cause that mountain to be given to a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*). The sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others are as before. Regarding this first [topic], concerning the patron, it is stated in the *Kālottaratantra*:
Alternatively, having bathed the Supreme Lord with one hundred and eight jars and having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite;
The wise preceptor should perform the offering one hundred and eight times with the offering mantra:
"Mahādeva, Mahārudra, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita."
Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, Bhavodbhava,
and Kapālīśa— these are to be known as the eleven Rudras.
One should worship him who is entirely possessed of all afflictions in due order;
having worshipped him upon a black antelope skin with sixteen additional offerings of sesame seeds.
Endowed with three gold pieces, wrapped in a pair of cloths,
beautified by flower garlands, and fully adorned with fruits.
Having meditated upon the eleven Rudras in their proper order,
one should cause them to be handed over to a twice-born Brahmin who is devoted to Śiva, tranquil, and learned in the Vedas.
Thus, whoever performs this with devotion, endowed with this ritual procedure,
shall experience longevity, prosperity, victory, and fame, and then go to Śiva.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the sesame-mountain as declared in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme sesame-mountain,
by the giving of which every sin shall be destroyed.
Whatever sin may have been committed within seven lifetimes, such as the killing of an embryo and so forth,
all of that comes to destruction through the gift of a mountain of sesame seeds.
On all auspicious occasions, and especially during an eclipse,
a mountain of sesame seeds should be diligently offered in a sacred place.
A wise person should have a pavilion constructed in front of the temple,
provided with four well-distributed doors and adorned with four archways.
It should be ten or twelve cubits in size, square and well-proportioned,
covered with a canopy, and with its canopy extending out in all directions.
Having placed two full jars at each of the doors,
one should perform the Puṇyāhavācana ceremony on the morning of the preceding day.
Then, having selected a preceptor who has mastered the Vedāṅgas, is self-controlled,
of virtuous conduct, youthful, and endowed with the auspicious marks,
one should also appoint eight officiating priests (ṛtvij) who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
He should announce his purpose to them, saying: "Tomorrow I shall bestow a mountain of sesame seeds."
Then, having worshipped the preceptor Mahādeva according to the prescribed rite,
as well as Vināyaka and Umā, one should then cast down the thread.
Having arranged nine compartments all around within the pavilion,
eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be prepared, with the ninth being in the northeast (īśāna).
Having spread white cloths everywhere across the central square,
one should diligently construct Mount Meru in the center using pure sesame seeds.
The highest [mountain] is made from three *bhāras* of gold; the middle and lowest are made from two and one [respectively].
Then, the surrounding Ring Mountains (*varṣaparvata*) are to be made with a sixth part of that.
Mālyavat, Niṣadha, Himavat, Hemakūṭaka,
the mountain Gandhamādana, Śṛṅgavat, and the two Śveta mountains.
It should be placed within the [sections] beginning with that of Indra, and one should cover the exterior with cloths;
the Kalpa-tree, however, is made of gold and adorned with all kinds of jewels.
Endowed with all flowers and fruits, it should be placed upon the summit of Mount Meru;
one should also designate golden deer, birds, and trees.
Whatever Mandāra trees, deer, birds, and so forth exist upon all the mountains,
they should be diligently placed there, being one-fourth the size of those on Mount Meru.
The measure of gold for the Sumeru [image] shall be twelve palas, eighteen, or ten, respectively,
for the superior, inferior, and middling [sizes].
Beneath the wish-fulfilling trees, one should visualize Hara seated comfortably upon a golden lotus, possessing four arms and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Having placed a golden image with three eyes and a gentle countenance, one should worship it;
Śiva by name should be in the center, while Bhava, Śambhu, and Trilocana [occupy the other positions].
Sthāṇu, Īśa, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, and Candraśekhara—
one should worship Mahādeva in the east and the other directions with these names.
During the day, he, along with his preceptor and the officiating priests, should consume sacrificial food (haviṣya),
specifically according to their own respective rules as prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras.
Having offered the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), he should perform everything as prescribed;
having honored them with garments, he should worship all the officiating priests and the preceptor.
One should give double to the teacher: earrings along with finger-rings, as well as sandals, an umbrella, a bed, seats, and wooden shoes.
Then, when the sun had risen and the auspicious time had arrived,
the sacrificer, his mind serene, was permitted by those brahmins.
Having bathed in water infused with all medicinal herbs, wearing linen garments and well-adorned,
he should circumambulate the mountain and diligently invite the Brahmins.
Having envisioned that deity as one who is wise, endowed with virtues, established in the self, free from greed, and learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
On the side of each respective mountain, one should worship it by its specific name;
first, one should offer Meru with the words, "May Śiva be well-pleased."
Having meditated upon Śiva for a Brahmin who is preeminent in virtues,
one should likewise cause the mountains of the eastern and other directions to be given with their respective names.
Thinking "May [the Lord] be pleased," he should conceive of those Brahmins as the respective deities,
and having offered the entire collection of ritual acts to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
Having first honored the twice-born, and then the poor, the blind, and the wretched, he,
accompanied by his kinsmen, was endowed with blessings and auspicious rites.
Whoever should give a mountain made of sesame seeds according to this rite,
for him there exists no sin whatsoever arising from seven lifetimes.
He who practices this without desire shall go to Śiva by means of a celestial chariot;
he who acts with desire obtains whatever desires he wishes for in his mind.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the sesame mountain as taught in the *Praśnottaratantra*. Now follows the procedure for the gift of the cotton mountain from the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"In this world, a superior cotton mountain consists of twenty *bhāras*."
The middling [type] is said to consist of ten, while the lowest is traditionally held to consist of five.
A man of little wealth should give according to his burden, avoiding any stinginess regarding his riches; O best of kings, everything should be prepared just like a mountain of grain.
When the night has turned to dawn, one should give [the gift] and utter this:
"Since you alone are always the conduct for the worlds here."
Therefore, O Karpāsācala, may you be the destroyer of the flood of my sins.
Thus, whoever should give this lord of mountains made of cotton on the occasion of a festival shall dwell in the world of Rudra for a kalpa, and thereafter become a king here on earth.
From the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
The Blessed One said,
"Henceforth I shall proclaim the supreme Karpāsācala."
It is the supreme among all gifts and the most beloved among all the days of the week.
Having secured the proper place and time, as well as wealth and faith with great effort,
this great gift should be bestowed for the sake of the deliverance of one's lineage.
[377] One should fashion a mountain there out of cotton according to the prescribed rule;
having performed everything according to the rule as previously described.
The wise should construct the best mountain out of twenty bhāras;
one should make the middling with ten, and likewise the lowest with five.
Indeed, it stands in the midst of a collection of all grains, surrounded by medicinal herbs,
endowed with juices and jewels, and likewise encircled by the world-protectors.
Likewise, Brahmā and the others should be fashioned from gold on the peak;
one should arrange the four Kulākulās using a fourth part [of the remaining material].
All the golden-peaked mountains, adorned with every kind of jewel,
their surfaces variegated with various minerals, and covered with all kinds of foods and delicacies.
A person [should offer oblations] into the fire with the *vyāhṛtis*, as well as with those deities [invoked by them],
and likewise with fragrance, clarified butter, and black sesame seeds.
There was a performance of ten thousand burnt offerings with fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and trumpets as well as the recitation of auspicious texts.
There, one should diligently celebrate a festival for one day;
then, on the occasion of the sacred festival (parvan), having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should make offerings.
Homage! Praised by the hosts of all the gods and beings dwelling in heaven, may the deities beginning with Brahmā always be granters of boons to me.
Having uttered this, a man or a woman should give according to the prescribed rule,
after having properly honored the twice-born with garments and ornaments.
Whoever bestows this gift according to this rite shall go to the abode of the Thirty-three, seated upon a celestial chariot.
Surrounded by hosts of Apsarases and attended by Gandharvas,
he shall dwell there in the abode of the gods for the duration of a Manvantara.
Having returned here to the earth due to the exhaustion of his merit, he enjoys the world together with its oceans;
handsome, fortunate, eloquent, illustrious, and possessed of incomparable prowess.
For five births he is born as a boatman; of this there is no doubt.
Listen further, O Indra among kings, to the divine Karpāsa mountain.
And he should perform that with exactly one hundred loads, or again with half;
the remainder he should perform entirely according to the previous rule, in due order.
And the fruit previously described indeed arises, O best of kings.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the mountain of cotton. Now follows the procedure for the gift of the mountain of ghee.
Pulastya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed mountain of ghee—
divine, consisting of fiery nectar, and the destroyer of great sins.
With twenty jars of ghee, the "Mountain of Ghee" (ghṛtācala) is considered the best;
with ten, it is declared to be middling; and with five, it is recorded as the lowest.
One with limited wealth should perform the rite according to the Meru arrangement using two [measures];
likewise, one should not fashion the supporting mountains (viṣkambhaparvatas) in a fourfold division.
One should place bowls of rice grains upon jars;
one should have them all arranged closely together according to the ritual rules and for the sake of beauty.
One should wrap it with white cloths and [adorn it] with sugarcane stalks, fruits, and so forth;
the remaining ritual procedure here is recited as being the same as that for the mountain of grain (dhānyaparvata).
In the same way, one should perform the acceptance [of offerings], as well as the fire-oblation and the worship of the deities.

In this context, a "pitcher of ghee" (*ghṛtakumbha*) is well known as ghee measuring one thousand *palas*. Since the term "pitcher" (*kumbha*) does not have a fixed measure, there would be the undesirable consequence of the meaning of the scripture being unsettled; furthermore, because it is a liquid substance, it requires a container. By the instruction that "one should place vessels of rice grains upon the pitcher," it is established that the pitcher serves as the base for the jar (*kalaśa*). The plural form "vessels of rice grains" (*taṇḍulapātrāṇi*) is used in reference to the five mountain-peaks. Then, when the night has turned to dawn, one should present it to the Guru.
In the same manner, with a peaceful mind, he should give the supporting mountains to the officiating priests.
Since ghee has arisen from the conjunction of the essence of nectar,
may Śaṅkara, the soul of the universe, be pleased here by this flame of ghee.
But you, who are the Brahman consisting of splendor established within the ghee,
in the form of a mountain of ghee— therefore, O upholder of the earth, protect us!
By this rite, one should offer the unsurpassed mountain of ghee;
even one burdened with great sins attains the world of Śaṅkara.
Mounted upon a celestial chariot yoked with swans and cranes, adorned with garlands of tinkling bells, and surrounded by apsarases, siddhas, and vidyādharas,
he shall sport together with his ancestors until the dissolution of the world at the end of the kalpa.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the mountain of ghee as declared in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
Now follows the procedure for the gift of the mountain of jewels.
Pulastya said:
Hereafter I shall describe the unsurpassed Jewel Mountain;
with a thousand pearls, the mountain here becomes excellent.
The middle [mountain range] is five hundred [yojanas], and the lowest is recorded as three hundred;
the peripheral mountains (viṣkambha-parvatas) should be on all sides at one-fourth [of the respective ranges].
To the east with *vajra-gomedaka* stones, and to the south with sapphires (*indranīla*) joined with topazes (*puṣparāga*),
the wise should fashion Mount Gandhamādana.
To the west, one should place the Vipulācala mountain interspersed with lapis lazuli and coral;
to the north, however, one should place it with rubies and gems of Suparṇa.

With an equal number of *vajra-gomedas*, according to the maxim that "equality should be maintained because it has not been otherwise heard"; this should be understood likewise for what follows. *Sauparṇa* means born of Garuḍa. In some places, the reading is *sauvarṇair* (with golden ones).
One should arrange everything here just as in the case of the Mountain of Grain (*dhānyaparvata*).
Likewise, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and [place] the dexterous deities made of gold.
One should worship with flowers and water, and perform the dismissal in the morning;
as before, one should recite these mantras to the preceptor and the officiating priests.
Just as all the hosts of gods abide even within all jewels,
and you are eternally composed of jewels, therefore protect us, O Great Mountain!
Since Hari brings about rain through the gift of jewels,
therefore protect us, O Mountain, by the gift of great jewels.
Whoever should give a mountain made of jewels according to this rite goes to the world of Viṣṇu, honored by the Lord of the Immortals.
O lord of men, he shall dwell here for a hundred and fifty kalpas,
endowed with beauty, health, and virtue, and become the sovereign of the seven continents.
Whatever [sin], such as the killing of a Brahmin, has been committed here or in the hereafter—
all that goes to destruction, just as a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Jewel Mountain as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the unsurpassed Silver Mountain.
By giving this, O best of the twice-born, a man goes to the world of Soma.
The best silver mountain is made of ten thousand palas;
the middling is said to be of five thousand, and the lowest is recorded as being half of that.
If one lacks the capacity, one should always have [the pillars] made beyond twenty according to one's means;
likewise, one should fashion the supporting mountains with a quarter of that measure.
As before, one should fashion Mount Mandara and the other mountains according to the prescribed rule;
there, the wise man should worship the World-Protectors made of gold.
*Kaladhauta* means gold.
Here, the hip should be made of gold, representing Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun;
for others, that which would otherwise be silver should all be made of gold here.
One should perform the remaining rites as before, such as the fire-oblation (homa) and the ritual vigil (jāgaraṇa);
likewise, at dawn, one should give a mountain of silver to the preceptor.
Having honored the supporting mountains with garments and ornaments for the officiating priests,
one who is free from envy and holds *darbha* grass in his hand should give them while reciting this mantra.
Since silver is dear to the ancestors, to Dharma, and to Śaṅkara,
therefore protect us from this ocean of worldly existence filled with sorrow.
Having thus dedicated this excellent royal mountain,
the person who gives it obtains the fruit of ten million cows.
In the world of the gods, that wise man shall dwell, being honored by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and hosts of Apsarases, until the dissolution of all things at the end of the kalpa.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Silver Mountain as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the excellent Gift of the Sugar Mountain.
By the giving of which Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra are always satisfied.
A great mountain (mahācala) should be made with eight loads of sugar for the best [type];
four loads are declared for the middling, and two loads are remembered for the lowest.
A man possessing only small wealth may construct the Viṣkambha mountains with one-fourth of the weight or half-weight that would otherwise be used.
Having prepared everything like a mountain of grain and combined it with ambrosia,
one should likewise place three golden trees upon Mount Meru.
The Mandāra, the Pārijāta, and the third, the Kalpapādapa—
these three trees one should place at the very top of all [the deities].
Two rows of yellow sandalwood trees (haricandana) should be planted on the eastern and western sides on all mountains, especially on the mountain of sugar (śarkarācala).
On Mandara, Kāmadeva shall always face west;
and on the peak of Gandhamādana, Dhanada shall face north.
On Vipulācala, the Swan, the embodiment of the Veda, should face the east;
on Supārśva, Surabhi, made of gold, should face the south.
Having performed all the rites, such as the invocation and the sacrifice, like those for a mountain of grain,
one should then give the middlemost of the excellent mountains to the preceptor.
To the officiating priests, he should recite these four verses concerning the mountains:
"This [mountain] is the essence of the nectar of good fortune, since it is the supreme sugar."
Therefore, O Lord of Mountains, may you always be a source of joy to me;
for those drops that fell to the earth while the gods were drinking the nectar of immortality— [may they become your peaks].
O Śarkarācala, drink our Soma which is equal to that of the gods;
may the essence (*madhu*) of that from which sugar (*śarkarā*) originated be mine.
O Great Mountain, you are composed of that; protect [the donor] from the ocean of saṃsāra!
That man who should give a mountain of sugar according to this rite—
Completely liberated from all sins, he ascends a vehicle resplendent like the moon and sun and proceeds to the abode of Śiva along with his attendants.
Impelled by Viṣṇu, the virtuous man should immediately embark upon the vehicle;
thereafter, at the end of a hundred kalpas, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
Endowed with long life and good health for as long as thirty thousand births,
one should provide food according to one's ability on every mountain, free from all envy.
Everywhere, he should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, with his permission.

"One should provide food" means that immediately after giving [the gift], one should provide food to the Brahmins according to one's ability. "One should also eat oneself [food] free from pungent salt" [is the meaning].
One should cause all the mountain-provisions to reach the abode of the Brahmins;
even if one is poor, one should behold these with devotion.
He who touches these [relics] being offered here by humans,
or hears of them with devotion, or bestows his mind upon them, becomes free from stain and goes to heaven.
A person attains the pacification of bad dreams by reciting these kings of mountains, which shatter the fear of existence;
what need is there to mention the one who would properly perform this here in the presence of the Sage with tawny hair?
The essence of all beings is the gift of the entire king of mountains.

Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the Sugar-Mountain as declared in the *Padma Purāṇa*. Now, the twelve gifts of Meru according to the Śaiva tradition are described. Regarding this, from the *Kālottara* Śaiva scripture:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the gift of Meru in its proper sequence."
Beginning from the month of Kārttika, one should perform the Meru-vrata.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, Ratnameru should be offered before Śiva;
now hear in due order the measurements for all these Merus.
Those known as diamond, ruby, great sapphire, blue sapphire, and rock crystal,
as well as emerald, pearl, and flowers, should be taken according to one's own means.
O son, one should collect [the materials] in the measure of one *prastha*, or even half or a quarter of a *prastha*;
or they may be given according to one's ability, without stinginess regarding wealth.
I shall describe the division of Meru and how one should worship it before Śiva:
one should place Meru upon the pericarp, adorned by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
Then everyone should worship the mountain named Mālyavat;
to its east is the one called Bhadra, and beyond that are the Aśva trees.
To the east of Meru, in the eastern quarter, the first three [peaks] extending northward have been described; specifically, they extend further toward the southern limit.

He attains the state of divine sovereignty born of a thousand sacrifices;

In this context, a *kumbha* is measured at twenty *droṇas*. This is demonstrated in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) by such statements as, "A *khārī* consists of sixteen *droṇas*, and twenty [such] *khārīs* are called a *kumbha*," and so forth. If one were to take the definition that a *kumbha* equals two *droṇas*, then defining twenty *droṇas* and so on as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) to the primary rule (*prathamakalpa*) would not be consistent. However, in the other case, it would be logical for the primary rule to consist of one and a half *kumbhas*, while twenty *droṇas* and so on would constitute the secondary alternative.

Salutation to Bhavānī for the feet; then to Kāminī for the knees;
likewise to Vāmadevī for the thighs; and to Jagatpriyā for the navel.

In this context, although by the word *dhenu* (cow) only a cow in its literal form (*svarūpa*) is denoted, nevertheless, due to the commonality of the term *dhenu*, it is appropriate to include even the "molasses-cow" (*guḍadhenu*) and others within this section. In this regard, the formulation of the speech of the gift is as follows:

This procedure for all cows is recited here;

[401] Thus, because of the general extension (*atideśa*) [of the rule]. The statement, "There should be jars (*kumbha*) for liquid cows, but heaps (*rāśi*) for others," is an explanation of the manner of placing a quantity of liquid substance measured by four *bhāras* or more into a jar as its receptacle. As for the mention in the *Padma Purāṇa* and other texts of a cow made of ghee and so forth using a single jar, or a cow made of sesame seeds using a *droṇa* measure, the *Kalpataru* explains that this refers to a different variety of cow from the one under discussion. However, the *Dānaviveka* has determined that a jar is measured at one thousand *palas*. Some, however, say that a jar consists of five hundred *palas* plus twelve. This is shown in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) beginning with, "Two *palas* make a handful (*prasṛti*)," and so forth.

after stating "The first [gift] should be a jaggery-cow," and so forth, [it continues]:

even in this world, one attains good fortune, long life, and health.
One who remembers Hari at the time of death attains the realm of Viṣṇu;
for ten thousand and eighteen billion years, the knower of dharma experiences neither sorrow nor suffering, nor is he born into a state of misfortune.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the molasses-cow and others. Now follows the gift of the sesame-cow, according to the Viṣṇudharma. Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, I shall now describe the sesame-cow (tiladhenu), which brings great satisfaction to Keśava; hear the supreme procedure for one who has given it.

Having given this, even one who has killed a Brahmin, a cow, or his father; one who has violated the teacher’s bed; one who has set fire to a house; one who has administered poison; or even one endowed with every possible sin [is purified].
One who is joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) and joined with minor sins (upapātaka) is indeed liberated from all evils and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
On the surface of the earth, which has been smeared and covered with cloth, antelope skin, and kuśa grass,
one should fashion a cow made of sesame seeds and adorned with all kinds of gems.
One should fashion a cow from a droṇa [of grain] and a calf from an āḍhaka;
likewise, it should have horns of gold, hooves of silver, and be provided with fragrant scents for its nostrils.
And one should fashion [the image] with a tongue of sugar, a mouth of molasses,
a woolen blanket for a garment, feet of sugarcane, a copper back, and eyes of pure pearls.
One should make [the image] auspicious, with ears adorned by praised leaves, possessing fruit-like teeth,
wearing a garland of flowers around its tail, and endowed with breasts made of fresh butter.
It has veins of white thread and hair like white mustard seeds;
it is adorned with charming fruits fit for alms, as well as jewels and pearls.
Having fashioned [the image] endowed with such a form— covered with a pair of white garments and adorned with ornaments of bells— one should be filled with faith.
Having given a brass milking vessel with the words, "May Keśava be pleased," [one should know that] she who is the Lakṣmī of all the gods and she who resides among the gods— [is that very one].
May that Goddess, who dwells within the body as Rudrāṇī, the eternal beloved of Śaṅkara, dispel my sin in the form of a cow.
May that Goddess, in the form of a cow, dispel my sin—
she who is Lakṣmī upon the chest of Viṣṇu, and Svāhā of the Fire-god.
That power of the Moon, the Sun, and Indra which takes the form of a cow is for the sake of prosperity;
it is the Lakṣmī of the Four-faced One and the Lakṣmī of the Giver of Wealth.
May that Lakṣmī who belongs to the world-protectors be this cow, granting boons to me;
you are the Svadhā of the foremost ancestors and likewise the Svāhā of those who enjoy the sacrifice.
The cow is the remover of all sins; therefore, grant me peace.

In the Vahnipurāṇa, however, this mantra is as follows: "Sesame seeds were created here by Brahmā for the sacrifice of cows (gosava) and have the ancestors as their deity; may the cow consisting of them, when given, please Keśava."
Then, having performed a circumambulation, having worshipped, and having prostrated,
one should dismiss [the deity] by saying, "This, together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), has been given by me to you."
Having given a sesame-cow according to this rite, the lord of men,
liberated from all sins, attains the supreme Brahman.
He who receives what is being given according to the rule shall rejoice;
and those who behold it being given with uplifted minds [shall likewise rejoice].
They too, being entirely freed from all evil, go to the supreme goal—
[to one who is] tranquil, well-disciplined, and a bearer of Vedic vows.
Having given a sesame-cow, one does not grieve over what has been done or left undone;
he who subsists on sesame for three nights becomes a donor of a sesame-cow.
Then, with his inner self absorbed in that, he ate them for one day;
O King, because of that gift, his sins were purified and he became a doer of merit.
Eating sesame seeds is said to be even more meritorious than the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa,
the Hotṛ said:
"O King, [I shall describe] the sesame-cow, the water-cow, and the juice-cow."
Give it quickly, so that you may be freed from hunger and thirst in heaven.
"He shall enjoy himself as long as the sun shines and the moon burns in the sky.
Having been addressed thus, the king then asked this question regarding the ritual procedure.
Listen, O lord of men, to how it was with the sesame-cow:
one *prastha* is proclaimed to be equal to four *setikās*.
These sixteen [bricks] shall constitute the cow, and four shall constitute the calf;
its legs are made of sugarcane stalks, and its auspicious teeth are made of flowers.
Its nose should consist of incense, its tongue likewise of molasses;
at the tail, there should be an arrangement of garlands, adorned with ornaments of bells.
Having fashioned her in this manner, one should provide a cow with golden horns,
a bronze milking vessel, and silver hooves, according to the previously prescribed ritual for a cow.
Then, having given a sesame-cow on the twelfth lunar day, being self-controlled and pure,
one shall deliver oneself from the difficult passage of hell and become a partaker of all desires.
A *setikā* is a *kuḍava*, and that is measured at twelve *prasṛtis*. In the *Mahābhārata*:
[She gave] a cow with excellent gifts, beautiful horns of gold, a bronze milking vessel, and a costly upper garment.
For one who gives a cow made of sesame seeds to a twice-born man,
the worlds of the Vasus become easily attainable.
Likewise,
having given a cow of equal measure to the measure of [the previous] cow, and also having given sesame seeds;
Likewise:
"And a mortal who [builds] a water-tank in the world of Yama does not undergo any torment."
Likewise: "He who, having consecrated a cow made of sesame seeds with the Gomatī-vidyā,
gives it away as consisting of essence and jewels, shall not grieve over what has been done or left undone."

The Gomatī-vidyā is also found in that very same place. It is as follows: "May cows with golden horns, yielding milk, fragrant and of the lineage of Surabhi, attend upon me, just as rivers flow toward the ocean."
I see cows constantly; may cows always see me.
Cows are ours, and we belong to them; where there are cows, there we are.
"Thus, whether by night or by day, in even or uneven circumstances,
and even in great terrors, a man who recites [this] is liberated from fear. Thus it is said in the Āditya Purāṇa.
Indeed, even a poor man who, being destitute, should give a sesame-cow—
having first smeared the ground with cow-dung, he should there draw the figure of a cow.
Having scattered sesame seeds over all its limbs and having fashioned it as a sesame-cow,
one should place gold indeed upon its hooves and horns.
One should present a sacrificial fee along with a garment to a Brahmin;
by giving a sesame-cow, one goes to the heavenly world.
One shall be liberated from all evils committed through action or mind;
indeed, for as many [tila seeds] as there are, so too for hundreds of crores.

He rejoices there in the world of the Vasus for many years; of this there is no doubt. Then, after the lapse of time, he may occasionally attain a human birth in a great family, indeed one abundant in wealth and grain.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the sesame-cow.
Pulastya said:
O lord of men, listen now to the ritual injunction for the sesame-cow.
A cow made of sixteen āḍhakas should have four calves made of four [āḍhakas] each.
Her feet were made of sugarcane stalks, her auspicious teeth were made of flowers,
her nose was made of fragrance, and likewise her tongue was made of molasses.
A garland should be fashioned for the tail, adorned with bells and ornaments;
having fashioned such [features], one should then provide the golden-horned cow.
Having prepared such a cow with silver hooves and a bronze milking vessel according to the ritual procedure for the primordial cow (pūrvadhenu), one should cause it to be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having placed the cow upon a black antelope skin, adorned it with beautiful garments, bound it with a thread, and provided it with the five precious gems;
One should cause [the food] to be given, endowed with all medicinal herbs and purified by mantras, [with the prayer]:
"May food be produced for me instantly, as well as drink and all flavors."
"O Goddess, fulfill our desires; I shall accept with devotion that sesame-cow offered to a twice-born man, especially for the sake of my family. [407]
"O Sesame-cow, support me with all my desires; salutations be unto you.
Thus, O best of kings, the sesame-cow is given according to the prescribed ritual.
It brings about the fulfillment of all desires; there is no doubt in this matter.
Likewise, the water-cow (jaladhenu) and the jar-cow (kumbhadhenu) are likewise prescribed here.
When given according to the prescribed rite, O lord of men, a cow indeed bestows all desires immediately; moreover, when a cow is given in truth on the full moon day, she grants them all.
A cow made of ghee, when given according to the prescribed rite by the wise, delivers one's ancestors from difficult states and becomes a granter of all desires, even from hell.
O King, by likewise giving a cow of nectar (rasadhenu) in the month of Kārttika, one attains all desires and becomes a bestower of splendor.
One obtains all desires and shall eternally partake in a happy rebirth.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the five cows as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Agastya said:
I shall now describe the sesame cow by which Durgā is propitiated.
Even one who has committed evil deeds becomes free from debt by giving her away.
Hear from me, O best of kings, that method by which the Goddess becomes directly manifest and brings about the happiness of sovereignty and sons; it occurs before long.
Having obtained permission from the God of gods, being well-bathed and having conquered his senses,

he should worship with flowers, perfumes, and various lamps and incenses; and having offered oblations into the fire for the Goddess, he should likewise fashion an image made of a *droṇa* measure [of grain].
Having made oblations in the fire and thus gratified the Goddess according to the previously described method of homa—
[O Vatsa, she shall be adorned with all jewels,
possessing golden horns, silver hooves, and a beautiful, fragrant-smelling nose. [408]
The face should be made of molasses, and likewise the tongue of food;
the blanket should be of fine thread, and the feet likewise of sugarcane.
Its back should be copper-colored, and its eyes should be adorned with gems and pearls;
its ears should be made of beautiful leaves, and likewise its teeth should be made of fruit.
One should fashion her breasts from fresh butter; make her out of flower garlands, and one should worship her with gems, pearls, and fruits for her tail.
Having fashioned [the image] endowed with such a form— one whose pair of beautiful eyebrows is concealed [by her hair] and who is adorned with lovely garments— one should act with full faith.
One should give a cow with a bronze milking vessel, saying, "May the Goddess be pleased with me";
having consecrated it with mantras, one should present it to a devotee of her.
As many particles of dust as there are on sesame husks, cotton seeds, and grains, roots, and fruits, for so long shall that man dwell in heaven.
Having freed his ancestors from sin, even those who have gone to the lower realms,
he shall, without hesitation, cause them to attain the auspicious worlds of the Goddess.
But in that state, O dear one, he delights as long as the moon and stars exist;
then, having returned here from that time, he is born as a lord of the earth.
Endowed with splendor right here, possessing many sons and filled with happiness,
he shall always delight in his queen and worship Acala according to the prescribed rite.
That supreme state which one attains through hundreds of yogic practices, one attains by reaching this.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the sesame-cow as declared in the Devīpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the sesame-cow in due order.
One should construct the previously described maṇḍala and perform the worship of Śiva in the western direction.
In front of him, having drawn a beautiful lotus in the middle of the ground,
the wise man should place that lotus, covered with cloths, in its center.

The sequence of the construction is as follows: one should worship Śiva facing east within the previously mentioned *maṇḍala*—specifically the *maṇḍala* prescribed for the *tulāpuruṣa* gift—located to the west of that [central] *maṇḍala*. In front of Śiva, in the central part of the *maṇḍala*, one should draw a lotus with rice-powder (*śālicūrṇa*) and other materials, cover it with cloths, and place a sesame-flower there.
Regarding the sesame-flower: "Having fashioned a golden flower, one should deposit it;
it should be made with thirty *niṣkas*, or else with half of that, or again half of that."
It should be made with five *niṣkas*, or again with half of that, or even half of that.
Having fashioned a lotus-flower consisting of a heap of sesame seeds measured by a *droṇa* or more, one should place a golden lotus upon it covered with cloth and other materials.
In front of that, the wise man should have a beautiful lotus made of sesame seeds constructed.
The food should be prepared with a droṇa measure; alternatively, one may have it prepared with a bhāra.
"Having covered it with cloths, one should place a golden lotus in its center," according to the Kāmika-tantra.
Having worshipped that [lotus] in due order with perfumes, flowers, and so forth according to the prescribed rite,
one should station eleven Brahmins in the northern direction of the lotus.
Having worshipped them in due order according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
and having covered the excellent horn, he should cause it to be given to the Brahmins in succession.
A turban should be offered and he should be adorned with earrings;
having given a golden ring to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rite.
Having spread eleven garments before them and having placed a khārī of sesame seeds separately upon each of those garments;
Having broken a bronze vessel weighing one hundred palas into eleven parts,
stalks of sugarcane should be given there, each separately.
One should have the two horns made of gold using two *niṣkas*,
and one should make the hooves of silver using two *niṣkas*.
Having thus given each separately, one should cast them into the sesame seeds.

A *khārī* consists of sixteen *droṇas*; the *kāṃsyapātra* is a milking vessel; "one-eleventh part of a hundred" means nine *palas* for each individual item. One should cast that into the sesame seeds.

In this manner, having placed one *khārī* of sesame seeds for each of the items beginning with the golden horns, one should fashion cows made of sesame seeds equipped with golden horns and so forth, and cause them to be given to the Brahmins while reciting the eleven Rudra mantras. Likewise, one should fashion cows in the eastern quarter of the lotus and cause them to be given to the Brahmins while reciting the eleven Rudra mantras.
Similarly, in the eastern quarter of the lotus, one should worship twelve suns.
And by this very path, one endowed with faith [should worship] them as well.
One should cause the deity itself to be offered [the oblation] with the *dvādaśāditya* mantra; furthermore,
one should again cause the sixteen Brahmins stationed in the eastern and southern directions to be offered [the oblation] as before, using the *mūrti* and *vidyeśa* mantras.

Here, in the eastern direction of the lotus, eleven Brahmins in the form of Rudras are to be worshipped; to them, one should give the previously mentioned offerings, such as a khārī of sesame seeds, divided elevenfold. The mantra, however, is "ye devāso divyekādaśasya" and so forth. Likewise, in the eastern direction of the lotus, one should honor twelve Brahmins in the form of the Ādityas. To them also, having divided a bronze vessel weighing one hundred palas into twelve parts, one should give a khārī of sesame seeds to each, as before, provided with golden horns and other ornaments.
