The mantra, characterized by the Ādityas, is "yajño devānām" and so forth. Similarly, in the southern part of the lotus, one should worship sixteen Brahmins in the form of the Mūrtis and Vighneśas.
The eight forms beginning with Bhava are as follows:
Bhava, Śarva, Rudra, Paśupati, and the one named Ugra; Mahādeva, Bhīma, and Īśāna is recorded as the eighth.

The names of the Lords of Obstacles (Vighneśas) will be mentioned in the section on the gift of Gaṇeśa. To each of them, one should likewise give a bronze vessel weighing one hundred palas, divided into sixteen parts, along with a khārī measure of sesame seeds provided with golden horns and other ornaments as before. The mantra, beginning with "To the god Bhava... and so forth, should be performed using their respective names preceded by the syllable *Oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*. All this should be performed by the patron (*yajamāna*) in due order.
Alternatively, there may be a gift solely to Rudra, or again, gifts to the Ādityas.
And one should give to the forms and other [deities] according to the extent of one's wealth;
having laid out a lotus with colored powder, the king should have the remainder executed as well.
And a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be given, along with an ornament made of five *niṣkas* of gold.

This entire procedure—from the lotus at the door up to the gift to Vighneśa—should be performed either as a gift dedicated to any one of the Rudras and others, or the central lotus alone may be offered. In all cases, the central lotus is to be given to the Guru, according to the statement in the *Vātula*: "Having performed [the rite] according to the injunction, one should give the golden lotus to the Guru. In all these alternatives, the ornament should be made of five *niṣkas* of gold; the worship of Śiva, the bathing, the fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth are to be done as before. The sacrificial fee is for the preceptor, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and others. Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
Having constructed a pavilion as before, one should indeed fashion it with a mandala;
likewise, one should perform the worship, the fire-oblation (homa), the ritual bathing, and so forth, in exactly the same manner.

"One should fashion the five-limbed ornament here with five *niṣkas*; one should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as before; whatever has not been mentioned shall be as previously stated. Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the sesame-cow (*tiladhenu*) as declared in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*.
Seven cows made of the seven kinds of grain are prescribed;
one should have these fashioned in exactly the same manner as the cow made of sesame seeds.
And that which consists of rice, another of wheat with sesame,
and likewise one made of mung beans and lentils, with priyaṅgu as the seventh;
The household utensils for all these [cows] are prescribed to be like those of the sesame-cow;
the limbs of these very cows are likewise like those of the sesame-cow.
The man who gives seven [offerings] made of rice in this world goes to the supreme abode, becoming like the wind and possessing a form of ether.
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the guru’s bed—
purified by the gift of a cow, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the seven-grain cow as proclaimed by Viśvāmitra. Now follows the procedure for the gift of the ghee-cow. Vasiṣṭha said:
In the absence of sesame seeds, one who is firm in his vows should likewise give a ghee-cow.
O King, listen now with a one-pointed mind to the procedure by which that [is accomplished].
Having worshipped Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as before with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings, a man should perform the consecration with ghee and milk.
Having fasted for a day and night and having praised the one named Ghṛtārcis, the mantra is:
"Obeisance to the god Ghṛtārcis, the Lord of the World.
[413] A jar of cow's clarified butter, adorned with flower garlands and other ornaments, [should be offered].
It was joined with a bronze lid and covered with a pair of white cloths.
It is accompanied by the Hiraṇyagarbha [image], along with gems, corals, and pearls.

Here, the water-jar (kumbha) measures one thousand *palas*; according to some, it is five hundred and twelve *palas*. This has been described in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). It is "accompanied by a bronze lid," meaning covered with a bronze vessel. "Accompanied by the Hiraṇyagarbha" means together with the gold [image] situated within; the remainder of the description is that it is "accompanied by gems, corals, and pearls. Furthermore, its legs are made of sugarcane and its hooves are likewise made of silver.
One should make the two eyes out of gold and the two horns out of aguru wood.
In this case, since the number of gold and other materials has not been specified, they should be provided according to one's capacity.

One should make the side-pieces out of seven kinds of grain and the blanket out of fine wool; the nose-piece should be made of *turuṣka* and camphor, while those [other parts] should be made of fruit.

Likewise, one should smear the tongue with sugar, the mouth with jaggery and milk, the tail with fine woolen cloth (*pattorṇa*) or washed silk (*dhautakauśeya*), the [body] with *turuṣka* and *sihlaka*,
and the hair with white mustard seeds tied with linen thread (*kṣaumasūtra*).
One endowed with faith should have the back made of copper vessels.
O lord of men, having thus conceived the form of the ghee-cow,
the wise man should likewise, through mental visualization, fashion the calf made of ghee.
The meaning is that it should be like a cow, provided with hooves, horns, and so forth. And that [image] should be made with one-fourth the size of a cow.
Having mentally envisioned that illustrious Brahmin as having the radiance of ghee, one should then, being self-restrained, present it to him.
O best of the twice-born, accept this for my benefit;
may the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Person whose flame is ghee, be pleased with me.
Having recited this, O lord of men, one should give a cow to a Brahmin.
This is the mantra from the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Cows produce ghee; ghee is established upon the earth."
Ghee, Agni, and the gods—may ghee be granted to me.
Viśvāmitra says:
"Ghee is Agni; ghee is Soma; all the deities consist of that [ghee].
By the gift of a cow of ghee, all the deities are satisfied. Thus it is said.
Having prepared a vessel of ghee and jewels with gold according to the proper ritual,
the lord of men, remaining for one night and subsisting solely on ghee, should offer it.
One is liberated from all sins; now hear likewise the fruit of giving:
there, rivers flow with ghee and milk, and their mud consists of milk-rice (pāyasa).
He is reborn in all those most meritorious worlds;
after his father’s passing, he leads seven generations both above and below him.
O King, he whose impurities have been destroyed leads them to those worlds;
O best of kings, this is the prosperity described for those who possess desires.
Men who give a cow of ghee without desire go to the world of Viṣṇu;
ghee is Agni, ghee is Soma, and all the deities have ghee as their essence.

By one who bestows clarified butter (ghṛta), all the deities become as if given. Gold is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) here, because it is prescribed according to one's capacity for those rites where no specific fee is mentioned. Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Ghee-Cow (ghṛtadhenu) as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Agastya said:
In the absence of sesame seeds, a wise man should give a cow of ghee;
having bathed Bhavānī with clarified butter and milk according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship with flower garlands and most enchanting food offerings;
one should procure all the necessary materials and prepare them there for her.
One should place that [consecrated water] into a jar of cow's ghee adorned with flower garlands,
and cover it with a bronze vessel and cloths.
One should fashion the feet out of sugarcane, adorned with gold, gems, corals, and pearls; one should fashion the hooves out of silver.
Likewise, golden eyes were placed upon two auspicious horns made of black agallochum;
on their sides were seven grains and a woolen blanket.
One should provide the nose with aloe-wood and camphor, the auspicious breasts with fruits,
the mouth with molasses and milk, and one should fashion the tongue from sugar.
The sugar shall be white;
the tail should be made of linen, and the hair from white mustard seeds;
with a copper-colored back and variegated markings—one of such a form, beautiful and pleasing.
One should fashion [the image] according to the rules, provided with ghee and marked with the proper characteristics;
having made it with these, and having likewise bowed and worshipped it according to the prescribed method.
This Maṅgalā should be given to one who is devoted to her and has mastered the scriptures;
please accept this for my benefit through my grace.
"May the goddess Nandinī be pleased, as well as Maṅgalā, Carcikā, and Umā. Having spoken thus, one should worship the cow, having made her pleasing to the mind.
By this rite, an excellent cow made of clarified butter should be given;
and a cow made of gold and jewels should also be bestowed according to this same procedure.
One is liberated from all sins and shall obtain all desires;
there, rivers flow with milk and there are lakes flowing with clarified butter.
In that world where the mud consists of milk-rice, he is glorified;
endowed with supreme joy, he attains lordship over them.
Having delivered ten generations of ancestors and himself as the twenty-first,
that man attains the status of a lord of the earth once again in this world.
This prosperity has been described for those with desires who give a cow;
however, one who gives a cow of ghee without desire attains the world of the Goddess.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a cow of ghee as stated in the Devīpurāṇa.
In the absence of a [real] cow, one should likewise diligently give a cow of ghee;
listen now with a focused mind to the ritual procedure by which it should be prepared.
Having worshipped Āditya, the Lord of the World, as before with flowers, perfumes, incense, and other offerings, a person should perform consecrations with ghee and milk.
Having fasted for a day and night and having bathed with the luster of clarified butter,
he should offer a jar of cow's ghee adorned with garlands of flowers.
It is joined with a bronze pillow and a pair of white cloths,
together with the Hiraṇyagarbha [image], and adorned with gems, coral, and pearls.
The legs should be made of sugarcane, and likewise the hooves of silver;
one should make the eyes of gold and the horns from aguru wood.
One should make the two sides out of the seven kinds of grain and the woolen blanket out of fine cotton cloth; the nose from *turuṣka* and camphor, and the breasts from fruit.
One should smear the tongue with sugar, the mouth with jaggery and milk,
the tail with linen thread, and the body hairs with white mustard seeds.
Endowed with faith, one should fashion a back made of copper.
Having thus conceived the form of such a beautiful ghee-cow, O lord of men, one should likewise,
through that same mental conception, fashion the calf for the cow.
And having mentally envisioned that illustrious Brahmin as Ghṛtārcis,
one should then, being self-restrained, offer [the oblation] to him.
"O best of the twice-born, accept this for my benefit;
may the Lord of Gods, whose flame is ghee and who is the supreme rain-cloud, be pleased with me."
Having recited this, O best of men, one should give a cow to a Brahmin;
having given it and stayed for one night, the lord of men should subsist on ghee.
He is liberated from all sins; hear now the fruit of his gift:
there, rivers flow with ghee and milk, and the mud consists of milk-rice porridge.
In those eternally meritorious worlds, he rejoices;
after his father’s passing, he shall lead seven generations of his kin, both those above him and those below.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a cow of ghee as taught by the illustrious Ādityapūrṇa.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "O King, according to the procedure for the ghee-cow (ghṛtadhenu), an auspicious cow made of fresh butter should be given, free from any deficiency or excess."
This very mantra has been specified, which is traditionally remembered in connection with the ghee-cow;
listen, O mighty-armed Pārtha, to the supreme fruit of this gift.
Where rivers flow with ghee and milk and have porridge for their mud,
there the giver of a cow of ghee goes, honored by all his desires.
After his father's death, he leads seven generations of his ancestors, as well as those who come after him;
having cleansed them of all impurity, he leads them to the most excellent worlds in this universe.
[418] O best of kings, this prosperity has been described for those with desires;
those who give it away without desire attain the stainless state.
Kātyāyana said: He who, when cows are unavailable, gives a cow made of ghee according to the prescribed rite,
is delivered from difficulties by that cow and rejoices in the celestial river.
But he who, being composed, gives a sesame-cow when ghee is unavailable,
shall be served by rivers flowing with all objects of desire while he dwells in heaven.
But if sesame seeds are unavailable, he who, with a concentrated mind, gives a water-cow (jaladhenu) attains all his desires; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
A man should give a cow made of ghee, a cow made of sesame seeds, and likewise a cow made of water, in due order; indeed, he who does so shall never fall from heaven.
Having duly given a cow made of clarified butter to a Vaiṣṇava who has conquered his senses and is tranquil, one attains the same world as Viṣṇu.
The righteous-souled one, by means of a cow of clarified butter, rescues his father, and likewise his grandfather, as well as seven generations on each side— seven before and seven after.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a cow made of ghee. Now follows the gift of a cow made of water. Vasiṣṭha said:
I shall now describe the water-cow, by the giving of which [Brahmā] is pleased.
The god of gods, Hṛṣīkeśa, is all-pervading and the creator of all beings.
O tiger among men, [he should offer] a water-pot filled with gold and silver,
containing gems within, and accompanied by all varieties of cultivated grain.
Covered with a pair of white garments, adorned with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass,
and joined with *kuṣṭha*, *māṃsī*, *uśīra*, *vālaka*, and *āmalaka*.
Accompanied by priyaṅgu leaves, wearing a white garment and a sacred thread,
holding an umbrella and wearing sandals, he is seated upon a bed of darbha grass.
O King, it is enclosed on four sides by four vessels of sesame seeds,
and is established with a vessel of curd at its mouth, containing ghee and honey.
Having fasted and honored Vāsudeva, the Lord of Waters,
with flowers, incense, and offerings according to his means, he should do so with due respect.
Having mentally conceived the water-cow and having worshipped that pitcher,
the wise man should likewise worship the calf and the pitcher consisting of water.
Having thus worshipped Govinda along with a water-cow and its calf,
one should be clad in white garments, tranquil, free from passion, and devoid of envy.
O Indra among kings, one should give [this] to a twice-born for the sake of pleasing the One who reclines upon the waters:
"May Keśava, the source of the universe, who reclines upon the waters, be pleased with me."
Having recited this, O Lord of the Earth, let it be bestowed upon the Brahmin;
thereafter, he shall subsist on uncooked food for a day and a night.

"Water-pot," and so forth; here, *kumbha* means a jar (*kalaśa*). Since there is no fixed measure for gold and silver, they should be prepared according to one's capacity. The five gems and the grains have been explained in the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). Now, although the instruction is given in general terms, nevertheless, according to the maxim "as it is in the case of that, so it is in the case of others because of their similarity," one should understand that the performance of non-contradictory attributes follows the model of the other *dhenu* (cow). Consequently, one should attend to the following: the horns are made of gold, the hooves of silver, the vessels for sesame seeds are made of copper, and the vessel for curds is made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*). Likewise, one should place the grains on both sides, the *kuṣṭha* and other herbs at the region of the nose, a leaf of *priyaṅgu* on the ear, and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) in the place of the head. The calf (*vatso*) also should be made with a fourth part [of the materials], following the same procedure as the *dhenu*.

In some versions, however, based on the reading, "The wise man should likewise worship that calf made of ghee," an option between ghee and water is understood; the formula for the gift is as before, and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) here is gold according to one's capacity.
Having given the water-cow by this rite, O lord of men, one obtains all desires, both those that are divine and those that are human.
When the water-cow has been given, there is no doubt that men obtain bodily health, the alleviation of afflictions, and the fulfillment of all desires.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the water-cow as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Bhānu said:
I shall now describe the water-cow, by the giving of which [Viṣṇu] is pleased.
The God of gods, the Lord of rays, all-pervading, and the creator of all beings.

"Having brought a water-pot," and so forth, has a meaning identical to that in the *Viṣṇudharma*. However, the specific detail is as follows: "Then, having worshipped the Sun, one should give a water-cow (*jaladhenu*) together with its calf to a Brahmin before the deity for the sake of pleasing Mihira (the Sun)."
May Mihira, the source of the universe, be forever pleased with the Sun.
Having recited this, O great sage, one should bestow that cow upon a brahmin; he who, by this rite, gives a water-cow—
A man obtains the merit of a gift made in the forenoon through his meditations;
being liberated from all sins, he [delivers] his father, his grandfather,
his great-grandfather, and the four preceding generations of ancestors.
O Lord of Sages, that man who gives a water-cow here saves himself, his son, his grandson, and four others below them.
And for one who receives it according to the rule, such [sons] as these shall likewise be born in his family;
and the same applies to one who gives it away or approves of its giving.
And those men who behold a water-cow being given away—
they too, liberated from all poverty, go to the supreme goal.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the water-cow as declared in the Āditya Purāṇa.
Agastya said:
"O child, listen to how the gift of the water-cow is made, so that the Goddess may be pleased."
A water-pot completely filled with water, provided with a pair of garments and jewels,
containing all kinds of seeds, and adorned with sprouts of dūrvā grass.
All seeds are all types of grain. [The vessel] should be joined with dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, curd, a conch shell, kuṣṭha, āmalaka, and sandalwood;
it should be provided with garlands, an umbrella, and vessels of sesame seeds.
One should prepare curd, milk, ghee, and leaves according to the prescribed rite;
likewise, the wise man should prepare for her a calf made of water.
Having worshipped the Goddess according to the rules, whether fasting or eating only at night,
he who gives [this] to a devotee of the Goddess shall obtain all his desires.
Victory to you, O Goddess Jayārisūdanī, the destroyer of the fear of the gods;
O Mother of the Vedas, O Excellent Durgā, O All-pervading One, O Auspicious One, salutations to you!
With this mantra, O child, one should consecrate [the image] by the name Nandā:
"May the auspicious Goddess, who bestows the fruits as described, be eternally pleased with me."
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the water-cow as declared in the Devīpurāṇa. In the Skandapurāṇa:
"Listen to the fruit of the gift of that person who gives a water-cow, or who constructs a water-station, a sacrificial session, a pond, or even a well of excellent capacity."
Having prepared water-jars and excellent vessels, adorned with perfumes and garlands.

A *prapā* is a water-shed; a *satra-śālā* is an assembly hall serving as a refuge for people. Having honored the best of the twice-born with flowers of various forms and having made them well-satisfied with various kinds of food and edibles, one should cause vessels of sesame seeds to be given to them.
One should give them a bountiful sacrificial fee and then recommend you to them.
"To these gods:
may the auspicious and gentle waters satisfy my ancestors;
may they be granters of desires for the sake of granting desires"—thus one should indeed say.
Having thus given that cow and having performed [the rites] once again,
he should then invoke the goddess Prapā, who bestows the world of Brahmā.
And having given sesame vessels, as well as a pair of auspicious garments,
the presence of gold, and various kinds of fruits;
Then, having bathed and become pure, one should give to the Brāhmaṇas according to the prescribed rule;
by giving in this manner, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Viśvāmitra: There is no doubt that when a water-cow is gifted, men enjoy bodily health and the perpetual alleviation of all afflictions.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a water-cow.
Now follows the gift of a milk-cow.
Vinītāśva said:
I shall describe the milk-cow; listen to it, O lord of men!
On the surface of the earth smeared with cow dung, O best of men.
Having strewn kuśa grass all around to the measure of a cow-hide,
O Great King, the wise man should place a black antelope skin upon it.
There, having first made a circular mark with cow dung,
one should then place a jar of milk, and a calf [made of clay] representing one-fourth of its size.
One should place upon a vessel of sesame seeds cows with golden faces and horns, smeared with sandalwood and aloe-wood paste, and adorned with ears made of excellent leaves.
Her face was made of molasses, her tongue likewise of sugar,
her excellent teeth were of fruit, and her eyes were made of pearls.
One whose feet are like sugarcane, whose hair is like *darbha* grass, who is covered with a white woolen blanket,
whose back is copper-colored, who has a bronze milking vessel, and likewise one adorned with silk thread;
And its tail, O tiger among kings, was made of butter;
it stood upon the earth with horns of gold, hooves of silver, and adorned with the five precious gems.
One should place four bowls of sesame seeds in the four directions as well;
one should scatter [offerings] consisting of seven grains in all directions.
One should thus prepare a milch cow endowed with these characteristics,
clothe her in a pair of garments, and worship her with perfumes and flowers.
Having offered incense, lamps, and other such items, one should present them to the Brāhmaṇa;
having clothed him and adorned him with rings and earrings.
Having given sandals, shoes, and an umbrella, one should present the gift;
with this very mantra, one should likewise offer a milch-cow made of milk.
"O bull among men, with the mantra beginning 'The prosperity that belongs to all beings' and with the mantra 'May you swell,' one should propitiate the milk-cow."
"O Goddess, I accept you with devotion"—thus the recipient should recite the mantra.
Having thus given the cow, one should then subsist on milk for one day.
O best of kings, those Brāhmaṇas who subsist on milk for three nights and behold [the gift] being given attain the supreme goal.
One should [offer] this with a thousand gold pieces, or a hundred, or according to one's own capacity;
or fifty, or twenty-five, or likewise fifteen, as one desires.
O great king, listen also to the fruit of that [act]: having given a cow, one is honored in the world of Rudra for a thousand divine years.
Together with his father and grandfather, he shall go to the abode of Brahmā,
mounted upon a divine celestial chariot and anointed with divine perfumes and unguents.
Having sported for a very long time, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu on celestial chariots adorned with excellent jewels,
which resemble the twelve suns.
Seated there amidst the sounds of singing and musical instruments, attended by hosts of Apsarases, that king shall attain union with Viṣṇu.
O King, whoever should hear this or recite it, permeated by devotion,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the milk-cow as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa. Now follows the gift of the curd-cow.
Vinītāśva said:
O great king, now hear the procedure for the curd-cow;
O lord of men, on a portion of ground smeared with cow dung.
Furthermore, having strewn the ground with a handful of flowers the size of a cow’s hide,
he should spread it over with *kuśa* grass and a black antelope skin.
Having placed a jar of curd upon a heap of seven kinds of grain, one should fashion a golden calf, joined with a golden face, measuring one-fourth [the size] of the jar.
[He saw] horses with praiseworthy ears, eyes made of pearls,
and bodies smeared with sandalwood and aloe-wood paste, their faces indeed garlanded with fragrance.
O King, the tongue [is satisfied] by sugar, the nose likewise by sandalwood,
the teeth by fruits and roots, and the blankets by white thread.
She has a copper-colored back, hair made of darbha grass, and a tail made of thread;
she has horns of gold, hooves of silver, and udders made of fresh butter.
Having well-prepared Ikṣupādā, adorned with all ornaments,
clothed in a pair of garments, and worshipped with flowers and perfumes;
One should cause such a gift to be given to a brahmin of noble birth, of virtuous conduct, wise, and disciplined in meditative concentration.
Having given sandals, shoes, and an umbrella to one seated at the region of the hips, with ear-rings as the only ornaments, one should recollect the mantra.
[426] With the mantra beginning "dadhikrāvṇo," one should cause a cow made of curd to be given.
O best of royal sages, having thus given a cow consisting of curd, one attains the highest state.
O prince, the sacrificer should remain for one day eating only curd;
O King, the best of the twice-born should stay for three days.
Those who behold her being given away also go to the supreme goal—
ten ancestors, ten descendants, and themselves as the twenty-first.
One attains the world of Viṣṇu until the dissolution of all that is summoned;
both the giver and the one who causes the gift to be given likewise go to the supreme goal.
Where there are rivers carrying honey and where the mud is made of milk-rice,
there go the givers of cows— the sages, the seers, and the perfected ones.
The person who hears this with devotion, or causes it to be heard,
shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice and go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the curd-cow as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Now, the gift of the honey-cow: I shall describe the honey-cow, which destroys all sins.
On the surface of the earth, which has been smeared [with cow dung] and covered with a black antelope skin and kuśa grass.
Having fashioned a cow made of honey and filled with a full jar,
one should likewise fashion a calf consisting of a fourth part of that.
Having made its face of gold, its horns of aloe-wood and sandalwood,
its back of copper, and its tail likewise of thread.
The feet should be made of sugarcane, covered with white woolen blankets;
having made the face out of molasses, the tongue should be provided with sugar.
Her eyes were pearls, her teeth were made of fruit,
the goddess possessed hair of *darbha* grass, and she was adorned with silver hooves.
One should cause her to be given seven kinds of grain— she who has ears like the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, breasts made of fresh butter, and who is endowed with all auspicious marks.
One should place four vessels of sesame seeds in the four directions,
covering them with a pair of cloths and adorning them with bells and ornaments.
Having given a brass milking vessel that has been honored with perfumes and flowers,
on the auspicious occasion of the solstices, the equinoxes, the *vyatīpāta* yoga, or the waning of the day;
During the transit of the sun, during eclipses, and at all times without weariness,
one should cause gifts to be given merely by sight, provided there is an abundance of wealth and worthy Brahmins present.
To a Brāhmaṇa who is poor, learned in the Vedas, a householder,
born in Āryāvarta, and one who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
O best of men, such a honey-cow should be given to one who is seated upon the tail, having been worshipped with perfumes, incense, and other offerings.
Having covered [the image] with a pair of garments and a ring for the ear,
one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, free from stinginess regarding wealth.
First, the water-offering must be performed; afterwards, one should present the gift.
She is the knower of the essence of all the gods, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
"May the ancestors and the gods be pleased; O Madhudhenu, salutations be unto you! Having uttered this, one should present that cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
I take you, O Goddess, especially for the sake of my family;
O yielder of desires, fulfill my wishes! O giver of honey, homage be to you!
Having caused her to be given with a restrained mind by means of the mantra "madhu vātā," O Great King, one should likewise give a cow, an umbrella, and sandals.
O lord of men, he who thus devoutly prepares the Madhudhenu and, having given it as a gift, passes the day with milk-rice (pāyasa) and honey; [attains the highest reward].
A Brahmin, moreover, [should eat] for three nights food combined with honey and milk-rice;
O lord of men, learn now what merit is gained when this is performed.
Where there are rivers carrying honey and where the mud is made of milk-rice,
there go the givers of cows— the seers, the sages, and the perfected ones.
There he enjoys excellent pleasures and dwells in the world of Brahmā;
having sported for a very long time, he returns once more to the state of a mortal.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures there, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
By the grace of the Madhudhenu, one leads ten ancestors, ten descendants, and oneself as the twenty-first to union with Viṣṇu.
The person who hears this with devotion, or even causes it to be heard,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Madhu-dhenu as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Now follows the gift of the Rasa-dhenu.
Vinītāśva said:
O Great King, I shall describe the cow of nectar (rasadhenu) in brief:
on a smeared surface of the earth, covered with a black antelope skin and a layer of kuśa grass.
O King, a wise man should likewise imagine a jar completely filled with sugarcane juice, and a calf equal to one-fourth of that amount.
Its legs are made of sugarcane, joined with silver hooves;
it has ornaments of gold on its horns, a tail of cloth, and breasts of clarified butter.
It was covered with a flower-woolen cloth, its snout and tongue were made of sugar,
its teeth were made of fruit, and its auspicious back was made of copper.

O Indra among kings, one should place four vessels of sesame seeds in the four directions before [the image] whose eyes are made of pearls, which is endowed with seven grains of rice, and adorned with all kinds of perfumes; this [image] has hair made of flowers.
To a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas, a master of the sacred scriptures, one who has maintained the sacred fires,
especially one who knows the Purāṇas, who is of virtuous conduct, and wise.
Such a milch-cow of nectar should be given to a householder;
the donor, freed from all sins, attains heaven.

Whether it be the giver or the receiver who eats a meal of savory food for even a single day, that shall be as if they had drunk the Soma; indeed, the entire fruit [of the ritual] shall accrue to them.
But those who see her being given away also go to the supreme destination,
after first worshipping the cow with perfumes, incense, garlands, and other offerings.
One should attentively recollect those very mantras previously mentioned;
having thus uttered them, they are indeed bestowed upon the best of the twice-born.
He leads ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first to the supreme state, from which one does not return again.
These, O King, have been described to you as the unsurpassed cow of nectar;
bestow them, O Great King, and may you attain a life of meritorious renown.
Whoever constantly recites this or listens to it with devotion,
being liberated from all sins, shall attain union with Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Rasa-dhenu as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa. [430] Now follows the gift of the Śarkarā-dhenu.
Vinītāśva said:
O King, one should likewise prepare a sugar-cow according to the prescribed rule,
upon a smeared surface of the earth covered with a black antelope skin and kuśa grass.
O King, a cow weighing four bhāras with sugar is always declared by the virtuous to be "excellent" (uttamā), and the calf is one-fourth of that weight.
Half of that is said to be the middle [size], and the smallest is by a fourth part;
in the same way, O child, a person should fashion the calf by a fourth part.
Alternatively, one should make the calf one-eighth the size of the cow;
one should have the cow made according to one's own capacity, so that it does not cause distress to oneself.
Having placed all the seeds on all four sides,
they should have golden faces and horns, and their eyes made of pearls.
The mouth should be made of jaggery, and likewise the tongue of flour;
she is adorned with a blanket of silk thread and decorated with bells and ornaments;
her feet are made of sugarcane, her hooves of silver, and her udders of fresh butter.
Adorned with white chowries and inscribed with eulogies,
it is endowed with the five jewels and provided with hair made of *darbha* grass.
With a bronze milking vessel, properly provided with perfumes and flowers,
and endowed with such a ritual arrangement, it is covered above with cloths.
Having adorned it with perfumes and flowers, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas, poor, of virtuous conduct, and wise.

It should be given specifically to one who is learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), who maintains the sacred fire (agnihotrī), and who is free from envy; it must certainly not be given to one possessed by malice.
O Six-faced One, during the solstices, the equinoxes, and the auspicious *vyatīpāta* yoga,
and at whatever other meritorious times there may be, one should likewise cause [the gift] to be bestowed.
The donor, standing facing either the east or the north,
should place the cow facing the east and position the calf to her north.
At the time of giving, one should recite those mantras and perform worship;
and having clothed that Brahmin, one should honor him with finger-rings and earrings.
One should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, along with fragrant flowers and sandalwood;
one should offer a cow and must not look at its face.
A Brahmin who subsists on sugar for one day may dwell [there] for three days;
such a cow removes all sins and bestows all desires.
One is born with all desires fulfilled; of this there is no doubt.
Even those who merely behold [this rite] being performed attain the supreme goal.
The person who hears this with devotion, or even reads it,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the sugar-cow as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa. Now follows the procedure for the gift of the cotton-cow.
Varāha said:
Henceforth, I shall describe the auspicious cotton-cow;
for the sake of guarding the secrets of the universe, Brahmā wore a garment of cotton.
That root of cotton is also considered by him to be the most excellent;
and that cow, along with a load of cotton, is proclaimed to be the best.
The middle [size] is half of that, and the smallest is half of that as well;
and the clothing, grain, and gold are likewise as before.
The calf, however, is prescribed to be one-fourth [of the quantity]; the mantra for its offering is enjoined as follows:
"One should fashion the calf as before, along with garments, grain, and other household requisites."
"As before" means as described for the *tiladhenu* (sesame-cow) in the *Varāhapurāṇa*. [The mantra is:

"O you who are born from the Ocean of Milk, O beloved of Soma, O cow named Sudhenu, O daughter of Surabhi, homage be to you! (Hemakundendradeveśa... kṣīrārṇavasamudbhave | somapriye sudhenvākhye saurabheyi namo 'stu te).
This is offered to Indranātha, to the one who is like the moon and the nectar;
salutations indeed to Soma-rāja, born from the eye of Atri.
The mantra for giving:
"He who, with such supreme devotion, bestows [this] upon a Brahmin,
goes to the world of Soma and rejoices together with Soma."
Neither a sick person, nor one with fever, nor one afflicted by leprosy shall be born in his family;
endowed with sons and wife, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a cotton-cow as declared in the Varāha Purāṇa. Now follows the gift of a salt-cow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, you who are learned in all the scriptures,
please tell me that which is proclaimed as the highest among gifts.

"O you of noble vows, tell me that by which, when given, all things indeed become given; by which there is the fulfillment of all desires and the destruction of all evils, and through which one becomes purified by expiation."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe here the ritual arrangement for Lavaṇa;
it is performed on ground smeared with cow dung and covered with a layer of darbha grass.
Having spread out a sheepskin and placed a cow facing the eastern direction, one should cover her with a cloth and position her in the center.
Whether one possesses great wealth or little, one should fashion [the cow] with exactly an *āḍhaka* [of gold];
she should have horns of gold, hooves of silver, feet of sugarcane, and breasts of fruit.
The tongue should be made with sugar, and likewise the sense of smell with fragrant substances;
one should wrap the ears with mother-of-pearl from the interior of the sea-shell.
One should provide two pieces of sandalwood for the horns, two auspicious pearls for the eyes,
two lumps of roasted flour for the cheeks, and barley grains for the mouth.
A woolen blanket with a silk thread around its neck, likewise a small parasol on its back,
a copper vessel on its hindquarters, and a lump of molasses at its anus.
One should give a woolen blanket on the tail, juices from the region of the udder,
honey at the region of the vulva, and one endowed with fruits all over.
Having thus properly established the cow made of salt,
a person should also place a calf made of one-fourth part [of salt].
Having thus worshipped the cow with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
one should bathe, perform the worship of the deity, and honor the Brahmins.
Having circumambulated the cow, O King, accompanied by his son and wife, he should present her to a virtuous Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with good conduct.
On all festival days, a person should give [this] with this mantra:
"In salt indeed are all tastes; in salt are all the deities."
"O Goddess who consists of all goddesses, O Goddess named Lavaṇā, homage be to you! Having thus recited this at the end of the mantra, one should present it to a Brahmin.
O King, O descendant of Bharata, by performing a complete circumambulation accompanied by a sacrificial fee,
one has effectively performed a circumambulation of the entire earth.
All gifts have been given, as well as the fruits of all seasons;
all tastes, all mantras, and all this world of the moving and the unmoving.
There is no doubt that by giving a cow made of mercury (rasadhenu), men attain good fortune, supreme prosperity, and the excellence of bodily health.
And there is certain residence in heaven until the dissolution of all things at the end of the kalpa,
for one who has made a garment of woolen cloth, silk, and blankets with salt water as its girdle,
having fashioned breasts of fruit upon it and a hide of the sheep (*avī*) on its back.
Having duly given a cow of nectar to a twice-born man,
he goes to the world of cows, which is endowed with every happiness.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the salt-cow as declared in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
Now follows the gift of the camphor-cow and others.
I shall describe the auspicious camphor-cow, which consists of all fragrant substances.
O Lord of the Earth, by giving vehicles, all types of perfumes are effectively given.
O Lord, one should give a cow adorned with camphor during a lunar or solar eclipse, on the full moon day of Kārttika, at the equinox, on the twelfth lunar day, or during the meritorious solstice.
For a poor brahmin who is devoted to virtuous conduct,
one should spread out upon the ground a beautiful cloth as white as a conch shell, having first covered it with a net.
The cow should be made of four palas, while the calf is one pala;
or else, the cow may be one pala and the calf should be made of one karṣa.
Its horns are of gold, its hooves of silver, its tail produced from saffron;
its tusks consist of musk, and its mouth is made of granthiparṇa wood.
The two eyes are made of *sihvakam*, the two ears from *aguru* wood,
the tail from *devadāru* wood, and the anus produced from *guggulu*.
Kuṣṭha is prescribed for the cheeks, and uśīra for the skin;
one should apply sandalwood to the abdomen, and indeed, the nail to the tips of the fingers.
Having thus formed this resolve, he should worship a camphor-cow adorned with cloth,
and likewise honor a Brahmin with that camphor and a pair of garments.
"O Lord of Brahmins, accept this well-worshipped camphor-cow;
may Kamalā, who resides within its flowers and fragrance, be pleased with me."
With this very mantra, one should cause a gift to be given to a Brahmin;
having given this cow, O King, one becomes equal to the Gandharvas.
One shall dwell in heaven for three kalpas and become a king of kings here on earth;
one attains all desires and is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
Likewise:
"A cow made of sugar is proclaimed to be the granter of all desires and the remover of all sins; therefore, one should give it with a concentrated mind."
[436] Here, as in the case of the jaggery-cow (guḍadhenu), one should perform the invocation and worship with mantras;
by giving a cow made of fruit, one shall partake in the fruits of all desires.
Likewise, O best of kings, one endowed with faith and wealth should give a musk-deer cow to a worthy recipient and utter this mantra:
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a cow made of camphor and other substances as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Now follows the gift of a cow made of gold.
The Blessed Lord said:
I shall tell you the secret concerning the golden cow, which is augmented by the merit of giving and which brings about the pacification of all sins.
O King of kings, that which was ordained by Brahmā and formerly established by Viṣṇu,
I shall relate to you in detail and in proper sequence, O King.
Of pure gold and gold, there is a conceptualized distinction:
one word "suvarṇa" denotes the substance (gold), while the other denotes the measure (weight).
[She was] joined with silver and pearls and adorned with pearls.
It was endowed with coral peaks and possessed eyes made of rubies.
She has vessels of ghee for breasts, camphor and agallochum for a nose, is endowed with a tongue of sugar-cane juice, and possesses a mouth full of savory food.
[One should worship] her who has a conch and a horn between [her breasts], whose forehead is fashioned with a pearl-oyster shell,
whose teeth are made of fruit, whose sides are adorned with a pair of garments, and who possesses fine linen and woolen blankets.
One whose feet are sugarcane, whose ears are coconuts, whose knees are molasses,
who has drunk the five products of the cow, and who possesses a back of bell-metal;

A man should bestow upon a Brahmin such a golden cow, which has a tail made of fine cotton thread, is provided with the seven kinds of grain, is endowed with fruits and flowers, and is equipped with a parasol and a water-pot.
"May the golden-seeded Puruṣa, the ancient one, dark-brown in hue,
possessing the luster of molten gold, the creator and soul of the universe, be pleased."
The gift of a cow with this very mantra is proclaimed;
one obtains, without doubt, the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
That wise man leads a thousand families to heaven; what need is there for many other gifts? A golden cow is sufficient.
Indeed, by giving a golden cow, a man becomes one who has fulfilled his duty;
he should proclaim, "May the Blessed Lord Hiraṇyagarbha be pleased."
O lord of men, one whose self is purified by fasting should give gifts during an eclipse of the moon or sun;
the rākṣasas and piśācas do not look upon his house.
One who is self-restrained should give on the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika;
by giving, one attains that state where, having gone, one does not grieve.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a golden cow as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Agastya said:
By performing which rite Manu attained the unsurpassed worlds.
O King, I shall now describe to you that procedure for the gift of a golden cow.
One should have a beautiful cow made of gold with silver hooves;

"beautiful" means fashioned from pure gold. Here, the inclusion of unstated details—such as the construction of the calf using a fourth part of the gold and other components—is to be understood from the previously mentioned golden cow (*suvarṇadhenu*).
Having clothed that cow in garments, one shall attain the highest world.
And with various multicolored flowers, perfumes, incense, and ointments,
one should likewise ask that Goddess for forgiveness and dedicate a cow there.
O Goddess, by your command it is given to your devotees;
furthermore, you should cause that same [gift] to be bestowed upon the king of Brahmins, who is a partaker of Śiva’s grace.
For one who brings about auspiciousness, for one who meditates upon Śiva,
and for the purification of penance by one desiring imperishable fruit—
this was indeed practiced by Manu; truly, men would attain success through it.
O child, having uplifted seven generations of ancestors and descendants who were established in the sin of Rudra, one should lead them to the unsurpassed world of the Goddess.

Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a golden cow as stated in the Devīpurāṇa. From the Vahnipurāṇa: "In this rite, a golden cow [is made] with fourteen *suvarṇas*; the middling [cow] is prescribed to be made with seven well-purified *suvarṇas*."
The Kanyasā is said to consist of four [parts], and the Vatsaka of a fourth part; when given according to the procedure for the Guḍadhenu, it bestows all fruits.
Viśvāmitra:
May the golden-seeded Puruṣa, the ancient one, dark-brown in hue,
possessing the luster of red gold, the creator and the soul of the universe, be pleased.
One should proclaim, "May the blessed Hiraṇyagarbha be pleased," and by giving a golden cow, a man shall have fulfilled his purpose.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a golden cow.
Now Vṛddhagautama says:
"Then, one should fashion a cow made of gold according to the previously mentioned rite."
[439] One with golden horns, richly adorned with jewels, and likewise with silver hooves.
And likewise, one should prepare the *tarṇaka* (the sacrificial vessel) with an eighth part as before;
[he should invite] a Brāhmaṇa endowed with Vedic learning, a Vaiṣṇava, and a householder.
Having invited to his home one who is possessed of good conduct, most righteous, and diligent in serving the twice-born, he should honor him according to the rules as before.
Just as before, gold should be offered according to one's means and with devotion; likewise, fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood should be properly offered with Vaiṣṇava mantras.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the one afflicted by urinary disease should offer it with this mantra:
"The Sudarśana discus, whose royal splendor likewise shines..."
May Viṣṇu, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, swiftly remove [the disease] premeha.
This is the mantra for the gift:
"This gift destroys the disease of prameha; it should be performed by the wise."
By performing this, even the most terrible afflictions here are pacified.
In this context, "as before" should be understood as being like the gift of a golden bull.
This concludes the procedure for the gift of a golden cow that cures urinary disorders (*prameha*).
Now, Baudhāyana says:
One should have a golden cow made from one pala or even half a pala;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, for if one does so, the fruit will not come to pass.
Having placed a cow with jeweled horns and silver hooves, adorned with various cloths,
upon the planets, one should arrange the nine grains.
The fire oblations (homa), however, should be performed as before for the benefit and pleasure of Govinda;
thus, [the mantras] "viṣṇu-pratad-viṣṇu" and "viṣṇor-nukam" are used in sequence.
Having offered the fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and the sacrificial porridge (caru), and indeed having completed the rite with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
the sick man should then, being pure, [invite] a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
One who is endowed with learning and good conduct, of noble birth, a speaker of dharma,
advanced in years, perfected in knowledge, and who causes no agitation among men.
Having personally brought [the offerings] with devotion, one should worship them with affection,
using rings, vessels, and the like, as well as sandals and umbrellas.
With this mantra, the patient, possessing self-control, should offer her into the vessel.
Meditating upon Govinda in my mind, we beheld him standing in the midst of the cows,
adorned with a crest of peacock feathers and intent on playing his flute.
O Govinda, beloved lord of the cowherd folk, slayer of the demon Kaṃsa, who today resembles the king of the gods, surrounded by the cowherd women and adorned with forest flowers!
O Compassionate One, being satisfied by this gift of my cow, grant me the destruction of hemorrhoids and may I diminish the host of my enemies.
The mantra for the gift:
"By this gift, the destruction of hemorrhoids is certain to arise;
therefore, one should perform it with effort for the sake of the relief of these hemorrhoids."
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the golden cow that removes hemorrhoids.
Now, in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
"And she who is barren in four ways becomes [fertile] through the separation from her calf."
I shall declare its remedy; learn from me its true nature.
The Guru said that one should have a sturdy cow made of gold according to one's means, together with its calf; the cow should be made from a pala of gold and the calf from a quarter-pala.
One should attach a jewel to the tail of a cow with silver hooves;
being pure and facing east, one should bind a bell to her ankle while she is accompanied by her calf.
With sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, with fragrant garlands,
and with the sixteen types of offerings, the food offering (naivedya) should consist of milk-rice (pāyasa).
And likewise, he placed the modaka, the apūpa, molasses, salt,
and cumin in a wide, sturdy winnowing basket made of bamboo.
One cow indeed should be given to Brahmin women;
immediately thereafter, one should give six, eight, or ten.
A Brahmin who is skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures, a knower of dharma,
endowed with learning and discipline, peaceful, and one who has conquered his senses.
Having summoned one who is free from greed, beloved by all people, and devoid of blemish, and having honored him with devotion through garments and other offerings, as well as perfumes and flowers;
With due reverence, he should cause the worship of the cow and the calf to be performed by that very person;
and there he should cause a fire-oblation (homa) to be performed, abounding in sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and cooked rice (caru).
Having recited the mantra "Somo dhenuṃ," he,
facing north, should then present her to the recipient who is seated facing east.
Having placed his hand upon the tail according to the rule with this mantra,
[he should know that] she who was the cow of Aṅgiras, as well as Surabhi, the cow of Vasiṣṭha.
She who is the daughter of the Sun, of Agni, and of Varuṇa;
and those cows that roam in the forests and groves.
May they always bring me joy, bestowing the happiness of sons and grandsons;
may they grant me an uninterrupted lineage day and night.
The mantra for giving:
Having thus given that gift, one should prostrate and dismiss it.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the Golden Cow, which removes barrenness.
Likewise:
"He whose hands and feet are perspiring who should steal mercury and other such substances..."
I shall explain its remedy through rites such as giving gifts and performing fire-oblations.
One should fashion a cow out of gold using half a *pala*, or half of that, or again half of that; the calf should be made from one-quarter of that amount.
Having done this, one should wrap that beautiful bow in cloth,
place it upon a mound of jaggery, and worship it with perfumes and incense;
the quantity of the jaggery should be forty palas.
Or it may be half of that, or even according to one's means;
as for the offerings to the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) and so forth, there should be the fourfold substances of ghee, curd, and milk.
Having placed [the substances] one by one on each of the feet, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise,
one should then smear its horns with saffron.
Having thus fashioned that cow in the form of gold,
the preceptor should commence the fire-oblation (homa) in a consecrated sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on an altar (sthaṇḍila).
Having performed the bringing forward of the fire, the preceptor— knowing all the Vedas,
conversant with dharma, learned in the ritual of sacrifice, skillful, and free from anger— [should proceed].
One who does not cause distress to men, who knows the meaning of the Purāṇas and understands the Vedic auxiliary sciences (aṅgas),
should perform the oblation of fuel-sticks with clarified butter and sesame seeds using these mantras in due order;
the oblation of fuel-sticks with the mantra "āyaṃ gauḥ" is highly recommended.
The wise should perform an oblation of clarified butter with the *śaibhedyeya* mantra,
and an oblation of sesame seeds with the *vyāhṛtis*, one thousand and eight times.
Having thus completed the fire sacrifice, the consecration of the one who has emerged [from the ritual] should be performed;
one should place an unblemished water-pot in the north-eastern region of the fire.
With a white garment, as well as clay and guggulu,
and when gorocanā is available, [one should perform the rite] with fuel-sticks of the five-bhaṅga tree.
Then, with the mantras "āpo hi ṣṭhā" consisting of three verses, and also with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" and the Pāvamānī hymns, he [should sprinkle] that sick person.
Having first performed the rite of pacification with the *śanno vātā* hymn,
one should then perform the consecration for the person wearing white garments.
One should smear one's hands and feet with the remnants of the oblations;
then, the sick person should worship that bow with devotion using perfumes, unbroken grains, and other offerings, while reciting the mantra: "The cows are indeed the fragrant ones."
Then, facing north, one should give her to the preceptor who faces east, according to the rule, after she has been worshipped with this mantra; of this there is no doubt.
Those who are the daughters of Āditya, as well as the cows of the gods,
and those of the ancestors, the yakṣas, and the gandharvas in their entirety.
Likewise, Vaśiṣṭha and Surabhi are the lords of the Yakṣas and Guhyakas;
may they all be quickly pleased with me by virtue of this gift of a cow.
Whatever deformity of the hands and feet has arisen from the theft of milk,
all that cows, when gratified in every way, quickly remove entirely.
The mantra for the gift:
For one who performs the gift of a golden cow according to this rite,
all suffering arising from the ripening of past karma is utterly destroyed.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brāhmaṇa according to one's ability and with devotion;
one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas and feed one's kinsmen as well.
Having bathed himself, he should eat pure food while remaining self-controlled;
by this act of giving, he will certainly be cured of the ailment born from the perspiration of his feet.
Then, by means of the perspiration from his feet, the sick were made well.
[444] Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a golden cow that destroys the sweat from one's feet.
Now, regarding the gift of a cow according to its actual nature, as stated in the Mahābhārata:
"Among all gifts here in this world, the gift of cows is distinguished as the most excellent."
Cows are the most excellent, pure, purifying, and the highest in the world.
Without curd and ghee, no sacrifice proceeds here;
therefore, they declare that the cow is indeed the root of the entire sacrifice.
Cows are superior to ascetics and indeed to all others;
therefore, the god Maheśvara dwells together with them.
O Bhārata, they provide service with milk, oblation, curd, dung, and even with hide,
bones, hair, and horns.
O King, I do not see any wealth in this world that is as imperishable as cows—
whether it be their praise, their hearing, their giving, or even their sight.
O hero, cows are highly praised as the supreme remover of all sins;
cows are always the root of prosperity, and no evil exists within them.
The utterances *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ* are eternally established in cows;
cows are indeed the leaders of the sacrifice, and likewise, the cow is the mouth of the sacrifice.
For they protect and carry the divine, imperishable nectar;
they are the abode of immortality and are honored by all the worlds.
It is my conviction that there is no gift superior to the gift of a cow;
such a cow, acquired by righteous means, delivers one's entire lineage when given away.
"The milk of cows is indeed nectar," so said Prajāpati;
therefore, he who gives a cow attains immortality.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"The fire-sanctuaries of Brahmins and the temples of the deities are honored by those women; what more could be given to them than a snake? (445)
Devala said:
"He who, desiring to go to heaven, ascends a supreme celestial chariot adorned with divine ornaments, should bestow the gift of a cow."
"O Vyāsa, there exists on earth either a greater gift or one equal to that of the donor; yet, this [gift] has certainly been ordained by the gods for her funeral rite."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa,
Brahmā said: "This earth is indeed celebrated as Gaurī, the daughter of Āditya."
She has appeared for the welfare of all the worlds and for the successful accomplishment of sacrifices.
The Brahmins and the cows constitute a single family divided into two parts:
on one side reside the sacred mantras, and on the other side resides the sacrificial oblation.
From cows sacrifices proceed; from cows the gods have arisen;
from cows the Vedas were uttered, together with the six auxiliary limbs and the Pada and Krama recitations.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu are eternally stationed at the base of the horns of cows;
at the tips of the horns reside all sacred fords, both mobile and immobile.
Mahādeva, who consists of all beings, resides in the center of the head;
the Goddess is situated on the tip of the forehead, and the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya) is in the portion of the nose.
The two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara well protect his nostrils;
the two gods Aśvinī protect his ears; and the Moon and Sun protect his eyes.
All the Vayus reside in the teeth; Varuṇa is situated in the tongue;
Sarasvatī is in the syllable *huṃ*; and Yama and Yakṣa are in the two cheeks.
Likewise, at the two junctions of day and night, Indra has taken recourse in the neck with his two lips;
the Rākṣasas are in the region of the armpits, while the Sādhyas are stationed upon the chest.
The entire Dharma with its four quarters stands itself upon his legs;
the Gandharvas are in the middle of his hooves, and the Pannagas are at the tips of his hooves.
Indeed, the hosts of Apsarases are stationed at the western tips of the hooves;
the eleven Rudras are on the back, and the Vasus are at all the joints.
The ancestors reside upon the slope of the hips; Soma rests upon the tail;
and the rays of the sun stand there as hair, gathered together in a mass.
The Gaṅgā is present directly in cow’s urine, and the Yamunā resides in cow dung;
the goddess Sarasvatī is in milk, and the Narmadā is situated in curd.
The consumer of oblations himself is the supreme preceptor of the Brahmins;
twenty-eight crores of gods reside within his pores.
The earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, is to be known as being within the belly;
and the four oceans are those which are the udders of the cows.
O tiger among gods, all this has been told by him— how the entire world, including the gods, asuras, and humans, is indeed established within the cows.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: They eat grass, they dwell in the forest,
and they drink waters that are not claimed as property.
They yield milk, they carry burdens, and they purify sin; the livelihood of those who live by their labor depends on the products of the cows.
Cows, when contented, pacify evil;
cows, when given as a gift, lead one to the third heaven; and cows, when well-protected, bring forth wealth.
There is no wealth at all that can be compared to cows.
He who constantly eats the young grass and gives it away—
which removes evil and increases friendship—
is indeed noble and is worthy of being honored.
There is no wealth whatsoever that can be compared to cows.
Having grazed upon dry grasses in the forest and even having drunk its waters, [the cows] flow with nectar;
for by means of their dung and other products, they purify the worlds.
There is no wealth whatsoever that is equal to cows.
Hārīta says:
He who indeed bestows cows yielding much milk upon a Brāhmaṇa shall deliver himself as well as seven generations of his lineage on both sides.
Devala says:
A wise man should give a cow that is well-behaved, endowed with auspicious marks, young, accompanied by its calf, yielding much milk, and gentle.
Vedavyāsa:
And he who, having sold himself, buys cows and bestows them [as gifts],
obtains those eternal cows which are equal to the sale of one's own self— so says Vṛddhakauśika.
Likewise: "He who, having acquired cows in battles, bestows them as gifts,
enjoys a reward equal in measure to the number of cows he touches."
"For that long" means for a period equal to the number of hairs on the aforementioned cow; this is the fruit of heaven for one year.
He who, having won or purchased cattle from a lightning-struck person, bestows them [as a gift], enjoys the fruit of ten thousand divine years, O Śakra.

Those born within [the herd], those obtained for a fair price, those purchased for a fee, those won by conquest, those born in the stable, and those rescued from hardship after being nourished—by these criteria, specific types of cows are praised. Regarding "those born within," the commentator on the *Bhārata* states they are pregnant. "Obtained for a fair price" means acquired through a purchase at the proper value; "purchased for a fee" means acquired through wages; "won by conquest" means [acquired] through battle and the like; "born in the stable" means born in the house; and "rescued from hardship after being nourished" refers to those who, having been overcome by the hardships of disease and so forth, were abandoned by their owners and subsequently acquired by oneself after providing them with nourishment.
One who is angry, wicked, weak, or diseased should not be given; nor one for whom the price has not been paid,
or she who subjects the Brahmin to hardships with [mere] fruits.
For him, the worlds are devoid of vigor and also fruitless.
The phrase "accepted for prices not paid" is the implied meaning. Likewise:
"One should certainly not give to a Brāhmaṇa a cow that is emaciated, one whose calf has died, one that is barren, one afflicted by disease, one with missing limbs, or one that is exhausted."
He who gives away a cow that has already served its purpose, is worn out, and is barren, shall enter into darkness; such a donor merely subjects the twice-born to hardship.

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: [One should not give a cow that is] one whose water has been drunk, one who has eaten grass, one whose milk has been sucked dry, one lacking senses, one that is frantic, one with missing limbs, one whose calf has died, or one that eats excessively.

One should avoid a cow that has long hair, whose dung smells of raw flesh, or who eats carrion; one that is miscarrying, barren, or has a ruptured udder; one that is a "pouch-cow" (a cow with a distended belly), one that gives birth to twins, or one whose teats are constantly discharging pus.

One should not give to Brāhmaṇas a bull that has faults, nor one that has already drunk water or eaten grass—this refers to the characteristic of old age. [449] Nor one whose milk is sucked dry, nor one that drinks from its own udder, nor a "great-eater" (mahāśanā) which eats much, nor a "bag-cow" (puṭadhenu), which is pregnant while still in the state of childhood. Viśvāmitra says:
One should not give a cow that has many horns, no horns at all, cracked eyes, or trembling hooves;
nor should one give a three-uddered cow; rather, one should cause only auspicious cows to be given.
In the Mahābhārata: "The powerful Ambarīṣa, having given eleven billion cows to the Brahmins, ascended to heaven together with his entire kingdom."
Having given away a hundred thousand cows along with their calves, King Prasenajit,
possessed of great majesty, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
Likewise:
"Where the palaces are made of gold, where the beds shine with jewels,
and where there are excellent apsarases— there go those who give cows."
One who gives a cow does not go to hell; having drunk milk, water, and lotus-water, O King, he shines in heaven upon a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
And hundreds of excellent women, beautifully dressed with shapely hips and adorned with divine ornaments, delight him as he stays in his celestial chariot.
Awakened from sleep by the sounds of flutes, lutes, and anklets,
as well as by the laughter of fawn-eyed women, he rises.
For as many hairs as there are on a cow,
for that many years one is honored in heaven; even when fallen from heaven, one remains so in the three worlds thereafter.
He will be born into a family possessing cattle.

Viṣṇu: “By the gift of a cow one attains heaven; by the gift of ten cows, Goloka; and by the gift of a hundred, the world of Brahmā. Jābāla: “He who gives a cow unasked for the purpose of the Agnihotra sacrifice has, without a doubt, given the entire earth filled with wealth three times over.”
Yājñavalkya says:
Having given a cow, whether it be a milch-cow or even one that does not yield milk,
provided it is healthy and free from blemish, the donor is glorified in heaven.
Aṅgiras said:
A cow should be given specifically to one who is learned in the Vedas;
for she indeed delivers seven ancestors, seven descendants, and seven more.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"That cow, when given to an unworthy recipient, leads the donor to hell;
yet it delivers the recipient, along with twenty-one generations of his lineage."
And when a cow, together with a sacrificial fee, is given to a worthy recipient according to the prescribed rite,
then it delivers living beings along with tens of thousands of lineages.
The vessels belonging to the inner self are primary; those of the pure Agnihotra-sacrificers are likewise foremost;
and the deities are similarly preeminent—for this gift of a cow is indeed supreme.
In the Mahābhārata:
"One distressed for a livelihood suffers excessively; and for the sake of poetic composition, one suffers at the time of the Soma-pressing due to the lack of oblations."
For the sake of the teacher or for the nourishment of children, one should give a cow; this is a distinguished time [for such a gift].

[451] At the Soma sacrifice during the *prasuti* rite; likewise: "O bull among men, a cow should not be given for the purpose of slaughter, nor to a farmer, nor to an atheist, nor to one who lives off cattle."

A *kīnāśa* is one who wields a plow. [The gift should go to] one of the Atri lineage, who is impoverished, who has many dependents, who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), who is fond of guests, and who is self-controlled; to such a person, a cow accompanied by molasses should be given.
A cow must never, under any circumstances, be given to one who is of low birth, to a fool, to a greedy person, to a slanderer, or to one who is excluded from offerings to the gods and ancestors.

Now, the procedure for the gift: Viśvāmitra says— having stationed a well-worshipped cow together with her calf facing the east, the donor, having bathed and tied his topknot, should indeed stand at the region of the tail.
The Brahmin, characterized by the auspicious marks of a vessel, should face north,
holding in his hand a vessel for clarified butter accompanied by gold.
Having cast his tail into that [fire] and having taken hold of it while it is smeared with ghee,
he should cause the hand of the Brahmin— containing sesame seeds— to be placed upon it with its fingers pointing toward the east.
Taking both sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass, he should perform the act of giving;
with this very mantra, he should pour water while holding the vessel in his hand.
May the Supreme God, who is of universal form, be pleased by this cow, which is the means for accomplishing sacrifice and the destroyer of all evil in the world.
Having followed that cow together with the Brāhmaṇa,
one should then, being restrained and pure, mutter the Gomatī-vidyā.
Then, O sinless one, having intended Vāsudeva as the recipient with the thought "May he be pleased," and having mentally envisioned a worthy recipient, one should pour water into the waters.
May the eternal Lord, who reclines upon the waters, the father of Brahmā, whose navel is a lotus,
and who rests upon the coils of Ananta, the Supreme Father, be pleased.
Yama said to Gomatī:
"Cows are eternally fragrant; cows possess the scent of guggulu resin.
Cows are the foundation of all beings; cows are a great means of securing well-being."
Cows are indeed the supreme food, the highest oblation for the gods;
they purify all beings and both carry and protect them.
With oblations purified by mantras, they gratify the immortals in heaven;
cows are the foundation of the fire-sacrifices of the seers who maintain the sacred fires.
Cows are the highest auspiciousness for all beings;
cows are the supreme purifier, cows are the highest auspiciousness.
Cows belong to the entire world; cows are blessed along with their vehicles.
Homage to the glorious cows and to the daughters of Surabhi.
Homage to the daughters of Brahmā, who are pure; homage, repeated homage! Both the Brāhmaṇas and the cows constitute a single lineage that has been divided into two.
In one place the mantras abide; in another place the sacrificial oblation abides.

There is also another *gomatī* mentioned in the *Mahābhārata*, which is shown in the context of the gift of a sesame-cow (*tiladhenu*). Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the performance of these two. Vasiṣṭha states the mantra common to all gifts of cows:
"Cows that yield ghee and milk, whose source is ghee, from whom ghee arises;
rivers of ghee with whirlpools of ghee—may they always be in my home."
Ghee is ever in my heart; ghee is established in my navel;
ghee is indeed everywhere within me; ghee resides in my mind.
Cows are always before me, and cows are behind me;
cows are on all sides of me, and I dwell in the midst of cows.
Thus, having sipped water and always reciting this prayer at evening and at dawn,
a person is liberated from whatever sin he commits during the day.
And the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) here is gold. As Vasiṣṭha says:
"They say that gold is the fee for the gift of a cow, which yields great fruit;
for gold is the supreme longevity, serving as the fee—of this there is no doubt."
The gift of a cow rescues seven preceding generations of men;
likewise, by giving gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), it is said to be twice as effective.
Gold is the supreme gift; gold is the highest sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
They say that gold is purifying, as well as the ultimate measure [of value].

In this context, if the word *suvarṇa* is a synonym for gold (*hiraṇya*), then the performance [of the rite] should be according to one's capacity. Others, however, say that since it is illogical to abandon the meaning of "measure" understood from the word *suvarṇa* when it is uttered only once, and because the word *suvarṇa*—being the object of the action expressed by "they say" (*prāhuḥ*) and so forth—is in the accusative case, its specific gender is determined; therefore, it is more reasonable that it refers specifically to a measure. This being the case, the contingency of an indefinite performance is avoided, and likewise, the phrase "in that manner" (*tathā*) as referring to the measure would also be consistent. On this point, some raise an objection:
This very same procedure shall apply, and those same implements are prescribed;
this rule is declared to be the same for all cows whatsoever.

According to this statement, since even a cow that is directly perceived would acquire all the characteristics of a "sugar-cow," one must likewise adopt [the practice of] having ears made of mother-of-pearl and feet made of sugarcane.

That is incorrect. By the phrase "the tenth [cow] would be by its own nature" (*svarūpataḥ*), the word *svarūpa* itself—by conveying the cow that possesses the form of a cow with her calf and is devoid of implements and so forth—excludes a counterfeit made of mother-of-pearl or the like. Furthermore, although the word "all" (*sarva*) depends on the context, it remains excluding the cow that is the actual substance (*svarūpa-dhenu*). Therefore, the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the molasses-cow (*guḍa-dhenu*) is to be performed according to that [procedure for the material cow]; however, the rule concerning the golden-horned [cow] to be mentioned later is indeed distinct. Thus, everything is faultless. This concludes the procedure for the gift of a cow (*godāna-vidhi*). Now, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
A cow with her calf, having a bronze bell-halter, golden horns, and silver hooves,
scented with fine silk and linen cloths, and provided with a bed and coverlets.
Having gratified the Brahmins with many flowers and fruits,
the man who then bestows a cow adorned with perfumes and garlands [attains great merit].
One should then bind it with a soft cord, having first secured it with both [types of] fastenings as used by all the gods.
O observer of noble vows, one should then offer kusha grass, golden seeds, sesame seeds, and siddhārthaka mustard seeds, along with water, while reciting this mantra.
She who consists of all the gods, the milch-cow of plenty, likewise composed of all the worlds,
the cause of all the worlds, and she who is saluted by all the gods.
"I bestow this auspicious, great being for the sake of the inexhaustible.
Having given a cow in this manner, wherever he may be reborn, [he shall obtain one].
Having gone to various places, she delivers those beings from fear;
having traveled through all the worlds, she rejoices just as a man does.
Thus born as a human being, he becomes possessed of a thousand cows, endowed with great strength,
handsome, wealthy, and blessed with many sons.
Kātyāyana says: [One should give] a cow endowed with good character, wearing a sacrificial upper garment, having a bronze milking vessel, and possessing horns tipped with gold.
O Blessed One, having given [this] to a beloved Brahmin,
one goes to the most meritorious and immortal worlds.
Saṃvarta:
He who gives a healthy, milch cow of good disposition, accompanied by her calf— her horns adorned with gold and her hooves with silver.
As many hairs as there are on that cow along with her calf,
for so many years does that man dwell in the presence of Brahmā.
Devala said:
Its two horns are made of gold,
its hooves are made of silver, its udder is made of bell-metal, its back is of copper, and it is provided with a pair of cloths.
Adorned with flower garlands and decorated with incense bells and fly-whisks,
it is given with the tail-end [of the cow] by one endowed with faith and accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having given thus, enriched by the enjoyment of his gift and surrounded by a multitude of celestial women,
he rejoices in heaven for as many years as there are hairs on the body of a calf.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a golden-horned cow,
according to the Nandipurāṇa. [456]
Whoever [gives] a cow with perfectly complete limbs, with horns adorned with gold, gentle-tempered, well-behaved, with silver hooves, and well-covered with variegated cloth;
One should likewise give a cow together with a copper vessel and a *kutapa* (a woolen blanket from Nepal) upon which her feet have been placed; by doing so, one shall attain imperishable heaven.
As many hairs as there are on a cow, for that many years does the donor dwell in heaven while remaining within the lineage of those who give birth; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a cow with golden horns;
the merit from the gift of a Kapila cow is remembered as being a hundred times greater than this.
Now, in the Matsya Purāṇa: "The two horns [of the cow] should consist of ten suvarṇas, the hooves should be provided with five palas each,
and the bell-metal or copper vessel should likewise weigh fifty palas."
The donor shall attain heaven until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the kalpa.

It should be understood that five palas of silver [are required]; copper for the back and bell-metal for the milking vessel; a pair of garments for clothing, and gold as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must also be known. This is the procedure for the gift of the cow with golden horns.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
One should give a cow to a householder Brahmin who is complete in the Vedas—
a cow whose horns are adorned with gold and which is accompanied by its calf and a bell.
[457] A cow that was recently delivered, thrice-blessed, satisfying the surface of the forehead [with milk],
having a bronze milking vessel, and satiated with salt, grass, and water;
Having grasped the tail of the cow with his hand, which holds gold,
the householder Brahmin learned in the Vedas should cause that acceptance of the gift to be performed.
This Gomātā, the destroyer of sins, bestows enjoyments and happiness;
Kṛṣṇā should be known as the giver of heaven, and Gaurī as the increaser of one's lineage.
