The red [stone] should be known as the bestower of beauty; the yellow is the destroyer of poverty;
the black antelope-colored one bestows sons; and the blue increases righteousness.
A tawny cow destroys all sins, and one of various colors bestows liberation.

"Fresh" means young in age; "possessing the three prosperities" means endowed with the quality of yielding the milk of moral conduct (*śīla*); "satisfied by salt, grass, and water" means always content with mowing and so forth.
This is the procedure for the gift of a cow with golden horns, according to the *Ādityapurāṇa*.
He who gives a black cow, covered with a cloth, well-adorned,
provided with a garland of bells, and decorated with flowers;
By giving [this] to the twice-born according to the prescribed rules, one does not see the world of Yama;
it bestows long life, health, sovereignty, and whatever desires are in the mind.
He who gives away a white-bodied [cow], adorned with divine jewels,
provided with garlands of bells, and likewise embellished with flowers;
Incense should be offered to its mouth, and its mouth should be filled with ghee;
it should be auspicious, adorned with golden horns and ornaments, and having silver hooves.
A beautiful cloth, covered with silk, should be given to one engaged in the practice of meditation.
Now hear the fruit of merit for him who gives a white cow.
Whatever sin has been committed since birth, whether inherited from one's mother or father,
perishes at that very moment for the hand raised against a noble family.
By the mere words, "I give a cow here," one is purified in every way—
father, grandfather, and likewise great-grandfather.
Those dwelling in hell are liberated and they go to the world of Soma;
indeed, that pure man who bestows a cow shall likewise attain Gaurī.
A man who has always observed ritual purity and fasted for a day and night [should give] a cow with horns tipped in gold,
hooves in silver, and adorned with a tail-string of pearls.
Adorned with garlands of bells and decorated with perfumes and flowers,
the wise man should spread out a woolen blanket and offer incense at its opening.
One should feed auspicious Brahmins with various kinds of food, both solid and liquid;
by the mere utterance of the words "I give a cow," one is purified in every respect.
Whatever misdeed there may be, whether committed against one's mother, one's father, or anyone else— that evil he burns away entirely, just as fire consumes fuel.
For thousands of millions of years, that man rejoices in heaven;
he is praised by all beings and provided with male and female servants and ornaments.
A man shall be born free from disease and endowed with splendor;
he should give a dark-colored cow that is milch, possessed of good character and virtues.
A cow with golden horns, silver hooves, and her tail adorned with pearls;
beautiful and gentle, covered with a silk cloth and decorated with strings of bells.
Adorned with a coil of thread of five colors,
it should be offered in the presence of Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.
By the mere words "I give a cow here," one is purified in every respect,
as are the father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather.
He who gives a blue cow is liberated from those dwelling in hell and remains in the world of Varuṇa for thousands of millions of years.
Rivers flowing with curd and milk exist everywhere at all times;
mountains of ghee and mountains of fresh butter appear.
One who partakes in agriculture becomes wealthy and does not experience bad food.
Thus ends the procedure for various gifts of cows.
In the Mahābhārata:
having given a tawny milch-cow accompanied by a calf of the same color...
One who is observant of good vows and endowed with fine garments is honored in the world of Brahmā.
One should give a milch cow that has a calf of the same age and the same color, a red cow with a matching calf,
one that is well-behaved and covered with a cloth; such a donor is glorified in the world of Indra.
Having given a brindled cow that has a calf of the same color, which is fertile,
well-behaved, and covered with cloth, one is glorified in the world of Soma.
Having given away a brindled, variegated, and milk-yielding cow that has a calf of the same color—
one that is well-behaved and covered with cloth— one is glorified in the world of Agni.
By giving away a cow that is golden-hued like a particle of wind-dust, accompanied by her calf, yielding all desires,
and covered with cloth, one is glorified in the world of Vāyu.
Having given a smoke-colored, milk-yielding cow with a calf of the same color,
well-behaved and accompanied by a garment, one is honored in the world of Yama.
By giving away a cow of golden hue, accompanied by its calf, capable of yielding all desires,
and covered with a cloth, one attains the world of Varuṇa.

The cow is worthy of honor; she is the yielder of all desires, yielding without effort. Having bestowed a golden-colored, tawny-eyed cow, accompanied by her calf and covered with cloth—one that yields all desires—one shall attain the world of Kubera.
By giving away a cow with a calf that has the color of straw-smoke and which grants all desires,
covered with a cloth, one is glorified in the world of the ancestors.
By giving away a fat cow with her calf, adorned and having a white throat,
one attains the excellent Vaiśvadeva station, which is free from all distress.
Having given a milch cow that is white-necked with a black throat, accompanied by a calf of equal age,
well-behaved, covered with cloth, and a Gaurī cow, one attains the world of the Vasus.
One who is well-behaved and easy to milk—
white as a woolen blanket, accompanied by her calf, granting all desires when milked,
and covered with cloth— having given such a cow, one attains the world of the Sādhyas.
By giving a blue-bodied cow with a calf, endowed with all kinds of jewels,
and having gifted the worlds of the Gandharvas and Apsarases, a human being attains them.
One who delights in the gift of cows goes forth after drinking from the masses of clouds;
O King, he shines in heaven upon a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
And a thousand excellent women, beautifully dressed and possessing shapely hips,
delighted that best of men, who was devoted to the gift of cows.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a cow with her calf according to the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Those who bestow a tawny cow, covered with cloth and well-adorned,"
With golden horns, silver hooves, and adorned with pearls on its tail.
She was clothed in white garments and accompanied by the sound of ringing bells.
Having given a thousand Kapila cows along with the sounds of bells and the clamor of their ringing, O observer of noble vows, the practitioner of yoga,
Brahmā— the best among the knowers of Brahman— spoke thus in the city at that very moment.
Indeed, for as many thousands of millions of years as there are pores on the body of Kapila, one rejoices in heaven.
A cow with horns adorned with gold, hooves of silver, and her tail decorated with jasmine flowers, provided with a bronze milking vessel, covered with a cloth, and fully ornamented.
By giving [this] to the best of the twice-born, a man is glorified in the heavenly world;
one tawny cow (kapilā) is considered equal to the gift of ten cows.
Yājñavalkya: A milch cow with golden horns, hooves of silver, well-behaved, accompanied by a garment and a bronze vessel, should be given along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The giver of this [cow] attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs on her body;
if she is a Kapila cow, moreover, he delivers his lineage up to the seventh generation.
Vyāsa says:
By giving away a tawny cow with golden horns, silver hooves,
and a copper milking vessel, along with her calf, one rescues seven generations of one's lineage.
Indeed, for as many hairs as there are on that cow together with her calf,
for that many years does she rejoice after reaching the world of Surabhi.
Supramundane;
joined with bells and fly-whisks, adorned with a network of tinkling bells;
endowed with divine garments, and decorated with golden mirrors.
A young, well-behaved, milk-yielding cow, accompanied by her calf—
specifically one that is tawny— should be given according to the prescribed rite in the presence of Śiva.
The mantra for the gift is found in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"O Kapilā, you are worthy of worship by all beings, O Rohiṇī;
since you consist of the holy fords and the gods, therefore grant me peace."
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a tawny cow (*kapilā*),
according to the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"The two horns [of the cow] shall consist of ten *suvarṇas*, and the hooves shall be provided with five *palas* of gold."
Copper weighing fifty palas, and bell-metal (kāṃsya) of exactly that same weight.
The cloth should be threefold [the size of the cow], and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) fourfold;
with these, one should adorn the cow, embellishing her with bells and ornaments.
By giving a tawny cow to a preeminent Brahmin, one may attain liberation;
a great tawny cow is traditionally defined as being endowed with double the usual household utensils.
Having given it to the foremost of Brahmins, she bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation;
she is released from the tenfold sins committed throughout seven lifetimes.
Whatever other desires a person prays for, he attains them all;
and in the end, he undoubtedly obtains the fruits of both heaven and liberation.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a tawny cow (kapilā-dāna). Now follows the gift of a cow dedicated to a deity. In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"To the south of the deity, a cow should be positioned facing north."
Having placed the calf facing westward and the Brāhmaṇa facing northward.
Then, facing eastward, the sacrificer should worship the Brāhmaṇa;
the Brāhmaṇa himself should accept [the gift] with the mantra beginning "Who gives? (ko dadāti).
The deity here is Maheśvara.
Having given such gifts as these, the donor goes to the abode of Śiva;
having enjoyed inexhaustible pleasures there, he finally attains the eternal Brahman.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"O King, [one should choose] a cow that is either blue, white, pale-red, or even tawny;
one that yields good milk, is affectionate toward her calf, is easy to milk, and has beautiful limbs."
Having taken [the image], one should worship the Goddess according to the rules with auspicious lotuses,
and with incense made of the five exudations, namely turuṣka, aguru, and candana.
Having first offered the mantra,
one should prepare the food offering (naivedya) consisting of milk-rice mixed with ghee, and likewise ask her for forgiveness.
One should present a cow with its calf, along with gold, cloth, and a bell-metal vessel, to a twice-born who is a devotee of Śiva; thus one shall attain great merit.
[464] For as many hairs as there are on that [image], for so long shall he dwell in the city of the Goddess;
having cast off his sins right here, O best of kings, he is reborn [in that state].
In the *Viṣṇudharma*, Māndhātṛ said:
"O best of the twice-born, tell me what gifts should be given for the purpose of pleasing Keśava and Śiva."
By whatever procedure a man’s gift brings happiness and secures attainment in this world and the next, it remains unimpaired.
Vasiṣṭha said: First, I shall describe the gift of a cow according to the sequence of direct practice, and by whatever procedure that is required for the cow, without excessive detail.
Then, O lord of men, having reached an auspicious day, having bathed and likewise offered libations to the ancestors,
and having observed a fast, one should consume the five products of the cow.
Having performed the consecration with ghee and milk for both Viṣṇu and Śiva,
one should worship him according to the rules, in due order, with flowers and other offerings.
Having positioned a milch cow that has calved once— *gṛṣṭi* meaning one who has given birth only once— facing either north or east,
together with her calf, clothed in garments, and wearing a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
With golden horns and silver hooves, it was established upon gold.
According to one's ability, one should present [the gift] to a Brāhmaṇa along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), saying:
"May cows be before me; may cows be behind me."
"May cows dwell within my heart; I abide in the midst of cows.
Having then performed a circumambulation of that cow and that best of brahmins, [he departed].
"Accept this cow given by me to you;
may Govinda be pleased with me for the removal of my sins."
In the Vahni Purāṇa, however, there is this additional mantra:
"O Goddess, that cow which belonged to Kāśyapa, Atri, or Gautama,
yields the fruit of all desires in this world and in the next."
Having addressed that brahmin Govinda in this manner, O King, one should provide for him;
and as he departs, O lord of men, one should follow him for eight steps.
He who bestows a cow upon a Brahmin according to this rite goes to the world of Viṣṇu, his self enriched with the fulfillment of all desires.
O Lord of the Earth, a man liberates seven descendants, seven ancestors, and himself from the sins committed during seven lifetimes.
"O King of kings, at every step a man obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha and Gosava sacrifices; thus did Hari speak to Dakṣa."
O King, it truly becomes a cow of plenty that milks all desires at all times,
and it is a remover of sins for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
For all sins committed unknowingly, this expiation is declared: namely, remorse, further increased by [virtuous conduct].
The fruit for all other gods follows one birth;
the fruit for Hāṭaka, Kṣiti, and Gaurī follows seven births.
O King, by giving this according to the prescribed rite, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other human beings have attained worlds that yield all desires.
Those learned in the scriptures declare that there is no gift in this world more purifying than that given to cows; thus,
the gods, desiring [to attain them], sought after them with great efforts.
It should always be given according to the prescribed rite to the most excellent of the twice-born.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a cow dedicated to a deity. Now follows the gift of a cow to the deities. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"He who gives a milch cow to Śiva or even to Viṣṇu..."
Having given a cow for the purpose of a ritual bath and offering, he goes to the Supreme Brahman.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"Whoever gives a young, milch cow to Sūrya,
by him the entire world, both moving and unmoving, becomes as if given."

"Saurī" means a cow born of the Sun, that is, the daughter of the Sun. Having given a beautiful, well-lactating, noble-bred tawny cow for the purpose of ritual bathing and fire-rites, it is as if a hundred cows have been given.
The man who, having thus adorned a cow, gives it to the Sun,
shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Likewise:
"He who gives a cow with both mouths to the Sun shall obtain that same fruit which is gained by giving the earth consisting of seven islands."
When two feet and half the head have emerged,
then that earth should be known as complete, along with its mountains, forests, and groves.
[467] Now, the gift of eleven bulls (*vṛṣabhaikādaśī-dāna*). From the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Ten cows together with one bull are known as the 'eleven-bull' gift."
Having thus offered it to Śiva with a pure inner self,
Possessing a self equal to the eleven Rudras through qualities such as power and enjoyment, he,
being self-controlled, rejoices at will in all the worlds beginning with Śiva.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "Ten cows together with one bull— that is, eleven bulls—
having been offered here to the Sun, hear what fruit one obtains."
With a self equal to the twelve Ādityas and endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest,
he rejoices at will in heaven throughout all the worlds, beginning with those of the Sun.
Now, the gift of one hundred cows and a bull. From the *Śivadharmottara*:
One should give a bull and a hundred very beautiful cows to Śiva;
hear what fruit one shall obtain, together with those born of twenty-one generations of one's lineage.
With celestial palaces resembling ten million suns, fulfilling all desires,
numbering many thousands of vehicles, and honored by both asuras and gods;
Endowed with the essence of the Śatarudra, like a second Vīrabhadra,
he shall go to the divine city of Śiva and become the sovereign of all without exception.

In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: O King, listen to what fruit one obtains by giving a hundred cows to the Sun-god, having gone there truthfully, together with those born of twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Resembling ten million suns, like a second maker of day,
the king goes to the beautiful city of the Sun and sports there like the Sun himself.
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures during the dissolution of all embodied beings,
he casts off the cloak of delusion and enters the solar orb.
The omniscient one, supreme as the sun, established within his own pure self,
is all-pervading due to his perfection and becomes radiant like the sun.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a cow to a deity.
Now follows the procedure for the three-night rite of the gift of a cow, as stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
[One should give] a cow with horns tipped in gold, hooves of silver, and adorned with ornaments of pearls on her tail.
She was clothed in unwashed garments and possessed a bronze milking vessel.
Having slept on the bare ground for three nights and subsisted on cow's milk for three nights,
he satisfies a satisfied Brahmin by giving him a gift while the latter is clothed in a garment.
O illustrious one, having sustained his life for three nights with milk products accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
O Brahmins, by giving a tawny cow (kapilā) in this manner, a person obtains a fruit even greater than the number of years equal to the hairs on that cow.
In the Mahābhārata:
[469] Having fasted for three nights with water and slept upon the ground, cows should be given to those who have been satisfied and gratified.
Having given milk for three days from cows whose calves have been suckled, which have good offspring, and which are well-tended, one should subsist on cow-products.
Likewise: Having honored the twice-born and informed him of the preparations for the following day, he,
firm in his vows, should engage Rohiṇī for the purpose of the gift.

Having announced that it is the next day’s ritual procedure and having made it known that the attendance must be performed at the time of dawn, he should utter the invocation: "O you who possess all limbs and are abundant! And having entered into the midst of the cows, he should recite this sacred text:
"The cow is my mother, the bull is my father;
heaven is my refuge, I take my stand upon it."
Having resorted to the single speech that is foremost among all words, the sage utters this regarding the gift of cows.
Indeed, he attains equality with the cows, sharing their friendship and their vows;
by traveling even a single short distance with them, he is immediately liberated from his impurity.

Indeed, a cow whose bull and calf have been released should be given away at the sight of the sun; for "utsṛṣṭa" means abandoned or released, and she is one by whom the bull and calf have been released. Furthermore, "ūrjasvinī" and "ūrjamedhā" refer to the sacrifice.
The embryo is the foundation of immortality in this world;
the streams are meritorious states belonging to Prajāpati— this is the meaning of the explanatory passage (arthavāda) found in the Śruti.
May the solar cows gladden my sins;
likewise, may those who are well-yoked be for my journey to heaven. May they, being invoked by me, grant protection as I give.
In that same way, may all my aspirations be fulfilled.
In the disposal of remains, in liberation from the body through ritual acts,
and in the pursuit of the highest good, you Sarasvatīs are fully engaged; you are eternally endowed with meritorious deeds.
Point out to me those regions inhabited by those who perform meritorious deeds.
Whoever you are, that am I today, being of one essence;
having given you, I am the giver of myself. You have been honored, and thus you have appeared within my very mind.
Protect [him], you who possess both gentle and fierce forms!
Thus, in the presence of that [Brahmin], the giver of cows, having first spoken the first half according to the rule and with the traditional vision,
the twice-born man should stand as a guarantor for the remaining half.
One who knows the ritual procedure for the gift of a cow should accept it.
The first half [of the verse] begins with "as far as you have come," and so forth.
One should say, "I give a cow," when bestowing the wealth of a cow during the *arghya* rite;
for there is an injunction that she must be bowed to as the "belonging to Viṣṇu" (*vaiṣṇavī*) from her udder.
One should proclaim her names in their proper order, one after another;
the fruits are thirty-six, eight, and twenty thousand [respective results].
Having thus understood these groups of cows and other animals in their proper order,
the giver of cows attains them all in the eighth stage.

*Arghyam* means worthy of honor; *usrvasu* means wealth in the form of cattle, which he was giving (*pradadat*). *Udhasyam* refers to milk; those possessing it are *udasyā*. [471] In the eighth step: when a cow has been given and is walking away, at the eighth stride—there, one who gives a cow is of virtuous character and fearless, a giver of honor, and one who bestows wealth upon a draft animal (*nasyota*) is indeed a lover.
O Dawn, you who bear the burden and lead as a wise one— those Vaiṣṇavas are indeed renowned as the worlds of the Moon.
Having given a cow, one should observe the cow-vow for three nights and dwell with them for one night;
on the Kāmyāṣṭamī, one should likewise conduct oneself for three nights.
Or with the fluids of cows, or with their dung, or with their secretions.
By the gift of a bull, one becomes devoted to the Vedic vows;
by the gift of a pair of cattle, one attains the Vedas; likewise, having followed the prescribed rite for cows, one becomes a performer of sacrifices.
One who does not know the ritual does not attain the highest worlds.

"Vasudā" means a giver of wealth. "Kāmī" means one who possesses the fruits of his desires. "Udhasya" means a bringer of the dawn; the meaning is one who causes the Gāyatrī to descend. "Kāmyāṣṭamī" is the eighth lunar day conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism. "Rasaiḥ" refers to curds and other such substances. "Prasravaiḥ" refers to milks. "Vedavratī" means one who possesses the fruits of Vedic vows. "Gavāṃ yajvā" means a sacrificer of cows, that is, a donor of cows.
He who indeed gives all earthly desires gathered in one place, as well as the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadughā*); [to him, the earth is given].
[472] Regarding those [women] who possess the flood of the qualities of a Samyaktva-Arhatī,
the bestowal of iron has been prescribed for them.
One should not assist one who is not a disciple, nor one who lacks the vows, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one whose intellect is crooked.
For this Dharma is secret to all the world; one should not conceptualize these dharmas here and there.
Thus ends the procedure for the three-night *godāna* ceremony.
Now Vṛddhagautama says:
[One should give] a milch cow, pleasing to the heart, adorned with ornaments such as a bell.
A man [should give] a cow with golden horns and silver hooves, wrapped in cloths.
One should give that [bed], accompanied by five *droṇas* of each of the nine kinds of grain and including gold, to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a family.
For one who is free from greed, peaceful, and especially knowledgeable in the Dharma,
the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed as before, with an abundance of sacrificial wood, clarified butter, and cooked rice.

"As before" means as in the case of the gift of a silver bull. To him who has been honored with rings, the one afflicted by disease should give a black cow to the one of black form, while reciting this mantra, having performed the fire-oblation.
O son of Devakī, destroyer of Cāṇūra, Kaṃsa, and Ariṣṭa, O Kṛṣṇa, who brings joy to the minds of the cowherd women, destroy this hemorrhagic fever!
The mantra for the offering:
By means of this gift, one attains the pacification of *grahaṇī*.
Therefore, this should always be performed by one suffering from *grahaṇī*.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the cow that removes *grahaṇī*.
Likewise:
The giver [should give] a milch cow that is red, with horns tipped in gold,
likewise with silver hooves, and adorned with a red cloth.
A person, having honored him, should give [this] to a Brāhmaṇa who is fire-colored,
using either a pala, half a pala, or even half of that again.
One should give it, bright and joined with gold, or according to one's own means,
to an excellent and most eminent twice-born who knows the meaning of all the scriptures.
Extremely delighted, he should with devotion offer that cow with this mantra:
"May cows be in my heart; may cows be behind me.
O Surabhi, come to the gods; by your grace, let there be no hemorrhoids for me."
The mantra for the *dāna* [remedy]:
It destroys even long-standing *asṛgdara* (menorrhagia).
Therefore, one afflicted by the disease of *asṛgdara* should perform this with diligence.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the cow that destroys menorrhagia. Now follows the gift of the Vaitaraṇī cow. Vyāsa says:
A cow with her calf should be given by one whose death is imminent, according to the previous [prescribed] method.
But in the absence of that, a cow alone indeed serves for deliverance from hell.
As before, according to the ritual for the golden-horned cow;
if at that time he is unable to give the Vaitaraṇī cow,
then another capable person who is free from illness should give it, for it is better to give it on behalf of the deceased.
"Arūk" means free from disease.
[474] Now, the mantra for giving:
At the gate of Yama, most terrible, lies the black river Vaitaraṇī.
"To cross over that Vaitaraṇī river, I give this cow to you."
In the *Brahmavaivarta*:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"That river Vaitaraṇī which is at the most terrible gate of Yama..."
What is its form, what is its measure, and how indeed is it censured?
How are they liberated from it? For whom is it always unfavorable? And for whom is it likewise favorable? Explain this in detail.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen to the measurement and the form of that river named Vaitaraṇī at the gate of Yama, which inspires terror in all beings.
That great river was a hundred yojanas in width;
it was unfathomable and infinite in form, inspiring terror the moment it was seen.
That river has pus and blood for its water and is formed from the mud of flesh;
it is further teeming with worms that have diamond-hard beaks and iron mouths.
It was filled with porpoises and crocodiles joined with thunderbolts and scissor-fish,
as well as other terrible aquatic creatures capable of piercing the vital organs.
There the demigods fall, wailing most piteously, repeatedly lamenting, "O son! O father! Alas, you have wandered away!"
Embodied beings sink deep within it for a long time and fall into exhaustion;
that great river is to be seen by the four classes of living beings.
[475] They cross over by means of giving to her; otherwise, they fall. Those who are righteous and possessed of the virtue of generosity, O best of men, cross over her.
Listen, O tiger among men, Yudhiṣṭhira, as I describe that by which the Vaitaraṇī river becomes favorable for human beings.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, auspicious conjunctions (vyatīpāta), the waning of the day,
and on other meritorious occasions, a gift is bestowed with reverence.
One should prepare a beautiful Vaitaraṇī cow, either pale-red or black,
with horns of gold, hooves of silver, and a bronze milking vessel.
Covered with a pair of black garments, provided with the seven kinds of grain,
and seated upon a copper vessel atop a drona-measure of cotton.
One should indeed fashion Yama out of gold, equipped with an iron staff,
mounted upon a great buffalo, and holding a noose in his hand.
Having constructed a raft made of sugarcane stalks bound together with cloth-straps,
one should place that cow, born from the body of the Sun, upon the raft.
Having prepared it, the learned man should cause it to be illuminated, provided with an umbrella and sandals.

"Seven grains" refers to a *droṇa* measure, as explained in the technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*). A "raft" (*uḍūpa*) is a small boat. Having taken up the circle of water, he should recite this mantra:
Having seen the river Vaitaraṇī at the most terrible gate of Yama,
desiring to cross it, I give this cow Vaitaraṇī to you.
The mantra for acceptance:
Oṃ, O you who are the form of Viṣṇu, best of the twice-born, god upon earth, purifier of the assembly!
This Vaitaraṇī river, together with a sacrificial fee, has been given by me to you.
The mantra for the gift:
Having circumambulated the King of Dharma, the Brahmin, the cow, and likewise the Vaitaraṇī river, one should present everything to the Brahmin.
Holding the tail of that cow and placing the Brāhmaṇa before her, one should say:
"O Dhenuke, wait for me at the great abode of the gate of Yama;
O Goddess Vaitaraṇī, salutations, salutations to you, as I desire to cross over."
The mantra for following [the departing guest]:
One should follow the one who is departing and bring everything back to his house;
when this is done, O protector of the earth, that river shall become a source of happiness.
And by that cow, she who carries the river-water flows;
she obtains all delights, both those divine and those human.
Furthermore, the sick man is freed from disease, and likewise, mindfulness shall be restored.
Thus has this meritorious gift of the Vaitaraṇī by your son Dharmasūnu been recounted by me;
whoever hears or reads this with devotion and with a smile, [attains the highest reward].
He goes to the immeasurable abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Vaitaraṇī cow.
Now, the gift of the "two-faced" (ubhayatomukhī) cow. In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He who gives a cow that is currently giving birth, which is two-faced..."
By means of the procedure as described, he shall obtain the recollection of his past lives.
In the Nandipurāṇa: "He who gives a cow with two faces to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas,
or to a beloved deity, [delivers] twenty-one generations of his lineage."
If a person, devoted to faith, remains near a Brahmin for eons equal in number to the hairs on his body, that man shall be uplifted from hell.
Yājñavalkya says: By giving a cow with its calf and its tail-hair intact according to the previously mentioned rite, one attains heaven for as many ages as there are hairs on their bodies.

According to the previously mentioned procedure—beginning with "having golden horns and silver hooves," as described for the actual cow—Viṣṇu states: "Now, a cow that is about to give birth becomes the Earth itself. Having adorned her and given her along with gold to a Brahmin, one obtains the fruit of the gift of the Earth. On this subject, there is a verse: "By giving a cow with her calf and two openings [teats] to a faithful and composed person, one attains heaven for as many ages as there are hairs on her body and her calf."
In the Mahābhārata:
"As long as a cow is half-given, so long is she considered to be the earth;
he who gives such a cow is deemed to have given the entire earth."
Devala said: As long as the calf has not entered the womb for the delivery of the fetus,
and as long as the cow has not given birth, so long does the earth remain possessed of all things mobile and immobile.

Having adorned it according to the prescribed rule, it should be given accompanied by three *pala* of gold; that with two *pala* is considered middling, and that with one *pala* more (three *pala*) is considered the lowest.
Having given this, a person dwells in heaven, honored by the immortals,
enjoying desired pleasures for as many eons as there are hairs on the body of a calf.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "O King, [one should give] a cow with golden horns, silver hooves, and adorned with a tail of pearls, along with a bronze milking vessel and her calf, to an eminent brahmin."
He who gives a cow accompanied by wealth while she is in the process of giving birth—
here, "wealth" refers to a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and since it will be stated later that this is "abundant," a considerable amount should be given—
as long as the calf has entered the womb and has not yet been released from the fetus.
In that state, the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, should be known as the cow.
He who gives a cow accompanied by wealth while she is in the process of calving,
[obtains] the earth with its oceans, caves, mountains, forests, and groves.
The earth bounded by the four oceans would be given away; of this there is no doubt, O lord of men—as many hairs as there are on the cow and her calf.
O Lord of the Earth, for that same number of yuga-cycles, he [dwells] in the world of the gods,
as do his fathers, grandfathers, and likewise his great-grandfathers.
Without a doubt, he who bestows abundant sacrificial fees shall rescue [his ancestors] from hell;
there, streams flow with ghee and milk, and the mud consists of curds and milk-rice.
Wherever that ascetic may be, he shall be a granter of all desired wishes;
for him, O King, Goloka and the world of Brahmā are easily attained.
And women, whose faces were like the moon and whose complexions resembled refined gold, with broad hips, full breasts, and slender waists, [waited upon him].
Those with eyes like lotuses constantly attend upon him.
In the Varāha Purāṇa:
Having fashioned a cow with golden horns and silver hooves, or alternatively,
having placed gold or even silver into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa...
Then, one should place the tail of a tawny cow in the hand of the Brahmin;
having poured water into his hand, he should cause him to recite [the formula] while endowed with faith.
By him, the earth—along with its oceans and forests, its mountains, woods, and groves, and filled with jewels—would have been given; of this there is no doubt.
By this gift, which is equal to the gift of the earth,
a man goes with his ancestors, who have been delivered, to the imperishable state called Viṣṇu.

One who seizes the property of a Brahmin, a killer of cows, a destroyer of an embryo, one who causes a breach in cooking, one joined with a great sin, a deceiver, and a defiler of the Veda— [these are all purified by this].
One who reviles Brahmins and defames their actions—
even if thus possessed of such a sin— is purified by the gift of cows.
And he who should give a cow with two faces, covered with refined gold,
on that day he should subsist on milk-rice or maintain himself on milk alone.
With a thousand pieces of gold, or even with half of that;
or half of that again, or a hundred, or fifty, or even half of that.
One should give according to one's ability, free from stinginess regarding wealth;
please accept this "both-mouthed" [cow], and may she indeed belong to me after you have bathed her.
"Be ever the bringer of well-being for me, whose lineage is pure.
Having recited "Irāvatī" and "Dhenumatī," one should then recite the *devasya tvā* mantra.
I accept you, O cow, especially for the sake of my family;
may there be perpetual well-being for you, O Mother of Rudra, salutations, salutations!
"O Vasundharā, one should mutter the mantra: 'I entrust this to you, O Heaven; Earth, you receive it. Who gives this to whom?'"
"O Goddess, one should release the Brāhmaṇa and lead the cow to his house;
one should give her with both heads [of the cord]," so says Cyavana in the continuation of the text.

Regarding the time for giving her away: the time of her calving is required and no other time need be awaited. [The auspicious times include] Vyatīpāta, the equinoxes (viṣuva), the solstices (ayana), the sixteenth beginnings of the lunar months (ṣaḍaśītimukha), Viṣṇupadī, and eclipses.

All times are indeed auspicious for merit; specifically, when she has given birth halfway through her pregnancy, the donor, having bathed, should speak to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning, character, truthfulness, purity, conduct, noble birth, ritual action, and other virtues. Having prostrated at the proper time, he should say: "O Lord, I am exceedingly terrified of this unfathomable and shoreless ocean of *saṃsāra*; may I deliver ten descendants, ten ancestors, and myself by resorting to you, O Master, as a worthy recipient of gifts. And he, with a mind of grace and not out of desire for wealth, should accept it. The donor should then consecrate it with these mantras: "You are the Great Earth, the Cow of the Universe (*viśvadhenu*"; "Who is this? From whom? When it has been accepted, he should pull a calf toward it with his right hand. While there is still a fetus within, he should mutter: "May there be no harm to living beings" (*mā hiṃsīḥ sattvānām*). Once it has emerged, he should kindle a fire and satisfy the gods, the ancestors, the rivers, the mountains, the trees, the oceans, the *nāgas*, and the medicinal herbs with their respective mantras. The mantra-padas for them are: "The gods who dwell in the eleven heavens" (*ye devāso divy ekādaśasthāḥ*); "Desiring you, we place you" (*uśantas tvā nidhīmahī*); "This my [gift], O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī" (*imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati*); "By the stones and our prayers, O Mother" (*adribhiḥ matibhiś ca nohite*); "O Tree, grow with a hundred calves" (*vanaspate śatavatsa niroha*); "Those whose chief is the ocean, from the midst of the waters, like a serpent with its coils, it encircles Rāhu" (*samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ salilasya madhyād ahir iva bhogaiḥ paryeti rāhum*); "The winds are honey-sweet for the one who follows the Truth" (*madhuvātā ṛtāyataḥ*). Following that, he should satisfy the Earth with verses addressed to the Earth: "Heaven and Earth, first-thought" (*dalair dyāvāpṛthivī pūrvacittam*); "Which two great ones, Heaven and Earth, for us" (*ye mahī dyau pṛthivī ca naḥ*); "The wide, broad, vast, and deep ends" (*urva pṛthvī bahule dare ante*); "The tawny one has lowed, fashioning the waters" (*gaurīr mimāya salilāni takṣatī*). With such verses, he offers eighty-four oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) and feeds the Brāhmaṇas, causing them to recite benedictions (*svastyayana*). Now they proclaim the fruit of this rite: it instantly purifies one who eats what is unfit to eat, one who drinks what is unfit to drink, a killer of a Brāhmaṇa, or a killer of a father. Having approached a teacher’s wife, a daughter, a friend’s wife, a mother, a maternal aunt, a maternal uncle’s wife, a sister, a sister’s daughter, a pupil’s wife, a nurse, or any other woman who should not be approached, one should give her—both her head and her attendants—to a Brāhmaṇa. Her "attendants" consist of gold, silver, jewels and the like, fields, villages, or grain, clothes, salt and other goods, sandalwood and other perfumes, a hundred cows, half of that, or even half of that, or all one's possessions, together with her, one should give to the Brāhmaṇa for the sake of liberation from great sins (*mahāpātaka*), for the sake of complete release.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a cow with two faces. Now, in connection with the gift of a cow, the gift of a bull is also described. Regarding this, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"Having produced the grain-crops, they graze upon the grass."
They carry that very same entire burden once again;
yet, untroubled by the weight, they do not utter a word.
Oh, how the world of living beings is sustained by oxen!
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "In ancient times, Brahmā fashioned a bull as the embodiment of Dharma—
white in color and four-footed, because it possesses the single quality of pure goodness (*sattva*)."
He said, "It is Dharma. He is Dharma; by Dharma the subjects are sustained.
Since he is the embodiment of Dharma and a bull (vṛṣa), he supports the subjects upon the earth.
Therefore, by the gift of a bull, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is considered given;
having placed an umbrella, sandals, and a blanket at its side there.
Having worshipped Vṛśa with flowers and other offerings, free from stinginess regarding wealth, the man who gives with faith— the King of Dharma does not release him from that.
He who conquers the giver [of gifts] through all kinds of crops and comforts is indeed a conqueror.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "He who indeed gives a well-behaved ox that carries its burden well,
having provided an umbrella, sandals, and a blanket for both its sides,"
When a man gives to a learned brahmin who is endowed with moral conduct and knowledge of the Vedas, who is joyful and disciplined,
under the Puṣya asterism, his own birth star, or during the solstices and equinoxes;
Having given that ox to him, adorned with all kinds of jewels,
having given that ox to him at that place, O great sage.
"Even for one afflicted by hunger and thirst, [a gift] is accepted in his presence;
having given it, one attains the worlds of Prajāpati, free from sorrow. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, [he has] a throat and a long-hanging dewlap.
Then, having given to a Brahmin a young, strong, and well-trained ox,
a bearer of the plough possessed of infinite power;
He attains the worlds of one who gives ten cows.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Having offered a bull endowed with excellent qualities to the refuge of Śiva,
one shall obtain the auspicious fruit of giving ten cows.
Bṛhaspati says:
One should become a knower of the Vedas by the gift of a bull;
the attainment of the Vedas occurs through the gift of a *yogudha*.
Devala said: Having given a pair of bulls or even a single bull, one shall go to the abode of the gods;
he who gives a pair of plow-oxen enjoys double the pleasures for the duration of a Manvantara.
Furthermore, he who gives two oxen, well-yoked with a plow,
adorned according to his means, possessing good limbs and auspicious marks, to a twice-born man;
With his soul purified of all sins and endowed with all desires,
he dwells in heaven for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
He who gives a virtuous bull, free from physical defects, according to the prescribed rite,
enjoys ten times the fruit of the gift of a cow.
A young bull, endowed with vigor, the leader of a herd accompanied by a hundred others,
a lord of cattle with massive horns and adorned, [was given] to the lord of Brahmins.
O scorcher of enemies, those who bestow a bull upon one learned in the Vedas are born again and again endowed with sovereign power.
"By a hundred," the remainder [of the sentence] is "female cows. "With many horns" means with golden horns. Yama says:
"By giving a tamed bull capable of bearing the yoke, together with an umbrella and sandals, one enjoys the same fruit as that which comes from the gift of ten cows."
From the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Janārdana, as I listen to this nectar of your words, I [am filled with joy]."
I do not attain satisfaction, for curiosity has indeed arisen within me.
[484] It is said that Govinda, the lord of cattle, renowned throughout the three worlds,
gladdens the triple world by the gift of a bull.
O Acyuta, please tell me the fruit of that gift of a bull.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen as I describe to you the divine fruit of the gift of a bull;
it is pure, purifying, and indeed the best of all gifts.
A single bull capable of bearing the yoke is equal to ten milch-cows;
indeed, one bull excels the gift of ten cows.
And the bull, O son of Pāṇḍu, was well-proportioned in limb,
healthy, young, auspicious, of good character, and free from all defects.
The bearer of the burden alone establishes a great lineage;
he becomes a protector in saṃsāra—of this there is no need for deliberation.
Having adorned a peaceful bull on an auspicious day that has arrived,
one should present it to a Brahmin, equipped with a silver-tipped tail.
O Indra among kings, listen to this mantra which I shall speak to you:
"You are Dharma in the form of a bull, the bringer of joy to the world."
"Therefore, O Eternal One, protect me as the abode of the eightfold form.
Having spoken thus, accompanied by the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and having prostrated, one should dismiss [the deity].
Whatever sin has been committed over seven lifetimes through the actions of speech, mind, and body—
all that indeed goes to dissolution by the merit of the gift of a cow.
Having ascended a divine vehicle, shining and most beautiful, yoked with bulls that moves according to one's will, he ascends to the heavenly world.
O Lord of the Earth, for as many hairs as there are on that bull,
for that many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of cows.
Having descended from Goloka, he is born here in this world as a twice-born,
a performer of the Sattrayajña sacrifice, possessed of great splendor, and honored by all brāhmaṇas.
Those who bestow a bull that is vigorous, capable of bearing burdens, firm-necked, and endowed with all the remaining qualities of a bull,
obtain the merit that results from the gift of ten cows.
Truly, those who exist on earth become partakers of the fruit thereof.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a bull.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now I shall describe, in brief, the gift of a golden bull.
Then, one should have the form of a bull fashioned out of a thousand pieces of gold.
Alternatively, the wise man may [worship] with half of that, or again with half of that,
or even with one hundred and eight [offerings], [representing] the bull who is the embodiment of Dharma.

In this context, however, it is not possible to determine the specific measure of the vessel by means of a number such as "thousand" applied to the gold; therefore, the expectation must be fulfilled by the word *niṣka* introduced previously, especially since we observe that in the gifts mentioned in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*, the transactions are conducted using *niṣkas* alone.
One should cause a mark (*puṇḍra*) in the shape of a crescent moon to be made on the forehead;
the hooves, moreover, should be made of crystal and silver.
The forehead mark (*puṇḍra*) should be made of *tilaka*, crystal, and silver for the hooves.
The neck should be adorned with a ruby (*padmarāga*), and the hump with *gomedaka*. Upon the neck, one should cause a bell and a circlet variegated with jewels to be fashioned.
One should have a bull-emblem fashioned there, with a serpent formed by small bells,
at the previously mentioned place and time, upon the mandala on top of the altar.
Maheśvara has the bull as his emblem. Viśvakarman describes the characteristics of that form:

"Maheśvara has three eyes, four arms, and is adorned with a circle of matted hair; he holds a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the phrase "at the previously mentioned place and time," the specifications for the location, time, sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), altar (*vedī*), and so forth, as prescribed for the *tulāpuruṣa* gift in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*, are to be understood here.
And one should station a bull there facing west in front;
one should worship with devotion the Lord who is mounted upon the bull and whose banner is the bull.
Having worshipped the Lord of Bulls with the Gāyatrī mantra and having paid obeisance with a concentrated mind, he remained composed.
Oṃ, let us know the one with the sharp horns; let us meditate upon the one whose feet are the Dharma;
may that Bull impel us forward.
Thus ends the Vṛṣagāyatrī.
By means of this mantra, the bull should be worshipped for the increase of dharma,
and oblations of ghee and other substances should be offered according to the extent of one's wealth.
The bull, having been fully worshipped, should be given to the Brahmins and to Śiva;
and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must also be given according to one's means.
He who performs this unsurpassed gift of a bull with devotion becomes an attendant of Śiva and rejoices there for a very long time.
One should place a bull facing west in front of Śiva, because it is to be placed behind Śiva. This is stated in the Vātula:
"A beautiful circle of small bells should be made all around the bull-emblem;
thereafter, one should worship the Lord situated in the western direction."
"Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should indeed perform the sacrifice of the bull (*vṛṣayāga*).

Here, the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "to Śiva and" (*śivāya ca*) serves as a conjunction for inclusion. In the *Kāmika*, however, there is also the option of a single fire (*ekāgni*), as it says:
"Alternatively, [one may offer] a single fire consisting of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge."
The ritual for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth is as previously described.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a golden bull as taught in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*.
Ambarīṣa said:
You ought to explain to me that gift which was proclaimed by Sūrya as bringing all happiness, [the practice] of both the wealthy and the destitute.
Vasiṣṭha said: O King, listen now to the manner in which the Lord or Hariḍru performs a gift endowed with all excellent qualities, according to the prescribed rule.
O best of kings, having performed the rite for a bull weighing three *palas* according to the prescribed rules, one should then give it along with a cow, or as much as one's means permit.
Indeed, as many cows as have been mentioned by me, so many bulls should likewise be dedicated; those cows should be assigned to Hari, and the bulls to Hara.
[488] Therefore, O King, best of monarchs, sesame vessels are constantly offered for the destruction of all sins because of their universal nature.
On a surface smeared with cow dung and covered with a fine cloth,
one should place there a bull made of gold or silver, adorned with jewels.
His two eyes were made of pearls upon his blue-hued horns;
his teeth were thirty-two auspicious cloths, and his nose was made of coral.
Its emerald body is described as being made of green stone, its two ears of yellow stone,
its feet of ruby, and its auspicious hooves of silver.
The silver [ornaments] and the hair are covered with linen cloth and a woolen blanket;
the tail is designated as being for the foot—this rule applies to all of them as well.
For crystal, the two testicles [of a bull] and the jewel on the penis are prescribed;
likewise, one should have a cow and a bull fashioned from gold.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the worship of the chosen deity;
O King of Kings, one should then present it to the twice-born with this mantra.
This bull, made of gold, which was the sacrificial gift of Śatānīka Niṣkala,
will undoubtedly deliver me.
Whoever, out of devotion, offers a gift according to their means— whether on a large scale or even when lacking the capacity— it is recorded that this yields infinite fruit.
Even one who is destitute, having thus given gifts without sloth, undoubtedly attains that same fruit as from a small gift; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a golden bull as declared in the Vahnipurāṇa.
[489] Sanatkumāra said:
On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, or of Kārttika, or of Phālguna,
this should be given according to the prescribed rule by those who possess faith and have conquered their anger.
Likewise, with thirty palas of pure Jāmbūnada gold,
or half of that, or half again, or according to one's ability with three palas.
The bull, beautiful in all its limbs, should be fashioned from two or one *pala* of gold;
it must not be made with less than a *pala*, for that brings about suffering, grief, and fear.
One should have a divine pavilion constructed, fashioned from the finest silk;
in its center, one should fashion an auspicious mandala with white rice grains.
Then, at the clear dawn, having risen with his senses conquered,
he put on white garments, bathed, and adorned himself with white garlands and unguents.
Having performed the daily rites, adorned with white garlands and jewels,
whether a man or a woman desiring divine enjoyments, [should proceed].
Then, having placed the bull covered with a pair of white garments in that golden pavilion, which was adorned with much gold;
Then one should worship properly with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and white flowers, using mantras originating from the Purāṇas.
Homage to you, O support of the world; you are beloved by those who perform meritorious deeds.
In this world bereft of you, no one attains anything auspicious.
Salutations to you, the King of Dharma, who indeed assumes the form of a bull;
O Lord of Gods, lift me up from this difficult ocean of saṃsāra.
O Lord of Gods, grant me fame, renown, wealth, grain, and whatever else remains; and in the hereafter, grant me an auspicious destiny.
[490] Having thus worshipped that god in the form of a bull according to the prescribed rites,
he spread out there an auspicious food offering (naivedya) prepared with sacrificial oblation (havis).
Having first fed the twice-born, one should then eat all seasonal roots and fruits from every side as an oblation of food for the gods.
Then, in the evening, one should construct an unsurpassed flower-pavilion,
adorned with auspicious white flowers and fragrances, swarming with bees intoxicated by the scent.
Other fruits and roots, as well as lamps provided with white wicks, should be offered;
and a vigil should be kept at night in the presence of the God of gods.
The courtesans, women of equal status, [offered] Gandharva songs that grant pleasure to the ear,
along with the sound of singing and musical instruments, and the resonant chanting of the Vedas.
Then he should pass that night with playful conversation and dances;
thereafter, at the rising of the dawn, he should rise, having conquered his senses.
Having honored the twice-born there with cows and gold, O best of men, [one should say]:
"May Dharma, who has the form of a bull, be pleased; may the Bull-bannered One be pleased."
Having uttered this supreme mantra, one should present it to the preceptor;
having given this gift correctly according to this rite, O King.
A Brahmin should undertake the conquest of the quarters and perform Vedic rites;
a Vaiśya should go to the ocean; and a Śūdra should perform work as he desires.
Or else, O best of men, one should give this gift on the full moon day of Phālguna;
for this was indeed designated as the "Fierce Rite" (raudra-karma) by Brahmā for Śaṅkara.
[491] Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a golden bull as stated in the *Garuḍapurāṇa*. Now follows the gift of a silver bull.
Now I shall describe the unsurpassed Vṛṣadāna, which removes leprosy;
it is that which should be performed by those afflicted with leprosy to bring happiness to the body.
One should have a palace constructed with three [materials], or with two, or even with one;
likewise, a bright silver bull with horns and hooves made of gold.
One should fashion two golden images presided over by Maheśvara and Umā, according to the sequence previously described.
According to one's means, a wise person should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; he should place those [offerings] in a bronze vessel weighing eight palas.
One should honor a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning, possessed of good conduct, and has his senses restrained, having adorned him with white flowers, unbroken grains, and white garments.
One who expounds all the scriptures, who turns away from accepting gifts,
who is self-controlled, of noble birth, knower of dharma, and who causes no agitation among men.
Having invited him to his home— one who is free from anger and greed and is skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures— he should worship him with devotion according to the prescribed rite.
With armlets, bracelets, garments, garlands, and finger-rings,
one should likewise perform the fire-oblation as before with the mantras dedicated to Maheśvara.
Seated facing north in the presence of Mahādeva,
the knower of Dharma, facing east, should give [the gift] while afflicted by disease, with this mantra.
The Great Lord Maheśāna, whose banner is the bull and who possesses eight forms, out of compassion [bestows] everything—
whether it be white, made of udumbara wood, or even variegated.
[492] And whatever skin diseases or circular patches may arise, O sinless one,
they all originate from the ripening of karma, O Lord of Pārvatī, O omnipresent one.
O Lord of All, be the destroyer of leprosy; O Lord of Pārvatī, protect me!
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a silver bull as stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa.
Baudhāyana says:
"On the eighth or the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, or again..."
With the hide, one should fashion a bull, resplendent with thick, shining hair.
With golden horns, beautiful golden eyes, and a face radiant with jewel-like blossoms,
it was indeed presided over by Maheśvara and Umā in their golden forms.
Then, in that case, one should prepare a single atom (paramāṇu) due to the lack of available materials.
Here, the form of Umā and Maheśvara should be understood as being without intervals, like the gift of a bull mentioned previously.
Having wrapped it with a cloth in a copper vessel consisting of eight palas, one should do so with devotion.
One [offering] for the God, one for the Bull, and indeed one for Pārvatī,
with white flowers, unbroken grains of rice, saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood.
One should worship with the root mantra and perform an oblation of sesame seeds,
offering one hundred and eight oblations mixed with clarified butter using the Āryaka mantra.
The teacher should be endowed with wealth, well-conducted, with senses restrained,
an expounder of the meaning of all scriptures, and likewise peaceful and self-controlled.
Dhiṣaṇa, however, was skilled in the Dharma and caused no agitation among men;
he was an expert in the application of the gift of bulls and was presided over by Haromā.
One should present a bull, equipped with a bell and adorned with a neck-ornament,
seated facing north in the presence of Mahādeva.
Facing east, afflicted by disease, and restrained, one should with devotion recite this mantra:
"O Eight-formed One, Great Lord, O Bull-bannered One, through your grace..."
Whether it be a disease like udumbara or vājina, or likewise daṇḍa and maṇḍalaka,
as well as whatever skin disorders arise from the ripening of past karma.
Whether arising from karma in this life, or again through the fault of the mother,
or through the fault of the father, or likewise everything arising from a disorder of the blood.
O Śaṅkara, beloved of Pārvatī, destroy this supreme body by means of the gift of the bull upon whom Umā is seated.
The mantra for giving:
One should also feed Brahmins, endowed with supreme devotion;
by performing this, leprosy-skins certainly go to destruction.
Therefore, they have declared this to be what must be done by those overcome by leprosy.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a silver bull,
according to the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Having fashioned an excellent bull out of eight *pala*s of silver..."
One should adorn it with pearls and beautiful rubies.
Having gone to the temple of Śiva, properly adorned with a golden ring and beautiful chowries, one should then perform worship to Śiva.
Having recited the Rudrādhyāya together with its secret six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga-rahasya),
the fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed to be performed with sesame seeds and clarified butter using the Śiva-mantra.
Then, having summoned an excellent brahmin who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
and having worshipped Śiva with garments, ornaments, garlands, and other offerings;
O Lord of Umā, Sovereign of the three worlds, Cause of the cause of the universe!
Be pleased by the gift of your own vehicle; salutations be unto you!
One should give that [gift] accompanied by this mantra and a gift of gold;
by the bestowing of this gift, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a silver bull according to the Skanda Purāṇa:
"By the gift of a silver ox, a person travels by means of a vehicle."
He attains imperishable worlds and rejoices together with Indra.
Having fashioned a bull out of silver, starting from thirty palas and ending at three palas, and having adorned it with all kinds of jewels.
Covered with linen cloth and adorned with an arrangement of grain,
one should present it to a worthy recipient at the time prescribed.
By giving gifts in this manner, a person shall obtain all desires;
at the time of giving, the wise one should recite this mantra of giving.
You are Dharma in the form of a bull, the bringer of joy to the world;
you are the eternal foundation of the eightfold forms, O Holy One.
Thus, he who gives a bull made of silver with devotion,
being liberated from all sins, rejoices in heaven like a god.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a bull made of silver, the fourth [type].
Now begins the supreme gift known as the gift of land. Regarding this, in the *Mahābhārata*, Bhīṣma said:
Among all supreme gifts, the gift of the earth is said to be the foremost;
for the earth is immovable and inexhaustible, milking forth unsurpassed desires.
The giver of land milks out garments, jewels, cattle, as well as rice and barley; he prospers eternally among all beings for many years.
As long as the life-span of the earth lasts, so long does the giver of land prosper;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there is nothing superior here on earth to the gift of land.
Those who formerly gave land are now those who enjoy the land;
by their own karma, men prosper both in this world and in the next.
Whoever, as a lord of the earth, should give this sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
having attained rebirth, he shall become a lord of the earth once again.
"In battle he may either abandon his body or give away this entire earth"—
this, they say, is the supreme blessing for those of the kṣatriya lineage.
"O best of men, it is said that the earth, when given, purifies the giver—
even one of sinful conduct, even a slayer of a Brahmin, or even a liar."
She alone delivers one from evil; she alone releases one from sin.
Even for kings who have committed wicked deeds, virtuous people accept them.
They desire no purifier other than the earth, for this is the supreme one;
"Priyadattā" is the eternal, secret name of this queen.
Whether it be giving or even non-giving, its name is supremely auspicious;
for he who takes the land of a virtuous person does not truly acquire land.
[496] By giving land to the virtuous, one indeed obtains land;
for the land always belongs to that righteous man whom the Brahmins instruct.
The enemies of that king do not rule over the earth;
for whatever sin a man, oppressed by the lack of livelihood, commits, [it falls upon him].
Even by the gift of a piece of land the size of a cow's hide, one is purified—
even those kings who have performed mixed deeds and those who have committed terrible acts.
To them, the gift of land—the supreme purifier—should be proclaimed;
the ancients of old considered this to be eternally of little distinction [from other meritorious acts].
Whoever should perform the horse sacrifice, or should give gold, silver, clothing, jewels, pearls, and garments to a virtuous person;
O protector of the earth, he who gives land bestows all of this:
the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, and the forests in their entirety.
O best of men, he who gives land bestows all of this:
medicinal herbs rich in milky sap, and trees endowed with flowers and fruit.
He who gives land including forests and foothills,
having performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees, [attains great merit].
One does not obtain that fruit from the gift of land which one enjoys through austerity,
sacrifice, sacred learning, virtuous conduct, freedom from greed, and truthfulness.
Those who worship their gurus and deities do not fail the giver of land;
those devoted to the supreme welfare of their master, having cast aside all self-interest, are slain in battle.
Even those who have reached the world of Brahmā do not transcend the giver of the ground,
just as a mother always nourishes her own son with her milk.
Just as the earth favors the giver with all its flavors,
so too does the rod of Death— terrible like fire and consisting of torment— act as his servant.
The terrible nooses of Varuṇa do not approach the giver of land;
he [reaches] the ancestors dwelling in the world of the fathers, and the deities in the world of the gods.
He who, with a tranquil soul, gives land to one who is excessively distressed, exhausted by lack of livelihood, and sinking in despair, truly satisfies the ancestors.
By giving land that provides a livelihood, a man becomes a perpetual provider;
just as a cow runs toward her calf, she constantly yields milk.
In this very way, O illustrious one, the earth supports the giver of land;
for having given land that has been ploughed by the furrow, provided with seed, and even bearing fruit.
Just as the increase of the moon occurs day after day, so too does a garden or a refuge become a granter of desires.

Likewise, a gift made upon prepared ground increases with every harvest; regarding this, those who know the past recite a verse concerning gifts made upon prepared ground: Just as a seed sown in well-prepared soil, Having been properly tended, yields abundant fruit, So too a gift bestowed upon prepared ground Increases manifold for the donor in this world and the next.
Having heard this, the son of Jamadagni indeed gave the earth to Kaśyapa;
kings give me alone, and by giving me, you shall obtain me.
O God, in this world, in the next, and thereafter in the state beyond rebirth,
[he attains that] who [knows] this Vedic utterance belonging to the Brāhmaṇas, which is established in Brahman.
When a śrāddha is performed for him, he attains union with Brahman;
or, for those accused by magic spells, it is a great pacification of ill-fortune.
Having given land as an expiation, he purifies ten generations on both sides;
so too does the Brahmin who knows this Vedic teaching.
The earth is indeed considered the eternal source of all beings;
having consecrated the king, one should cause him to hear this sacred tradition.
He who, having heard this, would give away the earth and not take it from a virtuous person—
he is of noble birth, he is a true man, he is a kinsman, and he is a doer of merit.
And that donor who gives away the earth is valiant;
such men shine upon the earth with splendor like the Ādityas.
Those who give fertile land to a twice-born man learned in the Vedas,
[reap rewards] just as seeds sown upon the surface of the earth sprout.
Those who have acquired merit through the gift of land obtain their desires as they wish;
[the fruits of such a gift are] Āditya, Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Soma, and Agni.
And the Lord Śūlapāṇi rejoices in the giver of land,
where there are golden palaces and showers of clothing that grant all desires.
Those who give land go wherever the Gandharvas and Apsarases dwell;
in this regard, they also cite this ancient history.
O Yudhiṣṭhira,
after performing a hundred great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
Maghavān questioned Bṛhaspati, the best among eloquent speakers, regarding this dialogue between himself and Bṛhaspati.
Indra said:
"O Blessed One, by what gift does one’s happiness increase after reaching heaven?
Tell me that, O best of speakers, which is inexhaustible and cannot be taken away."
Thus addressed by the lord of the gods,
Bṛhaspati, the priest of the deities and possessor of great splendor, then replied to Purandara.
Bṛhaspati said: O slayer of Vṛtra, that person of great wisdom who gives gifts of gold, gifts of cows, and gifts of land is liberated from all sins.
"O Lord, Indra of the gods, I consider nothing to be superior to the gift of land,
just as the wise have declared regarding Vasiṣṭha."
A man who bestows land here becomes more pure than the five original ancestors and the six who have gone to the earth; he surpasses these eleven by giving land.
O Purandara, he who gives the earth strewn with jewels is liberated from all impurities and is glorified in the heavenly world.
Just as a king who bestows the vast earth, endowed with all desirable qualities,
becomes a sovereign over kings, so too is the highest gift.
O Vāsava, he who gives a bronze vessel endowed with all desirable things,
all beings think, "He is giving me."
O Thousand-eyed One, that man who gives here this earth, which milks all desires and precedes the fulfillment of every wish, goes to heaven.
O Lord of the Gods, the rivers Madhu, Sarpiḥ, Pravāhinī, Payas,
and Dadhivahā likewise gratify those who bestow wealth upon this earth.
By the gift of land, a king is liberated from all sin;
indeed, no other gift excels the gift of land.
O Purandara, for him who gives land that is auspicious and possesses soft soil,
the worlds acquired through the merit of the gift of land are never exhausted.
In every way, O Śakra, a king who desires constant prosperity and seeks happiness must bestow land upon a worthy recipient according to the prescribed rites.
Even if a man has committed a sin, by giving land to a twice-born man,
he casts off that sin just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
The oceans, the rivers, the mountains, and various sacred fords—
these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the gift of land.
Therefore, O King, having obtained land, a wise man should indeed give it to a Brahmin;
the lord of the earth must never, under any circumstances, retain possession of that land himself.
Having performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma accompanied by ritual fees,
one does not obtain that fruit which one enjoys from the gift of land.
The donor benefits ten generations; likewise, one who seizes it destroys ten.
By taking away land previously given, one goes to hell.
He who does not give after having promised, or who takes back what he has given—
both of these are tormented by the nooses of Varuṇa under the command of Death.
In the waterless forests of the Vindhyas, black snakes dwelling in dried-out hollows are born; they are those who seize the earth.
When a field belonging to Brahmins is seized, tears fall from those who weep, are miserable, and are despondent; [such an act] destroys the family for three generations.
Those who bestow the earth, taking with them one who maintains the sacred fires, who has few servants, and who is fond of guests,
do not approach Yama.
Likewise: [He saw] land constantly filled with sugarcane, barley, wheat, and rice;
abounding in cow-pens and vehicles, and acquired through great prowess.
By giving land containing seeds and furnished with all kinds of jewels, one obtains inexhaustible worlds; for that is his "land-sacrifice."
Having shaken off all impurity, he shall become a king esteemed by the virtuous;
he who bestows the earth is honored by the good in this world.
Just as drops of oil fallen upon water spread out, O Śakra,
so does a gift bestowed upon the ground increase with every harvest.
O Lord of the Gods, women devoted to dance and song, adorned with divine garlands, always attend upon the man who bestows land.
And he who properly gives land here to a twice-born according to the prescribed rite rejoices in heaven, honored by gods and gandharvas, with a radiant countenance.
O Lord of the Gods, a hundred celestial nymphs adorned with divine garlands attend upon the giver of earth in the world of Brahmā.
Spiritual beings always attend upon the man who gives land:
the conch shell, the auspicious throne, the parasol, the earth, horses, and excellent elephants.
The merits of the gift of land, as well as heaps of gold,
result in commands that are always unimpeded and the sound of victory.
O Purandara, the flowers of the gift of land are its fruit: heaven itself;
moreover, the medicinal herbs have gold for their blossoms, and the grassy meadows are made of gold and kusha grass.
A person who gives land attains the ground that yields immortality;
there is no gift equal to land, and there is no teacher equal to sacrifice.
There is no dharma superior to truth; there is no treasure equal to generosity.
Having established this principle of the descendant of Aṅgiras, Vāsava [ruled] over this earth.
Then he gave [the earth], strewn with wealth and jewels, to the descendant of Aṅgiras.
Whoever causes this praise of the gift of land to be heard at a śrāddha ceremony—
for him there shall be no share for the rākṣasas, nor indeed for the asuras.
And what is given to the ancestors shall become inexhaustible; of this there is no doubt.
Devala said: The gift of land has been declared by the twice-born to be the most excellent of all excellent gifts;
having given that, a man is honored in heaven by the foremost of the thirty gods.
Even the ancestors, established in the heavenly world, desire this very thing:
that someone born of our lineage might become a founder of a monastery here.
Those dwelling in hell attain the world of the gods, and those dwelling in heaven reach the supreme state,
just as we who have passed away proceed by its power.
What is surprising in this, that the earth rescues the donor?
It carries across even the twice-born man who has accepted a gift.
The fruit that is obtained by givers through sacrifices, vows,
and gifts is not attained even by giving land measuring only three staffs;
for whatever gift is given here, its result indeed manifests right here in this very world.
Furthermore, by the gift of land, the fruit of all gifts is obtained;
they are blessed, they are doers of good deeds, and they have achieved their life's purpose—of this there is no doubt.
By those men who have bestowed the gift of land according to the prescribed rite upon a worthy recipient.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*,
Haṃsa said:
"O best of men, he who should give even a span's measure of land..."
By that very act, a person certainly attains the fruit of the gift of land.
By giving a plot of land the size of a cow’s hide, one shall attain the world of the Vasus;
by giving a field for vegetables, a man shall obtain the world of the Āṅgirasas.
Having given a grove of trees, one shall attain the world of Māruta;
he who gives a reservoir for the sake of water shall attain the world of Dāruṇa.
Whatever deity’s dwelling it was intended for, that deity he enjoys;
and by giving a pleasure grove, he rejoices together with the gandharvas.
Having given a source of jewels, one is honored in the world of Śakra;
so too for one who bestows upon other worlds a land that is a mine of treasures.
O twice-born ones, his destination in this world has been declared as the sacrificial fire;
and by giving a field for grain, one is glorified upon the back of a serpent.
O twice-born ones, that best of men who indeed bestows land containing mines of collyrium is honored by his ancestors while he remains in the world of Yama.
One who gives land for salt mines is honored in the world of Soma;
one who gives land for the source of medicinal herbs is honored in the world of the Aśvins.
By giving land with its sprouting vegetation to a lord of Śivīs, that best of men attains the world of the Sādhyas; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
He who knows the Dharma and bestows according to the Dharma the ground for all kinds of gifts is honored in the world of fire as one who has provided a mine of fuel.
A man who gives a field of sugarcane, or even a field of rice, attains great merit and goes to the world of Brahmā.
He who bestows land covered with thickets, flowers, and creepers attains the world of Soma and finds all his desires fulfilled.
Then, having given away the earth that yields flowers, fruits, and trees, he sports in the Nandana grove of the celestial mansion with hosts of apsarases.
Having fallen from the heavenly world, one may become a lord of a city;
by giving a house to a Brāhmaṇa, one enjoys the world of the Vasus.
The Brahmin who gives land of excellent quality sports in the Nandana grove;
the giver of a village becomes a king, and the giver of a city becomes a sovereign emperor.
One becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) ruling over the entire earth through the gift of sovereignty;
yet, whoever shall seize land given by himself or given by another, [incurs great sin].
Even if it were only the measure of a single finger, O Supreme Person, one who is deluded by negligence, ignorance, and delusion [fails] even regarding the Dharma for many thousands of years.
Likewise, together with his ancestors, he becomes a worm in excrement;
this occurs whether in his own kingdom or in a foreign realm, for having failed to honor the gods and the Brahmins.
A lord of the earth who seizes land falls into hell for a long time;
however, that man who, having acquired land, establishes [shrines] for the gods and Brahmins, attains merit.
Even a most cruel man attains the heavenly world;
the giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years.

Both the one who seizes it and the one who consents to it shall dwell in hell for as long as the time it takes for the earth to become covered with ripened crops after he has bestowed it, having adorned it.
He goes to the Brahma-world by means of a celestial chariot that moves at will.
In the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa:
[he dwells] on a thousand-yojana expanse where all crops grow.
One should give land endowed with fruit; that is called the gift of land.
When a certain king, having brought the earth under a single umbrella, bestows it upon the twice-born in its entirety,
that is called the gift of land (bhūmidāna).

In the Kūrma Purāṇa: Having divided a plot of land measuring a *gocarma* or more according to one's capacity into three parts, and having given it along with ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one shall go to the city of Śiva.
"Threefold with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)" means that it is accompanied by the sacrificial fee consisting of one, two, or three *suvarṇas* as previously mentioned. Bṛhaspati says:
"Even by the proper gift of a mere *gocarma* [of land], a human being..."
With his sins washed away and his self purified, he is glorified in the heavenly world.
Thirty daṇḍas measured by a staff of ten hastas constitute one nivartana;
ten of those indeed constitute a gocarma, which he who gives to the Brāhmaṇas [attains great merit].
Whatever sin a person, deluded by greed, may commit,
all of that is swiftly destroyed by the gift of land.
Kātyāyana says: A killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a killer of a father, or one who violates the teacher’s bed is liberated;
by giving land endowed with all excellent qualities, one is released from sin.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
With a staff of ten cubits, one should give five [such squares] on each side; this is called a *gocarma*.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Thirty daṇḍas measured by a staff of seven cubits is a *nivartana*;
Prajāpati has declared that three-quarters of this is the measure of a *gocarma*."
O wise one, for that person who gives a hundred nivartanas of land with this measure,
the entire accumulation of their sins is swiftly destroyed.
Or else, he may give half of that, or even just a piece of land the size of a cow-hide; by giving even a cow sufficient for the site of a house, he is liberated from sin.
Likewise: whatever sin a human being commits from birth onwards,
he is purified even by the gift of land the size of a cow-hide.
Where a hundred cows and one bull might stand unrestrained, [that is a herd].
