For those who know the Vedas say that it is indeed the size of a cow-hide.

And here, among these types of *gocarma* plots, the classification into superior, middling, and inferior should be understood; furthermore, gold is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in this case. As Māṇḍavya says:
"Indeed, there is no object superior to land, nor anything whatsoever superior to a cow or gold;
therefore, on earth, for land and for a cow, gold is considered the sacrificial fee by the wise."
The mantra for the gift of land is found in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the gift of land;
may there be peace for me here through the gift of land."
The formal application (prayoga) is right here.

"Oṃ! Today, at this time and in this place, I, of such-and-such lineage, of such-and-such *pravara*, and named such-and-such, being of such-and-such lineage, of such-and-such *pravara*, and named such-and-such, give this land, beloved by Datta and having Viṣṇu as its deity, for the sake of such-and-such desire, to you; it is not mine. Having spoken thus, he should place flowers, *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and water into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa. He (the recipient) should mentally circumambulate the land and perform the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*). If the land is nearby, he should circumambulate it in person. "Oṃ! Today, to one of such-and-such lineage," and so forth—"for the sake of the consecration of this gift of land, I give this gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to you; it is not mine."
Viśvāmitra said:
He who bestows upon a Brāhmaṇa even a piece of land the size of a cow-hide should be known as a giver of everything; like Śakra, he rejoices in heaven.
He who bestows a village or even a city,
or a field rich with crops, upon Brahmins is liberated from all sins.
Bṛhaspati said:
"The ancestors clap their hands and the grandfathers exult:
'A giver of land has been born in our family; he shall deliver us.'"
In the Nandipurāṇa: Having given land that is productive of crops, very pure, situated in a beautiful location, and delightful with fruit-bearing trees, a man attains supreme welfare.

Having given land that is free from saline soil and free from obstacles, endowed with many virtues, and even sufficient for the support of a single person, to a high-souled recipient who is a worthy vessel.
Free from sin, he shall dwell in heaven for ten kalpas.
In the Mahābhārata:
Having bestowed a well-prepared house-site capable of withstanding cold, wind, and heat,
one remains in the world of the gods and is not displaced even at the exhaustion of merit.
Likewise:
"He who gives even a piece of land the size of a span, provided it is unencumbered,
does not sink into hardship, nor does he encounter difficulties."
The wise man shines with joy and rejoices together with Śakra;
as many as are the particles of dust raised by the tip of the plough from the earth,
so many are the hairs on the body of the son of Bhāsa’s enemy.
For as many ages as that, the man who makes a gift of land here shall abide in the city of Śaṅkara.
Approaching a great celestial palace where hosts of gandharvas, kinnaras, asuras, and siddhas wave fly-whisks,
he is honored together with his father, grandfather, and kinsmen.
And the leader of the immortals shall go to the city of Śambhu.
He who seizes land, whether given by himself or given by another,
becomes a worm in excrement and sinks there along with his ancestors.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of land.
Regarding this, from the *Śivadharmottara*:
"He who [gives] land endowed with the word 'Śiva' and productive of all crops..."
A lord of the earth may give the earth; hear now the fruit of his merit.
As many *daṇḍas* as the earth would measure when measured all around,
for that many *kalpas* he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
In this manner, the result should be understood everywhere according to the measure of the staff;
one should report a village, a hamlet, a city, a field, a district, and so forth.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who gives a village endowed with all crops and water, and free from all afflictions, to Śiva.
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit comes from the gift of a village— [by this,
one becomes] endowed with ten million divine women, radiant like ten million suns.
Through the gift of a village, he is joined with many millions of celestial palaces endowed with all desirable things, together with seven times three generations of his family.
He sports at will in the world of Īśvara for imperishable time;
his merit from giving a village is more than a hundredfold that of one who gives a city.
It cannot be fully described even by the gift of the entire land;
for all things—jewels, food, drink, houses, horses, and so forth—are produced upon the earth.
Therefore, by the gift of land, a man becomes a giver of everything.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of land to Śiva.
In the Varāha Purāṇa: [One should give] a district, a village, or even half a village to Viṣṇu, according to one's capacity.
Having given it, he plays without harm in the regions adjacent to Vaikuṇṭha.
The illustrious lord of kings becomes free from disease, fortunate, happy,
a master of all sciences, and also renowned for his fame.
He who offers a thousand nivartanas to Viṣṇu sports among all the gods for the duration of a yuga.
He who propitiates Keśava even with a hundred nivartanas shall become a king upon the earth, extending over a hundred yojanas.
O King of kings, he who gives to Hari even a piece of land the size of a cow's hide is born prosperous for seven lifetimes.
That meritorious soul who, dedicating it to Viṣṇu, gives a field or even a house as an offering of enjoyment, is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the gift of land to Viṣṇu.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: He who [gives] to the Sun a land endowed with fruit and productive of all kinds of crops...
A lord of the earth may give away the earth; hear now the fruit of his merit.
O best of beings, for as many portions of land as shine upon the surface of the earth,
for that many thousands of yugas he is honored in the heavenly world.
In this manner, the result in all cases should be understood according to the substance [offered],
when reporting on villages, hamlets, cities, fields, provinces, and so forth.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who gives a village endowed with all kinds of grain and fruits, and free from all enemies, to the Sun.
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, whatever fruit is found in all vows,
and whatever merit is found in all acts of giving— one obtains that by the gift of a village.
Resembling ten million suns, crowded with ten million celestial women,
strewn with various jewels, and endowed with various mines.
By means of celestial chariots and through the gift of a village, surrounded by twenty-one generations of his kin,
he sports at will throughout all the worlds for an inexhaustible time.
The merit of giving a city is equal to two hundred gifts of villages;
the wise say that the fruit of giving a country is then infinite.
Thus ends the gift of land to the sun. Now begins the supreme gift known as the gift of knowledge (*vidyādāna*). Regarding this, it is said in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"There are three gifts equal [in merit], and three that yield equal fruit."
Truly, cows, the earth, and Sarasvatī are the yielders of all desires.
In the Nandipurāṇa: "That mortal who is devoted to merit, desirous of victory, and seeking to achieve fame,
should indeed bestow knowledge— which grants various desires— in accordance with the prescribed ritual."
The constant bestowal of knowledge indeed surpasses all other qualities of merit and desire;
one should strive to give it to a worthy recipient, for this is the supreme secret.
When a gift is given anywhere whatsoever dedicated to a deity,
by whom can the fruit of all that merit be described?
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"The wise know the gift of knowledge to be the supreme among all gifts;
they say that Śrī herself is the presiding deity of all branches of learning."
Just as Viṣṇu, the causal Puruṣa, is the most excellent among the gods,
so too is Kamalā, whose abode is the lotus, the most eminent among women.
They say that he is the best among the powerful, just as the sun is among luminous bodies;
just as this lord of rivers is the most excellent among reservoirs of water,
so too is the giver of knowledge the most excellent and the weightiest among those who are weighty.
He who bestows knowledge is meritorious everywhere;
they say that the wealth of knowledge is the true wealth, for it brings happiness and security both in this world and the next.
Endowed with stainless knowledge, the self-controlled one attains liberation;
through knowledge he reaches happiness, and through knowledge he reaches the supreme goal.
Knowledge is the foundation of all beings, and knowledge is the source of the deities;
therefore, the wise declare that in this world, the giver of knowledge is the giver of everything.
Bṛhaspati said: A thousand cows and a hundred oxen are equal;
a vehicle is equal to ten oxen; and a horse is equal to ten vehicles.
A maiden is equal to ten horses, and the gift of land is equal to that;
there is nothing equal to the gift of land, and the gift of knowledge is superior to that.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Knowledge is a cow that milks all desires; knowledge is the supreme eye.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of knowledge."
A man who possesses knowledge becomes a vessel for all desires;
therefore, by giving knowledge, everything is indeed given here in this world.
Whatever a man who is capable of teaching others consumes [as food],
that is considered his supreme austerity, equal to the world of Brahmā.
Among all gifts, O illustrious one, the gift of knowledge is supreme in this world, and likewise supreme among ascetic practices;
it bestows the fruit of all desires.

In the Devīpurāṇa: "Because one attains the fulfillment of all goals through the discernment of knowledge and the investigation of what is auspicious and inauspicious, knowledge is considered supreme."
There is no gift superior to the gift of knowledge to be found even in the three worlds;
by giving that, one attains Śiva, the supreme cause.
Likewise: "The established doctrines, treatises on liberation, the Vedas which are the means for attaining heaven and other goals,
the Vedāṅgas, and the Itihāsas should be given for the increase of Dharma."
O Bhairava, by teaching and giving away the Gāruḍa, Vāla, and Bhūta Tantras,
the Mothers bestow fruits upon men.
One attains the status of an astronomer, a physician, or a master of music;
by means of knowledge the world functions, and one discerns both dharma and adharma.
Therefore, knowledge should always be given by those who desire both visible and invisible fruits.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
By the gift of a Dharmaśāstra, one rejoices together with Dharma;
by the gift of the Siddhāntas, one attains Vedic liberation.
And by giving other sacred scriptures, a man is glorified in heaven.
In the Nandīpurāṇa:
"The fourteen branches of knowledge have been proclaimed in their proper order as they exist:
the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), the four Vedas, and the ancient treatise on Dharma."
Mīmāṃsā and Tarka—these are the fourteen sciences.

The Dharmaśāstras are the Smṛtis; the Purāṇas are the ancient ones. From within these very [sciences], thousands of other branches of knowledge have arisen, such as Āyurveda and Sasyaveda, which are proclaimed to have many divisions.
The science of crops is the treatise on agriculture;
and the knowledge of the Self is the soul of all, which destroys the fear of saṃsāra,
brings an end to all suffering, and annihilates all sins.
These sciences have been fully described, arising from many divisions and subdivisions;
likewise there are other sciences of the arts (kalā-vidyās), and others still, the sciences of crafts (śilpa-vidyās).
The science of arts (*śilpavidyā*) is the treatise on the construction of images and so forth.
All these [sciences] are highly auspicious; all accomplish every purpose, and they are considered to achieve distinguished results according to their relative gradations.
The science of the self is indeed preeminent, as are the compendiums of Ayurveda;
likewise, the arts that promote dharma and adharma are effective means for accomplishing crafts and worldly goals.
And the science of agriculture is widespread; these sciences yield great fruits, they are devoted to dharma and adharma, and they bring about the accomplishment of dharma and adharma.
By whatever means a single living being might somehow survive anywhere,
that very knowledge, even if it be insignificant, shall uplift a hundred lineages.
[515] A secondary science is subordinate;
yet whatever knowledge there may be, wherever it exists, because it is a means of awakening,
it shall lead one to imperishable worlds, whether practiced according to rule or otherwise.

Because it is awakening and because it is the cause of awakening; the sense of causation (*ṇyartha*) is inherent in the word "will go" (*prayāsyati*), and thus the meaning is "he will cause [them] to go.
Indeed, by imparting the knowledge of the arts, men go to the presence of Brahman.
By bestowing the knowledge of the arts, a person shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
Having given the science of agriculture, a man— endowed with contentment and possessed of his desires— will undoubtedly enjoy the pleasures of heaven for one kalpa.
By giving the Āyurveda, a man goes to the city of Prajāpati, delivers his ancestors from hell, and attains stainless worlds.

By giving the science of logic (tarkavidyā) to men, one attains the world of Varuṇa; by giving [gifts] such as divine garments to men during the divine Manvantara of the Aśvins, one attains that same realm.
Having given the Mīmāṃsā to a wise man, one may dwell in the city of Indra;
by giving a treatise on Dharma, a person is honored in the heavenly world.
By giving the knowledge of the Vedas, a man shall deliver his ancestors from hell for ten *manvantaras* and dwell in the three worlds of heaven.
And for one who bestows the knowledge of the Self,
it is impossible to fully describe the measure of that merit, even in tens of thousands of years.
This much can be said:
that for ten thousand supreme kalpas, a mortal may dwell in Satyaloka, where the Lord Brahmā resides.
Even by bringing a single living being, however lowly it may be, to the state of cessation [of suffering],
what could not be bestowed upon the earth through the power of Āyurveda?
Through the grace of the Sasyaveda, rice-crops flourish in abundance;
what indeed is not achieved there as eternal merit?
Having understood the greatness of the Mīmāṃsā system and its definitive conclusions regarding the Vedas,
what auspicious result indeed does not accrue to the donor who promotes the performance of sacrificial rites?
The ancient science of the Self and that which consists of the Dharmaśāstras—
these sciences, headed by the Trayī, [surpass] the fruits of all acts of giving.
Whatever dharma a man may practice after having understood the Dharmaśāstra,
the merit of that dharma for the one who bestowed the Dharmaśāstra is a hundredfold greater.
Those who are learned in the Purāṇas and traditional narratives, and who are devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods,
go to all the worlds filled with every desire, arising from the emergence of all that is auspicious.
Those who bestow the knowledge of the Purāṇas partake in infinite fruit;
likewise, those men who impart the knowledge of the Self do so by taking refuge in Dharma.
Furthermore, they do not enter the womb or the hell that is so difficult to transcend;
having crossed over all evils, they are together with their sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
They are liberated from countless terrible hells consisting of agonizing torments.
Likewise:
by giving a verse, a riddle, a stanza, or any other auspicious well-spoken word that brings joy, one goes to the auspicious world of the apsarases.
In the Varāha Purāṇa:
By giving the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, one is glorified in heaven;
as are those who give a Purāṇa, a treatise on logic (tarka-śāstra), prosody, poetics, and grammar.
O King, by bestowing the Vedas, the Mīmāṃsā, and the Śivadharma,
he shall indeed become the sovereign of kings over the earth with its seven continents.
By giving the Pāṇinian grammar, the Nirukta and other Vedāṅgas, as well as the Smṛtis,
one attains knowledge, especially that of the Vedānta.
O King of kings, cows, land, and knowledge should always be given as gifts.
Thus ends the praise of the gift of knowledge. Now, the gift of the Vedas is being examined. In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of the Veda is preeminent."
There is no need for [the exchange] of cattle, land, dwellings, sesame seeds, gold, or clarified butter.

The gift of Brahman is the gift of the Veda. Yājñavalkya says: Since Brahman, which consists of all dharmas, is superior to all other gifts, one who gives it attains the world of Brahman without falling away.
In the Mahābhārata: "He who imparts the righteous, divine Sarasvatī to a disciple enjoys a fruit equal to that of gifting the earth and cows."
The *brāhmī* [speech] follows the meaning of the Vedas. Likewise:
"Even he who, having studied the Vedas, explains them according to reason, being praised for his service to the teacher, is honored in heaven."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "By the gift of the Vedas, a man obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
by the gift of the Upavedas, he rejoices together with the Gandharvas."
And by the gift of the Vedāṅgas, one shall attain the world of Śakra.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"The supreme knowledge among all sciences is declared to be the knowledge of Brahman;
therefore, O King, from the gift of that [knowledge], the fruit of all gifts shall accrue."
They say that among all branches of knowledge, the Vedic science is unsurpassed;
therefore, for one who bestows it, there is indeed the attainment of both heaven and liberation.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"The Veda alone is the supreme means for the twice-born to attain the highest good;
therefore, through the practice of studying one's own [branch of] the Veda, one attains the Supreme Brahman."
The wise one should cultivate that very [nature] and cause it to be imparted to his disciples;
through its cultivation and its transmission, what is there that he does not attain?
He who knows the Veda in its entirety, together with its limbs and subsidiary limbs, is not smeared by sin; bestowing [the gift], he shall attain liberation.
Likewise,
Manu said:
"What is the nature of the Veda and its authority, according to the different enumerations of its auxiliary sciences (upāṅgas)?"
And also the auxiliary limbs of the Vedas; tell us those, O Eternal One.
Brahmā said: The Vedas originate from the syllable Oṃ; Gāyatrī originates from the Vedas.
Those six auxiliary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) have been fully described, as well as the secondary limbs (upāṅga).
Those born from the womb of Mātṛkā are remembered as being endowed with the characteristics of the *chandolakṣaṇa*.
That which was originally a single Veda was later made into four Vedas.
O child, for the sake of those with limited capacity, I have divided the Rig, Yajur, Sama, and Atharva Vedas so that they may be easily grasped without excessive prolixity.
In that regard, ten divisions of the Ṛgveda are proclaimed:
the Āstayas, the Sāṃkyacarcās, the Āvakas, and likewise the Carcakas.
The Āvaṇī, Avakrama, and Māṣa fasts— these six in forward order and six in reverse order,
together with the Daṇḍas— in brief, these constitute once again a single Pāraṇā.
O King, the branches are also threefold: the Śākalas, the Āṣkas, and the Māṇḍukas;
their instruction is proclaimed [to consist of] seventy maṇḍalas.
The enumeration of the carcās is twenty-four hundred;
the verses (ṛcs) number ten thousand and five hundred.
Eighty verses and one quarter—this is said to be the completion [of the recitation].
Now, while this is the number in the Ṛgveda, hear that of the Yajurveda.
By the command of Śiva, I have divided the sixty-four [tantras] according to their distinctions;
among them, the Carakas are tenfold, including the Kvarakas and the Hāridravīyas.
The Kaṭhas, the Prācyaṭhas, and likewise the Kapiṣṭhalakaṭhas;
the Nārāyaṇīyas, the Śvetas, and the Śvetāśvataras and Maitrāyaṇas.
Furthermore, the Maitrāyaṇīyas are proclaimed to have seven divisions:
the Mānavas, the Dundubhas, the Vārāhas, the Chāgeyas, and the Hāridravīyas.
The Śyāmas and the Śyāmāyanīyas—
those who know the Vedas have learned that their recitation consists of eighteen thousand readings.
Those who have mastered the Padas receive double [the reward], and those who have mastered the Kramas receive triple;
he who studies the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga) is called a knower of the six auxiliaries.
The Śikṣākalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Chandas, and Jyotiṣa—these are the six auxiliary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). Now listen, sir, to the secondary auxiliaries (upāṅga).
The Pratipadā, Anupada, and Chandobhāṣā,
along with Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, and Tarka, are proclaimed as the Upāṅgas.

And listen now to those eighteen supplementary treatises that have been enumerated: the *Yūpalakṣaṇa* (Characteristics of the Sacrificial Post), the *Chāgalakṣaṇa* (Characteristics of the Goat), the *Pratiṣṭhānuvāka-saṃkhyā* (Enumeration of the Consecration Hymns), the *Caraṇavyūha* (Arrangement of Vedic Schools), the *Śrāddhakalpa* (Ritual for Ancestral Offerings), the *Sūktas*, the *Pariṣad* (Assembly), the *Ṛgyajuṣa* (Ṛg and Yajur Vedas), the *Iṣṭakāpūraṇa* (Filling of the Bricks), the *Pravarādhyāya* (Chapter on Ancestral Lines), the *Uñchaśāstra* (Treatise on Gleaning), the *Kratusaṃkhyā* (Enumeration of Sacrifices), the *Niyamas* (Rules), the *Yajñapārśva* (Side of the Sacrifice), the *Hotṛka* (Duties of the Hotṛ Priest),
the *Vrata* (Vows), the *Prasava* (Impulse), the *Utkhāna* (Excavation), and the *Kūrmalakṣaṇa* (Characteristics of the Tortoise).
The remaining ones, however, have been declared to be nineteen in number.

Furthermore, O bull among sages, you should know that the Kaṭhas consist of forty-four [recensions], while the Vājasaneyins— divided into ten branches— comprise five groups consisting of those from the East, the North, and the Niruktas.
The Jābālas, Baudheyakas, Ānvīkṣakas, Mādhyandinas, Aśvaśāpeyas, Supāyins, those called Kapālas, the Pauṇḍras, Vasas, and Āvaṭikas.
The Paramāravikas, the Parāśaras, the Ṛddhyabaudhāyanīyas,
the Āyodhyas, and the Āyodheyas— these are their respective branches of study.
In the Vājasaneyaka Veda, which consists of two thousand verses less one hundred,
this collection of Ṛks has been enumerated, as well as the other Yajus formulas.

This is indeed the measure of the Yajus-mantras alone; it is reckoned as fourfold when including the Khilas and the Sukriyas, together with the Brāhmaṇas. Furthermore, the Taittirīyas are of two kinds.
The Ṛṣis, the Khāṇḍikeyas, and the Khaṇḍikas are further divided into five groups:
the Kāleyas, the Baudhāyanīyas, and likewise the Hiraṇyakeśas.
The Bhāradvājas and Āpastambas are proclaimed as their subdivisions;
likewise, there are the Saupitikas and the Prāvacaṇīyas.
In former times, the Sāmaveda was extensive, consisting of a thousand divisions;
it was then studied even during periods when study is forbidden by the wise Indra.
Those remaining who were struck down by Vajra—I shall describe them; listen with attention.
Listen further to the divisions therein: the Rāmāyaṇīyas and the Kauthumas.
O best of those who radiate heat, these seven types of lightning from the Rāmāyaṇa are easy to grasp:
Kālaveyā, Mahākāla, Vayālāṅgala, and Vaidyuta.
Among the Kauthumas, there are also seven [groups]: the Asuras, the Vānarāyaṇas, the Prajālāt, the Vainabhṛtyas, the Pariyogyas, and the Parikāyanas.
Now listen as I describe correctly how even their study was proclaimed:
there are eight thousand Sāmans and fourteen Sāmas.
Eight hundred and ninety plus ten, together with the Sālakhilyas, the Suparṇas, and the Prakhyas— these are known as the assembly of Sāma-singers.
Jajñalā, Brahmavedā, Śaunakī, Kanakhī,
Vedaṛṣi, and Autavidyā— listen now to their study.
There are five ritual manuals (kalpas):
the Nakṣatrakalpa, the Vaitāna, the Saṃhitāvidhi, the Āṅgirasa,
and the Śāntikalpa of the Atharvans.
Listen now to all the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (upavedas):
from the Ṛgveda comes Āyurveda, and likewise from the Yajurveda comes Dhanurveda.

The wise know that the Sāmaveda has the Gandharvas as its presiding deity, the Arthaśāstras as its subject matter, and the Atharvaveda likewise; they know that the lineage of the Ṛgveda is Ātreya and its deity is Soma.
Kāśyapa knew the Yajurveda, which they know as the Rudraveda;
and the Sāmaveda, by lineage Bhāradvāja, [knew] Purandara.
One should understand the ritual pertaining to the deities (adhidaiva) from the Atharvaveda;
one should understand the deity Brahman—now listen to me regarding our faults.
The Ṛgveda has eyes like lotus petals, a long belly, and is pure;
he has a curved neck, curly hair and beard, and his height is one span (vitasti).

Furthermore, the Yajurveda, adorned with five silver ornaments and pearls, should be worshipped for the sake of granting boons and bestowing worldly enjoyment upon the twice-born. He has tawny eyes, a slender waist, and thick neck and cheeks; his complexion is copper-red and elongated, and his feet are black due to his graciousness and the length of his strides.
Alternatively, he may be worshipped in a variegated linga, whereby one shall obtain all desires.
The Sāmaveda always has black feet due to his graciousness and the length of his strides.
Or else, he should worship at a variegated *liṅga* and obtain all his desires.
He is the Sāmaveda, eternally garlanded, firm in his vows, pure, wearing clean garments, patient, self-controlled, carrying a great staff, and having eyes like glass beads.
Having the color of the sun in hue, measuring six *aratnis*, it should be placed in either copper or a gem; when worshipped, it bestows auspiciousness.
The *Atharvaveda* has a sharp staff, can assume any form at will, is the soul of the universe, is dispassionate, and its flame blazes upward.

One who performs minor rites, is a composer of treatises, is steadfast, and is blue-lotus colored in appearance, being content with his own wife and having no desire for the wives of others, should worship Padmarāga;
he shall obtain all desires as prescribed in the Atharvaveda.
He who knows this name-and-form, which arises from lineage, the Vedas, and the authoritative means of knowledge, as well as each respective color, shall partake in the fruit of merit.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
Now I shall describe the procedure for giving gifts, which is considered the supreme secret;
by performing which a person does not approach the terrible hells.
Having properly fashioned golden images in accordance with the sacred tradition and the previously mentioned characteristics,
adorned with pure, precious gems.
Having arranged them according to the sequence of the Rigveda and the other Vedas.
The characteristics of the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas have been shown in the context of the gift of the jar of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Garments should be given in due order:
yellow, white, and then red.
Having likewise offered blue flowers and worshipped with perfumes, unbroken grains, incense, and lamps;
[524] Fragrant modakas, ghee with milk-rice,
then food with honey, and finally sacrificial post-ghee, in due order.
Having announced his purpose to them and having prostrated according to the rules,
the wise man should duly perform the rite of circumambulation.
O best among the wise, the ritual for their worship should be performed with the Gāyatrī;
having uttered the Vyāhṛtis, one should perform the invocation and the dismissal.
Then, with these mantras, one should perform the consecration (anumantraṇa) of these [objects]:
"O Ṛgveda, lotus-petal-eyed one, protect, protect; cast away what is inauspicious!"
I have come to you for refuge; grant me your wondrous benefit.
O Yajurveda, salutations be unto you, whose ultimate aim is the protection of the world!
By your grace, may all my endeavors be perpetually auspicious;
O Sāmaveda, O mighty-armed one, for you are indeed Adhokṣaja himself.
Becoming well-disposed with a gracious countenance, please favor me with your compassion.
O Atharvan, the welfare and misfortune of all beings depend upon you;
O Lord of Gods, grant peace and bestow the prosperity we desire.
Having thus offered prayers to the lords of the gods, one should present them to the Brahmins;
one should give one [image] to each [Brahmin], accompanied by three palas of gold.
In this case, one who is weak should give each [offering] with one *pala* added;
or else, the gift of these is prescribed according to one's own capacity.
This alone would be the authority for their fashioning of images;
this is the rule for the gift of the Vedas for one who has not studied them.
For one who is constantly engaged in study, the teacher alone is indeed the disciple;
being himself pure, having bathed in the morning and with senses restrained, he [should approach] the pure Brahmins.
Taking darbha grass in his hand, he should cause her to recite such [texts],
avoiding days when study is forbidden and not letting her hear anything vulgar.
Whoever bestows even a single verse according to this injunction,
by him the entire earth, filled with the three kinds of wealth, becomes given.
O Great-minded One, the fruit that one obtains from giving even a small portion of the Vedas cannot be described even in a thousand eons.
As many Vedic hymns and meritorious Vedic vows as there are,
so much shall one who is imbued with devotion obtain through the gift of the Vedas.
What has not been given by one who provides a livelihood for a preceptor in order to teach people—
that which is shown to be the goal of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha?
By giving students food, massage, clothing, or even alms, a person attains all their desires; of this there is no doubt.
Discrimination leads to a long life; one shall attain virtue, pleasure, and wealth.
Indeed, everything becomes as if given when food is provided for students.
In the Vahni Purāṇa: "O best of kings, he who, having risen in the morning, causes the Vedas or even the Vedāṅgas to be recited, shall obtain a fruit equal to the gift of the entire earth."
O King, he who provides a livelihood for those reciting the Veda takes the fruit of their sacrifice through his gifts of clothing and food.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth shall obtain wealth;
the unlearned attains knowledge; and the sorrowful is liberated from sorrow."
But one who is constantly engaged in study merges into the supreme Brahman;
thus ends the rule for the gift of the Veda.

Now, the gift of scripture (*śāstradāna*). Regarding this, the *Nandipurāṇa* states: "Since the entire world, with its auspicious and inauspicious [deeds], is dependent upon scripture, therefore scripture should be given with effort for the sake of virtuous action."
Yama said:
One might give this earth adorned with all kinds of jewels, and one might also give the scripture to the Brahmins; these two gifts are equal to each other.

That gift of land, adorned with all kinds of jewels, is equal to these previously mentioned gifts; this is the meaning of "equal to the gift of knowledge. For the treatise (śāstra) is indeed the eye of the worlds, illuminating the path to heaven;
by means of the treatise, the three worlds, including all that is moving and stationary, are surely sustained.
Even across a thousand yojanas and even in the course of hundreds of millions of years,
this scripture is capable of revealing an object that has suddenly vanished from sight.
Therefore, there is nothing whatsoever superior to this scripture in the three worlds;
it is proclaimed as the ship for crossing the dense darkness of saṃsāra.
A man who, being constantly attentive, gives this [work] by means of its application—
what would not have been given by him who bestows this jewel of a scripture?
In this regard, since it is the foremost among all branches of learning, the presentation of the Dharmaśāstra is discussed first.
In the Nandipurāṇa:
"Śruti and Smṛti are proclaimed to be the two eyes of the Brahmins."
One who is deficient by one [eye] there is called "one-eyed" (kāṇa), while one who is deficient by two is declared "blind" (andha).
[527] Likewise:
By giving a treatise on Dharma, a man is glorified in the heights of heaven;
for ten Manvantaras, that mortal shall deliver his ancestors from hell.
The ancient science of the Self and that which consists of the treatises on Dharma—
these three sciences are primary in the fruit of all acts of giving.
Whatever dharma a man may practice after having understood the Dharmaśāstra,
that dharma becomes a hundredfold for the one who has imparted the Dharmaśāstra.
Therefore, the wise and discerning should always study the Dharmaśāstra;
even Brahmā is not capable of enumerating its merit.
In the Agni Purāṇa: "O King, the giver of the Dharmaśāstra obtained all that fruit which is gained by the proper gift of a thousand Kapila cows."
In this regard, Śaṅkha and Likhita state their sequence by way of mentioning the authors of the Dharmaśāstras:

"The Smṛtis are the Dharmaśāstras. Their authors are Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, Dakṣa, Aṅgiras, Atri, Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Āpastamba, Vaśiṣṭha, Kātyāyana, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Saṃvarta, Gautama, Śātātapa, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Pracetas, and others."

By the word "and others" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of Budha, Devala, Soma, Prajāpati, Vṛddha-Śātātapa, Paiṭhīnasi, Chāgaleya, Cyavana, Marīci, Vatsa, Pāraskara, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and Ātreya. Paiṭhīnasi says:
"Among them are Manu, Aṅgiras, Vyāsa, Gautama, Ulikhita, Yama, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, and Parāśara."
Viṣṇu, Āpastamba, Hārīta, Śaṅkha, Kātyāyana, Guru, Pracetas,
Nārada, the Yogi, Baudhāyana, and Pitāmaha.
Sumantu, Kāśyapa, Babhru, Paiṭhīna, and Vyāghra;
Satyavrata, Bharadvāja, Gārgya, and likewise Kārṣṇājini.
Jābāli, Jamadagni, Laugākṣi, and Brahmasambhava—
these are remembered as the thirty-six sages who are the promulgators of Dharma.
In the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*, it is shown that there are thirty-six additional *smṛtis*:
"O son, those statements which are found within the eighteen *purāṇas*..."
Having examined those, O mighty-armed one, as well as other Smṛtis and the thirty-six Smṛtis proclaimed by Manu and others;
"Having examined their statements in sequence, I shall speak to you.
Thus said Manu.
Viṣṇu, Parāśara, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Vyāsa, and Hārīta [have also spoken].
Śātātapa, Vasiṣṭha, Yama, Āpastamba, and Gautama.
Devala, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Bharadvāja,
Uśanas, Trayī, Śaunaka, and Yājñavalkya— these are the eighteen authors of the Smṛtis.
Likewise, the Bhārgava, the Nāradīya, the Bārhaspatya,
and the Āṅgirasa are considered the four compendia (saṃhitās) of the Svāyambhuva Śāstra.
Aṅgiras, Jābāli, Nāciketas, Skanda, Laugākṣi, Kaśyapa, Vyāsa, Sanatkumāra, Śatarju, and likewise Janaka.
Vyāghra, Kātyāyana, Jātūkarṇya, Kapiñjala,
Baudhāyana, Kaṇāda, and likewise Viśvāmitra.
The wise call these the "applications of mindfulness."
Yama said: Those treatises on Dharma which were indeed composed by these [sages] in ancient times are the supreme authorities; they must not be refuted by mere reasoning.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The Smṛtis are the root of Dharma, for Dharma is the means of accomplishing all goals.
Therefore, when the Smṛtis are given, one obtains the fruit of every possible gift."
By rescuing even a single living being from the ocean of suffering, one obtains infinite fruit; how much more so for one who bestows knowledge upon many?
What follows from this? Is it indeed that dharma exists, or is it some such knowledge, or is there something else here that is seen in the Smṛtis?
Therefore, when these have been bestowed, the wise man is reborn;
having reached the further shore of the scriptures, he is glorified in the world of Brahman.
Thus ends the gift of the Smṛtis.
Now follows the gift of the Purāṇas. Regarding this, the Nāradīya [Purāṇa] states:
"O Goddess, the Vedas are established by means of the Purāṇas; there is no doubt in this matter."
The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "This man will deceive me."
This [dharma] was established as immovable in ancient times by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for indeed, that which is not seen in the Vedas is seen in the Smṛtis.
That which is indeed not perceived by both is sung of in the Purāṇas.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "The Purāṇa is remembered by Brahmā as the first of all scriptures;
immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths."
O sinless one, in this interval, there was indeed only one Purāṇa,
a meritorious means for achieving the three goals of life, with an extent of one hundred crores [of verses].
And when the worlds had been consumed by fire, I indeed assumed the form of a horse and [retrieved] the four Vedas, along with the Purāṇas and the extensive treatises on Nyāya.
Having taken up the Mīmāṃsā and the Dharmaśāstras and made them his own,
he [recovered them] again at the beginning of the Kalpa from the ocean of water in the form of a fish.
Having heard all this spoken by the one who had entered the water,
the four-faced Brahmā proclaimed it to the sages, verse by verse.
From that, the activity of all the scriptures and the Purāṇa arose;
then, seeing the corruption of the Purāṇa over time, falsehood [entered].
Assuming the form of Vyāsa, I bring about the withdrawal [of the Vedas] in age after age,
always in each Dvāpara Yuga, in a measure of four hundred thousand [verses].
Having divided that into eighteen parts, it is proclaimed here in this world of Bhūr;
even today, in the world of the gods, it has an extent of one billion verses.
The meaning of that has been briefly set forth here as four hundred thousand [verses];
now, those eighteen Purāṇas are being spoken of here.
I shall declare them by name; listen, O best of sages!
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "The Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata;
and another, the Nāradīya, and the Mārkaṇḍeya as the seventh."
The eighth is declared to be Āgneya, and likewise the ninth is Bhaviṣya;
the tenth is Brahmavaivarta, and the eleventh is Liṅga.
The Vārāha is declared as the twelfth, and the Skānda is the thirteenth here;
the Vāmana is the fourteenth, and likewise the Kaurma is the fifteenth.
The Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and likewise the eighteenth, the Brahmāṇḍa.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"That which was proclaimed by Vāyu as Śaiva, as well as the Vairiñca and the Vaiṣṇava,
and this which is called the Kālikā— these are remembered as the root Bhāgavata."
The Saura, the Nāradīya, the Mārkaṇḍeya, the Vahni (Bhaviṣya),
the Vāmana, the Kaurma, the Mātsya, and the seventeenth, the Gāruḍa.
The *Brahmāṇḍa* is to be known as the eighteenth Purāṇa; of this there is no doubt.
From the Saura Purāṇa:
"O twice-born ones, that which was previously spoken by Bhānu to his son Manu, I shall now fully declare; listen as I speak."
Primary creation, secondary creation, the genealogies, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the accounts of the dynasties' deeds— thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.
Having diligently written down the characteristics of the Upapurāṇas, they are remembered;
among them, the first is the Brāhma Purāṇa, adorned with two Saṃhitās.
Ten thousand verses containing various accounts of merit constitute the second section; the third is remembered as the Vaiṣṇava.
The fourth is proclaimed by Vāyu and is known as the Vāyavīya;
from that, two parts are proclaimed, adorned with two portions.
Immediately after that, the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa is said to consist of four sections;
then the Mārkaṇḍeya, the Āgneya, and after that the Nāradīya.
The tenth is the Brahmavaivarta, and the eleventh is remembered as the Liṅga;
then follows the excellent Vārāha in two parts.
The Skanda Purāṇa is extensive here, consisting of eight sections;
following that are the Vāmana and the Kūrma, which is distinguished by two parts.
The Matsya and the Gāruḍa have been proclaimed, and after that the Brahmāṇḍa;
the one designated as the Brahmāṇḍa is told in two parts.
The supplements (*khilāni*) and the minor Purāṇas that have been spoken by the wise—
this unsurpassed Saura [Purāṇa] is the supplement of the Brahmapurāṇa.
This meritorious work, based on the narratives of Śiva, is composed of two collections:
the first was spoken by Sanatkumāra, and the second was uttered by the Sun.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Other Upapurāṇas were indeed spoken by sages;
the first is that told by Sanatkumāra, and after that is the Nārasiṃha."
The third is designated as that spoken by Nārada,
while the fourth, known as the Śivadharmas, was spoken directly by Nandīśa himself.
The wonderful account spoken by Durvāsas, that which was spoken by Nārada thereafter, as well as the teachings of Kapila, of Manu, and likewise those set forth by Uśanas.
The Brahmāṇḍa, the Vāruṇa, and that called the Kāpila,
as well as the Māheśvara, the Śāmba, the Saura, and the Sārvarthasaṃcaya.
The two [works] spoken by Parāśara, namely the Pravara and the Bhāgavata—
this is declared to be the eighteenth Purāṇa, known as the Kaurma.
The merit of the *Saṃhitās* is established in four ways according to their divisions; as stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"That description of Narasiṃha which is proclaimed in the *Pādmapurāṇa*..."
Among those, the Narasimha Purana consisting of eighteen thousand verses is spoken of here.
That in which the greatness of Nandā is described by Kārttikeya is proclaimed by people as the Nandīpurāṇa.
O you who observe the vows of sages, that discourse which is delivered in this world by setting equality foremost will not fail anyone; indeed, it is equality itself that is proclaimed there.
Likewise, the one named Ādityasaṃjña is recited in that very same list;
however, as for the Purāṇa which is seen separately from the eighteen [Vidyās], [it is not included].
"Understand, O best of the twice-born, that this was composed from those [five];
it is the Purāṇa possessing five limbs, while the other is known as an Ākhyāna."
Cosmogony, secondary creation, genealogies,
the periods of the Manvantaras, and the history of the dynasties— thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.
The majesty of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra, as well as that of the world,
its dissolution, and the five-colored nature of the Purāṇa are clearly seen therein.
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are proclaimed in all the Purāṇas, as well as whatever fruit results from that which is contrary to them.
In the Sāttvika Kalpas, they know the majesty of Hari to be supreme;
and in the Rājasa Kalpas, they know the majesty of Brahmā to be supreme.
In the same way, the majesty of Agni is proclaimed in the Tāmasa Purāṇas, that of Śiva in the Sāttvika, that of Sarasvatī in the Saṃkīrṇa, and that of the Pitṛs in the Rājasa.
Likewise: "Having composed the eighteen Purāṇas, the son of Satyavatī composed the entire narrative known as the Bhārata, which was augmented by them."
That which was proclaimed by Vālmīki, known as the Rāmāyaṇa, is declared to be the supreme [work], augmented by the meaning of the Vedas through its single defining characteristic.
And that which was spoken by Brahmā was extracted from the expansion of a hundred crores by Nārada himself and repeated again and again to Vālmīki.
And by Vālmīki, for the sake of accomplishing virtue, pleasure, and wealth in the worlds,
these five [verses] together with one quarter were proclaimed as the illustrative examples (*lakṣya*) among them.
In the Matsya Purāṇa,
the sages said:
"O Sūta, recount in detail and in due order the number of the Purāṇas."
And the entirety of the Dharma concerning generosity, in its proper manner and successive order.
Sūta said: O sages, learn that which the Supreme Person, the Soul of the Universe, spoke in the past when he was questioned regarding this very same inquiry.
[535] Eighteen Purāṇas exist; they shall now be spoken of here.
O best of sages, listen as I declare them by name.
That portion of the Purāṇa which was previously spoken by Brahmā to Marīci,
consisting of ten thousand verses, is proclaimed as the Brāhma Purāṇa.
And whoever, having written this, should give it along with a water-cow on the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
When this very world became a lotus made of gold,
the account based on that event is likewise called the Pādma by the wise.
That Padma Purāṇa is recited here as consisting of fifty-five thousand verses;
and whoever should give that Purāṇa accompanied by a golden lotus—
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one who offers [food] mixed with sesame seeds shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
this was taught by Parāśara concerning the events of the Vārāha Kalpa.
That in which all dharmas are declared, they know that to be Vaiṣṇava;
and he who should give that [manuscript] in the month of Āṣāḍha, accompanied by a cow of ghee, [attains great merit].
On the full moon day, one whose self is purified attains the state of Varuṇa;
the wise know that Purāṇa to consist of twenty-three thousand verses.
In connection with the Śvetakalpa, Vāyu here proclaimed the dharmas,
wherein that which pertains to Vāyu is found, together with the majesty of Rudra.
That Purāṇa is said here to consist of twenty-four thousand verses;
on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, it should be accompanied by a cow made of jaggery.
The man who gives curd mixed with [other substances] to a Brahmin householder shall dwell for one kalpa in the world of Śiva as a purified soul.
That work in which the expansion of dharma is described with reference to the Gāyatrī,
and which includes the slaying of the asura Vṛtra, is called the Bhāgavata.
Whatever accounts of men and gods there may be within the Kalpa of Sarasvatī,
that which arises from those events is called the Bhāgavata in the world.
And whoever, having written this, should give it away on the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada together with a golden lion, goes to the supreme state.
That Purāṇa is proclaimed to consist of eighteen thousand verses,
wherein Nārada here expounds the dharmas based upon the Bṛhat-kalpa.
The Nāradīya consists of twenty-five thousand [verses];
whoever should give this, along with gold, on the fifteenth day [of the lunar fortnight].
One attains the supreme perfection from which return is difficult to find,
wherein, concerning birds, there is an investigation into dharma and adharma.
The Purāṇa called Mārkaṇḍeya, consisting of nine thousand verses, is spoken of here;
and he who, having transcribed it, should give it away together with a golden elephant, [attains great merit].
On the full moon day of Kārttika, one shall partake in the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice;
this is told with reference to the account of the Īśāna-kalpa.
That which was proclaimed by Agni to Vasiṣṭha is called the Āgneya;
whoever should have it written down and give it away, accompanied by a golden lotus.
Likewise, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform this according to the prescribed rite together with the sesame-cow offering;
this [collection] consists of sixteen thousand [verses] and bestows the fruit of all sacrifices.
In which the four-faced Lord of the World, taking the majesty of Āditya as his subject, spoke in connection with the narrative of the Aghora-kalpa.
In the ninth [chapter], he described the characteristics of the multitude of beings,
numbering fourteen thousand five hundred.
That which consists primarily of future conduct is here called "the future.
He who, free from envy, should give that on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa—
One who provides a jar of molasses obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice,
as well as [the merit of] relating the narrative of the Rathantara-kalpa.
Sāvarṇi [related this] to Nārada, together with the majesty of Kṛṣṇa,
wherein the deeds of Brahmavarāha are described repeatedly.
That Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa is said to consist of eighteen thousand verses;
he who should give this Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa in the month of Māgha—
On the full moon day, he is glorified in the abode of Brahmā’s world,
where the Lord Maheśvara, situated within the center of the fire-linga, spoke.
For the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and concerning the fire ritual (āgneya),
that Kalpa was spoken by Brahmā himself as the Laiṅga Purāṇa.
He who bestows that [manuscript] consisting of eleven thousand verses on the full moon day of Phālguna,
together with a sesame-cow, attains the nature of Śiva.
Furthermore, O best of sages, concerning the majesty of Mahāvarāha in connection with the Manava Kalpa.
Twenty-four thousand verses are said here to constitute that Purāṇa;
narrated by Viṣṇu to the Earth, it is called the Vārāha here.
Having fashioned a golden Garuḍa together with a sesame-cow,
and having given it to a Brahmin householder on the full moon day of the month of Caitra;
[538] By the grace of Varāha, one indeed attains the state of Viṣṇu, where,
concerning the duties of the devotees of Maheśvara, [the Lord] has spoken...
When that Puruṣa Kalpa had passed, the Purāṇa named Skānda was augmented by his deeds; it is said to consist of eighty-one thousand verses.
"One hundred and one thousand [years]"—thus it is recited among mortals;
and he who, having engraved it, should give it along with a golden trident, [attains this merit].
And when the sun enters Capricorn,
the four-faced Brahmā, having taken as his subject the majesty of Trivikrama, attains the state of Śiva.
Therein he proclaimed the Vāmana Purāṇa, celebrated as pertaining to the three aims of life (trivarga);
it consists of ten thousand verses, follows the Kūrma Kalpa, and is auspicious.
Whoever gives [this] on the autumnal equinox goes to the station of Viṣṇu,
where dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation [reside] even in the netherworld (rasātala).
In the presence of Indra, Janārdana, assuming the form of a tortoise, narrated the majesty [of the Lord] to the sages in connection with Indradyumna.
He who, during the solstice, should give a golden pitcher accompanied by a silver pitcher, along with seventeen thousand [coins], in connection with the Lakṣmī-kalpa;
That man shall obtain the fruit of the gift of a thousand cows,
wherein Janārdana, at the beginning of the kalpa, for the sake of setting the Vedas in motion—
And assuming the form of a fish, O you who observe the vows of sages, he spoke concerning the description of Narasiṃha, detailing the events of seven kalpas for the sake of Manu.
Know this to be its greatness: fourteen thousand [pounds] of gold, together with a golden fish and a cow, were offered to Viṣṇu.
[539] He who should give this [work] has given the entire earth;
for when, in the Gāruḍa Kalpa, Garuḍa’s birth occurred from the cosmic egg (viśvāṇḍa).
Kṛṣṇa spoke with reference to that [subject], and thus the Gāruḍa is described here;
it is recited in this world as consisting of eighteen thousand and one verses.
The man who gives to a learned person a pair of golden figures joined together attains supreme perfection and the presence of Śiva.
Brahmā spoke again concerning the majesty of the Brahmāṇḍa;
that Brahmāṇḍa consists of twelve thousand verses and two hundred more.
That Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, in which a detailed account of future kalpas is heard, was proclaimed by Brahmā himself.
And the man who gives a pair of woolen cloths during the Vyatīpāta yoga obtains the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
And that [gift], when accompanied by a golden cow, bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā.
In the Saura Purāṇa, referring to that very Purāṇa,
it says: "This most meritorious compendium, which destroys all sins,
was formerly narrated by the Sun to Vaivasvata Manu."
O twice-born ones, among all gifts, the gift of this Purāṇa is the most excellent for one who gives it to a Brāhmaṇa devoted to Śiva who is engaged in ascetic penance.
O best of the twice-born, whatever gifts are renowned in the worlds, one obtains the fruit of them all by [giving] on the fourteenth day; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever, having written down various other Upapurāṇas along with gold on festival days, should bestow them as gifts, shall become one who has reached the further shore of knowledge.
The person of meritorious intellect who bestows the *Śivadharmottara* and other such scriptures obtains infinite fruit through the illumination of the *Śivadharma*.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "The *Mahābhārata* is said to be the essence of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
by giving it alone, one becomes a giver of the Vedas and the Śāstras."
Having written out the entire Rāmāyaṇa, he who bestows it [upon another] finds Sarasvatī, bound by lotuses, becoming pleased with him.
In the Vahnipurāṇa: "The fruit that one obtains by giving away a Purāṇa, or even the Mahābhārata, or likewise the Rāmāyaṇa— that cannot be attained through all the great sacrifices."
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, referring to that very Purāṇa, it says:
"This sin-destroying *Saṃhitā* is both Brāhmī and Paurāṇikī;
he who, having written this, gives it as a gift in the month of Vaiśākha, O observer of noble vows..."
Learn now of his merit when given to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas:
he becomes liberated from all sins and endowed with all sovereign powers.
"Having enjoyed vast pleasures, one shall become possessed of knowledge and wealth.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a Purāṇa.
Now follows the gift of listening to a Purāṇa. Regarding this, it is said in the Mahābhārata:
Henceforth, O Bhārata, I shall declare those things which are to be given to the Brahmins while this is being recited, O King, at every sacred festival (parvan).
After the prescription for the Svasti-vācana and other rites has been performed, the ritual action proceeds;
then, when the festival day is concluded, one should satisfy the twice-born according to one's own capacity.
First, O King, having worshipped the reciter who is endowed with the essence of the rasa and the gandha, one should according to the rules feed him excellent honeyed milk-rice (madhupāyasa).

Then, O King, one should feed the believer with food consisting mostly of roots and fruits, as well as milk-rice (pāyasa), honey, and ghee; and one should also give him rice with molasses (guḍaudana).
Then, O king of kings, during the Sabhā Parva, one should feed the twice-born with sacrificial food accompanied by incense, cakes, and sweetmeats.
One should satisfy the best of the twice-born with wild roots and fruits;
and having arrived at the Āraṇyaka-parvan, one should cause water-pots to be given as gifts.
He should cause that man, endowed with all desirable qualities, to bestow upon the Brahmins principal offerings of water for libation, as well as grains, roots, and fruits.
Likewise, in the Virāṭa-parvan, there were various garments;
and in the Udyoga-parvan, O best of the Bharatas, he was provided with everything his heart desired.
O Indra among kings, on the Bhīṣma-parvan, one should feed the Brahmins, adorned with perfumes and garlands, after giving them excellent drink.
Then, one should give well-prepared food endowed with all excellent qualities,
and at the Droṇaparvan, a most refined meal to the Brahmins.
O Indra among kings, arrows, bows, and excellent swords should likewise be given;
and in the Karṇaparvan, food that fulfills all desires should also be provided.
O Indra among kings, one with a restrained mind should properly give refined food to the Brahmins at the Śalyaparvan, along with sweetmeats and rice mixed with jaggery.
One should cause all the food to be served with excellent condiments and gratifying drinks;
likewise, on the Gadāparvan day, one should cause food mixed with mung beans to be offered.
Likewise, in the Strīparvan, one should satisfy the twice-born according to the rules with jewels;
furthermore, in the Aiṣīka-parvan, one should again cause food mixed with rice to be given.
Then one should give well-prepared food endowed with all excellent qualities;
likewise, during the Śāntiparvan, one should feed the twice-born with sacrificial food (haviṣya).
Having obtained food that fulfills all desires at the site of the horse sacrifice,
one should likewise feed the twice-born with sacrificial oblations while residing in the hermitage.
In the Mausala-parvan, O Pārtha, there was fragrant incense, garlands, and ointments possessing every excellence; likewise, in the Harivaṃśa, there was the milk-rice (pāyasa) as a delicious meal.
O King, O bull of the Bharatas, at each and every conclusion of the recitation,
that expert in the scriptures, being purified, completed the entire collection according to the rules.
Then, having established it in an auspicious place and covered it with linen cloth and other materials,
one should become pure and well-adorned there, wearing white garments.
One should worship the volumes of the Saṃhitās individually with perfumes and garlands, according to the rule, out of devotion, being purified and well-composed in mind.
One should cause food, edibles, drinks, and various auspicious curiosities to be offered there,
and one should bestow silver, gold, and sacrificial fees as a gift.
One should invoke all the deities as well as Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
then, having well-adorned the best of the twice-born with perfumes and garlands, [one should honor them].
He should satisfy them with various desires as well as gifts of jewels and the like;
and when the Brahmins have eaten, he should duly distribute [the remaining food].
O best of the Bharatas, having fed the reciter after he has been well-adorned,
when the Brahmins are pleased, the deities become pleased with him.
[543] When the reciter is fully satisfied, there arises a supreme and auspicious joy;
thereafter, O bull of the Bharatas, the exposition of the Saṃhitās should be performed.
Having heard this history exactly as it occurred and in its proper sequence,
one who has restrained the self and become pure shall reach the further shore in the land of Bhārata.
O descendant of Bharata, having heard this account of the Bharatas, gifts should be given to the Brahmins by those who possess faith,
according to one's ability and with devotion, O bull of the Bharatas.
Great gifts should be bestowed, as well as various vehicles,
cows with bronze milking vessels, and most enchanting maidens.
There were various vehicles endowed with all the qualities of desire,
diverse palaces, and golden garments for dwelling upon the earth.
Vehicles should also be given, as well as charming, rutting elephants;
couches, palanquins, and well-adorned chariots.
Whatever excellent thing there may be in the house, whatever great wealth exists, that should be given to the twice-born; even one's own self, servants, and sons.

With supreme faith and a devoted heart, they gradually mastered the recitation; being well-disposed, possessing excellent learning, and free from envy, they applied themselves according to their ability.

Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of listening to the Purāṇas.
Now follows the procedure for the gift common to all Śāstras. Regarding this, it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
I shall proclaim the gift of knowledge by which the Mothers are satisfied;
O Lord, listen to the procedure by which it is written and bestowed.
Likewise:
devotion arises in those who hear; from that they worship the guru;
and he, O King, teaches the sciences and the scriptures to you who have taken refuge in him for the sake of knowledge and long life.
On a beautiful and even palm-leaf manuscript, with leaves well-arranged,
there was a variegated cloth-casing on the sides, enclosed within a leather cover.
With either red or black thread, soft and dyed,
bound with a firm string, and prepared according to this rite.
But he who causes the twelve-thousand-verse compendium to be written out and gives it to one who is devoted to it goes to the supreme goal.
In a region free from all obstacles and sloping toward the northeast,
the wise man should prepare a mandala with auspicious cow dung.
Within a square measuring one cubit (hasta) on each side, which is beautiful and auspicious,
one should draw a lotus in the center using white, red, white, and other colors.
One should adorn all directions with flowers produced from the desires of every season; one should cause a beautiful canopy, variegated and multicolored, to be spread over the head.
On the sides, one should properly arrange a beautiful display with white cloths,
as well as with balls, half-moons, mirrors, and chowries.
One should provide it on all sides with the sounds of bells and small tinkling bells;

The wise man should bind it with thread, fastened slightly at the bottom and well-secured at the top, adorned with a firm knot.
Above that, the wise one should place a beautifully written manuscript;
then, he should worship an image located right there according to the prescribed rite.
Likewise, with waterless flowers free from worms and insects,

In a secluded place, with a well-disposed and pure mind, day after day,

having done so, may the Vidyās, my Mothers, be pleased with me.
One should conceive that very scripture to which [the deity] is attached as a manuscript;

with that water, one should properly sprinkle the donor upon the head.

By the mere sight of him, he becomes the destroyer of the sins of all the worlds;
even after death, he goes to the abode honored by Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Having rescued seven preceding and seven succeeding generations of his own lineage, as well as everyone else,
from the mire of sin, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, for as many syllables as there are leaf-numbers,
for that long he sports in the worlds of Viṣṇu with various pleasures.
Then, having returned to the earth, he becomes devoted to the Goddess;
endowed with all enjoyments, he is born into a family of the learned.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"This merit which has just been declared regarding the gift of knowledge, the wise man [attains it] through the conjunction of place, time, ritual procedure, faith, and a worthy recipient. [548]
By diligently propitiating the guru who has reached the further shore of explaining the sciences, one obtains a fruit multiplied ten millionfold through the gift of knowledge.
One should undertake the gift of knowledge with one's power, devotion, and prostration.

Knowledge is the foremost of gifts; having heard the ritual from his teacher, the wise man, with a self purified by faith, should receive the knowledge according to the rule.
One should give those [gifts] to worthy recipients, especially to those endowed with virtuous qualities;
and whatever is suitable for a particular person, that one should bestow upon him.
In the abodes of the Siddhas, those who seek the fruit of great merit should diligently offer gifts according to the extent of their wealth.
On an auspicious lunar mansion and day, or on a favorable planetary conjunction, one should have [the manuscript] written after having worshipped the lords of the gods: Rudra, Brahmā, and Janārdana.
Having conquered the eastern direction, he became a knower of scripts, the best of scribes,
with hands and arms capable of restraint through his mastery in holding the ink-pot.
That best of scribes, who possesses solitude and the necessary materials,
should prepare an auspicious receptacle for knowledge made of gold or silver.
It may also be made of ivory or of auspicious wood;
it should be pleasing, made of fragrant aloe-wood, beautiful, and produced by the application of smooth machinery.
It should be joined with closing petals and endowed with blossoming ones; "made of *nāgadanta*" means fashioned from ivory. Therein, one should place the vidyā, established within a book.
And one should prepare its book, writing it with a width of two finger-breadths;
it should be auspicious, smooth, beautiful, black, or deep blue-black.
Alternatively, it should have the luster of a red lotus, adorned with black [pigments], auspicious, strung with cotton thread, and perfumed with various fragrances.
Adorned with dark-blue ornaments and decorated with the half-moon of a peacock, it was further embellished with many kinds of ink in four distinct colors,
as well as with numerous dark-blue designs joined by firm supports.
Fixing is the cause for the stability of the ink.
And with divine pens, indeed adorned with gold,
one should make the exterior of the book beautiful to behold.
Well-fastened and variegated with yellow, red, or brownish dyes,
it is beautiful, light, very spacious, and provided with knots that are not overly tight.
Then, in a delightful and secluded house with walls plastered with lime, one should place the previous manuscript containing the *vidyādhāra* and situated within its mechanical device.
Adorned with the sprouts of various passions, delightful with its pure reflection, fragrant with the pleasing scent of incense, and covered by a canopy.
The scribe shall be intelligent, bathed, resplendent in white flowers and garments,
adorned with golden and pearl armlets, and his fingers graced with signet rings.
When the ink-pot is well-kindled and provided with the weapon of the pen,
one should begin the worship of the gods and the ancestors amidst the sounding of musical instruments.
At the beginning, after having the Brahmins recite auspicious benedictions, the wise man should cause the scripture to be heard;
first, he should have the *Śrīka-pañcaka* or even the *Daśaka* written down.
Then, on the second day, in conjunction with an auspicious lunar mansion, one should write it down according to that very same procedure, accompanied by meritorious days and favorable omens.
Then, when the treatise has been completed, one should again perform a rite for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) during that same day and night, providing items such as food and drink.
"Or both [the plaintiff and defendant] should correct that document, making it consistent with what is recited;
the meaning is that while reading the document, both should correct it.

There is also the application [of the rule] through the statement of a deficient meaning, as well as by virtue of the suitability of the meter,
through the understanding of the meaning of other sūtras, and by means of the discernment of questions and answers.

Having examined the semantic proximity of words with multiple meanings,
and through the understanding of all the treatises, by means of the grammatical factors and so forth that are unimpaired;

having understood that desired connection of meters with the poetic feet.

should bestow it with divine riches upon the temples of the gods.
The arrangement of scripts from a manifest region is clearly called Nāgara;
it follows the manifest arrangement of scripts according to its specific location.
In the arrangement of the writing-tablet and in the formation of the letters, he was likewise skilled;
having placed [the image] upon a vehicle enriched with jewels, adorned with fine cloths,
graced with the beauty of bells and chowries, and provided with a jeweled-handled parasol.
Or [he may see him] mounted upon an elephant, a horse, or a chariot, endowed with great splendor,
preceded by song and dance and the sound of various musical instruments.
One should announce it to the god with auspicious sounds and the chanting of the Vedas;
having fully honored the dwellers of heaven with offerings of various forms.
And having given the book there, one should dedicate the merit to the ancestors and to beloved kinsmen, desiring for them infinite fruit.
Then, having bestowed that vidyā according to the prescribed rite in a temple of Śiva,
he should thereafter feed brahmins and men who are devotees of Rudra.
Festivals should be celebrated according to one's means within one's own homes;
however, the king should celebrate them in the city, and likewise the village headmen in their respective villages.
In every house, the festival should be celebrated by the householders together with their kinsmen;
they should be bathed, anointed with white unguents, adorned with garlands, and composed in mind.
Then, the scripture should be heard by those endowed with joy and possessed of faith;
there, one should honor the reciter according to the extent of one's wealth.
The wise one should honor the guru with devotion according to his ability and without guile;
thereafter, he should fully worship the disciples with flowers and incense.
The Brahmin beggar was wise, learned in the scriptures, and high-minded;
he had mastered the arrangement of syllables and was an expert in the treatises on poetic meter.

He understands the meaning of words, is eloquent, and is humble; moreover, he is endowed with intelligence, knows music, speaks words that are pleasant to hear, and his speech is not marred by faulty accents.
And the teacher shall be righteous, wise, learned in the scriptures, free from envy,
a Brahmin pure by nature, clean, and always smiling-faced.
He was of excellent conduct, knowledgeable in the treatises on proper behavior, and proficient in the science of grammar;
he had thoroughly mastered the multitude of scriptures and was skilled at advancing the subject matter at hand.
He who expresses the subject matter at hand, who provides an interpretation that maintains the sequence of the preceding and following parts,
who determines the purpose of the divisions of chapters and cantos,
who understands the meaning of words according to the treatise, who is wise, and who makes clear the meaning of both individual words and verses.
It conveys the meaning by designating the heart-substance— which is beyond syllables and arises from the collective, the miscellaneous, the primary, and the incidental meanings of the scriptures.
One who has mastered the classification of the meaning of the treatise from its commencement onward,
yet becomes an opponent by distorting the hidden meaning through a conceit of his own [limited] proficiency.
One whose speech is trustworthy, who is free from laziness, and who awakens the listener to proper conduct—
[such a person] [should teach] refined knowledge through refined expressions, and even common knowledge through common expressions.
The teacher who awakens his disciples through mere conversations and explanations,
as well as the teacher who awakens them through the tenfold arrangement of names;
He is the guru, he is the father, he is the mother; he is remembered as the wish-fulfilling gem—whosoever, having explained the means of the scriptures, delivers one from the hells.
Who in this world on earth is a kinsman equal to him,
by whose multitude of light-ray-like words the darkness within the heart is churned away?
He is the sun of great splendor arising from the night of the great saṃsāra;
one should not cause him to turn away by means of arrogance or harshness.
He should not feel aversion toward his diseases, sufferings, or impurities;
rather, he should pacify what is provoked and rescue those submerged in suffering.
And one should rescue them from diseases with effort and protection;
thus, having heard this excellent exposition from the mouth of the Guru, the best of men [should act].
But he who, desiring his own welfare in the next world, should contemplate what is to be practiced,
should listen with faith, being self-restrained and facing the teacher.
Not interrupting the discourse on what is beneficial to others, being vigilant and indeed tireless,
he should speak words with gentleness when doubt arises and inquire further.
And the Guru said: "In private, one who possesses faith should rely upon these words;
having performed this himself, he should act [further], provided with fuel and joined palms."
This was the deed of the Guru:
"He who should interrupt an irrelevant discourse in the presence of his Guru incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin, being one who lacks certainty regarding the words of his Guru."
And he who, having heard a scripture or acquired an auspicious refinement from another,
should produce fame for someone else, would be a slayer of a Brahmin in relation to his own teacher.
And he who, through delusion, causes one to forget even the supreme meaning of the treatise,
goes to a terrible, inexhaustible hell of fearsome appearance.
But whatever auspicious or inauspicious act a man performs after having understood the scripture,
that indeed becomes a hundredfold greater than for one who delights in mere intellectual knowledge.
In this manner, the wise speaker should express that all austerity, consisting of self-restraint, is the means for accomplishing results such as heaven and the like.
Having gently awakened him, one should speak of the inner self (*adhyātma*) and other such matters;
one should cause him to recite with a continuous flow (*dhārāvarta*), avoiding angry speech or the agitation of combat.
With the force of a continuous whirlpool,
one should cause her to speak with passionate and graceful words during their joined embrace; one should have her speak with a charm that accords with various poetic meters.

When the reciter has finished, O Bhīṣma, the wise man should speak thus;

One should say "well-heard, well-heard," and "let this be explained";
may the world proceed according to dharma, and may the king always be victorious.
"Virtuous, endowed with wealth, and a teacher free from disease here"—
having spoken thus, one should depart as one was born, having clearly understood this.
Disciples who are discerning should contemplate the scripture among themselves,

in this manner, a disciplined man should listen to the exposition day after day.
Through hearing the entirety of the scriptures,
a person’s mind here becomes dominated by faith and attains an inclination toward the nature of the scriptures.
And the defects perish in the twinkling of an eye.

upon the completion of the composition of that scripture—
And even at the arising of speech, his intellect has already passed away.
One who desires the welfare of his ancestors should thus worship Śakti for twelve kalpas and likewise honor the Guru with devotion.
This is declared to be the primary rule for the bestowal of knowledge;
by this very procedure, a Brahmin [should impart it] to one who is endowed with virtuous conduct.
One who awakens a person endowed with intelligence, skilled in reasoning, and conversant in the Vedic teachings,
should impart this auspicious scripture with the desire to attain great merit.
Having made a learned teacher well-satisfied with abundant wealth and honor, one should cause him to teach virtuous disciples who are of noble birth and possessed of intelligence.
Thus, the gift of knowledge is traditionally held to be the best of all gifts;
at all times, for all social classes, it is the supreme raft for crossing over hell.
Having bestowed the vidyā according to this rite, a man devoted to merit obtains the fruit of a hundred well-performed horse-sacrifices.
Whatever fruit is obtained from a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices properly performed,

Having given to the Brahmins land filled with all kinds of crops and adorned with all manner of jewels during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains through the gift of knowledge,
that same fruit is obtained for as many syllables as exist within the body of the scripture.
The giver of this knowledge shall dwell in heaven for as many thousands of years as there are lines of syllables contained within that book.
For as many auspicious folios as are found in the book, for that many thousands of ages his lineage rejoices in heaven.
Having rescued them from as many hells as there are, he leads them to heaven,
even for as many hundreds of births as were the sins committed by them.
All that perishes for that embodied being through the gift of knowledge;
he is born as a man in this world, he is blessed, and he is possessed of fame.
That supreme person who is devoted to the practice of giving the gift of knowledge should bestow that knowledge according to his means, free from all deceit.
He goes to the most meritorious worlds, which are imperishable and adorned with enjoyments.
In the Vahnipurāṇa,
Ambarīṣa said:
"O Sage, the gift of cows is of many kinds, as is the gift of land."
All things, beginning with the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), have been described by you to me.
Now I wish to hear of the great fruit of the gift of knowledge;
O great sage, please describe that various [fruit] according to the prescribed rule.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O best of kings, I shall now declare to you accurately the gift of knowledge—how it is to be given and what its fruit is; listen to that.
On an auspicious day and under an auspicious constellation, having constructed a pavilion with an auspicious altar— either square or with a canopy— one should smear that ground [with cow dung].

Whatever fruit belongs to a donor of jewels who gives according to this rite to a well-conducted Brahmin who is reciting and speaking eloquently—
The giver of even a single book obtains that fruit multiplied ten millionfold;
it is the same merit as that of those who travel to sacred pilgrimage sites and that of men who perform sacrifices.
The merit from the gift of knowledge is multiplied ten millionfold; there is no doubt about this, for it is equal to the fruit obtained by properly giving away a thousand tawny cows.
One attains that fruit by the single gift of a book.
Now, the gift of knowledge for one who possesses little wealth but has faith is described. Regarding this, the Devīpurāṇa states:
"He who makes a gift of knowledge according to his own means attains a fruit that is as difficult to achieve [for others] as for the wealthy; of this there is no doubt."
A woman shall obtain the fruit of the gift of knowledge by this very same method;
even one who is not authorized by her husband, or a widow, may do so with him [the husband] in mind.
One should always give clothing, oil for anointing, and food to one seeking knowledge;
likewise, an umbrella, water, and a lamp, because without these, one cannot traverse the earth.

By giving a well-measured and very beautiful book-cover,
a wise person obtains the merit of the gift of knowledge, as does one who provides it bound with thread.
A mechanical device, a seat, or even a staff-seat,
when given to one habitually devoted to the recitation of spells, bestows a kingdom.
Collyrium given for the eyes and feet to one devoted to learning bestows the fruit of the earth,
houses, fields, and the kingdom of heaven.
On whatever land one constantly establishes the gift of knowledge, that person also attains heaven through its power; of this there is no doubt.
In the Nandipurāṇa: "Even those who provide a leaf, an inkwell, a pen, a case,
or similar items to one intent upon studying a concise treatise are likewise givers of knowledge."
O lord of men, those mortals who possess merit go to auspicious worlds.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By the gift of a book, one obtains the merit of the gift of knowledge;
and he who teaches the arts shall obtain the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice."
Even by giving the tools of a craft, one obtains that fruit born of the gift of knowledge;
likewise, by turning back one who is intent on doing harm.
The fruit of the gift of knowledge has been proclaimed; no hesitation should be made in this matter.
Likewise, by giving supreme wisdom even to one of sinful conduct, [great merit is gained].
Having obtained the fruit of the gift of knowledge, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
