likewise, the giver of a vessel to one who lives by means of that vessel [obtains great merit].
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: A poor man, acting according to his means and avoiding stinginess regarding wealth,
shall obtain the fruit of the gift of knowledge by performing this rite with devotion.
According to whatever wealth one may possess, that is followed here;
having offered it, those highly fortunate ones are glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having given a book-covering (pustakāstaraṇa) measuring one thousand [units] in size,
or that same measure for a seat or a canopy, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
For as many thousands of eons as there are threads in those garments when counted all around, for that long shall one obtain great enjoyments.
Whoever should give a well-arranged collection of items produced from the *śrīparṇa* tree, having placed them in a casket made either of leather or carved out of a hollowed-out surface;
By giving a very smooth wooden plank to one devoted to the knowledge of Śiva for the purpose of studying it, one obtains the fruit of the gift of knowledge.
He who [offers] a golden casket, perfectly full, adorned with all kinds of jewels, complete with its lid, and serving as a repository for the treasury of knowledge;
Or one may have it made of silver or copper, square in shape,
or of bell-metal, brass, iron, or constructed from wood, bamboo, and the like.
With a new armor deeply dyed with excellent astringent, one should polish it both inside and out; this is the ever-new abode for the bestowal of knowledge.
One should construct a casket for the jewel of knowledge that is very firm, provided with a rim, secured by strong pillars, and equipped with a lock.
O King, having thus had that Seat of Knowledge constructed according to his means, the wise man should worship it there according to the prescribed rites.
In that place, with the proclamation of "an auspicious day," one should install the treasury of knowledge;
thus, whoever should construct an auspicious abode for the Śiva-vidyā.
Released from all sins, he shall obtain the fruit of the gift of knowledge by creating a mandala of knowledge in a pavilion for the exposition of knowledge.
Having worshipped the Śiva-vidyā there, one should then listen to its exposition;
he too goes to the abode of Śiva, endowed with all desired objects.
Whoever hears and proclaims this knowledge according to this method shall attain prosperity and happiness, and upon the end of the body, obtain liberation.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"Thus has been proclaimed the great merit of bestowing knowledge;
having heard this, one is certainly liberated from the principal sins born of seven lifetimes."
In the Devīpurāṇa: "Therefore, with every effort, knowledge should always be given by men;
in this very world one attains fame, and upon death, one goes to the supreme goal."
But he who shall perpetually promote the gift of knowledge in the house of the Goddess shall become worthy of worship by all the worlds and shall attain the state of the worshipful.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"All deities, beginning with Brahmā, are established in the gift of knowledge;
excluded from the gift of knowledge, they do not know dharma and adharma."
Therefore, O Indra among kings, one should bestow the gift of knowledge with every effort for as long as seventy-one cycles of the four ages.
O King, he shall sport for an inexhaustible time in the city of Viṣṇu;
and having returned to earth at the end of that time, he will become a king of kings.
In the Tretā Yuga, he is born again and again devoted to dharma;
born into a great family, he becomes a righteous king.
He was a donor of elephants, horses, and chariots, an enjoyer [of their fruits] free from envy;
he was the possessor of millions of excellent cities and indeed of many provinces.
Endowed with beauty and good fortune, he shall be long-lived and free from disease;
surrounded by sons and grandsons, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
One should give a fee to the scribe consisting of garments and ornaments;
and if one is able, one should also give a pair of garments along with a copy of the scripture.
Having had that treatise transcribed, it should always be given to one who possesses virtue,
who is devoted to austerity, who delights in the Dharma, and who is intent upon its preservation.
One should present the book wrapped in a pair of garments,
and one should likewise honor the reciter with clothing, ornaments, and decorations.
The scribe, being well-composed, should say, "May it be forgiven.
By this very procedure, one shall obtain the fruit from the gift of the vidyā.
In the Vahni Purāṇa:
"Whatever fruit results from a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices properly performed, that same fruit one attains through the gift of knowledge; of this there is no doubt."
Therefore, O King, if one desires one's own spiritual welfare, one should always cause the recitation of the Dharmaśāstra to be performed in the temple or while listening to it.
O best of kings, by that [act], cows, land, gold, garments, beds, and seats are given by him every day.
This world does not know dharma and adharma without knowledge;
therefore, O virtuous one, one should always be devoted to the gift of knowledge.
O best of kings, if the secrets within the Vedic scriptures did not exist, then what would be the condition of the world, blinded as it were by the darkness of ignorance?
All the gods beginning with Brahmā, the sages whose sins have been burnt away,
as well as humans and the ancestors, are established in the gift of knowledge.
O Indra among kings, after seventy-one cycles of the four yugas,
that best of gods, who has bestowed the Vedas and Shastras, is honored in heaven.
But having returned here from that time, he becomes a righteous king, rich in elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles; he is a donor, an enjoyer, and free from envy.
Endowed with beauty and good fortune, long-lived, free from disease, and happy, surrounded by sons and grandsons, he attains liberation at the proper time; of this there is no doubt.
In this world, there is no gift that yields such distinguished fruit as knowledge— which dwells within the lotus of the mouth—
excepting all other gifts such as cattle, land, gold, elephants, horses, chariots, and the like.
Therefore, O King, why would that which is being given not be considered as already bestowed?
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of knowledge (*vidyādāna*).

Thus [ends the section] in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrī Hemādri, the illustrious Mahādeva, the supreme king of great kings, the lord of all administrative powers, and the master of all branches of learning.
The Section on Giving, Chapter Eight: The Sub-section on Excessive Giving [564] The Section on Giving, the Eighth Chapter.
Now the ten great gifts are described:
such is that stainless family, possessing boundless knowledge and faultless form;
its speech is preeminent in sweetness, shaking the hosts of the army of poverty with its abundance.
Thus, because the virtues in this [work] assume greatness as if through a mutual desire to excel one another, Hemādri calls this the *vidhi* among the ten great gifts (*mahādāna*).

The summary verses regarding these are found in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Gold, sesame seeds, an elephant, a horse, a chariot, land, a house, a daughter, a tawny cow, and a milch-cow— these indeed are the ten great gifts (*mahādāna*)."
In that regard, since it was mentioned first, the gift of gold alone is discussed for now. In the *Vahni Purāṇa*, Rāma said:
"O best of eminent sages, this deed was performed by me out of anger."
How may I be liberated from that evil, such as the killing of living beings?
Having been thus addressed, those great seers, who knew the true nature of dharma, spoke to him regarding the supreme purifier of sins: the gift of gold in this world.
[565] We have heard that this peerless purifier has come into being here;
it is the supreme seed of Śambhu, the splendor, and the offspring of Jātavedas.
A thousand [beings] born from Rudra and Śukra belong to Kārttikeya;
because of their purity, they are worn by all the gods upon their crowns and other ornaments.
Agni is indeed all the deities, and gold is of his very nature;
therefore, by one who gives gold, all the deities shall be pleased.
"Those who bestow gold rescue ten ancestors and ten descendants from hell; so said Bṛhaspati."
Those who bestow gold grant all desires;
so the venerable Marīci, the son of the Grandfather, declared of old.
The man who constantly bestows gold upon Brahmins rejoices for a long time in heaven like a god— purified and wise.
The fruit of all other gifts follows one for only a single lifetime;
however, the fruit of gifts of gold, land, and a Gaurī image follows for seven lifetimes.
He who, out of greed, does not bestow the gift of knowledge or gold,
perishes through his sin and, enveloped by it, shall go to hell.
Even after committing a very great sin, he who gives gold is instantly liberated from that sin; there is no doubt about this.
"Having performed this for the sake of purification, O Bhārgava, give gold.
Thus addressed by those sages, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma, [acted accordingly].
He gave gold to the Brahmins and was thereby liberated from that sin;
therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should give gold to the twice-born.
If one desires the eternal goal, one should dedicate it to Viṣvaksena. From the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Gold is the supreme gift; gold is the highest sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
It is the most sacred of the sacred and the greatest of gifts; of this there is no doubt.
In a former birth, she was the daughter of Dakṣa named Satī; she was the devoted wife known as Umā, the daughter of Himavat.
And due to Dakṣa’s wrath, Satī abandoned her own body;
she was born as the daughter of Himavat, renowned in the world as Gaurī.
Having prostrated before the wielder of the Pināka bow, he too gave her to him;
he then caused the marriage of his daughter to be performed according to the prescribed rites.
The Grandfather offered oblations into the fire according to the marriage rite;
and as he was performing the homa, his mind became agitated by passion.
Then, upon seeing that form, the seed of the high-souled one was discharged by the goddess;
it was then trampled by her feet and thereby became manifold.
The high-souled Vālakhilyas and Marīcis were born there;
and the remainder fell into the fire, becoming as radiant as fire itself.
Seeing the son of Vibhāvasu blazing with brilliance,
they, being meritorious, took him upon their heads with joined palms.
And the gods, Gandharvas, and sages of firm vows said:
"O Vibhāvasu, the ornaments of you, the god, are the merit of your sacrifices and charitable works."
Likewise, the wives of the gods employed it thus for their ornaments;
in this manner, gold was produced from Agni as well as from Brahmā.
[567] There is no other purifying substance in the world equal to gold; indeed, there exists no kind of gift, offering, or ornament comparable to it.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"In the case of a house and the like, the fruit of merit shall be according to the value;
therefore, among all gifts, gold is remembered as the most excellent."
Just as the work of goldsmiths and others is accomplished with gold, so it is not through the gift of a house; therefore, gold is superior to that.
Vedavyāsa: "Those who bestow gold grant all desires;
for this indeed the venerable Atri, the son of the Grandfather (Brahmā), has declared."
Furthermore, gold has been proclaimed by Manu, the lord of men, to be a purifier, meritorious, and inexhaustible for the ancestors.
Manu: "The giver of land obtains everything; the giver of gold obtains long life. Saṃvarta: [as above].
A giver of gold attains great prosperity and long life. Viṣṇu says:
a giver of gold attains residence in the same world as Agni.
Bṛhaspati said: Gold is the first offspring of Agni;
the earth belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are the daughters of the Sun.
The three worlds are bestowed by him who gives gold, a cow, and land.
Viśvāmitra said:
O King, wherever in one's house there remains a written praise of the gift of gold,
the Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, and other such beings do not behold that place.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"Having ascertained the weight of gold and other materials, one should bestow them upon worthy recipients;
endowed with faith in the prescribed rite, one attains one's desired objects."
Vasiṣṭha said: "Therefore, we have heard that all the deities have Agni as their mouth;
for Agni was born from Brahmā, and gold was born from Agni."
Therefore, those who indeed bestow gold, which belongs to all the gods,
go to the worlds of that Creator and attain the supreme goal.
O Bhārgava, he would be consecrated with clarified butter as king in the heavenly world;
thus it continues in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
"This is pure, supremely meritorious, and was always [present] within bodies of old."
Since they all maintain it for the sake of auspiciousness and freedom from disease.
Therefore, all sins are purified when given to worthy recipients according to the prescribed rites, at the proper time and place, and in the presence of Hara.
Listen, O ascetic, to the manner in which gold was formerly bestowed by the high-souled Raicīka upon Rāma in the past.
Having performed a sacrifice consisting entirely of gold, the Brahmins were fully satisfied;
having honored them with golden ornaments, a hundredfold fruit was likewise bestowed.
Furthermore, having himself carefully placed [the weight] on the end of the scale,
he personally gave gold to the twice-born on the second side.
Furthermore, he then gave those very sun-dish vessels to the brahmins at the sacred fords such as Prabhāsa.
And of cows of ten colors, he gave ten thousand each, separately, all well-formed and accompanied by their calves.
Having bound the blanket and stepped upon it, he indeed gave eleven palas of gold, one for each [of the elephants] individually.
Having had nine lotuses made of gold, you placed them upon the tops of the various sacred lingas as you wandered.

Then, O giver of honor, having honored and satisfied the brahmins hundreds and thousands of times with ornaments made of that very substance, they were further gratified by him with that same [offering].
Having had lotuses, banners, and especially garlands prepared and assigned to the houses of Rudra and the others in every home;
By giving a sacred thread, a staff, a girdle, sandals,
as well as a pen and an inkwell to brahmins, one indeed attains that [merit].
Having caused thousands of items to be made, he gave away the entire collection of mental requisites, seats, and vessels fashioned from that very material to the twice-born.
Having fashioned numerous forms of the planets and the deities,
and having worshipped them according to the rules, they were installed in the temple of the twice-born.
Having surveyed the golden earth, complete with mountains and oceans and endowed with sacred medicinal forests, he bestowed it upon the brahmins.
In these and many other ways, gold was given in the past by those who had found a worthy recipient, for the purpose of removing their sins.

In the *Śrī Mahābhārata*, within the narration of the instruction given by his own father—whom he had seen in a dream and who was satisfied by the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*)—these are the words spoken by Bhīma to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"In the Vedas and the Upaniṣads, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is indeed required for all ritual acts;
and in all sacrifices, land, cows, and gold are prescribed as the offerings to be dedicated."
Furthermore, the supreme Vedic injunction is indeed that gold is the sacrificial fee;
therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, this has been properly undertaken by you today.
"However, for the sake of land and cattle, let gold be given;
thus it was with us, O knower of dharma, and with all our ancestors."
They have indeed been delivered and they shall be delivered; for that is the supreme purifier.
They deliver ten ancestors and ten others as well.
"Those who bestow gold"—thus did my ancestors speak to me regarding Rāma; these were the words of Vasiṣṭha concerning Rāma:
"Having extracted all jewels, he is endowed with a mass of splendor."
O best of Brahmins, gold is the most excellent and supreme jewel among these.
For this reason, the gods, gandharvas, uragas, rākṣasas,
humans, and piśācas, being self-restrained, uphold it.
O best of the Bhrigus, they shine here with crowns, armlets, and various kinds of ornaments fashioned from gold.
Therefore, it is remembered as the supreme purifier among all purifiers;
even after giving land, cows, and whatever else besides, [this remains the best].
O Lord, the gift of gold is distinguished as supreme;
gold is indeed inexhaustible and purifying, and it shines brilliantly.
Bestow this most excellent purifier upon the foremost of the twice-born;
for gold alone is prescribed everywhere as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Those who bestow gold indeed become all-possessing at all times.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"Five *māṣas* are known as one *kṛṣṇala*, and sixteen *māṣas* are remembered as one *suvarṇa*; by the gift of that, a donor shall attain heaven."
Likewise:
Therefore, one should always give gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a worthy recipient;
for if given to an unworthy recipient, that gold causes one to fall into the ocean of hell.
If, however, that [gold] is lost through negligence, one should provide an equivalent amount;
otherwise, one would be guilty of theft regarding the lost gold that was not returned.
For it was created solely for the purpose of giving; indeed, it is unstained and a means to attain heaven.
There exists no ritual superior to the gifting of gold.
Gold is the supreme gift; gold is the highest sacrificial fee.
This is the most excellent purifier; this is the great means of securing well-being.
O lord of the people, by giving [this] to brahmins, one may deliver ten preceding generations, ten succeeding generations, oneself, and even those who have committed a hundred sins.
Those men who bestow gold with a pure mind—by that [act], the deities are equal to them; of this we have heard, without a doubt.
For Agni is all the deities, and gold is the consumer of oblations;
therefore, by one who gives gold, all the deities are effectively given.

And in the absence of fire, those who know all the Vedas as authoritative perform [the rite] with gold in the places where fire is normally situated, according to the indications of the Śruti scriptures.
But those who, having kindled this fire, offer it at the rising of the sun while dedicating it to their vow, shall indeed attain all their desires.
"Referring to the vow" means having undertaken the vow.
The giver of gold enjoys his desired crows in the heavenly world;
clothed in a radiant garment, he wanders here and there.
He shone, resplendent in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun,
radiant and filled with throngs of Apsarases, by his own luminous splendor.
O best of men, traveling here and there in heaven by means of a celestial chariot drawn by swans and peacocks,
you shall move about carrying divine fragrances.
Therefore, men on earth should give gold according to their own capacity;
there is nothing else in this world that provides such immediate liberation from sin.
He who gives pure gold to one who possesses pure gold is honored in the heavenly world for many thousands of years.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: He who bestows gold upon gold is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the heavenly world.
By giving two pieces of gold, one attains an imperishable state;
likewise, by giving a hundred pieces of gold to the twice-born with a mind full of faith.
Having reached the world of Brahmā, he rejoices together with Brahmā.

First, by the word *suvarṇa*, gold is denoted; by the next, its purity of color is established; and the third refers to a specific measure. In this regard, the formula for the act of giving is as follows:

Oṃ. Today, in such-and-such a place, at such-and-such a time, I, [name] of such-and-such a lineage, [name], give this gold, whose deity is Agni, to you, [name] of such-and-such a lineage, [name], a Brāhmaṇa; it is yours, not mine. Oṃ. To [name] of such-and-such a lineage, etc.—this gold is given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the consecration of this gift of gold; I give it to you, it is not mine. Some say that silver is the sacrificial fee for the gift of gold. And this is the mantra for the gift: "The gold within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha is the seed of the Fire-god."
It yields infinite merit as its fruit; therefore, grant me peace.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "The gold should be one *pala*, or twice that, or thrice that, according to one's capacity;
it should be made of pure gold and accompanied by two or three [pala] of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)."
One may perform that [offering] either below the *pala* or with a *dakṣiṇā* according to one's preference;
for there is the maxim that "an increase in wealth entails an increase in the *pala*."
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of gold. In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"When sunrise has arrived, [the gift should be performed] preceded by the ritual rules and mantras."
He who indeed gives gold destroys bad dreams.
The evil of one who gives [gold] as soon as it has risen dissolves;
he who gives gold at midday destroys future sin.
He who, firm in his vows, gives gold during the final twilight,
attains residence in the same world as Brahmā, Vāyu, Agni, and Soma.
By giving gold, one attains inexhaustible and abundant worlds;
he who, having kindled the fire, performs the rite toward the northern solstice (udayana).
One should indeed give [the gift] with reference to a vow; one attains all desires.
Whatever deity one worships, through that [deity], and to whomever one gives [the gift].
He who gives [this] always dwells eternally in his world.
"Referring to the vow" means having undertaken the vow.
The giver of gold enjoys his desired pleasures in the heavenly world;
free from passion and clothed in excellent garments, he wanders here and there.
He shone brilliantly in a celestial chariot, sun-colored and radiant as the sun,
filled with throngs of apsaras and glowing with his own splendor.
Carrying a divine fragrance, that best of men traveled here and there through heaven in a vehicle that moved at will and was yoked with swans and peacocks.
Therefore, men on earth should give gold according to their own capacity;
there is nothing higher than this in the world for the immediate liberation from sin.
He who gives pure gold as a gift is honored in the heavenly world for many thousands of years.
Thus ends the rule for the daily gift of gold.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Now I shall describe the gift of gold, which was produced from my own seed."
It contains the essence of fire, is purifying, and increases longevity and health.
A purifier (pavitra) of one niṣka, or half of that, or even a quarter;
having filled a vessel with an āḍhaka measure of rice, one should place it into another vessel.
One should fill [the vessel] with half-an-āḍhaka of sesame seeds and place upon it a vessel filled with ghee;
into that ghee, one should place gold weighing half the measure of the sesame seeds.
On ground smeared with cow dung, one should place those three—
the Brahmin, that gold, and Śambhu— and, having recollected [the deity], worship them.
Having gazed upon one's own reflection, gold, sesame seeds, and rice, one should give them to a brahmin, saying: "May Śiva be well-pleased."
One should give [this] constantly according to this rule, whether monthly, at the solstice, or on the new moon day of the year; for from that comes supreme union with me.
At that time, there will be long life, health, and great joy;
thus, through the gift of gold, one should constantly bestow what is infinite.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of gold.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Then, freed from all exertion, [he attained] the state embraced by Rudra and Umā."
Listen as I speak of these [states] of the embodied being according to this method.
Restrained, placing either a *guñjā* or half a *guñjā* of gold upon the *liṅga* every day, one shall go to that supreme state.
One who gives away the earth filled with all kinds of crops, or even the two worlds accompanied by water,
or one who goes to Rohiṇī for the sake of Hara— he too shall go to that very state.
Likewise, having given great gifts to worthy recipients without doubt, one attains both enjoyments and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Gold is the first offspring of Agni;
the earth belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are the daughters of the Sun.
By [giving] that [gold], the three worlds would be considered given as a gift.
He who would give gold, cows, and land—
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of Śiva-gold from the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"The sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest were seated at a sacrificial session."
Śaunaka and the others questioned Ugraśravas as he was seated.
"Furthermore, we have heard here various teachings on the Dharma;
we now wish to hear further about the unsurpassed gift."
Thus addressed by the sages, the high-minded son of the Sūta spoke here of the wondrous greatness of giving, measured in hundreds.
O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim all that gift which the four-faced Parameṣṭhin formerly declared when questioned by Nārada.
Brahmā said: Listen attentively, O Nārada; I shall describe to you the gift known as the *śatamāna*, which destroys all sins.
It bestows long life, brings prosperity, is meritorious, grants health, and provides progeny;
it grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and is the cause of all auspiciousness.
One should always practice giving during all auspicious times, such as lunar and solar eclipses, and especially on one's own birth-star (janmarkṣa).
In all meritorious places, such as one's home, temples, and so forth—
wherever the necessary means for practice are available— one should perform acts of giving.
Having drawn a lotus on the ground with cow-dung, water, and white rice grains in the center,
adorned with filaments;
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus together with its pericarp.
Having placed a piece of gold weighing one hundred mānas upon it, and having meditated upon Him above that—
Brahmā, the Lord seated upon a lotus throne.
Having worshipped with devotion by means of perfumes and other offerings.
Having reflected upon a beloved person who knows the Vedas and having honored him with the thought that he is Viriñci himself,
one should give him a hundred mānas of gold.
Having uttered, "May the Self-born One be pleased," [he spoke].
It has been said that whoever gives a gift of a hundred measures of gold attains a full lifespan;
therefore, O Nārada, one should perform this rite at least once.
Daily, for a month, for a year, or according to one's ability.
Jāmbūnada, jātarūpa, suvarṇa, kāñcana,
and likewise hiraṇya— these, O Nārada, are [the types of gold] according to their capacity and in due order.
Thus ends the rule for the gift of a *śatamāna*.
Now Baudhāyana says:
And that which is measured as a *śatamāna* of imperishable gold,
one should properly place it in a bronze vessel together with an *āḍhaka* measure of sesame seeds.
They know the measure of a bronze vessel (kāṃsyapātra) to be eight palas;
upon it, one should place sesame seeds and unbroken grains of bright rice.
Having invoked the Lord of Gods, the sun, the imperishable jewel of light,
with fragrant perfumes and garlands, and especially with red garlands;
One should worship the immutable Sun with the sixteen services,
using the eight-syllabled Sāvitra mantra with supreme devotion.
Or else, having prostrated with a mantra bearing the marks of Savitṛ,
one should then perform worship for the Brāhmaṇa with auspicious perfumes and unbroken grains of rice.
And with various other [gifts], without detriment to his own family,
he honored that self-restrained man of good conduct who knew the Self.

Facing north himself, with a disciplined mind, he should perform the formal dedication (*saṃkalpa*) with this mantra for the sake of liberation from sins and diseases, [offering it] to one facing east.
Born from a lotus, holding a lotus in his hand, and having a chariot drawn by seven horses as his vehicle—
the Teacher of the Entire World is pleased when a hundred mānas are offered.
Whatever sin has been committed in this life or in another life— may he destroy all of that, whether through conviction or lack of conviction.
The mantra for the gift:
Then, having asked that Brahmin for forgiveness and prostrating before him, one should dismiss him;
one should arrange everything so that the fruit of the rite may be realized.
[579] Thus concludes the ritual procedure for bestowing a hundred measures that remove evil diseases,
according to the Vahnipurāṇa.
Indra said:
"O Blessed One, the entire fruit of the act of giving bulls has been explained.
I now ask about another meritorious matter that bestows eternal and inexhaustible results."
O Sage, tell me of that gift which increases the pleasure of Hara, the Lord of the three worlds, and by the giving of which the Master is thoroughly gratified.
Since Hari is the self of the guardians of the quarters and is eternally composed of existence and bliss,
how could he— being such— be a devotee made of gold?
By what gift, austerity, vow,
or sacrifice is one liberated from terrible sin that begins at birth and ends with death?
How may a man become illustrious, wise, possessed of sons, and powerful;
likewise long-lived, healthy, endowed with all sovereignty, and highly intelligent?
O Brahmin, if you consider me a devotee of Viṣṇu, I am indeed worthy to hear from whom that Supreme Person attains that station of Viṣṇu which is the highest.
Therefore, O Guru, be gracious and explain to me that gift which is complete in every respect.
Brahmā said: Bliss is the form of Brahman, eternally celebrated in the Vedas;
the all-pervading Lord, the abode of all, is manifestly established in bliss.

Therefore, bestow this meritorious gift, the supreme treasury of bliss, upon the Brahmin who is of imperishable form; increase his highest joy. O Śakra, by means of this gift, may you be endowed with the three realms.
Indra said:
O Brāhmaṇa, tell me the procedure for this great treasure of a gift,
how it should especially be given so as to bring joy to Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said:
Having reached a meritorious lunar day, such as the full moon, or during an eclipse of the moon or the sun;
At the beginnings of the four ages, or during the two solstices, at the time of Viṣṇu’s awakening or his sleep.
Then, one should fashion a water-pot made of udumbara wood,
filled with a weight of gold according to one's own capacity;
likewise, there should be an arrangement of fine silver.
One should not, however, fill it with a load of gold.
With fifty palas of gold, or twenty-five, or even twelve and a half, according to one's own capacity;
or with half of that, or half again, according to the power of one's wealth.
One may even perform half of three palas.
Having placed gold in a copper vessel, together with diamonds, sapphires, rubies, pearls,
lapis lazuli, and corals;
That silver vessel should be turned face down.

Thus, having placed that auspicious treasure upon a seat provided with a covering, topped with *kuśa* grass, and adorned with mirrors and chowries— the wise one, being well-informed, should act accordingly.
Together with sandals, shoes, and an umbrella.
Then, one should worship that [image], joined with a pair of the finest linen garments, with these excellent mantras;
first, however, [one worships] the primordial Viṣṇu with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Having bathed and duly worshipped the Lord who removes the cycle of existence,
and likewise having offered oblations into the sacred fire,
he should then address that auspicious treasure.
Having inscribed the five-syllabled name of Śrī with sandalwood paste, camphor, and saffron,
together with "namas" and the syllable *oṃ*, upon a vessel—
That shines even for a king; therefore, one should worship it.
By you, together with all the lords of the gods, siddhas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, uragas, and kiṃnaras,
as well as the lords of the gandharvas, vidyādharas, and dānavas.
This entire universe is joined with and encompassed by you; salutations to you!
You alone are the Māyā of the Lord, who brings about the entire cycle of worldly existence and is eternally composed of bliss;
you are the treasury of all auspiciousness and the state of meditative absorption.
O beloved of Hari, O auspicious one, salutations to you!
Having thus honored him according to the prescribed rite, one should then worship the Brahmin with bracelets,
armlets, excellent neck-ornaments, earrings, and finger-rings.
Then, having adorned Hari, who wears yellow garments,
the devoted practitioner should worship Acyuta after meditating upon him with this mantra.
"O Hari, you are eternally a god upon earth;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, source of compassion, remove my evil deeds, for salutations be unto you!"
O Bhūdeva, O Blessed One, O Lord who brings about the destruction of worldly existence,
O Conqueror who bestows prosperity upon the world, O All-powerful One, homage be to You!
Having thus worshipped and meditated upon that twice-born man as the very form of Viṣṇu within his heart,
the person should then bestow the Bhadranidhi with this mantra:
First, having uttered the name of the Great-Souled One together with his own lineage,
one should offer water along with barley, *darbha* grass, and sesame seeds.
For the sake of delivering my ancestors, for the increase of eternal bliss,
and for the destruction of the entire flood of sins, this gift to Viṣṇu has been made by me.
Therefore, with this [image] together with its jewels, endowed with the three realms,
accompanied by silken garments, and provided with a mirror and sandals;
May Lord Viṣṇu be pleased by this gift of a seat, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, and sandals, which provides eternal bliss.
Having recited this, one should give it to a twice-born man who is the very form of Hari;
one should give it according to the secret rite and should not proclaim the number of gold pieces.
When proclaimed, the fruit is said to be ten million times ten thousandfold; when kept secret, there is no doubt that it is multiplied by the number of kalpas.
Thus, a wise person should not proclaim this to one who is unworthy.
And whatever wealth was slain and deposited in the midst.
When this is done, that person becomes one who has perfected the self; he would never experience death,
but goes instead to that imperishable abode of Viṣṇu.
Consisting of the bliss whose nature is Śiva, together with its enumeration.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the gift of the auspicious treasure.
In that very Purāṇa,
Garuḍa said:
O Lord, be gracious, O Acyuta, creator of the universe! You are eternally majestic, the scorcher of the enemies of the gods;
grant me the answer to the question that I am about to ask.
O Mukunda, O All-pervading Lord, that is the most excellent answer.
O Lord of the World, how may people in this world be constantly in a state of great festival, always victorious and happy,
the abode of excellent prosperity and bliss, free from old age and immortal?
Tell me that auspicious means by which one becomes free from affliction.
Having heard these words of Garuḍa, Vibhu,
appearing with a gracious countenance, spoke this reply to him:
"O Suparṇa, as for this which you have asked— "
Listen well to that; there is nothing superior to giving.
Even here, and even there, a treasure has been accumulated somewhere, yet it is never obtained by anyone,
even in tens of thousands of ages or hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
While the donor who enjoys [the gift] does not diminish, the recipient diminishes;
whatever state of existence the donor goes to— whether in the next world or even in this one— he enters that very womb.
Whatever is given with great faith to the foremost of the twice-born at the end [of life], that very thing one follows after;
therefore, hear about the treasure [that results] from all forms of giving.
It bestows power and grants eternal fruit.
It bestows sovereignty and liberation, it is imperishable, and it consists of the three worlds as its many jewels for the giver.
One should have it performed at the end of Kārttika, or on the full moon of Māgha, or even in Mādhava;
or during the solstices, the equinoxes, or on the anniversaries of the Manvantaras and Yugas.

During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should, according to one's capacity, place a vessel made of udumbara wood with a silver lid, and likewise, one should set out a golden vessel in the center.
It was filled with various excellent jewels, surrounded by many different kinds [of ornaments],
and further enriched by vessels made of gold, silver, and copper.
"Various hundreds beyond even ten thousand, according to one's capacity.

The first *nānā* means "various," signifying many kinds; the second *nānā* means "coin" (*nāṇaka*) in the Mahārāṣṭra language. Therefore, the meaning is that one should fill [the vessel] with coins of various forms.
"According to capacity" means by a thousand *palas*, a hundred, or fifty.
Or half of that again, O King; one should not have it made with less than a pala.
That task was accomplished by him, free from deceit, using gold, then silver, then copper,
and finally with jewels, all covered with fine cloth.
Having placed various grains upon it, one should worship with the mantras prescribed for the Kalpa,
either by employing a reciter of the Purāṇas or by doing so oneself with his permission.
O bird-born one, having performed the preliminary rites in the presence of the fire, one who holds kuśa grass in hand and possesses a tranquil mind should recite this mantra to Viṣṇu or Īśa.
Oṃ, homage to you who increase all bliss and all prosperity!
Prosper us here with long life, fame, and glory.
Homage to you, whose continuum is infinite, who are ever-blissful and ever-arisen! Grant me here, through your continuity, long life and wealth that are ever-arisen.
Salutations, salutations to Padmanidhi, Dhaneśa, Śatakratu, Śaṅkara, and Nairṛteśa!
O Śaman, pacify our misfortune and ill-fortune.
O Lord Śaṅkara, be the granter of my desires.
Homage, homage to the immeasurable wielder of the noose; homage be to Rāma of the auspicious name;
homage to Samīra and to Hutāśana.
Homage be to the Infinite One, whose seat is the lotus!
Homage to the best of gods, to the Lord of Hari;
homage be to Sāvitrī, Śivā, and Śrī;
to Sarasvatī, Prīti, Rati, and Kriyā.
O you who are contentment, nourishment, mindfulness, peace, and fame!
You alone are the immeasurable treasury of all the immortals,
the father, sage, and lord of the ancestors;
you are the foundation of all that is moving and unmoving.
Since you are the source of the universe, I bow down to you.
Homage be to the Lord of Gods, a treasury of beauty;
homage be to the ocean, a treasury of profundity; homage again and again to the moon, a repository of splendor.
O Bhānu, treasure-house of splendor, I bow down to you.
Homage to Padma, the auspicious one; homage to you, Svastika;
homage to Śaṅkha, to Maṇi, and homage to you, Maṇibhadra.
Homage to Nandivivarta, to Nandāvarta, and to Vartin;
homage to Kaṭakakarṇa, and homage to you, Kaṇṭhāvarta.

Having thus worshipped the treasure-house of eternal bliss according to the prescribed rite, the wise one [should do so] with white mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, unbroken rice, and sandalwood paste.
O Lord of Birds, one should duly pour water upon the ground together with sesame seeds and parched grain, according to the ritual procedure stated in the Kalpa, while reciting this mantra.
Today, at this auspicious time, here in the presence of the twice-born, the gods, and the sacred fire,
for the sake of increasing the fame and welfare of my mother, father, and myself.
And salutations to those who expound the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Vedas, and to those belonging to various lineages who bestow knowledge.
I bestowed upon those brahmins, who possess manifold auspiciousness, that supreme state which grants eternal bliss,
covered with various kinds of garments.
A person who consists of the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva [should be fashioned] with gold, silver, and copper, together with gems, garments, and all necessary furnishings.
"May the imperishable Śrī Yajñapuruṣa be pleased by this gift of the treasure.
Having thus offered the water, he should present it to the Brahmins.
Having distributed [the wealth] according to the scriptures, one should not insult anyone;
since this is a "great gift," even a single person does not deserve it [to be withheld].
Furthermore, some others who have reached the further shore of all ritual injunctions—
whether through sacrifices, gifts, or vows— even such a single person deserves to dwell in that house.
Thus, he who performs such a gift, which is the supreme treasury of eternal bliss,
attains such prosperity continuously within this cycle of existence.
It is said that among all forms of giving without exception, this yields infinite fruit;
by bestowing the ordinance of eternal bliss, one partakes in liberation.
And whoever thus performs the rite of perpetual bliss here once,
he exercises sovereignty repeatedly in the imperishable station of the Creator.
In whatever manner one may act here, through the complete exhaustion of the qualities of one's own karma,
one then attains the sovereignty over the entire earth during that which is known as the Vrata [period].
Furthermore, having ruled the kingdom while remaining joined with his own duty and accompanied by his followers,
he attains the station of Īśāna, which is eternal, imperishable, and undecaying.
Therefore, having returned, he shall again obtain sovereignty in the rank of a Vidyādhara;
possessing no small splendor until the end of the kalpa, through the bestowal of the treasure of Śrī.
Again, at the end of the eon, he goes to the imperishable state of Viṣṇu,
where even those yogins who have departed attain the Supreme once more.
This, O Vainateya, has been declared by me with affection and effort as the "Treasure of Auspiciousness"; what else shall I tell you?
From the gift of the treasury of eternal bliss, eternal bliss is born;
he who should perform this shall possess imperishable life and attain a long lineage.
But he who recites this with devotion, or he who listens with a concentrated mind,
attains a long life and is liberated from all sins.
O Lord of Birds, may you and I together endure this most wonderful and beloved discourse concerning the subduing of the base;
for one who has easily obtained gold here acts [only in such a manner].
And he attains the station of Viṣṇu; oh, how easily attained it is!
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the treasure of bliss.
Now, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "He who bestows pure silver upon a brahmin..."
Having quickly shaken off his sins, he is glorified in the heavenly world.
He is born in this world handsome, fortunate, and glorious.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "A silver vessel for the ancestors, or one adorned with silver..."
Since it originated from the eye of Śiva, therefore it is dear to his father.
Silver is considered inauspicious in sacrifices and in rites for the gods; they say it is always to be avoided as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in rites for the ancestors.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of silver.
Now follows the procedure for the gift of a horse. Regarding this, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"He who indeed bestows a horse that is adorned with gold, well-characterized, and auspicious..."
By that deed, O Goddess, he attains the world of the Gandharvas.
In the Mahābhārata: "He who gives a horse to a brahmin— one that is young, free from defects, and equipped with all necessary trappings— is glorified in the heavenly world."
Likewise:
"O Lord of Men, as many hairs as there are on a horse,
so many abundant worlds do those who give horses attain in this world."
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "He who, being well-restrained, gives as a gift to Brahmins either a horse, or a pair [of oxen], or indeed beautiful sandals."
For him there shall be divine vehicles— chariots adorned with banners and flags—
and a difficult path shall never exist for him here.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "One should give a horse, or its value, or something less, middling, or superior, according to one's wealth, adorned with a multitude of stars."
"Tārāgaṇa" refers to a specific type of ornament that imitates a cluster of stars.
Adorned with silver hooves weighing five palas each and decorated with gold, it should be given in due order,
along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and cloth, to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fire (agnihotrī).
The giver of a horse attains heaven; the giver of a horse attains the same world as the horse.
Faith, the place, and the time are praised in all acts of giving.
The mantra for the gift is found in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"O Uccaiḥśravas, you who bring victory to horses and kings;
salutations to you, the vehicle of the Sun; therefore, grant me peace."
The threefold classification [of horses] based on their relative age and so forth should be understood as being like the gift of gold.
Thus ends the section on the gift of horses,
according to the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, as well as those that are secondary sins—
all of these certainly perish through the horse sacrifice.

In the Kali age, neither the horse sacrifice nor the cow sacrifice is performed; likewise, human sacrifice, the virgin bride, marriage by choice, and the procreation of sons through the husband’s brother are not practiced.
Indeed, this group of seven is censured: the Rājasūya sacrifice, the water-pot, and the Aśvamedha sacrifice—for one who is unable to perform them in the Kali age.
He should perform the gift of a horse here according to the prescribed rule;
I shall declare that rule, which was established by Brahmā in ancient times.
A beautiful white horse, bathed and adorned with a golden saddle-cloth,
with pure silver stirrups and decorated with ivory.
One should fashion Vajranetra with copper horns, a tail of linen, and beautiful garments;
he should be covered with a bright cloth and endowed with his own recitation.
One should present to a Brāhmaṇa such a horse, standing upon grain and jewels, with its girth fastened and well-adorned with fine cloth, and endowed with great luster.
It should be given to one who is handsome, well-conducted, learned, and possessed of keen intelligence;
it should be given to the foremost of mantra-holders and to Bhāskara.
At the beginning of the Manvantara, at the beginning of the Yuga, during the solstices and the equinoxes,
and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses, one shall become happy by giving a horse.

Now, the mantra for worship: Salutations to you, O Sūrya, the son of Mārtaṇḍa, who possesses great speed, the descendant of Kaśyapa, the triple-formed one, the twice-born of the world, and the embodiment of the three Vedas.

In this regard, [saying] "to one of such-and-such lineage," and so forth: "I, desiring heaven, bestow upon you, of such-and-such lineage, and so forth, this horse—adorned with golden ornaments, equipped with a frontal ornament, a neck-strap, and a saddle, decorated with perfumes, flowers, and the like, beautified by silver fetters and jewels, with diamond-like eyes, copper hooves, a silken tail, fine clothing, covered with a bright cloth, provided with its own weapons, standing atop grain and gems, girded with a belt, and well-fitted with a fine cloth. For the sake of the consecration of this gift of a horse, I bestow upon you this gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Thus one should recite the mantra and offer water with sesame seeds into the ear;
O son of Uccaiḥśravas, when the great ocean has arisen.
"I have given you to the foremost of Brahmins; O horse, be happy!
Homage to this Brahmin; this horse has been restored to you."
"O best of Brahmins, please accept this most beautiful [gift] given by me.
Having performed the offering into the ear, one should pour water into the hand of the Brahmin.
Thereafter, one should proceed with the horse in front for seventy-seven steps;
having meditated upon the Sun in the mind and looked back, one should go to one's own home.
He who gives a white horse shall obtain tenfold fruit;
by doing this, O tiger among men, a man shall go to the world of the Sun.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, as well as many others,
all of them perish by giving a horse according to the prescribed ritual.
By giving a horse in the proper manner, a son shall rescue his ancestors— thirty preceding him, thirty following him, and thirty more both before and after— from hell.
The ancestors dance, roll about, and laugh in heaven;
because a giver of horses was born in the Kali age, we have now become dwellers of celestial chariots.
By the son who bestows a horse, one is rescued from the ocean of hell;
for this is the fruit of the gift of a horse: that the worlds of men become inexhaustible.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a white horse. In the Āditya Purāṇa,
Durvāsas said:
O Lord, the gift-dharmas have been explained by you to me in detail;
O Maker of Day, so too have the gifts of horses and elephants.
Bhānu said:
"To one endowed with austerity, virtuous conduct, and good qualities; a worthy recipient who has mastered the Vedas;
an auspicious woman with all limbs complete, who is devoted to the agnihotra sacrifice."
With all his limbs complete, radiant, and possessing a luster equal to that of one who is indifferent;
well-proportioned, with beautiful hair, a slightly emaciated face, and exceedingly handsome.
Abounding in the splendor of all ornaments, anointed with divine garlands and unguents,
provided with all requisites, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
One should place pearls upon his teeth, coral upon his two lips, a diamond upon his two eyes, and lapis lazuli as well; however, if these are unavailable, one may use substitutes.
One should place gold and silver with the two hands and copper on the feet;
one should surround it with various egg-born and non-egg-born creatures, both individually and collectively.
The illustrious one should adorn the lord of mounts with fragrant scents and flowers, and offer it as desired.
Having turned toward the sun, one should announce it to the Brahmins;
there, one should prepare an offering (bali) with various kinds of foods and edibles.
One should feed the Brahmins there, especially those who are devotees of the Sun;
having eaten, one should say, "May Mihira be pleased forever," and then dismiss the twice-born.
O Great Sage, one should perform the gift of a horse according to this rite;
for as many hairs as there are on its body and for as many births as it has had, for that many thousands of eons one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Thus is another procedure for the gift of a horse. Now, from the *Śivadharmottara*: "He who, having adorned a horse, should offer it to Śiva on a festival day..."
He shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the gift of a horse to Śiva.
[594] Now, the gift of sesame seeds is described.
In the Āditya Purāṇa, Durvāsas said:
"How were the sesame seeds produced, and how were they brought down?"
Thus, O Lord, you ought to sever my doubt entirely.
Bhānu said:
Listen attentively, O Brahmin; I shall tell you everything without omission.
Formerly, in the Kṛta Yuga, O Brahmin, all the Pitṛs arrived.
They perform extensive penance for the sake of the sesame seeds; of this there is no doubt.
For a thousand divine years, those ascetics remain without food.
The best of sages perform intense penance for the sake of sesame seeds;
at that time, they are especially surrounded by all the gods.
"Prajāpati, Lord of the Fathers, the Grandfather himself, am truly well-pleased with you; I shall grant you what you desire—speak, for what is it that you wish?"
The ancestors said:
"O highly fortunate one, give us the sesame seeds we desire; of this there is no doubt. Without sesame seeds we do not live, nor does sesame seed remain in heaven."
The Grandfather said:
"Go indeed, O best of the twice-born; all of you have been given sesame seeds.
And the ancestors are fully satisfied by the acquisition of sesame seeds, O Lord of Creatures."
That man who offers sesame seeds, especially to the ancestors,
obtains the fruit of a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
He who offers sesame seeds mixed with honey to the foremost of the twice-born on the full moon day of Vaiśākha is liberated from all sins.
A man who gives sesame seeds to Dharmarāja is born with a share in agriculture and great wealth; of this there is no doubt.
They do not see the world of Yama; they go to the world of Brahmā, especially by giving sesame seeds on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
A person who offers sesame seeds to Brahmins in the month of Māgha obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
He who offers oblations to the ancestors with sesame seeds performs a sacrifice with all desirable things; he does not behold a hell crowded with all sentient beings.
A Śrāddha with sesame seeds must never be performed by one who is unwilling;
for these sesame seeds issued from the limbs of the great seer Kaśyapa.
Then, O Lord, sesame seeds possess a divine nature in acts of giving;
they are nourishing, bestowing beauty, and likewise destroyers of sin.
Therefore, the gift of sesame seeds excels all other gifts;
so say the wise Āpastamba, as well as Śaṅkha and Likhita.
The great seer Gautama was also always devoted to the gift of sesame seeds;
the brahmins were devoted to sesame oblations, and all were strictly restrained in sexual conduct.
Of all gifts, the gift of sesame seeds is remembered as supreme;
among all gifts, the gift of sesame seeds is said here to be inexhaustible.
[596] The great seers proclaim that sesame seeds are an incomparable purifier;
O Grandfather, tell me the fruit that results from their gift.
Bhīṣma said:
Of all gifts indeed, the gift of sesame seeds is remembered as supreme;
for it removes all sins, it is purifying, and it leads directly to heaven.
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"Kuśa grass and black sesame seeds are produced from the body of Viṣṇu;
the gods have declared that these are sufficient for the protection of Dharma."
Vyāsa says: These sesame seeds were formerly produced from the limbs of the great seer Kaśyapa; they attained a divine state and are thus remembered as being for the purpose of gifts.
Sesame seeds should be eaten and offered as oblations according to the prescribed rules;
they should also be given to Brahmins by men here who desire their own welfare.
Saṃvarta says:
By giving sesame seeds according to one's ability during obligatory, occasional, or optional rites,
a man always becomes possessed of progeny, sons, and wealth.
Vasiṣṭha said:
A man who constantly gives sesame seeds is honored in heaven. (From the Mahābhārata)
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for one who gives, sacrifices, takes, or receives, there shall be a golden drona of sesame seeds for every single sesame seed.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history:
the conversation between a brahmin and the high-souled Yama.
In the Middle Country, there was indeed a great village of Brahmins,
situated between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, at the foot of the Yamunā mountain.
Learned men and Brahmins lived there in great numbers at all times. Then Yama spoke to a certain man who was dark-brown in complexion:
"Go to the village of the Brahmins; having gone there, bring back a Brahmin who has blood-red eyes, whose body hair stands erect, and whose shanks, eyes, and nose are black."
That brahmin was of the Agasti lineage and Śālmalin by name;
he was a learned man settled on level ground, surrounded by students.
You should bring a kinsman from his side as a substitute,
for he is equal to him in terms of his qualities, his learning, and his birth.
"By his physical appearance, his conduct, and by everything about him, he is wise;
bring him here as instructed, for I must perform worship for my own welfare."
Having gone there, he acted contrary to that command of Yama;
having dragged him back, he brought him here, saying, "This course of mine has been forbidden."
Then Yama, the knower of dharma, having risen and performed worship for him, said: "Let him be led; let him be brought into the assembly."
When these words had been spoken by the King of Dharma, that twice-born man,
having indeed halted his journey, addressed the King of Dharma.
"Whatever time remains for me, I would dwell together with you.
Yama said:
Go, O Brahmin, this very day to your own abode, O great sage!
Speak your discourse as you please; what more may I do for you?
The Brahmin said:
"Tell me that by performing which great merit I might dwell in heaven;
for you are indeed the authority for all in the determination of dharma and adharma."
Listen, O brahmin-sage, to the supreme procedure for giving according to its true nature:
sesame seeds are the highest gift, and they are indeed meritorious and eternal in this world.
The great seers declare that sesame seeds are an incomparable purifier;
bestow them upon the Brahmins according to the ritual prescribed by rule.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, and at the northern solstice,
sesame seeds should be eaten and one should always perform self-anointing with them.
One should always perform the necessary rites with water in the home with one's whole being;
they praise the offering of sesame seeds at a śrāddha, for this gift is unsurpassed.
O bull among the twice-born, sesame seeds should be given daily according to one's ability;
through this constant giving, one shall again accomplish the fruit of all desires.
Listen to the secret of the Dharma which I shall tell you today:
sesame seeds are an incomparable purifier; let there be no doubt in you regarding this.
From sesame seeds, heaven is attained, and likewise from heaven, liberation; thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharma:
"Sesame seeds, cows, gold, food, a maiden, and the earth."
These, when given according to the prescribed rite, deliver one from great fear.
Likewise:
"O Prajāpati, when the moon is situated in Mūla and it is the month of Māgha,
on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, one should fast and subdue the senses."
By giving sesame seeds on the twelfth lunar day, one is liberated from all sins.
One who rubs with sesame, bathes with sesame, performs fire-offerings with sesame, offers water with sesame,
gives sesame as a gift, and eats sesame— these six uses of sesame are destroyers of sin.
Having repeatedly become a Ṣaṭtilī and being freed from all sins,
he is honored in the heavenly world for thirty thousand years.

In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "Having given sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, along with gold, honey, and clarified butter— one *droṇa* of each covered with a cloth— and likewise three such sets together with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."

"Threefold" means according to the distinction of inferior, middling, and superior—namely, one *droṇa*, two *droṇas*, and three *droṇas*. "Likewise, together with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)" means accompanied by one, two, or three *suvarṇas* respectively.
By giving this to a twice-born who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), one overcomes all evil deeds. And here is the formula for the gift: [The formula follows.]

Oṃ. Today, [I, the donor], for the sake of such-and-such gotra, and so forth—thus, I, desiring the destruction of all sins, give to you this gold placed upon a black antelope skin, combined with honey and clarified butter, covered with cloth, and consisting of one *droṇa* of sesame seeds; it is yours, not mine. Oṃ. Today, [I, the donor], for the sake of such-and-such gotra, and so forth—for the purpose of consecrating this gift of sesame—I give to you this gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); it is yours, not mine.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the gift of sesame. [600]
In that very same Purāṇa:
"Having fashioned a deer made of sesame seeds, provided with gold and silver,
one should give it spread over a woolen blanket or a black antelope skin."
He shall go to heaven in a celestial chariot that fulfills all desires;
upon the exhaustion of his lifespan, returning here, he shall once again become a king of kings.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of sesame seeds and deer.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who, endowed with faith, gives vessels of sesame seeds to Brahmins..."
Having reached the new moon day, being self-restrained and well-concentrated.
Having swiftly delivered his ancestors from the hells, O bull among men,
he attains the world of the fathers and enjoys happiness for a long time.
Atri:
"That man who, being well-composed, gives a full vessel of sesame seeds, certainly goes to heaven; of this there is no doubt."
Yama said:

He who, having placed Janārdana in his heart, should daily or on festival days give a vessel of sesame seeds along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) out of a sincere disposition, [attains the highest state].
Likewise, the word of the Dharma destroys the threefold evil.
In the Brahma Purāṇa:
"He who gives a copper vessel filled with a prastha measure of sesame seeds, along with gold, to a twice-born man according to his faith and wealth..."
One whose self is purified of all sins attains the supreme goal.

[601] Herein is the formula for the gift: *Oṃ, today, to you, who belong to such-and-such lineage, etc., I give this copper vessel filled with sesame seeds and containing gold, desiring the destruction of all sins; it is yours, not mine.*

"Oṃ, today, for the sake of the consecration of this gift of a copper vessel filled with sesame seeds belonging to [the donor] of such-and-such lineage, and so forth, I give this gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to you; it is not mine.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the sesame-vessel.
Now Viṣṇu says:
Having placed sesame seeds in a copper vessel weighing sixteen palas,
along with gold according to one’s means, one should present it to a Brahmin;
this destroys the threefold sin arising from speech, mind, and body.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: Having given a copper vessel filled with sesame seeds and accompanied by gold to a twice-born man in the morning according to the prescribed rite, one destroys an evil dream.
The sesame vessel is said to be of three kinds: inferior, superior, and middling;
a copper vessel weighing ten palas is proclaimed to be the lowest grade.
It is declared that for the middling [quality] it is double, and for the superior it is remembered as triple.
For the lowest quality, one should cast in one unit of gold; for the middling, two units.
Likewise, for the highest [grade], gold three times that amount is prescribed;
by giving gold as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the destruction of all sins occurs.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the gift of the great vessel of sesame seeds.
Pitāmaha said:
Listen, all you deities and sages whose wealth is asceticism,
to that by which men here are liberated from the debt owed to their mothers.
If one does not have the capacity to perform the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice,
then one may construct a great lake, a pond, a well, or a long reservoir.
When this has been done, the man becomes liberated from his mothers;
furthermore, by giving a bell-metal vessel along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he is fully released.
The sages said:
O Blessed One, please fully proclaim the ritual procedure for the bronze vessel—
its dimensions, its essential form, and at what time it is to be given.
To what kind of twice-born man this gift should be given,
by what kind of person it should be given, and to what kind of person one should not give it— [all this shall now be told].
The Grandfather said: The measure of the vessel made of pure bell-metal is specified here as twenty-five palas, and seven prasthas of sesame seeds.
One should place four gold māṣas upon the vessel;
one should wrap the vessel with a cloth, using the finest material and with great devotion.
Having bathed in a river or similar body of water, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
thereafter, one should worship Śambhu, Śaṅkara, and Hari as well.
Then, having smeared the entire middle of the house with cow dung,
one should draw a twelve-spoked lotus with saffron and sandalwood paste.
Then, having established the fire, one should perform the oblation with barley and sesame seeds;
having placed the vessel there, one should worship it endowed with devotion.
Adorned with perfumes, sandalwood, flowers, incense, and lamps,
he then summoned a well-restrained Brahmin who had many attendants.
Having duly adorned one who avoids the wives of others and is peaceful,
one should always avoid the hypocrite who is greedy for the pleasure of another's wife.
Having washed the feet of one who is base, envious by nature, fallen from the Veda, and devoid of purity, according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the *mātṛ-śrāddha*.
There, one should honor the Brahmin with flowers, incense, and ointments;
he should be clothed in soft garments that are worthy of respect.
Having adorned [the image] according to one's ability on the full moon day of Māgha or on the anniversary of death—
the "anniversary of death" being the day on which the mother passed away—
and during lunar or solar eclipses, at the transits of the sun, and on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Yugas.
Likewise, whatever else is given on the full moon day of Māgha in honor of one's mother, all that has inexhaustible fruit; so Maheśvara declared of old.
One should honor the living woman with garments, food, water, and ornaments;
for the deceased, everything should be given on the full moon day according to one's ability.
Just as I previously gave to the ancestors on the new moon day, so too was it given by me to the mothers on the full moon of Māgha; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whatever is given, recited, offered in sacrifice, performed as ritual bathing, or conducted as libation according to the rules—
all that becomes of inexhaustible fruit, and liberation itself is attained.
Having fully honored the brahmin, one should cause that vessel to be given to him;
having bowed according to the rule with devotion, one should utter this mantra:
"A bell-metal vessel was given by me out of a desire to discharge my debt to my mother;
O Blessed One, tell me how I may attain liberation through your word."
O best of the twice-born, while remaining in my mother’s womb for ten months and during my infancy, she was distressed by my drinking from her breast.
And whatever [deeds] I have committed, smeared with the defilement of excrement, urine, and so forth—
by your word today, may my liberation from that debt come to pass.
A bronze vessel, gold, sesame seeds, garments, a sacrificial fee, and the seven grains have been given by me; may there be liberation from debt for me.
By the gift of a bronze vessel, one attains the knowledge of reality and the subtle body;
likewise, by the gift of gold, one attains the imperishable Supreme Self.
The covering of the universe is this eternal secret;
by the gift of clothing to a Brahmin, the Supreme Self is perfectly worshipped.
My mother endured suffering for as many times as there are sesame seeds;
by the power of that gift of sesame, may I be liberated from my deeds.
Having fashioned it adorned with fruits and the like, and embellished with that water,
one should likewise present the leaf to a Brāhmaṇa as he departs.
Then the Brahmin should say:
"By the gift of this worthy recipient, you are released from the debt incurred toward your mother, according to the word of Maheśvara."
Having given the vessel to the Brahmin, he should diligently perform the fire-oblation (homa);
then, having asked for forgiveness and provided the Brahmin with the ritual accessories and betel, he should dismiss him.
He should also cause food and other offerings to be given to other Brahmins;
having honored those Brahmins with effort, with devotion, according to his capacity, and with due respect.
When this has been done, one is then released from debt to the gods; there is no doubt about this.
But regarding that which arises from one's mother, there is certainly no other way whatsoever.
In ancient times, a bronze vessel was given by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, whose mind was filled with apprehension regarding the sin arising from the slaughter of his mother.
In ancient times, after Viśvāmitra, the wise one, had slain the sons of Vasiṣṭha,
he gave this gift for the pacification of his vow of penance for the sin.
Having failed to carry out their mother’s command,
some of the serpents, overcome by fear, subsequently appeased their mother after being joined with a curse.
"Tell me the means of deliverance from the curse;
for the word that was spoken by you, O Goddess, a curse overcomes the wicked who have not discharged their debt."
She spoke to them at length regarding the bronze plate, saying:
"By giving this gift, one will be liberated; of this there is no doubt."
All that was done by the serpents at the command of their mother, though it was contemptible;
however, by the gift of the bronze vessel, he then became liberated from sin.
I have thus declared this entire procedure for the bronze vessel;
otherwise, how will they escape the debts arising from their mothers?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this, the gods and the great sages, Kaśyapa and the others, endowed with great luster and filled with joy, then departed for their own abodes.
Thus, O lord of the earth, I have explained to you everything regarding the gift of a worthy recipient;
perform this with every effort and never show contempt for it whatsoever.
[606] Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a bronze vessel as stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa*.
Yama says:
"The accumulation of all sins, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally..."
I shall declare its purification as well as the very means for attaining heaven.
In a level place, a heap of white and black sesame seeds, thirty-two finger-breadths high and one man’s length long, should be prepared.
According to the extent of one's wealth or according to one's ability,
men should install an image of Mādhava there made of gold, measuring eight finger-breadths.
Regarding the form of Mādhava, however, it is stated in the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]:
"Beginning from the upper left hand and proceeding in a counter-clockwise order,
Mādhava is traditionally described as holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus."
One should fill jars with honey, milk, curd, and clarified butter,
and place therein that gold, adorned with flowers, garlands, and cloth.
Or, having worshipped with devotion, one should give all of that to a learned Brāhmaṇa who is worthy of the arghya offering,
during the month of Māgha, or Vaiśākha, at the equinoxes, or during the sun’s northern course.
Whatever evil deed has been accumulated by me through ignorance, delusion, or greed, life after life, O Madhusūdana;
Having recited all this, one should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa;
whatever sin has been committed throughout one's life perishes at that very moment.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a heap of sesame seeds.
Now, in the Mahābhārata:
Yama said: O Brahmin, I shall describe to you that gift by giving which one obtains the merit found in all sacrifices and the fruit found in all acts of charity.
Listen as I declare the secret of all gifts:
in this meritorious land of Bhārata, water is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Known as the *tilapadma*, it is honored by gods and asuras;
O best of the twice-born, when the month of Māgha has arrived during its bright fortnight.
O Mahāmati, having prepared a square mandala of cow dung,
one should spread over it a new cloth together with a black antelope skin.
Having placed sesamum seeds in a vessel there upon a cloth,
one should fashion an auspicious eight-petaled lotus above its pericarp.
Then, one should establish three *niṣkas* of gold for Śrīnivāsa,
the Lord of the Universe, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should meditate upon the four-armed Lord Hari, the remover of the distress of those who bow to him—
the golden-wombed, the immortal, the one whose womb is Śrī, and the supreme beyond the supreme.
[He saw] Acyuta, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, clad in yellow garments,
marked with the Śrīvatsa, the seed of the universe, and the cause of all causes.
The ancient poet, the Lord of the universe, with eyes like lotus petals,
seated in the center of the pericarp, endowed with all powers.
Having joined his palms in reverence and having prostrated again and again,
he should worship the Supreme Lord according to his faith and the extent of his wealth.
Worship Janārdana, the God of gods, with sapphire, emerald, pearls, and other gems, according to your ability.
With perfumes, flowers, and likewise with lamps and delightful food offerings,
with milk-rice, foods cooked in ghee, and various kinds of divine fruits.
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods with a profusion of flowers, as well as with song, dance, and other such offerings, one should present betel.
Endowed with the five fragrant substances and with a mind purified by faith,
[one should offer] a prastha of oil, a prastha of ghee, and beyond that, an āḍhaka of curd.
One should place sixteen vessels of grain at its side;
having thus worshipped that auspicious lotus made of one *droṇa* of sesame seeds.
O twice-born one, for one night, two nights, or three nights,
he should first subsist on sesame seeds, or else observe a fast.
One should perform this for the sake of purifying one's own actions while recollecting Vāsudeva;
then, having become pure and composed, one should offer that lotus.
To a brahmin of known lineage and character, who is provided for his family,
has conquered his senses, is tranquil, serene, and a knower of the Self;
To one who is free from passion and hatred, specifically to a Vaiṣṇava endowed with these very qualities, [one should give] in this manner, according to suitability and in due order.
That sesame-lotus should be offered with diligence according to the prescribed rite,
while reciting, "May the god Mādhava be pleased," and keeping him in mind.
O Hiraṇyagarbha, Lord of gods, Padmanābha, Janārdana;
O Hiraṇyākṣa, support of all qualities, Sovereign of the foundation of all!
Abounding in wealth and grain, endowed with every prosperity,
accompanied by sons, grandsons, and the like, and provided with male and female servants.
Thinking, "Make me free from disease, well-disposed, and devoid of all suffering; make me most dear to you," he spoke thus.
Having thus propitiated Vāsudeva, the eternal Lord of Gods,
one should offer a lotus made of sesame seeds for the fulfillment of all desires.
A Brahmin, moreover, should accept [the gift] and cause it to be recited;
he should utter the Vedic mantra: "Who gave? To whom was it given?"
Thus, whoever offers a lotus made of sesame seeds according to the prescribed rite shall not behold the hell filled with all sentient beings.
The righteous-souled one becomes pure himself and then delivers his fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers,
as well as his entire lineage.
One who seeks dharma attains dharma; one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth;
one who seeks liberation attains liberation—there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
An outcaste is released from sin, as are the killer of a father and the violator of the guru’s bed;
even one devoted to every kind of evil is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
The ancestors desire sons, grandsons, and those born of their lineage, thinking:
"Someone born of our family will offer sesame and lotuses."
But that king who is a lord of wealth, prosperous and exceedingly righteous,
having propitiated a Brahmin according to the prescribed rule with garments, ornaments, and decorations;
O twice-born one, such is the fruit that arises for one devoted to giving, consisting of vehicles and other jewels, as well as villages, fields, and the like.
That [merit] shall indeed be concealed; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
But as for that righteous person who would duly offer this sesame-lotus, there is no end to be found here for the fruit of his gift.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of sesame and lotuses.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"Now I shall describe another supreme [gift], which requires few materials but yields great fruit."
Indeed, its ritual procedure is prescribed for the time when it is conjoined with the substance and the mantra.

The term "time" (*kāla*) is also an elliptical indication for "place" (*deśa*). Therefore, the meaning is that wherever and whenever there is a conjunction with a worthy recipient (*pātra*) who exists as a substantial reality (*dravyasat*), those alone constitute its place and time, and not those previously mentioned;
for it is stated here that [the rite] must be performed everywhere and at all times, according to the *Kāmika*.
Having smeared the ground with cow dung and scattered garments upon it,
one should place three auspicious *bhāras* of sesame seeds in the middle of that space.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus provided with a pericarp and filaments,
it should be made from ten niṣkas, or again, from half of that, or even half of that again.
One should place a lotus in the center of the sesame seeds and Maheśvara in the center of the lotus;
having worshipped the God according to the prescribed rite, one should worship Vāmā and the others.
One should have the form of Śakti fashioned from three niṣkas of gold;
and before them, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) should be made according to their respective divisions.
One should also have the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) fashioned according to the previously mentioned measurements of gold;
having worshipped them in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to the prescribed rite.

Regarding the phrase "Maheśvara in the center of the lotus": having placed Śiva, fashioned from a *niṣka* of gold weighing one hundred thousand or more [units], in the center of the lotus, one should place Manonmanī, made of half that measure of gold, on the left side of Śiva;
and to his north, one should have Manonmanī made with half of that [measure].
This is according to the statement in the Kāmika Āgama.
One should worship the eight powers, Vāmā and the others, all around that [central deity] as follows:
"Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālā, Vikaraṇī, the goddess Bala-prathamani, and Damanī, in due order. Thus it is said.
Outside of that, one should worship the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas). They are as follows:
"Now, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śiva, and also Ekanetraka;
Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍika. Thus [it is said].

"By the previously mentioned measure of gold" means by three *niṣkas*. The term "individually" (*pravibhāgaśaḥ*) also applies to the preceding [section]; therefore, the forms of the powers such as Vāmā and the *vidyeśvaras* should each be fashioned with three *niṣkas*. Among those, the form of Maheśvara has been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*; however, the forms of Manonmanī, Vāmā, and the others are described in the *Liṅga[purāṇa]*:
"All the goddesses have two arms and resemble the morning sun;
they hold a lotus and a conch, are peaceful, and are adorned with red garlands, garments, and ornaments."
The gift of Gaṇeśa for the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas) will be described [later].
