Thus ends the gift of the lower lotus with sesame seeds,
according to the Vāyupurāṇa.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the characteristics of the sesame-lotus;
by performing which one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt.
At the equinox, during an eclipse, at the Vyatīpāta yoga, on the day of the sun’s loss [of a lunar mansion], at the solstice, at one's birth asterism, or on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight;
At these times, in these regions, and at these meritorious shrines,
[one should offer] a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds with beautiful new cloths.
One should fashion an eight-petaled lotus adorned with a pericarp and petals;
upon that, a lotus fashioned from a *pala* of gold should be placed.
Adorned with half-petals and half-footed petals upon the pericarp,
one should there install the Lord of Gods, the moon-crested one, having invoked him.
One should worship the Lord, who has pale-white limbs, four arms, and is clothed in an animal skin,
with white lotuses, red lotuses, or hundred-petaled lotuses.
One should offer incense of guggulu smeared with ghee to the Supreme Lord;
having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods and performed a circumambulation.
Then, when an auspicious time had arrived, he summoned a brahmin and,
according to the prescribed rites, honored the brahmin just as he would a deity.
All acts, beginning with worship, should be performed with the root mantra;
having then recited this mantra, one should cause it to be given to that brahmin.
"This lotus is made of sesame seeds; Hara is present herein.
By the offering of this, may Śiva be perpetually pleased."
Just as that Blessed Lord dwells within all beings,
by that truth may my sin dissolve away in every respect.
Thus, whoever properly performs the ritual procedure for the sesame lotus,
being completely liberated from all sins, goes to the abode of Śiva.
There, for one hundred and fifty kalpas, he rejoices happily like Śiva.
Whatever sin he has committed by deed, thought, or word—
all that shall go to destruction through the gift of a sesame-seed lotus.
Thus ends the third [section] on the gift of the sesame-lotus.
Baudhāyana says:
One should have a golden lotus made, weighing one pala or half a pala.
Just as a wise person, according to his own ability, [fashions] an auspicious eight-petaled vessel.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; otherwise, it will be fruitless.
Even when there is a *droṇa* or more of sesame seeds, a copper vessel filled with water [should be offered].
In its center, one should place that lotus smeared with saffron,
along with a Brāhmaṇa who is accomplished in Vedic learning, though poor, and a maintainer of the sacred fire (agnihotrī).
Having summoned [the deity] with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings according to the prescribed rite and with great devotion,
one should then present a golden lotus accompanied by the mantra.
May the Sun— the bird, Pūṣan, the winged one, the twelve-fold self whose body is the triple Veda—
be pleased with me by this gift of a lotus.
The mantra for the gift:
By performing this, a person is liberated from difficulty in urination;
therefore, one afflicted by dysuria should perform this with great effort.
The gift of sesame seeds and lotuses removes the disease of dysuria;
thus it is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa.
Upon its exhaustion, one should present a silver lotus to a Brāhmaṇa;
that water which was upon the *āḍhaka* measure of sesame seeds should be placed in a vessel made of bell-metal.
Having performed [the rite] with a pala, or half of that, or according to one's ability,
and having placed a lotus there, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
O sinless one, born from the eye of Atri, by the gift of this golden lotus here, destroy for me the exhaustion born of the ripening of karma.
The mantra for the gift:
By performing this, one afflicted with consumption is swiftly liberated from the disease.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the gift of sesame and lotuses that removes the disease of consumption.
Baudhāyana said: One should have a beautiful lotus made with gold, or half that amount, or even half of that again; it should be clearly fashioned with eight petals and be auspicious.
One should fashion a pericarp in the center and a stalk made of silver;
one should prepare a lotus of this kind and place it upon a vessel of sesame seeds.
Having wrapped it in cloth with supreme devotion and a restrained mind,
[he should offer it] to a Brāhmaṇa who is established in knowledge and conduct, of good character, and whose senses are controlled.
One who knows the application of the lotus-gift should perform it on a Sunday;
having invited [the guests] down to the brahmins, one should worship them preceded by the offering of materials.
An oblation (homa) should be performed with clarified butter and sesame seeds one hundred and eight times;
one should invoke the god Bhāskara, the lord of the planets, with a lotus.
Come, come, Blessed One, O God; take your presence in this lotus, O Threefold One, Twelve-fold Self, for the welfare of all living beings!
The invocation mantra:
Having invoked the Lord of Gods therein, one should worship Him with red sandalwood,
with other red flowers, and with saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood.
One should offer milk-rice as the food offering, or, if that is unavailable, simply milk;
one should duly present a white lotus with this mantra according to the prescribed rite.
O Blessed One, Sun, Lord of Beings, Jewel of the Sky, Leader of the World! You are red in color, the sovereign of majesty, and the purifier of the three worlds.
Whatever medicine and such I have given to a worthy recipient for the sake of my very birth— all that has gone to waste because of that gift.
Then, having circumambulated the Brahmin with humility,
one should cause him to be served milk-rice mixed with jaggery for his meal.
Then, having bathed with auspicious rites and a declaration of merit performed with devotion,
she should consider her husband as a god and eat ghee and milk-rice.
By performing such a gift, there is no doubt that destruction will come;
by the gift of medicinal herbs, the blood-pain has been acquired.
"Therefore, this gift should be made by a woman afflicted with blood-pain.
Thus ends the gift of sesame and lotuses for the destruction of blood-pain.
Gautama said:
The man who causes suffering to cows by means of confinement or tethering will always suffer from ringworm and be afflicted with itching.
I shall describe the remedy for that through the act of giving a lotus and so forth:
one should fashion a very beautiful lotus using a conventional *niṣka* of gold.
One should not make it of silver, nor even its neck-ornament (*kaṇṭhaka*) with half that amount;
a jewel should be placed in the middle, or, if that is unavailable, a pearl.
Having washed it with fragrant sandalwood and saffron, one should indeed anoint it;
then, having placed it upon rice grains, or upon sesame seeds, it should be covered with a cloth.
Their measure is also held to be three *droṇas*;
if those are unavailable, two should be taken, or else according to one's own capacity.
One should worship with the sixteen services using the root mantra,
and one should invoke the Lord of Gods, Bhāskara, from the solar disc.
O God of gods, Lord of the world, jewel of the sky, purifier of the worlds!
O Sun, the eye of the worlds, please grant your presence in this lotus.
The invocation mantra:
Having thus invoked that Sun, Bhānu, who is beloved by all people,
one should worship him with the sixteen services using the root mantra.

Furthermore, the preceptor, who is well-versed in all the scriptures, should duly perform a fire sacrifice (homa) in the south-eastern direction of that [site] with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
One should perform the fire-oblation with the kindling mantra "Sūryaṃ te cakṣuḥ," and one should also perform the oblation of clarified butter with the mantra "Haṃsaḥ śuciṣat."
One should perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds using the *vyāhṛtis* ten thousand times,
and with sacrificial fuel sticks and clarified butter eight hundred or twenty-eight times.
Having offered the remnants of the oblations into this vessel,
one should smear the limbs of a person afflicted by the disease of ringworm with that [substance].

One should purify oneself with the *anuvāka* beginning with "akṣibhyām," according to the characteristics of the text, and likewise with an unwashed cloth; furthermore, one who has ringworm should do so with a handful [of water].
Immediately after worshipping with devotion, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as a food offering;
the sick person, facing north, should present that lotus to the deity facing east.
O God of gods, Lord of the world, embodiment of the gods, supreme beyond the supreme— you who have been worshipped according to the rules with this mantra and with extreme devotion.
O Lord, the sun-gem who brings supreme bliss to the worlds,
O Prabhākara, you who possess seven horses and whose charioteer is Aruṇa, the lord of gods!
Through confinements and bondages, as well as the deformities of the body,
and the impurities such as ringworm and scabs resulting from the ripening of past karma—
may you, being pleased by the gift of a lotus, quickly destroy these within the body.
The mantra for the gift:
Having thus given that lotus, one becomes free from the disease of ringworm;
free from itching, free from leprosy, and free from all skin disorders.
He immediately becomes handsome like the radiance of the sun;
such a mortal shall live for a hundred years, endowed with wealth and grain.
Immediately thereafter, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) to the Brahmins;
thus should one who performs this gift according to the procedure declared by Gautama.
And being liberated from other diseases as well, he rejoices on earth like the sun.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of sesame seeds and lotuses that destroys the disease of ringworm.
Furthermore, in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "One who destroys another's voice or steals their speech is born mute;
I shall describe the remedy for that, by which happiness is attained."
One should fashion a golden lotus weighing half a pala, a quarter of a pala, or half of that, according to one's means; one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
Having wrapped it in a red cloth, one should place it upon a copper vessel;
they know the measure of the copper vessel to be eight *palas*.
Or else, one should worship with red sandalwood according to one's own means;
having placed [the image] upon an *āḍhaka* measure of sesame seeds, one should wrap it with a yellow cloth.
The preceptor, who is learned in all the scriptures, knows the Dharma, is disciplined, compassionate, truthful in speech, and pure, [should perform the rite] with the sixteen services.
Facing east, adorned and pure, one should perform this according to the rule with this mantra:
"For you are indeed the abode of Brahmā, born from the noble lineage of Viṣṇu."
For you bring delight to the Sun, to Agni, and indeed to Rudra;
accept this worship, O destroyer of all afflictions!
The mantra for worship:
The practitioner of mantra-worship should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the south-eastern direction with fuel-sticks,
clarified butter, and sesame seeds, using the eight-syllable Sāvitrī mantra.
One should perform an oblation with kindled fire for the pacification of all diseases;
and an oblation of clarified butter should be performed with this verse beginning "citram."
Or else, with the *vyāhṛtis* beginning "Indra comes for the sesame seeds," the placement of the water-pot should take place to the north of the fire.
One should perform the consecration and other rites according to the previously mentioned procedure,
diligently carrying out the ritual actions from the *praṇītā* offering up to the final liberation.
Therefore, having bathed, being pure, wearing white garments, and adorned with ornaments,
one should give a lotus to that priest who has performed the oblation, while recollecting the Four-faced One (Brahmā).
O Lotus, you are the cause of delight for all the gods,
and especially for Brahmā, Sarasvatī, and Hari as well.

That deformity born of my body which arose prior to the cessation of speech, as well as that intense suffering produced by the breaking of my sin, and likewise that mine of diseases— [all these have vanished].
May Brahmā, Sūrya, Śiva, and Agni, as well as the gods beginning with the Thirty-three who possess sacrificial oblations on this earth, destroy all that here.
The mantra for the gift:
Having thus given that lotus to the preceptor with great devotion,
and having followed behind him, one is indeed liberated from the destruction of sins.
Thus did Padmodbhava speak to the high-souled Nārada.
Thus concludes the procedure for the offering of sesame and lotuses that removes muteness.
Now follows the procedure for the offering of the five three-petaled lotuses. Next, I shall proclaim the gift renowned as the "Three-Lotus" (Tripadma).
It bestows long life, brings prosperity, is meritorious, promotes health, and destroys evil.
One should especially perform [this rite] in the month of Māgha and on one's birth-star;
it should also be given when one is afflicted by disease, or upon seeing a bad dream or a portentous marvel.
[620] Now, if one perceives another danger, for the sake of pacifying all faults,
on ground smeared with cow dung, with a measure of *āḍhaka* of sesame seeds—
Having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus provided with a pericarp and filaments,
one should then place a golden lotus upon it.
Having wrapped [the image] in cloth, one should worship the Supreme Lord with perfumes and other offerings,
[using] a brahmin who maintains the sacrificial fires, who knows the Dharmaśāstras, and whose mind is tranquil.
Having worshipped him, one should cause [the gift] to be given to him and utter this mantra:
"May the Lord, the Self-born, the Four-faced One, be pleased with me."
By this gift, may the Lord of the World, the Creator of the universe whose self is everything, [be pleased];
likewise, another [offering] with rice grains, and the third with salt.
One should awaken [the image] with the gift-mantras: "To Viṣṇu and to Sthāṇu.
May the Blessed One, the Supreme Self who consists of the universe, be well-pleased with me.
By this gift, may the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara—the Supreme Soul, the Highest Person—be well-pleased with me; may he grant me prosperity.
Having recited the mantra, "By this gift, may the Soul of the Universe, whose crest is adorned with the half-moon [be pleased]," one should offer these [offerings] individually.
Having fashioned Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara out of gold—
O best of the twice-born, the merit that arises when this is done cannot be described even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Thus spoke the Blessed Lord Brahmā to the high-souled Nārada;
and I too have related all of that to you, O best of sages.
In this regard, the fashioning of the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara should be understood as being like that of the mountain of grain.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of three lotuses.
From the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"O Goddess, I shall now describe the tenfold gift of sesame seeds,
which is a secret that destroys all sins and brings about all auspiciousness."
One should perform [this rite] on one's birth-star, on the fourteenth day, and during the dark fortnight,
in the presence of Śiva, the God of gods and the Supreme Lord.
Having fashioned a lotus with twelve petals upon a wheel prepared from five-colored powders, he placed the *arañjaka* within it.
Having placed within it a flawless vessel filled with sesame seeds,
which is auspicious, and a golden mandala in the shape of the moon dedicated to the deity Śakra;
One should worship with perfumes, food offerings, lamps, flowers, and likewise with fruits.

The characteristics of Śakra have been shown in the context of the World-Guardians (*lokapāla*) during the gift of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍadāna*). One should prepare a mandala dedicated to Śakra, consisting of both a divine and an earthly mandala, which should be made quadrangular.
Having prepared incense from *sarjarasa*, one should offer it to that Śiva-yogin.
Īśāna, the Lord of the Earth, Fragrance, and Wealth, is the embodiment of Śakra and has sesame seeds as his abode.
"May that sin born of the earth, arising from [the ritual] nyāsa, remove my evil.
Having performed this, the sins born of the earth are destroyed.
For those beings, both stationary and moving, that are harmed during eating;
those that are harmed during scratching or vomiting; and those [killed] by the odors of corpses, wine, and so forth.
For every inhalation and exhalation of scent by a learned Vedic scholar or a sick person,
he shall dwell again in the City of Śiva for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
In all other cases as well, the general rule is traditionally taught;
however, O lady of pure smiles, I shall explain the specific details in their respective places.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the sesame-planting ground,
according to the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Next, I shall describe the sesame-ground on an auspicious pedestal made of heartwood."
On a pedestal measuring two *aratnis* in length, filled with sesame seeds and provided with side-walls,
one should worship Śiva in the form of Gaṇeśāna as the Lord of Space.
Regarding the form of Gaṇeśa, Ātreya says:
"He has four arms, an elephant face, stands upon a mouse, and has a protruding belly;
he holds a tusk, a rosary, an axe, and a breadfruit."
"May he become the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja)," [he should say].
With white perfumes and incense, one should likewise fumigate with camphor;
one should offer two linen garments and place a manuscript there.
May the Lord of the Sky-path, the white Gaṇanātha who rests upon sesame seeds,
dispel all evil that has reached the ears through the sound of the word "vyoma," O Lord!
Thus, when this is given, his sins born of space,
those arising from idle chatter, and stories of reviling others are destroyed.
Sins arising from false testimony and those produced by malicious slander,
as well as the reviling of the Vedas and the reviling of one's teacher, and listening to such [reviling] of those two.
By the gift of a sesame-press, one destroys all sins without exception and rejoices in the world of Śiva for fifteen kalpas.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the sesame pedestal. In that very Purāṇa:
"Now I shall further proclaim another unsurpassed gift of sesame."
On the previously described prepared pedestal, which is adorned with four water-jars.
Having placed a stainless mirror there, one should place the mind-made deity Śambhu,
who bears the form of Viṣṇu, and then arrange [the other deities] all around him.

The form of Viṣṇu was described by Nārada as follows: "The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his upper left arms, is to be visualized as the specific form among the various forms of ritual placement (nyāsa). Thus it is said.
One should worship a pair of yellow garments, the discus and other weapons placed upon five metals, and *tulasī* leaves in all directions.
O mind-made one, salutations be unto you, O gentle-formed one whose banner is the bull;
quickly destroy all the evils committed by the mind.
When this has been given, those mental actions committed by him—
which were directed toward harming others and arisen from desire and greed— will indeed perish.
And all sins born of anger, especially those consisting of speaking what should not be spoken and those arising from improper study and meditation.
All objects of meditation, even when their cycles have been completed, perish;
yet one may dwell in the world of Śiva for ten billion years according to one's desire.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of sesame and a mirror, according to the Vāyu Purāṇa. Now I shall describe the jar of sesame: when the jar has been placed as before, [one should proceed].
In the Varuṇa maṇḍala, one should worship the deity in the form of Varuṇa.
One should worship with white flowers, fruits, fragrances, and camphor.

The characteristics of Varuṇa have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*: "Having reached the Varuṇa-maṇḍala, that maṇḍala should be made in the shape of a half-moon. Having placed the six flavors (rasas) all around, one should then mutter this mantra:
'Homage to the one whose form is Varuṇa; homage to the lord of liquids and waters.'"
May my sins, caused by the consumption of liquids, go to destruction;
be gracious, O Supreme Lord, through this gift of a jar of sesame seeds.
Thus, when [water] is given away, the sins arising from violence committed by aquatic creatures during bathing, drinking, cooking, and immersion are destroyed.
O Lord of Gods, for those who consume the essences as food and desire even forbidden drinks, every medicinal herb shall become pure;
they shall dwell in the world of Śiva for fifteen hundred kalpas at minimum.
Thus ends the ritual for the gift of the jar of sesame seeds,
according to the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"A water-pot filled with sesame seeds [should be placed] upon the mandala dedicated to the deity Agni."
Having established Śiva like fire, one should worship him with oleanders;
one should fumigate him with the scent of red sandalwood and resinous exudations.

The "mandala of the deity Fire" means a triangular mandala. The phrase "Śiva like fire" means having placed Śiva in the form of fire. His form is described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*: "Resin is the resin of the *sarja* tree;
and then one should offer a mirror and four lamps. Śambhu, the Lord in the form of fire, is of the nature of fire and has sesame seeds as his support."
"May it dispel the sin caused by the form of fire and that which pertains to the eye.
When this is given, the sins committed by fire are destroyed.
Indeed, those trees that are consumed by fire during cooking and burnt offerings,
as well as those produced from charcoal, forest fires, and the like, [are not to be used].
Those arising from the performance of forbidden acts, those produced by the application of cosmetics,
and those born from seeing another's wife, another's property, or another's son.
O King, he who, restrained in his vows and out of devotion to Śiva, performs such a gift— even if it arises from seeing a corpse or the like, or is caused by a defect of the eyes—
shall dwell in the world of Śiva for three kalpas without fear.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a sesame-water jar,
according to the Vāyu Purāṇa.
Hereafter, I shall describe to you the gift known as Ahaṃkāra.
Upon a seat prepared as before, one should place [the offering] on top of sesame seeds.
A pure silver mandala, eight finger-breadths long on all sides;
there, one should meditate upon the deity Ahaṃkāra, whose form holds a thunderbolt and a spear.
Having installed the others made of silver, one should install around him Naigameśa,
Viśākha, Kumāra, and Guha.

"As before" means as in the case of the offering of the sesame pedestal (*tilapīṭha*). *Pavi* is the thunderbolt (*vajra*), and Ahaṃkāra, in human form, should be depicted with two arms, holding a thunderbolt and a spear (*śakti*). The characteristics of Naigameṣa and the others have been described by Viśvakarman:
"From that, the Skanda-grahas were born—terrible, with deformed faces;
they have the faces of Naigameṣa and others, hold spears, and likewise possess two arms."
One should offer two saffron-colored garments and place a bell all around;
saffron should be used for the purpose of fragrance, and the flower should be that of the *karavīra*.
O Lord, master of egoism, you who take the form of the cave and are the ender of all things; O Sovereign, protect me from every fault born of self-conceit.
[627] Thus, when this is given, those sins born of egoism perish,
as well as those arising from harshness, the prohibition against women, and offenses against Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
All those sins that arise from transgressing one's duties,
as well as those arising from the notion of self in what is not-self through attachment to house, field, and so forth—
whatever other sins there may be— all of them perish completely.
Those sins are destroyed, and the man shall dwell in the world of Śiva for one hundred kalpas; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the ego (ahaṃkāra).
From the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed gift of sesame seeds (tiladāna).
Having given this, whether a man or a woman, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.
This merit-bestowing rite grants long life and health, destroys all sins,
brings delight to Śiva for men, and auspiciously increases one's progeny.
Then, with the thought that they are the eleven Rudras, the wise man, facing east, should worship the eleven Brahmins seated facing west with perfumes and other offerings.
Likewise, one should place two *prasthas* of sesame seeds in each bowl;
furthermore, one should offer a golden mandala in each of the bowls.
Having thus honored the vessels with the thought that they are Śiva, one should offer them in due order,
preceded by water, while reciting the eleven Rudra mantras.
The eleven mantras of Rudra are to be known by the names that will be mentioned hereafter, ending with "namas" (salutation):
Mṛgavyādha, Sarva, Nairṛti, Mahāyaśas, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Paraṃtapa.
Vahana, Īśvara, Kapālī of great splendor,
Sthāṇu, and the blessed Bhava— these are known as the eleven Rudras.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of eleven sesame seeds to Rudra. In that very Purāṇa:
"Hereafter I shall proclaim the unsurpassed [rite] containing sesame seeds."
By giving which as a gift, a person may obtain a long life.
This secret method, known as Tilagarbha, is a means for conquering untimely death, capable of liberating one from disease, and a destroyer of sins.
When there is a most severe planetary obstruction of one's birth star,
or the onset of diseases, or even the rising of portents;
Then the *tilagarbha* rite should be performed for the pacification of all defects;
immediately after the omen (*nimitta*), one should carry out the sequence of the ritual procedure (*naimittika-vidhi*).
Having smeared the ground with cow dung and spread two cloths over it,
one should place an *āḍhaka* of rice grains in the center and half of that amount of husked rice.
Upon them, one should spread out a lotus with eight petals and a beautiful pericarp;
upon the pericarp, one should place a lotus made of gold according to one's means.
The nine jewels should be carefully placed within that lotus;
thereafter, one should arrange pure sesame seeds all around its exterior.
Then, having wrapped it again with a cloth as if it were a fetus,
one should slowly place that embryo according to the ritual rules, using the Yoni-mantra.
Then, having seated the man whose fists have been tightly clenched by Kṛṣṇa,
one should apply the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra to his limbs in successive order.
Having visualized that god Virūpākṣa, adorned with the crescent moon,
one should reverently recite the mantra with the five Brahmās.
The *yonimantra* is well known among the Vājasaneyins, beginning with: "O you whose womb is fit for sacrifice, whose womb is golden... Śaunaka describes the *mṛtyuñjaya-nyāsa*:

one should place [the mantra] "tryambakaṃ yajāmahe" on the tuft of hair (*śikhā*); "sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanam" on the heart; "urvārukam iva bandhanāt" on the two arms; and "mṛtyor mukṣīya mā'mṛtāt" on the navel.
In the feet and ankles, in the shanks, thighs, and hips,
in the waist and genitals, in the navel, in the two sides of the belly, in the flanks, in the armpits, in the breasts, and in the heart.
On the shoulders, at the nape of the neck, at the elbows, and at the wrists;
on the little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, the index finger, and the thumb of both hands.
One should then place the syllables of the mantra upon the throat, the chin, the mouth, the nose, the ears, the eyes, the forehead, the crown of the head, and the topknot.

Thus, either the placement of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra as stated in the Devīpurāṇa is adopted, or that which is found in the Gāruḍapurāṇa regarding the Tulāpuruṣa gift for curing various diseases; that should be consulted. There are five Brāhmaṇas representing the Tatpuruṣa and other mantras.
Upon its head, a golden lotus is fashioned as before.
One should place it there, wrap it with cloth, and fill it again with sesame seeds.
The knower of mantras should further worship that embryo, having contemplated it as arising from nectar—
the moon who causes the flow of nectar— using its own mantra.
Then, having recited the unsurpassed Mṛtyuñjaya mantra one hundred times, he,
being composed in mind, should raise [the fetus] from that place within the womb.
Having sprinkled [himself] again with the Vāruṇī and the Pāvamānī verses, he should contemplate:
"I am Śaṅkara, liberated from my former body."
One should bestow all that, beginning with sesame seeds, upon a disciplined Brahmin who possesses knowledge, is free from anger, and is established in the Brahman.
"May the Blessed Lord Śambhu, the moon-crested one, be pleased," he said.

In that regard, there is the seating of the *tilagarbha* [the vessel containing sesame seeds]. The meditation is "I am Śaṃkara," and the rising is accompanied by mantras. The offering of sesame seeds and so forth is to be performed by the patron (*yajamāna*). The preceptor (*ācārya*) should perform everything else.
Whoever undertakes the *tilagarbha* according to this rite shall not suffer untimely death; of this there is no doubt.
There will certainly be liberation from diseases, even great ones;
the afflictions of the planets are destroyed, and the planets become propitious once again.
The pacification of all three kinds of portents occurs instantaneously—
namely, those of the earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens.
This is the ritual procedure for the offering of the *tilagarbha*.

Thus ends the section on gifts, beginning with the gift of the *tilagarbha*, in the *Dānakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Mahādeva, the sovereign of great kings, the lord of all faculties, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
[632] The Ninth Chapter, the Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), begins with the first [sub-section].
Now, the gift of an elephant. In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"One should give an elephant at the value prescribed in the Purāṇas, or five hundred [gold coins], according to one's wealth; even in that case, there are the lowest, highest, and middle grades."

The price prescribed in the Purāṇas for this mantra is two hundred gold *māṣas*. Furthermore, there are three grades according to one’s wealth, including the gift of an elephant in its actual form (*svarūpa-gaja-dāna*). Among these, the gift of an elephant in its actual form is the superior option; five hundred [gold *māṣas*] is the middling option, and two hundred is the inferior. Regarding the "five hundred" mentioned here, it should be understood that they refer to gold *māṣas*. Having given a silver pillar adorned with stars and clusters of gems, along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one’s financial capacity, one shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
The pillar is the rope; the elephant is a cluster of stars fashioned from pearls and the like—a particular kind of ornament. Thus ends the ritual for giving an elephant.
Now, in the Liṅga Purāṇa: "I shall proclaim the gift of an elephant correctly and in due order;
it should be given either to a twice-born man or, again, to the God of gods."
One should have an elephant made, endowed with the auspicious marks, either of gold or of silver,
weighing one thousand *niṣkas* or even half of that.
Or one may make it with half of that half, adorned with all the auspicious characteristics;
and at the previously mentioned place and time, one should offer it to the deity.
Or on the eighth day, it should be offered to Śiva, the Supreme Lord,
to a poor Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas and maintains the sacred fires.
It should be given with Śiva in mind, after having worshipped Śiva as before.
"As before" means as described in the *Liṅga Purāṇa* regarding the gift of the *tulāpuruṣa*.
He who performs this gift, endowed with devotion to Śiva,
having dwelt for a long time in heaven, shall become a king, a lord of elephants.
Thus ends another procedure for the gift of an elephant,
as stated in the Viṣṇusaṃhitā: [An elephant] bound by ropes at its flanks and provided with a beautiful seat.
Adorned with garlands of jewels and gold, and with chowries upon its ears.
Whoever offers an elephant adorned with strips of cloth and flowers— even if it is devoid of lamps or provided only according to what is available— [attains great merit].
By giving to a poor Brahmin, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
upon the exhaustion of that karma, having returned here, he becomes a great king, a lord of hosts,
liberated from all sins— of this there is no doubt.
Now, in the Vātula-śāstra:
"I shall now describe the gift of an elephant in brief; listen to the procedure according to the rule.
It should be given specifically to the twice-born, for it brings pleasure to the gods."
It brings prosperity, is supremely auspicious, increases strength and nourishment,
destroys diseases, grants progeny, and eliminates the calamities of the world.
An elephant endowed with auspicious marks, born in a pure land,
young, possessed of beauty, and adorned with all ornaments.
And at the previously mentioned place and time, near the temple,
having brought the king of elephants born from the lineage of Airāvata;
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should cause it to be given to a preeminent Brahmin;
furthermore, a declaration of auspiciousness (puṇyāha) should be performed there, as well as the worship of Śiva.
And here, the worship of the teacher must be performed according to the prescribed ritual.
Now, in the Mahābhārata:
"He who, according to his ability, bestows elephants, horses, carts, and so forth,
upon a distinguished twice-born man who is learned in the Vedas and maintains the sacred fires."
Listen as I describe in detail the fruit one attains there:
having enjoyed pleasures in the city of the gods for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years, he returns here as a king upon the exhaustion of his time.
And here is the formula for the gift: *Oṃ, today, to [Name], of such-and-such lineage,* and so forth.

*This elephant, together with its axle, rope, and firm seat, adorned with a golden garland, decorated with chowries, perfumes, and flowers, having Prajāpati as its deity—I, desiring imperishable heaven, give this to you; it is no longer mine.* *Oṃ, today, to [Name], of such-and-such lineage,* and so forth. *For the purpose of consecrating this gift of an elephant, I give this gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to you; it is no longer mine.* Thus ends the ritual procedure for the gift of an elephant.
Then Baudhāyana said:
"A man who has committed an offense against the speech of his teacher shall become afflicted with a disease of the mouth;
the remedy for this is prescribed by means of a gift, which is now being described."
One should have a gentle elephant made of gold, silver, or copper, weighing one *pala* or half a *pala*, or according to one's means.
One should have its two tusks made of pure silver,
its tail of pearls, and likewise its two eyes of gems.

Having wrapped it with a yellow cloth, one should worship it—situated upon a heap of grain—with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings; eight *droṇas* of grain are prescribed for this heap.
A Brahmin who is perfected in learning and conduct, whose senses are restrained,
self-controlled, of noble birth, most righteous, and who causes no agitation among men.
Having summoned [the artisan] with supreme devotion and honored him with garments, ornaments, and decorations,
one should, being purified, have this rite performed by him.
With that [mixture] of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, he should also perform the fire-oblation;
having thus established fire within fire, he moves through the stages of the clarified butter in due order.
These mantras have been specified; sacrificial fuel from the *aśvattha* tree is desired.
Having performed the *apraṇomya* rite, there should then follow the worship of the elephant.
[636] Having sipped water and performed the ritual acts, as well as the sprinkling of the *praṇītā* water,
he then put on white garments and applied white garlands and unguents.
To that one who has offered the oblation, he should duly give that elephant along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
especially to one facing the east, while reciting this mantra according to the prescribed rule.
O lordly elephant of beautiful countenance, you are consecrated by the Sarasvatī;
you are the eternal vehicle of Indra and are worshipped by all the gods.
By this gift being given, destroy the disease of the mouth.
The mantra for the gift:
"At the conclusion, one should feed the Brahmins and then eat together with one's kinsmen.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the elephant-gift that removes diseases of the mouth.
Then Vṛddhagautama said:
"One should have a golden elephant made with four tusks, weighing one pala, or half of that, or even half of that again."
The tusks should be made of gold and adorned with various kinds of gems;
and the elephant, equipped with all ornaments, should be one that is serviceable.
When that [offering] is made as a gift of all things, one should, being composed, worship it at its side with the sixteen services, including perfumes and flowers.
Then, having summoned a brahmin who was learned in the meaning of all the scriptures,
endowed with sacred learning and virtuous conduct, and who caused no distress to men;
Having worshipped with devotion using garments and other offerings, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with those [materials],
properly employing the Puranic mantras enjoined in the Saṃhitās and Śāstras.
The four elephants of the quarters, those such as Puṣpadanta and others, and those such as Sārvabhauma— having brought these, I shall satisfy them.
An oblation with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds shall be for the pleasure of the elephant;
one who has properly offered it to him, being diligent, acts for the sake of pleasing the Sun.
Endowed with devotion, one should offer [the gift] according to the rule with this mantra:
"To the one facing east, the wounded man [offers] the vehicle of Indra, facing north."
Having followed Airāvata, the preceptor, filled with joy,
should feed the Brahmins and then eat himself while maintaining silence.
When this is done, [the poison] spreads from the wound at that very moment due to the irritation;
therefore, those with wounds must certainly perform this for the sake of their recovery.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of an elephant to one afflicted by wounds. Now follows the gift of an elephant to the deities, according to the *Śivadharmottara*:
"He who offers an elephant adorned with gold and other ornaments out of devotion..."
Listen to the meritorious fruit obtained by him on an auspicious festival day.
He sports with hundreds of magnificent great vehicles, yoked to many beautiful elephants resembling the intoxicated Airāvata.
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
he shall dwell in the world of Rudra, and at the end of that time, he shall become a lord of the gods here.
At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, that lord of men, having attained heaven,
shall become equal to Indra, endowed with glory, beauty, and valor.
Thus ends the gift of the elephant to Śiva.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"The high-minded person who bestows an elephant upon the treasure-house of the world..."
Born from the Bhadrajāti breed, [he was given] to Padmanābha according to his ability.
A small elephant, rich in strength and beauty, adorned with bells and chowries,
equipped with a leather girth and a goad, and decorated with many golden ornaments.
Having performed the great worship of Viṣṇu on the eleventh day of the month of Kārttika, abounding in various ornaments and filled with the resonant sound of charming drums.
On the twelfth day, one should offer that [image] to the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus:
"O Lord of the three worlds, O Sovereign of gods, O treasure-house of compassion for all beings!"
"O you who are pleased by the gift of an elephant, grant me my desire!
Having uttered this, he then gave it away and prostrated before the Lord of the World.
Having reached the realm of the Lord of Suras, he sports there for an inexhaustible time;
having sported for many hundreds of billions of years in heaven for a very long duration, he remains.
Then, having reached the world of mortals, he shall become a sovereign king.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of Viṣṇu’s elephant. In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"He who offers an elephant adorned with gold and other ornaments with devotion..."
Listen to the fruit of his merit on a festival day dedicated to the Sun.
He sports with hundreds of magnificent great vehicles, yoked to many elephants resembling the intoxicated Airāvata.
He shall become a sovereign of the earth consisting of seven islands and oceans;
having enjoyed vast pleasures, when the dissolution of the world has arrived, he shall depart.
Having attained union with the Sun, he is dissolved right there.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a sun-temple elephant.
Now follows the gift of a female slave. Regarding this, the Vahnipurāṇa states:
"The gift of a house has been heard, O King; now hear concerning the gift of a female slave."
Out of devotion to you, I shall proclaim that which bestows great happiness.
For among the four stages of life, the householder is said to be the best;
and within the home, O King, the excellent wife is superior to the house itself.
Devoid of gold, without female slaves, with little food and no dairy products—
this is another ordinance for hell for those who live as wretched householders.
A village without a magistrate, a household without a female slave,
and a meal that lacks clarified butter— in my opinion, these are all in vain.
In that house which her handmaidens, adorned with shimmering ornaments, attend upon,
dwells Lakṣmī, who rests upon the ocean of milk and holds a lotus in her hand.
In that house there is neither cleanliness nor the happiness born of worldly affairs,
where there is no female servant who always performs all the work.
The work that has been performed by servants for which they were hired does not accomplish as much here as that which a single female servant, having been hired by the householder, performs alone.
For one whose village is abundant with provisions, whose home is filled with male and female servants,
and whose intellect is filled with righteousness— what can possibly cause him distress?
In whose house the wife is skillful, the female servant is devoted to her task, and the employees have their hands raised for virtuous effort— in that place the three aims of life are accomplished.
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is dear to one in one's home—
that very thing should be given to a virtuous person by one who desires that it become inexhaustible.
Having reflected upon this in one's heart, one should give a maidservant to a twice-born man when the moon is joined with a fixed asterism and endowed with the influence of auspicious planets.
The virtuous praise the time for giving, especially on festival days,
after having adorned [the recipient] according to one's ability with garments and ornaments.
She should be given to a Brahmin with devotion and according to the mantra:
"This illustrious slave girl is bestowed by me upon you."
Always performing her duties and being enjoyed as desired, she attains prosperity.
This is the formula for the gift here:

*Oṃ, today, to [Name], of such-and-such lineage, etc., desiring the attainment of imperishable happiness, I give this female slave, adorned with golden ornaments and decorated with perfumes, flowers, and so forth; she is yours, not mine.* *Oṃ, today, to [Name], of such-and-such lineage, etc., for the sake of consecrating this gift of a female slave, I give this gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); it is yours, not mine.*
She who is more than five years old but not exceeding forty years of age should be given as a slave-girl to a twice-born man; this same rule applies to the gift of a male slave as well.
Having given [these], he should afterwards ask the Brahmin for forgiveness with garments and gold;
then, having followed him to the boundary, he should dismiss the twice-born man.
Having given thus, O Great King, a man becomes one who has fulfilled his duty;
both in this world and in the next, he remains unbroken for seven births.
One should give a young, beautiful female servant,
provided with abundant liquid assets and accompanied by a village house.
He who, having observed a maidservant who is highly skilled in household duties, gives her to a Brahmin of noble lineage and virtuous conduct,
shall be honored by the lords of learning and wisdom.
A mortal goes to the world of Viṣṇu together with his kinsmen.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"One should give a beautiful maidservant according to one's capacity, adorned with ornaments,
together with gold and silver, and accompanied by the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)."
Having given her to a Brahmin householder according to his means,
he rejoices in the world of the Apsarases for as long as three hundred kalpas.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of male and female slaves.
Now, in the *Kālottara*: "He who, having adorned a woman, should present her to Śambhu as the most excellent [offering],"
He shall obtain a hundredfold the fruit of the horse-sacrifice.
One should offer a well-disciplined female slave for the sake of a hired task;
one shall obtain a hundredfold the fruit of the human sacrifice (naramedha).
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of female and male slaves.
Now follows the gift of a chariot. In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"A chariot mounted by four oxen, covered with grain, and having three tiers..."
And it was equipped with all the necessary chariot accessories, according to their means.
And having given [the gift] along with a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin, one shall go to the city of Śiva.

Regarding "surrounded by grain" (*dhānyavṛta*): the eighteen types of grain have been explained in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). "In three ways" (*tridhā*) means that there is a threefold division into superior, middling, and inferior, according to whether the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of three, two, or one *suvarṇa*. "Requisite parts of the chariot" (*rathopakaraṇāni*) refers to the yoke, the thongs, the whip, the leather straps, and so forth. Now follows the formula for the gift: "Today, [I, the donor], desiring the unimpeded happiness of heaven and other realms, give this chariot—whose deity is Viśvakarman—to you, [O recipient of such-and-such lineage] and so forth, yoked with four oxen, surrounded by the eighteen grains, and complete with all its own accessories; it is yours, not mine."

"O you of such-and-such lineage," and so forth; for the sake of the consecration of this gift of a chariot, I bestow upon you this gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); it is yours, not mine. [643] Thus it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Salutations to you, the chariot, the lord of the chariot, the architect of the universe;
salutations again and again to the lord who is the soul of all beings, to Aruṇa.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"He who gives a carriage yoked with horses to a twice-born man is born on earth as a king whose soul is enriched by the fulfillment of all desires."
A *gantrī* is a specific type of chariot;
it is known as having wheels, equipped with a yoke, adorned with intoxicated elephants,
spread with a canopy of tree-bark, fitted with a harness, and provided with a *kūvara*.
One should bestow upon a twice-born man a chariot yoked with four horses, or two according to one's ability, or even one joined with oxen.
On an auspicious day, having invited a Brahmin and adorned him with garments and other ornaments,
one should give [the gift] along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability, with a disciplined mind.
The mantra for the gift:
"I bestow this cart, of which Viśvakarman is the presiding deity;
by this gift, may the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, be pleased with me."
Having thus duly offered a palanquin with the mantra,
a man rejoices in heaven like a god, traveling in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
In this world, one shall become a powerful king devoted to righteousness.
In the Mahābhārata:
"The gift of a cart is distinguished above all gifts."
Thus spoke the illustrious and venerable seer Śāṇḍilya.
Whoever gives a cart yoked with draft animals to a twice-born man shall possess an auspicious celestial chariot made entirely of gold in heaven.
O best of Brahmins, it stands filled with celestial women, adorned with all kinds of jewels,
and bestows the fruits of all desires.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a chariot.
Now, in connection with the gift of a chariot, the gift of a palanquin is described. In the Vahnipurāṇa, Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen further, O protector of the earth, to another unsurpassed great gift,
by the mere giving of which one is indeed liberated from the ocean of hell.
Having fasted on the day of Hari during the auspicious fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa,
or likewise in Māgha, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, or during the autumn months.
On the twelfth day, having worshipped Hari— who holds the conch,
the Śārṅga bow, the mace, and the discus— made of gold according to one's means and seated upon a water-pot (kalaśa).
Then, having brought a palanquin made of straight wood from a curved bamboo frame,
equipped with an auspicious umbrella, into the presence of Viṣṇu.
Having adorned her with that ornament, he should cause a vigil to be held there,
[selecting] one who is endowed with learning and noble birth, clever, and most proficient in the scriptures.
Having worshipped in the morning one who is firm in his commands, pure, skillful, adorned with a wife and children, together with his wife, with garments and ear-ornaments;
Sandals, a small knife, a sword, a belt, a tunic, a braid,
a mirror, a pouch, a drinking vessel, and a bronze bowl.
Four bulls and cows endowed with auspicious marks should be given,
as well as bearers for palanquins and likewise umbrella-bearers.
A livelihood as well as food sufficient for a year should be given to the Brāhmaṇa;
and every year, this very same thing must again be given to the Brāhmaṇa.
Even if my livelihood is not fully secured, may this annual offering be accepted year after year;
O Lord Keśava, grant me protection from the heat of suffering in this world and the next.

This auspicious umbrella has been given by me to a Brāhmaṇa for your pleasure. O God of gods, Lord of the world, Soul of the universe, O Lord Janārdana, be pleased by this palanquin that has been offered.
Thus is the mantra for the gift. Having given [it] to one who is learned in knowledge, accompanied by his wife and possessing sons,
[one is purified even if] he be a drinker of spirits, a thief, a socializer with outcasts, a killer of a Brahmin, or a violator of the Guru’s bed.
By the greatness of the gift of a palanquin, one is clearly liberated from evil;
one shall deliver one’s paternal kin, maternal kin, and likewise one’s wife’s kin,
as well as oneself and one’s circle of relatives, from the ocean of hell.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures that bestow happiness in this world and the next, he,
together with his wife and his father, attains union with Viṣṇu.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a palanquin.

Now, since the great gift (*mahādāna*) that follows in sequence has been discussed in the section on "Exceedingly Great Gifts" (*atidāna*), the gift of a house is commenced immediately after the gift of a chariot. Regarding this, Saṃvarta says:
"The giver of a house is happy, wise, and free from craving for all things."
Therefore, for the sake of increasing the bliss of wisdom, one should give from one's home into the alms bowl.
Bṛhaspati:
He who bestows upon a brāhmaṇa a house provided with juices and utensils—
his lineage does not perish, and he attains unsurpassed heaven.
Vedavyāsa:
Having given a golden mansion fully provided with all objects of desire to Mudgala,
the high-minded Śatadyumna went to heaven.
Having given all kinds of gems, bulls, *darbha* grass, young horses, beloved women, and even a delightful dwelling, he has ascended to that world.
In the Mahābhārata:
"And that man who gives a lodging endowed with all excellent qualities to a twice-born person..."
O King, for him as well— who possesses the virtues of Vedic study and right conduct— there are worlds in Kurujāṅgala.
That man who gives to a twice-born a house that is not devoid of seeds, provided with beds,
delightful with its finest features, and filled with many jewels;
O King, he shall obtain the supreme empowerment.
Likewise:
"But he who bestows a pure dwelling upon a Brāhmaṇa is honored in the heavenly world for thirty crores of years."
Then, having descended at the proper time, he comes to the world of humans;
he will certainly become a glorious lord of cities, a king of kings.
Vyāsa said: A house filled with lamps, radiance, beds, seats, and vessels, along with household utensils and stocked with all kinds of grain;

All types of grain have been mentioned. Household utensils include: beds, mattresses, pillows, seats, vessels of bell-metal and other materials, lamps, grinding-mills, containers for measuring grain and other goods, pestles, mortars, earthenware pots, jars, water-cisterns, winnowing-fans, fans, umbrellas, sandals, swords, daggers, brooms, cattle, bulls, buffaloes, rice, clarified butter, oil, full vessels, gifts of clothing, sandalwood and other fragrant substances, betel-leaf accessories, wooden stoves, male and female slaves, and so forth.
He who gives these to a poor Brāhmaṇa of virtuous character—
Likewise, hear now what the fruit is for one whose habit is study.
Joined by the gods, the hosts of ancestors, the celestial rishis, and the human rishis,
they remain satisfied and free from disease for exactly one thousand years.
Therefore, having come here, one shall become the sovereign of the seven islands,
a great giver, possessed of abundant wealth, or a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas.
In the Garuḍa Purāṇa: "Whoever, according to his ability, should give a spacious house made of brick, wood, or even clay, provided with all necessary furnishings..."
Having sported for a very long time in heaven, he returns to the world of men as a learned householder who is poor;
he becomes one whose sovereignty is unimpeded and who is endowed with all his desires fulfilled.

In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "By giving even a house filled with all kinds of wealth according to one's ability, along with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), to a twice-born man in three ways, a person shall go to the world of Brahmā."
"With all one's possessions" means with all one's household utensils. "In three ways" refers to the distinctions of superior, middling, and so forth, as previously stated.
This is according to the *Brahmavaivarta* and *Vahni Purāṇas*:
"There is no duty higher than that of the householder, nor is there any gift greater than that given from the home."
There is no sin greater than falsehood; there is none more worthy of honor than a Brahmin.
A home endowed with wealth and grain, filled with wife and children, and crowded with herds of cows, elephants, and horses, is superior even to heaven.
Just as all living beings live by depending on their mother,
so do all the other stages of life (āśramas) live by depending on the householder.
"O King, the householder stage of life, which yields dharma, artha, and kāma, as well as mixed and renowned fame, should always be resorted to by men who have attained their desires."
O best of kings, neither dharma, nor wealth and pleasure, nor happiness is attained without a house; likewise, the course of worldly life, fame, and heaven are not obtained without it.
Neither in heaven nor in liberation, nor even in other abodes,
is there such happiness for those sleeping at night in their own homes with their feet stretched out as [is found here].
Those days are truly counted which pass in the householder's stage of life;
even for one who cooks only vegetables, there is supreme happiness in one's own home.
Thinking thus, O Great King, one who desires great prosperity should have a very beautiful mansion built and give it to a Brahmin.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: Having built a house with auspicious pillars, many paintings, and great beauty, provided with walls and gateways, and secured with doors, bolts, and mechanical devices.
It was plastered with white lime, spacious, graced by a large assembly of people,
provided with auspicious entrances and exits, and equipped with auxiliary buildings and the like.

Having given a house richly adorned with the beauty of intoxicated elephants and decorated with windows and other features to a preeminent among the twice-born, one does not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: Having constructed a dwelling made of baked bricks, or stone, or wood, or even of clay, endowed with auspicious characteristics.
Abounding with offerings of food and flowers, provided with a cow,
and adorned with *arjuna*, *sarala*, *sāla*, and other beautiful trees.
It is endowed with the characteristics of a dwelling site (vāstu), produced in an auspicious location, and possessed of *timiṣa*, *sarja* trees, *kadamba*, and *vañjula* trees.
One should perform the installation according to the rule, as well as the beautification of the ground;
one should carry out the sweeping and the sprinkling with water that produces progeny.

Having worshipped, according to the prescribed rule, auspicious offerings and those prescribed by the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā), as well as the five deities together with the forty [subsidiary ones] therein, the householder should then bestow the house.
The characteristics of the site (*vāstulakṣaṇa*) involve forty-five deities, and the sequence for this is found in that very Purāṇa:
"Having divided [the ground] into eighty-one squares using dust and gold,
one should subsequently smear it with flour, having stirred it all around with a thread."
There are ten lines extending east-west and ten extending north-south;
in all divisions of the site-plan, these should be understood as nine-square units.
Having divided the site into eighty-one squares, the architect, knowledgeable in all sites,
should worship the deities occupying those squares— thirty-five in total;
thirty-two are to be worshipped on the outside, and thirteen are to be worshipped within.
In this regard, the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows:

First, one should examine a plot of ground that is free from impurities such as cremation grounds, not saline, and endowed with auspicious characteristics such as color and fragrance; it should be square and sloping toward the northeast. Having smeared it with cow dung and other substances, one should lay down ten threads with equal intervals, coated in lime, running east-west. Likewise, one should lay down ten threads running north-south. Thus, in nine rows of nine squares, the entire mandala consisting of eighty-one sections is produced. Therein, having set aside the central group of nine squares, one should establish a [specific] section of nine squares; this should be unified with the two adjacent squares situated to its east. The southeast square, however, remains as one. In this manner, having unified the three squares each in the south, west, and north, and leaving one square remaining in each of the corners, one should complete the enclosure of the Brahma-position. Externally, having left four squares each in the corners starting from the northeast (Īśāna), one should arrange five squares each in rows of clods in the directions starting from the east. Thereby, forty-five squares are produced.
In the center, there is one square of nine parts; four squares of three parts each are prescribed;
twenty squares of one part each are prescribed; and as many squares of two parts each are prescribed.
Thus established are the forty-five gods;
I shall declare them by name, so listen to their locations as well.
One should worship the deities starting from the northeast corner in successive order:
Śikhin, Parjanya, Jayanta, and Kuliśāyudha.
Sūrya, Satya, Bhṛśa, Ākāśa, Vāyu,
Pūṣan, Vitatha, and both Gṛhakṣata and Yama.
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, Mṛga, and likewise Pitṛgaṇa;
then Dauvārika, Sugrīva, and Puṣpadanta, who belongs to Varuṇa.
Āsura, Śoṣa, Pāpayakṣman,
Avaroga, Bhallāṭha, Soma, Nāga, Aditi, and likewise Diti.
Phaṇāvān, Mukhya, Bhalvāṭa, and the two other Soma-nāgas,
as well as Aditi and Diti, are to be installed with the Praṇava at their navels.
These thirty-two are on the outside; now hear the four within them:
Āpa, Śāvitra, Jaya, and likewise Rudra.
Aryaman, Savitṛ, Vivasvat, the lord of the gods (Indra),
Mitra, Rājayakṣman, and likewise Pṛthvīdhara follow in sequence.
The eighth is Āpavatsa; these are remembered as being around Brahmā.

In this regard, first, on the outer perimeter of the thirty-two squares, having established Śaśin in the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa), one should install the deities beginning with Parjanya in a clockwise sequence. Within that, there are four: in the square immediately west of Parjanya is Āpaḥ; west of Ākāśa is Sāvitra; east of Dauvārika is Jaya; and east of Āpaḥ is Rudra. Thus, one should install these four deities around Brahmā on the outer perimeter. Having established Aryaman in front of Brahmā, who resides in the central square, one should install eight deities in a clockwise sequence.
Then he summarizes:
Water, the calf of water, Parjanya, Agni, and likewise Diti—this is the group for the foot-soldiers;
thus it is in all the corners without exception.
In the center of that, however, is the Barhis with twenty feet on all sides;
and there are Aryaman, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Pṛthvidhara.
And all around Brahmā, in every direction, there are likewise three steps on all sides.

"Of the one-footed," and so forth. This group of five one-footed deities is situated in the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa). Likewise, in the corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya), there are also five one-footed deities, with *barhis* in their center. In the middle of the corners, on the outer enclosure (*paridhi*), there are twenty two-footed deities; the four beginning with *Ava* are three-footed, and in the center is Brahmā, occupying nine squares (*pada*). Having thus worshipped these forty-five deities with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, one should commence the building of the house according to the method taught in the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*). As stated in that very Purāṇa:

Once the site has been properly examined, the wise man should perform the pacification of the site (vāstūpaśamana) within the house-site, using sacrificial fuel-sticks and the offering of oblations (balikarma).
Likewise, in the restoration of what is dilapidated, in the consecration [of a deity], and in a new residence;
in a newly built palace or mansion, and in the renovation of a temple.
Likewise, at the construction of gates, as well as in palaces and houses,
a wise person should first perform the pacification of the site (vāstu).
Having drawn the diagram of eighty-one squares in the center of the site with flour-paste,
an oblation (homa) should be performed in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit and having three tiers (mekhalā).
With barley and black sesame seeds, with sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from milk-exuding trees—
whether from the Palāśa, Khadira, Apāmārga, or Udumbara trees.
Or it may be performed with five brahmins using blades of kuśa and dūrvā grass combined with honey and ghee, or even with five bilva seeds.
At the conclusion of the fire offering (homa), one should present an oblation (bali) consisting of various kinds of food and edibles in the area of the Vāstu;
likewise, one should offer this special sacrificial gift (naivedya) in the prescribed sequence.
In the northeast corner, one should offer that [oblation] smeared with ghee to Śikhin;
to Parjanya, one should give cooked rice accompanied by blue lotuses and mixed with ghee.
One should place a yellow banner for Jayanta and a cake-effigy of a tortoise;
likewise, one should place five gems for Indra and a cake-effigy of a thunderbolt.
One should offer a canopy to Sūrya, as well as incense and parched grain;
one should offer ghee and wheat to Satya, and fish to Bhṛśa.
One should offer *saṣkulya* cakes to Antarikṣa and roasted barley flour (*saktu*) to Vāyu; parched grain (*lāja*) should be given to Pūṣan, and chickpea-rice (*caṇakaudana*) to Vitatha.
One should offer honeyed food to Gṛhakṣata, meat-rice to Yama,
fragrant rice to Gāndharva, and the tongue of a ram to Ṛṅga.
One should give a tooth-stick to the doorkeeper, as well as a flour-cake and a black offering;
one should give barley-gruel to the deer and likewise kṛśara to the ancestors.
One should offer cakes to Sugrīva and milk-rice to Puṣpadanta;
likewise, one should offer a lotus together with a bunch of Kuśa grass to Vāruṇa.
One should give a cake made of flour and golden ornaments to Asura, liquor and spirits to Śoṣa, rice cooked with ghee to Śoṣa, and barley to Pāpayakṣman.
Ghee-filled sweetmeats (laḍḍukas) should be offered to Rogā, and Nāgapuṣpa flowers to Phaṇāvat;
food should be given to Mukhya, and after that, rice with mung beans.
At the station of Bhallāṭa, one should offer honeyed milk-rice to Soma;
to Nāga, rice-flour cakes; and likewise, fried cakes to Aditi.
One should say, "One should give a *pūrikā*"; thus is the external offering (*bali*).
Having offered the milk, curd should indeed be given to the one with the calf (*āpavatsāya*).
One should offer sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas) to Sāvitra, water infused with kuśa grass and black pepper;
to Savitṛ, molasses cakes; and to Jaya, ghee and sandalwood.
One should further give red sandalwood and milk-rice to Vivasvat;
one should give a mixture of yellow orpiment and ghee to Indra.
One should offer rice with jaggery to Mitra, milk-porridge with ghee to Rudra,
and likewise raw or cooked meat to Rājayakṣman.
One should cause meats and pumpkins to be offered to Pṛthvīdhara;
one should give milk-rice with sugar to Aryaman, and indeed a drink alone.
One should present to the Brahmin the five products of the cow, barley, sesame seeds, unbroken grains, sacrificial oblation, cooked rice, and various kinds of food fit for eating and chewing.
Thus worshipped, the gods always bestow peace;
one should give gold to all [the deities] and a milch cow to Brahmā.
An offering to the Rākṣasas should consist of meat and rice;
and in the northeast, one should present a sacrificial oblation (caru) to the Nāga Mothers.
Having approached the southern direction, one should offer meat-rice, blood, and turmeric-rice after tearing open [the ground].
One should offer a yellowish-red oblation consisting of curd-rice mixed with blood and fish entrails to the Rākṣasī named Pūtanā.
In the northwest, fish, meat, liquor, and fermented spirits, as well as milk-rice, should be offered to the evil Rākṣasī by her own name, in due order, on all sides.
One intent on the *namaskāra* and beginning with the *praṇava* should offer, in every respect,
meat and boiled rice to Skanda in the east, and likewise to the other [deity] in the south.
One should offer kṛśara and apūpa with the root mantra to Aryaman;
however, one should give meat along with blood to Jṛmbhaka in the west.

In a vessel made of *pilipiccha* wood, one should offer a *bali* oblation to the lords of the directions with various kinds of food and drink, both smeared and ground with red pigment, using their respective mantras.
For all [the goddesses], milk-rice with clarified butter should be offered when the aforementioned oblation is unavailable;
in its absence, the offering consists of *darbha* grass, flowers, curd, unbroken rice, and clarified butter.

On the ground to the east, having smeared it with cow dung, one should offer all the ritual oblations (bali), beginning with those for the elements, preceded by perfumes and other offerings upon the mandalas.
Homage again and again to the spirits and to the ancestors, to the rākṣasas,
to the piśācas, to the mothers, and to the various hosts individually.
Then, with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, [one should perform the bathing] for the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial [deities];
thereafter, one should cause the patron (*yajamāna*) to undergo a bath with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*).
One should worship with devotion the twice-born and others who have come to the house;
having thus performed this pacification of the site (vāstu), one should carry out the ritual action.
At the commencement of palaces, mansions, and gardens, during renovations,
and upon entering a city or a house, [one should perform this] for the pacification of all defects.
Having performed the pacification of the site, one should then encircle the house and other structures with thread,
using the *Rakṣoghna* and *Pāvamāna* hymns.
One should perform the recitation by Brahmins accompanied by dances and auspicious musical instruments;
the wise man who performs this according to the prescribed rule every year, [attains the fruit].
Whether one performs it in the home or in a sanctuary, that person shall not encounter suffering;
nor shall he have fear of disease, nor shall there be any loss of kinsmen or wealth.
Such a man shall live for a hundred years and dwell in heaven for one kalpa.
Now, in the Brahmavaivarta:
Having caused beautiful houses to be built in numbers equal to the seasons,
the Vasus, and the suns (12), and eighteen worlds and thirty [others] in numbers corresponding to their respective lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
According to one's capacity, one should construct up to a hundred or a thousand diverse multi-storied buildings featuring walls, pillars, windows, and so forth.
[He saw] houses with walls and gateways, fitted with door-panels, bolts, and mechanical devices;
white as plaster, beautiful, and possessing spacious courtyards and enclosures.
With vessels made of the seven metals, endowed with the five jewels,
as well as those made of leather, wood, ivory, and cloth.
They were strewn with earthenware utensils, provided with garments and implements,
and adorned with an abundance of all kinds of equipment, hemp, and bark-cloth.
They were adorned with grass and stones, provided with heaps of wood,
and graced by granaries filled with all kinds of grain.
[He saw] auspicious and excellent mansions, firm, provided with cows, buffaloes, horses, bulls, servants, and female slaves, and situated near fields, groves, and water.
It should be completely filled with the seven types of grain, along with ghee, oil, molasses, and so forth— namely, sesame, rice, śāli rice, sugarcane, mung beans, wheat, and mustard seeds.
With *priyaṅgu*, wild rice (*yavānī*), *nīvāra*, *niṣpāva*, and *rājamudga*;
with *masūra*, *caṇaka*, *āvarta*, *kuṣṭhaka*, and *kulotthaka*.
With salt, fresh ginger, dates, grapes, cumin, and coriander;
and with bathing liquids consisting of asafoetida, saffron, camphor, and sandalwood.
With silver utensils, couches, cotton mattresses, and pillows;
with stoves, cutting tools, churning-sticks, fine seats, and stools.
With cooking pots, mortars, plates, winnowing baskets, mirrors, and mechanical devices; with pestles, swords, daggers, arrows, staffs, bows, and mallets.
[658] With household hearths, ladles, platters, clods of earth, and hands;
with wandering mendicants, time, iron, Indra’s lightning, firebrands, and water-jars.
Likewise, the mortar and pestle, the water-jar and the broom, as well as the chests, the jars, and the swings together with the primary vessels for ritual sipping.
According to one's capacity— with a thousand pieces of gold, or a hundred, or fifty, or twenty-five— one should fashion them joined with silver, using a pure mind.
In this manner, one should give complete houses to those who seek welfare and other such benefits.
In the Vahnipurāṇa:
"When the moon possesses strength, when it is conjoined with a fixed asterism,
on an auspicious day declared by a Brahmin, the time for giving is praised."
On the third day of the bright fortnight, or on the full moon day,
having thus prepared the necessary provisions and invited the best of the twice-born to his home;
One should invite a hundred persons endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct,
who are learned in the Vedas and Shastras, and have mastered the Puranas and Smritis.

O King, what is given to those who are devoted to the duties of householders, who are self-controlled, though lacking wealth yet having large families, and who are without other support, yields great fruit.
Having adorned those accompanied by their wives with garments, ornaments, and earrings,
and having again performed the fire-sacrifice and worshipped the site according to the prescribed rite;
Uttering this, the donor, free from pride, should perform [the rite], saying:
"May Govinda, the Lord of the World, who dwells in the household, be pleased."
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Having caused a single sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a girdle (*mekhalā*) to be constructed in the courtyard of the house,
the domestic sacrifice (*gṛhayajña*) should always be performed, which brings about satisfaction and nourishment."
The procedure for the domestic sacrifice (gṛhayajña) should be consulted in the [relevant] section.
Then, the Brahmins should recite the hymns that destroy demons (rakṣoghnasūktas).
The worship of Vāstu must be performed, and one should offer oblations (bali) to the guardians of the directions (dikpālas).
Then, with the proclamation of an auspicious day, those Brahmins,
having led them into those houses, should cause them to sit upon the couches together with their wives.
Then the wise patron, pure and wearing white garments,
should bestow upon each person that which was previously ordained for them.
In this regard, the formula for the gift is as follows:

"Oṃ, today, to [Name], of such-and-such lineage, etc., I give this house, complete with beds, seats, vessels, and utensils, filled with all kinds of grain, and dedicated to all the deities, for the sake of [Name] desire; it is yours, not mine. Having said this, one should recite the mantra to be spoken later:
"Oṃ, today, to [Name], of such-and-such lineage, etc.; for the sake of consecrating this gift of a house, I give this gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); it is yours, not mine."

The number of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) has indeed been shown according to one's capacity by the passage beginning with "with a thousand pieces of gold" and so forth. Having said "May it be well" (*svasti*), the recipient should recite the mantra well-known in the Yajurveda: "Who gave?
(*ko dāt*). "O Brahmin, accept this house, complete with all its furnishings; through your grace, may my desired fruit be attained."
Having thus given [the gifts] one by one and prostrated, he should offer them;
the Brahmins, being honored, should say "May there be well-being" and "Who has given?"
Furthermore, in the Bṛhaspati-smṛti, this mantra is as follows:
"O best of the twice-born, accept this house for the sake of my prosperity;
may Janārdana, the source of the universe, who takes the form of the site (vāstu), be pleased with me."
In the Matsya Purāṇa: When the day for the gift has arrived, one should prepare in the northeast a square pit, equal in size to a cubit, adorned with a girdle and a yoni.
To the northeast, a sacrificial altar (vedī) measuring one cubit (hastimitā) is for the worship of the Lord of the Gods (Deveśvara) and others;
there is the worship of the icons (arcārcana) of Brahmā, Śiva, and Acyuta.
The function of the sun is [fulfilled] by fruits, flowers, and fragrances.
The characteristics of the images of Brahmā and the others have been described in the *Tulāpuruṣa* [chapter]. Furthermore, archways (toraṇas) should be constructed at the gates,
even using the leaves of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīravanaspati*).
And having placed a full water-jar in the center,
provided with garlands, perfumes, incense, garments, and jewels;
Having performed the opening of the fire (agnimukha) according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras,
one should then cook a divine sacrificial oblation (caru) of sthālīpāka with cow’s milk.
And then I offer that very sacrificial oblation (caru) to the household deities situated in the center, as well as the ritual offering (bali),
according to the correct application of the rules.
But one should offer [the oblation] surrounded by a stream of milk.
One should first honor the Brahmin and ask for his forgiveness once he is fully satisfied.
Then, on the southern side, one should provide a bed equipped with a pillow and a lamp,
covered with white cloths and accompanied by images of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.

The characteristics of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa will be described in the section on the gift of deities, specifically in the rite of the gift of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa; having fashioned that form out of gold according to one's capacity,
it should be dressed in white garments and adorned with earrings, golden ornaments, armlets, and beautiful neck-ornaments.
And taking him together with his wife by the hand,
the householder donor should recite this mantra:
Come, come, O Nārāyaṇa of divine form,
whose lotus feet are worshipped by all the immortals;
O steadfast one, the abode of the nectar of auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, and bliss!
Accompanied by Lakṣmī, you indeed take possession of this house.
Salutations to the Lord Kaustubha, and to the one clad in golden armor;
salutations again and again to the sustainer of the world who sleeps upon the ocean of milk.
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, salutations indeed to the Lord of the World;
salutations to him who has become the abode of the world of the moving and the unmoving.
The worlds, headed by the Bhūrloka, are situated within your body;
they shall rejoice until the end of the kalpa, and you likewise remain as their master therein.
O Lord of Gods, by your grace, this householder, joined by his sons and grandsons and engaged in the performance of the five great sacrifices, shall dwell [here] as long as the moon and stars exist.
Having spoken thus to the Lord of Gods together with his consort, he seated that best of the twice-born upon a bed placed atop a prastha of sesame seeds.
Then he spoke these words: "O best of the twice-born, accept this house, which is filled with all kinds of grain and provided with every household utensil."
There, one should offer all household utensils for the couple,
along with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, ornaments, seats, and vessels.
Having recited, "May it be complete, endowed with wealth, furnished with household utensils and ornaments,
and entirely perfect," one should then make the formal offering.

In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: "The great sages maintain that even for the instructor, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be equal to the household utensils, excluding the house itself, because he is the root of that [instruction]."
