Having honored the virtuous women, one should then go to one's own home;
according to this rite, one may give many or even just a single house.
A restriction regarding number must be established; here, capacity is the regulating factor.
Having given a thatch hut that wards off cold, wind, and sun, [one attains the fruit].
One obtains desired objects and is glorified in heaven after death;
[this is] either that which is measured by the Ṛgveda, or that which has the Yajus in its midst and is adorned with the tones of the Sāmaveda.
Having attained ultimate happiness, one should bestow the beloved city of Brahmā. Gifts of cattle, land, and gold, as well as religious observances and self-restraints,
O son of Kuntī, do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of giving a house.
In the Vahni Purāṇa:
"O King, having thus given a house equipped with all furnishings,
a man goes to the city of Viṣṇu, being served by hosts of apsarases."
Having enjoyed there for three kalpas pleasures that are very difficult even for the gods to obtain,
he returns here in due course of time and becomes a righteous king.
Furthermore, having attained Viṣṇu’s city after seven births,
the king becomes endowed with beauty and good fortune, long-lived, and free from affliction.
O Great King, a man shall be happy, free from separation from prosperity through his sons and grandsons;
therefore, a house is bestowed.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "He who thus dedicates cooked food endowed with all [excellences] is honored in the world of Brahmā for as long as a hundred crores of kalpas."
Whoever offers [a vessel] made of stone or even wood according to the prescribed rite shall dwell in the delightful Ocean of Milk in the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
And he who gives a house made of clay, complete with household utensils,
shall dwell out of affection in the cities of the world-protectors for the duration of a Manvantara.
Freed from the impurities of the Kali age, honored by the assemblies of perfected beings (siddhas), and fanned by celestial nymphs (apsarases) with *sāla* tree branches,
he [delivers] even his hundred ancestors, his kinsmen, and his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons.
Even one alone may rescue those who are submerged in hell.
Having enjoyed divine pleasures thereafter, he shall become a king of kings on earth;
endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa, devoted to Nārāyaṇa,
and attached to the stories of Nārāyaṇa, he shall live happily for a hundred years.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"He who should cause to be built a city for the twice-born, which is like a very firm palace, highly significant, inhabited by the virtuous, and fit to be enjoyed by noble people..."
With his heart's desires gladdened by divine apsarases, he attains the state of non-attainment belonging to the Moon-crested Lord.
[664] Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a house.
Sumantu said:
Having constructed a house for Ananta made of clay, wood, stone, or even baked brick, according to the extent of one's available wealth;
Having thus given a house equipped with all utensils and provided with every kind of grain to the Sun, one shall obtain all desires.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a sun-house as stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*. Likewise, in the *Mahābhārata*:
"Similarly, for the sake of cows, one should provide a beautiful shelter that wards off cold and wind."
Having delivered his lineage up to the seventh generation, O best of the Bharatas.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
He who, having caused to be made a very firm and extensive level ground,
which wards off cold, wind, and heat, and is most soft with sand—
It removes the itching of the body, is filled with a multitude of pillars,
and possesses a staff-like support made of various grasses fashioned as food.

He took recourse in that excellent seat as a refuge to ward off mosquitoes and other insects with smoke, and to dispel the prickly goads of the fear of being bitten by snakes, which provide the touch of supreme bliss.
It was provided with constructed wells, drinking pools, and other reservoirs of water; it was filled with laborers who removed refuse and kept the area free of litter.
Provided with a livelihood capable of sustaining grass, water,
and other necessities, such a place was exceedingly beautiful, adorned with walls and gates.
He who builds a house for the sake of cows and offers it on a sacred festival day becomes a king of kings, endowed with good fortune and health.
Having reached the world of the Surabhis, endowed with divine enjoyments,
and having sported there for a very long time, he then returns to the human state;
possessed of wealth and beauty, he is born into a great family.
Thus ends the gift of a cow-house.
Now, the gift of a shelter. Regarding that, the Kālikā Purāṇa states:
"There is nothing superior to Śaṅkara; therefore, one should offer it to him."
Or having constructed a dwelling for ascetics made of baked bricks;
Discrimination, resolve,
excellent conduct, and a beautiful, windless place provided with attendants,
joined with a pavilion for exposition, and furnished with various seats.
A village endowed with flower gardens and watered by streams, together with a temple of Śaṅkara,
[should be given] for the sake of lamps, fuel, and so forth, as well as for the maintenance of servants.
One should employ it for the sake of obtaining a loincloth, sandals, and other such necessities;
then, having honored the ascetics with devotion, one should especially feed them.
Having worshipped the Lord with vajras and with devotion, one should offer them to him, saying:
"May Mahādeva, the moon-crested Maheśvara, be pleased with me."
Having spoken thus and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) on an auspicious day,
a man— endowed with all his desires through this gift of shelter—
shall go to that abode and enjoy the pleasures of the worlds of the immortals.
Therefore, that is the abode of Śaṅkara. In the Śaiva Purāṇa it is said:
"The *liṅga* is said to be of two kinds: stationary (*sthāvara*) and mobile (*jaṅgama*).
The stationary should be established in a temple (*prāsāda*), while the mobile is beneficial in a monastery (*maṭha*)."
The great seers have declared that the mobile is superior to the immobile;
[this includes] the establishment of the directions and so forth, as well as the illumination of knowledge and action.
But it should proceed from a mobile [image]; therefore, there is a superiority in the case of a mobile one.
Consequently, for the protection of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), [it should be taken] from mobile lingas.
Having caused a divine monastery to be built of pure stone and brick,
provided with beds and seats, and beautified by flower gardens and the like.
Endowed with supreme faith, one should bestow it at an auspicious time.
Regarding the gift of a monastery (*maṭha*), Mārkaṇḍeya states in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"For as long as that monastery remains on the earth, frequented by people,
for that same number of years the donor shall partake in auspiciousness."
He who causes a stone monastery to be built in the vicinity of a temple of Śiva shall attain the state of Śiva and dwell there for a hundred times ten thousand kalpas.

Therefore, upon the exhaustion of that merit, one who is dear to the Lord shall obtain this earth; though long afflicted by illness, he shall attain health, prosperity, sovereignty, and a continuous lineage.
In the Tretā Yuga, O lord of kings, he shall become a performer of a thousand sacrifices;
having built a monastery in the presence of the holy abode of Viṣṇu,
he shall forever be the repository of all sovereign splendors and riches.
In the Bhagavatī Purāṇa:
"For the sake of victory alone, one should establish meritorious gardens, monasteries, and the like;
therefore, a person should cause such monasteries, gardens, and so forth to be provided with water."
Having diligently constructed a monastery equipped with beds and seats,
one should then present it to Brahmins or to ascetics during an auspicious time.
One who possesses all desires attains them all; one who is free from desire shall attain liberation.
As stated by Brahmā:
Having caused a monastery or even a shelter to be constructed, complete with all necessary implements,
one should dedicate it to the twice-born at an auspicious time.
The worlds attained by him through his meritorious deeds never perish.
Agastya said:
He who builds a temple for the gods and a shelter for ascetics always attains all his desires and achieves success.
He who builds a sacrificial pavilion, or even one who sports in excellent houses, [attains these rewards].
In the Devīpurāṇa: "Those who worship [the deity] in a temple, a pavilion, a house, a monastery, on a painted stone slab, in a loft, or in a cloth tent— [all of them attain the fruit]."
A monastery three stories high, provided with its own women and water within,
was established as a sanctuary of peace through the recitation of the treasury of knowledge and other rites, which were like fire itself.
It is fitting that this, which bestows all desires,
pacifies great sins, and removes the impurities of the entire earth, should be given to the Lord.
The recitation [of this] likewise increases sovereignty, longevity, progeny, and good fortune;
they do not perform it in vain, nor in a place devoid of a monastery and a garden.
O King, he acts as an obstacle to all people, bringing fear to the world;
likewise,
he would cause ten million temples of the gods to be adorned with golden egg-shaped ornaments.
One has made the abode of the Lord of All; this is the superior fruit thereof.
Whatever merit is proclaimed to come from bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā, that same merit one obtains by having her bathed by her own kinsmen; thus she attains the state of Īśāna.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, concerning the gift of a monastery (*maṭha*), it says:
"He who should cause to be built a great and beautiful monastery, well-established upon a pedestal, five stories high or three stories high, for those whose souls delight in the knowledge of Śiva."
It was provided with secret inner chambers, endowed with locations for the recitation of mantras,
divided according to the science of architecture, and surrounded by a perimeter wall.
To the east, the sacrificial circle (satramaṇḍala) should be provided with a smoke-vent;
in the northeast, a house for perfumes and flowers should be constructed together with a monastery (maṭha).
The treasury should be in the north, the granary in the northwest,
and the water reservoir, provided with a wind-vehicle, in the west.
In the southwest (Nairṛti) should be the place for fuel such as sacrificial grass and wood, as well as for weapons;
and there should also be a delightful guest-house provided with beds.
To the right, there should be ponds, fires, and lamps;
all the interior rooms should be provided with water-filled plantain bowers.
One should arrange it so that it is adorned with flowers of five colors,
and one should provide an outer enclosure measuring five cubits in size.
And outside the enclosure wall, in all directions on every side,
one should fashion the divine, auspicious refuge of Rāma, adorned with various flowers.
It was endowed with flowers of every season and possessed various kinds of trees,
including priyaṅgu, śikhara, aśoka, putrajīvaka, and kariṣṭaka.
With *punnāga*, *vakula*, *pāṭala*, *bilva*, and *campaka*; with white *mandāra*, *vijaya*, *jātī*, *tagara*, and *kuṣṭha*.
With golden and white yūthīs, with kuraṇṭakas whose colors do not fade,
with karavīras and karṇikāras of many various colors in great abundance.

It was endowed with various kinds of trees possessing well-placed arrangements and conduct, joined with the foundation of the true path, and provided with water in all directions and intermediate points.
It was filled with white jewel-lotuses and blue and red water-lilies,
and in various places there were small pavilions formed by the canopies of creeping vines.
Adorned with plantains, sections of pillars, pomegranates, and other such fruits,
having thus prepared the exterior, one should cause a great enclosure wall to be constructed.
Above the third city, there shall be a pavilion for the exposition of knowledge, provided with gates and watchtowers, and equipped with moats and ditches.
One should fashion a wonderful structure provided with windows for the exit;
and fifth, one should construct a house for Śiva to dwell in, located outside the city.
One should install Śiva there according to the prescribed rite, fashioned from clay, wood, or stone, upon a wooden pedestal measuring six or eight cubits.
To the knower of all sciences, the omniscient Lord of the family,
who was surrounded by disciples and grand-disciples, and whose hands were raised in readiness for exposition;

Having thus established the hermitage of Śiva, one should represent the Guru seated in the lotus posture, brilliantly white and with a serene countenance, according to one's devotion and financial means.
Thereafter, one should perform its consecration, characterized by worship and ornaments;
having created a splendor before the monastery with the riches mentioned for the gift of knowledge.
Having established it in the northeastern direction with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in sequence,
one should bathe it with perfumed water and other substances as prescribed in the Śiva scriptures.
Having brought him there with the sounds of musical instruments, one should place him in a pavilion of flowers;
then, having worshipped him with sandalwood, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Having recited the fivefold hymn of praise, he should then make this request to Śiva:
"O Lord, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) takes place today; tomorrow shall be your installation."
Out of compassion for his devotees, he should manifest his presence;
having bathed the Lord of Gods in the morning and worshipped him, he should cause him to enter.
One should establish [the deity] upon the altar with five purifiers, beginning from the feet;
thereafter, the temple of Śiva should always be purified with perfumes, incense, and other offerings.
One should worship Śiva with flowers, accompanied by a bath and a pair of garments; having prostrated before that Lord along with his consort, the Guru should commence the exposition.
Facing either the east or the north before Śiva for the sake of a meritorious day,
the patron himself should then worship the Guru with devotion.
One should honor them with various sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) and offerings such as food;
thereafter, one should offer a dwelling place for all the Śiva-yogins.
Even with all his resources, a wealthy man who, having prostrated before this [liṅga] again and again,
causes it to be thus established, shall attain the great and glorious city of Śiva.
Completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva,
accompanied by twenty members of his own lineage and surrounded by his servants and retinue.
Accompanied by his sons, friends, and others, serene and surrounded by his retinue,
he [proceeds] in countless, most wonderful Great Vehicles that provide all desires.
Endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, he sports with enjoyments like Śiva;
then, after a long time, by the power of the gift of knowledge (*vidyādāna*).
Having attained the yoga of knowledge, one is liberated right there;
[even] architects, masons, trees, oxen, and those engaged in ritual action [are so].
All those men who are supervisors there go to the city of Rudra;
and others as well, such as laborers and servants engaged in the work of Śiva’s sanctuary—
they too, upon death, go to heaven by the power of their service to Śiva.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: Having caused to be built a firm and auspicious monastery made of baked bricks, resembling the back of a tortoise and illuminating the horizons;
One should give [a dwelling] smeared with lime, well-protected, and adorned with comfortable halls;
this bestows infinite fruit upon Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and Yogic practitioners.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: One should construct a monastery (maṭha) that is three-storied, two-storied, or even single-storied;
it should be enriched with various halls, resplendent, and adorned with *mattavāraṇa* (elephant-ornaments).
Adorned with places for meditation, study, fire-offerings, and exposition,
its ground was fashioned equally either with plaster or with stone.
It was filled with fresh materials used as book-rests arranged about it,
and adorned by circles of garden rows teeming with various fruits.
It was a reservoir filled with pure, sweet, and abundant water,
serving as a dwelling for ascetics and for travelers who had arrived there.
For the sake of obtaining sandals, shoes, umbrellas, loincloths, fuel, clothing,
and other such useful articles.
Endowed with faith, one should give a village or a vast tract of land;
thus providing a refuge that brings benefit to the ascetics.
To others as well—those in the world who suffer and seek a refuge—I grant a secure shelter; may the Treasure of the World be pleased with me.
Having thus given such a wonderfully diverse refuge, O Great King,
one obtains without doubt the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Having resided in the city of Viṣṇu as Śiva, possessing his form, strength, and prowess,
and having enjoyed manifold pleasures, he attains supreme liberation.
He who should cause to be built a temple for Murāri, crowded with rows of various and vast pillars, and provided with beautiful walls and canopies,
shall then be surrounded by celestial maidens.
Having reached the further shore of the waters of the ocean of existence, he attains happiness.
[673] Thus concludes the gift of a dwelling place.
Now follows the gift of a shelter. Regarding this, in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
When a very spacious shelter has been constructed, complete with water and fuel for the sake of the poor and the helpless, what then would remain that has not already been accomplished?
In the Vahni Purāṇa: Having caused to be constructed a firm pillar made of baked bricks,
a very spacious shelter with auspicious ground endowed with the proper characteristics.
One should give [a dwelling] plastered with lime, well-protected, and adorned with comfortable halls;
this bestows infinite fruit upon Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and yogic practitioners.
Having caused a very spacious shelter to be built— a beautiful house provided with excellent food and abundant water for the sake of the poor and the helpless—
one should offer it to travelers, a charming dwelling with auspicious gates.
In the *Devīpurāṇa*,
Śakra said:
"To the western part of the city, or to the south, or else to the north."
Whether they build a shelter in the east or even in the middle, [they do so].

O best of the twice-born, which deities should be installed there and which should not? Tell me regarding their placement according to the divisions of the directions, so that he may become a bestower of peace.
Brahmā said:
O Lord of the Gods, this sanctuary for him should be constructed to the south, north, east, or west;
or else, Śakra should be placed in the center.
Those who provide shelter for twice-born men who are weary and exhausted shall dwell in heaven for a long time.
Therefore, those who seek both visible and invisible fruits should construct a shelter;
for Śakra, when presided over by a deity, becomes the bestower of all happiness.
Three deities are prescribed; a fourth is not appropriate.
One should likewise have Mahiṣaghnī, a Yakṣa, and the Nāyaka fashioned here.
Mahiṣaghnī should be placed in the center, in the position of Jyeṣṭha, and not otherwise;
she should be positioned toward the left direction, and likewise, Yakṣarāja should be on the right.
Alternatively, it may be performed facing the cardinal directions; regarding that as well, I shall tell you:
one should install the Goddess there at whichever door is directly in front.
No yakṣa or leader should be made; they should stand in the middle between the two doors.
When this is done, who is able to describe the fruit that results?
The fruit of this alone is happiness, sovereignty, fame, and prosperity.
Yama says:
He who provides these five— a seat, water for washing the feet, a lamp, food, and shelter— performs a sacrifice accompanied by five sacrificial fees.
The giver of food is to be known as the giver of life; the giver of form is remembered as the giver of clothing.
Indeed, he who gives shelter is called the giver of everything.
A man who provides lodging for yogis gains the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices,
and a thousand Puṇḍarīka sacrifices.
Viṣṇu says: By the gift of each of these— a shelter, as well as a bed, foot-unguent, and a lamp—
one obtains a fruit equal to the gift of a cow.
Dakṣa said:

"If even for a moment a renunciant enters into the hermitage of one who possesses this [knowledge], what need has he for any other dharma? For he is considered to have accomplished all that was to be done."
Whatever sin has been accumulated by a householder since birth, a mendicant who is satisfied for even a single night wipes all of that away.
Likewise: one emaciated by austerities and recitations, one afflicted by disease, one who is infirm, an old man, one possessed by a spirit, and likewise another whose sense faculties are impaired.
A mendicant who is healthy and young is not worthy of a dwelling;
being healthy and young, he perishes through the loss of his celibacy.
But a monk who, having lived in the monastery, indulges in sexual intercourse, being ruined by his failure in celibacy, shall destroy both his family and his lineage.
He cuts away even the very roots of that destruction of his dwelling.
Bṛhaspati said:
One should give a seat to the one who has arrived, and likewise a bed to the weary;
one should give water to the thirsty and food to the hungry.
One should give sight, one should give mind, and one should give pleasant speech;
Manu has declared this to be the common duty for all four social classes.
Agni is pleased by a welcome; Śatakratu by a seat;
the ancestors by the washing of the feet; and Prajāpati by the food.
Manu, Viṣṇu, and Śātātapa [state]:
"Those among the Brahmins from whose house a guest departs without having eaten,
they indeed attain the state of a donkey, a camel, or a horse."
In whosever house a Brahmin stays without being fed,
neither the gods nor the ancestors will partake of his offerings to the gods (havya) or to the ancestors (kavya).
In whatever village a guest indeed lies down hungry despite having been diligently sought for alms, the sin of killing a Brahmin is ordained there.
Whether cooking only vegetables or living by gleaning grains,
a guest should never dwell in one's own country or in a foreign land with a troubled mind.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is considered a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore called a guest.
Yama said:
That high-souled person by whom all lunar days, festivals, and celebrations have been abandoned is a guest for all beings; they know the rest to be mere visitors.
A practitioner of vows or an ascetic who stays for only one night is called a *atithi*;
because he does not stay permanently, they know him as a guest (*atithi*).

The *parvan* days are those such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and others; festivals are marriages and the like; and the lunar day (*tithi*) is that distinct from these, such as the first day of the festival of lights (*dīpālikā-pratipad*). The meaning is that he who, being devoted to dharma, has renounced these occasions for obtaining special food—that person is a guest (*atithi*). Gautama states:
"A guest is one from a different village, staying for only one night, who waits upon the sun while remaining under a tree."
"Ekarātrika" means one who is habituated to staying for only one night. "Adhivṛkṣa" refers to the sound of the sun [at its zenith], indicating the evening time.
He is skillful. I shall describe the substances for nectar when a learned guest has arrived at the house.
One should offer this fourfold gift: the mind, the eye, the face, and gentle speech.

The articles for the nectar-offering are those that can be obtained without effort. Rising to greet them, welcoming them with kind words upon their arrival, attending to them, and following them when they depart— these duties should be performed with diligence.
Attendance consists of remaining in his presence.
Other minor services include the earth, water, grass,
washing the feet, as well as anointing with oil, shelter, and a bed.
And "slight things" are so called because they can be accomplished with little effort.
At night, he should eat something according to his ability; he should not remain in the house without eating.
Manu says: No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of one's ability with a seat, food, a bed, water, or roots and fruits.
In the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
One should construct a guest-house for travelers that brings them benefit;
or else, one should provide lodging for virtuous wayfarers within a portion of one's own home.
Inexhaustible merit is declared for him, which bestows both heaven and liberation;
enriched with all his desires, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
Thus concludes the gift of a superior quality.
Now, the gift of a body is described. Bṛhaspati says:
A thousand cows and a hundred oxen are equal [in merit].
A vehicle is equal to ten oxen; a horse is equal to ten vehicles.
A maiden is equal to ten vehicles, and the gift of land is equal to that;
therefore, among all gifts, the gift of a maiden is preeminent.
Atri said:
A heap of sand as large as the constellation of the Seven Sages [the Great Bear] is reduced by one *pala* every thousand years once it has passed.
And its exhaustion is observed; it does not exist in the giving away of a daughter.
In the Mahābhārata: Karandhama’s son was King Maruta;
having given his daughter to Aṅgiras, he quickly ascended to heaven.
And King Mitrasaha, having given his beloved Damayantī to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, departed for heaven along with her.
And the royal sage Madirāśva, having given his slender-waisted daughter to Hiraṇyahasta, went to the worlds praised by the gods.
And the lordly royal sage Lomapāda, having given his daughter Śāntā to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga,
was endowed with all his great desires.
Kaśyapa says:
By giving away a maiden adorned with mantras and oblations, one obtains a hundred times a hundredfold the merit of performing a hundred Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.
The gift of ten thousand oxen capable of bearing the yoke,
given to a worthy recipient according to the prescribed rite, is equal to the gift of a daughter in marriage.
Devala said:
Having protected three daughters according to the law and having provided for them,
neither the father nor the woman who gives birth to daughters goes to hell.
Vasiṣṭha said: The fruit of all gifts whatsoever follows one for a single birth;
however, the fruit of gifts of gold, land, and cows follows one for seven births.
Saṃvarta says:
But he who, having adorned a maiden with ornaments, clothing, and food,
gives her away, attains heaven and is honored by Indra and the other gods.
In the Vahni Purāṇa: "O best of the twice-born, those who bestow a maiden, well-adorned according to their means, as a gift for a Brahmin, go to the world of Brahmā."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"By giving a decorated maiden, adorned according to his financial capacity and with festive rites,
to a virtuous Brāhmaṇa, one attains the world of Gaurī."
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"Of the four stages of life (āśramas), the householder is said to be the best;
of all houses, the home is the best; and of all homes, excellent women are the best."
Therefore, no other gift is considered equal to the giving away of a daughter;
hence, a daughter should be given in marriage by the wise who desire all goals.
Yājñavalkya: The father, the grandfather, the brother, a sapinda relative, and likewise the mother;
in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent person is the giver of the maiden, provided they are of sound mind.
Nārada says: The father himself should give away the daughter, or the brother with the father’s permission;
likewise the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the paternal kinsmen, and other relatives.
But in the absence of all these, if the mother remains in her natural state,
then while she is not in that state, those of his own caste should give the girl in marriage.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Having made her one's own by means of gold, even one who is not of the same lineage is fit to give away another's daughter according to the righteous rite.
Manu states who is entitled to marry:
"Having studied the Vedas— either all of them, two of them, or even one— in due order,
and having remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy, he shall enter the stage of the householder."
Having been permitted by his teacher, having bathed, and having returned home according to the prescribed rule,
the twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks.
Yājñavalkya also says: "Having mastered the Veda, or the vows, or both,
and having remained pure in his student life (brahmacarya), he should marry a woman of auspicious marks."
Viśvāmitra said:
O lord of men, having summoned a Brahmin seeking knowledge and having given him a decorated maiden, that is called the gift of a daughter (kanyādāna).
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "O lord of men, one should give a decorated maiden to a twice-born man who is learned in the Vedas, without taking anything in return; that is called the gift of a maiden."
One should give one's daughter, who is still a maiden and a follower of dharma, to a man of virtue;
one should not withhold her until she has reached the age of menstruation, even if he is devoid of virtues.
Likewise:
"A maiden should be given to a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), a Brahmin, an ascetic,
one who has directly studied the Vedas, and a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), according to the prescribed rule."
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Having adorned a maiden with supreme devotion and great care,
one should give her to a man of noble birth, handsome appearance, and especially one who recognizes virtue."
To one who seeks a maiden in marriage, she should be given; this is the prescribed rule.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"A daughter should be given with great effort to one who is well-behaved, of good conduct, possessed of learning, and ascetic; never to anyone else under any circumstances."
The characteristics of a maiden to be married are stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"One who seeks dharma and worldly prosperity should marry a maiden who is beautiful, endowed with auspicious marks, free from physical defects, born of a noble family, and has a brother."
She had wide eyes, a beautiful face, and dark, curly hair;
her palms and the tips of her feet were copper-colored, her neck was shaped like a conch shell, and she possessed a slender waist.
She had broad hips, was adorned with beautiful buttocks,
possessed slender ankles and teeth, and had lips and palate that were slightly dark.

The wise declare that a maiden who has eyes that are not too tawny, who is not reddish-brown, whose feet do not quiver, who is auspicious, and whose cheeks and tip of the nose are not thick, is praiseworthy;
one should marry such a girl who is free from disease and defects.
The description of girls who are to be avoided is given in the Vahnipurāṇa:
"Even if they are great and prosperous in terms of cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain—
one should avoid these ten families in forming a marriage alliance."
For those who cause distress to people of low birth, heretics, and virtuous men, there shall be families afflicted with hypocrisy, disease, constant censurability, vitiligo, and leprosy.
A wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother and whose father is unknown, for fear of the practice of *putrikā* (the sonless daughter).
As Saṃvarta has said:
"At eight years she becomes a Gaurī; at nine she becomes a Nagnikā;
at ten she is called a Kanyakā; and at twelve she is known as a Vṛṣalī."
Āṅgirā said:
A girl who has not yet reached puberty is called Gaurī; once puberty has arrived, she is Rohiṇī;
one who has not developed secondary sexual characteristics is Śyāmā; and one who lacks breasts is Nagnikā.
Kāśyapa says: A girl of seven years is called *gorī*, one of ten years is a *kanyakā*,
but upon reaching twelve years, she is designated as a *kumārī*.
When the time of menstruation has arrived, Soma enjoys the maiden;
during the period of menses, the Gandharvas; and when the breasts appear, Śakra.
Therefore, one should marry off a maiden before she reaches puberty;
indeed, marriage for an eight-year-old girl is commended by the wise.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Learn from me in brief these eight forms of marriage for women, which are beneficial or harmful both in this world and the next for all four castes."
The Brāhma, the Daiva, the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya,
the Āsura, the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca is considered the eighth.
The wise know that the first four [forms of marriage] are recommended for a Brāhmaṇa;
likewise, the Rākṣasa form is for a Kṣatriya, and the Āsura form for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Of the five [forms of marriage], three are righteous and two are unrighteous as established here;
namely, the Paiśāca and the Āsura, which should never be performed under any circumstances.
The two forms of marriage previously mentioned—
the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa— whether performed separately or mixed together, are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya.
Paiṭhīnasi says: "The Gāndharva and Āsura forms are for the Rājanya; the Rākṣasa for the Vaiśya; the Paiśāca for the Śūdra; and the Ārṣa is authoritative for all. Pracetās says:
The Paiśāca rite is for those born of mixed marriages in the reverse order (*pratiloma*) from those produced by the *saṃskṛta* (Vedic) rites.
Manu says: "Whatever merit has been proclaimed by Manu for each of these forms of marriage..."
Listen attentively, O Brahmins, to everything as I proclaim it.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman who performs meritorious deeds delivers ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first— from sin.
A son born of a wife wed according to the Daiva rite propagates seven generations before and seven after himself;
a son born of a wife wed according to the Ārṣa rite propagates three before and three after; and a son born of a wife wed according to the Kāya (Gāndharva) rite propagates six.
In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma form, taken in their proper order,
sons endowed with Vedic luster and esteemed by the learned are born.
Endowed with beauty, strength, and virtue, wealthy and renowned,
possessing abundant enjoyments and most righteous, they live for a hundred years.
Moreover, among the remaining types of improper marriages, sons who are cruel, speakers of falsehood,
and haters of the Veda and dharma are born.
Through blameless marriages with women, one's offspring become blameless; through blameworthy ones, they become blameworthy among men. Therefore, one should avoid those who are blameworthy.
Now, their characteristics: therein, Viṣṇu says: "Having invited a man of virtue, the giving away of a daughter is the Brāhma [form of marriage]. Baudhāyana says:

"Having ascertained that he possesses learning and virtuous conduct and is a seeker of the Vedic way (*brahmavārin*), one should give [the daughter] to him who asks—this is the *brāhma* [wedding]. Thus said Pracetas.
One should give an unmarried girl (*nagnikā*) with water to a man of the same caste; that is the *brāhma* marriage.
Vyāsa says:
Having clothed and adorned her, and having circumambulated the fire three times while pronouncing her name and lineage, one should give her away; this is the Brāhma rite.
Manu says: "When a sacrifice has been properly commenced and the officiating priest is performing the ritual,
the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the 'Daiva' form of marriage."
Having taken one or two pairs of cattle from the bridegroom according to the law,
the giving of the daughter according to the rule— this is called the Ārṣa rite.

Hārīta says: Having given a pair of garments according to the rule, without considering them as something blameworthy by others, one should practice the Dharma together with her; this is the Prājāpatya form.
Manu says:
Having addressed the words, "May you both practice dharma together," and having honored the gift of the maiden, this is remembered as the Prajāpatya rite.
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability,
the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the Āsura dharma.
The mutual union of the maiden and the groom through their own desire is to be known as the Gāndharva form; it arises from passion and is characterized by sexual union.
Having killed, cut, and pierced [the guardians], and having forcibly abducted a maiden from her home while she is crying out and weeping— this is called the Rākṣasa rite.
Where one is led away after being carried off by deceit while asleep or intoxicated in secret,
that is the most sinful of marriages, known as the eighth, the Paiśāca.
Furthermore, in the Vahni Purāṇa:
"He who gives away his daughter in the Brāhma form of marriage shall quickly go to the world of Brahmā, honored by the gods, beginning with Brahmā."
But he who gives away his daughter through the *daiva* marriage,
having pierced the gate of the sun, goes to the heavenly world.
He who gives away his daughter by the Gāndharva rite,
having reached the world of the Gandharvas, sports for a long time like a god.
He who, having given his daughter for a bride-price, subsequently honors her properly,
sports with Kinnaras and Gandharvas for an inexhaustible time.
In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa: Having examined the auspiciousness of the lineage, the lunar mansion, the compatibility of the zodiac signs, and so forth,
one should bestow [the gift] according to the prescribed rule at an excellent moment and during a favorable conjunction.
The grasping of the hand (marriage) of an eight-year-old maiden is recommended for both parties, preceded by the mental aspiration for prosperity.
Paiṭhīnasi says:
"The sacramental rite of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste;
this following rule is to be known for the marriage ceremony with women of different castes."
An arrow should be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by a Vaiśya maiden,
and the hem of a garment by a Śūdra woman when marrying a man of higher caste.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
Having pronounced the excellent lineage beginning with the great-grandfather,
the learned man should indeed proclaim the name of the girl as well.
The giver should stand facing east, while the bridegroom should face west;
therefore, he should give her, honored with madhuparka and accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, taking a vessel of water, he should cause it to be given with this mantra:
"O Brahmin, [I give] this maiden Gaurī, adorned according to my ability."
"To that Gotra-Śarman, may [this] be given, providing a refuge for Brahmins.
This is the formula for the act of giving here.

"Oṃ! Today, I, [Name], desiring [Name], give this girl—belonging to the [Name] lineage (*sagotra*), of the [Name] *pravara*, named [Name], adorned with ornaments, whose deity is Prajāpati—to you, [Name], of the [Name] lineage, of the [Name] *pravara*, [Name], the grandson’s grandson of [Name], of the [Name] lineage, of the [Name] *pravara*, [Name]; the grandson’s son of [Name], of the [Name] lineage, of the [Name] *pravara*, [Name]; and the daughter’s daughter of [Name], of the [Name] lineage, of the [Name] *pravara*, [Name]. This is for the sake of establishing the gift of the girl; I give this gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) saying, 'It is not mine. Having recited this, he should chant the mantra of giving. The recipient, however, having first uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and said "Svasti," should recite the mantra beginning with "Who gave? (*kodāt*).
According to one's capacity, one should give land, cows, female slaves, garments, buffaloes, horses, and even gold and jewels.
Then, one should have the rites beginning with the fire-oblation (homa) performed according to the rules of one's own *gṛhya* tradition;
likewise, auspicious ceremonies and festive decorations should be carried out in accordance with local custom.
In the Liṅgapurāṇa: Having obtained the consent of the parents and having given a great amount of wealth, one should give a girl who is endowed with auspicious marks and free from all defects.
Having made it one's own and established it, having given a new, auspicious garment,
and having adorned it with ornaments, one should then worship it with perfumes and garlands.
Then, having examined the auspicious signs, the family lineage, the birth constellations, and so forth,
and having considered the minds of both parties, one should worship both with great effort.
The ear-ring should be given to a Brahmin who is an ascetic,
who has personally studied the Vedas, and who is a celibate student according to the prescribed rule.
One should cause female and male servants, seats and the like, and especially ornaments,
as well as fields, wealth, or other such things to be given.
Furthermore, for as many hairs as there are on the body of the maiden,
for that many thousands of years she is glorified in the world of Rudra.
In the Vahni Purāṇa: "Thus, those who bestow their daughter, well-adorned according to their means,
when the time for marriage has arrived and a suitable man is found as prescribed,"
In due succession, they obtain a hundred sacrifices one after another.
Upon hearing of the giving away of their daughter, fathers and grandfathers are liberated from all sins and go to the world of Brahmā.
Likewise:
one should not cause them to feel resentment, and they should always be honored in the home;
especially Brahmā and the other [deities], and there should always be a meal for the Brahmins.
One should never eat from the hands of a childless daughter;
having seen the face of your grandson, why do you grieve?
Surrounded by great beings, you have no fear of hell;
having crossed over all sufferings, you shall attain the supreme heaven.
The ancestors always rejoice at the gift given by a daughter's son;
whatever gift he bestows is destined for infinity.
Having given away his daughter, he should not grieve, even if she becomes hungry, or is beaten,
or is overwhelmed by various miseries, or likewise remains unprotected and emaciated.
One should not harbor anger toward her, and one should support those who have come to her;
where the female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes.
Wherever they do not eat, there they burn [the household] if they are not honored;
therefore, these [goddesses] should always be worshipped with ornaments, clothing, and food.
Men desiring prosperity should always be content with their own sons and grandsons;
likewise, they should be honored during śrāddha rites and festivals.
In whatever family this [practice] is constantly maintained, there indeed prosperity is certain;
O best of the twice-born, in this world there is fame, and in the next world, heaven.
Suppose a heap of sesame seeds were piled as high as the sun;
when it is gathered again at the end of a year, the time it takes for even a single seed from that heap to be removed is [the duration of a kalpa].
He will certainly attain the destruction of the Brahma-world,
measured at a hundred yojanas, by means of the accumulated hairs of the bull.
The giver of a maiden likewise remains in the world of Tura for as many years as there are hairs on his body;
he shall attain heaven until the exhaustion of all those hairs.
The chariots of the giver of land, the giver of cows, and the giver of a maiden—
these three chariots travel together equally, following after the gift of a maiden.
Then, for one who gives what has been gathered, for one who speaks the truth,
and for one whose constant habit is the private study of the Vedas— these three go together in a chariot.
The builder of a sacrificial hall, the performer of the horse sacrifice, and the giver of life to the twice-born—these three indeed go to equal merit; there is no doubt in this matter.

The giver of a daughter is called *kūkuda* when he has adorned her before giving her away. He who bestows a well-adorned maiden upon a poor man attains the merit of *pūrta* dharma, performed exactly according to the prescribed ritual.
Therefore, one who desires their own welfare should bestow a daughter with great care.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Or he who, being compassionate, gives a gift for the purpose of marriage,
[travels] by means of a variegated celestial chariot garlanded with networks of tinkling bells.
He goes to the abode of Mahendra, being served by hosts of Apsaras.
Thus concludes the procedure for the giving away of a daughter in marriage.
Now follows the installation of the twice-born (dvija). Regarding this, Dakṣa states:
"One who is bereft of mother and father [should be established] by means of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), marriage, and so forth."
For one who establishes [this], no limit to their merit is found here in this world.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Having likewise performed the marriage ceremony for [the images] in families of Śrotriyas—
twice-born men who possess Vedic learning, speech, character, and conduct— there should be eleven such [images]."
One should construct eleven delightful wind-houses;
having had them built, one should fill them with various kinds of grain.
Female slaves, cows, buffaloes, as well as beds, seats, and sandals;
and various vessels made of copper and clay.
Bowls for the purpose of eating, all kinds of utensils,
as well as iron, gold, and especially garments.
Having gathered these excellent provisions, he should employ them in those households;
or else, according to his ability, he should provide a hundred [provisions] for each, for the sake of their livelihood.
Each separately, from fifty nivartanas of ploughing,
[one may grant] a district, a karvaṭa, a kheṭa, a village, or even half a village.
One should indeed join the form of Soma with the twice-born who have been meditated upon;
there are exactly eleven of them, consisting of couples whose nature is that of Umā and Hara.
Having reflected with supreme devotion, he should cause them to enter those houses;
having ushered in these best of the twice-born, he should have them perform the *agnihotra* sacrifices.
A man should act for his own welfare according to the rule and in accordance with the law;
this is the ancient ordinance concerning those born of unblemished lineage.
One should always cause the twice-born who are distinguished by devotion to Śiva to perform [the rites];
for that fool who employs unworthy twice-born men for the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).

The fruit of that would not exist for him; moreover, the Vedic scripture is certain regarding whatever consists of sacrifice, charity, vows, and so forth, as well as pilgrimages to sacred sites and the like.
But the person who causes another to act in this way has performed everything himself;
he goes to a celestial chariot that shines like the sun and is garlanded with jewels.
Having ascended that meritorious station adorned by celestial women,
he is surrounded by thousands of other divine celestial chariots.
Having enjoyed all the pleasures available in the world, he attains that [state] after realizing the capacity of his own wealth; he should marry one Brahmin.
By that, a man devoted to Śiva certainly attains that state;
through the place [granted] by the prescribed rite, the attainment of that state comes to pass.

Now, the installation of a king. In the *Āditya Purāṇa* and in the *Bṛhaspati-śruti*: "He who reinstates a protector of the earth who has been displaced from his kingdom shall dwell here on the back of the celestial vault among the lords of sages; of this there is no doubt."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "He who reinstates a king fallen from his kingdom in his own sovereignty goes to the same world as Śakra for as long as fourteen Indras endure."
Then, having attained human birth, he becomes a righteous king;
therefore, one who desires prosperity should give gifts even to those devoid of fortune.
That which is given to those bereft of fortune is proclaimed to be infinite.
Likewise:
"The man who restores one who has fallen from his station to that position again attains the heavenly world for a long time through this deed."

In connection with the gift of a maiden (*kanyādāna*), the establishment of the twice-born (*dvijāti*) has been mentioned; since the gift of a *kapilā* cow follows in due order, it has been described in the section on the gift of cows (*godāna*). Thus, the "Ten Great Gifts" (*daśamahādānāni*) are concluded.

Thus ends [this section] in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri—the venerable Hemādri, who is the sovereign of all faculties, a master of all branches of knowledge, and the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Mahādeva.
The Section on Giving: The Chapter on the Ten Great Gifts.
[693] Now begins the tenth chapter. Next, the gifts of the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina) are described.

He who constantly considers the deerskins— softer even than linen garments— to be superior during the consecrations of the sacrifice, thinks that this golden mountain is nothing at all; thus has everything been said in its entirety.
He states the procedure for the gift of the black antelope skin and other items.
The summary verses for these are found in the Saura Purāṇa:
"A black antelope skin, a buffalo, a ewe, and ten cows—
as well as the Tulāpuruṣa gift— bestow the world of Brahmā."
Regarding the gift of a black antelope skin in that regard, Yama says:
"He who gives even a single path [of land] accompanied by a cow, land, and gold—
even if he has performed every kind of evil deed— shall attain union with Brahman."
Marīci: Whoever gives a black antelope skin with hair on both sides to one who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni),
the sin committed over seven lifetimes perishes at that very moment.
Kātyāyana says:
Those who place sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, along with gold, honey, and clarified butter,
and bestow them upon a Brahmin, need not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
Moving like a bird at will, he travels through all the worlds;
he is honored in the heavenly realm until the dissolution of the universe.
There is no gift in the three worlds equal to the black antelope skin;
likewise, those who know the Vedas understand that the acceptance of such a gift is even more sinful.
He who, out of devotion, bestows a black antelope skin upon a Brāhmaṇa shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
Whoever beholds a black antelope skin being given away with devotion shall also be liberated from sins, even those accumulated since birth.
The black antelope skin was fashioned by Brahmā as the primary requisite for the perfection of yogas and for the successful accomplishment of śrāddha rites.
O lord of men, its white form is day, its dark body is night,
and its multiform aspect is to be understood as the twilight.
The deer, whose body is the Vedas, moves about with the Sāman chants as its black antelope skin, the Ṛg verses as its white [spots], and the Yajus formulas as its many-colored forms.
That land where one may enjoy oneself according to one's own will is known as the land of the sacrificers (yājñika);
all others are lands of the Mlecchas, devoid of the Vedic dharma.
O King, without Kṛṣṇa there is no sacrifice, no ancestral rite (śrāddha), and no ritual action anywhere; nor do the treatises on dharma or the Vedic rites exist.
That gift is superior to all other gifts and to the performance of Vedic rites.
Viṣṇu said:

Then, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, having prepared the skin of a black antelope together with its hooves and horns—its hooves plated with silver and its tail adorned with pearls—one should spread it out upon a stretched woolen cloth. Then one should cover it with sesame seeds. One should make a golden navel and cover it with a pair of unwashed garments. One should decorate it with all kinds of gems and perfumes. Having placed four metallic vessels filled with milk, curd, honey, and clarified butter in the four directions, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires and is covered with a pair of garments.
And furthermore, there are these verses:
"But he who should give a black antelope skin, complete with hooves and horns,
covered with sesame seeds and cloths, and adorned with all kinds of jewels;"
By him the earth, together with its oceans, caves, mountains, forests, and groves, extending to its four boundaries, would have been given; of this there is no doubt.
He who places sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter upon a black antelope skin and gives them to a Brahmin overcomes all evil deeds.
In the Matsya Purāṇa,
Manu said:
"O sinless one, tell me the procedure and the fruit of the gift of a black antelope skin."
And explain to me what constitutes a Brāhmaṇa, for I have a great doubt regarding that matter.
Matsya said: The full moon day of Vaiśākha, an eclipse of the moon or the sun, the full moon day of Māgha, as well as those of Āṣāḍha and Kārttika; [696]
Or on the twelfth day of the sun’s northern course; what is given on that day yields great fruit.
O King, it should be given to that twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires.
Listen as I describe the manner and the ritual procedure by which it is done,
O King, on a pure spot smeared with cow dung.
First, having spread out a beautiful woolen cloth,
he then placed upon it a black antelope skin together with its horns and hooves.
It should be made with golden horns and silver tusks;
its tail should be adorned with pearls and likewise covered with sesame seeds.
Having made [the image] equal in size to himself with sesame seeds, the wise man should cover it with cloth;
some read the text as "having made a pinnacle out of sesame seeds.
He should make it have a golden navel and should especially adorn it.
One should place jewels and perfumes in its various directions according to one's ability;
one should also offer four bell-metal vessels in the directions in due order.
And having duly offered ghee, milk, curd, and honey, respectively, into earthen vessels starting from the east and so forth;

In this regard, one should place bronze vessels containing jewels in the four directions; furthermore, other earthen vessels filled respectively with ghee, milk, curd, and honey should be established in the directions starting from the east. Likewise, having performed the ritual attendance to Brahmā, one of auspicious wealth should establish the five eyes, a branch, and a flawless water-pot.
And one should wipe all the limbs with a worn-out yellow cloth.

Regarding the term *brāhmopasthānakam*: it refers to a specific water-jar (*kumbha*) located outside the area where the gift was given; it is so called because its placement (*upasthāna*) is near (*upa*, i.e., close to) that spot. "He should cleanse it" means that immediately after giving the gift, having bathed, he should cover it with a worn-out cloth. He should cause vessels made of metal to be placed at its feet [with this prayer]:
"Whatever sinful deeds I have committed out of greed for the sake of my desires."
"By the gift of an iron vessel, may my [sins] indeed perish quickly!
Having filled it with sesame seeds, one should place it under the left foot."
Whatever sinful desires have arisen from my ears and whatever [sins] have been committed,
may they always perish through the gift of a bronze vessel.
Having filled that [vessel] with honey, one should place it indeed on the right foot.
These two vessels are to be placed at the two back feet.
[This is for the sake of avoiding] slander of others, calumny, and the eating of the flesh of the back.
May whatever sin has arisen therein perish from this copper vessel:
the falsehood regarding a maiden, the theft of cows, and the violation of another's wife.
By the gift of a silver vessel, may these two [obstacles] of mine go quickly to destruction;
for in this rite, there are vessels of copper and silver with their openings turned upward.

Regarding "ūrdhvapāde" (on the upper foot), the singular number used for "the two feet" is not intended here. In this case, a copper vessel filled with honey should be placed on the upper foot; a silver vessel filled with sesame seeds should be placed on the right foot; and [another] on the left foot.
"O Janārdana, may the sin committed by my deluded mind throughout thousands of births be destroyed quickly through the gift of this golden vessel."
And one should place this golden vessel filled with unbroken grains in the center.
Gold, pearls, coral, pomegranate, citron,
auspicious leaves, and *śṛṅgāṭaka* fruits should be placed on the ears and the hooves.
Having done this according to what was stated, the learned best of the twice-born who maintains the sacred fires and knows the rules for accepting gifts [should accept] all the vegetables and fruits.
Having bathed, clothed in a pair of garments, and adorned according to his means,
O Lord of the Earth, the acceptance of the gift is prescribed for him at the tail-end of the bull.
One should give [this] with a golden navel, saying, "May the Bull-bannered Lord be pleased."
This is the formula for giving here.

"Oṃ! Today, [I, the donor], for the sake of [the recipient] of such-and-such lineage (gotra), and so forth—this black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), which rests upon a woolen blanket spread over *kuśa* grass; which is covered by a pair of garments over a heap of sesame seeds; which has golden horns, silver hooves, silver teeth, and a pearl-ornamented tail-tip; which has a golden navel and is adorned with the five gems; which is accompanied by perfumes and flowers; which is provided with four vessels filled with ghee, milk, curd, and honey situated in the four directions; and which is together with a bronze bowl—this [skin], whose deity is Śiva, I bestow upon you, [named] So-and-so, who desires such-and-such, saying: 'It is yours, not mine. Today, [I, the donor], for the sake of [the recipient] of such-and-such lineage, and so forth—for the purpose of establishing the gift of this black antelope skin—I bestow this gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon you, saying: 'It is yours, not mine.'"
According to this procedure, one should duly offer a black antelope;
for that twice-born man, O King, must not be touched, as he is equal to a sacrificial post on a funeral pyre.
At the time of the ancestral rite (śrāddha), one should avoid [the donor] from afar while giving;
having sent that Brahmin away from one's own house, one should perform the ritual bath within the sacred circle (maṇḍala).
Having taken that garment together with the jar, it should be cast away at a crossroads.
"Unwashed" means not yet worn and not yet washed; "vītaḥ" means one who has put on [the garment]. As for the number of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), it is stated in the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:
"Endowed with a hundred *niṣkas*, or even half of that, or again half of that."
Therefore, one should not give less than this, for a greater fruit has been earned.
The skin of the black antelope should be given as the best quality for one hundred [coins], the middling for half of that,
and the lowest for half of that again.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth for the sake of avoiding the loss of its fruit.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"O best of kings, even the gods are not able to describe the satisfaction that arises from this [rite]; nevertheless, listen as I speak of it in brief."
A human being obtains the fruit of a gift of the entire earth;
like a bird, he travels through all the worlds, moving according to his will.
One who is summoned reaches heaven along with his kinsmen without a doubt; there shall be no death of father or son, nor separation from one's wife.
And he shall never, anywhere in this world, suffer the loss of wealth or country.
Having given the skin of a black antelope to a composed and eminent brahmin,
one will not grieve over this death as it has been described.
One attains that desired fruit of the mind.
In the section on the Vaiṣṇava path,
the Kālikā Purāṇa states: "Those who, having offered oblations into the fire upon a plate of gold and the like, present it [to the deity]..."
It should be accompanied by one drona measure of sesame seeds and wrapped in a pair of garments.
Then, having covered half, or a quarter, or even a half-pala of gold as the measure of wealth,
one should clothe the twice-born with a pair of fine garments or another cloth.
Having placed another piece of gold along with water and sesame seeds into his hand,
he should then give a black antelope skin accompanied by a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds.
Having given [the gift], one should feed [the recipient] there, and having bowed, one should dismiss him;
likewise during the solstices, the equinoxes, and the eclipses of the moon and sun.
Or those who, at the beginning of a Yuga, bestow [the gift] upon a twice-born according to the prescribed rite—
they too, having attained that state, shall enjoy a tenth part of the lifespan of Brahmā.
Endowed with the qualities of arts and beauty, they sport with various enjoyments;
and by this procedure, one becomes a bestower of ten *droṇas*.
He who offers a jar filled with water and adorned with a golden lotus rejoices in that supreme city for as long as the world of Brahmā endures.
Having honored him with a pair of garments, he too shall certainly go [to that state].
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Those who give a gift of sesame seeds on the full moon day of Vaiśākha,
having covered it completely with a black antelope skin and eight measures of sesame."
With golden horns, silver hooves, and its tail adorned with pearls,
it is provided with a pair of white cloths and decorated with black cloth and other ornaments.
And a set of four iron vessels filled with ghee and honey,
and likewise completely filled with curd and milk thereafter.
To Parīkṣit— a brāhmaṇa who was a vessel of virtues, perfectly composed,
devoted to the agnihotra sacrifice, tranquil, and dedicated to the gods and the twice-born— [he spoke].
To him who bathes daily, who is devoted to purity, and who is adorned by mastery of all the scriptures—
that unsurpassed gift of a black antelope skin is bestowed.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving away the earth, filled with jewels, together with its seven islands, oceans, mountains, forests, and groves— [that fruit one obtains by this].
Having rescued one hundred and one generations from the terrible hell,
he goes to the world of Brahmā in celestial chariots resembling the moon.
Fanned by yak-tail whisks, accompanied by the delightful sounds of songs and flutes,
he was surrounded by apsarases amidst a multitude of banners and standards.
And a cry of victory is raised before him by the gods and kinnaras;
then, having reached the world of Brahmā, he enters this city.
O Sage, it was divine, blazing with all kinds of jewels, adorned with networks of pearls,
richly beautified by pillars of coral, and decorated with gold.
Formerly, there were three billion and eighty million [beings];
he was seated upon a lion throne, draped in white garments.
He indeed dwells there for as long as the time until the dissolution of all things;
yet, if by the turn of time he should ever attain human birth again.
One is born into a family of great lineage, a household of those learned in the four Vedas;
one becomes handsome, strong, long-lived, and pleasing to behold.
He was beloved by all women, as well as a giver and an enjoyer.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a black antelope skin. Now, in the Vahni Purāṇa,
Brahmā said:
By what rite should sesame seeds accompanied by a black antelope skin be given?
Tell me all this, O Lord, if you are pleased with me.
Yama said: During an eclipse, at the solstices, at the transits of the sun, on all festival days (parvan),
at the beginnings and ends of the Yugas, and on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), one should remain self-restrained and pure.
Having observed the fast and having worshipped Keśava, the remover of sins,
especially on the twelfth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight.
Then, having smeared the ground with cow dung to the measure of four cubits,
one should spread cloths upon the earth and place a deerskin there.
Having covered it with rice grains and sesame seeds,
one should place upon it a vessel made of gold or likewise of udumbara wood, filled with honey and clarified butter.
One should cast gold there—either one *pala*, three *palas*, or a hundred;
for giving according to one's ability is indeed the cause of devotion in this matter.
Having covered that [image] with beautiful cloths, one should place it wearing the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) along with its vessel;
likewise, eight jars, accompanied by their vessels and wrapped in cloths, should be placed in the cardinal directions.
"I am black by my deed, O Black One; therefore, accept this black antelope skin together with black sesame seeds. May Kṛṣṇa be well-pleased."
Having given thus to the twice-born, one should afterwards give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
there one should subsist on sesame seeds and then feed the Brāhmaṇas.
Having thus given a black antelope skin, a man, freed from all taint, uplifts his ancestors and goes to heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Having enjoyed there the pleasures accumulated by his fathers and grandfathers,
that man, chosen by them, indeed goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu through its power.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the secondary black antelope skin;
now follows the gift of the primary black antelope skin. Regarding this, Pulastya says:

Now, therefore, we shall describe the procedure for the gift of a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). On the full moon day of Kārttika or Vaiśākha, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), or at the solstices (*ayana*), one should prepare a black deer skin that has its hooves and horns, is free of wounds, and is beautiful. It should have golden horns, silver hooves, and be adorned with a pearl on its tail; it should be fleshy on the inside and hairy on the outside, with the neck facing east. Having smeared the ground with cow dung, having spread out *kutapa* grass upon it, and having spread a woolen cloth (*avika*) over that, one should place the skin upon it with the golden center facing up. Covering it with sesame seeds and fashioning it into that form, one should cover the sesame seeds with a pair of garments. In the four directions, one should place four vessels—of copper, silver, bronze, or gold according to one’s means: filled with milk in the eastern direction, curd in the southern, ghee in the western, and honey in the northern. One should place four heifers that have calved once in the four directions. Having established a well-kindled fire in the western part, swept around it, sprinkled water, and strewn grass around it, one should offer sesame seeds mixed with ghee upon *darbha* grass with the tips pointing east, using the *mahāvyāhṛti* formulas; for a Śūdra, this is done with a simple salutation (*namaskāra*). Then, one should give [the gift] to a learned Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires, who is complete in all limbs, possesses the ritual vessels, is covered by a pair of garments, and is adorned, saying: "I give this black antelope skin, distinguished by all qualities. While touching the navel, the recipient should say: "I accept the black antelope skin for Aditi," and he should cause the formula for acceptance to be recited.

[704] Here, in the passage beginning with "hiraṇyaśṛṅgam" (the golden-horned one), the measurement of the gold and other items should be performed according to one's inclination, without stinginess regarding wealth. "Bahirloma" means having hair on the upper side; "kutapāḥ" refers to *kuśa* grass. "Āvikam" is a woolen cloth or blanket. "Gṛṣṭiḥ" is a cow that has calved once. Regarding the phrase "touching the navel," the meaning is that the giver, while touching the navel made of sesame seeds and adorned with gold and other ornaments, should recite the mantra. "For Aditi, a black antelope skin"—this is the mantra for acceptance. Saying "Asau" (so-and-so), the recipient, pronouncing his own name, should accept it by the tail-end.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O Mādhava, tell me, who am asking you, the rules for the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*),
as well as other gifts that remove all sins."
The Blessed Lord said:
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, on the full moon day of Kārttika, as well as at the equinoxes,
the solstices, or during an eclipse, one should offer the skin of a black antelope.
Having spread darbha grass upon the ground smeared with cow dung,
a person should likewise spread an unbleached woolen cloth there with its fringes pointing toward the east.
Upon that, O King, one should spread out a fleshless black antelope skin,
with its neck pointing eastward, facing north, and likewise provided with horns and hooves.

Having covered it with black sesame seeds according to one's ability and according to the prescribed rite, [one should offer] a bull with golden horns, silver hooves, and adorned with a tail of pearls.
One should cause a golden vessel for milk to be given in the eastern direction;
one should cause a silver vessel for curd to be given in the eastern direction.
One should place a copper vessel filled with clarified butter in the west;
likewise, a conch with a beautiful navel and a fine mouth, filled with milk, in the north.
[705] Likewise, in the four directions, there should be four young cows (gṛṣṭikā) in sequence;
their form, O King of Kings, is that they are covered with sesame seeds and a cloth.
Then, having established the fire according to the ritual rule in that western portion,
one should, with a concentrated mind, offer sesame seeds smeared with ghee while reciting the vyāhṛtis.
Then [he should invite] a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, whose limbs are unimpaired, who is an excellent reciter, an expounder,
a performer of sacrifices, a donor, and one supremely learned in the Smṛtis.
Having honored him with a pair of garments and beautiful ornaments,
one should sprinkle the directions with water mixed with sesame seeds while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.
"O best of the twice-born, I give this black antelope skin together with the head and the heifer that has calved for the first time; please accept it, and may the King of Dharma be pleased."
Touching his navel, he should pour that [water] out, saying, "May such-and-such a person accept it.
Then he should mutter, "Aditi is heaven," beginning with the syllable Om.
The recipient of those two should mutter the *praṇava* mantra at the beginning of the acceptance.

He who gives this path accompanied by cows, land, and gold— here, "accompanied by cows, land, and gold" means that the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of cows, land, and gold according to one's capacity— he shall attain union with Brahman (*sāyujya*), even if he has committed every kind of sinful deed.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a medium-sized black antelope skin.
Now follows the gift of a large black antelope skin, as stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Blessed Lord said:
O giver of honor, I shall now declare that very expiation which was previously prescribed for the shaving of the head in the case of the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
One should smear a pure ground that slopes toward the east with cow dung;
upon it, one should carefully spread out bundles of green *darbha* grass.
In the center, O King, having spread out a black antelope skin— unwetted, firm in all its parts,
complete with its horns, and with its head facing east— along with its neck;
One should first invite a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with the auspicious marks of his lineage;
"invited" (ketita) means summoned.
Having washed his feet, one should give him two black garments.
Golden earrings should be given, as well as a necklace;
golden bracelets should be given, as well as hand ornaments.
Having worshipped with garlands of flowers at the middle of the two horns,
one should place a golden-horned deer facing eastward before a Brāhmaṇa.
One should cover the head of the Brahmin with black sesame seeds;
O King, when the head of the Brahmin has been submerged [in the water], [then one should proceed].
Being composed in mind, one should indeed mutter either the root mantra or the Gāyatrī,
while mentally reflecting upon the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
Having dug up [the earth] to the depth of the navel, one should cover it again with sesame seeds;
once it has been covered, O Brahmin, one should recite the mantra as before.
O King, having again lifted the Brahmin up so that he stands waist-deep,
one should once more cover his head with black sesame seeds.
Having thus immersed himself three times, the donor should give the deer-skin;
having meditated upon the recipient in his mind, he should cast water into the waters.
"May Viśvakarman, the soul of the universe, who assumes all forms, be pleased.
By giving a black antelope skin in this manner, one dispels the sin of killing a Brahmin.
"Even the most wicked person goes to the supreme state where one does not grieve.
Thus has this secret been told to you: the gift that destroys all evil.
But when a Brāhmaṇa has been killed by one who has undergone the tonsure,
he must certainly give a thousand as a sacrificial fee to a Brāhmaṇa after performing the Kṛcchra penance.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājinadānavidhi*).
Now, in connection with the black antelope skin, the gift of a deer is described. Baudhāyana says:
"One should have a deer fashioned from copper weighing ten *palas*."
On each of its two firm, silver peaks, [there is a palace] half that size, and on those, again half that size.
Having placed it upon the rice, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa;
either three āḍhakas or half of that, according to one's own capacity.
Having placed four bronze vessels upon the four sandals,
one should perform a fire offering (homa) there with mantras dedicated to Vāyu as the deity.
O twice-born one, having prepared fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations,
or alternatively twenty-eight, with the mantra for the gift.
O Vāyu, purifier of the world, you move within all beings;
by the gift of this vehicle, destroy my affliction caused by wind.
By merely performing this according to the prescribed ritual as stated,
one is liberated from wind-related diseases and, being free from ailment, enjoys happiness.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a deer.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"By falsely insisting upon [the service of] his guru, a man shall become an apatantrī."
I shall describe its remedy, consisting of gifts together with fire-offerings and other rites.
One should have the excellent vehicle of Vāyu fashioned from gold, weighing one pala, or half of that, or again, half of that.
And having placed it upon rice on a silver vessel adorned with three mountains, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having placed four bronze vessels at the four corners, each containing either three *āḍhakas* or half of that, according to one's capacity;
And there the twice-born should perform a fire-oblation with mantras dedicated to the deity Vāyu,
having offered one hundred and eight oblations of sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and cooked rice.
The preceptor should be one who knows all the scriptures, is firmly established in all branches of knowledge,
understands the application of this ritual of giving, and has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
In the north-eastern direction from the fire, the wise one should place a beautiful water-pot;
nine gems should be offered within it, or, if they are unavailable, gold alone.
One should also cast down earth, as well as yellow pigment (rocanā) and guggulu resin;
and with four Brahmins, one should perform the rite for pacification (śāntikarma).
With the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," with [the substances] such as gold,
with the Pavamāna-anuvāka, and indeed with the mantra "devasya tvā."
Then, having placed [the disciple] upon the seat, four attentive brahmins, taking up a jar wrapped in a cloth, should perform the consecration.
Then, a man wearing white garments and anointed with white unguents should,
together with the preceptor, perform the worship of Hariṇa.
Then, with a hundred recitations of the Vāyu mantra, or else with its specific indicative mantra,
one facing north should present that deer to the recipient facing east.
Then, according to this rite and with devotion, one should offer [the oblation] to the preceptor with this mantra:
"O Vāyu, you move within all beings; you are the purifier of the world."
O Lord Māruta, whatever falsehood was committed by me in a previous birth through the designations of prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna, and so forth— [may it be purified].
For you indeed know all this, just as the Supreme Self does;
by the gift of a vehicle, destroy the lack of a chariot.
And he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his ability to the four Brahmins;
the teacher, however, shall take an unwashed garment that is indeed white.
With that [mantra], the wise one should diligently apply the limbs to his [the deity's] corresponding parts according to their indicative marks,
using the *anuvāka* for the eyes according to their respective marks.
With a handful of darbha tips and also with bunches of darbha grass,
and again with pure, golden-leaved [grass], [one should use] the [mantra] beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
With the Pavamāna-anuvāka, with the verse "āpo asmān," and likewise with other purificatory mantras and Yajus hymns honored by the world;
A man should also feed Brahmins according to his means;
by doing so, he is certainly liberated from the danger of falling.
O Lord, the person who performs this gift during great diseases or other ailments becomes endowed with long life and health, remains in good condition,
and is liberated from those respective defects, becoming free from disease.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a doe.
Now follows the gift of a buffalo-cow. Viśvāmitra says:
O King, [one should give] a buffalo-cow that has good offspring, is rich in milk, and is likewise young.
And having given away a cow together with household utensils on the full moon day of Kārttika, [one obtains the fruit].
One enjoys the same fruit as that obtained by the gift of ten cows;
one attains sons and grandsons and goes to the world of the Sun.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa,
the Blessed One said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe the majesty of the gift of a buffalo-cow."
It is meritorious, purifying, life-prolonging, and bestows all desires and happiness.
During a lunar or solar eclipse, on the auspicious full moon day of Kārttika, likewise at the solstices,
on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, and on the day of the sun's transit (saṅkrānti).
O descendant of Kuru, as soon as wealth and the [right] mind arise,
one who fears the terrors of saṃsāra should immediately give away his queen.
She who has beautiful udders, beautiful hips, beautiful horns, and beautiful hooves;
who has calved for the first time, is young, well-behaved, and free from defects.
