Adorned with golden horns and a tilaka mark, decorated with bells and ornaments,
covered in beautiful red cloth, and provided with a copper milking vessel.
Equipped with a basket of oil-cake, accompanied by gold according to one's means,
and filled with seven kinds of grain, it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
Likewise, it should be given to one who recites the Purāṇas or to one who knows the science of astrology;
it must never be given to one devoid of the Vedas, nor to one who observes the "heron-vow" (hypocrisy).
O King of kings, on an auspicious day, one should give these substances combined together according to the prescribed ritual and with the mantra recited in the Purāṇas.
May she who is the auspicious queen of the world-protectors, Indra and the others,
grant all my desires through the greatness of this gift of a buffalo.
May she, whose son is established in the service of the King of Dharma and who is the mother of Mahiṣāsura, be the granter of boons to me.
The mantra for the gift:
Having circumambulated her, one should give that milch cow to a Brahmin;
the acceptance of her was ordained by the Self-Existent One upon her back.

In this regard, the formula for the gift is as follows: "Om! Today, I, [Name], of such-and-such lineage, etc., give unto you, O Yamadevatā, this buffalo-cow—her first calf, young, with golden horns, a golden tilaka-mark, and golden ornaments, equipped with a bell and a copper milking vessel, provided with a basket of oil-cake, filled with the seven grains, and possessing wooden sandals; for the fulfillment of my desire, [Name]—I bestow her upon you, not for myself. Having spoken thus, he should recite the previously mentioned mantra.
"O you of such-and-such lineage," and so forth; "for the sake of the consecration of this gift of a buffalo, I bestow this gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon you; it is not mine.
Having given thus according to the ritual procedure, one should lead the Brahmin to his home.
Then, one should ask the Brahmins for forgiveness, saying, "May you be well-pleased."
Having bestowed a buffalo upon an eminent brahmin according to this rite,
one attains all desires in this world and in the next.
O King, that woman who gives a buffalo shall become a queen;
likewise, a man shall become a great king, according to the words of Vyāsa.
The Brahmin shall become a performer of sacrifices; the Kṣatriya shall be victorious;
the Vaiśya shall be submissive, possessed of grain and wealth; and the Śūdra shall be endowed with all objects of desire.
Therefore, a man who possesses wealth and desires his own welfare for the sake of his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, should give away a buffalo-cow.
O King, Nārada declared a buffalo to be equal to ten cows;
the wise Vyāsa declared it to be equal to twenty cows, the best of all gifts.
By Sagara, Kakutstha, Dhundhumāra, and Gādhi,
these buffaloes that grant all desires were given to the Brahmins after being consecrated.
The man who always hears the greatness of the gift of a buffalo is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva.

Having given to an eminent brahmin a buffalo that yields abundant milk, which has the hue of a fresh cloud, possesses contented calves, delights with its broad haunches, and is adorned with a golden tilaka;
And he conquers both worlds here in this life—what wonder is there in this?
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a buffalo.
Now follows the gift of a ewe. Regarding this, Kaśyapa says:
"Furthermore, he who should give a pleasing ewe here to a Brāhmaṇa..."
Having reached the world of Agni, he too enjoys most splendid pleasures.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By giving a ewe that destroys all sins, one goes to the supreme station;
by giving a ram, O best of men, one attains the world of Varuṇa."
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa, the Blessed One said:
"Listen, O Pārtha, to the supreme gift that destroys all sins."
By giving which, various kinds of evil immediately go to destruction.
One with golden hair, golden in color, visibly most beautiful,
adorned with a golden tilaka, and decorated with all ornaments.
She was clothed in silk garments, adorned with divine sandalwood paste,
offered divine flowers, and endowed with all mineral pigments.
One should diligently have that [image] fashioned out of a hundred measures of gold, provided with the seven types of grain and likewise adorned with fruits and flowers.
Or one may perform it according to one's ability, but must not practice stinginess regarding wealth;
[this applies] during the solstices, the equinoxes, and on the auspicious occasions of lunar or solar eclipses.
Upon seeing an evil dream, during one's birth star (janmarkṣa), at the waning of a lunar day (tithi),
or whenever wealth arises accompanied by a mind endowed with faith.
At that very moment it should be a time for giving, for life is indeed impermanent;
one should give at a sacred site, in one's home, or wherever the mind finds delight.
There he installed Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, together with Umā;
likewise Brahmā with Gāyatrī, and Śrīdhara accompanied by Śrī.
Having likewise worshipped Ananga together with Rati, as well as the world-protectors and the planets, according to the prescribed ritual with perfumes, flowers, and food offerings;
Viśvakarman describes the form of Umā and Śaṅkara:
"Clad in a garment of skin, four-armed, and holding a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a noose;
marked with ashes, Śaṅkara shall have Gaurī seated upon his left lap."

The form of Brahmā as Gāyatrī is to be seen in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna* described in the *Padmapurāṇa*. The forms of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa are [described] in the *Hemahastirathadāna*; those of Rati and Anaṅga in the *Kalpapādapadāna*; and those of the World-Guardians (*lokapāla*) and the planets (*graha*) in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna* and the various planetary gifts (*grahadāna*), which will be explained later. These should be fashioned out of gold according to one's capacity.
Prior to that, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) on the ground with sesame seeds and clarified butter, having adorned and fully worshipped a peaceful Brahmin with garments.
And when the fire has blazed up, an oblation (homa) should be performed with mantras containing their respective marks;
then, those [offerings] placed in the jar of sesame seeds should be positioned facing toward the salt.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should recite this mantra:
"With my hair, skin, flesh, marrow, and all other constituent parts, I am always [offered]."
Since you have set out for the sake of the world, I therefore pray for your auspiciousness regarding whatever evil deed I have committed through speech, mind, or body.
"May all that [evil] go to destruction through the service of your gift.
Having recited this, one should give it to a Brahmin who has a family.
The statement regarding the gift should be understood as being like the gift of a queen (mahiṣī), with the sole difference that the term "ewe" (meṣī) is used in place of "queen.
Having given [the gift], one should not speak to [the recipient] nor look upon his face;
a Brahmin who accepts such a wicked gift becomes a sinner.
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) that is deficient in wool or lacking in its proper measure should not be given, nor should it be given contrary to the prescribed rule.
A sacrificial fee given deficiently according to the rule brings about suffering and grief.
In former times, this gift was given by Gaurī while she was living in the house of Dakṣa;
by that merit, she obtained a husband who is auspicious and honored by all the gods.
A hundred golden-haired cows were given by Indrāṇī according to the prescribed rites;
she obtained the lord of all the gods and even today rejoices in heaven.
Indeed, having given this kingdom to Nala, he departed for heaven;
thus I have obtained Rukmiṇī as my husband, as well as incomparable good fortune.
By the power of this gift, one obtains sons endowed with great strength;
the childless obtains a son, and the destitute obtains wealth.
Having given gifts that result in beautiful limbs, vast [merit], and likewise great prosperity,
one who constantly hears this unsurpassed ritual manual on giving (dānakalpa) [attains these].
One is liberated from the sins committed during a day and night; there is no doubt about this.

O joy of the Kurus, give with reverence that ewe, which is highly praised for its ability to remove all impurities, and which is always endowed with the essence of minerals and grains when given as a gift; having given her, [attain the highest state].
By which you shine like the sun, having dispelled the darkness of sin.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a ewe.
Now follows the gift of a ram. Regarding this, Baudhāyana states:
"If there should be a dullness of the fire belonging to one who has destroyed the three sacred fires (tretāgni),"
I shall declare its remedy, as it was told by Brahmā in the past.
Furthermore, one should have an excellent, gentle silver vehicle for Agni made with half a *pala*, or half of that, or even half of that again.
The hooves should be made of gold and wrapped in white cloth;
one should offer white garlands, white perfumes, and honey-sweet incense.
Having placed it upon the rice, the wise one should worship it again;
the measure of the rice is declared to be two *droṇas*.
And in the southeastern direction, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter,
and sesame seeds by the preceptor, who is humble and a knower of the meaning of all the scriptures.
And it should be performed by one who is learned in the Rigveda; hear these mantras for that purpose:
the offering of fuel with the mantra beginning "Agnirmūrdhā" is highly praised.
The oblation of clarified butter with the mantra "agne naya" is performed using fire and sesame seeds along with unbroken grains (akṣata);
the installation of the fire shall be carried out with the mantra prescribed in the Mantrādhyāya.
One should place an auspicious water-pot in the north-eastern direction of the fire;
once the rites up to the release of the *praṇītā* vessel have been performed, the ritual bath is prescribed.
Then, one should purify the sick person with the verse beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," the four verses beginning with "hiraṇya," and the Pavamāna-anuvāka.
One should also perform the propitiatory rite (śānti) with the *Śaṃno devīr* hymn;
then, for that officiant who has performed the oblation and is facing east, the sick person should offer a gift along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having worshipped [the deity] according to one's ability, one should give that [gift] along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
for Agni, the bearer of oblations, who is honored by all, is the mouth of the gods.
You are his venerable vehicle, worshipped by the gods including Indra and by the great seers;
it is that which arose from the ripening of my former karma, and which now belongs to me.
Destroy all of that quickly and increase the digestive fire within the stomach.
The mantra for the gift:
"Whoever should thus give this supreme vehicle to Agni to a Brahmin,
that powerful mortal possessing the fire shall live for a hundred years more."
Then, having bathed together with his own kinsmen and the Brahmins, the man should eat.
Thus ends the gift of a ram.
Now, since the ten gifts of cows that follow in sequence have already been mentioned, and following the context of the gift of a ewe, the gift of a goat is commenced. Regarding this, Sumantu said:
"Prajāpati, having performed austerities and having produced offspring with great effort..."
Having designated that son as the sacrificial animal for the sake of the sacrifice, he was prepared for the performance of the rite.
The skin of the black antelope, smooth and from a young animal, is of two kinds;
[it is used] until the completion of sacrifices, sacrificial sessions, and ancestral rites.
That which is ordained by the gods is equal to that; it is called the gift of a goat.
Indeed, Ajāpāla, the protector of the earth, went to heaven through the gifts of goats.
The gift of a goat is recommended during the solstices, at the equinoxes, at the beginning of the Yugas,
during eclipses, on the new moon day, and on the full moon day.
I shall describe its ritual procedure as ordained by Viśvāmitra:
it is endowed with all kinds of jewels and placed upon seven types of grain.
And [he gave] Paśujānakī, adorned with garments, garlands, and ornaments,
who had eyes like diamonds, golden horns, a copper-colored back, and was always ready for milking.
One who is self-restrained should offer water with sesame seeds into the belly [of the image] which has silver feet and is accompanied by its son;
he should perform this like the Godāna rite, using the following mantra.
O goat, fragrant with mantras, gentle, auspicious, and the bringer of perfection in sacrifice—
being thus created, burn away my sin committed throughout hundreds of previous births.
[718] The mantra for the gift: One should thus recite with devotion and pour water into the hand of the twice-born, saying:
"May it be pleasing to Yajñanātha; obeisance indeed to Vāsudeva."
Having thus circumambulated the sun, one should look upon it;
then, recollecting Hari, the person should go to his own home.
Whatever sins were committed in childhood, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
or whatever transgression was committed in youth or the infatuation of old age, even through mere association;
Through the greatness of giving a goat, a man becomes free from sin;
endowed with sons and grandsons, he remains for a very long time possessed of a mind inclined toward virtuous conduct.
In the Mahābhārata:
"By giving a decorated goat, one is glorified in the world of Agni;
by giving a goat according to the prescribed rite, a man attains that very world."
One obtains all desires whatsoever that are established in the mind.
Likewise:
"Having given goats, sheep, and buffaloes to a Brahmin according to his capacity,
he rejoices wherever rivers flowing with ghee and milk exist."

In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "He who gives a camel or even a donkey to a twice-born man, or likewise a goat, a ram, or a *tugara*, according to his ability and accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),"
Having reached Alakā, he rejoices together with the lords of the Yakṣas;
his soul fulfilled by all desires, he obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
Therefore, bestow a goat upon him; then you shall obtain everything, having adorned it according to the ritual with this mantra and according to your own means.
In former times you were created by Brahmā as the supreme purifier;
since the sacrifices arise from what is produced by you, therefore be a bringer of peace.
And the best of the twice-born should indeed receive it upon his back.
The formula for the gift should be understood as being like the formula for the gift of a buffalo.
Having thus bestowed [the gift] upon a Brahmin, one is liberated from all sins;
having obtained the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, one rejoices in the city of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a goat.

Thus [ends the section] in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the venerable Mahādeva, the supreme king of great kings, the sovereign of all faculties, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
The Section on the Gift of the Black Antelope Skin and Other Items within the Chapter on Giving.
[720] Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Now, the gifts to the deities.

In whose sacrifices the foremost of the hosts of gods returned only with great difficulty, having been called away from their children— whom they had set aside after making them somehow limp— with their hearts longing for the enjoyment of incessant embraces with proud celestial women; and who were purified by his deeds that conquered the three worlds.
Having reached their nurse, they are so astonished that they immediately forget their departure for their own home.
Now, by that Hemādri Śūri, whose nature is to benefit the entire world,
the gift of deities is described in due order.
Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:
A man, according to his means, should have a staff made of gold, silver, copper, or even bell-metal; or he may make the staff from the wood of the arka or mūlaka trees.
One should fashion a lotus out of gold, with two eyes made of refined gold;
and one should fashion a rat for it, just as it was fashioned when it was to be given.
One who possesses a grove should fashion for him a sacred thread made of *nāga* fibers;
immediately thereafter, he should honor him with garments, sandalwood, and *aguru*.

To a Brahmin who has performed the fire-oblation, who is peaceful, who knows the meaning of all the scriptures, and who has been honored according to one's own capacity, [one should give] together with gold.
[721] With this mantra, according to the prescribed rite, one should offer it to the one facing south:
"O Vināyaka, O Gaṇeśāna, you who are saluted by all the gods!"
O son of Pārvatī, quickly destroy my abscess.
The mantra for giving:
By means of this act of giving, a person becomes free from disease.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the offering to Vināyaka.
Likewise:
"Indeed, by obstructing the breath of a Brāhmaṇa, a man may become afflicted with epilepsy."
I shall describe its remedy through acts such as giving gifts and performing fire-oblations.
One should fashion a beautiful image of Vināyaka out of gold, weighing one pala, or half of that, or even half of that again.
One should fashion a silver *nāga* as the sacred thread (*upavīta*);
one should fashion the *puṣkara* with a ruby and the hand with gems.
One should fashion the eye of the deity according to half the measure of the Vināyaka;
likewise, various jewels should be applied to its limbs.
One should fashion two beautiful eyes for it out of rubies;
on the day prior, one should construct a firm pavilion with sixteen cloths.
Alternatively, one should diligently construct it with twelve or eight [pillars];
one should also arrange a pedestal that constitutes one-fourth of the pavilion.
At night, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of Vināyaka is also desired;
it should be performed by the preceptor, who is learned in all the scriptures, together with four Brahmins.
For the teacher himself should be one who knows the Dharma, truthful in speech,
pure, of noble birth, not aged, and devoted to the welfare of all living beings.
Having kept a vigil at night, one should offer an oblation at midnight,
consisting of fish and meat, as well as milk-rice.
The preceptor, having become purified and restrained by this mantra,
should offer that all-fulfilling bali-oblation in the eastern direction.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and all the gods;
all the piśācas, ḍākinīs, śākinīs, and deities of travelers.
May the deities of epilepsy, the vetālas, and the nairṛtas likewise bring peace in every way through this offered sacrificial gift.
The mantra for the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna):
Then, at the clear dawn, having bathed, wearing garments with their own hands,
and properly adorned with bracelets, sacred threads, and rings;
One should construct four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the cardinal directions, provided with girdles (mekhalās);
in these, they always perform oblations with their respective mantras.
In the former [rite], the Bahvṛca should perform the offering of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice,
addressing Vināyaka with the mantra beginning "gaṇānāṃ tvā."
Let us know that Tatpuruṣa; let us meditate upon Vakratuṇḍa; may that Dantī inspire us.
The Adhvaryu priest, being composed, should perform the oblation in the southern pit;
or the Chandoga priest may do so in the western one, offering with the mantra dedicated to that deity.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the northern pit for the god Vināyaka,
who is the benefactor of all beings.
To him appointed to the office of Gaṇapati: HŪM PHAṬ SVASTI SVADHĀ NAMAḤ.
Having offered the sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and the oblation of cooked rice, up until the final full-oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
the preceptor, joined by the Brahmins, [performs the rite] for the images.
Having placed [the vessel] upon sesame seeds in the center of the seat, which is beautifully adorned with canopies and the like, one should worship it with perfumes and garlands.
With various kinds of white garments, armlets, bracelets, and so forth;
with the sixteen types of ritual services, and sweetmeats for the food offering.
Just as one would arrange ornaments and so forth for the deity, so too should one arrange them for the Ācārya;
the Ācārya, with supreme devotion, should offer these to Gaṇeśa.
One should likewise have cakes and other such foods prepared for the eaters and others;
having offered these to Pārvatī as well as Maheśvara, the God of gods.
One should indeed personally worship the preceptor with supreme devotion;
likewise, the afflicted person, through devotion, should fully worship Gaṇanāyaka.
A Śūdra, however, should worship silently with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā.
Then, when midday has arrived, [he should offer] the image along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
And with this mantra, that sick person himself, facing east,
should offer [the gift] with great devotion to a Brāhmaṇa seated facing north.
O Vināyaka, remover of the suffering of those who have sought refuge, O Lord of Obstacles! You were proclaimed of old by the gods, who were intent on overcoming all impediments.
Due to the obstruction of the Brahmin’s breath, that transformation which arose in me—
namely epilepsy, intoxication, and so forth— was indeed the ripening of my past karma.
Whether it be dullness, deafness, or a nasal voice—
by the offering of your worship, quickly destroy this disease.
Having thus given an offering to Gaṇapati along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to four Brahmins according to his ability, a mortal shall become happy.
Thus is the ritual procedure for the gift to Vināyaka:
a man, according to his means, [should fashion] an image of Vighna from gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or brass, or even from the wood of the arka or mūlaka trees.
One should fashion a lotus out of gold, with two eyes made of refined gold;
and one should fashion a rat for it, made of gold from a [specific] portion of the foot.
One should fashion a sacred thread (*upavīta*) in the form of a serpent out of gold;
one should place it upon a pair of garments over two *āḍhaka* measures of sesame seeds.
On the ground, in a pure place, with devotion and a restrained mind, the wise man,
having wrapped [the image] in a cloth, should worship that Vināyaka.
One should fumigate with sandalwood, agallochum, and incense, and anoint with saffron;
one should worship the vehicle just as one would the deity itself.
The preceptor, however, should perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds one hundred and eight times,
using the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," and likewise offer oblations of clarified butter in the same sequence.
To him who had performed the fire-oblation, who was tranquil, self-restrained,
proficient in the treatises on dharma, and a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
One should arrange all of this for one who is well-conducted, highly learned, and facing the south,
on the fourth day of the bright fortnight.
One who is self-restrained and pure should honor that teacher with a garment,
both as a result of the ripening of past actions and by virtue of the actions performed in this life.

Dropsy, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, and stones, as well as whatever diseases of the belly there may be—those are quickly destroyed by giving gifts and giving gifts; of this there is no doubt.
Endowed with supreme devotion, one should perform this according to the rule by means of this mantra:
"O Vināyaka, O Gaṇeśāna, you who are saluted by all the gods!"
O son of Pārvatī, pacify my abdominal disease—
whether it be a tumor, splenic enlargement, or a stone-like growth, whatever collection of ailments arises in the abdomen.
O Lord, O Son of Maheśāna, by means of this great gift endowed with devotion and performed without hesitation, quickly destroy the obstacles of your devotee.
The mantra for the gift:
"In this manner, one should perform the gift to Gaṇapati, which brings liberation from disease.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the gift to Vighneśa.
Now, the gift of Sarasvatī. In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"A man who has committed an offense against the speech of his guru shall become a person with stammering speech;
I shall describe for him the remedy through a gift as spoken by the sages."
Furthermore, one should fashion an image of Sarasvatī with four arms, using either a pala, half of that, or half of that again [in weight].
She holds the gesture of granting boons (varada) and a rosary (akṣasūtra) in her right hands,
and carries a book and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in her left hands, seated upon a swan (haṃsa).
The seat should be made of very bright silver or of counterfeit gold;
and one should fashion an excellent lotus-seat out of gold.
And having placed upon him the supreme Goddess Vāgīśvarī, her limbs adorned with strings of pearls and clothed in white garments; [726]
One should worship with the Vāgīśvara mantra using white rice,
white flowers, and white perfumes, having consecrated them according to the prescribed ritual.
A Brahmin who is learned in all the scriptures, skillful, esteemed by all,
and proficient in the practice of mantras— through him one should have the fire-oblation performed.
One should offer milk-rice one hundred and eight times, as well as oblations made of śāli rice;
likewise, one should also offer sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
Or the mantra "sarasvatī predam ava" is desired;
once the dismissal of Brahman has been performed, one should present that [conch] to the teacher.
Having properly honored the Brahmin according to the rules with this mantra, while facing north, for one facing east, preceded by the offering of garments and ornaments.
She who is the Goddess in the mouth of Brahmā is that supreme Vāgīśvarī,
worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, and adored by all.
May she be satisfied by this supreme gift of speech that I have given—
namely, my faltering speech resulting from having committed an offense against the words of my guru.
Exhaust all of that quickly, for you are the divine power of Brahma, the purifier of the world.
Likewise is the mantra for giving:
having obtained permission from that brahmin, the man should eat himself.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of Sarasvatī.
Likewise: "One who destroys the musical notes and steals speech is born mute."
O best of men, I shall describe its remedy through gifts and fire-offerings.
Alternatively, one should fashion an auspicious image out of very pure silver, using half that amount, or half of that again, or even half of that once more.
One should [visualize] Sarasvatī with four hands, holding a noose, a goad, and a water-pot,
likewise with one hand in the gesture of fearlessness, and draped in white garments.
One should worship with white garlands and white perfumes using the root mantra;
and there one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) abounding in sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice.
And the mantra "Sarasvatī predam ava" is prescribed;
the teacher should be learned in all scriptures, of good conduct, and with his senses restrained.
One who knows the Dharma, speaks the truth, is intelligent, and likewise possesses eloquence—
one endowed with such characteristics is desired as a teacher in all matters.
Having prostrated and brought [the deity] home, one should worship with devotion;
and having thus performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should worship Sarasvatī.
With the mantra "Obeisance to Sarasvatī," according to its specific gender,
he should give that goddess, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), to the one who has performed the oblation.
With this mantra, according to the prescribed rule, one facing north [should offer] to [the deity] facing east:
"O gentle goddess, highly fortunate one, who is saluted by all the gods!"
O you who sit upon the lotus throne and remove the suffering of all living beings,
dispel my dullness of wisdom caused by the impairment of my voice.
The mantra for the offering:
Having thus diligently offered the natural form of Sarasvatī,
one is liberated from the dullness of wisdom born from injury to the vocal tones.
This gift brings about wisdom for all, and especially so;
furthermore, this specific excellence that has been proclaimed shall serve as the commencement of the recitation.
Having first performed this offering, one should commence the recitation;
one should present milk-rice as the food offering and consume it oneself.
On the preceding day, one should undertake the practice only after having observed the fast;
and purification of the body must be performed until it becomes free from salt.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of another Sarasvatī. Now follows the gift of the bell (*ghaṇṭādāna*). In the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*:
"He who practices the study of the Vedas without being authorized by his teacher..."
But that man who is devoid of wisdom is born again in the cycle of existence.
I shall describe the remedy for that: one should have a beautiful, sturdy bell made of pure bronze, adorned with auspicious lines.
One should construct the palace with twenty or thirty [pillars], or half of that;
it should have a beautiful-sounding end and be very smooth, and one should wash it with the five products of the cow.
One should place them, wrapped in white cloth, upon rice;
the quantity of rice shall be exactly three *droṇas*.
Alternatively, half of that measure may be taken according to one's own capacity.
The preceptor should be a knower of all scriptures and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Skilled in the treatises on dharma, of virtuous conduct, and with senses fully restrained,
he went to the house himself, having been summoned with supreme devotion.

With that very [bell], one should perform the worship according to the injunctions of the scriptures, using the sixteen services with devotion and this mantra: [729] One should cause the worship of the bell to be performed with the sixteen services as enjoined by the scriptures, with devotion and with this mantra.
One should invoke Vāgīśā, the supreme goddess, into the bell:
"Come, come, O Goddess, Sovereign of All; take up your residence within this bell."
You are the benefactor of all sentient beings, O Seal of Wisdom, beyond the reach of falling.
The invocation mantra:
Having thus invoked her, one should worship that bell and the Brahmin as well;
having worshipped the bell with the *brahmayajñāna* mantra, one should likewise worship the garment.
Then, having installed [the deity] with devotion according to the path taught in the Mantrādhyāya,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with diligence using sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), and sesame seeds (tila).
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as a food offering (naivedya) to the Goddess and likewise to Brahmā;
the mantra "Sarasvati, please accept this" is approved for all instances.
To that one who has offered the oblation and has been worshipped, the sick person— purified and facing the east— should duly give that bell while reciting this mantra.
Furthermore, for one seated facing north, [the recitation] is performed with devotion;
however, that study of the Veda which is done with disrespect toward the guru [is likewise ineffective].
O Sarasvatī, Mother of the World, you who remove the world’s dullness,
you are the manifest consort of Brahmā, praised by Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the other gods.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, remove this dullness born of my lack of study;
you, O Brahmāṇī, purifier of the world, are pleased by the gift of the bell.
Having thus given the gift and having asked that teacher for forgiveness, [he should proceed].
One should give to others according to one's ability, as well as food to Brāhmaṇas;
thereafter, having bathed together with one's own kinsmen, the man should eat.
Thus, even one who makes such a gift while being devoid of wisdom or dull-witted,
becomes a wise and non-dull person, like Vākpati;
and a flow of eloquence arises within him, as if he were personally causing the Gaṅgā to descend.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the bell.
Now follows the gift of Lakṣmī, as stated in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"I shall proclaim the gift of Lakṣmī, which greatly increases sovereignty."
This has been specifically proclaimed by Śiva for the destruction of wounds such as those caused by spider venom.
Having constructed the previously described pavilion, one should fashion the incomparable Śrīdevī out of gold according to the prescribed rite upon the mandala on the sacrificial altar.
Or again, with a thousand, half of that, half of that again,
or even with one hundred and eight [beads], she is endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
One should place Lakṣmī, adorned with all ornaments, within the mandala;
then, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to her right, one should worship Viṣṇu.

Regarding the phrase "as previously stated," it should be understood that the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), mandala, altar (*vedikā*), canopy (*vitāna*), and so forth, is to be performed according to the *Tulāpuruṣa* rite prescribed in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*. Furthermore, the count of one thousand and so on mentioned here is to be fulfilled in *niṣkas*, since it is observed that in the gifts prescribed in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*, transactions are generally conducted using those very coins.
The characteristics of Lakṣmī have been described in the section on the gift of the *Kalpapādapa* (Wish-Fulfilling Tree):
"Having worshipped the Goddess of the Gods according to the ritual with the *Śrīsūkta*..."
One should worship Viṣṇu, the teacher of the universe, Hari, with the Viṣṇugāyatrī mantra.
Having propitiated [the deity] according to the prescribed rule, one should first begin the fire-oblation (*homa*).
With kindled fuel according to the ritual injunction, one should perform the offering of clarified butter (*ājya-huti*).
An excellent Brahmin should offer the oblations separately one hundred and eight times for each.

The *Śrīsūkta* begins with "hiraṇyavarṇāṃ hariṇīm" and so forth. The *Viṣṇugāyatrī*, however, is stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* itself: "We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva; may that Viṣṇu impel us. Having placed Lakṣmī within the previously mentioned maṇḍala, one should worship the deity Viṣṇu on an altar to the south of her using the *Gāyatrī* dedicated to Viṣṇu. Then, one should worship Śrī with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) in due order using the fifteen-verse *Śrīsūkta*. Once she has been worshipped, she becomes "accomplished" (*siddha*), and thus she is Siddhilakṣmī. But when there is a specific desire (*kāmita*):
One should worship Lakṣmī with the Śrī-mantra, or otherwise honor her with the Śrī-sūkta;
the worship of Śiva and the fire-oblation (homa) are performed as before, with particular emphasis.
"Or the Guru should perform a single *homam* according to the previously mentioned procedure;
having worshipped Śrī with a thousand jars and other offerings, he should bestow prosperity.
And the *homam* is performed with the *Śrīsūkta* itself, after having summoned the patron to a place to the east of her [the image].
Therefore, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground before that Goddess;
having bowed, one should worship Viṣṇu situated there and Śiva as before.
The phrase "as before" means as described in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* regarding the *tulāpuruṣa* rite.
A twentieth part of that [fee] is indeed proclaimed as the priestly fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
a tenth part of that should be given to the others according to their merit.
Then one should feed those Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
according to a portion equal to one-twentieth of that image of Lakṣmī.

One should give other wealth as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Guru in the measure of a tenth part, and to each of the other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), as well as to the door-reciters, half of that amount for the priests. As it is stated in the Vātula:
"Having bowed to Lakṣmī, one should present [the fee] to learned scholars and those well-versed in the Vedas (*śrotriya*);
from that, however, the sacrificial fee for the Preceptor (*deśika*) shall indeed be a twentieth part."
The best among the knowers of the Vedas, having performed the recitation, should give one-tenth of that as a fee;
likewise, he should cause the reciters of the *puṇyāha* to be given what was previously mentioned.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of Lakṣmī.
Now follows the gift of Nārāyaṇa, as proclaimed by Brahmā: A mortal who causes obstacles to a sacrifice is born with an enlargement of the intestines (*antravṛddhi*).
I shall describe its remedy through rites such as giving gifts and performing fire-oblations.
One should fashion an auspicious golden image of Nārāyaṇa using two vyāvahārika niṣkas, or one, or even half of that.
The characteristics of Nārāyaṇa have been described in the context of the gift of a golden elephant-chariot:
having washed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should place it upon saffron;
having wrapped it in a white cloth, one should worship it with perfumes and garlands.
The Vaiṣṇava preceptor, pure and well-versed in the true meaning of all scriptures, should be firmly established in the knowledge of Brahman and perform the rites with the sixteen services.

And one should perform the fire sacrifice there in the southeastern direction according to the scriptures, using sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and sesame seeds; indeed, the fuel-stick is offered with the root mantra.
One should offer clarified butter with the mantra "Nārāyaṇāya" and sesame seeds with the *vyāhṛtis*;
likewise, the sick person should worship the god Nārāyaṇa, who is free from disease.
The food offering (naivedya) and the sacrificial porridge (caru) are prescribed according to the rule by means of the root mantra (mūlamantra).
The root mantra is proclaimed to be the name ending with "namaḥ" and preceded by the syllable "oṃ."
Then, facing north, one should duly present that image to a person facing east,
endowed with supreme devotion, using this mantra according to the prescribed rule.
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace!
Whatever [fault] was indeed committed by me due to obstacles to sacrifice and other rites in a previous birth—
O Lord of the World, whose hand holds the discus and who wields the mace, being gratified by this gift, quickly pacify the great disease of intestinal hernia.
The mantra for the gift:
Having thus given [the gift] to that deity and having asked the Brahmin for forgiveness, one should then provide a meal for the Brahmins;
having bathed, one should eat together with one's kinsmen.
By acting thus, a man on earth attains freedom from disease;
endowed with health, he always prospers in purity and happiness for a long time.
Thus ends the ritual for the gift of the image of Nārāyaṇa.
Now follows the gift of the image of Gopāla. Likewise:
blindness at night occurs for him who [damages] the two eyes of cows.
He performs the hurling of the trident; I shall describe the expiation for that.
One should fashion an image of Viṣṇu in his glorious cowherd attire, intent upon playing the flute, out of devotion and according to one's capacity, using gold.
Having caused an image to be made— possessing two arms, standing upright, adorned with a crest of peacock feathers, and of auspicious form— one should wash it with pure water.
Then, having wrapped it in cloth, one should worship it with perfumes and garlands;
having placed it upon rice, one should do so oneself according to one's means.
The preceptor, who is learned in all the scriptures and has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, should perform the worship of the deity with devotion using the root mantra.
Having brought one who is thus qualified, he should perform worship for him and also carry out a fire-oblation with sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
The installation of the fire should be performed according to the sequence of the mantras "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," "pratadviṣṇuḥ," and "viṣṇor nukam," following the method taught in the section on mantras.
Having performed [the rite] up to the sublime liberation, one should worship the deity;
one should offer the entire oblation as a food-offering to the deity on all sides.
Having heard this, the sick person— self-controlled and pure— should perform oblations one hundred and eight times with the root mantra, facing the east.
Wearing white garments and adorned with white perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
he, facing north, should give those [gifts] along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to one facing east.
Having prostrated according to the rule with this mantra and with supreme devotion, |||
O Govinda, Lord of the beloved of the cowherd women,
slayer of the demon Kaṃsa, worshipped by the king of the gods, sole uprooter of the preeminent mountain Govardhana!
She is the protector of the entire host of cows.
By the sin born of the total obstruction of the eyes of those who wander, may this blindness of mine be destroyed;
through your gift, may my form become truly radiant.
May this bring about night-blindness.
The mantra for the gift:
Having thus performed this remedy for one wearing the guise of a cowherd, he indeed becomes happy at that very moment; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the Gopāla image. Now follows the gift of Varāha, according to the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall relate the gift of the primordial Boar,
which was formerly proclaimed by me upon the earth while I assumed the form of the Boar.
It is meritorious, purifying, and life-prolonging; it is the most excellent among all gifts, the destroyer of the stains of great sins and other evils, and is honored by the best of sages.
One should give gifts during the transit of the sun, during an eclipse, on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī),
at sacrifices, festivals, and weddings, or upon seeing an evil dream or a portentous marvel.
Or rather, when wealth arises accompanied by a mind endowed with faith,
that very moment should be his time for practice, since life is uncertain.
In sacred fords such as Kurukṣetra, in rivers such as the Gaṅgā,
or likewise in a cow-pen, a temple, or even in a pleasant courtyard of one's home.
It should be given according to the ancient rite to a Brahmin who has a family,
who is free from physical defects, who is of virtuous conduct, and who is a reciter of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
The proper place, time, and recipient have been correctly described by me to you;
now hear the supreme, meritorious rite of giving, which removes all sins.
One should smear with cow dung a ground that slopes toward the northeast,
and having strewn it with kuśa grass on its side, one should consecrate it with the syllable *praṇava*.
Above those, one should fashion a boar out of sesame seeds,
using four *droṇas* or, alternatively, half of that amount.
One may also fashion it with an āḍhaka of gold, but one must not practice stinginess regarding the wealth spent.
The two forearms should be made of gold, equipped with the discus and the mace.
One should have a silver tusk fashioned, adorned with rubies;
one should place a conch shell at the side and a golden garland of forest flowers.
The wise man should likewise have the two feet made of silver with flowers,
and he should have the auspicious earth depicted as clinging to the tips of the fangs made of gold.
Endowed with the essence of all grains, her form adorned with garments and ornaments.

The characteristics of the *droṇa* and other measures have been stated in the *Paribhāṣā*. The characteristics of the earth (*pṛthvī*) should be consulted in the section on the gift of land (*dharādāna*).

Having covered the Lord of Gods, Varāha, who grants all desires, with cloths, and having fashioned a line of hair (*romarājī*) with *kuśa* grass, one should then worship him with perfumes and flowers.
A sacrifice to the nine planets (navagrahamakha) should be performed, and an oblation with sesame seeds is prescribed for this occasion;
having thus installed [the deity] according to the rules, one should then recite the hymn of praise.
O Boar, crush, crush all remaining evils and the fruits of every sin, O you with great tusks and radiant golden earrings!
Salutations to the one who holds the conch, discus, and sword in his hands; to the destroyer of Hiraṇyākṣa;
to the Lord of the Earth raised up by his tusks; and to the embodiment of the three Vedas.
Having recited this and paid homage, and having performed the circumambulation three times,
he should then give that [image], adorned with ornaments, to a Brāhmaṇa.
And the supreme sages have declared that the acceptance of this gift consists in touching his feet;
having thus given the boar along with a sacrificial fee according to this rite.
Then, having honored the preceptor and prostrated before him, one should ask for his forgiveness;
O Lord of the Earth, having thus given the Varāha image which grants all desires.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving to the god Janārdana, just as the goddess Vasundharā was uplifted by the Boar; [that same fruit one obtains].
Likewise, having uplifted one's family, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
This gift is common to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, and the Śūdra people, as well as to Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava yogins.
Having assumed the form of a man-lion for the sake of a brahmin learned in the Vedas,
and having given him sesame seeds, gold, and fine garments,
he rescued his ancestors along with their wives and friends.
He attains the realm of Viṣṇu, which is frequented by gods and Siddhas.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of Varāha. Now follows the gift of Narasiṃha, according to the Kālikā Purāṇa.
Then, having fashioned a golden image of the four-armed, all-pervading Lord Nṛsiṃha,
one should install it in a copper vessel and provide silver tusks.
The two eyes were made of ruby, the nails likewise of coral;
the region of the eyebrows was of topaz, and both earrings were of diamond.
Regarding the form of Nṛsiṃha, according to the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"The Lord Viṣṇu should be fashioned bearing the body of a man-lion,
with thick shoulders, hips, and neck, a slender waist, and a lean belly."
The lion-throne is the human body, clothed in blue garments and endowed with radiance;
it stands in the ālīḍha posture and is adorned with all ornaments.
With a face surrounded by garlands of flames and a circle of blazing manes,
he tore open the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu with his exceedingly sharp claws.
"Hiraṇyakaśipu should likewise be made with knees reaching up to the deity;
and the deity, adorned with the conch and discus, should have two half-arms. Thus it is said.
One should likewise cause a vigil to be observed there with perfumes, flowers, and incense.
The royal road is of lapis lazuli, and the summit is of sapphire.
Having fashioned this beautiful form, the wise one should fill that vessel with honey mixed with sugar-candy,
and then install the deity therein once more.
One should seat [the deity], covered with a pair of garments, upon a throne;
the wise one should then prepare an excellent food offering consisting of various kinds of edibles.
One should worship it, joined with a canopy above and adorned with garlands of flowers;
likewise, having performed the vigil, one should honor it with perfumes, flowers, and incense.
Having performed all this, one should offer it to Hari as before;
whatever was previously specified, one should perform all of that here as well.

"Previously specified" refers to worship with the Vaiṣṇava mantra, the offering of one hundred and eight oblations of sesame and clarified butter with the root mantra, and the gift of food along with a sacrificial fee to twelve Brahmins.
By properly performing this rite on either the twelfth day (dvādaśī) coinciding with the full moon of Kārttika or that of Vaiśākha, one certainly attains that supreme state.
Whether in the forest, in battle, or surrounded by thieves and beasts of prey,
no fear arises for him who performs this once.
Having torn away the terrible arrows from the bow, he bestows wealth, long life, progeny, beauty, good fortune, and the fulfillment of one's desires.
Whatever merit arises from the gift of the form of Nṛsiṃha,
by that embodied beings, having attained the station of Viṣṇu, sport there.
Having heard this great merit, one is liberated from all sins;
wealth and lifespan shall increase, especially for a disciple. One should give offerings to the disciple according to one's ability for the sake of one's own prosperity.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of Nṛsiṃha.
Now follows the gift of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. Regarding this, Baudhāyana states:
"One should fashion the form of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa out of gold."
[740] The form of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is described in the Kāmika: "One should fashion the God of gods, four-armed and seated upon a lotus throne, using one pala, or half of that, or again half of that."
One should place a lotus in the lower right hand and a conch in the upper right hand;
there should be a discus in the upper left hand, while the other hand rests upon the back of Lakṣmī.
"Lakṣmī, with a jewel-vessel in her hand, should be seated on the left lap; and the right arm of the Goddess should rest upon the back of the Discus-wielder. Thus it is said.
One should fashion Garuḍa, the vehicle of the God of gods, out of silver.
His wings were made of gold, and his beak was likewise golden.
Having clothed the pair, who are the very essence of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, with most beautiful garments with great eagerness, one should worship them with flowers.
Then, having summoned a brahmin who was serene, charming, well-behaved, and endowed with auspicious marks, [he saw him] seated upon a Garuda.
One who possesses proper conduct, knows the Dharma, has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
abstains from accepting gifts, and abides on the path of the Śruti and Smṛti.
Having personally brought [the image] with devotion, one should worship it with garments and earrings,
with saffron, agallochum, and camphor, as well as with a sacred thread and a ring.
One should perform the fire-oblation there according to the previously mentioned procedure;
with this mantra, one should offer that which is honored by all the worlds.
O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Sovereign of the Son of Devakī, O You who recline upon the Ocean of Milk, O You who are beyond the reach of words—
O Govinda, O Dāmodara, [cure] the vāta-rakta!
Destroy them quickly, O you who have exhausted the host of enemies!
The mantra for the gift:
By thus giving an image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa with great devotion, one becomes healthy and happy forever; there is no doubt about this.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa image.
Now follows the gift of Garuḍa. In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"A wise person should have a Garuḍa fashioned, either of gold or even of silver."
Or with copper, O Nārada, weighing one pala, or according to one's own capacity.
One should fashion the nose out of gold, and likewise, one should fashion the two eyes.

The characteristics of the Garuḍa image should be consulted in the section on gifts according to lunar days (*tithidāna-prakaraṇa*), specifically in the *Gāruḍa-dāna* prescribed for the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*).
It should be wrapped in a white cloth and placed upon a copper vessel,
[anointed] with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and especially adorned with white garlands.
One should worship the one named Garuḍa with supreme devotion using the Gāyatrī mantra,
and likewise perform a fire sacrifice (homa) right there with sacrificial fuel sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
The Brāhmaṇa was skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures, possessed of a stainless soul,
a devotee of Viṣṇu, righteous, peaceful, of good conduct, and with his senses fully controlled.

We know that Puruṣa; we meditate upon the King of Birds. May that Suparṇa inspire us. We know that Puruṣa; we meditate upon the one with the speed of the wind. May that churner of nectar inspire us. We know that Puruṣa; we meditate upon the son of Vinatā. May that Tārkṣya inspire us.
These are the mantras for the fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, respectively;
thereafter, [the officiant] shall wear white garments and be anointed with white perfumes.
The sacrificer himself, pure and with a restrained mind,
should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa with devotion, while remembering Nārāyaṇa in his heart.
Having worshipped with this mantra and with garments and other offerings according to one's ability:
"O King of Birds, Lord of Avians, Son of Suparṇī, O Master!"
Whatever was done by me in a previous birth— namely, the stealing of divine property and the consumption of snakes, gems, and pearls— it is because of that which this has been done to me.
"O vehicle of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, quickly destroy all [sins] of mine;
then, having become free from stain, a man becomes free from disease."
Since this deformity has indeed arisen from sins committed over seven lifetimes,
one should devoutly feed Brahmins according to one's own capacity, especially so.
Thus ends the procedure for the offering to Garuḍa.
Now Vṛddhagautama says:
"One who steals food becomes afflicted with desire; I shall declare the expiation for that."
And one should fashion the supreme vehicle of Viṣṇu from two śatamānas.
On the two wings, there are two pearls made of extremely pure gold;
likewise, on the nose is a diamond, and the upper garment is silver.
Having done this, one should place Garuḍa upon a vessel of ghee,
wrap him in a white cloth, and worship him with white garlands.
A Vaiṣṇava who knows the true meaning of all the scriptures and recites the Dharma should be honored with devotion by the patron according to his capacity.
Likewise, one should honor the twice-born with the sixteen services;
and the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed on an auspicious sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the south-eastern direction.

There, with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds—and indeed with *palāśa* fuel-sticks as well—the *mantra* is the *Garuḍagāyatrī*; the fuel-stick and the clarified butter are thus proclaimed. An oblation of sesame seeds should be performed with the *vyāhṛtis*, and one should sacrifice to *Sviṣṭakṛt*.
The *Garuḍagāyatrī* has been previously mentioned.
One should place a flawless water-pot wrapped in a white cloth;
one should then deposit within it the nine gems, as well as earth and yellow pigment (*rocanā*).
From a stable for horses, from a stable for elephants, from an anthill, from a confluence, and from a lake—
one should obtain the five barks and sprouts, and fill them with water from sacred bathing sites (tīrtha).
With those [mantras], one should perform the consecration in sequence with the verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*,
and indeed with the verse *hiraṇyavarṇā* and the *pavamāna*.
Then, having bathed and become pure, the sick person, filled with joy, should present the supreme vehicle of Viṣṇu, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), to one facing the east.
Facing north, one should indeed offer [the gift] to the preceptor according to the rule with this mantra:
"O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, supreme bliss, protector of the world!"
Whatever sin of stealing devotees' offerings was committed by me in a previous birth, it is because of that that I have obtained this very form of deformity, which is indeed most difficult to endure.
O Lord Kṛṣṇa, you are indeed the protector of the worlds; by the gift of this vehicle of yours, quickly destroy this realm of desire for me.
The mantra for the gift:
Having thus performed the gift of the Garuḍa, a mortal shall become happy;
and having fed the preceptor and prostrated before him, one should dismiss him.
Thus ends the procedure for the secondary Garuḍa-dāna.
Now, in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Indeed, eye-pain arises due to the obstruction [of merit] from a previous birth."
I shall perform a sacrifice as a remedy for that, as was spoken by Brahmā in the past.
One should have a Garuḍa, the vehicle of Viṣṇu, fashioned from gold;
likewise, its two very broad wings should be made of silver and adorned with jewels.
One should fashion a pair of eyes from two rubies,
and one should provide golden anklets for the feet adorned with two gems.
One should place a golden neck-ornament (graiveyaka) upon the neck;
one should fashion the nose with diamond and lapis lazuli set above a pearl.
Having adorned the Lord of Mountains with various kinds of garments and decorated him so that he possesses an auspicious appearance, one should place him before Viṣṇu for the sake of his pleasure.

The most excellent Brāhmaṇa— skilled in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and firmly established in the knowledge of Brahman— should worship with perfumes, flowers, and unhusked grains scattered in the prescribed manner.
And there, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with auspicious mantras expressive of that [deity],
or else with the Garuḍa-gāyatrī, using sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and so forth.
The installation of the fire must be performed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra.
The Garuḍa-gāyatrī has been shown in the context of the first offering to Garuḍa.
The Puṇyāha-vācana (declaration of an auspicious day) should be performed by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.

Having worshipped him with devotion according to the rules, with armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments, one should, being attentive, give [the gift] to that priest who has offered the oblation for the sake of pleasing Śauri.
With this mantra, according to the prescribed rite, one afflicted with eye disease [should offer] facing the east:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, Beloved of Lakṣmī, Supreme beyond the supreme!"
O Lord of the World, Nārāyaṇa, who pervades the universe, you were pleased by the gift of a vehicle and [thus cured] the eye disease born from the ripening of karma.
Whether it be *puṣpa*, *paṭala*, or *vātarakta*, or blood disorders,
night-blindness (*naktāndhya*), or other conditions such as *budbuda* and the like.
The mantra for the gift:
Then, O best of Brahmins, having dismissed [the deities] along with his remaining beloved kinsmen,
and having bathed and fed the Brahmins, a person becomes happy.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the image of Garuḍa. Now follows the gift of Umā and Maheśvara. Baudhāyana says:
"He who injures the limbs of a Brāhmaṇa shall indeed become afflicted with the disease of ringworm (dadru)."
I shall describe its pacification; one should have it fashioned out of gold.
Or again, with half of that, or half of that, or half of that half,
one may fashion the form of Umāmaheśvara presided over by the bull.
The wise artist should depict Umā as either four-armed or two-armed;
in her two right hands, she should hold a rosary and a trident.
One hand is placed upon the back of the Goddess, while the other bestows boons;
the Goddess rests on his left lap, with one hand placed upon the back of Śiva.
And here, a bull made of silver should be fashioned, equipped with bells and other ornaments;
however, for one who acts with stinginess regarding wealth according to their own capacity, it shall be fruitless.
There too, having placed the Lord of Gods together with Umā,
one should worship the Master with garments, garlands, and likewise with perfumes, using the root mantra at the end.
Then, having summoned a brahmin who was poor yet learned in the Dharma,
endowed with Vedic learning and right conduct, peaceful, and a knower of the Self;
One should devoutly perform worship for him with garments and finger-rings,
and one should also have a fire-oblation performed with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
And the mantra is the Rudra-gāyatrī; this is the settled conclusion for all cases.
The Rudra-gāyatrī is found in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"We know the Lord of All; we meditate upon the one who holds a trident in his hand; may that Rudra inspire us.
Alternatively, the wise man should offer fuel-sticks with the Tryambaka mantra itself.
One should attentively offer clarified butter with the mantra beginning "kadrudrāya."
And sesame seeds [should be offered] with the root mantra; this sequence should apply everywhere.
Likewise, at the conclusion of the dismissal of Brahmā, a pair [of garments] should be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
One who suffers from ringworm, being self-controlled, should with devotion offer an image standing upon a bull according to the rule by means of this mantra.
May the supreme Lord, the dweller of Kailāsa, accompanied by Umā and the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, swiftly dispel the disease of ringworm.
The mantra for the gift:
Then, having prostrated correctly before the Brahmin, one should ask for his forgiveness;
one should also feed the Brahmins and eat oneself while maintaining silence.
Having thus given this great gift, one is liberated from the disease of leprosy.
Thus ends the ritual for the gift of Umā and Maheśvara. Now follows the gift of the form of Rudra. In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"He who is a thief of food becomes suddenly emaciated."
I shall describe its remedy through gifts, fire-oblations, and ritual ablutions.
With gold, or half of that, or again half of that,
one should devoutly fashion an image of Rudra using the same metal.
Or else, with the essence of one's wealth, [one should worship] the three-eyed,
four-faced, and four-armed [deity], supreme in meditation, seated upon a comfortable throne.
Clad in a tiger skin and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
one should wrap him in a white cloth and place him upon the rice.
The measure of rice should be four *droṇas*,
or one should arrange the worship there according to one's own means.
The preceptor, who is learned in all the scriptures, should [worship] with fragrant perfumes and garlands, as well as various kinds of white [flowers], and with the sixteen types of ritual services.
One should perform all rites, such as worship and the like, with the root mantra;
and there, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed upon a well-prepared sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
The installation of the fire should take place according to the path described in the Mantrādhyāya;
there, one should employ these following mantras with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
"Āmbakam," "Kadrudrāya," and "Vāmadeva" are the [mantras] in sequence;
here, one hundred and eight repetitions are prescribed for each.
Having offered oblations repeatedly from the remnants of the fire, and having placed them in the vessel according to the prescribed rule,
one should firmly establish the entire collection in the north-eastern quarter of the fire.
And having wrapped it in a cloth together with the five sprouts,
[one should take earth] from a horse-stable, an elephant-stable, an anthill, a confluence, and a lake.
At the conclusion of the oblation, the preceptor himself should perform the pouring [of water],
likewise with the *Āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses and with the *Hiraṇya* verses.
Indeed, by means of the Pavamāna-anuvāka and the Śanno-vāka,
one should effect the union of the two bodies with the people through the complete integration of all their elements.
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
the patron, having become pure, should worship the Lord of Gods with devotion.
And furthermore, when he has offered oblations and performed worship with the root mantra,
one should give that image of Śaṅkara, the God of gods, to him.
With this mantra, facing north, one should [offer] according to the rules to him who faces east:
"O God of gods, Maheśāna, Vṛṣabhadhvaja, Śaṅkara!"
Whatever sin was committed by me in another birth through the theft of food,
and whatever unbearable emaciation of my body has been produced by that,
I have become stout through the gift bestowed by you; protect this sinner!
The mantra for the gift:
"In this manner, the man who bestows an image of Śaṅkara upon an excellent Brahmin according to this rite is liberated from emaciation."
Having performed the Puṇyāhavācana rite, one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the form of Rudra.
Now follows the gift of the Dakṣiṇāmūrti. In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Listen to the supreme secret, the gift that is the most excellent among all."
Having paid homage, I shall proclaim [the glory] of the God of gods, the wielder of the trident.
That by which the destruction of all sins is brought about—
that expiation for sins has been proclaimed by the sages who perceive the truth of the scriptures.
For that [practice] consisting primarily of austerity, fire-offerings, and recitation should indeed be performed with diligence;
this is the unsurpassed atonement for all sins.
In the case of the faults of the great sins (mahāpātaka), the secondary sins (pātaka), and the minor sins (upapātaka),
as well as for other faults, expiation is provided.
O Lord of Gods, one should fashion [the image] out of three palas of gold—
[representing] Īśāna, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the All-Knowing One, the Witness of the World.
Having placed a lotus upon the ground smeared with cow dung,
one should then set down a white lotus in its center using various powders.
Upon its pericarp, one should worship the Lord of Gods in the form of gold—
the omniscient, all-pervading, peaceful one, the cause of all causes,
who is saluted by all the gods and who knows the innermost essence of all the gods.
The great fire that consumes the fuel of sin, the one who carries across the ocean of saṃsāra,
the great ocean of the flood of compassion, the moon-crested Maheśvara.

Having thus meditated upon the Lord of Gods, whose hands are raised in the gesture of granting boons and whose entire body is like the great ocean, one should worship him with lotuses of the Brahmā-mantra.
One should offer white, blooming lotuses, water scented with white sandalwood,
and agallochum perfumed with camphor for the purpose of incense.
One should offer garments of linen and present milk-rice;
then, having performed a circumambulation, one should dedicate it to the Supreme Self.
Having first honored oneself, one should then honor the brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, peaceful, and devoted to Śiva.

Having conceived that very person— who has burnt away his karma through knowledge and who delights in obligatory and occasional rites— as the deity itself, one should worship him according to the prescribed rules.
Having prostrated before that deity, one should then utter this mantra:
"O Blessed One, knower of all beings, omniscient nectar, Śaṅkara!"
By your grace,
O Śaṅkara, may all the remaining sin arising from my speech, mind, and body be destroyed in every way.
Through the gift of your form, may all my [sins] dissolve from every side,
for I, ignorant, sinful, and devoid of right conduct, have come to you alone for refuge.
"O Maheśvara, show compassion toward me by destroying the flood of all [sufferings].
Having thus addressed him, one should then say: "May Śiva be well-pleased."
One should offer to that Śambhu, whose form is the universe, the entire collection of ritual acts, one's very self, and all accumulated impurities.
Whoever should offer this complete expiation according to this rule, all his sins will perish; of this there is no doubt.
Just as all darkness perishes in the presence of the sun,
so may every sin be destroyed by this gift dedicated to Śiva.
Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes in an instant,
so does the Blessed Lord Śambhu [reduce] the evil deeds of those who have come for refuge.
One who is devoid of all [conceptual] dharmas is liberated from all evils,
even if he has been intent upon all evils with his mind.
By means of the boat of Śiva alone, one will cross over all evil;
therefore, he who abandons everything and goes for refuge to Śaṅkara [will do so].
Through supreme devotion to him, no fear exists anywhere;
for as long as one lives, sin inevitably accrues to a human being.
For that sin, there is indeed no expiation other than its exhaustion;
therefore, one should diligently perform an atonement every year.
Since life, prosperity, and even health are impermanent,
one who desires their own welfare must act to cross over from hell.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the gift of Dakṣiṇāmūrti. Now follows the gift of the axe (paraśu), according to the Vāyu Purāṇa.
The sages said:
O Samīraṇa, homage to you! That expiation which was proclaimed by you regarding the vow has been fully confirmed by us.
O gracious-faced Lord, O best of gods, you ought to speak to us further concerning that mental sin which is committed intentionally.
You ought to speak so that, through that gift, there may be the destruction of his evil.
Vāyu said:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, because the mind is difficult to discern and is manifold,
even the resolve of the great inevitably becomes otherwise."
Without giving, one proceeds once again toward hell;
therefore, I shall now explain giving as the means for its exhaustion.
By means of which the sin associated with minor offenses (upapātaka) is destroyed:
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, in the forenoon, [one should offer] śāli rice grains.
With three pieces of cloth, one should fashion the form of the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva),
having four arms and three eyes, seated comfortably upon a lotus.
Having fashioned an axe made of a pala of gold for his right hand, one should then perform the worship.
The entire rite of propitiation for Paraśuhasta should be performed with mantras;
one should also worship the Supreme Lord with bilva leaves and kuśa grass.
Having worshipped the axe separately with red flowers, with a tranquil mind,
and having honored a Brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva and a master of the Vedas separately according to the previous rites, one should then utter the mantra.
O Lord of Gods, blue-and-red in hue, remover of the fear of all sins;
with an axe held ready in your hand, I have come to you for refuge.
O Lord, O All-pervading One, whatever evil I have committed with my mind since birth,
may you destroy all of that without remainder by granting me this axe.
By this, destroy all mental sins;
O Lord, show compassion toward me, the wretched one, today through your grace.
Having spoken thus, he gave that axe, the rice and other offerings,
the water-pot of the three Vedas, and that best of the twice-born, a god upon earth, to the lord of the brahmins.
Thus has been described the gift of the axe, which destroys the sins committed by the mind;
whatever sin one has previously committed with the mind since birth.
This gift is the diligent means for the expiation of that sin; therefore,
O ascetics, this gift should be given month after month,
or even year after year, for the removal of all faults.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the axe. Now follows the gift of the trident, according to the Vāyu Purāṇa.
The sages said:
O Samīraṇa, life-breath of the world, all-pervading Lord of the purifying action,
you ought to tell us the gift by which one casts off evil.
O Lord, you ought to tell us the means for the destruction of that evil which may have been committed through action, mind, or speech out of ignorance.
For there is no exhaustion of sinful karma except through the enjoyment [of its fruit],
or else by means of punishment, verbal [confession], or again, through expiation.
O Lord of the Earth, royal punishment was declared of old for manifest sin; as for that sin which is unintentional and committed through ignorance, [it is different].
For him for whom no atonement has been made, the Lord Vaivasvata [Yama] is the master;
therefore, O wanderer of the sky, you must state the means of his purification.
Vāyu said:
O best of sages, listen as I shall tell you that atonement for sins committed through lack of wisdom.
Whatever sin has been committed, it is entirely destroyed by the bestowal of that weapon of the trident-bearing God which is known as the Pāśupata.
On the fourteenth or the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
one should fashion a trident endowed with the proper characteristics using twelve niṣkas of gold.
Terrible, bringing about the end of the age, capable of destroying sins and obstacles,
one should place a full vessel made of copper filled with sesame seeds upon the hub of a wheel fashioned from various powders and adorned with six spokes.
One should place a vessel equal in capacity to an āḍhaka there and insert a trident;
one should then perform its worship in due order with that very mantra.
And one should worship the Lord of Kamalā at his side without visualizing a form,
having prostrated at the conclusion of the worship with the mantra beginning "aghorebhyaḥ."

The Aghora mantra, however, is found in the Liṅga Purāṇa: "Oṃ! To the non-terrible ones, to the terrible ones, and to those more terrible than the terrible, to all of them everywhere—to you who possess the forms of Rudra, let there be salutation! Thus it is said.
O best of sages, having likewise honored a learned Brahmin who is a kinsman,
one should then circumambulate him and recite this mantra:
O Blessed One, destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, crusher of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, O Śaṅkara, by the granting of this weapon to me, may my sin be destroyed.
By you, at the end of the eon, the destruction of the world's end was accomplished;
since this has been digested by me as well, by that [power], destroy my sin.
By that Pāśupati, by whom the three cities— difficult even for the gods to conquer— were burnt in half a moment, may my sin be swiftly destroyed.
Whatever sin has been committed by my unawakened mind while I was ignorant,
may all of that come to an end through the offering of this trident to you.
Having thus addressed him, he should then give that trident to the twice-born man, [reciting:
"Whatever sin may have been committed by me previously through ignorance."
The expiation for all of that is considered to be this offering of a spit (śūla);
since a human being inevitably commits sin through ignorance,
one should therefore offer it year after year for the removal of each such transgression.
Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the trident.
Baudhāyana says:
"From this point forward, everything arising from the ripening [of karma] is the destroyer of the trident."
I shall now correctly explain that gift which was proclaimed by Brahmā.
One should diligently fashion a trident out of gold or silver,
according to one's means, or even with half a *pala* of metal.
One should fashion the weapon of Mahādeva using either copper, iron, or even khadira wood; it should be prepared in that manner.
Having wrapped it in a red cloth and smeared it with red sandalwood paste,
and having encircled it with a red garland, one should place it upon sesame seeds.
A pure Brahmin should worship according to his capacity with a measure of sesame seeds— either one *droṇa*, half of that, or half of that again.
Having performed the sixteen services, beginning with the *arghya*, using the root mantra,
and having worshipped the officiating Brahmin who is skilled in the ritual procedures, the performer should prepare for the fire-oblation (*homa*).
To the south of the funeral pyre, the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni) is brought forward;
having offered fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, one indeed offers the fuel-stick with the verse beginning "puruṣasya."
One should perform an oblation of clarified butter with the Tryambaka mantra;
and with the mantra "yat indreṇa," one should offer sesame seeds, and with "śaṃ naḥ," one should provide peace.
Then a person should sprinkle water upon the patient suffering from colic;
thereafter, having worshipped the fire-oblation according to one's ability, [one should offer] the colic-pain itself.
Facing north, one should give that [gift] along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to one facing east,
with supreme devotion and while recollecting the Supreme All through this mantra.
You are the trident created by Brahmā; you are the ancient destroyer, the eternal weapon of Śaṅkara against the Daityas and Dānavas.
Whether it resides in my belly, or at my side, or is attached to my back— destroy that colic for me which was borne by Mahādeva.
Then, having bathed, he should eat together with Brahmins and kinsmen;
this will quickly destroy the pain arising from the injury caused by the stake.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the iron trident (paraśūla).
Now follows the gift of the image of the Sun (sūryamūrtidāna). Vṛddhagautama said:
"He who, being foolish, causes others to suffer by the application of medicinal herbs and the like..."
For that embodied being, an extremely unbearable wandering arises.
I shall describe its remedy through rites such as giving gifts and performing oblations,
using either three or two *niṣkas* of conventional currency.
Or, according to his own capacity, he should fashion a beautiful image of the Sun with two hands,
elevated and well-adorned with two lotuses.
She stood upon the chariot, adorned with red garments,
marked with saffron, and properly decorated with garlands of jewels.
Having bathed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should place it upon a copper vessel;
as for the measurement of that vessel, they know it to be eight times the amount of sesame seeds.
Whether it be half of that or half of that again, according to one's means,
one should place a vessel of sesame seeds upon a surface strewn with *darbha* grass.
The wise preceptor should worship that image thus transformed with fragrant perfumes and garlands, reciting the verse: "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad" (RV 4.40.5).
One should offer milk-rice as a food offering with the sixteen types of service;
and for those desiring auspiciousness, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed in the south-eastern direction.
[758] And with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, one should offer oblations with these mantras in their proper order:
"That wondrous eye of the gods," "The upward-rising," and "To Jātavedas."
And whatever *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation is prescribed for this rite,
it should be placed in a water-pot situated to the north of the fire.
All rites, beginning with the consecration (abhiṣeka) and preceded by pacifying rituals (śāntikarma),
should be performed by auspicious Brahmins for one seated upon a comfortable seat.
The dismissal of Brahmā includes everything up to the excellent liberation;
then, having bathed, pure, joyful, and anointed with white perfumes, [he should proceed].
Adorned with white garlands, he should present the auspicious image to the preceptor, who is seated facing east,
while he himself faces north.
The thousand-rayed god, the sky-goer, Pūṣan, the radiant one;
he who consists of all the gods, the Brahman, the eye of the world, whose body is the triple Veda.
Formerly, when I was wandering by means of the application of medicinal herbs and other such means, I worshipped the feet of the Brahmins; that was my previous wandering.
May the god Bṛhaspati, pleased by the gift of an image, dispel all wandering within the body; may Vāsudeva remove it.
The mantra for the gift:
Having thus given that gift to the preceptor with extreme devotion,
