one should follow him as far as the boundary of the monastery, prostrate, and ask for forgiveness.
One should also give to other brahmins a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability. Having given such a gift in the past with great devotion, a mortal,
having abandoned the delusion arising from the ripening of former karma, shall become happy.
[759] Thus ends the ritual procedure for the gift of the form of the Sun. Likewise:
The man who causes a Brahmin to be killed is born with leprosy;
I shall describe the remedy for that, namely the ritual gift of the Sun according to the prescribed rules.
One should fashion an image of the Sun using a pala, or half of that, or even half of that again; and one should place a plantain tree in its vicinity.
For the sake of pacifying those whose bodies are afflicted by leprosy,
one should have an auspicious [image] fashioned out of half a pala of gold, adorned with leaves and flowers.
The Sun, however, should be depicted with two arms, seated upon a shining chariot;
he should be wrapped in red cloth and anointed with saffron.
Having placed Rambhā upon rice, covered with a white cloth, adorned with white flowers and sandalwood paste, and provided with various fruits;
The measure of rice is proclaimed to be one *droṇa*;
[he should offer it] to a Brāhmaṇa endowed with Vedic learning and study, who possesses a tranquil mind.
Having invited to his home a poor Agnihotrin who is skilled in all branches of knowledge, one should worship him with devotion using garments and garlands.
Then one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice grains;
having offered parched grain mixed with honey, one hundred and eight times.

And with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should offer oblations to Durgā, the planets, and the presiding deities; thereafter, with devotion, one should also offer sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice.
In the same way, with the mantra "O you who have fallen into the clarified butter, you are protected," one should perform the anointing according to the characteristic marks on the body.
One should perform the propitiatory rite (śānti) specifically with the *Śanno devī* hymn;
the sick person, having offered the oblation, should give it to him with devotion.
Facing north, one should [offer] according to the rule with this mantra to him who faces east:
"O Āditya, Sūrya, Jewel of the Sky, Destroyer of All Diseases!"
O thousand-rayed one, friend of the lotus, destroyer of darkness!
O twelve-fold self, embodiment of the three Vedas, eye of the world, possessor of two hands!
Swiftly destroy this leprosy arising from the ripening of past karma.
Thus ends the mantra for the gift of the image of the Sun.
The plantain tree is the bestower of all happiness to all the gods, to the Mothers,
to Lakṣmī, Śacī, Pārvatī, and likewise to the celestial maidens.
In former times, she was worshipped for the sake of a specific purpose by Sāvitrī and Rambhā;
she dispelled every kind of leprosy arising from the limbs and minor members of the body.
The mantra for the gift of a plantain tree:
Then, having bathed, one should eat together with Brahmins and kinsmen.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the image of the secondary Sun.
Now follows the gift of the image of Fire. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:
"A wise man should fashion the image out of gold or copper."
Or again, with half a pala, or even a quarter-pala, of the essence of Vibhūti (ash).
[761] The characteristics of Vahni (Fire) have already been shown in the context of the Lokapālas during the description of the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa.
Likewise, she is surrounded by flames, smeared with red sandalwood paste,
draped in a red cloth, and seated upon a ram.
It was covered with garlands of *taktamālya* flowers, adorned with strings of pearls,
possessing the luster of the golden mountain [Meru], and as auspicious as twelve suns.
To a Brahmin endowed with celibacy, devoted to ritual action,
maintaining the sacred fire, and adorned with rings, garments, and other ornaments, one should offer her.

With this mantra, according to the prescribed rite, you, the adorable Agni in the form of the threefold fire (tretā), who are worthy of being pleased, have been honored; indeed, you move within all men.
"You know my past sin; destroy this dysentery.
By acting thus, a man properly dispels dysentery;
free from disease and always very happy, he attains a long life.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the form of Agni.
Now follows the gift of the Kālapuruṣa (the Person of Time). In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, tell me of other gifts that are supreme—
those which are auspicious, purifying, and destroyers of all sins.
O Mādhava, there is no one else here besides you who is the cause for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra and who possesses complete knowledge of dharma and adharma.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Various kinds of gifts have been described by me to you;
I shall speak of them once again, if you have any curiosity.
I have spoken these to you, and I shall speak them further for you;
they are accomplished through great purpose and bestow a great fruit.
O Pārtha, the ritual for giving performed exactly according to the rules for the sake of desired results has been proclaimed by the sages; when performed otherwise, it leads to fear.
O Pārtha, one hundred niṣkas should be known as the supreme rule for gifts;
that which is half of that is middling, and half of that again is recorded as the lowest.
And likewise upon a ewe, upon the Kālapuruṣa, and upon other great beings;
similarly upon a tree, a chariot, an egg, a cow, and a black antelope skin.
"O lord of men, even for one who is incapable, this rite of five gold pieces is prescribed by Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, he who gives a great gift with even less than that [attains the same merit]."
Or if he should accept it, it will bring him suffering and grief.
O son of Pāṇḍu, having reached an auspicious day, on level and pleasant ground, on the fourteenth or the fourth lunar day, or under the Viṣṭi yoga;
The *viṣṭi* is the *bhadrākaraṇa*.
A male figure should be fashioned out of black sesame seeds, with silver teeth and golden eyes;
here, the proportions for the gold and other materials should be prepared according to one's capacity.
With a sword raised in his hand, tall in stature, and wearing earrings of hibiscus flowers;
clad in red garments, adorned with garlands, and decorated with a necklace of conch shells; his cheeks were stained with streams of blood from the binding of sharp dagger-blades.
She has a daughter and a knife;
her feet are provided with a pair of sandals, and she has a black woolen blanket at her side;
likewise, she holds a lump of meat in her left palm.
Having performed such [rites], the patron, with palms joined in homage and a tranquil mind, should utter this mantra.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers and having offered the food oblation, you perceive everything; therefore, you are called Kāla by virtue of your end.
O you of noble vows, you are unassailable even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others;
you have been worshipped by me with devotion, and likewise, O King, you have attained happiness.
O Lord, you know that; therefore, do it. Salutations, salutations! Having thus worshipped him, one should present [the offering] to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having first honored the Brahmin with garments and ornaments,
one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, and after prostrating, bid him farewell.
The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of gold coins (*niṣka*) and so forth, as previously mentioned.
For whoever bestows this gift according to this rite,
there shall be no fear of death, nor shall there be anything caused by disease.
He becomes one whose sovereignty is unimpeded and who is free from all afflictions;
at the end of the body, having pierced the abode of the Sun, he goes to the supreme state.
Having returned here upon the exhaustion of his merit, he becomes a righteous king,
a performer of sacrificial sessions, endowed with glory, and accompanied by sons and grandsons.
Having worshipped the Person of Time according to the rules and having given to a brahmin that which is the cause for the arising of auspicious and inauspicious fruits,
[one should act] toward this body, which is afflicted by disease and composed of all defects.
The embodied being does not fall into delusion because of its power.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Kālapuruṣa. Now follows the gift of the Kālacakra. From the Mṛtyuñjaya [Tantra]:
"Having fashioned a wheel made of silver, consisting of rays of pearls..."
Having placed the autumnal moon upon his head, situated within the midst of its rays.
But the skin and flesh on his limbs all around become silver;
thus, for him who possesses such meditation, even the moon would turn black.
Immediately after that, standing behind him and circumambulating the Brahmin from left to right,

this gift called Kālacakra is the destroyer of death.
Uttering these words: "I give this silver vessel, lunar and filled with a network of rays, for the destruction of untimely death," he should present it.
One should present gold accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brāhmaṇa;

Therefore, for that reason, it should always be given by those afflicted with the fear of untimely death,
or by those seized by diseases such as fever, or even by those fallen into great calamity.
Then, one should establish the fire according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras;
one should offer oblations with sesame seeds one hundred and eight times, using the name of Kāla.
Then, one should devoutly feed Brahmins to the number of twelve;
one should oneself eat only once, avoiding pungent and salty food.
When this is done, a man will surely live for a long time—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Kālacakra. Now, the gift of Yama. From the Mṛtyuñjaya [Tantra]:
"Brass placed in an iron vessel, and upon it a lotus made of silver."
At that time, Kāleśvara assumed a human form made of gold.
The form of Yama has been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*:
he is provided with garments and ornaments, holding terrifying weapons on all sides,
and flanked by male figures made of the three metals acting as messengers of Death (*kāladūta*).

The weapons that cause fear are the sword, the dagger, and so forth. "Triple-metal" refers to copper, bell-metal, and brass. The messengers of Death are three men in human form, holding staffs in their hands.
Having placed a buffalo upon its back, one should offer it while addressing Yama.
Whoever performs this according to the prescribed rite on the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day, [attains the desired fruit].

He is certainly liberated from destruction by giving an additional jar of ghee. This means that while addressing Yama—referring to Yama who is seated upon the back of a buffalo and mounted upon a lotus placed in a bronze vessel—he should utter, "I give [this]. Regarding the phrase "to the north of the jar of ghee," the author of the *Dānaviveka* explains that this refers to the place for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Others, however, say it refers to gold as the fee.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift to Yama.
Now, the gift of a water-pot (*udakumbha-dāna*) according to the *Śaunakīya*:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O Blessed One, by what gift, by what austerity, or by what deed [is this attained]?"
Without having reached the terrible hell, the human being attains heaven.
O Sage, O divine seer, living beings are constantly being cooked in the hells;
if there is a remedy for this with little effort, please speak.
Sūta said:
Having been thus addressed by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya,
the Blessed One then spoke to Nārada concerning a gift that yields great fruit even for one with limited wealth.
O sinless Mārkaṇḍeya, listen to this which was spoken of old by the Blessed Lord Śambhu when he was thus questioned by both Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Listen, O observer of virtuous vows; I shall describe the gift known as the water-pot, by performing which a man or a woman never goes to hell at any time.
It leads to heaven, brings fame, longevity, and health; it destroys sin, is meritorious, pleasing to me, and likewise dear to you both.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, on the full moon day of Kārtika,
or on that same day during one's own birthday, as well as upon seeing a bad dream or a miraculous portent, this rite should be performed.
On ground smeared with cow dung, the wise man should place a water-pot,
wrapped in a white cloth and adorned with flowers and fruits;
according to the prescribed rite, he should also deposit there a heap of sesame seeds mixed with rice.
One should install the god Dharmarāja, fashioned from gold according to one's means,
with a pleasant countenance, two arms, seated, and holding a staff in his hand.
One who grants boons, endowed with compassion, and acting for the welfare of devotees—
having thus prepared seven jars, one should then worship them with perfumes and other offerings.
One should cause the Brahmins to receive the jars with these mantras in due order:
"To Yama, to Dharmarāja, to Mṛtyu, and to Antaka."
To Vaivasvata Kāla, the destroyer of all beings—
having thus propitiated them, one should offer those jars preceded by water.
"May the Blessed One himself be pleased"—thus one should recite at the conclusion of the mantra.
In this way, by the offering of the water-pot (kumbha), that God of gods is satisfied.
The one who performs [the rite] and the one who causes it to be performed attains heaven; of this there is no doubt.
He does not go to a terrible hell, nor does he encounter anything inauspicious anywhere.
The Lord, who is Yama himself, becomes truly pleased with him who gives the gift of a water-pot to Brahmins according to the prescribed rite.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the water-pot.
Now follows the gift of the crocodile. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:
"One should properly fashion a crocodile out of silver or indeed copper."
With three syllables, or with two, or even with one, [one should meditate on] the auspicious form.
Jewels should be given for the tail; one should have the waist made of silver;
the eyes should be made of gold, and the tongue should be fashioned accordingly.
One should place the feet there into a vessel of ghee in front of the two [deities],
having wrapped them in a black cloth and smeared them with sandalwood and agallochum.
Then, one should place a beautiful makara in a copper vessel or a water-vessel,
[and invite] a brahmin who is endowed with good conduct, elderly, self-controlled, and free from greed.
One should worship with garments, bracelets, armlets, and finger-rings;
the fire-oblation (homa) is performed according to the method taught in the chapter on mantras, using deities belonging to the water-sphere (vāruṇa).
Then, one should offer that crocodile to the Brahmin representing the belly, saying:
"O Lord of the waters, O Lord of gods, O All-pervading Master of the western quarter!
Being gratified by this gift, grant me the destruction of my abdominal disease."
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Makara. Now follows the gift of the image of Dhanada (the Giver of Wealth). In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"That mortal who creates an obstacle to giving is born poor."
Listen to me regarding that action by which sovereignty is produced.
One should fashion an auspicious image of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) made of gold, measuring half a pala, or half of that, or again, half of that.
She has two arms, is accompanied by her vehicle, and brings joy to the eyes;
[769] the characteristics of the god of wealth (Kubera) are to be observed in the gift of the mountain of grain. She is joined on both sides by the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma.
Having wrapped it in a white cloth, one should place it upon rice.
The quantity of rice should be four *droṇas*, or half of that, or half of that again; one should not practice stinginess regarding the wealth spent.
One should worship [the deity] by anointing it with fragrances and adorning it with white garlands;
furthermore, an oblation (homa) in the southeastern direction should be performed with sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
The mantra "Obeisance to the King of Kings" (mantro rājādhirājāya) should be employed together with the appropriate gendered designations;
furthermore, those desiring wealth should perform the oblation of sesame seeds accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis*.
The teacher should be a knower of all scriptures, disciplined, honored by all,
born of a noble family, a knower of the Dharma, truthful in speech, and pure.
With great devotion, one should have the worship of Dhanada performed by him using the mantra dedicated to that deity; thus, he shall become a lord of his desires.
To him who has performed the oblation, one facing north should duly present that image to him who faces east, with this mantra.
O Lord Kubera, master of the northern quarter, whose vehicle is a man,
you are the lord of the Padma and Śaṅkha treasures, the beloved of Śrīkaṇṭha.
By means of giving and other virtues, whatever poverty has been acquired that brings me suffering—
by the gift of yourself, quickly destroy all that evil.
The mantra for the gift:
"In this way, the mortal who performs the gift of Kubera according to the prescribed ritual becomes equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) at that very moment."
[770] Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the gift of the image of Dhanada. Now follows the gift of the Naga; regarding this, Vṛddha-Baudhāyana says:
But the man who is bitten by serpents shall become afflicted with erysipelas (visarpa);
its pacification should be performed through charity and especially through fire-offerings (homa).
One should fashion a Nāga out of gold weighing one pala, or half of that, or again half of that, provided with five hoods.
And rubies should be given on each of the five hoods;
likewise, a gem should be placed on the tail, and a diamond on the two eyes.
Having thus fashioned the auspicious serpent, one should smear it with saffron,
wrap it in a red cloth, and place it upon a copper vessel.
They know the measure of the vessel to be eight *pala*s;
one should worship the supreme Naga with the sixteen services (*upacāra*s).
The preceptor, who is learned in all the scriptures and devoted to the treatises on Dharma,
should also perform the fire-oblation with auspicious sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
With the three mantras beginning with "Namo 'stu sarpebhyaḥ," one should [recite] either one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight times, respectively.
Alternatively, the measure may be twenty-eight separately;
having offered with the falling of oblations, one should personally unify them in the vessel.
Having anointed the patient suffering from visarpa with the oils associated with the Śrīsūkta,
one should [anoint] him in sequence with the verses beginning with "bhūmir bhūmnā" and all the verses addressed to Rājñī.
So that he may become healthy and his limbs free from disease,
one should cast in guggulu, fragrant substances, and leafy wood.
Having prepared a water-pot, one should perform the consecration with auspicious waters,
using the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ sarpebhyaḥ" and also with oblations accompanied by mantras containing the deity's specific marks.
One should recite the *Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, the *Śucayaḥ*, the *Pavamāna* section,
the *Āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, and the *Śaṃ no vātaḥ*.
Having rubbed his beautiful limbs with aloe-wood and sandalwood,
he should then wear white garments and apply white garlands and unguents.
Then the preceptor should also worship with effort using perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth,
employing the mantra dedicated to Śarada.
One should present that Ananta, the king of serpents,
who supports the entire earth with its mountains, forests, and groves, to the teacher.
May that Nāga, whose bed is in the Ocean of Milk and who belongs to Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow—
being pleased by his own gift— dispel my ailment.

May she dispel my disease of erysipelas, whether it be born from a fault of speech, or arisen from a disorder of the blood, or even originating from my mother or father, and whatever ailment has manifested in my limbs and their members.
The mantra for the gift:
Having thus given that nāga to the preceptor along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and having bowed his head to the ground, he should slowly walk a hundred paces.
Having been permitted by the preceptor, the wise man should enter his own home;
having fed the Brahmins, he should then eat himself together with his kinsmen.
[772] Thus ends the procedure for the gift of an elephant.
Now follows the gift of one's own image, according to the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall now fully describe to you that gift which increases one's merit and which, known as the "Self-Image," was not mentioned to anyone previously.
The sages have proclaimed that for him, every moment is always a time for giving;
O Pārtha, a meritorious day is attained through merits within this fleeting life.
Then, O King, having had a beautiful golden image fashioned,
mounted upon his favorite vehicle and adorned with his preferred ornaments;
Accompanied by her beloved ones and provided with all necessary utensils— "accompanied by her beloved ones" means accompanied by those dear to her—
there she is covered with silk cloths and garments, and adorned with garlands.
Her limbs were anointed with saffron and perfumed with camphor and agallochum.
If it is a woman who gives, he should have her herself prepare the bed;
whatever is most dear to him, all that he should place by his side.
Whatever may be beneficial for women and men,
one should personally reflect upon it in the mind and set all of that aside.
Having brought all these together, one should assign them each to their respective places,
after having worshipped the world-protectors, the planets, the Goddess, and Vināyaka.
[773] Here, by the word *devī*, Durgā is meant, because of her association with Vināyaka.
Then, having bathed and put on white garments, holding a handful of flowers and standing before a Brahmin, he should recite this mantra:
This image of yourself, complete with all its appurtenances and endowed with every kind of jewel, has been presented to you, O beloved.
The Self is Śambhu, Śiva, Śauri, and Śakra, joined by the hosts of Śiva;
therefore, by the gift of my own self, may my own self be propitiated.
Having recited this, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should then give [the gift] to a Brāhmaṇa;
and the Brāhmaṇa receives it while reciting, "Who shall give? (kodāt).
"From whom [did you receive it]?"—this refers to the mantra well-known in the Vājasaneyi school.
Then, having circumambulated [the recipient] from left to right and prostrated, one should dismiss them.
O King of Kings, by means of this ritual procedure, one bestows this gift.
Whatever man or woman should hear this, they shall obtain the fruit [of their merit] for two hundred and fifty years, surrounded by all the worlds and the gods.
By granting the desired fruit, one becomes a partaker of the desired fruit;
for wherever a living being is born at the moment when their karma has reached its exhaustion, [there they shall attain it].
In that very place, O King, he shall enjoy the fruits of all his desires,
and never experience separation from his beloved kinsmen.
O King, such a person attains [this] and enjoys infinite heaven.
And whoever, having fashioned a golden image of himself seated upon a choice vehicle, filled with wealth and grain and provided with all appurtenances,
gives it with devotion to an excellent brahmin;
That king of kings shines in the sky like the moon and the sun.
[774] Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the image of the Self.
Now follows the gift to the Aśvins, as stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
Then those sages performing the sacrificial session in the Naimiṣa forest questioned the son of Suta;
O Ugraśravas, we ask you.
How should a wise person pacify the affliction of disease?
Thus questioned by the sages, the son of Sūta spoke this regarding the greatness of giving:
"Listen, I shall tell you about that gift."
Having performed which, he is liberated from the multitude of diseases.
The performer attains the fulfillment of his desires in this world, gains longevity and supreme health,
and all fierce [obstacles] come to rest.
By which means the donor may likewise attain prosperity.
When the moon or sun is eclipsed by Svarbhānu, or when the sun enters another zodiac sign, or during a solar eclipse,
or when afflicted by diseases, or during any of the three kinds of portents;
In whatever stage the mind constantly delights, [that is its nature].
In that place, which is a pure location smeared with cow dung, one should perform the gift known as the Āśvina on two altars,
each measuring one cubit on all sides.
Having prepared [the offering] with sesame seeds and rice known as *āḍhaka*.
There, having worshipped the two Aśvin deities, who are golden and facing westward, [one should offer] two golden ones;
that is, two golden [images] made of gold. Their characteristics are described in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
The two divine physicians should be depicted with two arms and beautiful eyes;
in their right hands, divine medicinal herbs should be held.
O twice-born one, two beautiful books should be made for the two [deities] in their left hands;
O Yādava, one should be on the right side of one, and the other on the left side of the other.
A pair of women should be fashioned, beautiful and pleasing to behold;
their names, as well as their physical perfection and appearance, have been declared.
"A jewel-casket should be placed in the hand, and likewise a garment as white as the moon. Thus it is said.
Having performed circumambulation with perfumes, garments, flowers, incense, and lamps, one should also do so for the two chief deities.
Having bowed down and honored the two Brahmins with reverence, the two of them offered a handful of flowers.
In this rite, one should give a single piece of gold for each [deity], preceded by the offering of water;
then, one should recite the mantra in due order.
The donor, having composed his mind, [should give with] a serene heart.
O Nāsatyas, destroyers of falsehood, through the gift of the golden-formed Yuga cows, may there be peace for me;
just as you two became the physicians of the gods.
And so, for the sake of quelling my disease, [I pray to] the two gods.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Aśvins.
Now follows the gift of the Moon and the Sun, according to the Viṣṇudharmottara. The Blessed One said:
Henceforth, O King, lord of men, I shall proclaim that gift by giving which King Bali indeed attained the sovereignty of Śakra.
And Śakra, having given the kingdom to Bali, regained it once again,
as [happens] during an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the equinox, or at the solstice.
On the twelfth lunar day, on the new moon, on the full moon of Vaiśākha, upon the birth of a son,
on the full moon of Kārttika, on the great Māghī, and likewise on the seventh lunar day known as Jayā.
The two Ādityas should also be given;
the Sun is said to be made of gold, while the orb of the Moon should be made of pure silver.
The mandala for both [the male and female deities] is twelve finger-breadths in circumference;
the two circles are shaped like lotuses, with a pericarp in the center.
The wise man should place the sun in a copper vessel filled with ghee,
and he should place the moon upon the Gaṅgā in a vessel filled with milk.
One should worship the Sun with red flowers and likewise the Moon with white ones;
furthermore, one should cause fragrant incense to be offered to Āditya.
For Soma, white resin (guggulu) should be offered as fragrance; likewise for Aja.
For Pataṅga, however, saffron and a lamp with ghee should be given.
Having thus worshipped the Moon and Sun separately with effort,
one should worship Soma with the mantra ending in "mano'ntena" as the embodiment of nectar (amṛtamūrti).
Having repeatedly invoked the Sun with the mantra "khakholkāya" ending in "namaḥ," one should then devoutly invite a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Having honored with flowers and incense the householder who is poor, as well as one who maintains the sacred fires— a twice-born man who is like a second sun—
O King, having indeed gazed upon the orb of the sun and the orb of the moon reflected in clarified butter,
one should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa with this mantra.
The Rukma, the Puruṣa, the Parṇa, and the Puṣkara—
these three are the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, which constitute the limbs of that one whose form is the universe.
"O Brahmin, may that god Caṇḍakara be pleased without delay";
having uttered this, one should present [the gift] to the Brāhmaṇa while addressing the Sun.
O best of the twice-born, I also give you the god of gods born from milk, as well as the king of the twice-born, the cool-rayed moon who is the embodiment of nectar.
O Lord, the eclipse of the sun occurs through the Gāyatrī,
while that of the moon occurs by reciting the Taratsamandīya with a pure mind.
Thus, having given the moon and the sun, Bali indeed obtained the kingdom;
for he who should give the moon and the sun would have given everything.
O King, best of men, by him everything has been performed, by him everything has been heard,
and by him every sacrifice has been offered with sacrificial fees throughout the cycle of existence.
He is worshipped by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Ṛṣis, Devas, and Dānavas.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the moon and the sun.
Now follows the gift of the banner and the noose. Baudhāyana says:
"One should indeed make the banner and the noose from one *pala* of silver."
Or else, with half a pala of pure crystal-like [mercury], one should proceed with care.
One should properly fasten emeralds with jewels all over the limbs [of the image],
and one should place there a water-pot containing five *droṇas* of sesame seeds.
And a beautiful banner with a noose should be placed upon the pitcher;
both of these, together with gold, one should present to a Brāhmaṇa.
One should wrap the water-pot with a cloth and honor it with perfumes, garlands, and unbroken grains;
[then present it] to a learned householder who is endowed with Vedic knowledge and virtuous conduct.
One should likewise offer it for the pleasure of Varuṇa and Vāyu:
"Salutations to you, the bearer of the noose; salutations to you, the bearer of the banner."
To you, the Lord of Waters, and to Vāyu, who is beloved by all people—
these two, a banner and a noose, shining like pure silver, are given for the pleasure of both of you.
"May asthma and cough, who take refuge in all people, remove my [suffering] out of affection. By performing this, one shall become free from disease at that very moment.
[779] Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the banner and the noose. Now follows the gift of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, as stated in the Liṅga Purāṇa.
Now I shall further proclaim another [rite], the most excellent among all gifts;
it should be performed according to the rules in a pavilion, at the proper place and time, as previously described.
At a water-shed, in the middle of a mountain peak, on a sacrificial mound, or in the presence of Śiva—
having first worshipped Viṣṇu and thereafter the lotus-born Brahmā.
By means of those two mantras according to the prescribed rite, beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.

Here, by the word "as before" (*pūrvavat*), everything—including the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and so forth—enjoined for the *tulāpuruṣa* gift in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* is included, because that [description] is read within that very context. The terms *prācī* and *prākūṭa* refer to specific types of pavilions. The implied meaning is: having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in such a specific pavilion as described, one should worship Brahmā and Viṣṇu in the presence of Śiva. By the phrase "in the presence of Śiva," the making of an image of Śiva is also understood. Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
Within the mandala, one should place a golden Śiva, with Brahmā and Keśava on either side;
dedicating it to them, a great amount of wealth should be given to those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).

The highest [sacrificial ground] is three thousand [bow-lengths], the middle is two thousand, and the lowest is said to be one thousand; this is stated by me in brief. As before, there is the worship of Śiva, as well as the sacrificial fees for the officiating priests and the preceptor.

"With both mantras"—meaning with both that are about to be mentioned—one should worship Viṣṇu and Brahmā. "Beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*" is an adverbial phrase qualifying the action. "May we know Nārāyaṇa; may we meditate upon Vāsudeva; may that Viṣṇu inspire us.
"To you, Brahmā, the giver of wealth, who is vast and the cause of expansion."
Svāhā to Śiva-Hari; Svadhā, Vauṣaṭ, Vaṣaṭ, and Namaḥ!
Thus are the mantras of Viṣṇu and Brahmā. Regarding Śiva, however, the author will state, "having recited the Rudras.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should thereafter commence the fire-oblation (homa).
All the ritual substances (dravya) should be offered into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the two [mantras] according to the rule.
Having recited the Rudra hymns with self-restraint, his mind fixed solely on Śiva,
he should appoint two officiating priests who are endowed with excellent qualities and have mastered the Vedas.
Having designated them, one should cause wealth to be given to the Brahmins according to the rule—
one hundred and eight excellent [coins] to each of them individually.
Adorned with garments and ornaments according to the full extent of one's wealth,
the preceptor and the two officiating priests [should worship] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
To each of them one should give gifts separately and also feed Brāhmaṇas;
furthermore, the worship of Śiva must be performed, including the ritual bathing and so forth, in the proper sequence.

"Every substance," and so forth: every substance is described in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* in the section on the *Tulāpuruṣa* gift. "In two [fires] at the sacrificial pit" means that the oblation should be offered by two officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) into a single pit. "With reference to them," and so forth: with reference to those—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—one should cause wealth to be given, one hundred and eight times for each deity, to Brahmins other than the officiating priests and the preceptor (*ācārya*), individually and separately. Although no specific caste or quantity is mentioned here by the word "wealth" (*dhana*), since *niṣkas* have been introduced frequently throughout, the total of one hundred and eight should be completed with those alone. "And the preceptor," and so forth: having fashioned golden images of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara for the one preceptor and the two officiating priests, one should give them. Their characteristics have been stated in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*; for them, the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the feeding of Brahmins, and the recitation of auspicious prayers (*svastivācana*) must be performed. Having worshipped the teacher as before, one should also worship the two officiating priests.
The wise man should worship the Brahmins who proclaim the *puṇyāha* as before;
for thus it is stated in the Vātula:
"By performing it in this manner, a person obtains the fruit of all sacrifices."
One attains all desires and realizes nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the gift of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Now follows the gift of the Threefold Form (Trimūrti) from the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa. Sūta said:
All the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest respectfully questioned Ugraśravas, the son of Romaharṣaṇa, as he sat there.
"You have described to us various kinds of gifts,
yet you have not indeed mentioned the gift of an image, O best among the knowers of Brahman."
"When, where, or how should this task be performed as a means for accomplishing the Dharma?
Tell us, O Knower of All Dharmas; we are eager to hear about generosity and service."
O son of Sūta, having been thus addressed by the powerful ones headed by Śaunaka,
he spoke of the greatness of giving to the sages.
Let all the sages listen to this gift, which grants the accomplishment of all aims,
removes all sins, is auspicious, and bestows complete liberation.
Long ago, in the Deva-yuga, the divine Madhusūdana spoke to the high-souled Viriñci, who was seated upon the lotus from his own navel.
In the same way, I shall tell you all; listen, O sinless ones!
The gift of the Three Forms (Trimūrti) is said to be the most excellent among all gifts.
One should perform it at the equinoxes or solstices, during lunar and solar eclipses and the like, or regularly on the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight and under one's own birth asterism.
One should cause a gift to be made in a temple, on a riverbank, in sacred shrines, or in one's own home; it should consist of five layers and be pure.
One should smear a level, square piece of ground with cow dung;
there, one should scatter handfuls of flowers along with unbroken grains (akṣata) on all sides.
Therein, the triple altar (trivedikā) should be one or two cubits wide and three times that in length;
it should be mixed with white rice and extend across the area.
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Lord Murāri, made of gold, are to be installed there;
they should have four arms and be richly adorned with their own characteristic weapons and ornaments.
And also of Kirīṭin, in due order.
The characteristics of Brahmā and the others have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*.
Having worshipped them with devotion using water for bathing, water for the feet, water for sipping, clothing, perfumes, and so forth— [783]—
Having circumambulated [the deity] with flowers in hand,
having prostrated and performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsana), one should then present [the offering].
Having thus honored each one individually after they have previously given much, you, the creator of the world, should give this of your own accord in due order.
You alone are the grandfather of all.
You alone are the creator of the worlds and you alone are their transformer; you alone are the sustainer and the ordainer of the worlds.
Through your gift, may I become sinless.
And through you, O Lord, he attains union.
O Lord, grant the grace of the best of gods to me who have come to you for refuge;
for by you this entire world has been attained.
The virtuous indeed say that you are Viṣṇu.
O God of infinite form, all things abide in you; they declare that the entire universe is sustained by you.
Through your grace, I become sinless.
Just as [he is] the Lord, the cause of the cause of the world.
O Lord, O best of gods, act thus toward me who have sought refuge;
show favor by providing the nectar of immortality for mortals.
Because the hālāhala poison is indeed concentrated.
Likewise, O Lord, for the sake of the welfare of the world, the triple city of the Asuras was burnt by you with a single arrow;
and through the granting of your own form, I too have become entirely so.
I take refuge in those hosts who are liberated from defects.
"O Lord, O best of gods, act thus and grant your grace to me who have sought refuge;
having spoken thus, he offers [the gift] according to the prescribed rite."
He then attains union with the Trimūrti.
To that most excellent of Brahmins who should cause [this] to be performed,
one should respectfully give gold calculated by the count of its weight, as well as a pair of garments.
When it has been performed in this way, one obtains that fruit.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Three Forms (Trimūrti). Now follows the procedure for the gift of the Three Persons (Tripuruṣa), according to the Mṛtyuñjaya [Tantra]:
"With one hundred *raktikās* of gold, or according to one's capacity..."
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Śaṅkara are to be made [from it].
One should have a pedestal made of iron, measuring twelve *pala*s,
circular like a wheel, for the purpose of installing the deities.
There, Brahmā and the others are to be installed; one should place the messenger of Yama in front.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) has four faces and four arms, with a lotus in his hand.
Śaṅkara has two arms, carries a trident, is mounted upon a bull, and has three eyes;
Viṣṇu has four arms, wields a discus, holds a mace, and has Garuḍa as his vehicle.
The messenger of Yama, holding a noose and a staff, with a distorted face and made of iron,
should be depicted as terrified and bound before him.
Then, having performed the worship of the gods with flowers, fruits, and other offerings,
the sacrificer took a sharp, new sword in his hand.
Having uttered, "I shall cut off this head of this wicked-souled messenger," he severed the messenger's head while facing the direction of Yama.
Then, the recitation by the Brahmins (brāhmaṇavācana) should be performed by four Brahmins;
thereafter, one should diligently make offerings to the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
Whether in a temple, a house, at a sacred ford, or anywhere else,
one should give those [gifts] to a Brāhmaṇa who possesses divine limbs and is virtuous.
He who, terrified by the fear of untimely death, should give these three deities, beginning with Brahmā, in due order, accompanied by a sacrificial fee of gold;
His death shall perish through this gift; of this there is no doubt.
Even a man being seized by Death clearly continues to live.
The person who, having fashioned three images of gold, performs here the gift of [the deities] beginning with Brahmā,
casts away all diseases, even those that are difficult to overcome.
A man never encounters the fear of untimely death.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the three persons.
Now follows the gift of the four forms, according to the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"The sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest were seated at a sacrificial session."
The best of sages questioned Ugraśravas as he sat.
"O son of Romaharṣaṇa, you are a great ocean of all knowledge.
Thus addressed by the sages, Sūta, the best among speakers, replied.
As the Blessed One Brahmā, the grandfather of Nārada, said:
"Listen, Nārada—may you be blessed—the gift that destroys all evil."
O high-minded one, we are all desirous of hearing the Dharma from you;
by what means, then, might we cross this ocean of saṃsāra without effort?
"O man, speak of either a gift, or a vow, or indeed sacred learning.
Thus addressed by the sages, Sūta, the best among speakers, replied.
As the Blessed One Brahmā, the Grandfather, said to Nārada:
"Listen, Nārada—may prosperity be yours—to this gift which destroys all evil."
That rite of the fourfold form is a cause of auspiciousness for women;
it bestows wealth, health, long life, and the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It bestows sons, brings prosperity, is meritorious, grants desired fruits,
and is auspicious during all holy times, such as lunar and solar eclipses.
One should perform the gift-offering in places such as a temple or in one's own home;
[one should prepare] a square, level piece of ground smeared with cow-dung water.
There should be four lines there, equal and oriented toward the east and north;
there should be nine squares, and one should exclude the corner squares.
There, one should install their images in the four directions—
starting from the east and ending with the north— auspiciously fashioned out of gold.
One should place them upon white rice-lotuses adorned with flowers;
first Vāsudeva, and after that Saṅkarṣaṇa.
And [he saw] Pradyumna and Aniruddha, the fourfold form in due order,
holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, clad in yellow garments, the infallible Acyuta.
The god Ananta has the Śrīvatsa mark, four arms, and is radiant with armlets and a crown; he wears blue garments and holds a mace as his weapon.
Saṅkarṣaṇa has four arms and is adorned with bracelets and other ornaments;
Pradyumna and Aniruddha likewise bear the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Wearing yellow and white garments and adorned with armlets and other ornaments—
one should thus fashion the fourfold form with four arms and worship it.
Constructed with gold according to one's capacity from half a *pala* onwards,
the sequence of worship for the deities begins from the east and extends to the north.
The propitiation of the deities with their respective mantras in due order [includes] bathing,
a pair of garments, water for the arghya offering, and water for the pādya and ācamanīya offerings.
One should offer jasmine flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings;
likewise, one should present three streams of pure water and betel leaf.
Then one should worship the world-protectors on all sides with perfumes and other offerings;
having circumambulated three times clockwise, one should hold a handful of flowers.
Having dismissed the Brahmins and honored them, one should give [the gift] and utter this mantra:
"Homage be to Vāsudeva; homage to the Lord of the worlds."
From the chanting of your name and from giving gifts, may there always be welfare for me. O Saṅkarṣaṇa, salutations be to you, whose activity is the maintenance and destruction of the world.
O Lord, by your gift, may it become the remover of all sins for Pradyumna,
the ruler of all, who takes away the suffering of his devotees.
Homage be to the God of gods, who removes the suffering of his devotees;
always homage be to the cause of the creation, preservation, and end of the world.
If one endowed with faith should offer the fourfold form to the god Aniruddha, who is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, O Nārada.
"Whether a woman or a man, one enjoys the fruit as described.
Thus spoke Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, to Nārada.
"Just as all that was told to me by the best of sages," thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the fourfold form (*caturmūrtidāna*).
Now follows the gift that bestows long life (*āyuṣkaradāna*), according to the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*.
Sūta said: Now, O best of sages, listen as I shall proclaim the gift (dāna) known as "Bestower of Longevity," which grants health and all perfections.
One should perform the act of giving at a place where the means for accomplishment are established;
on the ground smeared with cow dung, auspiciously oriented from south to north.
Having placed there four golden mandalas filled with white rice using both hands, one should set them down upon those [spots].
Then one should worship the golden deities in due order,
beginning there with the Self-born (Brahmā) together with Viṣṭaraśravas (Viṣṇu).
Kṛttivāsas, Īśāna, Vajrapāṇi, and Śatakratu;

[789] Ātmabhū is Brahmā, Viṣṭaraśravas is Viṣṇu, and Īśāna is the well-known Śiva. Their characteristics have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*. These should be fashioned out of gold according to one's capacity.
Then, having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, they should be placed in order from south to north.
Having propitiated them with devotion, one should give one [coin] to each of the Brahmins individually.
Having meditated upon each respective deity, one should recite these mantras;
one should then utter: "May the Blessed One, the Self-born, be well-pleased with me."
"May the Lord Viṣṭaraśravas, who pervades the world, be well-pleased;
may the Blessed One clad in animal skin be well-pleased with me"—thus he said with certainty.
"May the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, be pleased with me.
Thus spoke Brahmā in the past to the celestial sage Nārada;
and all of that has now been told by me to you, O bulls among sages.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift that bestows long life.
Now follows the gift of the five forms (*pañcamūrtidāna*), according to the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*:
"Now I shall proclaim the gift known as the five forms."
By performing which, a man or a woman shall attain all accomplishments.
Whatever evil was previously committed by means of mind, speech, and action throughout thousands of other births, all that goes to total destruction.
Just as in the past the Lord was questioned by the high-souled Nārada,
so too was the Blessed One, the lotus-born Grandfather, questioned by him.
In that same way, O bulls among sages, I too shall proclaim all of that to you— the Great God who is heard of as having five forms.
Listen, O divine sage, to this gift which destroys all sins;
it bestows health and long life, brings about prosperity, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the equinoxes, the solstices, and other such occasions;
on all meritorious days, whether in one's own home or in sacred shrines.
One should choose a Brahmin as the preceptor, and having obtained his permission,
one should have everything performed by him alone, for he is endowed with both learning and humility.

One should smear the level ground with cow dung and water. There, four lines should be drawn—eastward and northward—and they should all be equal, measuring three cubits each; thus, there shall be nine squares.
In that case, only five [squares] are to be taken; one should avoid the four corners.
Within those five compartments, one should place a lotus in each.
Upon heaps of white rice, one should place an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
within those rice-lotuses, one should install the five forms.
Having fashioned five golden images according to the prescribed rite,
he made the Lord of gold, seated and resplendent with armlets and a crown.
With four arms and noble limbs, adorned with bracelets and other ornaments,
he holds an axe in his right hand and a young deer in his left.
One should assign the gesture of fearlessness to the right [hand] and the trident to the left, as well as the three eyes;
likewise, one should assign Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, and Puruṣa.
One should fashion them from gold according to half a māna in weight:
Sadyojāta in the west, Vāmadeva in the north, and likewise Aghora in the south.
"Sadya" means "newly born.
One should place the Puruṣa denoted by the word "tat" (that) in the eastern compartment,
and likewise Īśāna in the middle of them.
Having honored the five forms in sequence with bathing, clothing, incense, lamps, and sacrificial food,
preceded by the measure [of offerings], one should worship them with the five Brahma-mantras.
And having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
And the Vedas, beginning with the *savya*, should be recited in their proper order.

The characteristics of Sadyojāta and the others have been described in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* regarding the gift of the mountain of sesame seeds (*tilaparvata*). There are five Brahmins for the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, which are well known among the Taittirīyas. Having performed all this himself, the donor—whether a woman or a man—should personally make the gift when the time for giving has arrived.
He was bathed by that teacher with kusha-grass water purified by mantras.
Having honored the Brahmin with perfumes and other offerings, one should recite these mantras;
a single image of the deity should be given to each one in succession.
Homage be to Sadyojāta, to Bhava, who is attached to worldly existence;
through the granting of your form, may there be for me attachment to worldly existence.
To Soma, to Vāmadeva, to Śiva, who is the embodiment of auspiciousness—
may there always be only auspiciousness for me through the granting of your form.
Homage to you, who are both non-terrible and terrible, whose activity is the dissolution of the world!
I have come to you for refuge; remove my fear without hesitation.
To the primordial Puruṣa, to Hara, the bestower of boons—to you, may there be salutation;
through the granting of your form to me, may there be prosperity.
The Lord of the worlds, the Sovereign of the gods who grants fearlessness—
O Lord of all remaining beings, protect me who have come to you for refuge.
Having circumambulated three times clockwise and holding a handful of flowers,
one should then prostrate and offer them with these mantras in due order.
One should give the middle portion to the preceptor, or cause it to be given to another;
one should also give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor, consisting of gold and two garments.
Whether a man or a woman, whoever should perform this here on earth,
shall be liberated from all sins and attain union with Śiva.
Thus have the sages described the fourfold gift to Nārada;
and just as he spoke it, so too has that fivefold form been declared by me.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the five forms. Now follows the gift of the directions (*digdāna*), according to the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"On the full moon day of Kārttika, under the deity Agni, [one should perform the rite] for Viṣṇu, Brahmā, or Antaka."
One should designate the four directions, beginning with the east, together with the earth.
And auspicious figures in female attire should be made, holding full water-jars in their hands;
the Earth, in the form of a cow, should be fashioned, endowed with all the characteristic marks.
Having fashioned five lotus-shaped objects out of two pieces of gold,
one should then honor five brahmins with fine garments and ornaments.
O King, he who places a copper vessel upon a leaf of the plantain tree and gives it away along with a seat, by him the entire earth has been gifted.
The ancestors dwelling in the world of the fathers and the gods dwelling in the celestial realm,
being satisfied, gratify him with wealth, sons, and desired riches.
Having given this according to the prescribed rule, one should eat food that is free from black gram.
Thus ends the procedure for the burning of the quarters. Now follows the gift dedicated to the five deities, according to the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Now I shall proclaim the gift; let the stainless sages listen."
"The fivefold divinity" was thus declared by the Self-born One to Nārada.
It bestows physical health, longevity, prosperity, and destroys evil;
by performing it, a man or a woman may attain a full lifespan.
On all auspicious occasions, and especially on one's birth-star,
one should always practice giving in a sacred place or at home.
But for one who has seen a bad dream or a portentous marvel, in order to pacify all defects,
one should perform this gift equally, endowed with supreme faith.
Having bathed in the morning with water infused with *kuśa* grass, wearing clean garments and with a serene mind,
he should worship a learned Brahmin and obtain his permission.
Agni, Soma, Varuṇa, the goddess Sarasvatī,
and Agni-Viṣṇu— these, O Brāhmaṇas, are declared to be the five deities.

The characteristics of Agni and others have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*; the characteristics of Sarasvatī have been described in the *Sarasvatīdāna*. The characteristics of Agni and Viṣṇu have been stated by Aparājita:
"Agni and Viṣṇu are to be fashioned standing together upon a lotus;
therein, Agni has a sacrificial ladle (*śruk*) in his hand, while he holds a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*)."
"Viṣṇu is the bearer of the mace and the lotus, as well as the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Having thus designated these five [deities] and having propitiated the Brahmins, one should cause them to be given.
For each [deity], two bright garments with gold [ornaments] should be offered in due order, saying:
"May this divine Lord Soma be pleased."
He should give that same sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin who acts as the instructor.
He should have five twice-born men recite for him the auspicious day, well-being, and prosperity;
and to them also, a sacrificial fee should be given according to their merit.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the five deities.
Now follows the gift of the eight world-protectors (*lokapālāṣṭaka*), according to the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"The divine group of the eight world-protectors is directly [manifested] and is exceedingly difficult to obtain."
It brings about all prosperity, is secret, and destroys the armies of adversaries.
The constant protection of one’s own country, the increase of elephants and horses,
the bringing forth of sons, merit, and the promotion of the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
At the previously mentioned place and time, having worshipped Śiva in the center of the mandala upon the altar, according to the rule and in due order.
One should prepare altars made of sand in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
having invited eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, the gods, and the Vedāṅgas.
Those who had conquered their senses, born of noble lineage, endowed with all auspicious marks,
seated facing Shiva, and dressed in unwashed garments;
One should worship the world-protectors with divine garments and ornaments using their respective mantras,
and one should worship the Brahmins in due order with perfumes, flowers, and incense.

In this rite, the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the mandala, the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the altar (*vedikā*), the canopy (*vitāna*), and so forth, should be understood as being like that described for the *tulāpuruṣa* gift in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*. Regarding the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) here: having prepared eight altars (*sthaṇḍila*) around the Śiva-altar, one should install there eight world-guardians (*lokapāla*) fashioned from gold according to one’s capacity, seated upon new cloths and facing Śiva; having worshipped them with garments and other offerings, one should then honor the Brāhmaṇas. The characteristics of the world-guardians have been stated in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*:
"To the east, one should offer oblations into the fire with the mantras of the eight world-guardians."
The oblation should be offered with fuel sticks and clarified butter, following the sequence of the fire-ritual.
Having thus performed the rite according to the injunctions, the sacrificer, adorned with all ornaments, should invite Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas.
Having prepared them and worshipped them, one should then cause wealth to be given to the twice-born;
specifically, ten niṣkas and ornaments for each, accompanied by their respective mantras.
With ten niṣkas, one should separately provide clothing and the like, as well as a seat and a woolen blanket;
there, the ritual bathing of Śiva must be performed according to the prescribed rules.
And a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to the extent of one's wealth.

[796] The sequence for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) begins with the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*) and ends with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). In the *Kāmika*, however, one should perform the *homa* on a single sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or in a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*). In the *Vātula*, the preceptor should perform the *homa* in the direction starting from the east (the quarter of Śakra).

With the mantras of the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*), one hundred and eight oblations should be offered separately with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and clarified butter (*ghṛta*); at the end, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Regarding the phrase "with ten *niṣkas*": having honored those Brahmins who are *lokeśas*, the patron (*yajamāna*) should give to each of them an ornament consisting of ten *niṣkas*, along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of gold equal in value to that, as well as garments and other items. The term "sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇā*) here refers to the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*), which should be given according to one's wealth. However, in the *Kāmika-tantra*, it is stated that the sacrificial fee should consist of ten *niṣkas* accompanied by ornaments. In the *Vātula-tantra*, on the other hand, a fee of one hundred *niṣkas* for each of the nine teachers is prescribed.
The man who makes this gift to the Lords of the World with devotion,
having established himself firmly as a Lord of the World in those stations,
shall dwell happily for a kalpa in the City of Śiva and then become a sovereign ruler upon the earth.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the eight world-protectors (lokapālas).
Now, from the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Listen, O Nārada, may it be well with you; I shall describe the gift that destroys all sins."
It is auspicious in every way, bestowing long life, health, prosperity, and goodness.
[797] For this is the supreme among gifts, the highest means for accomplishing all success;
whether it be a woman who gives this gift, she shall attain union with Brahman.
At the equinoxes, at the solstices, during the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
on other auspicious occasions, and especially on one's own birth-star.
One should perform the act of giving in a temple, on a riverbank, or in one's own home,
O Nārada, in all those meritorious places mentioned in the Purāṇas.
A square, level ground, smeared with cow-dung water,
measuring six cubits, eight hands, ten, or twelve cubits [in size].
Four equal lines should be drawn toward the east and the north;
there, nine squares should be formed using heaps of white rice grains.
One should arrange auspicious lotuses provided with eight white petals;
in the central square of those, one should place the golden image of the Lord, the imperishable creator of the world.
Brahmā seated upon a lotus;
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa,
Vāyu, Soma, and Rudra, in due order, starting from the east and so forth.
One should fashion eight deities made of gold, equipped with their own weapons,
weighing three palas each of gold, or fashioned according to one's capacity.
One should establish all of them facing toward Brahmā in all [the directions].
[He should fashion] images made of gold and of refined gold. The characteristics of Brahmā and the world-protectors have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*.
Having wrapped each one individually in a cloth and having sprinkled them with water mixed with *kuśa* grass, the wise man who causes this to be done should perform it in this manner.
When the time for giving has arrived, the donor, having bathed with water infused with *kuśa* grass,
with a serene mind and countenance, [should honor] those headed by Parameṣṭhin.
Having worshipped with devotion using their own names as mantras ending in "namas," and having honored the Brahmins with perfumes and other offerings in due order;
"May he be well-pleased with me," having spoken thus.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to that brahmin who causes [the rite] to be performed:
gold calculated by weight, as well as two garments.
I have already described to you the gift called "of the World Guardians" (lokapāla), which was taught by the divine sages;
now tell me this, if you wish to hear it in its proper sequence.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Now follows the gift of the eight Rudras, according to the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Listen, O divine sage, to this secret gift which bestows all goals upon men."
This is known as the Rudrāṣṭaka, together with their wives and sons.

There, one should fashion lotuses upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) using rice grains. One should place a golden image of Brahmā in the central square, and on its side, one should fashion the altar of the Vedas (*chandovedī*) with half that size.
And [one should worship] the goddess Chandodevī and Gāyatrī. Their characteristics are described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*:
"One should fashion eight golden Rudras, made with half the size of Brahmā, and arrange them all around, starting from the east and ending in the northeast."
With half of that [quantity], one should fashion golden [images] for each side of Rudra;
having fashioned their goddesses and sons, a man should worship them.
The worship should be performed with their respective mantras accompanied by salutations;
one should worship Brahmā and the others with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.
Then, having performed circumambulation and prostrated in due order,

Having honored the instructor, one should give the middle [offering] with the mantra:
"May the Blessed Lord Brahmā, the Supreme Abider, the Grandfather, be pleased."
Thus, one should give the gift accompanied by the eight Rudras according to the prescribed rite;
thereby, being completely liberated from all sins and having attained all perfections, [one attains the supreme goal].
Endowed with long life and health, possessed of sons and wealth, and happy,
he enjoys pleasures as he desires and attains both heaven and liberation.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the eight Rudras.
Now follows the gift of the planets, according to the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
Sūta said:

Rāma should be depicted as a youth with a serene countenance, possessing the shoulders of a lion and great strength; his arms should reach down to his knees, and he should be holding a bow and an arrow.

and possessing two long arms.

seated in the lotus posture, two-armed, and absorbed in meditation— such is the Buddha as he is proclaimed.

With fragrant flowers, incense, and likewise with lamps,

just as salt thrown into milk dissolves it without leaving a trace.

For this all-pervading Lord has a body composed of the entire world.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the gift of the ten incarnations.
Now follows the gift of the Viśvāmaras, according to the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:

By performing which, a man or a woman may attain the world of Brahmā.

Just as the Blessed Lord Brahmā spoke to the celestial sage Nārada,

One should propitiate [the deity] in the north at the conclusion.
"Six to the south," and so forth: having drawn six lines extending from south to north, and having laid down four lines extending from east to west, one should produce fifteen squares.

Having fashioned as many lotuses made of rice-grains as there are [deities] among them, one should install the deities to be described hereafter. Among these, the characteristics of Āditya and Vasu have been stated in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*; the characteristic of Rudra has been stated in the *Viśvacakra*; their names are given in the *Tulāpuruṣadāna*; the characteristics and names of the Viśvedevas are in the *Viśvāmaradāna*; the characteristics and names of the Maruts are in the *Maruddāna*; and those of the Sādhyas are in the *Sādhyadāna*.
Then, one should worship Mahendra, the sovereign lord of the worlds, together with the hosts of gods.
Having honored him, one should give to that preceptor a pair of garments and golden ornaments.
Then that brahmin, his limbs adorned with ornaments and wrapped in a pair of garments,
should worship the foremost leaders of the hosts of gods.
Then one should commence the fire offering for the deities.
One should offer a bath, clothing, water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, water for sipping, fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and food; among these,
one should present the middle portion to the God of gods.
One should worship according to the ritual prescribed by the scriptures.
Having established the fire and swept around it, one should strew it with *darbha* grass; then,
having taken clarified butter and honored the ladle according to the rule, [one should fill it] with ghee.
And for each [of these], there is one offering of ten oblations.
Having likewise offered one hundred or ten oblations to the Gaṇas,
and having completed the sacrifice to Indra according to the prescribed rite;
The remaining [oblations] are likewise offered with the *vyāhṛtis* collectively.
Thus, this must be performed by the preceptor himself;
or else, the donor himself may perform the act of giving here,
having bathed and been sprinkled with water by the preceptor while wearing fresh garments.
With purifying water from kusa grass and with Yajus mantras.
Having worshipped each one of the preeminent brahmins in turn, [the gift] should be given;
and together with the hosts of gods, a circumambulation should be performed.
Having offered [them] with palms joined in reverence and accompanied by flowers.
Having said, "May he be pleased with me," one should give everything here preceded by water;
then, having caused this to be given to the teacher, [one should proceed].
And one should have the Brahmins recite the *svasti* benediction with five verses.
Having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to those reciters,
one should then worship the Brahmins and the preceptor (*guru*);
likewise, having performed the offering to the gods (*devadāna*) in this manner.
Then, one is liberated from all multitudes of diseases.
Having performed this gift to the Lord of the hosts of gods,
he attains the highest longevity and health,
and after enjoying abundant worldly pleasures, he reaches the pinnacle.
From there, one shall go to the vast world of Brahmā.
Thus, O best of eminent sages, this gift known as Gaṇeśa was formerly proclaimed by the celestial rishis and even by Brahmā himself, the Self-Existent.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Lord of the Hosts of Devas. Now follows the gift of the Nignābha, according to the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
Now I shall proclaim another gift;
let all the sages assembled here listen,
just as [I once spoke] to the seer Nārada in the past.
The creator of the world, the lotus-born one, spoke thus.
Having performed this, whether a man or a woman, one obtains the desired fruit in both worlds,
and furthermore, one attains a full lifespan free from diseases.
He is liberated and attains the world of the Moon.
During the [astrological] periods, such as those beginning with a solar eclipse, one should perform this gift;
likewise, one should perform it at that which is designated as *nirnābha*.
In various places, such as temples and other sacred sites.
Or, wherever he may take pleasure in his home,
one should give to a twice-born man who is skilled in the Vedas and Purāṇas and devoted to the sacrificial rites the *Anumāna* [text] that appears in the *Nimna*.
Having respectfully embraced the brahmin preceptor.
With that very same brahmin, the sacrificer should diligently have everything performed;
he himself should personally make the gift known as the *nirnābha*.
On the ground smeared with cow dung, one should cause ten and five lotuses to be made with white rice grains, arranged equally from south to north.
One should fashion mandalas out of gold according to one's capacity;
within them, one should place three mandalas for each lotus.
Whatever principles such as life-force (āyus) and the rest truly exist within the body,
one should meditate upon them and then worship them with scents and other offerings, using mantras that are not [specifically] prescribed.
These are life-force (*āyus*) and the others, beginning with the ear, according to the scriptural statement: "The ear is life-force. Their sequence is given in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these are the sequence."
"Space, wind, fire, water, and earth— in this sequence,
the sages know these to be the fifteen principles (tattvas).
Having honored the brahmins, [the gift] should be given to each one in due order.
One should cause the disciple to recite the mantras for the gift of fire, as instructed by the Guru.
One should have the recitation of the *svastivācana* performed by five [priests] together with the preceptor;
and one should give a gift consisting of a cow, gold, and two garments.
Alternatively, one may cause a pair of lotuses to be given even to each individual;
or one may give everything to the guru after making a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) regarding that for which the recitation is performed.
O sinless one, if one should give one [portion] to the preceptor and give the others to many [others],
the performer obtains the fulfillment of his desires through that gift.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of Nignābha.
Now, the gift of Gaṇeśa is described in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"I shall fully explain the gift of Gaṇeśa in the pavilion previously mentioned."
Having fully worshipped the Lord of the gods of gods, who is surrounded by the guardians of the world;
Having fashioned an image of Vighneśvara adorned with all ornaments according to the scriptures using ten niṣkas, one should then worship it according to the prescribed rite.

In this matter, the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the mandala, the altar (*vedikā*), the canopy (*vitāna*), and so forth, should be understood as prescribed in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* for the *Tulāpuruṣa* rite.
Having worshipped Maheśvara, the Lord of the gods of gods, together with the Lokapālas made of gold, one should worship the Lords of Obstacles (*Vighneśas*) in the eight directions surrounding him.
Because they are lords over the hosts of obstructors (*vighna*) consisting of seventy million mantras, they are therefore called *Gaṇeśas*. And they are as follows:
"Now, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śiva, and also Ekanetraka;
Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍaka. Thus it is said.

The Gaṇeśas mentioned here are the Vighneśas spoken of by Śiva; each of them should be fashioned from ten niṣkas of gold. As it is stated in the Kāmika: "The Guru [should worship] these individually within their own enclosure, having fashioned them separately from ten niṣkas of gold, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings."

"One should offer oblations to Īśa in the principal [direction] and to the Lords of Obstacles (Vighneśas) in the eight directions. As for their characteristics, they are [described] in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
"In the left hand [he holds] a water-pot (*kuṇḍī*), a noose, a goad, and a trident."
In some cases, the [four] right hands hold a spear, a vajra, a rosary, a sword, and a discus.
Wearing a leopard skin, seated upon a lotus, with a serpent as his sacred thread,
having one face or five faces, three eyes, and bearing matted hair and the moon— such is Śiva.
In the four cardinal directions are Ananta and the others, red, blue, white, and crimson;
and in the corners are Ekarudra and the others, white, blood-red, blue, and dark red.
All [the deities] should be depicted with eight arms, four faces, and matted hair;
they bear the weapons of Śiva and possess three eyes, though in some cases they are without the goad and the sword.
[824] The lords of obstacles (vighneśas) are of various colors, have matted hair, possess three eyes, and carry tridents; all of them have single faces and join their palms in reverence.
The characteristics of the world-protectors have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*.
One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) as before in eight sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) located in the eight directions,
following the path of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*) and according to the traditional succession.
"As before" means as described in the *Liṅga Purāṇa* regarding the *Tulāpuruṣa* rite. Having worshipped seven Brahmins and likewise one maiden in the north,
he should cause all the Tantras to be given in due order with their respective mantras.
By giving in this manner, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt about this.

The meaning is as follows: one should perform the worship of Śiva—who is endowed with five enclosures (āvaraṇas) beginning with the Five Brahmans—and the fire-oblation (homa) in the central principal pit; however, in the directional pits, there is a homa for the Vighneśas who are joined with their respective five enclosures as taught by the lineage of gurus. Having worshipped seven Brahmins in the seven directions starting from Īśāna and one girl in the northern direction, one should give all the Tantras and the Vighneśas who consist of all the Tantras to those eight persons—the seven Brahmins and the girl—each with their own respective mantra. There is a reading, "dāpayet sarvavidyeśān" (one should cause [them] to give all the Vidyeśas), because of the statement in the *Kāmika*: "One should give the Vidyeśas to them in sequence with their own respective mantras. Furthermore, the worship of the five enclosures should be understood as that described in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*.
Having examined the ground according to rule by its fragrance, color, taste, and other qualities, one should prepare a place there that is pleasing to the mind, with a canopy spread across the sky.
On the surface of the earth, which has been well-smeared and resembles the surface of a mirror,
one should draw the eastern line according to the method seen in the ancient scriptures.
Having prepared a mandala measuring either one cubit or two cubits,
one should draw a large eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
With powders such as red powder, gathered according to availability,
combined with *prativāruṇa*, and endowed with great beauty.
The Siddhis are to be assigned to the petals,
and the Rudras, Vāma and the rest, eight in number along with their Śaktis, are to be placed upon the filaments in order, starting from the east and proceeding around.
In the pericarp is Vairūpya; in the seeds are the nine Śaktis;
in the bulb is Dharma whose nature is Śiva; and in the stalk is Jñāna which has Śiva as its refuge.
Above the pericarp are the mandalas of Fire, Sun, and Moon;
beyond these are the three principles known as Śiva-tattva, Vidyā-tattva, and Ātman-tattva.
Facing upward above all the seats and adorned with various flowers,
it is exceedingly radiant through the Vidyā within the expanse of the supreme ether.
Having imagined a seat and invoked the Supreme Lord in embodied form,
one should worship Him together with the Mother according to the path of the five colors.
Resembling pure crystal, serene, and cool-rayed;
resembling a circle of lightning, adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Equipped with the finest of divine weapons, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents,
clad in a tiger skin, his lotus-like face bore a slight smile.
With the soles of his feet and palms resembling the petals of a red lotus,
endowed with all the primary marks, and adorned with every ornament.
Five-faced and ten-armed, with a crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
possessing an unprecedented countenance that is serene and radiant like the rising sun.
Abounding with lotus-like eyes, adorned with the crescent moon as a crest-ornament,
and possessing a southern face with a luster as beautiful as a dark blue cloud.
Terrible, with a face contorted by a frown, possessing three round red eyes,
formidable with bared fangs, and with quivering sprout-like lips.
The upper face resembles coral, adorned with dark locks of hair;
it possesses three playful eyes and has a crescent moon as its crest-ornament.
The western face has the luster of the full moon, radiant with three eyes;
it is exceedingly serene, blossoming, and brilliant with three eyes.
On the right [hand], he holds a trident, an axe, a vajra, and a sword, blazing with fire;
he bears the crescent moon, is gentle, and is captivating with a mild smile.
The fifth [wheel] resembles crystal and is illuminated by the crescent moon;
on the left, it shines with the serpent, the iron arrow, the bell, the noose, and the goad.
It extends from the knees up to the navel through the Nivṛtti [kalā], and from the navel up to the heart through the Pratiṣṭhā [kalā].
Likewise, [the body] up to the throat is [pervaded] by Vidyā; up to the forehead by Śānti;
and above that, by the supreme kalā known as Śāntyatītā.
Therefore, it pervades the five paths and has the form of the pentad of kalās.
The god whose crown is Īśāna is the ancient one called Puruṣa;
likewise, Aghora is his heart, and Vāma is the secret organ of Maheśvara.
Then [he should meditate on] Sadyojāta and the rest, whose form consists of thirty-eight kalās,
