which consists of the Mātṛkās, which is Īśāna, and which consists of the five Brahmans.
And this very one called Oṃkāra, the Haṃsa endowed with Śakti—
the Lord consisting of five syllables, or indeed consisting of six syllables.
Endowed with the six limbs and possessed of the six births,
by what power do I desire to mount that water-pot?
One should directly perceive Sadāśiva, whose form is the Vidyā, as consisting of the three principles: through the one called Jñāna on the right and through the one called Kriyā on the left.
Having conceived [the deity] as having form and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa through the rite,
one should worship according to the rule with the root-vidyā up to the offering of arghya.
Having invoked there Mahādeva— who is Śiva himself in embodied form, together with his supreme Śakti, and who is devoid of the manifestation of existence and non-existence— [one should worship him].
Having performed the five-fold service (pañcopacāra), one should worship the Supreme Lord with the [five] Brahma-mantras,
the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), and also with the Mātṛkā.
By means of the Praṇava, by Śiva himself joined with Śakti in due order,
by the Śānta mantra, and likewise by all other divine mantras in their entirety.
One should worship the supreme deity either with Śiva alone,
having made Īśāna the face beginning with Sadyojāta, or else without the ritual bathing.
One should then commence the worship of the five obstructions (pañcāvaraṇa-pūjā) in due order;
therein, first, on the right and left sides of the two Śivas respectively.
First, one should worship the deities Heramba and Ṣaṇmukha with perfumes and other offerings; thereafter, one should worship the Brahmāṇīs in order, starting from Īśāna and proceeding around them.
One should worship the [deities] together with their powers (śaktis) up to Sadyojāta in the first enclosure;
likewise, one should worship the six limbs, beginning with the heart, in that very same place in their proper sequence.
One should worship Śiva and Śivā in the Vāmā and other directions.

Therein, one may or may not worship the eight Rudras, beginning with Vāma, together with their powers (śaktis), such as Vāmā and the rest, subsequently, in order, surrounding the area starting from the east.
The six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and the Rudras beginning with Vāma are shown in that very [text]:
"The heart, the head, the crest-lock, the armor, and the eye—
these six limbs have been declared by the wise as 'Svasti me' and so forth."
Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, as well as Rudra, Kāla, Vikaraṇa,
Balavikaraṇa, and likewise Balapramathana.
The subduer of all beings and those eight Śaktis of such a kind constitute the first enclosure; now hear about the second enclosure.
One should worship Ananta together with Śakti on the petal of the eastern direction,
and likewise worship Ekanetra on the petal of the northern direction in that very same place.
One should worship Ekanetra and his Śakti on the petal in the northeast direction, and Trimūrti and his Śakti on the petal in the southeast direction.
One should worship Śrīkaṇṭha on the southwestern petal and his Śakti to his left; then, one should likewise worship Śikhaṇḍīśa on the northwestern petal.
In the first enclosure, there is no worship, or alternatively, those [gods] of the universal monarchs;
in the third enclosure, the eight forms [of Śiva] are to be worshipped along with their Śaktis.
In the eight [directions] are Śarva, Īśāna, Rudra, Paśupati, Ugra, Bhīma, and Mahādeva; these are the eight forms in sequence.
And in the intervals between these, the eleven forms beginning with Mahādeva, together with their Śaktis, are to be worshipped in succession.
Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita,
Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, and Bhavodbhava.
And Kapālīśa are likewise said to be the eleven Śaktis;
among them, eight are to be worshipped first, beginning with the southeast (Āgneyī) in due order.
Devadeva is on the eastern petal; Īśāna is in the southeast;
Bhavodbhava is between those two; and Kapālīśa is beyond that.
Within that enclosure, one should further worship the Lord of Bulls (Śiva) in front;
Nandin to his right, and likewise Mahākāla to the north.
The Teacher [Śākyamuni] is on the petal in the southeast; [the deity] Mātṛkā (? is on the southern petal;
Gajānana is on the southwestern petal; and then Ṣaṇmukha is on the western petal.
One should worship Jyeṣṭhā on the petal of Vāyu (the northwest), Gaurī in the north, Caṇḍa in the northeast, and Munīndra and Vṛṣabha between Śāstṛ and Nandīśa.
One should worship Piṅgala to the north of Mahākāla,
and then Bhṛṅgīśvara in the midst of the assembly of the Teacher’s Mothers.
One should worship Vīrabhadra between Mātṛkā and Vighneśa;
one should conquer Goddess Sarasvatī between Skanda and Vighneśa.
One should worship Mahāmodī between Jyeṣṭhā and Kumāra;
one should worship the goddess Durgā between Gaṇāmbā and Caṇḍa.
In that very same obscuration (āvaraṇa), there is further the assembly of Śiva’s attendants,
known as the first ground of Rudra, which is threefold and consists of his own powers (śakti).
One should worship the circle of Śivā’s companions after meditating upon them on all sides;
thus, when the third enclosure has been expanded and worshipped in this manner.
Having meditated upon the fourth enclosure, one should worship outside of it:
Bhānu is to be worshipped on the eastern petal, and the four-faced Brahmā on the south.
Rudra is on the petal in the direction of Varuṇa, and Viṣṇu is on the petal in the northern direction;
now follow the individual enclosures for each of these four deities.
Immediately after that worship, one should perform [the rite] according to the method prescribed in its own scripture;
or else, having worshipped the Sun, one should sacrifice in the first enclosure.
In his own self, there are first six [powers], beginning with Dīptā and the others;
namely, Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jyā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, and Vimalā, in due order.
Amoghā and Vidyutā are likewise situated around the east and the other directions;
these four forms are to be worshipped in sequence in the second enclosure.
Beyond that are the powers (śaktis) starting from the east and ending with the north;
then, in successive order, Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, and Ravi.
Arka, Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu are thus the sons of Vivasvat;
they are situated in the eastern quarter by way of expansion, or else they stand in the south.
One should nourish Bodhanī in the western part, and then Āpyāyinī in the north;
likewise Uṣā, Prabhā, Prajñā, and Saṃdhyā thereafter.
In the second enclosure, one should worship in the corners beginning with Īśāna:
Soma, Aṅgāraka, and Budha, the best among the wise.
Bṛhaspati of vast intellect, Mārgava, the treasury of splendors,
as well as Śanaiścara, Rāhu, Ketu, and the terrifying Dhūmra.
One should worship these in order around the entire third enclosure;
or alternatively, one should worship the twelve Ādityas in the second enclosure.
And in the third enclosure, one should worship the twelve zodiac signs,
and also the hosts of the seven planets all around its exterior.
The sages, gods, and gandharvas; the pannagas and hosts of apsarases; the grāmaṇīs, as well as the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and horses.
One should worship the Vālakhilyas, who consist of the seven meters;
thus, having fully honored the Sun-god with three enclosures.
One should then worship Brahmā together with his three enclosures:
Hiraṇyagarbha in the east and Virāj in the south.
One should worship Kāla in the western quarter and Puruṣa in the north;
Hiraṇyavarṇa is the first, and Brahmā resembles a lotus.
Time is like collyrium made from birth; the Puruṣa is like crystal.
He consists of the three qualities: indeed, he is rājasa, tāmasa, and likewise sāttvika.
These four are situated respectively in the first enclosure;
in the second enclosure, they are to be worshipped in order, starting from the east and proceeding around.
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana—
one should worship these Prajāpatis in the third enclosure from the west.
The eight ancestors, however, are: Pūrvā, Trīṇi, Prāk, Paścāt, and Uttara in sequence;
then Dakṣa, Ruci, Bhṛgu, Marīci, and Aṅgiras.
Paulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Atri, Kaśyapa,
and Vasiṣṭha— these are renowned as the lords of progeny.
Their wives, together with them, are to be honored in due order:
Prasūti, Kūti, Khyāti, and Saṃbhūti.
Smṛti, Prīti, Kṣamā, Santati, Anasūyā, Devamātā, and Arundhatī— all of them were indeed devoted to their vows.
One should worship the four Vedas as his attendants in the first enclosure— those who are constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, illustrious, and of pleasing appearance.
Furthermore, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are in the second enclosure;
thereafter, in the third enclosure, are those preceded by the Dharmaśāstras.
All Vedic sciences are indeed to be honored on all sides;
however, the Vedas are to be revered starting from the east and proceeding around, while others may be honored according to one's preference.
Having divided [the area] into eight or four parts and having worshipped [it] on all sides,
one should thus honor Brahmā together with his three enclosures.
One should subsequently worship Rudra with his enclosures in the south and west;
his six Brahma-aṅgas are known as the first enclosure.
The second enclosure likewise consists of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras);
as for the distinction found in the third enclosure, it is now described.
Her four forms are to be worshipped in order, starting from the east;
the three-fold, manifest deity in the front is known by the name Śiva.
The Rajasic Brahma, the creator, is always worshipped in the south;
the Tamasic Agni, the destroyer Hara, is to be worshipped in the west.
Sāttvika, Sukhakṛt, Saumya, Viṣṇu, Viśvapati, and Mṛḍa— thus,
in the western quarter, are the twenty-six auspicious forms of Śambhu.
Having worshipped thoroughly, one should then worship Vaikuṇṭha in the northern quarter;
one should sacrifice to Vāsudeva in the first enclosure in front of him.
One should worship Aniruddha in the south, Pradyumna in the west from there, and Saṃkarṣaṇa in the north; or alternatively, one may worship these two [Pradyumna and Saṃkarṣaṇa] here.
The first enclosure has been described; now hear of the second enclosure:
Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nārasiṃha, and Vāmana.
Kṛṣṇa is one among the Rāmas, and you are also horse-faced;
one should worship one [deity] in the eastern part of the third enclosure.
One should worship the weapon named Nārāyaṇa in the south, which is in some cases unimpeded;
and Pāñcajanya in the west, and the Śārṅga bow in the north.
Thus, having fashioned the image of the supreme Hari known as Viṣṇu— who possesses three enclosures,
who is Mahāviṣṇu, and who is the eternal Viṣṇu— one should worship him.
Having thus worshipped the fourfold group of four emanations in sequence as the four forms,
one should then worship their four powers in order.
One should worship Prabhā in the south-eastern quarter, Sarasvatī in the south-west,
Gaṇāmbikā in the north-west, and Lakṣmī in the north-east.

Having thus performed the worship of the forms of Bhānu and the others, as well as their respective powers, one should immediately thereafter worship the Lords of the World (lokeśas) in that very same enclosure.
One should worship Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa,
Vāyu, Soma, Kubera, and Īśāna in the western direction.
Having thus worshipped the fourth enclosure according to the prescribed rite,
one should worship the weapons of Maheśa outside the lotus.
One should worship the glorious trident in the northeast, the vajra in the direction of Mahendra (the east), the axe in the region of the fire (southeast), and the arrow in the south.
One should worship Aṅkuśa in the western quarter and Pināka in the northern quarter;
having thus worshipped the enclosure, one should thereafter worship outside.
One should worship Kṣetrapāla facing west in the fierce [direction],
either outside all the surrounding deities or specifically in the west.
One should worship together with the five mother-cows in front of a great bull;
they are Nandā, Subhadrā, Surabhī, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā.
These five mothers of cattle are established in the world of Śiva;
therefore, all those of divine origin are indeed to be worshipped on every side.
The sky-faring ṛṣis, the Siddhas, the Daityas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas,
as well as the lords of the Nāgas beginning with Ananta, together with the Nāgas born of their lineages, were there.
The ḍākinīs, bhūtas, vaitālas, pretas, and bhairava leaders,
as well as others dwelling in the subterranean realms (pātāla) who have arisen from various wombs.
Rivers, oceans, mountains, forests, and lakes;
beasts, birds, trees, insects, and other beings of lowly birth.
And there are men of various forms and animals of low birth;
these are the worlds within the cosmic egg, and from that arise millions of cosmic eggs.
The external cosmic eggs are enumerated by the great lords;
the Rudras who support the Brahmāṇḍa are stationed in the ten directions.
Whatever is secondary, whatever is to be given through the sacrificial cup, or whatever is possible beyond that—
whatever meaning whatsoever belongs to a word, whether it be a sentence consisting of conscious or unconscious elements.
Having understood all that in the presence of Śiva and Śivā, one should worship them collectively;
all [the deities] should be visualized with palms joined in reverence and with smiling faces.
And always gazing with reverence upon the God and the Goddess—
having thus worshipped the enclosures for the sake of pacifying all misfortune.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more, one should utter the five-syllabled mantra;
thereafter, one should offer to Śiva and Śivā that which is like nectar.
The great *caru* oblation should consist of pure rice with its seasonings and six flavors;
the best is thirty-two *āḍhaka*s in measure, while the middling is at least one *āḍhaka*.
Having prepared it according to one's means, one should offer it with faith;
then, having offered water for drinking and betel leaves along with their stalks.
Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and other rites, one should complete the remainder of the worship;
one should procure specifically those substances that are useful for yoga.
A wise person should not practice stinginess with wealth when they possess it,
even toward Śiva, who remains indifferent and may even perform defective rites.
It is the teaching of the virtuous that rites performed for the sake of desire do not bear fruit at all;
therefore, having abandoned deceit and indifference, one should practice through the application of all limbs.
One should perform rites for specific desires if one wishes for the attainment of their fruits;
having thus completed the worship and bowed to the God and the Goddess.
Having completed the worship with devotion, one should then recite the hymn;
thereafter, at the conclusion of the hymn-recitation, the excellent number is one hundred and eight.
Eagerly, one should recite the five-syllable mantra more than a thousand times;
having performed worship of the Guru, one should subsequently offer worship according to the prescribed order.
One should also honor the members of the assembly according to one's means and according to their faith;
then, having bid farewell to the Lord of Gods together with all his retinues.
One should present the mandala to the guru together with the implements of yoga;
or alternatively, one may give it to those who have taken refuge in Śiva, all of them according to their respective fitness.
Alternatively, one should offer it for the sake of Śiva alone in a sacred field of Śiva (śivakṣetra),
or one should worship the Lord in the Śiva-fire with the seven substances for oblation (homadravya).
Having worshipped all the deities of the enclosure as before,
Yogeśvara thus became renowned throughout the three worlds.
Therefore, there is no yoga whatsoever superior to this anywhere in the world; indeed, there is nothing in this universe that cannot be accomplished by means of it.
Whether the fruit be something pertaining to this life or even to the next life,
it cannot be determined that "this is its fruit" and "that is not."
This [practice] is the most excellent means for accomplishing all forms of the highest good; however,
it can be said that whatever is offered by a person from this [practice],
like a wish-fulfilling gem, that very fruit is obtained by him.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of Gaṇeśa.
Now follows the gift of Marut from the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain; listen, O best of sages."
This is proclaimed as the "Gift of the Maruts," which destroys all sins.
[837] Formerly, in the age of the gods, the divine Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
being questioned by the sage Nārada, spoke this to Nārada.
Listen, Nārada—blessings be upon you—the gift that bestows all fruits;
whatever the giver desires, he obtains that very fruit.
On all auspicious occasions, especially on one's birth-star,
and in all sacred places or at home, one should perform the act of giving.
There were forty-nine gods, equal in splendor to the Lord of the Gods;
they were the Maruts, brothers of Puruhūta, possessing the brilliance of the sun.
Adorned with crowns, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments, they constantly carry swords and shields; these are the eternal attendants of Śakra.
One should have images of them fashioned in the form of paramours;
all those gifts for them should be performed by the Brahmin alone.
In a clean place, having smeared a level area with cow-dung water,
one should draw six equal lines there, running from south to north.
First, there should be eleven lines; this is called a grid of fifty squares.
All squares are equal and four-cornered, measuring three cubits.
In the middle row of the enclosure, situated in the sixth [cell] from the north, is what is called the seat of Indra; the others are likewise the Maruts.
Having fashioned lotuses in all the enclosures with circles of white rice,
one should begin the seat of the deity.
One should establish them upon those [supports] in their proper sequence.

Here, having drawn six lines from south to north, fifty squares are produced by means of eleven lines extending east to west. There, in the central row, in the sixth square from the north, is the seat of Indra; the remaining squares are for the Maruts. Regarding the seats of the Maruts and their names, they are [found] in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Then they assigned their names individually according to their parents, and indeed by means of corresponding rites, ending with the Maruts."
Śukrajyotis, as well as Āditya; Citrajyotis, another;
Satyajyotis, Jyotisman, Satyaha, and likewise Ṛtapāḥ.
This first group has been declared; now learn the second:
Ṛtajit, Satyajit, Suṣeṇa, and likewise Senajit.
For there is the enemy who is close by, the enemy who is distant, and another who is the enemy within a group;
learn now concerning this third one.
Ṛta, Satya, Dhruva, Dhartṛ, Vidhartṛ, and Vidhāraya; Dharuṇa is the third, but now learn from me the fourth.
The Dhvāntas, the Dhunitas, and likewise the Sabharas as a host;
such are the Puruvas and the Anyādṛkṣas who come hither.
The Maruts are well-proportioned, with equal eyes and matching gazes; indeed, they are a host led by Indra, sharing their burden, and beyond them lie the divine clans.

"Yajña, Anuvartman, and likewise another, Mānuṣīviśa—these are declared to be the Daityas and Devas. These seven groups of seven constitute the forty-nine Maruts according to my tradition. Thus it is said.
Having first performed all the ritual actions here in this manner, starting from the east and proceeding to the north-east,
and having then wrapped [the object] with cloths and sprinkled it with water mixed with *kuśa* grass;
Having sprinkled [it] with Yajus mantras containing that [specific] indicative mark.

In the center is Mahendra, armed with the thunderbolt, bearing a spear, and wearing a diadem; his limbs are adorned with necklaces, armlets, and other ornaments, and he is made of gold of triple quality.
The lord of gods, the master of the world, is profoundly tranquil.
The word "kāryam" (should be done) is to be supplied. Having first worshipped the gods and the Maruts,
and immediately thereafter likewise the best of Brahmins.
One should offer each of these individually, performing circumambulation toward the northeast.
Then, when an auspicious and meritorious time has arrived, the donor,
having bathed and holding flowers in his hand, should circumambulate [the recipient] with water mixed with sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass.
Having indeed performed [the rite] together with the brahmin for all of them.
Having prostrated with a handful of flowers, one should cause the entire host of deities to be worshipped in sequence;
likewise for each of the preeminent brahmins.
Having prostrated, one should indeed recite the mantra.
He chose one god among the Maruts; likewise, O Lord, show favor to me, O God!
By your grace, may there be for me the destruction of my sins.
But the lords of the immortals are always of golden form.
Having spoken thus, the best of Brahmins should first offer [the image] to the Maruts and then offer the deity to Mahendra; he who should cause this to be done for him—
And the Brahmins, having first uttered the word "Svati," [proceeded].
Then, having honored the preceptor with an appropriate sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
he likewise gave suitable fees to the Brahmins who recited the benedictions (svastivācaka).
May the King of the Three Worlds, the sovereign of the universe, the lord of the gods, and the slayer of the hosts of Daityas,
the Divine One, bestow blessings upon me.
The elder brother of the gods, the wielder of the thunderbolt, is profoundly peaceful.
Having uttered this, one should then offer [the oblation] to the god Hari, the wielder of the vajra;
this mantra is proclaimed for use even by one who is capable of performing the worship.
Whoever performs such a gift for the Maruts according to the prescribed rite,
being endowed with all desires, rejoices like a god in heaven.
Just as Brahmā spoke the Veda to Nārada, the celestial sage,
so too have I related all of this to you, O best of sages.
Thus ends the procedure for the Maruts and Dānavas.
Now follows the procedure for the installation of the World (Bhuvanapratiṣṭhā) from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
By what gift, O Madhusūdana, does one obtain eternal stability in this world and the next, as well as wonderful fame?
And how all their fathers and grandfathers attain a good rebirth,
as well as an inexhaustible lineage in this world and abundant prosperity.
O delighter of the Yadus, O highly fortunate one, tell me how the installation of all the gods may be performed— whether by means of a gift or by means of a religious observance.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O King, you have asked well; it is beneficial for the worlds.
Listen with a focused mind to this most secret and supreme teaching."
I shall tell you in brief the foundation of the worlds:
the gods, asuras, nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
Pretas, Piśācas, and Bhūtas have undoubtedly been established during an auspicious moment of victory that is favorable to the performer.
On an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, and on a day joined by benign planets,
one should have a cloth made seven cubits long and square, well-woven and firm.
O King of kings, one should have all the worlds engraved upon that [disc], which has its parts distinct, is very firm, pure, and possesses the luster of pure crystal.
Having brought four-colored pigments for the variegated work of painting,
one should select a young, healthy, auspicious, and capable painter.
Having worshipped with effort using flowers, garments, and ornaments,
he should apply himself to that ritual while reciting it together with the best of the twice-born.
With the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, the resonant tones of auspicious songs,
and the proclamations of "Auspicious Day" and "Victory," he diligently honored the Brahmins.
Having honored the preceptor as well with garments and ornaments,
O King, one should cause the commencement of the work on that cloth exactly as prescribed.
O King, following the ancient ritual, one should have Jambudvīpa depicted in detail in its center, according to the proper sequence of the worlds.
Mount Meru stands in its center; above Meru are the deities;
and in the cardinal directions are the eight cities of the world-protectors, inhabited by gods.
The earth with its seven continents, the seven great mountain ranges,
the seven oceans, and the delightful rivers along with the seas are all contained herein.
There are indeed seven netherworlds (pātālas) and seven celestial realms (svarga-vibhūtis),
as well as the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, in their proper order.
Likewise, the sun follows its fixed course, surrounded by the planets and hosts of stars;
as do the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas.
The sages, the seers, the cows, and the mothers of the gods;
the birds beginning with Suparṇa, and the elephants beginning with Airāvata.
One should have the eight elephants of the quarters depicted right here, adorned with jewels;
O King, having had such a beautiful cloth-painting made in this manner, [one should proceed].
All this is enveloped by water ten times greater [in extent];
that [water] is further enveloped on all sides by fire, which is vast and fierce.
Fire is enveloped by wind, and wind is encompassed by space;
likewise, space is [enveloped] by the source of the elements (bhūtādi), and that source by the Great One (mahat).
The Great Principle, characterized by intellect, is indeed pervaded by the Unmanifest;
the Unmanifest is pervaded by Tamas, and Tamas likewise by Rajas.
That which is pervaded by the quality of goodness (sattva) is said to be the threefold primordial nature (prakṛti).
Thus, O King, the entire cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is endowed with these veils.
The wise man, having thus rendered everything— both external and internal— as a painted image situated upon a cloth, [should contemplate] that all is pervaded by the Puruṣa.
On the full moon of Kārtika, at the solstices, at the equinoxes, and likewise during eclipses—
listen to me as I briefly describe the ritual by which one should perform worship.
The wise one should have a variegated mandala made for him to the east;
he should have nine sacrificial pits made, four of which are square.
Among them, he should appoint two Brāhmaṇas at a time who have mastered the Vedas,
who are provided with sacrificial implements, and who are adorned with garments and ornaments.

All of them, with self-restraint and observing silence, should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) using the names of those residing on the cloth, preceded by the syllable Om and accompanied by their respective mantras.
Then the patron, adorned with all ornaments,
should together with the preceptor perform worship before the cloth painting.
Having worshipped with flowers and garments, one should utter this mantra:
"Whatever worlds exist here within the interior of the cosmic egg,"
May these, being present here, be honored for my sake:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the Ādityas and the Vasus.
"May they, being worshipped, remain forever established for me.
Having thus worshipped according to the rule and having performed a circumambulation, [he should proceed].
One should cause various kinds of foods and offerings to be presented there;
then, one should arrange a vigil accompanied by the sounds of conchs and trumpets.
With various sounds of Vedic chanting and the resonant tones of auspicious songs,
he bathed again at the clear dawn, pure and adorned.
Having again worshipped that cloth-painting according to the previously mentioned procedure,
the wise officiating priest (ṛtvij) should then perform the worship with a hundred cows.
Alternatively, one should give a pair of well-adorned cows to each individual,
as well as sandals, an umbrella, and household utensils.
Whatever is most beloved, all that the wise man should give;
from that, he should arrange a gift for the Nāgas, well-adorned.

If it is not obtained, one should mount the cloth-painting after giving a thousand as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and having prepared a chariot yoked with horses, adorned with banners, flags, and garlands.
Or else, a wise man should lead a Brahmin to the temple with his semen;
having led him there, he should establish it and worship it with perfumes and flowers.
O King, one should offer food oblations there as well and celebrate a great festival in whichever temple his consecration is performed.
One who desires prosperity should perform a great worship there as well;
the wise person should cause a moonlight-canopy, a bell, a banner, and so forth, to be offered.
And according to his ability, O Indra among kings, the monarch, showing reverence to his preceptor and honoring him with sacrificial fees,
should dismiss the Brahmins.
On that day, food should be given without restriction to the poor, the blind, and the wretched, as well as to friends, kinsmen, and relatives.
Whosoever, whether man or woman, being faithful and having conquered the senses, should perform this consecration for the benefit of all the world according to this rite;
By him the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, are established;
and by him, along with his sons, O Yudhiṣṭhira, his lineage has been delivered.
As long as this cloth painting remains worshipped in a temple,
so long shall his inexhaustible fame spread throughout the three worlds.
For as many days as one's fame is sung among mortals in the world of men,
for that many thousands of years is one honored in the world of the Sun.
Being sung of by the Gandharvas and attended by hosts of Apsarases,
he shall dwell there with a joyful mind for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
Having returned here from the exhaustion of his merit, he is born as a king of kings,
endowed with sons and grandsons, illustrious, long-lived, and exceedingly righteous.
O Indra among kings, for ten births he is born with his thorns removed;
prosperity attends him eternally, and his splendor remains unimpeded upon the earth.
Strength, intelligence, wealth, grain, as well as excellent sons and grandsons—
one who is most excellent among the gods attains all this by performing this.
His fame shall indeed be celebrated and his strength shall be great;
moreover, in seven other births, he shall become a king.
Afterwards, having entered the order of ascetics, one attains supreme Nirvana;
there is nothing higher than this in the three worlds.
Having performed this, the sages attained the supreme state;
by the power of this alone, the ancient universal monarchs [attained their goal].
Having attained such a state, they spread their fame throughout the world. All this that you asked me has been related to you.
Whether it be a woman or even a man,
whoever performs the installation of a golden image according to the prescribed rite will certainly become one who has fulfilled his purpose.
It increases the Dharma and upholds hundreds of dharmas; it inspires clarity and removes evil.
And it proclaims one's exceptional steadfastness throughout the worlds.
There is nothing that he does not perform for the establishment of the world.
Thus ends the procedure for the installation of the world-symbols (*bhuvanapratiṣṭhā*).
Now, regarding the gift of the *Kalpa* (the Matsya Purāṇa):
"I shall proclaim the recitation of the *Kalpas*, which destroys all sins."
By the mere recitation of which one becomes endowed with the merit of the Vedas.
The first is the Śvetakalpa, the second is the Nīlalohita,
the third is Vāmadeva, and after that is the other, Rathantara.
Raurava is declared the fifth; the sixth is remembered as Prāṇa;
then the seventh is Bṛhatkalpa, and the eighth is called Kandarpa.
Madya is declared as the ninth, and Īśāna is remembered as the tenth;
Vyāna is declared as the eleventh, and likewise Sārasvata is the next.
The thirteenth is indeed the Udāna, and the fourteenth is the Gāruḍa;
the fifteenth is to be known as the Kūrma, from which the Paurṇamāsī is born.
The sixteenth is the Nārasiṃha Kalpa, and after that follows the Samāna;
the eighteenth is declared to be the Āgneya, and likewise the next is the Somakalpa.
Mānava is said to be twenty [in number], and another is called Tatpuruṣa;
likewise there is Vaikuṇṭha, and another is Lakṣmīkalpa.
The twenty-fourth is likewise proclaimed as the one known as the Sāvitrī-kalpa;
in the twenty-fifth is the Ghora, and after that, the Vārāha.
Then the twenty-seventh is the Vairāja-kalpa, and another is the Gaurī-kalpa;
after that, the Māheśvara-kalpa is proclaimed, wherein Tripura was destroyed.
The *pitṛkalpa* as well as that which is remembered as the *kuhū* of Brahmā—
this is the month of Brahmā, which destroys all sins.
In the beginning, Brahmā assigned the name of that particular Kalpa according to the greatness that was ordained for it.
But he who, having fashioned these [images] out of gold, should give them on every festival day,
shall dwell for a kalpa in the city of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, honored by sages in heaven.
Since the gift of ritual manuals (kalpa-dāna) brings about the destruction of all evil,
the wise person, having fashioned images of the Munis, should then bestow the ritual manuals.
The form of a sage, the abundance of a sage, and the characteristics of a sage have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*. Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Kalpa-tree.
Thus [ends the work] of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādeva, the sovereign lord of all faculties and the possessor of all...
The Section on the Gift of Deities within the Dānakhaṇḍa of the Caturvargacintāmaṇi, composed by Śrī Hemādri, who is proficient in the sciences.
Now, specific types of giving according to specific times are described:

by honoring guests according to the prescribed rite, by arranging auspicious conjunctions of lunar days and constellations, and by repeatedly offering generously on the days of the week, one who delights the preceptor with affection for his person delights the wise man.
Bearing a home that is beautiful due to the constant reflection of the circle of his dear friends,
and being truly skilled in the application of the treasury (śrī-karaṇa), he alone on earth is like gold (hema) and other precious things.
Therefore, on lunar days, weekdays, astrological mansions, and yogas, as well as during the *karaṇas* and at times such as the solar transits (*saṅkrānti*), the collection of gifts is performed.

In that regard, the gifts associated with the lunar days (*tithi*) are first described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O giver of honor, on the first day (*pratipad*) one should give flowers; on the second, ghee;
on the fifth, fruits; and on the sixth, a bath."
On the seventh day, there were cakes; on the eighth, molasses;
on the ninth, boiled grain; and on the tenth, various foods.
On the eleventh day [one should give] gold, on the twelfth day clothing,
on the thirteenth day perfumes, and immediately after that, white sugar.
The gift of excellent food on the fifteenth day yields great fruit. [850] In the *Bhaviṣyottara*,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe to you the gift of lunar days (tithidāna),
which pacifies all sins and destroys all obstacles.
Whatever sin may arise from mental, verbal, or physical action,
O Pāṇḍava, it all comes to rest through this act of giving.
In the months of Śrāvaṇa, Kārttika, Caitra, Vaiśākha, and likewise Phālguna,
that gift which increases prosperity should be given during the bright fortnight.
The gift, the companion of faith, the attainment of a worthy recipient,
and likewise the time for giving— these have always been declared here by the seers of reality.
O best of men, whatever a self-controlled person gives at a sacred ford, in a sanctuary, in a cow-pen, or in his own home, that becomes infinite in its merit.
Having honored the twice-born on the sacred days (pratipad) and having worshipped Prajāpati,
one should have a golden eight-petaled lotus fashioned.
The characteristics of Prajāpati have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*:
"Having prepared [an image] in a vessel made of udumbara wood filled with fragrant ghee,
and having worshipped it with flowers and incense, one should present it to a Brahmin."
An *audumbara* vessel is a copper bowl.
Having offered a lotus to the Abode of Kamalā according to this rite, one who has desires obtains his desired objects; one free from desire attains identity with Brahman.

Having worshipped the fire on the second day, and having offered a hundred oblations of sesame and clarified butter in the sequence of *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, one should then offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
O King, one should place a golden image of Vaiśvānara upon a copper vessel filled with jaggery and clarified butter, which rests atop a water-filled jar.
Having filled it with garments, garlands, and various kinds of foods and edibles, one should then give it to a Brahmin, saying: "May Agni be pleased with me."

The characteristics of the Vaiśvānara [image] have been described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*: "One is liberated from all sins committed throughout one's life; there is no doubt about this. Upon death, one goes to the city of Fire. Thus spoke the sage Nārada.
On the third day, O Great King, one should place a beautiful golden lizard upon a copper vessel and set it upon salt.
One should place cumin, pieces of myrobalan, and jaggery at its sides;
it should be covered with a pair of red cloths and adorned with saffron.
O Pārtha, who can describe the fruit that one obtains by worshipping a twice-born with flowers, incense, and food offerings, and then making a gift to him?
Where there are palaces made of gold and rivers with milk as their mud,
where Gandharvas and sages dwell— there those men go.
Having brought [the merit] from heaven, one shall become handsome and fortunate in this world;
a giver and enjoyer of abundant wealth, endowed with sons and grandsons.
Or a woman endowed with those same qualities becomes so; of this there is no doubt. In the Vahni Purāṇa:
"He who gives sandals to the twice-born on the third lunar day..."
In the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should [offer] together with an umbrella and the requisite ritual implements.
No mental anguish arises for him when he is born in the world of mortals;
freed from all diseases, he obtains prosperity and sons. O best of the twice-born, in due time he comes here to my own world.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O best of the twice-born, whatever a man gives on the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha,
O foremost of men, he enjoys that as inexhaustible."
But it is specifically proclaimed that [this merit] belongs to those who have eaten through the act of giving.
Viṣṇu said:

"Having fasted on the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, one who worships Vāsudeva with unbroken grains (akṣata), and having offered those very same grains as oblations, becomes purified from all sins; furthermore, whatever one gives away on this day, that becomes inexhaustible. Thus it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
O King, on the third day of the month of Māgha, the giving of molasses and salt brings great merit to both women and men.
The four-faced Lord is surely pleased with jaggery and salt;
likewise, an offering of jaggery should be presented in the month of Bhādrapada.
On the third lunar day, for the gratification of Vāmadeva, the offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) is recommended;
however, O Bhārata, the offering of sweetmeats (modaka) is likewise praised.
O Indra among kings, on the third lunar day of the month of Vaiśākha, a Brahmin is pleased by sandalwood paste and water, while Bhīma himself is indeed pleased by sweetmeats (modaka).
O tiger among the Kurus, there is no doubt that this lunar day in the month of Vaiśākha is indeed superior even to sandalwood here in the lotus-born abode.
The third [stage], which is with destruction, is celebrated in the world by the gods.
O mighty-armed one of excellent vows, [give] a vessel of great value, abundant silver, gold, as well as food, and especially ghee, to a worthy recipient.
Candra is gold, and kaladhauta is silver.
Whatever is given on this [day] shall become inexhaustible; therefore, it is known as Akṣayā.
Whatever gift is given, whether small or great—
All that becomes inexhaustible; therefore, this is known as "Inexhaustible."
O hero, that man who gives water-pots provided with water-vessels here goes indeed to the world of Hemamālī.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: On the fourth lunar day, having had a beautiful golden elephant made weighing half a pala and equipped with a goad,
one should place it upon a drona-measure of oil.
Having worshipped with garments and flowers and having offered the food oblation,
one should then give [the remainder] to a Brāhmaṇa, saying, "May Gaṇeśa be pleased."
In all undertakings he shall meet with no obstacles.
For seven births he shall be an elephant, intoxicated with rut;
and mounted upon that lord of elephants, he shall be a conqueror of the three worlds.

And in this regard—the rule concerning the months, which was stated at the beginning of the section on gifts on lunar days (tithi-dāna) such as Śrāvaṇa, Kārtika, and Caitra, is to be understood as applicable to all the tithi-dānas mentioned in the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
[On the fifth day, one should have a complete serpent fashioned from a single piece of gold;
having placed it in the midst of a vessel containing milk and clarified butter, one should worship it and cause it to be given to a Brahmin.]
Having honored the twice-born with garments, prostrated before him, and asked for his forgiveness,
one brings happiness through this gift both in this world and in the next.
Śambhu has likewise proclaimed this expiation for one bitten by a snake, which drives away the afflictions of serpents and destroys all that is evil.
On the sixth [lunar day], having had Kumāra fashioned according to one's ability— accompanied by Śakti, mounted upon his peacock, and adorned with a golden garland—
The characteristics of Kumāra are described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Kumāra should be depicted with six faces, adorned with a topknot;
he should be dressed in red garments and mounted upon a noble peacock."
"A cock and likewise a bell should be placed in his two right hands;
a Vaijayantī banner and a spear (śakti) should be fashioned for his two left [hands].
Having thus worshipped with garments upon the crest of a drona-measure of rice according to one's means, [one should proceed].
Then, having paid homage, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa who has a family.
Having attained prosperity in this world, he is glorified in heaven after death;
a Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa becomes a partaker of the world of Brahman.
On the seventh [lunar day], having likewise worshipped the Sun and an excellent Brahmin,
one should give [the horse] with its neck adorned, equipped with a saddle, and accompanied by a ritual fee.
The mantra for the gift should be understood from the section on the gift of a horse:
"He attains the world of the Sun and rejoices together with the Sun;
the Gandharva attains satisfaction when a well-adorned horse is given."
On the eighth day, one should offer a white bull with unimpaired limbs, capable of bearing the yoke,
covered with a pair of white garments, and adorned with bells and ornaments.
Having prostrated, one should give [the gift] to a Brahmin, saying, "May the Bull-bannered Lord be pleased.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should follow him as far as the entrance of his house.
O King, through this gift, the world of Śiva is not difficult to attain;
for upon the shoulders of the Bull reside the fourteen worlds.
Therefore, O descendant of Bharata, by the gift of a bull one becomes a true donor;
having had a golden lion fashioned according to one's means on the ninth lunar day.
Adorned with eight pearls and wrapped in blue cloth,
one should offer it while recollecting the Goddess, the destroyer of wicked demons.
By giving [this] thus to a twice-born, one attains all desires,
even on paths through wildernesses, forests, and difficult terrains, which are infested with thieves and wild beasts.
And even those who are harmful do not harm him through the power of this gift;
having died, he goes to the city of the gods, being honored by both deities and asuras.
Having returned here from that state due to the exhaustion of his merit, he becomes a righteous king;
O tiger among kings, on the tenth [day], having given directions fashioned of gold.

Having worshipped with garments, flowers, and other offerings salt, molasses, coriander, flat beans, sesame seeds, the three products of the cow, and rice grains placed atop black gram, one should present them to a brahmin.

The *āśās* are the directions. Their characteristics have been described in the *Āśā-daśamī-vrata*: "They are female in form and marked by the weapons and vehicles of their presiding deities. This means that, in order starting from the east, they are marked by the weapons and so forth of their respective presiding deities, such as Śakti and the others. The weapons and vehicles of Śakti and the others should also be observed in the *Brahmāṇḍa-dāna*.
[The prayer is: "May the *āśās* always be favorable to us; may my heart's desire be accomplished. By your grace, may there always be auspiciousness."
The mantra for the offering of worship:
O King of kings, listen to the fruit of merit for that man or woman who, by this ritual procedure, performs the act of quenching [the fire].
Having attained the foremost [state] in this world, he is honored in heaven after death;
all the various hopes that were situated in his mind become fruitful.
Then, having come here from heaven, one is born into a great family after having had a golden image of Garuḍa fashioned on the eleventh lunar day.
According to one's capacity, having worshipped it upon a vessel of copper filled with ghee,
one should especially offer it to a preceptor who is a Brahmin devoted to the five fires.
Having given this, what need is there for much speaking? One is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The form of Garuḍa is described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Tārkṣya has the luster of emerald, and his nose is shaped like an owl's."
He should be depicted with four arms, and likewise with round eyes and face.
With his knees either on the ground or raised upward, adorned with two wings,
he is devoid of the golden halo that usually abides in radiance.
At the edge of the parasol, one should have a full water-jar made for him;
his two hands should be fashioned such that they are joined in the añjali gesture.
"If Viṣṇu is to be placed in front, he should be depicted with two arms and his hands joined in the gesture of reverence (añjali).
[One should offer] a cow, a bull, a buffalo, gold, the seven types of grain, goats and sheep, a mare, all kinds of molasses and juices, as well as many fruits."
Having gathered pure flowers and various kinds of forest fragrances,
he covered her with devotion using new garments.
On the twelfth day, one should present these twelve [items] to Brāhmaṇas;
O Great King, listen now to the fruit that comes from giving to even a single one.
The mantras for these [offerings] are to be sought in the sections concerning those specific gifts.
Having attained supreme fame in this world and having enjoyed pleasures as desired,
he then goes to the city of Viṣṇu, served by hosts of celestial nymphs.
Upon the exhaustion of that karma, having come here, he becomes a righteous king—
a performer of sacrifices and a lord of charity— who shall live for a hundred autumns.
In the months of Śrāvaṇa, Kārttika, Caitra, Vaiśākha, and likewise Phālguna, this should be offered during the bright fortnight; it increases one's spiritual welfare.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"A man who gives variegated garments on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra obtains inexhaustible fruit and goes to the world of the Nāgas."
Likewise, on the twelfth day of the month of Vaiśākha, there is the gift of gold;
and for the king, there is the gift of an umbrella and sandals in the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Having given a well-spread bed, one should please the Lord who reclines upon his couch;
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one is glorified in Śvetadvīpa.
By the gift of clothing in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
O twice-born ones, the giver of a cow goes to Goloka in the month of Bhādrapada.
By giving a horse to the Aśvinī deities during the month of Aśvina, one pleases the horse-headed Lord (Hayagrīva),
attains the world of Viṣṇu, and uplifts one's own lineage.
By the gift of cotton cloth in the month of Kārttika, one attains heaven;
the gift of salt alone in Mārgaśīrṣa yields great fruit.
Likewise, by the gift of grains in the month of Pauṣa, of wood in the month of Māgha,
and of all types of perfumes in Phālguna on the twelfth lunar day, one becomes happy; thus, by giving as prescribed, the donor is glorified in heaven.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"The two months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Vaiśākha are dear to me;
he who, with self-restraint, [observes the vow] on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) of these two months..."
O Vasundharā, he who gives to twelve Brahmins an excellent cow for each one, provided with all necessary utensils—
A pair of garments and sandals, as well as an ear-ornament,
a parasol, two wooden shoes, and a finger-ring.
Having smeared himself with ashes and donned the sacred thread, meditating upon me with devotion,
he should offer [the oblation] to five, three, or two [deities], according to his capacity.
But if one is unable, then [one may give] to a single person who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
who is free from anger, established in his vows, and especially so if he is one who provides refuge.
O Goddess, listen to the fruit of merit for that man who gives according to this rite in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or the month of Vaiśākha.
Twenty-two crores of Manvantaras abide within my body;
all of them, including Śanaiścara, reside upon my head in the Liṅga.
All of them attain gentleness by means of this rite on the twelfth day.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should worship Puruṣottama on the twelfth day through the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa with offerings of sugar, ghee, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
This lunar day, the twelfth (dvādaśī) in the bright fortnight, belongs indeed to Viṣṇu; on that day, one should diligently worship the Lord Janārdana.
Whatever is given in this manner to a pure Brahmin dedicated to Īśāna,
or even to Viṣṇu, that bestows infinite fruit.
Therefore, on this lunar day, those seeking auspicious results should give fried food. Viṣṇu says:

When the full moon of Pauṣa has passed, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, one who has fasted and bathed with sesame seeds should offer water with sesame, worship Vāsudeva with sesame seeds, and having offered oblations of those same seeds and eaten, becomes purified from all sins. When the full moon of Māgha has passed, having reached the twelfth day of the dark fortnight conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇā, one should present a gift of lamps before Vāsudeva using two large wicks. On the right side, one should give a measure of oil increased by eight [palas] along with a complete garment dyed with saffron; on the left side, one should give a measure of ghee increased by eight [palas] along with a complete white garment. Having performed this, in whatever kingdom, in whatever region, and in whatever family one is born, one becomes radiant there.
With the words "on the right side," etc., he describes two great wicks: one dyed with great silver and the other dyed with safflower, each weighing a hundred *tulā-palas*. [Regarding] Yama:
having offered sesame seeds into the fire on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, and having given sesame seeds to the Brahmins, one is liberated from all sins.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O King, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, for the sake of pleasing Govinda,
the gift of a cow was previously described to you."
One obtains all that fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
From the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
On the thirteenth day, one should bathe thirteen Brahmins in the morning;
having clothed them in new garments, one should then honor them with perfumes and flowers.
One should feed them delicious food and present a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
according to one's ability, the righteous-souled person should offer pieces of gold, saying, "May [the deity] be pleased."
To Dharmarāja, to Kāla, to Citragupta, to Mṛtyu, to Kṣaya, to Kṣayarūpa, to Antaka, and to Yama.
To the Lord of the Pretas, to the Fierce One, and likewise to Vaivasvata;
to the one mounted upon a buffalo, and to Citra—thus are the thirteen names.
Having recited this with faith and having prostrated, one should dismiss [the deity];
O Great King, whoever performs this delightful worship, [attains the fruit].
Having lived happily in the mortal world, free from disease,
that man does not later experience the suffering that lies on the path of Yama.
He does not see the city of the hungry ghosts nor does he go to the world of the ancestors;
having returned here from the exhaustion of his merit, he becomes happy and free from disease.
Likewise: On the fourteenth day, one should prepare an auspicious earthen jar filled with milk,
mixed with one karṣa [of the prescribed substance], and adorned with a fine cloth.
Whoever should give [this bull], richly adorned with ornaments of bells and accompanied by a bull, to a Brāhmaṇa householding devotee of Śiva;
"Made of earth" means earthen. "Filled with milk" means full of milk. "Combined with one karṣa" means joined with gold of the measure of one karṣa.
One should give a jar together with gold, filled with milk on the fourteenth day (bhūta), according to the Vātula-tantra.
Having given this, O best of men, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having remained there for a long time, one eventually returns to the surface of the earth.
Endowed with health and wealth, he is born into a great family,
his self fulfilled in all desires for as long as three hundred lifetimes.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"He who, having bathed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, worships the Lord who wields the Pināka bow through the mouth of a twice-born brahmin, has no further rebirth."
Especially on the Kṛṣṭamī day, having bathed and honored according to the rules a righteous twice-born man with the washing of his feet and other rites;
"May Mahādeva be pleased with me; may he grant his own wealth.
Thus liberated from all sins, one attains the supreme goal."

"One should propitiate through the mouth of a twice-born" means that for the sake of pleasing Śiva, one should satisfy the twice-born with those gifts. "Material goods" refers to cows, land, gold, and so forth. Now, from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
Having reached the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, a man—having fasted and subdued his senses—should give a pair of variegated garments.
By bowing to Brāhmaṇas, one shall obtain good fortune;
specifically on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should honor five or seven Brāhmaṇas.
One should cause [the deceased] to recite with black sesame seeds mixed with honey, or with others;
saying, "May Dharmarāja be pleased," or whatever else dwells in one's mind.
One is liberated from the evil committed throughout one's entire life at that very moment.

"One should cause the Brahmins to recite" means that one should have them perform the *svastivācana* (ritual for auspiciousness). [863] With black sesame seeds mixed with honey—that is, accompanied by honey—and "with others," meaning with white sesame seeds, one should gratify the Brahmins; this is the remainder of the sense. At that very time, having covered a black antelope skin complete with its hooves with sesame seeds, and having adorned it with garments and all kinds of jewels—
Whoever should give [this], by him the earth, together with its sacrificial altars and gold, would have been given.
The detailed procedure for this, however, should be seen in the section on the gift of a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). Yama says:
"On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one who has fasted for three nights, having bathed, being self-controlled and pure, should according to the rule feed ten Brāhmaṇas with *kṛsara*."
Having given white or black sesame seeds mixed with honey to ten Brahmins, one should have them pronounce a blessing of well-being over those very seeds.
One should satisfy the ancestors and the gods with the thought, "May the King of Dharma be pleased";
by this, one is released from the sins committed throughout one's entire life at that very moment.
He shall remain for ten million times ten million years and be honored in the heavenly world;
he shall behold me alone and shall not be defiled by sin.
Jābāla said:
By offering cooked food and a water-pot, especially on the full moon day of Vaiśākha,
and dedicating it to Dharmarāja, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
Raw food and cooked food;
by satisfying seven or five Brahmins with water-pots containing gold and sesame seeds, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
In the Mahābhārata:
"On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, having given sesame seeds to the twice-born,
one should always eat sesame seeds and perform anointing with them."
Those who desire their own welfare should always strive with all their soul for what must be done within the home.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Likewise, having observed a fast on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one who gives sandals and an umbrella adorned with *tulasī* shall become exceedingly happy."
By the gift of food on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, one obtains abundant food;
by the gift of a water-cow on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, one attains heaven.
The gift of a cow on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada yields great fruit;
likewise, on the full moon day of Āśvayuja, one should give a brass vessel filled with ghee to a twice-born man.
Having likewise given [a gift] together with gold, one is born here with radiant splendor;
on the full moon day of Kārttika, one becomes as bright as the moon, or even of another [golden] hue.
Having prepared [the offerings] with jewels, perfumes, grains, seeds, and likewise with garments,
and having performed what was prescribed, one should offer a bull and lamps on all sides.
By giving at the rising of the moon, a man is liberated from all sins;
by that merit, he travels happily through the wilderness on the path of Yama,
obtains sons and grandsons, and goes to the world of the Sun.
Likewise, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the moon is full during the winter season,
one is honored with a garment dyed with the blood of a great king.
Having covered it with a bronze vessel and prepared the *soma* with a concentrated mind—

using either dye from great kings (*mahārājatarakta*) or safflower dye (*kusumbharakta*)— the mark of the moon will be described hereafter among the offerings of water. As for the primary salt, one should fill a black vessel (*kṛṣṇamārgaka*) completely.
"Of the principal salt" means of *saindhava* (rock salt);
having given a golden-navel [ornament] to that very same twice-born man.
A man who has rubbed his body with a paste of white mustard seeds in the month of Pauṣa becomes endowed with good fortune, beauty, and charm.
"Ucchādita" means rubbed with unguents;
and after that, he was consecrated with a jar that had no cracks.
Likewise, having been cleansed, he was bathed with waters containing all kinds of seeds.
Having cleansed it and removed all oiliness,
and having subsequently anointed it with perfumes, jewels, fruits, and ghee,
one should then fashion a golden image and present it to a twice-born man.
The grammatical connection is: "anointed with ghee in the midst of gold. By the word "that," the material object under discussion, such as the water-pot and so forth, is referred to.
Then, one should worship Viṣṇu, who has been bathed with ghee, according to one's capacity;
thereafter, one should offer ghee into the fire and give ghee to the twice-born.
One who knows the Dharma, being self-controlled and fasting, should give a pair of garments to the performer; by this act, he is liberated from all sins.
By performing a Śrāddha with sesame seeds on the full moon day of Māgha, one is liberated from all sins;
and by giving a well-spread bed to a Brāhmaṇa on the full moon day of Phālguna.

A man who knows the Dharma obtains a wife endowed with beauty and wealth, as well as one who is devoted to his side; indeed, he attains the most excellent prosperity along with many kinsmen on his side.
Likewise,
a wife should not even look at her husband on full-moon days in the month of Caitra that coincide with the lunar mansions; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
The fruit of these very same gifts becomes tenfold;
when given to those same women who have previously performed great meritorious deeds, one enjoys inexhaustible fruit.

"When the full moon day is conjoined with the lunar mansion of the month and it falls on a Thursday, that is called 'Mahāpūrvā'; for it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara: 'When the full moon is conjoined with the lunar mansion of the month and Jupiter, it is indeed Mahāpūrvā. Thus said Viṣṇu.

On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the moon is conjoined with the asterism Mṛgaśiras, one should present at moonrise a *prastha* of powdered salt with a golden center to a Brāhmaṇa. By this rite, one is born endowed with beauty and good fortune. If the full moon of Pauṣa should be conjoined with Puṣya, on that day one whose body has been anointed with a paste of white mustard seeds, who has been sprinkled with a jar full of cow’s ghee, and who has bathed with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*), all perfumes (*sarvagandha*), and all seeds, should bathe the blessed Vāsudeva with ghee. Having worshipped him with flowers, perfumes, incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, and having offered oblations into the fire with Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, and Bārhaspatya mantras, one should cause a Brāhmaṇa to pronounce a blessing (*svasti*) with gold and ghee, and give a pair of garments to the officiant. By this rite, one prospers. If the full moon of Māgha should be conjoined with Maghā, by performing a *śrāddha* with sesame seeds (*tila*) on that day, one becomes purified. By giving sesame seeds for the purpose of the meal during the *śrāddha*, one becomes beloved by all people. If the full moon of Phālguna should be conjoined with Phālgunī, by presenting to a Brāhmaṇa a well-prepared bed with a fine mattress on that day, one obtains a charming wife who is virtuous and wealthy; and a woman likewise obtains a husband. If the full moon of Caitra should be conjoined with Citrā, by the gift of variegated garments on that day, one obtains good fortune. On the full moon of Vaiśākha, by satiating seven Brāhmaṇas with sesame seeds mixed with honey and pleasing Dharmarāja, one becomes purified from sins. If the full moon of Jyaiṣṭha should be conjoined with Jyeṣṭhā, by the gift of an umbrella and sandals on that day, one obtains lordship over a city. On the full moon of Āṣāḍha conjoined with Āṣāḍhā, by the gift of food and drink, one obtains that very same [lordship] in an inexhaustible form. On the full moon of Śrāvaṇa conjoined with Śravaṇa, by giving a water-cow (*jaladhenu*) accompanied by a pair of garments and food, one attains the heavenly world (*svargaloka*). On the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada conjoined with that [asterism], by the gift of a cow, one becomes completely freed from all sins. On the full moon of Āśvayuja, when the moon has entered Aśvinī, by giving a vessel filled with ghee along with gold to a Brāhmaṇa, one becomes possessed of a blazing digestive fire. If the full moon of Kārttika should be conjoined with Kṛttikā, on that day at moonrise, one should give to a Brāhmaṇa a white bull or one of another color, provided with all kinds of grain, jewels, and perfumes, in the middle of an island. One does not behold the fear of the wilderness.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: Having performed the ritual release of a bull according to the prescribed rules on the full moon day,
one should fashion a beautiful silver image of the Moon weighing one pala.
One should worship with fragrant flowers and offer an oblation of food.
As for the characteristics of the form of the Moon, they should be consulted in the section on the offering of the door that follows.
O King of kings, one should honor a Brahmin with garments, ornaments, and decorations, and give [the image] to him while reciting this mantra; listen now as it is proclaimed by me.
Born from the ocean of milk, illuminator of the courtyard of the three worlds,
crest-jewel upon the head of Umā’s consort, and [source] of Śivā as well— homage, homage to you!
By this gift, the king shines like the moon in the sky,
surrounded by Apsarases until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the kalpa.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "He who, with a pure mind and well-composed, having reached the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) of the dark fortnight, should give vessels of sesame seeds to the twice-born."
Having gratified the ancestors, that bull among men attains the world of the ancestors inexhaustibly and prospers in happiness for a long time.
[The phrase] "of black sesame seeds" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Having reached the new moon day, one should give whatever [gift] to an ascetic Brahmin, dedicating it to Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Gods."
May the Lord of Lords, Soma, the eternal Mahādeva, be pleased;
the sin committed throughout seven lifetimes perishes at that very moment.
Soma, accompanied by Umā, [spoke]. In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"Those of pure nature who, according to the sequence of the first lunar day (*pratipad*), duly bestow these gifts upon the most excellent of the twice-born..."
Having sported happily in the realms of Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
they later become excellent kings on earth, endowed with beautiful forms.
Thus end the gifts for lunar days (*tithi*). Now, the gift for the first day of the *yuga* (*yugādi-tithi*),
according to the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord of Gods, speak again to me, whose soul is purified by devotion to you;
I desire to hear this great and auspicious dharma being told here.
For even if only a tiny amount is given there, or even if it is merely recited, it becomes truly great.
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen, O Pāṇḍava, I shall tell you this secret fashioned by the gods,
which I have never spoken to anyone, O Bhārata, not even to one who is very dear to me.
The third day of the month of Vaiśākha, the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
and [the ninth day] of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya.
And the thirteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Māgha.
It should be noted that [the Vaiśākha-tṛtīyā] refers to the third day of the bright fortnight, while the Māgha-pañcadaśī refers to the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight.
"The Vaiśākha-tṛtīyā is equal to the Kṛta-yuga,
and the Kārttika-navamī is equal to the Tretā-yuga."
The thirteenth day of the month of Nabhasya is considered equal to the Dvāpara age;
O King, the fifteenth day of Māgha is said to be the beginning of the Kali age.
O Indra among kings, these four are remembered as the origins of the yugas;
for this reason, they are called "the beginnings of the yugas" by all the learned sages.
Fasting, austerity, charity, recitation, fire-offerings, and other such rites—
whatever is performed during these [lunar days] becomes ten million times more meritorious.
On the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, you should worship Nārāyaṇa, the Teacher of the World accompanied by Śrī, with flowers, perfumes, ointments, and other offerings.
With collections of garments and ornaments, as well as various kinds of food offerings.

[Nārāyaṇa] accompanied by Śrī is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. His form should be understood from the section on the gift of deities (*devatādāna*) concerning the gift of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. Then, O best of the Kuru lineage, a cow should be made before him with one *āḍhaka* of salt, and the calf with a fourth part thereof.
Having placed it upon a human skin and prepared it according to the prescribed rite,
one should cause it to be given to a Brāhmaṇa by means of the application of the sequence taught in the scriptures.
"May Śrīdhara, Śrīpati, the glorious Śrīmān, and the Lord of Śrī be well-pleased"—
having given the cow to the Brahmin according to this rite, O Bhārata.
A man who observes the *nakta* fast on the ninth day of the month of Kārttika attains in this world a reward ten times that of giving a thousand cows; of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed again in rivers, lakes, or natural pools dug by the gods,
one should then worship the blue-throated Lord, the bestower of boons, who is accompanied by Umā.
One should worship the blameless Śaṅkara, the auspicious Śiva, characterized as Umāmaheśvara, with flowers, incense, food offerings, and so forth,
as described in the section on the gift of deities regarding the gift of Umāmaheśvara.
One should give a cow made of sesame seeds according to the procedure prescribed in the Purāṇas.
One should proclaim: "May the eight-formed Nīlakaṇṭha be pleased."
O Pārtha, by whom can the merit obtained here be described?
By giving a cow made of ghee, one shall attain the realm of Śiva.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Nabhasya, one should worship Kṛṣṇa.
The form of Kṛṣṇa is described in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Kṛṣṇa, bearing the discus, should be depicted with the luster of a blue lotus petal;
he has two arms, a gentle face, and is adorned with two earrings. Thus it is said.
One should devotedly feed Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences with offerings of food and honey for the sake of the ancestors.
O Great King, a young cow that is easy to milk and possesses abundant milk, along with her calf, should be given in person for the sake of the ancestors.
"May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather be pleased by this gift of a cow"; having said this, one should give the gift and dismiss [the Brahmins].
O King of kings, by what means could the merit obtained by men through this performance be calculated, even in hundreds of millions of years?
A man obtains here sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, as well as vast and desired wealth,
and in the hereafter, he attains an auspicious state.
On the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha, having worshipped the Grandfather—
the God accompanied by Gāyatrī and adorned with the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas— [one attains the fruit].

The definition of Brahmā and the Vedāṅgas has been stated in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*; the definition of Gāyatrī is found in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna* as described in the *Padmapurāṇa*; and Gāyatrī as the embodiment of the Vedas is mentioned in the *Mahābhūtaghaṭadāna*:
"One should present to a Brāhmaṇa a cow made of fresh butter, endowed with various kinds of fruits, together with gold and her calf."
One should recite: "May the lotus-born Grandfather be pleased with this;
whatever is in heaven, whatever is in the netherworld, and whatever is rare in the mortal realm."
One undoubtedly attains that through the grace of the Lotus-born,
as well as whatever other very numerous gifts have been bestowed.
O Great King, at the beginnings of the eons, gifts indeed become inexhaustible;
for even one who is destitute should give whatever little he has, however small it may be.
And everything shall become inexhaustible during the beginnings of the Yugas; of this there is no doubt, even for one who is a king, provided he performs it according to his own means and wealth.
In accordance with one's wealth, through an unsurpassable meditative concentration,
land, gold, a house, clothing, beds, seats,
umbrellas, vehicles, and yokes should be given as gifts to the twice-born.
Having thus given according to one's ability and having fed the twice-born as well,
one should afterwards eat a substantial meal, restrained in speech, together with one's own kinsmen.
Whatever sin there may be— whether mental, verbal, or physical—
all that comes to destruction through the worship performed on the lunar day marking the beginning of a Yuga.
Being sung of by Gandharvas and praised by gods and asuras, he enjoys himself for an imperishable time in the heavenly world; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever is given, they say that becomes ten millionfold;
likewise, bathing, recitation, and sacrifice all become inexhaustible,
O King, when performed on the Yugādi lunar days.
Vyāsa and other eminent sages declare thus.
Thus concludes the procedure for giving gifts on the beginnings of the Yugas. Now, regarding gifts on the days of the week. In that regard, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"On the days of the week beginning with the Sun, [gifts] should always be accompanied by gold."
The planets indeed become pleased with one who offers images of them.
One should assign the Sun to the Sun, the Moon to the Moon, and Mars to Mars;
likewise, one should assign Mercury and the others, and to Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, and Śanaiścara.
In the Brahma Purāṇa: "He who, having fashioned the planets out of gold, bestows them upon Brahmins on their respective days according to his capacity, attains all his desires."
Their characteristics are described in the *Brahmāṇḍadāna*:
"The Sun should always have two arms, be seated upon a lotus, hold a lotus in his hand, possess a splendor like the interior of a lotus, and have seven horses and seven reins."
Śaśin should be depicted as white, wearing white garments, possessing ten horses, and adorned with white ornaments;
he has two arms, holds a mace in his hand, and bestows boons.
Wearing red garlands and garments, holding a spear, a trident, and a mace,
four-armed and mounted upon a ram, the son of the Earth (Mars) shall be the bestower of boons.
Wearing yellow garlands and garments, with the luster of the petals of the Karṇikāra flower,
holding a sword, shield, and mace in his hands, and seated upon a lion, the planet Mercury bestows boons.
Likewise, the preceptors of the gods and the Daityas should be depicted as yellow and white, four-armed, holding staffs,
granting boons, and carrying rosaries and water-pots.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) should always be depicted as having the luster of sapphire, holding a trident and granting boons, riding upon a vulture, and bearing an arrow and a bow.
With a terrifying face, bearing a sword, shield, and trident, and bestowing boons,
the blue Rāhu is praised here as seated upon a lion-throne.
All smoke-colored, two-armed, wielding maces, and having deformed faces;
seated eternally upon vultures, these banners shall be bestowers of boons.
All the planets, which bring welfare to the world, should be depicted wearing crowns;
they should all always be one hundred and eight units in height, measured by their own finger-breadths.

The eight [planets] beginning with Āditya and the hundred *ketus*—both together amounting to one hundred and eight; some say there are one hundred and one *ketus*, or even just one *ketu*. In either of these two views, images of the deities should be fashioned using one hundred and nine [units], measured by the sacrificer’s own fingers (*svāṅgula*). The mantras for their donation are to be found in the *Grahadāna* section of the *Brahmaprokti*. On a Sunday, having fashioned an image of Āditya out of gold, one should present a red cloth and a ruby (*padmarāga*) to a Brāhmaṇa. Alternatively, by giving a tawny cow (*kapilā*), one attains all desires in the world of the Sun; if free from desire, one attains liberation (*mokṣa*). On a Monday, [one should give] a silver image of Soma or a conch shell; on Tuesday, a golden image of Maṅgala or a red *duraṃdhara* horse; on Wednesday, for the attainment of knowledge, one should give a golden image of Budha; on Thursday, a golden image of Bṛhaspati or a yellow cloth; on Friday, for his pleasure, a silver image of Śukra or a white horse; on Saturday, a golden image of Śanaiścara joined with a sapphire (*indranīla*) or a black-limbed cow; on that same day, one should give Rāhu accompanied by iron, and the *ketus* accompanied by goats for their pleasure. In this context, Rāhu and the *ketus* should also be made of gold. By such specific donations, one shall attain all desires.
Then Yama said:
"Yama is indeed pleased with him who always first gives gold to a Brahmin on a Sunday."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "A man who, on a Sunday, gives a cake prepared with salt, clarified butter, and jaggery, along with gold, is not overcome by diseases."
By giving such a gift on a Monday, one shall obtain good fortune;
by giving wood on a Monday, one shall achieve the destruction of enemies.
The wise praise the gift of toys to children;
furthermore, by the gift of clothing on the day of one's birth, one attains supreme satisfaction.
By giving a woman sexual pleasure on a Friday, one obtains every boon;
by giving an oil massage on a Saturday, one attains long life.
Thus end the gifts according to the days of the week. Now follow the gifts according to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). In that regard, the *Mahābhārata* states:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
I have heard from your words the procedure for the gift of food;
now, tell me the ritual for the gift associated with the lunar mansions.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Devakī and the celestial sage Nārada.
When Nārada, who has the vision of a god, arrived at Dvārakā, Devakī, who perceives the dharma, asked him this question: "Tell me the answer to this inquiry."
As she was thus questioning him, the celestial sage Nārada duly explained everything to her; listen to that, O lord of the people.
Nārada said:
O illustrious lady, by gratifying virtuous Brāhmaṇas with milk-rice mixed with ghee under the asterism of Kṛttikā, one attains unsurpassed worlds.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, on the day of Rohiṇī, one should give beans, gems, and ghee, along with milk as a drink,
to a twice-born man for the sake of discharging one's debt.
A man who gives away a milch cow together with her calf under the lunar mansion presided over by Soma (Mṛgaśiras) attains the unsurpassed heaven, seated within a solar celestial chariot.
Mṛgaśīrṣa has Soma as its presiding deity.
By offering kṛsara mixed with sesame while composed in mind under the asterism Ārdrā,
a man crosses over difficulties and mountains with edges like razors.
Furthermore, by giving a well-cooked cake filled with ghee under the constellation Punarvasu,
one is born into a family that is illustrious, endowed with beauty, and possesses abundant food.
Having given gold, whether fashioned or unfashioned, upon a flower,
he shines like the moon in worlds where there is no light.
"Made" means fashioned; "unmade" means unfashioned.
Under the asterism Aśleṣā, one likewise gives silver or a bull;
such a person is liberated from all fears and is born learned in the scriptures.
By giving bronze vessels filled with sesame seeds under the Maghā asterism, a man is born possessed of cattle and endowed with sons.
