Having fasted on the occasion of the full moon of Phālguna and having given edible foods mixed with molasses to Brāhmaṇas, one attains good fortune.
Having offered sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭikaudana) mixed with ghee and milk according to the prescribed rite in the region of Uttarā, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Furthermore, whatever gift is bestowed by men in the region of Uttara, its fruit is always infinite; this is the certain conclusion here.
"At the time of Phālgunī-pūrva" means at the time of Pūrvā-phalgunī. "Phāṇita" is a derivative of molasses. Regarding "Uttarā," it means at the time of Uttarā-phalgunī.
Having fasted and given an elephant-chariot yoked with four [animals] under the asterism of Hasta, a man crosses over difficulties and the razor-edged mountains.
O Bhārata, having given a bull yoked with four— that is, harnessed to four— elephants at the constellation Citrā, as well as a meritorious-limbed cow,
one wanders in the world of the Apsarases and sports and rejoices in the forest.

"A meritorious limb" means a cow whose body is marked with auspicious characteristics; that is to say, a milch cow. Furthermore, by giving wealth that is most dear to oneself under the asterism Svātī, one attains very beautiful worlds and great renown even in this world.
Under the asterism Viśākhā, having given a draft ox, a milch cow,
a cart equipped with a yoke-pole, along with grain and cloth;
The *prāsaṅga* is the wooden pole of the yoke;
it gratifies both the ancestors and the gods, and after death one attains infinity.
One does not encounter difficulties and goes to the heavenly world.
Having given the desired means of subsistence to the Brahmins as prescribed, he attains it;
it is certain that he does not undergo the sufferings of the hell-beings.
Having fasted and given an excellent cloak or garment under the asterism Anurādhā,
a man is honored in heaven for even a hundred yugas.

A *prāvāra* is a cloak, a superior garment such as an undergarment or the like. By giving *kālaśāka* (black pot-herb) together with its roots to Brahmins while reciting the mantras on the day of Jyeṣṭhā, one destroys death and attains the desired goal.
Having offered roots and fruits at the root [of the tree] to the Brahmins with a concentrated mind,
O God, he gratifies his ancestors and attains his desired goal.
Then, under the Pūrvāṣāḍhā constellation, one who has fasted should offer vessels of curd to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with noble lineage and conduct and is a master of the Vedas.
By giving [this], one is born into an excellent family abounding in many virtues;
surrounded by sons and grandsons, one likewise becomes possessed of cattle and wealth.
By giving a stirred drink mixed with ghee, honey,
and molasses under the Uttarāṣāḍhā constellation, one shall attain all worlds.
Udamantha is barley meal mixed with water; phāṇita is a product of milk and sugar-candy.
Having given milk, saturated with honey and ghee, under the conjunction of the Abhijit asterism, one who is devoted to dharma is glorified in the heavenly world by the wise.

This is the meaning: the fourth quarter of the lunar mansion Uttarāṣāḍhā, the first four ghaṭikās of Śravaṇa, and the conjunction of Abhijit constitute this time. Having given a woolen blanket (kambala) under Śravaṇa, even when it is covered by another cloth, one goes by means of a white vehicle to the unobstructed heavenly worlds.
Having given a vehicle yoked with oxen under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā while composed in mind,
and having given new clothing therein, one attains a kingdom after death.
Having offered incense along with agallochum and sandalwood during the conjunction of Śatabhiṣaj,
one attains the world of the Apsarases after death and eternal fragrances.
Having indeed given rajamāṣa beans during the conjunction with Pūrvabhādrapadā,
one becomes endowed with all kinds of food and fruits and shall truly be happy after death.
He who offers the meat of a ram under the Uttarā constellation gratifies all the ancestors and attains infinity after death.
An *urabhra* is a ram; its meat is *aurabhra*.
He who gives a cow with a bronze milking vessel during the *Revatī* asterism returns after death, taking with him all desires, and stands before the donor.
Having given a chariot yoked with horses on the day of Aśvinī,
that best of men is born into a family endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots, and is possessed of splendor.
By giving a sesame-cow to the twice-born under the asterism Bharaṇī,
a man indeed obtains cattle that have recently calved, as well as fame, after death.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus has this summary of the characteristics regarding the conjunctions with the lunar mansions been declared by Nārada to Devakī; she, in turn, spoke this to her daughters-in-law.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "The gift of gold under the asterism Kṛttikā is remembered as yielding great fruit;
likewise, the gift of red cloth under Rohiṇī, and of salt under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras)."
Likewise, [the gift] of kṛsara on Ārdrā, of silver when the Sun is in the sky,
of ghee under Puṣya, and of perfumes under Āśleṣā;
Likewise, sesame seeds are for the ancestors (Pitṛs), priyaṅgu for Bhaga,
ghee-cakes for the Āryas, and milk-rice (pāyasa) for Savitṛ.
Under Citrā, one should offer variegated garments; under the deity Vāyu, parched grain (saktu);
under Indra, fire, and metal; and under Maitra, garlands and fruit.
Likewise, the gift of an umbrella, as well as roots and fruits,
and gold combined with honey, yields great fruit when given under the Āpya constellation.
O Brahmins, food and drink are auspicious in Viśveśvara; clothing is auspicious in Śravaṇa; grain is auspicious in Vāsava; and medicinal herbs are auspicious in Vāruṇa.
Today is the day for seeds of the Purāṇas; immediately thereafter, for grains;
likewise on the day of Puṣya, for products of the cow; and then on the day of Aśvinī, for ritual ablutions.
The gift of sesame seeds always yields great fruit under the asterism Bharanī.
Viṣṇu says:
"Every month, when the moon is in conjunction with Revatī, one who feeds Brāhmaṇas with *paramānna* mixed with honey and ghee, and thereby pleases Revatī, becomes possessed of beauty."
Yama says: By feeding Brahmins with milk-rice mixed with ghee and accompanied by ritual fees every month under the asterism Revatī, one is born endowed with beauty.

Thus end the gifts associated with the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). Now follow the gifts associated with the astrological conjunctions (*yoga*). In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "The practice of giving during the conjunctions beginning with Viṣkumbha yields great fruit."
I shall explain that to you; listen, O best of sages!
The gift of all kinds of grain during the *viṣkumbha* yoga destroys all sins;
likewise, the gift of food and drink during *prīti*, and of ghee during *āyuṣmat*.

The gift of saffron brings good fortune, and the gift of barley brings beauty, O auspicious one; the gift of garments brings freedom from disease, and the gift of milk-rice brings success in one's work.
The gift of silver is prescribed for Ghṛti; the gift of roots and so forth for Śūla;
the gift of ornaments for Gaṇḍa; and the gift of a cow is desired for Vṛddhi.
In Dhruva, there should be five jewels; in Vyāghāta, molasses;
in Harṣaṇa, the offering of perfumes; and in Vajra, one should also give gems.
During Siddhi one should give white mustard seeds; during Vyatīpāta, gold;
during Varīyas, sesame seeds; and likewise, during Parigha, garments.
Water-pots should be given when [the deity is] Śiva; when [the deity is] Siddha, prepared food is desired;
when [the deity is] Sādhya, ornaments; and when [the deity is] Śubha, the gift of an umbrella is auspicious.
On the day of Śukra, one should give sandals; on the day of Brahmā, a weapon and clarified butter;
on the day of Indra, one should give lamps; and on the day of Viṣṇu, gold is beneficial to give.
O best of the twice-born, having given gifts according to one's ability to these yogis with devotion to a brahmin, one dwells in the world of the Wielder of the Discus.
Thus end the gifts of yoga.
Now, the gifts of instruments (*karaṇadāna*). In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim the gifts for those who are compassionate."
On the eighth lunar day (Yava), there should be a gift of milk-rice; on the ninth (Bālava), a gift of parched barley flour.
One should give milk products during Kaulava; sesame seeds during the period named Taitila;
salt during the one called Gara; and clothing should be given during Vaṇija.
In Viṣṭi, the gift of sixty-day rice is recommended; in Śakuni, clarified butter;
in Catuṣpāda, the gift of honey; and in Nāga, the gift of garments.
"O best of the twice-born, the gift of priyaṅgu is said to be the most excellent in Kiṃtughna.
[883] Thus end the gifts according to the lunar days (karaṇa).
Now, regarding gifts at the transits (saṃkrānti): on this point, Viśvāmitra says:
"At the transit of the sun into Aries, the gift of a ram yields great fruit;
likewise, at the transit into Taurus, the gift of cows is prescribed."
The giving of clothing, food, and drink is prescribed for the sign Gemini;
and the gift of a cow with ghee is highly praised for Cancer.
The gift of a golden umbrella is always prescribed even for a lion;
likewise, at the entrance of a maiden, the gift of garments and fragrant substances is ordained.
At the entry of the sun into Libra, the gift of grains and seeds is most excellent;
at the entry of the insects, the gift of garments and houses is likewise prescribed.
In this [zodiac], Cancer is the scorpion;
upon the entry of Sagittarius, there is great fruit for garments and vehicles;
and upon the entry of Pisces, likewise, there is the giving of wood and fire.
Jhaṣa refers to the Makara.
Upon the entry [of the Sun] into Aquarius (Kumbha), the gift of cows, water, and grass is prescribed;
upon the entry into Pisces (Mīna), bathing and excellent garlands are likewise recommended.
O best of the twice-born, having bestowed these gifts at the proper time,
a man obtains the desires cherished in his mind.
Therefore, they indeed praise giving at the proper time.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "O King, he who gives a cow made of sesame seeds during the northern course of the sun attains all his desires and finds supreme happiness."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O Brahmins, during the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), the gift of clothing yields great fruit;
by giving a bull filled with sesame seeds, one is liberated from diseases."
Thus end the gifts for the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*).
Now, the monthly gifts. In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By the gift of sesame seeds in the month of Māgha, one does not go to the world of Yama."
By giving priyaṅgu in the month of Phālguna, one becomes beloved on this earth.
By giving variegated garments in the month of Caitra, one enjoys good fortune;
by the offering of cakes in Vaiśākha, one attains heaven.
Likewise, by the gift of an umbrella in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one enjoys all desires;
and the very great fruit of giving clothing in Śrāvaṇa has been proclaimed.
Likewise, by the gift of molasses in the month of Prauṣṭhapada,
and by the gift of ghee in the month of Āśvina, one is born endowed with beauty.
By offering a lamp in the month of Kārttika, one attains all radiance;
and by giving salt in Mārgaśīrṣa, one enjoys good fortune.
In the month of Pauṣa, by the gift of gold one attains supreme nourishment;
likewise, the gift of flowers during the bright fortnight is remembered as bringing about prosperity.
Similarly, the gift of fruits during the dark fortnight yields great fruit.
In the Vāmana Purāṇa: "In the month of Māgha, sesame seeds are commended, as is the gift of a cow made of sesame;
likewise, other items such as sacrificial fuel and firewood are for the purpose of pleasing Mādhava."
O bull among the Bharatas, in the month of Phālguna, rice, cows, and clothing accompanied by a black antelope skin should be given for the sake of pleasing Govinda.
In the month of Caitra, for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu, one should then give these divine things— variegated garments, beds, and seats— to Brāhmaṇas.
Fragrances should be given to the foremost of the twice-born for the satisfaction of Madhusūdana; moreover,
a water-pot, a cow, and a palm-leaf fan with sandalwood paste should always be given by the virtuous for the pleasure of Trivikrama.
A palm-leaf fan,
a pair of sandals, an umbrella, salt,
and myrobalan fruits should be given with devotion in the month of Āṣāḍha for the pleasure of Vāmana.
Clarified butter, jars of milk, a cow made of ghee, and fruits should be given to a wise man in the month of Śrāvaṇa for the pleasure of Śrīdhara.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa), honey, and clarified butter,
as well as salt and rice with jaggery, for the purpose of pleasing Hṛṣīkeśa.
In the month of Āśvayuja, sesame seeds, horses, bulls, curd, copper, iron, and so forth should be given by men for the sake of pleasing Padmanābha.
In the month of Kārttika, a person should offer silver, gold, lamps, gems, pearls, and so forth, for the sake of pleasing Dāmodara.
Men should give donkeys, camels, mules, elephants, pigs, horses, goats, and sheep month by month in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa for the pleasure of Keśava.
Palaces, cities, and the like, as well as houses and garments,
should be diligently offered in the month of Pauṣa for the sake of pleasing Nārāyaṇa.
Male and female servants, ornaments, and food endowed with the six flavors should be given at all times for the sake of pleasing Puruṣottama.
Whatever is most beloved and whatever else is auspicious in the home,
that indeed should be given for the sake of pleasing the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "One should give the best of juices (rasottama) in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, and ghee in Pauṣa yields great fruit.
Here, "the best of juices" refers to salt.
O best of sages, one should offer sesame seeds in the month of Māgha and the seven types of grain in Phālguna.
And one should give various garments to an excellent Brahmin in the month of Caitra;
in Vaiśākha, wheat; and in Jyeṣṭha, a jar filled with water.

In the month of Āṣāḍha, sandalwood mixed with camphor should be given, which yields great fruit; in the month of Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa), fresh butter is prescribed, and in Prauṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada), an umbrella is recommended.
O Sage, he who offers laddukas rich in the colors of jaggery and sugar during the month of Āśvina,
and who bestows the gift of lamps in Kārttika, gains great merit.
One obtains all desires; this has been declared in due order.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a beautiful cow along with its calf and a brass milking vessel.
One should cause [the recipient] to give a cow with her calf and a garland according to this procedure,
and likewise worship the Goddess, Brahmā, the Sun, or Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped the best of the twice-born according to the prescribed rules, [the gift] should be given to one who is pure by nature, free from passion, and devoid of desire and anger.
To one who is humble, well-behaved, and observant of religious vows,
a donor of cows obtains his desires and delightful pleasures in Goloka.
At the conclusion of the vow known as the "Month-Gift," upon the completion of the observance,
one should likewise give a water-cow in the month of Āṣāḍha and ghee in Bhādrapada.
In the month of Māgha, there should be a sesame-cow; he who gives it obtains benefit. For example:
"One should give a cow made of sesame in Māgha, specifically during the northern course of the sun."

O Sage, one obtains all desires by offering an image made of sesame seeds on the full moon of Jyeṣṭha; likewise, one should offer an image made of ghee on the auspicious day of the full moon of Pauṣa according to the prescribed rite.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "One should give sesame seeds in the month of Jyeṣṭha, especially on the full moon day;
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, of this there is no doubt."
Yama said:
One should always give ghee to a twice-born man in the month of Āśvayuja;
having gratified the two gods, the Aśvins, one is born possessing beauty.
Viṣṇu said:

By giving ghee daily to Brahmins throughout the entire month of Āśvina and thereby pleasing the two Aśvins, one becomes possessed of beauty. In that same month, by feeding Brahmins daily with products of the cow, one becomes possessed of health. Likewise, in the month of Māgha, by offering oblations of sesame seeds into the fire daily and feeding Brahmins with ghee and *kulmāṣa* (sour gruel), one becomes possessed of a radiant digestive fire.
The wise one said:
"A man who gives sesame seeds indeed obtains his desired offspring,
especially in the month of Māgha, and most especially on the day mixed with [the previous] Taitila."
In the *Mahābhārata*: "He who offers sesame seeds to Brahmins in the month of Māgha does not behold the hell crowded with all manner of beings."
Thus ends the procedure for monthly gifts. Now, the gifts according to the seasons. In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"The giving of baths, ointments, and so forth, is prescribed for the spring."
Likewise, in the summer, [the gift] of water-pots, and immediately thereafter, of umbrellas.

In the Devīpurāṇa: "Furthermore, O child, he who, according to the prescribed rule during the rainy season, bestows sesame seeds and other gifts upon Brahmins and Brahmin maidens for the sake of the Goddess,"
That goddess will indeed be pleased with that vidyā before long.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O knowers of dharma, having made an external gift of food in autumn and of garments in winter, a man [should do so] at the rising of the sun."
The external gift consists of giving fire for the purpose of dispelling cold;
likewise, during the winter season, one should constantly satisfy the fire with sesame seeds and,
according to one's ability, give boiled grain with ghee to the twice-born.
One attains the radiance and clarity of the bodily fire and the destruction of enemies by consuming parched grain flour mixed with white sugar-candy, cucumber, and vāraka.
O best of the twice-born, one who has bathed during the rainy season and constantly offers [this] combined with salt and clarified butter,
placed upon a water-pot, attains indeed imperishable fruit.
Yama says:
Having fed the twice-born with rice mixed with sesame and meat according to his ability during the winter season,
one attains a blazing digestive fire and goes to the heavenly world.
[890] Thus end the gifts according to the seasons. Now follow the gifts according to the year, as stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
O best of the twice-born, the gift of sesame seeds by donors for a full year yields great fruit; likewise, the gift of barley at the end of that period does so as well.

The term *pari-pūrva* means "a full year" (*parivatsara*). It is taught that the gift of garments and grains in successive order, as well as the gift of silver preceded by the word *it*, yields great fruit.

Regarding "idāpūrva" and so forth: *idā* refers to the year (*vatsara*), the *anuvatsara*, and the *idvatsara*. These, along with the *saṃvatsara* and others, are well-known in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
Thus end the gifts of the years.
Thus [ends the section] of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādeva, the sovereign lord of all instruments, the entirety...

In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrī Hemādri, who is proficient in the sciences, within the section on giving (*dānakhaṇḍa*), this is the chapter on the specific times for giving (*kālaviśeṣa*).
[891] Chapter Thirteen: Now, the gifts that yield infinite fruit.
By which the ponds, delightful with groves and with serpents submerged in their surrounding ripples,
surpass the playful, effortless movement of the horses of the sun’s chariot;
and by which the wells are expert in the constant task of providing water for hundreds of the king’s armies.
The rows of palaces were constructed so as to touch the stars and to be beneficial to the dwellings of the twice-born.
This Hemādri, a marvelous and peerless scholar, has made even those gifts— which are worthy of being circulated through the channels of fame—
guests of his very eyes.
Now he speaks of the collection of gifts that yield infinite fruit.
In response to the inquiry as to what those [benefits] are, it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"One should, by means of religious observances, accomplish health, the means of enjoyment,
fearlessness, service to travelers, and food, water, and trees."
The wise say that these gifts yield infinite fruit.
Now, the gift of health (*ārogyadāna*). Regarding that, the gift of health is first explained. Viśvāmitra says:
[892] "There is no gift anywhere superior to the gift of health;
therefore, one should give health to those afflicted by disease for the increase of their fortune."
He who provides medicine, wholesome food, oil massage,
and shelter to the sick shall be free from disease.
Saṃvarta says:
One who gives medicine, oil, or food to the sick for the sake of curing their disease becomes free from illness, happy, and long-lived.
Agastya said:
Those who provide food and medicine go to happiness, free from disease.
In the Saura Purāṇa: "He who provides medicine for the sake of curing the disease of a sick person becomes free from disease, long-lived, and always happy."
In the Nandipurāṇa: "That high-minded man who gives collyrium to a Brahmin for the sake of curing an eye disease goes to the world of the Sun."
Such a man is born divine, fortunate, and possessing the eye of health.
Health is the means for achieving virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
therefore, by the gift of health, a person becomes endowed with all these at all times.
He establishes a hospital equipped with excellent medicines and provisions,
staffed by skilled physicians and provided with dwellings for the attendants.
But the physician should be learned in the scriptures, wise, one who has witnessed the efficacy of medicines,
one who knows the colors of medicinal roots, and one who knows the proper time for extraction.
The wise one who knows the tastes, potencies, and post-digestive effects of rice, meat, herbs, and gems,
and who understands their application, enters the bodies of embodied beings with his intellect.
He who knows the elements and what is wholesome for them, who understands the primary causes [of disease], who is unwearied,
who recognizes the early signs of diseases, and who knows the subsequent methods of treatment;
One who knows the place, time, and procedure, as well as the science of medicine;
one who is a knower of the eight branches of Ayurveda and a knower of the application of medicinal formulations.

The Ayurveda has eight branches, as stated by Suśruta: surgery (śalya), ophthalmology and otolaryngology (śālākya), internal medicine (kāyacikitsā), demonology (bhūtavidyā), pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), toxicology (agadatantra), rejuvenation therapy (rasāyaṇatantra), and aphrodisiac therapy (vājīkaraṇatantra).
A physician of such auspicious qualities should be appointed there;
one who adheres to the warrior code (yodhadharma) should thus establish a medical hall (ārogyaśālā).
That man is righteous in the world, he has accomplished his purpose, and he is wise,
having been properly treated with medicines that soothe and digest within the clinic of perfect health.
Having rendered even a single sick person free from pain, one endowed with compassion goes to the abode of Brahmā together with seven generations of his lineage.
The wealthy man, according to his means, becomes a sharer of the fruit for the poor;
for the poor man, where is there a house, or a young physician for his health?
Furthermore, even if a mortal has been restored to health by someone through the use of roots or by means of massages and other treatments, he shall attain the aforementioned imperishable world.

He who, by means of even a small effort, liberates those afflicted by disease— whose conditions vary according to the accumulation or depletion of wind, bile, phlegm, and the like— he too goes to auspicious worlds that are unattainable even for those who perform sacrifices.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Listen to the fruit of the merit of him who establishes a hospital for the sick, presided over by great physicians and equipped with all necessary implements.
Since health is the means for achieving virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, therefore,
by the gift of health, all four of these are given.
Then, by diligently restoring a single learned man who is afflicted,
one attains very great merit that is infinite and free from decay.
Whoever restores to health a peaceful Śiva-yogin who is afflicted by disease and devoted to the yoga of knowledge shall likewise obtain the fruit of all possible gifts.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, all the gods, diseases, kinsmen, and kings—these are the great obstacles to yoga; they are not [obstacles] for yogis.
The great merit that one obtains by protecting Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are afflicted by disease cannot be attained even through all the great sacrifices.
Just as no end of space can be found even by the gods,
so too no end whatsoever exists for the gift of health.
By this great merit, having gone to the city of Śiva, a person rejoices with various enjoyments and celestial chariots that fulfill all desires.
Endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage and accompanied by his servants,
he remains protected in the city of Śiva for as long as the dissolution of all things at the call of the end of the aeon.
Then, having always remained disciplined and devoted to the remnants of his own duty,
knowledge arises for him as he serves the Rudras.
Detached from worldly existence through knowledge and having resorted to the meditation on Śiva,
one casts off one's own body like a blade of grass and attains the end of all suffering.
Freed from all suffering, pure, established in one's own self,
omniscient, and perfect— one is designated as "liberated."
Therefore, for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should attend to those afflicted by disease,
and especially so toward a lord of yogis, with both body and wealth.
A wise man should never feel aversion toward the sick, even those who are weak; he should always regard them as his own teacher because of their suffering. In this way, righteousness proceeds.
He who, day by day, approaches [the teacher] while considering himself as one who has been favored—
even if he is afflicted by disease— by him the ocean of existence has been crossed.
Thus ends the gift of health.
Now, the gifts that remove diseases. In the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*,
Brahmā said:
O Blessed One, all living beings here are afflicted by disease;
therefore, O Lord of the World, what should be done for their relief?
O best of sages, having been thus addressed by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
I shall tell him all that the Blessed One said to him.
Mental anxieties and physical ailments indeed cause the body to wither;
one who desires their own welfare should perform meritorious deeds for the sake of avoiding them.
Fever, diarrhea, consumption, abdominal tumors, colic, fistula-in-ano, leprosy,
diseases of the digestive fire, wind-disorders, throat-pain, and smallpox;
Diseases of the throat, teeth, eyes, and ears, as well as diseases of the head and the upajihvikā (ranula),
all of which arise from the three doṣas, are terrifying to living beings.
Glands, dysuria, bladder disease, and abdominal enlargement—
these and many others, possessing great speed and great strength.
Diseases numbering in the hundreds are indeed causes of death;
therefore, whatever may bring about the pacification of disease should be performed by the wise.

Medicine, recitation, burnt offerings, and the like, as well as charity and the worship of deities, all serve to pacify every disease; yet the gift of gold is said to be the supreme remedy for them all.
In cases of fever, erysipelas, and consumption, that [iron] is prescribed;
likewise, iron is declared for abdominal tumors, while silver is said to be used for skin diseases.
Through the gift of jewels, all ailments arising in the rectum are entirely pacified;
O Lotus-Seated One, through the gift of land, there shall be a complete cessation of disease at its very end.
For the sake of pacifying wind-related diseases,
the gift of clothing is prescribed by one who desires the alleviation of ailments arising from the throat, tongue, and so forth.
Grain, clothing, or gold should be given with great effort;
the gift of gold is the cause of pacification for all diseases.
Therefore, O Lotus-born One, with every effort one should give clarified butter mixed with gold for the diseases arising in the eyes.
Water, milk-rice, mung beans combined with sugar and ghee,
and indeed sugar-candy along with a pillow, [should be offered] during all instances of aching in the limbs.
O Lotus-born One, one should offer a woolen blanket for the diseases of Vaikuṇṭha,
as well as gems and silver, according to one's capacity and in a fitting manner.
And having fashioned an image of the disease, one should diligently give it to a Brahmin for a hundred [gold pieces],
or half of that, or thirty in number.
One should have an image of the disease fashioned out of gold;
having placed it in a vessel filled with rice and one hundred silver coins.
And having adorned the golden image with applications of aloe-wood incense,
wrapped it in a pair of garments, and decorated it with many ornaments of gold;
Having given [the gift] to a decorated Brahmin, one should utter this mantra:
"Those diseases that afflict me, constantly and pervasively residing within my body..."
"O best of the twice-born, take those diseases in exchange for your own form.
"So be it," he replied, and he accepted that form along with the ailments.
[898] From that very act, one becomes free from disease, a donor, and attains long life;
thus, O Lotus-Seated One, it serves as a manifold means for the pacification of diseases.
"I have told you what must be done for them; what else shall I tell you?
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the World, [spoke].
All that was spoken by me to Nārada has been related here in its entirety.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift that removes disease. Now follow the gifts that bestow enjoyment (*bhoga*). Regarding these, Jābāli first speaks of the gift of jewels:
"A person should give highly valuable jewels to a twice-born man."
Or, for the sake of ornament, [one may offer] to the deities with great effort.
Freed from the torment of sin, he attains liberation itself;
there is no object superior to the jewels, nor is there anything else in the three worlds.
Therefore, by virtue of that gift, who could possibly describe its fruit?
Viśvāmitra said:
He who bestows jewels upon the Brahmins with great effort obtains sons endowed with all virtues and rejoices.
Saṃvarta says:
A man free from defilement, by giving jewels produced from the ocean to a great Brahmin, attains great prosperity.
[899] Vedavyāsa said: O lord of men, it is declared that the gift of jewels is a source of very great merit;
for a Brāhmaṇa who bestows fearlessness performs sacrifice by selling those [jewels].
In the Skanda Purāṇa: By the gift of coral, a man goes to the world of Rudra;
freed from all sins, he is born [again] through the gift of pearls.
By means of a gift of a *vajra-gomeda*, a man attains the world of Vajrin, the wielder of the thunderbolt;
likewise, by giving *gomeda* gems, he rejoices and delights in the forest.
All the planets are propitiated by the gift of a puṣparāga gem;
with emeralds, one certainly conquers Indra through prosperity.
One attains the world of the sun through lapis lazuli, and freedom from disease through rubies.
The word "given" (*dattaiḥ*) is to be supplied [to the following].
By the gift of sapphires (*indranīla*), one becomes a vessel for playful delights;
by the gift of a conch shell, one becomes happy; and by the gift of a pearl-oyster (*śukti*), one gains power (*śakti*).
Thus ends the gift of jewels.
Now Vṛddhagautama said:
"A ruby, a lotus-gem (padmarāga), a diamond, and likewise lapis lazuli..."
Mauktika, gomeda, puṣparāga, and likewise marakata.
One should place these nine green items upon a golden vessel;
or alternatively, one may fill a silver or copper vessel with clarified butter.
Created of old by Brahmā for the sake of pleasing the nine planets,
one should worship that [image] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, incense, and food offerings.
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed as before with their own respective insignia and mantras;
"as before" means by the method described in the *grahayajña*.
Then, having summoned a Brāhmaṇa who is well-versed in the meaning of all the scriptures...
May all the planets, beginning with the Sun, being delighted by the offering of the nine gems, swiftly destroy my fistula.
The mantra for the offering:
By this rite, when truly performed according to the rules,
a man undoubtedly attains freedom from hemorrhoids and fistula.
Thus ends the gift for the removal of hemorrhoids. Likewise:
A ruby accompanied by a diamond, flawless and auspicious by its very nature, should be wrapped in a red cloth and placed upon five *khārikās* [of grain].
Alternatively, having placed a ruby upon a heap of barley with its most precious part facing upward,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, preceded by devotion.
Having summoned a Brahmin who is endowed with Vedic learning, of good conduct, with senses restrained, and modest in appearance, he should do so with devotion and a disciplined mind.
Having worshipped him according to the rules with a golden sacred thread, as well as garments and rings, just as before for one who has performed the fire-oblation;
With this mantra, the person with the wound should duly offer auspicious [substances] to him, saying:
"O God Sūrya, Lord of the World, honored by all the worlds!"
"By the gift of rubies and diamonds, may you destroy my wound.
This is the mantra for giving.
"Even those wounds which may be caused by weapons smeared with poison in battle..."
They too grow pure, just as was declared by Vāyu.
Thus ends the gift of the jewel that destroys wounds.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "A man who steals substances from the throat becomes one with a goiter."
I shall describe the remedy for that through generosity; listen, O Bhāskara.
Māṇikya, padmarāga, vajra, and likewise gomedaka;
vaidūrya, puṣparāga, pearl, and similarly emerald.
With these one should fashion a garland; the thread for it should also be silver.
If that is unavailable, one should prepare the garland with any other material such as pearls and so forth.
One should arrange silver thread everywhere according to the prescriptions of the gods;
having placed it in a copper vessel, one should set it upon the sesame seeds.
The quantity of sesame seeds is prescribed as five *droṇas*,
or it may be half of that, or one should have it performed according to one's own capacity.
Likewise, one should perform a great propitiatory rite for peace through Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
"Great peace" means the pacification of the nine planets.
And the preceptor should be pure, skillful, a knower of the true meaning of all scriptures,
endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, and devoted to the welfare of all living beings.
Having worshipped in this manner with garments, garlands, and ointments,
one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with that [substance], abounding in sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice.
The mantra "Ā satyena" and likewise "Gaṇānām idam," as well as the mantras beginning with "Somaṃ rājānam," should be joined together in their proper sequence.
Facing north, one who suffers from a goiter, remaining silent, should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with this mantra according to the rule to one facing east.
This Mālā belongs to all the deities—by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others;
by Rudra and the other world-protectors (Lokapālas); and likewise by all the immortals (Amaras).
"Whether constantly worn around the neck or cherished with affection,
may this [image], when given to a Brāhmaṇa, dispel goiters.
This is the mantra for the gift.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those by whom the pacification of the planets (grahaśānti) has been performed;
having performed the recitation for an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), one should eat together with one's kinsmen.
Thus ends the gift of the jewel that destroys goiters.
Now, the gift of ornaments. In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
"He who gives brilliant ornaments to the twice-born..."
Thus adorned, he sports in the heavenly world with hosts of apsarases.
By the gift of ornaments one becomes handsome and fortunate;
likewise, by the gift of ornaments one obtains long life.
Sadāśiva attains satisfaction through the gift of ornaments for men,
while the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain is pleased by the giving of ornaments for women.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Though young, though possessing all his limbs intact, and though bearing a radiant body,
one truly does not possess a charming splendor without ornaments."
Human birth is difficult to obtain; even therein, a handsome appearance is rare;
and even for that, O best of men, youth serves as its ornament.
All this would be in vain and without ornament for human beings;
therefore, with every effort, one should indeed bestow ornaments.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By the gift of a head-ornament, one shall attain the status of a consecrated monarch;
by those for the ears, there shall be fame reaching to the ears; and through those for the neck, unimpeded fortune."

With his palms he would conquer those who conquer with palms; with his hips he would conquer the Unborn (Viṣṇu); with his knees he would conquer men; and with his feet he would conquer those born from feet.
In the world of men, there is nothing more desirable than well-adorned preeminent men;
yet that [desirability] cannot be obtained without giving.
Therefore, the ornaments should be bestowed.
Thus ends the gift of ornaments.
[904] Now, the gift of clothing. Devala says:
One who gives a garment becomes endowed with beauty, fortunate, and glorious.
In the *Nandipurāṇa* it is said:
"He who gives a garment, whether white or as he pleases, to one who asks for it..."
He shall become wealthy and illustrious, and he shall dwell in the city of Bṛhaspati.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "And for those men who give garments to yogis and to the poor,
there shall be divine garments— fragrant and soft."
And indeed, a fragrant wind blows, truly like nectar.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"One should give clothing, water, and a sacred thread to a Śiva-yogin;
he obtains great enjoyment and, in the end, eternal yoga."
In the Mahābhārata: "We have heard that by the gift of garments, a man who is devoted to his own wife becomes well-clothed and well-attired."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "One should give garments of middling or superior quality that are unwashed;
by that very act, one obtains abundant fruit in accordance with that [gift]."
[905] From the Viṣṇudharmottara: Haṃsa said:
"The gift of clothing is proclaimed to be the best among gifts in this world."
For clothing is said to belong to all the deities and is fit for all purposes.
A donor of clothing shall be well-attired, endowed with beauty and wealth,
possessed of charm and good fortune, and likewise free from disease, O twice-born one.
One should not give blue, red, or worn-out [garments] to a Brāhmaṇa;
rather, a superior garment should be given, for [the donor] goes to the world of Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras.
Having given a garment of cotton, one is honored in the heavenly world;
by giving one with the wool still upon it, the fruit there shall be tenfold.
By giving a garment of sheep's wool, one attains the world of the Bhṛgus;
by giving a goat, the world of Aṅgiras; and by giving a linen garment, the world of Bṛhaspati.
By giving garments of kuśa grass or silk, one attains the world of the Vasus;
likewise, by giving cloth made from insects (silk), one is glorified in the world of Soma.
By giving even a garment made of deer-hair, one attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
by giving a garment made of bark, one shall attain the world of the Vasus.
Having given samocaka, kadali, and so forth, as well as a deerskin,
a pair of trousers, a breastplate, and likewise a helmet;
One who gives footwear obtains the fruit of a separate sacrifice;
the gift of clothing is purifying and even delivers one's ancestors.
By giving [a gift] dyed with safflower, one shall obtain great good fortune;
by the gift of that which is dyed with saffron, one shall obtain great beauty.
By applying other colors and red lac, one shall become happy;
for in this world, the more a garment becomes highly valuable, [the greater the merit].
To whatever extent there is purity, to that same extent the fruit of merit is great;
this alone is proclaimed as superior to all other forms of giving.
O knowers of dharma, since one who gives clothing everywhere is said to be a giver of everything, and because he obtains that [everything] from such a gift, it is therefore distinguished as superior.
The giver of clothing, having enjoyed divine happiness on earth for a very long time,
travels in a radiant celestial chariot, sun-colored and drawn by swans.
Having attained human birth, he becomes free from disease,
yet possessed of sorrow and deprived of supreme happiness;
nevertheless, he is pleasing to people and well-attired.
And he is always to be honored in the world by the wise.
Thus concludes the gift of clothing. Now, regarding the rite for purification:
Īśvara said:
I shall proclaim the gift of clothing, which increases my joy,
bestows long life and health upon men, and is the supreme cause of happiness.
One should provide a pair of fine white garments for each of the eleven Brahmins who embody the eleven forms of Rudra.
Having adorned them with perfumes and flowers and having fed them according to the prescribed rite,
one should then cause garments to be given to them while reciting the aforementioned mantra.
May Bhava, the wearer of the elephant hide, be forever gracious toward us;
may Śaṅkara accept the garments offered by us.
A man who gives garments equal in number to the threads [of which they are woven],
having become as powerful as Rudra, is glorified in the world of Rudra.
The names of the eleven Rudras are to be found in the ritual for the offering of sesame seeds to the eleven Rudras.
Thus concludes the procedure for the offering of garments to the eleven Rudras.
Now follows the offering of garments to the deities, as stated in the Āditya Purāṇa.
By the gift of clothing to a fire-priest (*vahnin*), one attains the world of Brahmā. In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"But garments that are variegated, substantial, and soft..."
Having bathed them, one should offer two new sheaths to Śiva.
For as many thousands of years as there are threads in that garment, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "He who gives garments of linen or of fine wool, or even those made of cotton, with devotion to the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), according to his means."
In that garment, for as many atoms as there are in its threads, for so many thousands of years is one honored in the heavenly world.
In the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa: "He who, being wealthy, gives new and unwashed cloth to the Sun,
having reached the world of Hari, is honored even by the gods."

In the *Devīpurāṇa*: "O Śakra, by worshipping the Daughter of the Mountain with garments made of silk or even those born of eggs (wool), and adorning her with ornaments, one shall attain the status of a universal monarch."
Now, the gift of garments that remove sorrow. Regarding this, Vṛddha-Baudhāyana says:
"A man who creates obstacles for those consuming food becomes sorrowful;
for him, the following is the supreme remedy to destroy the disease arising from the ripening of his karma."
I shall describe in its entirety the gift that destroys all sorrow;
having procured a linen garment of great value, such as it deserves.
One should tie pearls at all four corners along the edge of the cloth,
properly marked with saffron and fumigated with camphor and agallochum incense.
Having placed [the image] upon the rice and [offering] as much rice as he can afford,
the preceptor should joyfully worship it with the sixteen services;
they know that the worship is performed with the two mantras beginning with *yuvam* and *yuvā suvāsāḥ*.
"yuvam vastrāṇi" is one mantra, and "yuvāsuvāsā" is another mantra.
One should also perform the fire-oblation with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds,
using the mantras "udbuddhasva," "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and "āpasmint sapta."
One should offer oblations in sequence with the mantras, as well as the Sviṣṭakṛt offering which belongs to it.
Having offered oblations repeatedly and having placed all the remnants in a vessel,
he should perform the count exactly one hundred and eight times for the sake of the patient.

With the hymn beginning "By the falling [of the arrow]" (*sampātena*), one should likewise apply it to every limb and marrow of the patient, as well as to the eyes, according to the specific symptoms.
One should perform the cleansing of the garments; one should cleanse them with handfuls of *darbha* grass.
Then, being sorrowful, one should give that garment to the teacher along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Facing south, pure and according to the prescribed rite, with this mantra: "May Agastya, the preeminent among sages, the lord and husband of Lopāmudrā,
being pleased by the gift of this linen garment, dispel my disease."
The mantra for the gift:
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability to the Brahmins as well as to others.
Then, having bathed, become pure, and adorned with garments and garlands—
He should eat together with the Brahmins and his kinsmen with the utmost devotion.
Thus ends the gift of clothing.
Now, the gift of the turban. In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"Mortals who give turbans are born radiant with crowns."
In that extensive royal lineage, they were characterized by the foremost mark of the white parasol.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"He who should give various turbans to the twice-born—
whether they be red, white, or even saffron-colored— "
Having attained supreme beauty, he shall become beloved by women;
for those who give turbans, O King, possess beautiful hair and beautiful faces.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, strive to make gifts of them.

Now follows the gift of a woolen garment. Kāśyapa said: Even he who, out of devotion, gives a woolen cloak to a twice-born man attains supreme perfection, which is very difficult for other mortals to obtain.
But he who gives a divine woolen cloak, which wards off cold, wind, and heat, to ascetics who live in a state of total possessionlessness—
With the entire flood of suffering cast aside, he becomes a possessor of great wealth.
In the Vahni Purāṇa: "He who bestows a new, fine,
and very large blanket upon an eminent Brahmin on a day afflicted by cold provides them with happiness on their journey."
He who, out of compassion, gives woolen clothing to the destitute and the wretched who are afflicted by cold, wind, and intense heat;
Even the gods of the thirty-three cannot describe his merit;
freed from mental and physical afflictions, he enjoys imperishable happiness.
Now, the gift of a bed. Vedavyāsa says:
That man who gives a bed, provided with fragrant and variegated coverlets, to a twice-born man—
He shall obtain a wife endowed with beauty, possessed of wings, charming, and acquired without effort.
Now, in the Viṣṇusaṃhitā:
Listen also in detail regarding the gift of a bed;
it should be given at all times as well as on auspicious days.
The limbs, feet, and arches should be fashioned from ivory, coral, gold, or silver, and they should be accompanied by ritual gifts.
Even if they cannot be obtained, auspicious seats made of wood of equal quality should be prepared,
covered with beautiful carpets that have the appearance of layers of twilight clouds.
It was provided with neck-like ramparts that were well-extended and draped with cloth,
and equipped with vessels made of jewels, gold, silver, and copper.
With fragrant fruits and flowers, with extensive offerings such as betel and the like,
with mirrors, foot-protectors, and various substances and ornaments;
Having established them in the four corners according to one's ability, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
[one should place] vessels filled with ghee, saffron, wheat, and water.
Having fully worshipped the bed, my devotee who is intent upon me should,
with palms joined in reverence, perform a circumambulation of the bed.

Having prostrated toward the four directions with the words "Homage to the Goddess of Valid Cognition," [he should offer it] to a poor Brāhmaṇa who is distinguished by his learning and study of the Vedas.
Likewise, a wise person should provide a bed to one who is learned in wisdom;
the merit of that gift is a celestial mansion radiant with gold.
It was strewn with various jewels, endowed with various flowers,
frequented by various divine apsarases, and covered with various gems.
He ascends a celestial chariot endowed with various precious substances;
from there, he goes to the city of Indra, being attended by throngs of apsarases.
Having sported at his pleasure for sixty thousand years,
he falls from the world of Indra and becomes a king in this world.
In a mandala sixty yojanas in extent, he becomes a sovereign;
he is a knower of dharma, one who has conquered his servants, as well as radiant and handsome.
In the Mahābhārata: Listen now to the fruit that belongs to one who gives a bed, provided with a mattress and well-covered with a fine canopy, to a brahmin.
Handsome, fortunate, and beloved by women, surrounded by thousands of women,
he is honored in the heavenly world for ten thousand years.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "O descendant of the Pāṇḍu lineage, I shall describe to you the gift of a bed;
by giving it, one becomes a partaker of auspiciousness both in this world and in the next."
The best of the twice-born always praise the gift of a bed, because life is transient; who else will provide it later?
O Bhārata, he is a kinsman and he is a father only so long as he lives;
once he is known to be dead, affection ceases in an instant.
Therefore, having reflected in one's mind that "the self alone is the kinsman of the self," one should personally provide bedding, food, water, and so forth.
If one does not honor oneself with gifts and enjoyments,
who else is more beneficial than that [self] which will honor [oneself] later?
Therefore, having reached a bed made of strong sal-wood,
beautiful, adorned with ivory inlays and decorated with bands of gold;
Upon a bed covered with swan-down feathers and perfumed with incense and other fragrances,
one should place a golden image of Hari accompanied by Lakṣmī;
at the head of the bed, one should arrange a water-pot filled with ghee.
The form of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa should be understood from the section on the gift of deities (*devatādāna*) concerning the gift of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, it should be known by the wise that [the vessel] contains a jar with a lid,
along with betel, saffron, camphor, musk, agallochum, and sandalwood.
One should devoutly place a lamp, sandals, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, and a vessel, as well as the seven types of grain, at the sides.
Whatever else is helpful to one lying on a bed,
such as the *bhṛṅgāra* and *karaka* vessels, destroys the five colors [of the body].
Having prepared such a bed, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa together with his wife on an auspicious day, having honored him according to the prescribed ritual.
Just as the bed of Kṛṣṇa is never empty of the daughter of the ocean,
so may my bed also be never empty in birth after birth.
Since the bed of Keśava and Śiva is never empty,
may my own bed likewise be never empty in birth after birth.
Having thus offered a pure bed and prostrated, one should bid them farewell;
this is the prescribed procedure for the gift of a bed that has been proclaimed.
By the power of giving a bed, that living being dwells happily in heaven, in the abode of Indra, and likewise in the residence of the Son of the Sun.
In the abode of the Son of the Sun, likewise in the city of Vaivasvata,
the terrifying-faced messengers of Yama do not torment him.
That man is never oppressed by heat or cold;
even if he is joined with sin, he goes to the heavenly world.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot and served by hosts of apsarases,
he shall remain there, freed from all sin, until the dissolution of the world.
O son of Pāṇḍu, the stainless gift of a bed has been proclaimed by you as the source of all happiness; indeed,
he who himself bestows it according to the prescribed rite shall dwell in heaven.
Free from conceptual construction, that mortal shines forth for an eon.
Now, the gift of Śiva’s bed. From the *Śivadharma*:
One should offer a bed for Śiva that is provided with a goose-feather mattress, a soft couch, well-adorned, and equipped with all necessary furnishings.
Having made Śiva, joined with the Goddess, joyful, one should present [the offering].
The form of Śivadevī is to be seen in the section on the gift of deities (*devatādāna*) within the ritual for the gift of Umāmaheśvara.

Having worshipped the preceptor (*ācārya*), who knows the reality of the purpose of Śiva-knowledge and is endowed with compassion, with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as garments, ornaments, and chowries;
Then, one should offer a bed with all kinds of foods, both solid and soft;
for as many thousands of years as there are threads in the wool, cotton, or cloth of that bed, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
The Gift of the Sun’s Bed. In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "One should prepare a bed for the Sun, well-constructed with a soft mattress filled with swan-down, and equipped with all necessary furnishings."
Then one should offer a bed joined with a royal consort to the compassionate preceptor, who knows the reality of the meaning of the solar knowledge.
Having worshipped him with flowers, perfumes, and the like, with garments, ornaments, and chowries,
as well as with various kinds of food— both solid and soft— and drinks endowed with manifold flavors;
The form of the Queen was described by Viśvakarman:
"The Queen should be depicted with two arms, wearing a deer skin and a crown,
holding the gesture of granting boons (varada) in her own hand, and seated upon a lotus."
For as many thousands of yugas as there are threads in that garment of wool or cotton, for so long is he honored in the world of the Sun.
Having enjoyed all pleasures without exception in all the worlds, beginning with that of the Sun,
he returns in due course to this world and becomes a king upon the earth.
Now, the gift of a seat. In the *Liṅga Purāṇa*: "He who gives a seat and a bed to one who is illustrious, and who is equal toward all beings—for him no suffering exists."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who offers a covered seat to a Brāhmaṇa indeed attains the station of self-sovereignty, becoming radiant and free from all affliction."
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "He who gives a seat adorned with fragrant and variegated ornaments to one who knows the Vedas..."
He quickly obtains the lordship of a village,
and he shall attain complete greatness within his family.
Viṣṇu [states]: "The seat is the locus of giving. The word "fruit" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Now, the gift of a mirror. In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"The man who gives a stainless mirror to a twice-born person, having reached the world of the Moon, rejoices for a hundred autumns."
In the *Nandiprokta*:
"One should place a beautiful, stainless mirror before Śiva,
having adorned its perimeter with white garlands and sandalwood paste."
Stainless as the rays of the moon, glorious, fortunate, and assuming forms at will,
he is honored in the world of Rudra for ten thousand times ten thousand kalpas.

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Having worshipped Viṣṇu with devotion on a lunar mansion presided over by Viṣṇu that resembles the orb of the moon, or on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) during an auspicious time..."
The man who gives a mirror adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste is born handsome, fortunate, illustrious, and possessed of wisdom.
[918] Now, the gift of a fan. In the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"He who devoutly bestows a palm-leaf fan upon the twice-born..."
Free from disease, he always enjoys union with divine pleasures.
Nothing other than the breeze from a palm-leaf fan is capable of delighting a king, who is otherwise exhausted by great austerities and intent on uprooting the nature of worldly existence.
Nothing other than the fanning of a fan would be able to remove the fatigue, thick with perspiration, arising from the enjoyment of her lotus-stalk-like thighs.
Therefore, always filled with joy, one should give a palm-leaf fan to a twice-born man,
free from all blame, as a means for attaining the enjoyment of liberation.
O highly fortunate one! He who gives a fan that delights all beings to the foremost of the twice-born shall dwell in heaven with a mind rejoicing in the fragrance of the Nandana grove.
Free from all taint, he shall dwell for the duration of all kalpas, satiating [the ancestors].
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By giving a fan made of bamboo, one is born into a great lineage;
by giving a fan made of leather, one attains the perfection of all actions."
Likewise, when a peacock feather is given, his lifespan does not diminish;
by means of a vessel he attains the status of a son, and by means of a garment he becomes free from contempt among women.
Therefore, one should offer that [gift] by giving a fan here in this world.
[919] Now, the gift of chowries. In the Mahābhārata:
"He who, with devotion, should give a radiant chowrie to the foremost of the twice-born..."
He attains sovereignty over the entire circle of the earth.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"He who offers a chowrie to Śiva, the Lord of Chowries,
shall dwell upon the slopes of the Golden Mountain with all his desires fulfilled."
Whoever offers a peacock-feather whisk to Śiva shall mount an excellent celestial chariot and be fanned by hosts of apsarases.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
By offering an excellent chowrie with faith to Viṣṇu,
a person attains the supreme state, which is difficult even for the gods to reach.
This is more beloved to the God of gods than all other ritual offerings.
The gift of a canopy. In the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
"A canopy that is beautifully expansive, likewise painted with colors, adorned with hanging clusters of pearls, and filled with jewels."
[920] Adorned with the binding of well-dyed silk threads and other materials, it is distinguished by the various arrangements of mandalas, foremost among which is the Sarvatobhadra.
It was likewise resplendent, filled with variegated leafy creepers,
and graced by the heads of pairs of yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
Having fashioned such a canopy, which caused great wonder on all sides due to its embroidered decorations, he then presented it to the twice-born man.
On an auspicious day, one should offer [this] to Śiva or to Viṣṇu;
he certainly delivers his own ancestors from [saṃsāra].
Having personally enjoyed delightful pleasures in the beautiful city of Śiva,
one shall eventually return to this world and become happy, wise, and wealthy.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "That person of meritorious intellect who devoutly offers the 'Moonrise' (candrodaya) gift— no end to his auspicious states ever arises."
Now, the gift of fragrance. Saṃvarta says:
"He who, knowing the Dharma, gives fragrances, ornaments, and so forth, is born wherever he may be endowed with a sweet and pervasive scent."
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "By the gift of fragrance, a man shall obtain a fragrant body;
he will always be possessed of enjoyments, and his body shall never suffer."
In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"Indeed, by the gift of unguents and perfumes,
a human being never experiences a burning of the mind or a burning of the body."
By the offering of fragrant incense, one shall go to the world of the apsarases.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By the gift of ointment, a man is born handsome;
by the gift of sandalwood, he is liberated from all sins."
The gift of saffron is declared to bring about good fortune;
likewise, by the gift of camphor, one shall attain all desires.
By the gift of musk, one shines with glory upon the earth;
by the gift of yakṣakardama, one enjoys extensive sovereignty.
Now, the offering of betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*). In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"The man who, endowed with self-restraint, offers betel-leaf daily to the gods and to the twice-born, attains great fortune."
In this world of transmigrating beings, the human state is extremely difficult to attain; yet, through the gift of betel, that state arises for men without further effort.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "He who, with a concentrated mind, offers bright betel-leaf to Brahmins,
as well as to Śiva and Keśava, is honored in the heavenly world."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By the gift of betel, one also obtains good fortune;
by giving nutmeg, O Brahmins, one finds that one's actions bear fruit."
By the gift of mouth-perfume, one shall obtain fragrance of the mouth.
Now, regarding the offering of flowers. In the *Mahābhārata*: "Because they gladden the mind and bestow prosperity, they are therefore called *sumanas* (well-minded) by men of virtuous deeds."
The pure man who offers flowers to the deities attains all his desires and is glorified in heaven after death.
Therefore, they are called *sumanasaḥ* because the deities are pleased by them; O Lord, whichever deity one has in mind when these *sumanasaḥ* flowers are offered, [to that deity they go].
O Lord of Daityas, he becomes pleased with him for the sake of his welfare.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*: "The giver of incense is always fragrant; the giver of flowers is ever fortunate. Therefore, those who desire happiness should give these to a deity and to a brāhmaṇa."
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"Nourishment shall be constant at all times through the offering of perfumes and garlands. [923] Yama says:
By offering flowers to the deities, one is born endowed with prosperity;
and that man who offers incense attains an upward rebirth.
Viśvāmitra said:
Flowers should always be offered by men who seek meritorious fruits;
for what deity is there who is not pleased by flowers?
Now, the gift of song and so forth. In the Nandipurāṇa:
"The wise man who gives song and instrumental music to a Brāhmaṇa shall go to the city of the Gandharvas and dwell there for three yugas."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Just as one goes to one's home singing, drinking, or eating,
so too does he who performs vocal music for Brahmins at the time of their meal."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "He who sings a very sweet song in a temple of the gods or in the houses of Brahmins shall dwell in the city of the Gandharvas."
O King, by pleasing the twice-born and the deities with the science of instrumental music,
he reaches the heavenly world and is entertained by the gods and others.
Whoever constantly performs dance before the deities or before the twice-born,
the hosts of apsarases shall eternally entertain him in heaven.
He who causes singing, instrumental music, and dancing to be performed by paying a fee shall dwell in the abode of Śakra until the dissolution of all that is summoned.
Or whoever entertains a deity with mouth-music, having washed away the stains of impurity, shall go to heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, he who praises the virtues of the virtuous with pleasing words,
or who praises the deity with hymns composed either by himself or by others;
By whom can the incalculable merit of that meritorious one be counted?

Now, the gift of the parasol and sandals. Bṛhaspati says: A man who gives a parasol and sandals crosses the path of the Forest of Sword-Leaves (Asipatravana), which is lined with razor edges, and the scorching heat.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "He who bestows a water-pot during the summer heat or the rainy season never experiences any mental distress whatsoever."
In the Mahābhārata: "He who bestows sandals upon Brahmins with diligence tramples down all thorns, even while crossing over uneven terrain."
By him, indeed, a cart yoked with draft animals has been given;
for him, a vehicle yoked with mules shall be prepared in heaven.
O son of Kuntī, those who give wooden sandals adorned with silver and gold to a virtuous Brāhmaṇa go to heaven,
enjoying pleasures, by means of a divine vehicle.
In the dialogue between Jamadagni— who was provoked by not seeing the dust heated by the sun's rays—
and the Sun, the Sun said:
"O Great Seer, let this umbrella, which wards off my rays, be a protection for your head."
And accept these leather sandals as protection for your feet.
From this day forward, this shall circulate throughout the worlds during meritorious times and shall indeed be supremely inexhaustible.
O Bhārata, these sandals and this umbrella were indeed employed here by Bhūri; they are renowned as meritorious throughout the three worlds.
Therefore, bestow excellent umbrellas and sandals upon the Brahmins;
your merit will be very great, of this I have no doubt.
For he who gives a white umbrella with a hundred ribs to a member of the twice-born, O tiger among men, prospers in happiness after passing away.
O bull of the Bharatas, he dwells in the world of Śakra, constantly honored by the twice-born, by the Apsarases, and by the gods.
O mighty-armed one, he who bestows a pair of sandals upon a Brahmin who is being scorched by heat— a twice-born Snātaka of rigid vows— [attains great merit].
He too attains worlds honored even by the gods;
he dwells in Goloka for a kalpa, O Bhārata, and likewise in each heaven.
[926] This fruit of the gift of an umbrella and sandals, O best of the Bharatas, has been recounted by me to you in its entirety, O most excellent of the Bharatas.
In the Vahni Purāṇa: One should give an umbrella that provides protection from heat, rain, and sun to a twice-born man;
being liberated from all diseases, he obtains prosperity and sons.
And by means of a divine celestial chariot, garlanded with networks of wish-fulfilling gems,
he goes to the abode of Mahendra, being attended by hosts of apsarases.
For one who gives a pair of sandals to a Brahmin whose feet are burning,
no burning of the mind ever arises.
O brahmin-sage, a splendid chariot yoked with mules, made of gold and adorned with every kind of jewel, stands ready for him.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*: "O Nārada, by the gift of an umbrella during the rainy season as well as in the summer,
those [beings] shall remain for ten thousand days of the entire year, endowed with all their desires."
He who bestows an umbrella obtains sons and prosperity;
he does not suffer from eye disease and partakes in the portion of the sacrifice.
"And he shall obtain liberation from both hardship and misfortune;
thus spoke the illustrious and venerable sage Śāṇḍilya."
Kātyāyana says:
One should give an umbrella that protects against wind, rain, and heat to a twice-born man;
he becomes free from all diseases and obtains prosperity and sons.
Devala says: "The giver of an umbrella travels with shade; the giver of shoes travels by vehicle.
Yama says:

The giver of an umbrella obtains a house, and likewise the giver of a house obtains a city— so says Jamadagni. He who bestows a pair of sandals upon a Brahmin whose feet are being scorched [by the heat] [attains great merit].
To that Snātaka of firm vows, O mighty-armed one, who was a twice-born man.
He attains the worlds and is honored even by the gods;
indeed, O Bhārata, he dwells in Goloka filled with joy.
Atri:
He who gives food and sandals at the times for ancestral rites (śrāddha) shall indeed obtain abundant merit and reap the fruit of the gift of a horse.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: He who bestows wooden sandals as footwear upon an eminent brahmin goes happily to my abode by means of a great, excellent horse.
Now, the gift of a vessel. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"He who gives a golden vessel adorned with jewels rejoices in heaven in a celestial chariot crowded with hundreds of *apsarases*."
He who bestows a beautiful silver vessel upon Brahmins,
having attained the station of a Gandharva, rejoices together with Urvaśī.
He who gives a copper vessel, especially to Brahmins,
shall become a lord of the Yakṣa king, endowed with splendor.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By giving vessels made of radiant metal and of beautiful color,
one becomes a vessel for all desires and shall attain great loveliness."
For one who gives metallic vessels filled with oil,
excellent health is proclaimed, as well as supreme beauty.
O twice-born ones, for one who gives metallic vessels filled with clarified butter,
supreme health is proclaimed, as well as residence in heaven.
For one who offers vessels made of refined metal that are perfectly balanced,
supreme beauty is said to be attained, as well as supreme good fortune.
Now, the gift of vessels made of gold and other materials. In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"One who should offer a golden vessel filled with milk, a silver one filled with curd, a hundred pearls, and a pair of garments..."
Then, with the sounding of the *puṇyāha* drum and auspicious sounds such as cries of victory,
one should diligently worship Hari after having installed him upon a golden lotus.
The form of Viṣṇu has indeed been described in the context of the Tulāpuruṣa gift.
Then, taking that vessel himself amidst the sounds of musical instruments and Vedic chants,
he should perform a circumambulation for that powerful Viṣṇu.
Then, having addressed him according to the rules, one should worship him especially;
thus, having fully honored the Brahmin and bowed down, one should ask for his forgiveness.
Having fed other Brahmins, he should also give them gold as a sacrificial fee;
and having honored those observing vows with gifts of food, clothing, and so forth, he should satisfy them.
One should give food without restriction to the poor, the blind, and the wretched,
having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha and on the full moon day.
He who performs this rite correctly shall go to the abode of Hari;
however, he who mocks the gods, the Brahmins, and ascetics [is excluded].
This vow of the form of the alms-bowl must never be given to them;
it bestows the form of wisdom and grants longevity, wealth, and good fortune.
This [vow], when practiced according to the prescribed rule, bestows sons and happiness;
one should honor the teacher of this vow, who is endowed with tranquility and virtuous qualities.
One desiring prosperity should worship with sandals, garments, and gold;
and likewise, a vessel made of silver filled with clarified butter and joined with a sapphire.
But in the absence of gold, one should worship the cloth with half a karṣa.
In the absence of a sapphire, the central part should be adorned with half a *karṣa* of gold.
Having brought a pair of new, fine cloths strewn with heaps of flowers,
one should place that vessel there in a clean location.
Then one should keep a vigil with auspicious songs, instrumental music, and other such ceremonies;
at dawn, one should carry that vessel to the great temple of Hari.
Having bathed the Lord Viṣṇu with milk and other substances, and having worshipped him, one should present that vessel and utter: "May he be pleased."
Then, having offered various kinds of foods along with fragrant boiled rice mixed with curds,
sugar-candy, and other ingredients, one should present the food offering (naivedya) and the sacrificial oblation (bali).
Then, having bowed, he should go home; having arrived, he should bow again.
Having bowed, he should devotedly feed those observing the vow together with the twice-born brahmins.
Then, one should duly honor the preceptor with gold, garments, and other gifts, without restriction, for the sake of all who are distressed, blind, or miserable.
And likewise, according to one's ability, for one who desires to live a long life—
this is to be known as the *pātravrata*, and it has been revealed here as a secret.
It should not be given to those of wicked intellect, to enemies, or to those of sinful deeds;
but it should always be given to a devotee of Viṣṇu, a devotee of Śiva, a devotee of Sūrya, or a devotee of the Bhagavat.
This should be given according to the prescribed rite for the increase of longevity and wealth;
[it is not for] those foolish men who hate Viṣṇu or the Bull-bannered Lord.
They are surely devotees of Viṣṇu, those who carry Viṣṇu himself;
by this very vow, they shall attain that supreme state.
The long-lived and wealthy person rejoices here for a very long time.
Now, the gift of vessels (*bhāṇḍadāna*). Vasiṣṭha states: "The giver of copper vessels shall become a vessel for jewels.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
The giver of vessels made of copper and iron shall become a lord of yakṣas;
he attains a supreme station and is endowed with great glory.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "He who gives vessels made of udumbara wood or even those made of iron attains great prosperity, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: He who gives a vessel made of gold or silver for the sake of the deities reaches the world of Kubera and rejoices there for many years.
Now, the gift of cooked food. From the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord of Gods, tell me that by which, when given, human beings [attain their goal]."
He is born with many sons, great wealth, and many servants.
The Blessed Lord said: Formerly, in this land of Bhārata-varṣa, there was a king named Babhruvāhana.
He obtained the kingdom of his father and grandfather, free from all thorns.
In his country there are no learned men, nor is there any fear arising from enemies;
likewise, there is no great disease in the body, nor any that causes internal distress.
While he was governing his kingdom in this manner, the merit acquired through his past actions remained;
there was no servant capable of bearing the burden who could carry the weight of the entire realm.
There is no son who acts for one's pleasure, no minister with sweet speech,
no friend capable of accomplishing one's task, and likewise no well-wisher.
When the time for eating has arrived, there was no food that fulfilled all desires;
nor was there any meal accompanied by leaves and fruits, nor any ambrosial garment.
He did not cause wealth to be expended on the accumulation of jewels for the sake of social connections;
while he ruled his kingdom in this manner, his actions remained unimpeded.
Then one day, the highly renowned and great-souled Brahmin Pippalāda,
a master of great yoga, approached the presence of the king.
Seeing that the Sage had arrived, the king’s queen, Śubhāvatī,
honored him in every way by offering water for his feet, the guest-offering, and a seat.
And at the conclusion of a certain conversation, Śubhāvatī said to him:
"O Blessed One, this kingdom of mine is free from all afflictions."
And why, O twice-born one, do servants, sons, ministers, friends,
and the like not provide such enjoyment as that which endures for all time?
Pippalāda said:
"Whatever has been ordained by one's past actions, that very fruit one obtains.
O Queen, this is the land of karma; therefore, you ought not to grieve."
Neither kings, nor heirs, nor enemies,
nor kinsmen, nor friends can undo that which was done by oneself in the past.
Therefore, that supreme kingdom which was given by you has been obtained;
but the relationship with servants, friends, and others was not given—how could it be obtained?
Śubhāvatī said:
"O brahmin-sage, why even now is that not taught?
By means of it, may I have many sons, wealth, and servants."
Whether it be a friend, the company of kinsmen, a vow, charity, or fasting—
O one of pure intellect, tell me by which happiness is attained.
Then Pippalāda, the best of the twice-born,
related the great gift known as Āpāka, which bestows all forms of prosperity.
O tiger among the Kurus, whether it be a woman or a man, one who acts with faith through such a gift shall become the recipient of manifold fortunes.
Then, having heard this, the king gave him an excellent *āpāka* oblation;
by it, one obtains many sons, servants, ministers, friends, and well-wishers.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe the great gift known as Āpāka,
by the giving of which one’s sons become the recipients of all desires.
Having obtained the strength of the planets and stars, one should worship the potter with garments,
ornaments, flowers, agallochum, and sandalwood.
One should speak thus regarding this commonality so that he becomes pleased:
"You [have given] my various vessels, both heavy and light."
Jeweled vessels and other bright objects, as well as most beautiful cooking pots, small jars, water-pitchers, ritual water-vessels, and bowls.
Bowls such as shallow dishes, various kinds of vessels and utensils, water-jars, pitchers, and other types of pots.
"O illustrious one, please provide whatever else may be required for enjoyment in the house; for you alone are indeed Viśvakarman."
The descendant of Bhṛgu, too, with great effort, should prepare an auspicious oven equipped with a multitude of vessels,
according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule.
Having set aside one thousand vessels, the wise man,
at the time of twilight, should churn [the fire] or indeed offer oblations into the sacrificial fire.
One should keep a vigil at night with the sounds of songs and auspicious music;
then, at the clear dawn, having bathed and offered hundreds of funeral libations (nirvāpa).
Having approached with red garments, one should worship with flower garlands;
then the patron, having bathed, pure and wearing white clothes, [should proceed].
Having placed around it vessels made of gold and silver, as well as those made of copper and iron, according to one's capacity, sixteen *ṭaṇis* [of grain].
One should place those four in each [direction] according to the sequence of the cardinal directions, beginning with the east,
having worshipped them with diligence or having prepared them with great care.
And having brought noble women there who have not lost their virginity, one should worship them;
then, having performed a circumambulation, one should worship with this mantra.
You are the very essence of the cooking-pot and Brahmā; may these vessels be living beings, and may there be nourishment for your progeny as well as imperishable heaven for me.
Indeed, those vessels which were fashioned here by me have become suited to living beings; let them now be presented to you.

[935] Herein is the formula for the gift: *Oṃ, today I, desiring auspiciousness, freedom from widowhood, the attainment of a house endowed with all virtues, and the fitness for sovereignty over a lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth, release this cooking-pot (*āpāka*), fashioned with various vessels and dedicated to Viṣṇu,
unto various people.* Whichever person is in need of whichever vessel, that one should bestow it upon him.
Let them take it according to their own will; no one is to be restrained.
O King, he who bestows this gift according to this rite shall have Viśvakarman pleased with him for three lifetimes.
And by giving a woman, one attains incomparable good fortune,
as well as a home endowed with every excellence and surrounded by servants and friends.
One shall always obtain non-separation from one's husband and unsurpassed beauty;
