this gift has been prescribed for you, O sinless one, in this manner.
O best of men, this earth is divided into many different regions.
That excellent woman who, having diligently prepared a superior collection of vessels, gives them away here before they have been baked,
shall obtain the happiness of increasing wealth in sons, grandsons, and cattle.
Having passed away, she quickly dwells forever in happiness together with her husband.

Now follows the gift of the cooking vessel (*sthālīdāna*). From the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "Henceforth, I shall describe to you that which destroys all sins and bestows auspiciousness—a gift that confers honor upon men and grants all desires."
Having fashioned a copper vessel weighing five hundred palas,
one who is unable to do so may instead use half of that weight or even a fourth part.
But one who is devoid of all means may have [the image] made even of clay,
provided it has very deep and wide cavities and a firm handle and scoop.
By the term *daṇḍakaḍacchaka*, ladles are denoted.
[One should offer] those filled with milk made from soft rice,
accompanied by side-dishes and water, and provided with vessels of clarified butter.
Having placed her on a side that has been prepared, washed, and smeared with sandalwood paste,
one should then worship her with mandalas, perfumes, flowers, and incense.
On a Sunday, during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on the fourteenth, eighth, eleventh,
or third lunar days, one should bestow it upon a Brahmin.
Even with grains that are blazing beside a fire and even when accompanied by water,
there can be no accomplishment of food for living beings without a cooking pot.
You are the accomplishment for those desiring accomplishment; you are the contentment for those seeking contentment.
Therefore, bowing before you, I entreat you: do as I say.
O bestower of boons, may you be such that I do not eat while my kinsmen, relatives, circles of friends, Brahmins, and my own people have not yet eaten.
Having uttered this, the pot should be presented to the best of the twice-born;
it bestows contentment and nourishment upon men who desire all their wishes.
Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, she did exactly so;
she gave a cooking pot to many Brahmins along with abundant sacrificial fees.
Those who give to the twice-born a large-mouthed vessel along with a ladle, filled with sweet-smelling food,
shall have their meal attended by friends, kinsmen, and Brahmins.
Even while being enjoyed, O Kṛṣṇa, it does not go to destruction.
Now, the gift of the fire-brand (*agniṣṭikā*). From the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Pārtha, I shall describe the fire-brand; listen to it."
In whatever manner and by whatever rite she bestows happiness upon all sentient beings.
First, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on an auspicious day, one should have a beautiful,
firm, and comfortable-seated fire-pit constructed.
In a courtyard of the gods, in a monastery, in a marketplace, or likewise in a spacious square,
one should arrange a well-dried heap of wood during both twilights.
Then one should kindle the fire and offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* in due order;
one should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability and give them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having performed [the rite] according to this procedure, one should then kindle the fire every day;
if anyone should be afflicted by hunger, one should provide food there for them.
This is the formula for the donation here:

"Oṃ! From today onwards, for the duration of the two seasons known as Hemanta and Śiśira, or for all time, or as long as is pleasing, for the sake of warming all sentient beings, I, free from desire, relinquish this fire-pit dedicated to the deity Viṣṇu, so that [the recipient] may attain the world of Brahmā, where enjoyment is immeasurable in time, and may become a Brāhmaṇa learned in the four Vedas, perfected in all aims.
There, the people sit at ease, freed from cold and likewise free from fever.
O Pārtha, those stories she tells cannot be recounted by me.
One who knows the *liṅga* may speak at will while sitting comfortably about kings, dharma, or people;
he is not restrained by anyone.
O King, listen to me as I describe the meritorious fruit for that man who gives a fire-brand according to this procedure.
Mounted upon a celestial chariot radiant as the sun in that great forest,
he remained for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years.
Having been honored and being utterly satisfied, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
and when descending to this world, he becomes a twice-born man learned in the four Vedas.
He was free from disease and a performer of the Sattrayajña sacrifice, by virtue of the power of the fire's brilliance.
Those who provide auspicious fires, abundant with wood, at shrines, temples, assembly halls, and dwellings,
which bring comfort to people during the winter and early spring seasons;
They attain a stainless body with the radiance of a blazing fire.
Kātyāyana says: He who bestows the sacred fire during the winter and the cool season for the sake of the austerity of all the world shall attain a meritorious state.
He who gives firewood to Brahmins for the purpose of kindling the sacred fires achieves success in all his aims and is born endowed with splendor.
In the Vahnipurāṇa:
"He who bestows fuel and wood upon Brāhmaṇas for the sake of providing heat for all people shall attain a meritorious state."
Saṃvarta says:
And during the cold season, one should diligently provide much wood for the fire;
thus one shall obtain the radiance of the bodily fire, wisdom, beauty, and good fortune.
And he who gives fuel to the twice-born at the onset of the cold season always conquers in battle and shines, endowed with prosperity.
Viṣṇu: By providing fuel, one's fire becomes kindled; one attains auspiciousness in battle. Yama: [The same].
By the offering of fuel, a fire blazes forth upon the earth. As stated in the Mahābhārata: "And he who gives wood to Brahmins for the purpose of fuel..."
O Indra among kings, when the cold season has set in for the purpose of causing intense heat, a man [suffers].
His goals are always accomplished, as are his various undertakings;
and he shines with his very body above all his enemies.
And being present, the fire becomes ever quickly well-pleased;
animals do not abandon him, and he is victorious even in battles.
Now, the offering of lamps. In the Mahābhārata:
[940] I shall describe the unsurpassed connection with the fruits of the gift of lamps—how, by whom, when, and to what kind of person they are to be given.
Light (*jyotis*) is described as brilliance or radiance, and also by its upward movement;
therefore, the giving of light increases the brilliance of men.
In the blinding darkness, the thick gloom, and during the southern solstice as well as the northern solstice,
the offering of lamps is highly praised.
Since that [gift] leads upward and is indeed the remedy for darkness,
it is certain that the giver shall attain an upward course there.
Since the gods are radiant, powerful, and illuminating—
being both characterized by darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas)— therefore a lamp is offered.
By looking at [the recipient] and giving, a man becomes possessed of sight and endowed with radiance;
having given it, he should not make use of it himself, nor take it back, nor cause it to be destroyed.
One who steals a lamp shall become blind and go to the realm of darkness, which is inauspicious;
one who gives a lamp shines like a garland of lamps throughout all the worlds.
One who desires prosperity for oneself should always be a giver of lamps at mountain precipices, in dense forests, at sacred shrines, and at crossroads.
He whose soul is purified by illuminating his lineage attains luminosity;
he who is ever devoted to the gift of lamps attains union with the celestial lights.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "In the temples of deities such as Śiva, in the hermitages of ascetics (*yatis*),
in the house of one who maintains the sacred fire (*agnihotrin*), and likewise in a shelter (*pratiśraya*)."
Reflecting that Śaṅkara dwells visibly everywhere,
one should constantly offer lamps in the houses of those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).
Devala says:
A man who performs the act of sweeping becomes a king who provides the illumination of lamps.
Vedavyāsa says:
Just as one praises lamps out of a desire for the welfare of our ancestors,
therefore the giver of lamps constantly delivers his ancestors across [to liberation].
Therefore, O best of the Bharatas, lamps should always be offered to the gods and the ancestors; for they are considered to be pleasing to their sight, O Lord.
By the gift of the light of a lamp, a man is born with sight.
Yama says: "In this world, even one who possesses sight becomes illuminated by means of a lamp.
[From] the Nandipurāṇa.
That mortal who offers a lamp with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken grains, water, and the delightful scents of incense in the dwellings of the gods and Brahmins;
But he, traveling by a divine vehicle shining with great luster,
goes to incomparable heaven and shall dwell there for a hundred years.
Those who give lamps go by that path which belongs to Yama, consisting of darkness, terrible, difficult to traverse, and full of great fear— yet they proceed along it with joy.
In the *Skandapurāṇa*:
"Those who give lamps go forth illuminating all directions at crossroads, at sacred shrines (*caityas*), and in the dwellings of Brahmins. [942]
Indeed, by the gift of lamps in tree-lined groves, cow-pens, and dense forests, one obtains great fruit everywhere.
The wise declare that for one who offers a lamp in the house of a Brahmin during the month of Kārttika, there is the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
He who offers a lamp at the twilight hours shall go to the supreme state.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa: By the liberation of Nīlakaṇṭha, by offerings of water with sesame seeds at Gayā,
and by the offering of lamps during the rainy season, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
But he who offers a garland of lamps in the houses of Brahmins,
having dispelled terrible darkness, shall attain the world of luminaries.
Saṃvarta says:
By offering a lamp at a temple or at a crossroads for the sake of the twice-born,
one shall always be intelligent, endowed with knowledge, and possessed of keen vision.
From the Viṣṇudharmottara:
A great lamp should always be offered, which yields great fruit for the protector of the earth;
especially during the dark fortnight, and particularly on those [specific] days.
The new moon day and the twelfth day are also specified as yielding great fruit;
they may occur either after the month of Āśvayuja has passed or during its dark fortnight.
[943] Then the new moon day is meritorious, and especially so the twelfth day;
on the right side of the deity, offerings accompanied by a balance of oil should be presented.
O King, one should cause a wick made of eight *palas* of cloth dyed entirely with the blood of a great king to be offered right there.
And on the left side of the deity, O King, a tulā of ghee should be offered;
there, one should likewise cause a white wick weighing eight palas to be presented.
O lord of the earth, having fasted and subdued his senses, he who gives this pair of great wicks together with a complete garment once—
Having enjoyed the heavenly realm for a very long time, when he is born again upon the earth,
he becomes endowed with fortune, beauty, and good luck.
O tiger among kings, O Lord, in whatever kingdom, region, city, or family he is born, there he shall be possessed of light.
He becomes exceedingly brilliant in battles and in disputes,
and he always attains renown in the world through the excellent virtues of the virtuous.
Furthermore, O sinless one, he who would give even a single desired gift to these two obtains everything in the human state that has been described by me to you.
O Yādava, O King, one likewise attains enjoyment and duration of time in heaven;
indeed, the gift of even an ordinary lamp yields great fruit.
How much more so for that great fruit whose end is not known?
The gift of a lamp is a supreme merit, certain even among other gods.
How much more so, then, for the God of gods, the infinite and great-souled one,
should [offerings] be given upon mountain peaks and on the sandy banks of rivers?
At crossroads, on streets, and in the houses of Brahmins;
at the roots of trees, in cow-pens, and in dense wildernesses.
By the gift of a lamp, one enjoys great fruit everywhere;
for as many moments as the eye blinks while the lamp continues to burn.
For that many years, O Indra among kings, he rejoices in heaven;
by the gift of a lamp, O Indra among kings, he is born here with sight.
Those men who offer a garland of lamps at the abode of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow become endowed with beauty and good fortune, and are provided with wealth and grain.
Having offered a beautiful lamp-tree at the temple of Keśava, those who possess honor attain heaven and become like the moon.
Having reached heaven, that man shines exceedingly with splendor,
having offered a lamp that is auspicious and resembles a sacrificial fire-pit.
Having reached the abode of Keśava, he shines in heaven like Śakra;
and by the gift of lamps, a human being always shines brilliantly like a lamp.
Thus, one is born eternally radiant in the world, even upon the vault of heaven;
for indeed, it is only in a place provided with a lamp that the eyes bear fruit.
Likewise, O King, those who give lamps become possessed of fruitful vision,
just as the flame of a lamp always moves upward.
In the same way, for the giver of a lamp, there is an excellent upward progression;
therefore, O Lord of Men, lamps should be given with every effort.
O King, O Indra among kings, from the passing of the month of Āśvayuja until the full moon of Kārttika,
the specific fruit for one who offers lamps has been declared.
Those who always offer a lamp at night for that duration on an elevated place outside shall obtain a great fruit of merit.
O tiger among the Yadus, that in which luminosity arises within dense darkness— indeed, by means of that luminosity do people attain happiness.
By offering a lamp at the confluence of two rivers in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
one is born endowed with brilliance, fame, and beauty.
Lamps should be offered in rivers, especially on the full moon day of Kārttika,
continuing until the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja.
Lamps should always be offered at the openings of the subterranean chambers according to the prescribed rite; by offering lamps elsewhere as well, one shall always obtain the fruit of great merit.
O delight of the Yadus, on the occasion of Śravaṇa-dvādaśī, especially during the dark fortnight,
lamps should be offered with ghee or with oils.
Lamps should never be offered with fat, marrow, and the like;
having offered a lamp, one who understands the ritual must not perform that [impure] act again.
Extinguishing a lamp and causing injury are both censurable acts;
he who commits such an act shall become one with flower-like eyes.
One who steals a lamp becomes blind; one who extinguishes it becomes one-eyed. There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of a lamp.
The wise should offer lamps in the houses of Brahmins. Those who offer lamps in the dwellings of the twice-born during the month of Kārttika—
the wise declare that for them there is the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
One should avoid lamp-wicks made from animal products or those that are blue or red;
O King, they should especially be made from lotus fibers.
By offering a lamp with a wick made from lotus fibers soaked in fragrant oil,
a person becomes free from disease and fortunate.
O Lord of the gods of gods, by washing the lamp with camphor,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and uplifts one’s entire lineage.
O moon of the Yadu dynasty, I have thus described to you in its entirety the fruit of offering lamps;
having heard this correctly, it should indeed be constantly practiced.
Lamps were offered by you in the dwellings of Brahmins and gods.
Thus the gifts of enjoyment are completed.
Now, the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*). Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:
"The gift of fearlessness is superior to all other gifts; by giving that, one attains the desired world."
Saṃvarta says:
By granting fearlessness to living beings, one shall obtain all desires;
one attains long life and shall always be happy.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*: "For the subtle bodies of the Maruts, as well as for those afflicted by disease, for the violent,
and for those of gentle form, [the gift] indeed yields fruitless fear."
It is better to protect the life and grant fearlessness to a single sentient being than to give a thousand cows along with sacrificial fees to a thousand Brahmins.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: Fie upon the life of that man who does not grant favor to one who is suffering and seeking refuge— even if he is certainly on the side of an enemy!
Sacrifices, charity, and austerities do not lead to well-being, either in this world or the next,
for one whose mind is not intent on the protection of the needy.
In the Mahābhārata: "The wise declare that for one who, out of greed, hatred, or even fear, abandons one who has sought refuge, the sin is equal to that of killing a Brahmin."
In the scriptures, expiation is seen even for those who have committed great sins;
however, for those who kill one who has sought refuge, no expiation is seen anywhere.
Even the fruit of sacrifices to the Maruts perishes with time;
but for one who grants fearlessness to the frightened, there is no decay at all.
Likewise:
"For the wise have said that he who, though capable, remains indifferent while a living being is being slain, goes to a terrible hell."
He who might give away this entire earth, bounded by the four oceans,
and he who grants fearlessness to sentient beings— of these two, the giver of fearlessness is superior.
In the Rāmāyaṇa: "Remembering the duty of the virtuous, one should not kill an offender who has come for refuge, even if he is wretched, pleading with palms joined in supplication."
Whether he be afflicted or terrified, one who has come for refuge from others must be protected by one of noble character, even at the cost of his own life.
If, out of fear, delusion, or desire, one does not protect that person oneself according to one's ability and in accordance with what is right, that is a sin condemned by the world.
He who does not protect one who has come for refuge is ruined while looking on;
taking all the merit from that unprotected person, he departs.
The fruit of a horse-sacrifice properly performed with full authorization does not equal that fruit which is obtained when one who has come for refuge is protected while filled with terror.

"Of one to whom [the gift] has been fully and completely bestowed" means: he is such a person for whom the bestowed gift (*nisṛṣṭa-dāna*) is "fully and completely" (*suparyāpta*), that is, perfectly fulfilled.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"Of all gifts whatsoever, this alone is the single most excellent."
There is no gift for all living beings superior to the granting of fearlessness.
He who grants fearlessness to all beings, both moving and unmoving,
is liberated from all fears and attains the supreme Brahman.
From the Vahni Purāṇa: Gavī said:
"On one side are all the sacrifices, completed with the bestowal of excellent sacrificial fees."
The protection of the life of a living being who is terrified on one side.
There is no other dharma on this earth more weighty than that which grants fearlessness to living beings who are terrified by fear.
The gift of fearlessness regarding life has been bestowed upon a living being;
this is not equal to a thousand decorated cows given to a thousand Brahmins.
Givers of golden cows, land, and other such gifts are easy to find on earth;
rare in this world is the man who grants fearlessness to all living beings.
The fruit of even great sacrifices perishes with time;
however, for the gift of fearlessness to those who are afraid, there is no decay at all.
For one who is devoted to compassion and grants fearlessness to all beings,
there is no destruction from any quarter once he is liberated from the body.
Whatever has been given as a gift, whatever sacrifice has been performed, whatever austerity has been practiced, and likewise whatever is based on visiting sacred fords—
all these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the gift of fearlessness.
One who gives this earth bounded by the four oceans does not give as much as one who grants fearlessness to all living beings.
I would rather renounce my kingdom or even my own body, which is so difficult to give up,
than abandon this poor pigeon, who is terrified with fear.
By whatever merit I possess, in birth after birth,
may I become a savior for those in great distress, for the sake of destroying the suffering of embodied beings.
For I do not desire sovereignty, nor heaven, nor even liberation from rebirth;
I desire only the destruction of the suffering of living beings who are tormented by pain.
Just as I have not uttered this speech falsely here,
by this truth may the Blessed Lord Maheśvara be gracious to me.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "He alone is the foremost person in the world among all upholders of dharma,
that best of men who provides protection for one terrified of being killed."
That man remains in the world of Śakra for as long as fourteen Indras endure,
having been protected from the fear of entering into darkness.
One attains the world of Brahmā; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Causing entry into darkness means blinding by means of gouging out the eyes and so forth.
Even more sinful than killing is the total deprivation of sight;
a king should never, under any circumstances, do this to anyone.
Having caused others to enter into darkness, that lowest of men certainly incurs blindness wherever he may be born;
indeed, he remains bound by darkness for thousands of eons.
"By creating a phantom for the protection of one who fears the cutting off of limbs, one attains the world of Rudra for the remainder of a kalpa; such is the sacred tradition."
Then, at the beginning of the creation of the eon, that best of men becomes endowed with knowledge after having provided protection for those terrified by bondage.
Completely liberated from all bonds, he is glorified in the world of Vāyu.
By providing protection for one who has been obstructed, a person likewise becomes liberated from all suffering and attains the world of the Sādhyas.
But he who provides protection for one who is afraid of being beaten shall be liberated from all suffering and attain the world of the Bhṛgus.
And by providing protection to one who fears exile,
a man likewise attains the entire world and the highest station among humanity.
Having provided protection to one who fears the loss of his wealth,
the best of men obtains the merit of giving, as well as the world of generosity and self-restraint.
By providing protection to one who fears humiliation,
the best of men attains the heavenly world as well as honor from the hosts of gods.
Whatever merit a man who has failed to provide protection might perform,
the one who did not protect shall have no share in that meritorious deed.
Furthermore, by providing protection for cattle, wild animals, birds, as well as grasses, trees, and creepers, a twice-born man becomes an inhabitant of heaven.
Having rescued a beast from the hand of a slaughterer,
that best of men attains the heavenly realm and is born everywhere in happiness.
For as many hairs as there are on the animal's body, for that many years does the human being attain all the worlds, he who provides protection for it.
Even by providing protection for a mere insect or moth, one attains heaven for many thousands of years; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
O Brahmins, he who liberates one seized by thieves, seized by kings, seized by enemies,
or likewise seized by serpents, shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
By providing medicine for one who is diseased, one obtains the fruit of giving the gift of life.

O twice-born ones, having provided such instruction and thereby granting the gift of life without seeking any fee from the physician, one attains the fruit of saving lives and is glorified in the heavenly world.
Those men who were devoted to protection and went to the aid of the timid have reached the world of the Lord of the Thirty-three;
yet even today, those heroic men continue to protect.
Even at the [proper] time, there is no passing away for them.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of fearlessness. Now follows the service to travelers, according to the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*.
He who attends to a traveler with bedding, seating, and food conquers those who perform Vedic sacrifices with very little effort.
Having prepared a pleasant shelter that is well-protected from the wind, with a pure ground surface,
for the fire-drilling apparatus, one immediately burns away sin.
In the rainy season, during the most intense heat of winter and the cold spells,
and in the summer when the ground is cool, he provides rest for the traveler and attains the celestial realm.
By giving clothing to the naked, medical treatment to the sick,
sweet water to the thirsty, and delicious food to the hungry,
as well as wealth to the traveler, one overcomes all evil deeds.
Even on a journey, by honoring a guest with vegetables, roots, fruits, or water,
or even by greeting them once with kind words, one becomes a vessel for spiritual welfare.
For the sake of the comfort of travelers, there were those who provided hospitality on the road,
and for their movement across deep waters, there were those in charge of boats.
O King, those men who construct water-stations for travelers, filled with various kinds of flavorful drinks, all share in the merit of heaven.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Having constructed a bridge easily on a path, one obtains the fruit of the *Vājapeya* sacrifice;
that best of men who constructs a bridge for crossing water [obtains the same]."
Having crossed over all sufferings, he attains the world of the gods.
Likewise,
by diligently removing pebbles, clods of earth, stones, and gravel from the path, a person obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
By massaging one who is weary, a person obtains that very same fruit;
likewise, by fanning a traveler with a palm-leaf fan,
or even by carrying a weary person on one's shoulders, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Furthermore, by carrying those who are exhausted from perspiration with a vehicle or a carriage,
one reaches the world of the Sādhyas and enjoys divine pleasures.
By giving food to one who is weary, a person attains the eternal state;
when the weary one is satisfied, that human being attains well-being.
By providing sandals and an umbrella to a weary person,
and by establishing them in auspicious places, a man shall obtain great fruit in an instant.
O best of Brahmins, he who takes up a burden and carries it for one exhausted by a heavy load attains the heavenly world through that very action.
The wise man who, having transported another's burden for a price,
shall obtain tenfold the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Having provided protection to travelers along the road,
that best of men attains supreme prosperity in this world and is glorified in the realm of Rudra.
Having provided protection from thieves, a man is honored in the world of Śakra;
likewise, by ferrying travelers across riverbanks on their journey.
He who constructs a boat equipped with all necessary gear on the riverbank quickly crosses over difficult terrains, even mountains with razor-sharp edges.
That man obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice from that deed.
The wise person who constructs delightful assembly halls and various wonderful gardens is honored in the world of Śakra.
By providing things worthy of being seen, one obtains memory and intelligence. Indeed, compassion should be shown toward travelers by whatever means possible;
for a traveler who has departed from his own home is the supreme object of mercy.
Whether he be a bearer of sectarian marks or a student of sacred knowledge, he is to be treated as a traveler by those who are discerning of the path;
indeed, a traveler is to be honored in every way through the telling of edifying tales.
Having performed worship of the traveler Puruṣa and having reached the abode of Purandara,
one attains divine enjoyments in heaven through merits.
Therefore, travelers are most worthy of honor in the world of men.
Thus end the various services.
Now follows the offering of an oil massage. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Having given an oil massage with auspiciously scented oil to a twice-born man..."
Having rubbed [the body] with auspicious powder and bathed it with lukewarm water,
one attains the splendor of the moon until the dissolution of all beings.
But the wise man who anoints with oil a twice-born person exhausted by the road and worn out by the village will rejoice happily for a long time.
And that meritorious soul who bathes a twice-born, or Keśava, or Śiva with oil from cooked food— what need has he for many sacrifices?
He who on the twelfth day anoints Viṣṇu with devotion using a fragrant oil, or ghee from a cow according to his means,
or sesame oil, rejoices in the world of the Gandharvas.
Having reached the northern solstice, he who anoints Dhūrjaṭi with the ghee of a tawny cow or otherwise with other ghee, [attains the highest goal].
By performing a great worship with ghee on that very auspicious day,
a person obtains a kingdom from which all thorns have been removed.
By performing a great ablution (mahāsnāna) for Govinda or Śiva with a thousand palas of clarified butter, a man casts off even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"For him who bathes the deity with the Brahmakūrca on a sacred festival day,
the worlds of that merit-maker never perish."
The constant bathing of all the deities with the five nectars, or again at auspicious times, is the destroyer of great sins.
The *brahmakūrca* and *pañcāmṛta* have been explained in the *Paribhāṣā*.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"By means of anointing the heads of Brahmins, especially those who are away from home..."
The man is born handsome, fortunate, illustrious, and radiant.
[956] Now, the gift of foot-massage. Kātyāyana says:
"By means of foot-massages, head-massages, and by gifts, honors, worship, and so forth..."
The best of the twice-born are especially worthy of honor with refined speech.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"He who provides an oil massage for the feet to a weary traveler shall have his feet eternally worshipped by bards with auspicious ornaments."
He shall become a highly fortunate king over a realm extending ten yojanas.
A man who, after massaging one who is exhausted, provides an oil massage for the feet and so forth,
attains the city of Dharma, resplendent with all desirable qualities.
By giving water for sipping, water for touching the face, and oil for massaging the feet to a twice-born man,
as well as by wiping away his remnants, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
In the Nāndīyapurāṇa:
Having diligently offered a foot-massage to a twice-born man or even to ascetics,
one attains the world of the Lord of the Gods and rejoices, free from all suffering.
He who provides service to those whose feet are cracked by the journey ascends a celestial palace (vimāna) filled with every enjoyment.
Now follows the gift of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
Baudhāyana says: [957] "He says..."
By the gift of a sacred thread, one becomes endowed with spiritual luster;
therefore, those [threads] should be given by a wise Brāhmaṇa.
Without the sacred thread, all ritual acts are fruitless;
without the sacred thread, one is indeed deprived of Brahminhood.
Therefore, the great seers declare that the gift of it is most meritorious.
Atri said:
Whoever should give a very beautiful sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*)— whether made of linen, cotton, or even silk (*paṭṭasūtra*)— and colored with ghee;
By performing according to the injunctions to the best of one's ability, one shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"A man undoubtedly performs dharma for ten years by giving a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) to a twice-born according to the prescribed rule."
Likewise: By the gift of a sacred thread to the gods or to a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahmin learned in the four Vedas with a purified intellect; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having given a sacred thread (*upavīta*) made of triple-stranded silk thread or the like, white or bright yellow, to Rudra, one becomes a master of the Vedānta.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "One should give as a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) one made of linen, or cotton, or even silk; those who do so will not be harmed by crows."
In the *Vāyuprokta*:
"At the *upākarma* ceremony, one should give a sacred thread (*yajñopavītaka*) to the Brahmins;
by that act, a man becomes long-lived on earth."
Likewise:
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
one should perform the ritual offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) for the deities in due order according to the prescribed rule.
Agni, Brahmā, Ambikā, Īśa, Apsu, Pannaga, Skanda, and Bhānu;
Durgā, Yama, Indra, Govinda, Kāmeśa, and the Pitṛs are remembered [as the lords of the quarters].
Thus, by performing the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) to these deities during the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
one goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

Now, the gift of a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) for the alleviation of diseases of the head. In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "The sacred thread should be made of gold weighing half a *pala*, or half of that, or half of that again, or according to one's means."
And one should present to a Brahmin who knows the Veda and is well-versed in the scriptures an upper garment made of silver, equal in number to that [same quantity].
When he has been duly worshipped with this mantra and with finger-rings,
may Dhātṛ, the Ordainer, the Supreme Self of the worlds, the four-faced one,
swiftly destroy the onset of disease located in my head.
The mantra for the gift:
Now follows the gift of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) for the rite of proclaiming the conception. One should have a golden sacred thread made according to one's means.
And a silver upper garment, endowed with an exceedingly beautiful color.
Furthermore, pearls and diamonds should be set at the joints of the knot using a space equal to half a *pala*, or half of that, or even half of the latter.
Having washed it with the five products of the cow while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra, one should place the image of the correct proportions into that vessel amidst clarified butter.
The well-worshiped sacred thread (upavīta) should be placed upon the clarified butter (ājya),
with great devotion, using perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, incense, and food offerings.
Then, having summoned a brahmin, one should have him perform a fire sacrifice there with one hundred and eight oblations mixed with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and honey.
To that person who has offered the oblation and has been honored with garments and other gifts,
one should duly present the sacred thread while facing east, accompanied by this mantra.
"This supreme sacred thread was worn by Brahmā in ancient times;
who is this Cyavana that he should sustain a fetus through the gift of it?"
The mantra for the gift:
At whatever time one causes fruits to be given to the Brahmins,
one should likewise follow the teacher, prostrate, and ask for his forgiveness.
By acting in this way, one is liberated from the fault arising from the proclamation of the embryo.
Now, regarding the gift of a staff: In the Nāndipurāṇa it is said,
"The man who, being compassionate, gives a staff to an elderly person,
shall always experience constant prosperity and, free from fear, attain heaven."
In the *Āditya Purāṇa*: "For those who provide a staff to one who is sightless or weak,
their path shall be fruitless, though adorned with fruits and roots."
In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: Those who are compassionate toward the lame, travelers, and the destitute,
and who provide them with staffs, will undoubtedly remain free from disease.
A cripple always performs the functions of walking with the aid of a staff;
and by the holding of the staff, protection from cows, serpents, and other dangers arises.
For those who are afraid, she is a refuge; for those traveling at night or in the forest, she is a staff.
This very [staff] dispels the suspicion arising from defects such as mud and the like. Therefore, whoever gives a flawless staff that brings satisfaction [is blessed].
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Having given a bamboo staff to ascetics and a small knife to the twice-born,
one does not encounter the rod of Yama in the next world.
He who bestows punishment upon a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) according to his caste becomes a great Brāhmaṇa and enjoys spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa).
Now, regarding the shaving of ascetics and others. Yama says:
"A man who causes the shaving of the head for celibate students (brahmacārins) and ascetics (yatis) becomes endowed with keen vision when he has his nails trimmed."
Viśvāmitra said:
By performing the clipping of hair for ascetics, students, travelers, and likewise for other distressed people, [one attains merit].
By performing the cleansing of the nails, one becomes endowed with beauty;
he who, for the sake of all people, [trims] his hair, beard, nails, and so forth.
He who, endowed with supreme faith, provides wages to a barber for the purpose of performing a ritual in a temple or at a sacred ford,
shall dwell in the world of Āśvina for a hundred years, free from sorrow.
Now, in connection with the service of travelers, the care of cows is described. Regarding this, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"Cows are to be saluted, worshipped, and constantly served;
he who performs a circumambulation of cows standing in their pen [attains great merit]."
Cows are purifying and auspicious; the worlds are established upon the cow. Cows extend the sacrifices; cows are the destroyers of all evil.
Cow urine, cow dung, clarified butter, milk, curd, and yellow pigment (rocanā)—
these six constituents of the cow are supremely auspicious at all times.
The water from a cow's horn is meritorious and destroys all sins;
scratching a cow also destroys all impurities.
By giving a morsel of food to a cow, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"O King, cows should always be saluted with this mantra:
'Salutations to the glorious cows, the daughters of Surabhi.'"
Salutations to the daughters of Brahmā, and again, and yet again, salutations!
By the mere recollection of this mantra, one shall obtain the fruit of gifting a cow.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "And those who, according to their capacity, give salt to cows—
those performers of merit go to the world of cows."
He who, being devoted, always observes the cow-vow, speaks the truth, remains peaceful and awakened, and gives even a small amount of the first portion [of food] to cows,
gains the merit of a thousand cows.
One whose character is rooted in righteousness shall attain it within a year.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"He who does not cause smoke [from cow dung] in the cow-pen of his cows, O Gopālaka,
shall be devoured by flies in the Makṣikālīna hell."
But that lowest of men who, having subdued a cow that has recently lost its calf, drinks her milk while she is still bearing the burden of her young,
shall indeed remain for a long time afflicted by hunger.
In the Mahābhārata:
"O lord of the earth, he who creates an obstacle for a herd of cows afflicted by thirst at the edge of water, they call him a slayer of a Brahmin."
Having constructed a large shelter for the sake of cows, capable of withstanding cold winds,
one rescues one's lineage up to the seventh generation, O best of the Bharatas.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "A cow born in one's house, even if she possesses defects, must always be personally maintained;
likewise, a twice-born man, even if he is ill-behaved, is worthy of honor, but never a Śūdra, however self-restrained he may be."
In the winter season, one should diligently construct a shelter for cattle that have no protector,
wherein grass, water, and fuel are provided for the sake of merit.
Hārīta says: One should cause the calf to drink for two months; in the third month, one should let it suckle from two teats;
and in the fourth month, from three teats, according to the rule and according to its strength.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "On the full moon days of Āṣāḍha, Āśvayuja, Pauṣa, and Māgha, one should never take the milk of cows; one should give it all to the calves."
One should not drive eunuchs [as draft animals], nor should one oppress a cow with excessive burden;
this applies especially on the beginnings of the Yugas, at the ends of the Yugas, and during the Ṣaḍaśītimukha periods.
When the sun moves southward or northward, as well as during both equinoxes,
at all transits (saṃkrāntis), and during eclipses of the moon and the sun.
On the fifteenth, fourteenth, twelfth, and eighth days of each month,
the ritual service for the cows should be performed in due order.
Four palas of salt and eight of ghee,
as well as sixteen of another person's milk, should be given.
Having first considered the thirty-two palas of cold water, as well as the quantity of the milk, one's strength, and one's appetite.
However, for the sake of merit, a daily offering of fodder for cows should be given spontaneously;
where salt is offered in the morning, water should also be given from that same source.
Then [he provided] grass, fodder, and nourishment devoid of meat;
at night, there was a lamp with a lute, as well as divine recitations from the Purāṇas.
When this is done, the fruit shall be equal to that which results from giving the entire earth filled with jewels,
or the merit that arises from the protection of cows through the gift of cows.
Cattle must be protected with great effort by humans, even at the cost of grass and their own bodies;
they should always be given away, honored, nourished, and preserved.
Likewise:
"In forests abounding in grass, water, and the like, let the cows— along with their bulls and calves— sport in intoxication."
May they emit milk, may they sleep in peace,
and may they be liberated from the fears of cold, heat, and disease.
That pure-souled one, being constantly composed in meditation, should recite this mantra while walking,
standing, reciting, smelling, eating, playing, or even while voiding excrement.
In all great dangers, whether in times of equality or adversity,
and likewise at the time of departure, this hymn that bestows fearlessness should be recited.
Likewise: fodder, mouthfuls of grain, and so forth should be given; at night, a brightly shining lamp should be provided;
and there should be an exposition of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas accompanied by lute music.
Those who are inwardly content should serve according to their ability and in due order;
they should never, even in a dream, experience beating, abuse, or exhaustion.
One should never feel any aversion toward their urine or excrement;
furthermore, the cow-pen must always be cleaned with dry ash, alkaline substances, and the like.
In summer, one should stay in a house surrounded by trees with cool water and free from mud;
likewise in the rainy season and the cold season, in a place that is pleasantly warm and sheltered from the wind.
One should discard food leavings, urine, feces, phlegm, and filth there, nor should one do so in that place. A woman in her courses, an outcaste, or an unchaste woman must not enter.
One should not step over a calf’s tethering rope, nor play in the vicinity of a cow-pen;
one must not enter among the cows wearing sandals or wooden shoes.
[966] At times, one should travel by means of elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles with canopies; otherwise, one should proceed on foot, keeping to the right and remaining humble.
Cows afflicted by exhaustion from plowing must be protected with faith like one's own father and mother,
for they are distressed by fears of mountain precipices, lions, bears, cold, and heat.
During a terrible great tumult, a fierce storm, or a national calamity,
fodder and cool water should be given to cows.
From the Viṣṇudharmottara: Puṣkara said:
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, the protection of cows must indeed be performed by the king."
Cows are purifying and auspicious; the worlds are established upon cows.
Cows extend the sacrifice; cows are the mothers of the universe.
Their dung and urine are supreme, the ultimate dispeller of misfortune.
For that [place] is indeed pure through effort, and Lakṣmī is established there;
one should not feel agitation due to ignorance regarding feces and urine.
One should not discard the urine or dung of cows, nor their spittle and so forth;
the dust of cows is supremely meritorious and destroys misfortune and obstacles.
Scratching the bodies of cows indeed destroys all impurities;
O Rāma, the water from a cow's horns is equal to the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—
these, O Bhārgava, should be known as the supreme purifiers for bathing and drinking.
This is a destroyer of Rākṣasas, auspicious, and a dispeller of the sufferings of the Kali age;
likewise, Rocanā is blessed and removes the poison of Rākṣasa-diseases.
But he who, having risen at dawn, gazes upon his face in clarified butter—
for him misfortune perishes and his sin does not increase.

By the gift of a herd of cows, he enjoys great merit. As many cows as one is able to maintain comfortably in one's home, so many should one always maintain; one should not maintain them if they are hungry.
Where cows live in misery within the house of a twice-born man, he falls into hell; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having given a village to another cow, he enjoys great merit.
By giving fodder to another’s cow throughout the entire winter season,
one attains heaven for six hundred years.
By always giving the first portion of food, as well as [the first portion] of cows,
a man obtains for eight years a residence endowed with the celestial world.
Twice a day—at evening and at dawn—is the meal prescribed for humans by the Veda;
likewise, one should always untiringly give a single meal to cows.
The man who eats a second meal attains the world of cows for as many years as there are in a Manvantara, O twice-born one.
O best of men, by providing shelter from the cold for cows in his house,
and by providing water at a watering place for cows, O best of men,
he attains the world of Varuṇa and sports with hosts of apsarases.
O Bhārgava, he who creates an obstacle for cows that have set out to drink commits the sin of killing a Brahmin; he becomes terrible and,
wherever he is born, he attains supreme satisfaction.
Having plowed the pasture land of cows with a plow or similar implements,
one attains a great hell for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras.
A man who rescues a cow terrified by lions or tigers, or one stuck in mud or fallen into water,
enjoys celestial pleasures for an eon in heaven.
O best of the twice-born, by the gift of salt to cows, one is born handsome; he attains great good fortune and physical charm.
Likewise, by giving medicine, one becomes free from disease;
he provides medicine, salt, water, and food.
If, while they are grazing together in the forest and have been penned in,
a wolf should spring upon and kill one of them, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter.
By killing a cow, a man goes to twenty-one hells;
therefore, with every effort, their protection must be ensured.
O Rāma, by selling cows one falls into hell;
yet by merely praising them, a man is liberated from sin.
Touching them is auspicious and destroys all impurities;
likewise, by giving them away, one may uplift even entire families.
In that house where even a single cow dwells, there shall be no fault regarding women in their courses or those who have recently given birth, nor any defect of the ground, nor any other such faults.
By the wind from the breath of cows, supreme peace shall prevail in the home;
that is proclaimed as the highest lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) in all places.
O Rāma, by the touch of cows, the impurity of men is destroyed.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with a one-night fast— when these are practiced individually as separate penances, it is known as the *sāntapana*. This purifies even a dog-eater (*śvapāka*).
O Rāma, having performed the *atikṛcchra* penance for twenty-one days on milk, one obtains the fulfillment of all desires and the destruction of all inauspiciousness.
By practicing that, the best of men become stainless.
One should drink warm urine for three days, drink warm ghee for three days,
drink warm milk for three days, and subsist on air alone for the final three days.
This is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra* penance, which destroys all inauspiciousness.
In the same manner, this cold austerity (śītakṛcchra) is proclaimed to be performed by means of cold [substances] in succession;
it was created by Brahmā himself for the destruction of all that is inauspicious.
One should perform one's bath with cow urine and sustain oneself on the products of the cow;
one should remain standing when they have risen, and remain seated when they are seated.
One should not eat while others have not eaten, nor should one drink while they have not drunk;
one should provide protection for oneself and rescue those who are afflicted by fear.
Even by sacrificing one's own life, that cow-vow is proclaimed;
it pacifies all sins in a single month, O Bhārgava.
By the fulfillment of this vow, O Rāma, a person shall go to Goloka, or else to whatever is desired, for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
By eating barley every day, abstaining from the food of cows,
one obtains within a month whatever one desires in one's mind.
Likewise, one should recite the Gomatī-vidyā in the evening and in the morning;
a person attains Goloka—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Above all the worlds of cows,
a realm is proclaimed where cows dwell eternally, moving through the sky in the heavens within diverse celestial chariots surrounded by throngs of apsarases.
The rivers, variegated with networks of tinkling bells, lutes, and musical instruments, always yield the fruits of desire, with mud made of milk and milk-rice.
There are beautiful lotus ponds with cool, pure water and golden sands, filled with blue and white lotuses made of beryl.
And likewise, O best of the Bhṛgus, mental perfection is attained there in that world;
men go to that world through devotion to cows, of this there is no doubt.
I shall proclaim the Gomatī, which destroys all sins;
O Brahmin, listen with a well-composed mind as I recite it.
Cows are eternally fragrant; cows possess the scent of guggulu resin.
Cows are the foundation of all beings; cows are the supreme means of transcendence.
Cows are indeed the supreme food and the highest sacrificial offering for the gods;
they purify all the deities and both carry and protect them.
In the world of the gods, they gratify the immortals with oblations purified by mantras;
in the fire-sacrifices of the sages, cows are employed for the oblation.
Cows are the supreme refuge for all living beings;
cows are the highest purifier, and cows are the greatest auspiciousness.
Cows are the stairs to heaven; cows are auspicious and eternal. Salutations to the glorious cows, to the daughters of Surabhi, and salutations again and again to the pure daughters of Brahmā.
The Brahmins and the cows constitute a single family divided into two parts:
on one side reside the sacred mantras, and on the other resides the sacrificial oblation.
Since the entire world is indeed sustained by gods, brahmins, cows, virtuous men, and virtuous women,
why are all of them considered most worthy of worship?
At that sacred ford where thirsty cows always drink water,
or by which they cross over, there the Sarasvatī stands.
For here, the Gaṅgā is present in the bathing-place of cows;
likewise, nourishment is increased in their dust;
prosperity is in their dung, and dharma is in bowing down to them.
And one should constantly pay homage to them.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa,
Brahmā said: "Having touched a cow and paid homage, he who performs a circumambulation..."
By him, the earth together with its islands has been circumambulated in a clockwise direction.
O best of men, because sin is destroyed by the sound of the cows' "hum" and by their glance, one should look at them and touch them.
How could there be sin for one whose home is adorned,
constantly decorated by young women with children at their breasts?
All the sacred fords on earth, including the oceans and the lakes,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of bathing with water from a cow's horn.
One should not step over the bone of a cow, nor should one avoid its scent;
for as long as one smells that odor, for that long one is joined with merit.
Scratching the bodies of cows is auspicious and yields the fruit of the gift of a cow;
likewise, protecting them from fear, disease, and other harms is equal to the gift of a hundred cows.
Whoever provides a cow’s daily ration consisting of grass, water, and so forth, should know that he obtains the fruit of giving a hundred Kapila cows; of this there is no doubt.
O auspicious one, composed of the five elements, meritorious, pure, and born of the Sun;
accept this which is given by me, O daughter of Surabhi; salutations be to you!
And what is the use of saying more? Cows must be protected with great effort; likewise, they should be given away, guarded, honored, and accepted in every way.
Those who strike cows here, the mothers of all the world, go to the hell named Raurava; of this there is no doubt.
Whosoever, out of delusion, should strike her, or any other lowest of men, he shall go to the terrible hell known as Saṃpīḍaka; such is the sacred tradition.
He who, upon seeing a cow approaching with the intent to kill at night,
says, "Forgive me, O Mother," goes to the supreme state.
In the Varāha Purāṇa,
Yama said:
"Cows are purifying, auspicious, and the deities even of the gods."
He who serves them with devotion is liberated from sins;
the evil committed throughout his entire life perishes at that very moment.
The man who receives upon his head the water raised up by the tail [of a cow] is indeed liberated from the sins committed during the autumn season.
A man who bathes at Prasravaṇa on the earth during the Rohiṇī asterism quickly burns away all the faults incurred by his sinful deeds; of this there is no doubt.
That man who receives upon his head the stream of milk issuing from the udder of a cow is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the service to cows.
Now follows the gift of food, from the *Dānadharma* section of the *Śāntiparvan* in the *Mahābhārata*.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the Bharatas, what gifts should the king Dārukāma give to the Brahmins who are superior in merit in this world?
By what are you immediately satisfied, and when satisfied, what do you bestow?
Tell me this, O mighty-armed one: what is the great fruit of performing meritorious deeds?
O King, what gift is fruitful both in this world and in the next?
I wish to hear from you; tell me that in detail.
Bhīṣma said: O Bhārata, listen as I relate that which Nārada, who beholds the gods, spoke in the past when he was questioned on this very matter.
Nārada said:
The gods, the hosts of sages, and the asuras all praise food alone;
for the world-ordinances and all designations are established in food.
A gift equal to food has never existed, nor will it ever exist;
therefore, human beings especially desire to give food.
In this world, food provides vigor, and the vital breaths are established in food;
by food, O Lord, this entire universe and all this world are sustained.
From food, O mendicants, do householders in this world arise;
from that very food, life-breath originates—this is perceptible, there is no doubt in this.
Even by causing distress to one's family, food should be given to a high-souled Brahmin and to a mendicant by one who desires his own prosperity.
Whoever gives food to a worthy Brahmin who asks for it,
provides for himself the most excellent treasure in the world beyond.
Seeking prosperity, one should honor an afflicted, elderly, and learned Brahmin who has arrived at one's home while returning from a journey.
Having abandoned arisen anger, being well-behaved and free from envy,
the giver of food, O King, attains that happiness both in heaven and here on earth.
One should not despise a person who has approached for alms, nor should one ever turn them away;
even if it be a dog-cooker or a dog, a gift never goes to waste.
Whoever should give unblemished food to one traveling on a road who is weary and has not seen such a person before, that person shall attain the great Dharma.
O lord of men, that man who gratifies the ancestors, the gods, the brahmins, and the sacred fords with food, his meritorious fruit is great.
Even after committing a sinful deed, he who gives food to one who asks—
especially to a Brāhmaṇa— is not joined with that sin.
A gift of food given to Brahmins is inexhaustible, while food given to a Śūdra yields great fruit;
indeed, the gift of food to Brahmins is superior even to that given to a Śūdra.
One should not inquire about [the guest's] lineage, conduct, sacred study, or even his native land; when a brahmin has requested alms here, one should simply give food and let him depart.
O King, for one who gives food, trees that yield all desired fruits arise both in this world and in the next; of this there is no doubt.
For the ancestors hope, just as farmers long for good rain:
"May our son or our grandson provide us with food."
For a Brahmin is indeed a great being; he himself begs, saying, "Give.
Whether one is free from desire or possessed of desire, by giving, one obtains merit.
The Brahmin is the guest of all beings and is entitled to eat first from the offerings;
for the Brahmins always come to his house seeking alms.
When they are honored, they turn back; therefore, that [merit] proceeds exceedingly.
O Bhārata, after death, one obtains birth in a family of great enjoyments.
Having given food in this world, a man likewise attains the unsurpassed state;
as a giver of desired food, he dwells honored in heaven.
Food is indeed the life-force of men; everything is established upon food.
The giver of food becomes possessed of cattle, sons, wealth, and enjoyments as well.
O King, such a giver of food becomes possessed of vital breath and likewise endowed with beauty;
he is proclaimed in the world as a giver of life and a giver of all.
For by giving food to a guest who is a Brāhmaṇa according to the prescribed rule,
the donor attains happiness and is honored even by the gods.
For the Brahmin is a great being who moves about like one with feet;
whatever seed is sown in him indeed yields a great fruit of merit.
Furthermore, food alone generates immediate joy for those who eat it;
therefore, all other gifts of food bear fruit only in the unseen future.
Know, O King, that progeny indeed arises from food; know that pleasure comes from food;
know that both dharma and artha arise from food, as does the destruction of disease.
For in ancient times, Prajāpati said that food is indeed nectar;
food sustains the five-elemental body of the world.
Food is indeed divine, for the entire person is established in food;
upon the destruction of food, the five elements in the body fall apart.
In this world, even the strength of the powerful perishes through the loss of food;
likewise, the Āvahā, Vicāhā, and Yajña sacrifices do not endure in the end without [sustenance].
O best of men, O Brahmin, they do not perish, nor does their food run out;
for the giver of food [obtains] all this, whatever is stationary or moving.
Therefore, food should be given for the sake of Dharma in the three worlds by the wise;
for the man who gives food possesses strength, vigor, fame, and happiness.
O King, the fame of one who does not take [the sacrificial] oblations increases throughout the three worlds;
for Śiva does not cause the fall of living beings when they have not been given [as offerings].
Nor does Śakra rain down water that has already entered the clouds, O Bhārata.
The sun draws up the terrestrial moisture with its own rays;
and from the sun, the wind—the divine Prajāpati who moves within—draws it forth.
O descendant of Bharata, when water has fallen from the clouds upon the earth, then the goddess Earth becomes moist.
From that, the crops grow, by which this world subsists;
from that, moreover, there arises the manifestation of flesh, fat, bone, and semen.
From that semen, O lord of the earth, living beings come into existence;
for Agni and Soma nourish that semen as the means of procreation.
Thus, food, the sun, the wind,
and indeed everything else are considered a single aggregate, from which all beings were born.
O bull among the Bharatas, he who quickly gives food to a seeker who has arrived at his home bestows life upon all beings and increases their progeny.
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, having been thus addressed by Nārada, I always gave food.
You are food, as is the Sun; therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, give food."
O King, O Lord, by giving food to the twice-born according to the rules and in a fitting manner,
you too shall attain heaven.
O lord of men, hear now of those worlds that are attained through the gift of food.
The palaces of those great-souled ones shine in heaven,
possessing various forms and structures, and endowed with various pillars.
[978] They were as white as the lunar disc and possessed networks of tinkling bells;
they had the color of the rising sun and were both stationary and moving.
They consist of many hundreds of stories, contain internal waters and groves,
possess the brilliance of lapis lazuli and the sun, and are composed of gold and silver.
Moreover, trees yielding all desired fruits stood within the dwellings;
there were ponds, pathways, assembly halls, water-stations, and oblong lakes on every side.
And there were thousands of resonant vehicles yoked for the journey,
as well as halls filled with food and drink, garments, and ornaments.
Rivers flowing with milk, mountains of food,
palaces of white splendor, and couches radiant with gold—
those who give food attain these; therefore, become a giver of food.
These worlds belong to the high-souled doers of merit who give food;
therefore, food especially should be given by men on this earth.
From the Agni Purāṇa:
O sinless one, I shall relate to you the greatness of the gift of food, which has been declared by all the best of sages to be the source of happiness and joy for everyone.
"Give food, give food, give food, O best of kings!
What is the use of anything else you might give, when that which instantly brings satisfaction in this world is at hand?"
In a former age, that which was spoken by Rāma according to the prescribed rule out of world-weariness— though he was a god among gods— I shall nevertheless relate it to you.
"O son of Sumitrā, although the earth is filled with food, we still long for more; surely we have not offered oblations into the mouths of brahmins."
Whatever is sown in one's own wife, its fruit is inevitably obtained by men;
this has been observed by us, for what is offered into the mouth of a Brahmin does not yield such a result.
That which is not to be obtained cannot be obtained either by knowledge or by human effort;
this popular saying in the world is true: what has not been given does not come to one.
O King, among all kinds of food, the gift of cooked rice is supremely conducive to merit;
other gifts of various other types of edibles are likewise beneficial.
For men who have bathed, anointed themselves, and adorned with ornaments,
there can be neither happiness nor contentment without food.
Food is the supreme means for attaining virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation;
food is Prajāpati himself, and likewise, food is Viṣṇu and Śiva.
Therefore, food should especially be given by men on this earth.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"The gift of food is beneficial for men and superior to all other gifts;
for from food, the generation of life-force for men always arises."
But he who gives even a mere means of sustaining life to a Brahmin—
especially during a famine— must be honored by men on this earth.
Devala said:
But he who, having committed a sinful deed, gives desired food—
especially to Brahmins— he destroys his own darkness.
Food that is offered with reverence and devotion delights the limbs; it is not so when it is devoid of human care, even if it were nectar itself.
A giver who gives with joy is rare, and those who enjoy with joy are even rarer;
both the joyful giver and the joyful enjoyer are inhabitants of heaven.
The food of one who eats what is highly esteemed, who does not despise the food,
and who gives the food with joy— his food stands ready for him.
He who gives food with joy and he who receives it with reverence both eat inexhaustibly with pleasure;
being honored, he attains heaven.
He who gives food with displeasure and he who does not welcome the food—
both of them shall dwell submerged in hell for a hundred autumns.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Of all gifts indeed, the gift of food is remembered as supreme;
it provides immediate gratification, is divine, and increases strength and intelligence.
There is no gift equal to the gift of food found within the three worlds;
from food all beings come into existence, and they die for lack of it.
Those dwelling in the womb, those being born, children, the elderly, and those in their middle age—
even gods, dānavas, and ascetics— all long for food.
For hunger is considered the most preeminent of all diseases;
its remedy is proclaimed to be the application of the medicine of food.
The giver of food is declared to be the giver of life, and the giver of life is the giver of everything;
therefore, by the gift of food, one obtains the fruit of all possible gifts.
The body is the supreme means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
its maintenance depends upon food and drink, and therefore that [food and drink] is the means for everything.
Food is Prajāpati himself; food is Viṣṇu; food is Śiva himself.
Therefore, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to the gift of food.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara,
Haṃsa said:
"Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of food is preeminent."
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of food.
In this matter, there should be no examination of the recipient, nor any restriction regarding time;
nor should the location be scrutinized here—the food should always be given.
Food should indeed always be given to dogs, to those who cook dogs, to the fallen, and likewise to worms, insects, and moths.
For food is life in this world, and the vital breaths are dependent upon food;
thus, the giver of food is a giver of life in this world, and the giver of food is likewise a giver of everything.

O best of the twice-born, it should be understood, O most excellent of Brahmins, that for whom one eats food, for him one's progeny is born; the offspring belongs to the one whose food has been consumed.
Gifts should be given to all castes, but food should be eaten by a Brāhmaṇa alone.
O twice-born ones, if a Brāhmaṇa dies with another's food remaining in his stomach, he enters that person's womb; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

The giver of solid food attains heaven; the giver of soft food attains the world of Śakra; the giver of food to be licked attains the world of the Apsarases; and the giver of food to be sucked attains the world of the Vasus.
A man who drinks [alcohol] likewise attains the world of Varuṇa;
he who offers fragrant and cool beverages becomes enriched with all desires— of this there is no doubt.
By the gift of *paramānna*, eternal satisfaction is attained;
one does not die of thirst and is glorified in the world of cows.
Likewise, the giver of molasses bestows health; the giver of honey fulfills all desires;
the giver of ghee grants long life; and the giver of oil likewise bestows health.
He who bestows salt obtains all his desires;
he who gives flour-meal attains satisfaction, and likewise he who gives sand attains fame. By giving other things not specifically mentioned here, one shall attain heaven.
Now, in the Bhagavatī Purāṇa: "O Bhārata, salt, ghee, oil, jaggery, asafoetida, pieces of ginger, cumin, leaves, and beautiful vegetables [are permitted]."
"Having given [these], one shall be happy"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"By giving jaggery, sugarcane juice, salt, condiments, and fragrant drinks, one shall become exceedingly happy."
Yama said:
By the gift of dairy products, one attains unsurpassed satisfaction;
likewise, by the gift of clarified butter, one finds a long life.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
[983] Those who give salt, sesame seeds, and likewise clarified butter,
are born radiant, possessed of enjoyments, and long-lived.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Blood, flesh, fat, and semen arise from food in succession;
from semen beings are born; therefore, the world consists of food."
Even when all these things— gold, jewels, horses, lordly elephants, moon-garlands, sandalwood, and so forth— are obtained, those who are hungry do not find delight in them.
There is no suffering equal to hunger; there is no disease equal to hunger.
There is no happiness equal to food; there is no enemy equal to anger.
Therefore, there is great merit from the giving of food,
because all embodied beings die when tormented by the fire of hunger.
Whatever jewels, enjoyments, women, and vehicles exist in the three worlds,
the giver of food enjoys all of them both in this world and the next.
When one whose limbs are nourished by another's food and drink accumulates a store of merit, half of that belongs to the giver of the food and half to the doer; of this there is no doubt.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "He whose food a hundred Brahmins eat for many years,
given with a joyful mind, shall not fall into the state of an animal."
O bull among men, ten thousand Brahmins should be fed;
by this, even a man who is always devoted to sinful deeds shall be liberated from unrighteousness.
O King, having fed a thousand men who are knowers of Brahman—
those who understand justice, those who know the Dharma, and likewise those who are learned in the Smṛtis and the Bhāṣyas— [one attains the fruit].
He does not go to a terrible hell, nor does he undergo the cycles of saṃsāra.
A householder should always offer food to a Brāhmaṇa first before eating;
a person should make each day fruitful by the gift of food.
The Brahmin who, having collected food through alms,
bestows it upon other Brahmins and remains devoted to the study of the Vedas, prospers in happiness here in this world after having given.
In every circumstance, a person should always place food that has been acquired through righteous means into the hands of a worthy recipient; for food is indeed the supreme refuge.
Likewise:
"He who, moreover, gives food during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
crosses over all difficulties and enjoys infinity after death."
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"Beings are born from food; indeed, the gods desire food.
No rule regarding vessels and such is proclaimed for that [food] except in the context of a *śrāddha*."
Likewise: "Even by giving food to insects, moths, dogs, and those born of the Cāṇḍāla womb,
one briefly attains the world of Prajāpati."
For those who bestow food upon kinsmen, guests, friends,
and the poor, the blind, and the wretched, there shall be heaven for those givers of food.
By giving even a single mouthful of food to beings who are greedy for food,
a person shall dwell in heaven for a hundred years with delightful enjoyments.
Indeed, this fruit has been duly proclaimed for every morsel;
this merit and its weight have been declared to you by the God as being twofold.
If one gives food at the appropriate time and place to a person who is emaciated due to lack of food,
it is said that the fruit is fivefold and endowed with all auspicious qualities.

The meaning is that [the recipient] is endowed with the state of being a king and so forth. Furthermore, he who, filled with faith, gives food and other provisions to the deities, shall dwell for a hundred thousand years together with the immortals, even for every single grain of rice.
The merit from food accompanied by condiments is ten times this;
this merit is proclaimed to be equal to that obtained from giving to one's chosen deity.
Whoever should give food to a Brāhmaṇa, his reward is twofold;
therefore, by giving food to Viṣṇu, one enjoys twice that reward.
By the offering of food to Rudra, this fruit is fourfold,
due to the conjunction of faith and the proper time, and through the inclusion of various side dishes.
The merit of those who properly give food shall be equal to a hundredfold.
Laghuhārīta says:
Just as one eats food that has been properly prepared when it is served,
so too one should not give away as leavings food from which the essence has been drunk, nor should one offer it in the fire sacrifice.
Vyāsa says: He who, in a single row, gives unequally—
whether out of affection, fear, or for the sake of wealth— [is at fault].
It has been seen by the gods and sung by the sages;
the sages declare that to be the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Atri:
That king should punish the village where twice-born men wander for alms without observing vows and without sacred mantras; for such a village provides sustenance for thieves.
Having studied the four Vedas and understood the true essence of the meaning of all the scriptures,
one who has feasted in the palace of a king is born as a worm in excrement.
The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster;
and he who eats the food of his own daughter eats the impurity of the earth.
Devala says:
A householder who feeds a Brahmin without clarified butter in his own home, even though ghee is available,
shall fall into a terrible hell in the hereafter.
Having himself eaten fine food,
if a fool subsequently feeds Brahmins poor and meager fare, he shall dwell for a long time in hell.
He who gives delicious food to the foremost of the twice-born, or to the gods, or to guests,
shall increase with sons and grandsons.
He attains equality with the enemy of Vṛtra.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of cooked food. Now follows the gift of uncooked food, according to the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Haṃsa said:
The gift of grain is declared by the best of the twice-born to be the most excellent of gifts;
and among grains, red śāli rice is proclaimed to be the supreme grain.
By giving red śāli rice, a man is honored in the world of the Sun;
likewise, by giving fragrant substances, he rejoices together with the gandharvas.
By the gift of *kāla* rice, one is glorified in the world of Śakra;
by the gift of *mahāśāli* rice, one shall attain the world of the Vasus.
By likewise giving black śāli rice, one rejoices in Alakā;
by the gift of grain and the donation of crops, one shall attain heaven.
By the gift of barley, a man is glorified in the world of Śakra;
likewise, by the gift of wheat, he shall attain the world of the Vasus.
He who gives priyaṅgu becomes beloved by the world;
but he who gives śyāmāka, the deities are pleased with him.
A man who is intent on giving other types of awned grain attains the heavenly world; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The giver of mung beans attains the world of Śakra, while the giver of māṣa beans attains the world of Yama;
likewise, O Brahmin, the giver of sesame seeds attains whatever world he desires.
By the gift of sixty-day rice, one attains the world of Nirṛti;
by giving rice mixed with chickpeas, one reaches the world of Varuṇa.
By giving lentils, black gram, and parched grain, one attains the world of Vāyu;
and by the gift of other pulse-grains, one shall attain heaven.
By the gift of sugarcane and grapes, one shall attain supreme good fortune.
In the world of men, the gift of cooked food is said to yield fruit; for through this, one attains that [cooked food].
Therefore, the best of the twice-born perform sacrifices with offerings.
Therefore, that is declared to be most meritorious.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of cooked food.
Now follows the gift of water. Regarding this, Manu says:
"He who offers water, which sustains the life-breaths of living beings..."
It is cool during the summer season; now hear the fruit of his merit.
Whatever merit is indeed prescribed for the gift of ten million tawny cows,
one who provides drinking water obtains that very fruit of merit;
he ascends a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) as radiant as the full moon, free from all darkness.
In the Saura Purāṇa: "The gift of water is remembered as supreme, superior to all other gifts;
therefore, one who knows the Dharma should likewise fetch and give water."
Vedavyāsa said: "O dear one, water is indeed difficult to obtain, especially in the hereafter;
by the gift of water, eternal satisfaction is attained."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "Water is the life-breath of living beings; therefore, let that be given there, since this alone is superior to all other gifts."
Likewise: He who bestows water during the summer and the spring seasons—
his merit cannot be described even with a thousand tongues.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"Listen to the fruit of the gift of him who bestows upon Brahmins fragrant, cool [waters] endowed with divine flavors."
Having ascended a celestial chariot, radiant as the sun and frequented by hosts of Apsarases,
he goes to heaven to dwell in the same world as Varuṇa.
In the Nandipurāṇa: "Any man who gives a drink of water to one afflicted by thirst dwells in heaven, eternally satisfied, for a hundred yugas."
In the Mahābhārata:
"Manu has declared that food is indeed superior to all gifts;
and from food, O best of the Kurus, even water comes into being."
For indeed, O dear one, nothing at all proceeds without water;
and the blessed Soma, the lord of the host of planets, was born from water.
Amṛta, the earth itself, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā;
food, medicinal herbs, O great king, and creepers born from water—
from these, O lord of the people, the life-breaths of living beings arise.
For the food of the gods is indeed ambrosia (amṛta), and likewise that of the nāgas is sudhā;
svadhā is declared to be the food of the ancestors (pitṛs), and for animals it is plants.
The wise say that food alone is the life-breath of human beings;
and all of that, O tiger among men, originates from water.
Therefore, there is indeed nothing more auspicious than the gift of water;
a man who desires his own welfare should give it constantly.
O lord of the people, O son of Kuntī, the gift of water brings merit, fame, and long life; indeed, the giver of water dwells in heaven even beyond Śakra.
He obtains all desires and eternal fame in this world;
after death, he attains infinity and is liberated from all evils.
"O tiger among men, O one of great splendor, having gone to heaven,
he attains imperishable worlds," so said Manu.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
