"Water alone is the fruitful fruit of the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving;
both the stationary and the mobile are transformations of water."
In this world, there is never any subsistence here without water.
For worms, insects, and moths, water alone is the ultimate refuge;
wherever there is water, all the gods are established there.
Where there is water, there likewise are the sages of great vows;
and that is difficult for people to attain in the next world, O best of the twice-born.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa: "He who, having acquired merit through wealth, bestows the gift of water,
goes to the realm of the Moon, clothed in auspicious, radiant garments."
Rivers of milk flow toward him and likewise rivers of honey;
oceans of ghee, curd, and water are at his command.
It is said that people can indeed live for many days deprived of food;
however, one cannot live even a single day without water.
O tiger among men, the giver of water is proclaimed to be a giver of everything;
for all seeds exist within water—such is the figurative tradition.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Water is remembered as the life of all three worlds;
it is pure and nectarine. Therefore, one who desires merit should give it."
Now, the gifts of the water-strainer (*karapavitraka*) and so forth. Devala says:
"That man who gives a water-strainer containing water to a Brahmin traveler certainly obtains the merit of having excavated a well."
In the Mahābhārata: "O Bhārata, there is great delight for the venerable Bṛhaspati, as well as for Pūṣan, Bhaga, the Aśvins, and Agni."
This is the supreme medicine for the priest, the highest of sacrifices;
by it they do not die of thirst, and their own desire is fulfilled.
He who offers water-pots shall not meet with misfortune.
Endowed with faith, you should give water-pots to the foremost of Brahmins;
such a person always obtains a sixth part of the merit of ritual ablutions.
Kātyāyana says: He who, having fed the twice-born,
gives them water-pots filled with very cool water, shall also attain a happy state.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "He who gives a water-pot, a vessel, a *kuṇḍikā*, or a *karakā* [water-jar] obtains cool water for one afflicted by thirst during the summer heat."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who, having honored a jar filled with water placed within a golden vessel and gifted it along with a pair of garments, will certainly go to heaven."
Now, the gift of the Dharma-jar. Viṣṇu said: A jar filled with cool, fragrant water, its body smeared with white sandalwood paste and adorned with garlands of flowers.
One should prepare a shallow bowl filled with curd and rice,
and upon it, one should fashion a water-pot called Dharma, provided with a pair of sandals and an umbrella.
Having taken flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), one should utter this mantra:
"Oṃ, homage to you who have the form of Viṣṇu; homage to you, O son of the ocean!
Lift me up from this ocean of suffering saṃsāra, which is full of water."
A water-pot was given by me day after day during the summer season;
through this gift of a water-pot, may Madhusūdana be pleased.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: Every day, a jar of Dharma, its mouth wrapped in cloth,
containing cool and pure water, should be carried to the house of a Brāhmaṇa.
The person who provides water during the interval between spring and summer obtains the fruit of one pala of gold for every single drop.
Whoever should offer a water-pot beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa shall obtain,
day by day, the meritorious fruit of giving a thousand cows.
O best of men, the concluding rite (udyāpana) for that very vow should be performed month after month,
offering *maṇḍakas* and bricks, along with cooked foods that fulfill all desires,
dedicated to Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, or the ancestors.
Having sprinkled [the water] with sesame seeds while reciting this mantra, the man [should proceed].
This [water] from the Dharma-pitcher, whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, has been given;
by its offering, may my desires be constantly fulfilled.
Whoever bestows the Dharma-jar according to this rite during the spring or the summer season shall obtain the fruit of providing a water-station;
he too attains the fruit of providing a water-station here, of this there is no doubt.
Now, regarding the watering of the *aśvattha* tree. In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"Indeed, that man who may be incapable even of the gift of a water-pot should daily water the root of the *aśvattha* tree, having conquered his self."
It pacifies all sins, destroys all suffering,
alleviates all diseases, and constantly increases one's progeny.
"May the Blessed One Janārdana, who takes the form of the Aśvattha tree, be pleased with me.
Having uttered this and having offered salutation, [one performs] daily [the rite] which destroys sin.
Whoever performs the watering at the root of a tree for four months, he too obtains that fruit; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
Now, the taking of the water-pitcher:
likewise, I shall further describe another supreme method for the offering of water.
Having recognized the spring season, one should go to a supreme temple.
There, having filled a jar with water for that self-manifested (svāyaṃbhuva) or sage-worshipped (ārṣa) linga which is honored by the gods, [one should place it] within its inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
One should cause that water, scented with fragrant perfumes, filtered through a cloth,
and flowing continuously day and night, to fall upon the top of the *liṅga*.
Thus, whoever, endowed with faith and devotion, should have a water-pot made for Śiva,
Viṣṇu, the Sun, or for one’s chosen deity;
One should cause a pitcher to flow continuously upon the head of the deity;
by giving [this] according to this rite for four months, a person [attains the fruit].
Then, when the month of Karkaṭaka has arrived, one should bathe the Lord with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
worship Him with perfumes and delightful food offerings,
prostrate before Maheśāna, and recite this mantra:
Oṃ, salutations! May Śaṅkara, Śambhu, Bhava, Dhātṛ, Śiva, and Hara be pleased with me through this offering of a water-pitcher, O Mahādeva.
Having made this resolve, the donor, having subsequently returned home,
should feed, according to his capacity, devotees of Śiva and the foremost of Brahmins.

O Lord of Men, he who performs the rite of offering water to Śiva in this manner during the summer shall dwell in the world of Śaṅkara for as many millions of years as there are drops that fall upon the linga; of this there is no doubt.

Now, the gift of a water-jar (*maṇika*). Regarding this, Devala says: "He who gives a water-jar filled with water to the house of a twice-born at the commencement of summer obtains the fruit of one who has constructed a pond."
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By one who is unable to provide water-stations (*prapā*) but desires to attain a specific merit..."
O Janārdana, tell me how the gift of a jeweled vessel is to be given, at what time it is bestowed, and what fruit results from that gift.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one who is unable to provide water-stations but desires to perform a specific religious duty should instead practice the gift of a water-jar.
Especially on the third day of Vaiśākha and on the full moon,
as well as during the spring and summer seasons, the water-pot (maṇika) is offered there.
The best [image] is said to be made with forty jars, the middling with thirty, and the inferior with twenty; one should not have it made with fewer than that.
Then, one should fill it with water according to one's capacity, including gold;
its body should be smeared with white sandalwood paste and adorned with garlands of flowers.
Having completely covered it with garments and placed vessels of cooked food upon them,
one should place an image of the god Varuṇa made of gold on top of that;
then, meditating upon Keśava, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The waters are called Nārā; may Āditya, Varuṇa, Yama, the water-jar, and the Earth grant peace to the giver of all.
The worship mantra:
Oṃ! Water is the purifier of the worlds; Janārdana rests within the waters.
May the One Who Lies upon the Waters be pleased by the gift of this water-jar.
The mantra for the gift:
Having given a water-jar according to this rite to an eminent brahmin,
O best of men, hear what fruit the donor obtains.
He never experiences separation from his sons, brothers, or wealth;
nor does that man ever suffer a deficiency in his household provisions.
Listen to the fruit of merit for that woman who gives a water-jar:
a childless woman obtains a son, and an unfortunate woman becomes fortunate.
A widow who gives a water-pot shall not be reborn for seven lifetimes;
having obtained the fruit of giving a house, she is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O bull of the Bharatas, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja,
one shall dwell in the divine city of Ākhaṇḍala, where flowers are in full bloom.
Thus ends the gift of a water-pot.
Now follows the gift of a water-shed (*prapā*). In the *Mahābhārata*:
"O best of the twice-born, water-sheds should be established for the purpose of giving at all times."
And especially after they have eaten, drinks are offered to them.
He who provides water without restriction during the heat of the summer season does not encounter difficult, treacherous, or painful circumstances anywhere.
Yama said: One who constructs wells, gardens, and rest-houses, as well as one who plants trees,
gives away a maiden in marriage, and builds bridges, attains heaven without a doubt.
For example:
"Those who possess ponds, water-stations, auspicious groves, wells, and shelters..."
The giving of food and sweet speech [bring] both this world and the next for them.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"O lord of men, water and boiled rice should be given with one's whole being;
this is exceedingly difficult to obtain in the world beyond."
Therefore, wells, tanks, ponds, and water-stations should be constructed according to one's ability by men who desire their own welfare.
Whether in a village, a city, or on a path devoid of water,
he who causes a delightful water-station (prapā) to be built shall attain a meritorious state.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By constructing a beautiful water-shed (*prapā*) on the road, one is glorified in the world of the gods;
by establishing a beautiful site for a water-shed, one attains an eternal station."
It is proclaimed that by consecrating that place, there is an increase of fruit;
having performed the smearing of that spot, one is liberated from all sins.
By giving a rope at a place for a water-shed, a man becomes a possessor of cattle;
likewise, by giving a water-vessel, he obtains that very same fruit.
By the gift of a water-pot, one's desires always become fulfilled.
And likewise, by providing a water-station and a male attendant,
one enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
O best of the twice-born, he who gives increasing vessels at a water-station attains threefold growth through splendor, fame, and prosperity.
By the gift of salt, one obtains eternal flavors;
therein, by the gift of green vegetables, one may attain the world of cows.
Likewise, by the gift of fruit, one obtains the merit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice;
by the gift of barley meal (saktu), a man obtains the merit of giving a hundred cows;
and by the gift of dairy products, he shall attain Goloka.
By providing various kinds of beds and seats at a water-station, one attains the heavenly world of the Vasus; of this there is no doubt.
Having performed the fire-ritual there in that manner for protection against the cold,
a person shall likewise attain the radiance and clarity of the body's internal fire, as well as good fortune.
By providing fuel, one is not overcome by enemies;
by giving useful articles there, one attains heaven;
and by the gift of betel leaves and such, one reaches the world of Indra.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord of Gods, tell me something of the majesty of the gift of a water-station (*prapā*)."
How should it be given? When should it be given? And what is the fruit of that gift?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
When the month of Phālguna has passed and the great festival has arrived,
on an auspicious day declared by the Brahmins, endowed with the strength of the planets and the moon.
The wise man should have a pavilion constructed— providing dense shade and beautiful to behold—
either in the center of the city, on a road, or at the foot of a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa).
One should place beautiful and auspicious jeweled jars in the center of that delightful area, which has a very cool surface and is furnished with various seats.

[1000] Having provided wages as prescribed to a Brahmin endowed with virtuous conduct, one should appoint a guardian of the water-station (prapā-pāla), who has many sons and attendants, using cloths to wrap the faces of the water-jars whose bases are not exposed.
He who causes men to drink water without fatigue, having constructed such a water-station on an auspicious day according to the prescribed rites;
O best of men, at the commencement of the rite, one should feed the twice-born according to one's ability;
thereafter, the wise man should dismiss them with this mantra: "Anena mānavah."
This water, common to all, has been offered to the beings;
by its offering, may the fathers and grandfathers be satisfied.
This is the formula for the declaration of the gift (*dānavākya*) here:

"From this day forward, for the duration of four months, desiring to attain the world of Indra—which is to be enjoyed for a period of thirty million years—and desiring the status of a Brāhmaṇa learned in the four Vedas in the mortal world, I relinquish to all beings this water-station (*prapā*) provided with drinking water, food, condiments, and so forth; whether three, two, or one person [shall drink] each day.
Thereafter, water should be given unimpeded for the four months.
Or, O Great King, three fortnights is the maximum lifespan for living beings.
One should offer [food] that is rich in fragrance, delicious, and cool, placed upon a beautiful vessel;
one should give it without obstruction while not looking at the recipient's face.
One should cause the twice-born to eat from that [vessel] every day according to one's ability.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for him who, according to this rite, gives excellent water that destroys the heat during the summer season.
Whatever fruit results from the gift of a hundred tawny cows properly bestowed,
that same fruit of merit one attains, being highly honored by all the gods.
Having ascended a celestial chariot resembling the full moon,
he goes to the city of the Lord of the Gods, being honored by hosts of apsarases.
For thirty crores of years, one is served by yakṣas and gandharvas;
then, upon the exhaustion of merit, having returned here, one becomes a twice-born master of the four Vedas. Thereafter, one attains that state from which a return is difficult to find.
O Pārtha, on the road at the edge of the city, in a place belonging to the king, there is a water-station with sweet, cool water that dispels fatigue,
which is enjoyed by all people.
That Dharmottara indeed lives in the world of the living.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of water-stalls (*prapā*). Now follows the construction of reservoirs. Regarding that, first the well is described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Without water, there is no livelihood at all in either of the two worlds."
Therefore, reservoirs of water should be constructed by a wise man.
A well is equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, and in a desert, it is equal to the Aśvamedha;
a well with flowing water removes all evil deeds.
The maker of a well, having attained heaven, enjoys all pleasures;
even there, proficiency in enjoyment is proclaimed to result from practice in that very place.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The man who should construct a beautiful well filled with water,
and having fed excellent Brahmins according to the prescribed rule, should present it to them."
Adorned with eight most variegated banners,
O best of men, by giving this [gift], one delivers fifty ancestors;
he goes among the Apsarases and attains the same world as Varuṇa through song.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*: "The man who causes a pond or a well to be dug in a place devoid of water goes to heaven after death for a hundred years."
He is always equal to the gods, being incomparable and free from thirst and hunger.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Those who are devoted to the Setubandha, those who are intent on purity at sacred fords (tīrtha),
and those who construct tanks and wells— they are liberated from the fear of thirst."
Viṣṇu: Now, for the one who digs a well, when water flows forth from it, his evil deeds perish. The maker of a tank, being eternally satisfied, attains the world of Varuṇa.
The giver of water is always satisfied.
When that has proceeded— that is, when it has issued forth from that well— likewise: in wells,
groves, ponds, and in temples of the deities.
And one who performs the re-consecration obtains the fruit of the stake.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"O best of gods, one should construct a well and a grove just as they are praised, so that the builder may be born in this world and it may become beautiful."
One should perform [the rite] by relying on the eastern direction, or even on its northern path;
one should not cause a deviation from the east, nor should one do so from a temple or a house.
Whatever is done that causes fear in the world— such as the danger from fire or water,
or even that which pertains to the wind— is produced as a source of fear for the deity.
Garga said: A wise man should construct a well, circular or oblong in shape, which brings happiness to all living beings, with a depth of more than five cubits and up to twenty-five cubits.
Thus ends the procedure for the construction of a well. Now follows the construction of a pond (*vāpī*), as described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Those who construct reservoirs of water do not behold the world of Yama."
Therefore, O King, one should take great care to construct a well of beautiful form.
A pond is likewise proclaimed to be equal to ten wells.
In the Devīpurāṇa: A well is that which is five cubits or more in depth;
a pond is that which is ten *dhanus* or more in depth, as established by the best of kings.
The *uttarā* should be performed in all cases—twice, thrice, once, or even otherwise;
it may be known as *saṃbhadraka*, or others [may perform] it in *vṛtta* or in any other manner whatsoever.
The path of the cow should be made in the shape of a plowshare, a half-moon, or a wheel, using the finest available materials; it should provide all desired objects.
The radius should be such that it is eight [units] less than the diameter of the wheel;
the well or the axle-pin should be provided so that the rim is firm.
The temple, constructed with wood and stone, features a high-piled pedestal;
it is well-designed, adorned with archways, and filled with the dwellings of the lords of the Gaṇas.
O best of gods, the auspicious pond Bhadrā is adorned with the dwellings of nāgas and yakṣas, filled with the sounds of divine play, and it grants all desires to men.
Bhadrā, Padmā, Śubhā, Kāntā, Vijayā, Maṅgalā,
as well as Jayā and Yoktrī— these bring auspiciousness to kings and others.
Ponds that are circular, oblong, or square are considered to be for general use; the remaining types are according to specific desires, while a circular well is conducive to auspiciousness.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"Or he who should duly present a step-well (*vāpī*) accompanied by fire,
having worshipped with faith the oceans situated in the water-pitchers at the corners."
By him the earth, bounded by the four oceans, becomes as if given away;
having honored the twice-born in his presence according to the rules with food and drink,
he goes to the world of Varuṇa, endowed with divine desires.
Now, the construction of the Bhadrā tank. Regarding this, Yama says:
"He whose water remains constantly in a tank attains the world of heaven; no deliberation is required on this point."
The builder of a pond dwells in heaven for four yugas.
Wherever a Brahmin or a cow drinks water,
by constructing a pond at such a spot, one shall dwell in heaven for ten yugas.
In the Mahābhārata:
Gods, humans, ancestors, Gandharvas, serpents, and Rākṣasas,
as well as immobile beings, all take refuge in a reservoir of water.
He whose excavated reservoir of water always provides water for cows to drink and for virtuous men shall deliver his entire lineage.
He whose thirsty cows, as well as deer, birds, and humans, drink water from his pond, shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Whatever water people drink there, whatever they bathe in, and whatever they rest in—
all that belongs to the owner of the pond and conduces to his infinite reward after death.
Likewise: "The wise have said that for him whose water remains in a pond during the rainy season, there is the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice."
He who has water remaining in his pond during the spring season enjoys the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
The great seers know that for one who has water remaining in a pond during the summer season, the fruit is equal to that of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"By constructing a tank, the best of the twice-born likewise enjoys the world of Varuṇa for ten thousand years, or even for the duration of a kalpa."
One obtains even greater merit than that from constructing a reservoir by making one on a path.
O twice-born ones, he in whose desert tank water remains indeed goes to the world of Brahmā by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
Even during the rainy season, for that man in whose pond water remains,
the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is proclaimed.
The fruit of a twelve-day sacrifice belongs to him whose [sacred fire] remains kindled during the winter season.

O twice-born ones, he in whose [house] it remains during the springtime obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice; and he in whose [house] it remains during the summer obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
When a river channel is thus constructed for the purpose of irrigating crops,
the donor becomes a giver of food, a giver of drink, and a giver of life;
he undoubtedly attains the worlds of Bhāgīratha.
O twice-born ones, having purified the water in a lake created by the gods,
a man obtains the fruit arising from the gift of ten cows.
By constructing an ancient reservoir made of wood or stone that is easy to use, a person is glorified in the heavenly world.
By constructing a water channel there, one attains unsurpassed satisfaction;
one acquires great merit and is honored in the heavenly world.
The wise man who constructs a pond dug by his own arm obtains the fruit of both the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Moreover, whoever else should perform a meritorious act at someone's reservoir,
he too becomes a sharer in a portion of the merit belonging to the owner of that reservoir.
O best of the twice-born, even when a small reservoir is constructed, a man attains supreme satisfaction and likewise reaches those worlds belonging to the Lord of Waters.
From that, however, [he created] the world of waters and the world of men.
Now, the door-binding (dvārībandha). In the Devīpurāṇa, Brahmā said:
"O best of gods, goddesses are praised as the accomplishers of all desires."
For their enjoyment, one should have water-vessels made.
O Śakra, the Puṣkariṇīs, Nagas, and auspicious Talakhātas are considered nourishing when provided with gates, embankments, and so forth;
a pond (taḍāga) without a protective wall is also deemed nourishing. A Dīrghikā is said to be rich in beauty, while a Vāpikā is square.
Wells are those lacking feet, while those with feet and provided with arches are considered *jhiraṃtīs*;
the *jhiriṭikā* is thought to be so called because it causes Indra’s [elephant] Airāvata to tremble.
The gate situated within the mountain is Sasphoṭa, as well as Haraka;
Cakramarda is Sacalaka, and Argalā is Citimant, the last.
The Vajra-nāga, moving downwards, never attains success;
likewise, the Holā-ātman and the Cakra are proclaimed to be easily accomplished.
That [vowel] which is superior, inferior, or middling, and is short in duration, is easy to grasp;
however, that which is long in duration and bound by a consonant is proclaimed as middling.
O dear one, a door that extends for a hundred thousand [units], consisting of two or eight double-frames,
is considered superior or inferior depending on whether it has many joints.
One should carefully avoid ground that is covered with sand, mud, or cracks;
for it is auspicious when measured by its length and breadth, and one should cultivate friendship there.
The best type of binding is proclaimed to extend to three, five, or eight [fingers];
the auspicious *pālī* consists of two hundred [units], while the lowest consists of seven.
The extent of the palībandha has been described in the treatise by the learned:
the rampart, the turret, the tunnel, the covered passage, and the collection of defensive mounds.
The path of the back would be the Bond-Dharmacandra together with Kambala;
O Śakra, when the earth-eater is in the sky, there is the station of water-restraint.
A vessel made of stone, one fashioned from a bilva-wood tree,
or that which is constructed from stones bound together, wide and expansive in its accumulation.
The wise one, having mastered the supreme union of vajra-connection which brings an end to all disputes and endures the time of debate, should perform the striking of the belly.
One should not cause [the ritual] to be performed upon a pit dug in the heart of the earth, nor even upon a woolen blanket;
for that brings great misfortune and causes fear to the one who acts as the mediator.
Effort should be made in pounding, such as kneading with clay and so forth;
iron struck by a pestle should be placed within the tubes.
The king should cause stones to be excavated until the completion of the process;
otherwise, the foundation would not be firm, and it would leak, causing harm.
Therefore, one should make the foundation firm, with the back of the house not being shaken;
first, one should deposit gold in the shape of a tortoise and a bull.
At the commencement of this great worship, one should perform the rites for Śyenaka and the others;
and one should always perform the recitation of the sacrificial mantra dedicated to Varuṇa and the Nāgadeva.
O Śakra, it must be completed; otherwise, it would bring fear to the kingdom and its people, and the gateway would not be secure.
Then, for the sake of visible results, Śakti should fashion images of the Vināyakas without their characteristic marks, just as Mahālakṣmī did previously in the city.
In this world, the water of the Nandā brings auspiciousness; likewise, an Āgama, a gateway, a pond, or a well containing a great serpent bestows welfare.
At the door-panels, the rite of releasing cows (gopradānika) should be performed;
one should give a thousand auspicious cows, as well as land and gold as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The Śyenaka and Nāgayajña [forms] are always auspicious when the door is bound;
they are provided with four archways and adorned with banners and other ornaments.
The ritual disposal [of offerings] is prescribed at the threshold; otherwise, it does not lead to auspicious results.
The bali offering should be presented with a cart, preceded by the slaughter of an animal.
One should employ there the throbbing mantra of the Heart of Nāgas;
then everything becomes complete, including whatever was done deficiently or in excess.
And whatever fruit might arise here from a horse sacrifice that has been performed,
one obtains that entirely when the construction of a door-bolt (dvārībandha) is completed.
In this world, O King, there shall be fame, all auspiciousness, and freedom from enemies;
those who construct door-archways rejoice together with their progeny.
A pond equipped with water-channels and provided with a surrounding walkway,
joined with a temple and a grove, bestows all desires.
When the gate-bond is very extensive, it is always auspicious and free from burning;
otherwise, O Śakra, there would be no firmness in the binding of the embankment.
In the center, a well-arranged watercourse for carrying water should be constructed,
either of stone or of baked brick, for the pleasure of the kings.
One should fashion beautiful bamboo poles for the insertion of the auspicious leaves;
the railing of the stairs should be made wide for the purposes of bathing and eating.
Endowed with superior beauty, it should be placed upon the *kūrca* according to the prescribed rule;
likewise, a firm binding should be made upon the back of the knot, enduring for a thousand eons.
In this way, one attains merit through what was performed during the period of stability;
just as the horse-sacrifice (*vājimedha*) is a ritual that bestows merit, so too shall this [practice] be a giver of merit.
Then, O dear one, the construction of the gateway-bond arises as a merit-giver for men;
through that merit they attain success, and that [merit] results from the dedication of Nanda and the others.
Jayantī, Āditadāga, and the other eight are destroyers of sin;
among them, Dvārī is the most excellent, being endowed with divine groves.
Provided with water from wells and tanks, it always bestows sons, long life, and fame;
that [fortress], established as the residence for the king's retinue, is measured out according to his honor.
For the sake of the success of the gods of cities and ports, this auspicious [earth] arises;
it is the earth not traversed by Viṣṇu, which is filled with rivers and the abodes of the Siddhas.
The water that circles eight times around the door-post of good fortune is welcomed by the ancestors, the gods, and human beings alike.
O Śakra, it becomes purifying; otherwise, it is considered fruitless.
In places where the outlets have not been opened, the water would be undrinkable;
therefore, the water that has been released is drinkable, and the opening of the outlets during the rainy season is auspicious.
Its front should face north, its rear situated in the northeast, or it may also extend toward the east;
and the linga should indeed be on the south, for a Shiva-mukhi [shrine] is always auspicious.
In the west is the one named Subhagā; as it is in the north, so it is there.
Those seeking auspiciousness should not perform [the rite] in the south, the southwest, or the southeast.
One should always plant auspicious [trees] in the east by proceeding clockwise;
otherwise, the doer incurs quarrels, agitation, or even death.
Therefore, an orchard established to the west, north, or east brings sovereignty, long life, auspiciousness, and increases the lineage of sons.
Provided with gateways, enclosures, and towers, and joined by powerful leaders,
it is then adorned with wells, water, and gardens, granting all desires.
O tiger among gods, he who constructs such a city, endowed with Brahmā, Sūrya, and Antaka,
shall obtain his desired fruit.
In this world, O Brahmin, it brings fame and virtuous sons; in the next world, it grants the supreme goal. Through the binding of the door, the fruit shall be equal to that of a horse sacrifice.
When performed according to the rite, it effects the destruction of all sins, and one becomes like a god;
therefore, the king must provide water at the gate.
Accompanied by the mantra, the rite seen in the treatises shall become fruitful.

Likewise, one should perform the worship of Śyenaka and others; one should mutter the heart-mantra marked with the serpent for the sake of accomplishing the binding of the gate, otherwise the performed rite will not be obtained.
O best of gods, since the sealing of the gateway is accomplished through merits,
one should therefore perform meritorious rites such as recitation, fire-offerings, and vows.
By the command of Śiva, the auspicious work of constructing a dwelling for the regional deities (deśaroga) should be undertaken;
for the sake of the success of the Nāgas at the gateway, the well of Nandā should be constructed.
In that case, the door would be meritless; however, it is the means for resolving doubt.
That which is made [weak] decays over time; therefore, it should always be made firm.
If that staff (daṇḍa) is situated in the west, southwest, or south relative to the practitioner, it will bring death;
if it is in the west or east, it bestows pleasure, sons, and wealth;
and if it is in the south or north, it causes the destruction of one's wife and wealth.
The direction going toward the Yakṣa (North-East) and Varuṇa (West), known as Bhadra, bestows long life and sons;
it should be given when facing North-East, and is considered to grant happiness and wealth.
In the west, there is Nanda, who brings about union and increases the treasury of wealth;
when situated in water or wind, he bestows gold and provides riches.
The *rakṣovāyu* [diagram] brings wealth and eradicates crows;
the *agnivāruṇika* [diagram] causes burning, consumes, and increases fame.
The malefic influence situated in the tenth house (deśadāha) causes sin as well as distress regarding wealth;
likewise, the fiery influence situated in the seventh house (vāyudāha) destroys wealth, gold, and elephants.
Relying on these characteristics, one should construct named groves that always bring auspiciousness to the builder, resulting in the attainment of wealth, long life, and offspring.
In this world, under the sovereignty of enmity, wealth always brings intoxication to the one who acquires it;
therefore, one should not destroy the auspicious merit of the king, the kingdom, and the people through improper conduct.
One should have the female door-guardian fashioned together with Rudra and accompanied by Gaṇanātha;
one should also properly fashion Jaya, Vijaya, and Gārya, along with the entire kingdom.
Having recited the heart-mantra known as Nāga, which vibrates with power, it is auspicious for the installation;
the armies, marriages, and goddesses should be gratified with offerings of milk and vows.

Those who desire the firm establishment of the boundary embankment (*pālībandha*) should hold a great festival in the enclosure with various kinds of garments, perfumes, fruits, incense, and other offerings.
O Śakra, gifts should be bestowed, which bring happiness to the king and the kingdom.
O best of gods, the gift of a cow, the gift of land, and the gift of a maiden should be bestowed at the consecration of a gateway; each shall yield a millionfold merit.
The gift of elephants, horses, and jewels, as well as the gift of food, should be bestowed with great effort at the doorways and enclosures; all such gifts shall become multiplied ten millionfold.
O Śakra, the merit that arises from the Gomedha, Naramedha, and likewise the Hayamedha sacrifice is even greater than that which comes from binding a door-bolt.
Ponds, wells, tanks, and temples—
these are auspicious and fruit-bearing among the duties of one's livelihood.
Charity should be given according to the prescribed rules to the poor, the blind, the elderly, and those who are fearful;
there, a single gift produces merit a millionfold—of this there is no doubt.
This, O Śakra, has been told to you regarding the fruit of binding the door;
the manifestation of the goddesses, their casting [of obstacles], and their majesty have been proclaimed.
The man who properly hears this auspicious manifestation of Śivadūtī shall fully obtain the fruit of all merit.
O dear one, wells, groves, tanks, and the like, as well as water-stations, fire-sanctuaries, and shelters—
when all these are consecrated, they yield infinite fruit.
One who constructs a hundred reservoirs with gates for irrigation,
having provided water for the Lord of All, shall obtain merit even greater than that.
Joined with Śiva, Sūrya, Hari, and Brahmā,
this primordial form is indeed supreme, all-granting, pervasive, and the abode of all mantras.
O Śakra, when it is installed, it becomes dedicated to all the deities, surrounded by Brahmā and the others, and serves to destroy all sins and fears.
Thus concludes the procedure for the binding of the gateway. Now follows the consecration of tanks and other such works, as stated in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
He spoke to Viṣṇu, the son of the Sun, regarding the course of reservoirs of water—
concerning ponds, groves, wells, and lotus-filled step-wells.
O Lord of Gods, I ask about the ritual procedure for temples;
who should be appointed as the officiating priests there, and what should the sacrificial altar be like?
"Who are those with southern bracelets? What is the location, and what is the preceptor? Please explain all such auspicious matters according to their true nature."
Matsya said:
Listen, O mighty-armed King, to the procedure regarding tanks and other such works as described in the Vahni Purāṇa.
When an auspicious day, an auspicious lunar mansion, and an auspicious moment coincide,
it is prescribed that the ritual for constructing ponds, wells, and tanks should take place at that time.
When the [sign] is completed, the desires of the doer shall be fulfilled;
in Cancer there is the gain of a son, while in Capricorn there will be happiness.
In Pisces there is the gain of fame and wealth; in Aquarius, an abundance of water;
in Taurus and Gemini, prosperity; and in Scorpio, it shall be devoid of water.
Satisfaction is found in Virgo, while in Libra there is eternal progress;
O twice-born one, Leo, Aries, and Sagittarius bring about the destruction of water.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"When the auspicious bright fortnight of Māgha has passed and the sun is in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa),
on a meritorious day declared by a Brahmin, having performed the *brāhmaṇavācana*..."
In a region sloping toward the northeast, near a pond,
one should prepare an auspicious altar measuring four cubits, square in shape, and facing the four directions.
Likewise, the pavilion should be sixteen cubits in size and have four openings;
and around the altar there should be a trench one *ratni* in depth, with three tiers.
O Prince, the vulva (yoni) may be nine, seven, or five [finger-breadths] deep;
the vulva should be one span (vitasti) in length and six or seven finger-breadths in width.
One should cause ten doors to be made for each side of the pavilion, fashioned from the branches of the aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, and vaṭa trees.
There, eight auspicious Hotṛ priests and likewise eight gatekeepers should be appointed;
furthermore, eight Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas should be made reciters (jāpaka).
Endowed with all auspicious marks, possessing the sacred mantras, with senses subdued,
and possessed of noble lineage and virtuous conduct— such are the best of the twice-born for the consecrator.
On an auspicious day, at a favorable moment (*lagna*) and so forth, there is the recitation by Brahmins.

On the day prior to the actual dedication (*utsarga*), the patron (*yajamāna*), having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that he will perform the dedication of the tank and other works, should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*—the rite for prosperity—and then conduct the recitation by the Brahmins. Furthermore, the worship of the site (*vāstu-pūjā*) must be performed here;
for it is heard in the *Matsya Purāṇa* that a fault arises if this is not done.

"One who does not perform the *vāstupūjā* shall become your food. The procedure for that is shown in the section on the gift of a house (*gṛhadāna*). The characteristics of the hand and so forth have been stated in the *paribhāṣā*. The *gartas* are the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*). One should construct five of them: four in the four cardinal directions and a fifth in the northeast, which is the pit for the preceptor (*ācāryakuṇḍa*). As for the banners (*patākās*), one should make them yellow, red, black, blue, resembling collyrium, white, black, green, and multicolored, in the directions starting from the east and proceeding clockwise through the cardinal and intermediate points. The flagstaff (*dhvaja*), however, should be adorned with small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*).

Having offered [the invitation], saying, "I, so-and-so, shall perform a sacrifice for a specific purpose; may you serve as my officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) therein," and so forth, he should honor twenty-five Brahmins led by the *ācārya* with the *madhuparka*. In each pit, there should be a water-pot (*kalaśa*), sacrificial implements, two fans, and two bright seats upon a very large copper plate.
Then, the wise preceptor, having consecrated them with mantras, should scatter upon the ground bracelets of many colors, one for each deity.
The sacrificial post (yūpa) should be one cubit (aratni) in length, fashioned from a milky tree;
or, desiring prosperity, it may be established at the height of the sacrificer.
Twenty-five officiating priests (ṛtvij) adorned with golden ornaments should be appointed;
they should also be provided with golden earrings, armlets, and bracelets.
Likewise:
"One should honor all [the priests] equally with rings, purificatory threads, and various garments; however, one should give double to the teacher."
One should give [the gift] together with a bed, as well as whatever is dear to oneself;
two golden tortoises and crocodiles, and two silver fish and *ḍuṇḍubha* eels.
The two copper-colored creatures, the crab and the frog, and the crow and the porpoise—
having encountered all of them in this manner at the very outset, O lord of the people.
Wearing white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes and unguents,
he was bathed by the preeminent Vedic scholars with water containing all medicinal herbs.
The sacrificer, together with his wife and accompanied by his sons and grandsons,
should enter the sacrificial pavilion by resorting to the western door.
Then, with the sound of auspicious cries and the beating of kettledrums, [he set out].

Regarding the passage beginning with *pratigarta*, one should place two seats, two copper vessels, two bundles of grass (*viṣṭara*), a fan, a cloth, and a water-pot containing five gems (*pañcaratna*)—all adorned with garlands, sandalwood, and other ornaments—at each pit (*kuṇḍa*). One should likewise prepare the sacrificial implements, such as the *pavitra* (strainer), the *chedana* (cutting) and *prokṣaṇī* (sprinkling) vessels, the *praṇītā* vessel, the cooking pot (*sthālī*), the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the fuel-wood (*idhma*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the kindling-sticks (*samidh*), the clarified butter (*ājya*), and so forth; as well as the *argha* offerings and oblations (*bali*) for the deities who are to be installed, various colors, perfumes, incense, lamps, and garlands, and a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) fashioned from a milky tree. After the offering of oblations to the deities, one should bury that sacrificial post in the eastern direction from the previous pits, having first cast into the hole auspicious stars [*text torn*]. Furthermore, having placed within a golden vessel containing the five gems, one should set down the *ḍuṇḍubha* (a type of lizard), *rājila* (a striped snake), *kulīra* (crab), *karkaṭaka* (crab), *kūrma* (tortoise), and others. In this manner, one should procure all other materials necessary for the commencement of the rite beforehand. All medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*) have been shown in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*).
The knower of reality should draw a mandala with five-colored powders;
it should be a sixteen-spoked wheel, containing a lotus at its center and having four faces.
Having made it square on the outside, circular in the middle, and very beautiful,
one should place the planets and the lords of the worlds upon the altar.
The wise one should place all [the deities] according to the mantra in every direction;
relying on the Varuna mantra, he should install Jhaṣa and the others in the center.
The wise man should install Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu right there,
as well as Vināyaka, Kamalā, and Ambikā.
Then, for the sake of the peace of all worlds, one should arrange the assembly of spirits;
having thus provided them with flowers, food, and fruits, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
And having wrapped those jars containing precious gems with cloths,
and having adorned them all around with perfumes and flowers, [he appointed] door-keepers at every entrance.
When they have settled there, the teacher should speak thus to them and honor them:
"The two *Bahvṛcas* should be stationed to the east, and the two knowers of the *Yajus* to the south."
The two Sāmavedins should be stationed in the west, and the two Atharvavedins in the north;
the sacrificer should sit down to the south, facing north.

"By means of *rajas*" and so forth; *rajas* refers to the powder of rice and other grains. The method for this has been shown in the *Paribhāṣā*. "The planets," namely Āditya and the others, together with their presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) and secondary deities (*pratyadhidevatā*). "The world-protectors and so forth," namely Indra and the others. The procedure for their invocation and so on should be observed in the *Tulāpuruṣa* rite. "The *jhaṣa* and so forth," namely the *makara* and other signs of the zodiac. "Kamalā," that is, Lakṣmī. "Ambikā," that is, Durgā. "Those"—namely, the jars situated near the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*). One should station two Hotṛ priests from the *Bahvṛca* school at the eastern pit. Having seated the Hotṛs in the southern and other pits according to their respective Vedas, this same sequence is to be understood to apply to the chanters (*jāpa*), the officiants (*dakṣa*), and the gatekeepers (*dvārapāla*).
He should say "Sacrifice! to those who are the *hotṛ* priests, but to the reciters (*jāpaka*), he should say, "Remain [engaged] in the muttering of the superior mantra."
Having thus instructed them all and applied the fire with the appropriate mantras,
he should offer oblations of clarified butter and likewise fuel-sticks with the Vāruṇa mantras.
And oblations should be offered to the officiating priests with *vāruṇa* mantras in every respect;
having offered according to rule to the planets, and likewise to Indra and Īśvara,
to the Maruts, to the world-protectors, and to Viśvakarman according to rule.
The teacher should offer oblations—this is the remainder of the sense.

The Vāruṇa mantras are: the five beginning with *tat tvā yāmi brahmaṇā vandyamānaḥ*; the two beginning with *tvaṃ no agne varuṇasya vidvān*; and *imaṃ me varuṇa śrudhi*. Regarding the number of oblations, having prescribed one hundred and eight for the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and clarified butter (*ājya*), twenty-eight oblations each should be offered to the planets (*graha*) and the other deities. The mantras for the planets and others are those stated in the *Tulāpuruṣa* [chapter].
The Viśvakarman mantra and the Raudra hymn beginning with *imā rudrāya*, etc., as well as the Pāvamāna hymn, constitute the auspicious hymns (*maṅgalasūkta*).
They should recite the Rātrisūkta, the Raudrasūkta, the Pāvamānasūkta, and the auspicious Puruṣasūkta; one should offer oblations separately from the eastward direction.

The *Rātrisūkta*, beginning with "rātrī vāsaḥ prayacchati," and so forth; the well-known *Puruṣasūkta*, beginning with "saṃjñānam ajaniṣṭa," and so forth; the *Śakrasūkta*, the *Raudrasūkta*, the *Saumyasūkta*, the *Kauṣmāṇḍasūkta*, the *Jātavedasasūkta*, and the *Sūryasūkta*—these should be recited by those learned in the Yajurveda on the southern side.

The *Śakrasūkta* consists of the *Indra naḥ viśvatas* and the *Rītyanuvāka*, with the *Udadhnuśakra* as its defining characteristic (*liṅgaka*). The *Raudrasūkta* consists of six verses beginning with *imā rudrāya sthiradhanvane*. The *Saumyasūkta* consists of six verses beginning with *somo dhenum*. The *Kauṣmāṇḍasūkta* consists of four *anuvākas* beginning with *yad devā devaheḍanam*. The *Jātavedasasūkta* is the *anuvāka* beginning with *yas tvā hṛdākīriṇā*. The *Sūrasūkta* consists of six verses beginning with *sūryo devīm*. These *sūktas* are well known among the followers of the Taittirīya school.
The Vairāja, the Pauruṣa Sūkta, the Sauvarṇa, the Rudrasaṃhitā, the Śaiśava, the Pañcanidhana, the Gāyatra, and the Jyeṣṭhasāman.
The Vāmadevya, the Bṛhat-saumya, the Raurava, the Saura-ṛthaṃtara, the Gavām-vrata, the Vikarṇa, the Rakṣoghna, and likewise the Yaśas.
"O King, let the Sāma-singers, stationed at the western gate, sing."

The *Vairāja* is well known in the verse beginning with "indrasya somaṃ piba. The *Sauparṇa* verses are those beginning with "ud hy eṣām abhiśrutā madaḥ"; there are three such *Sāmans* in the *Saṃhitā*. The [verse] beginning with "āvīr rājānam" is well known. The *Śaiva* is well known in the verse "uccā te jātam andhasaḥ," or else it has five *nidhanas*. The *Vāmadevya* is well known in the verse "kayā naścitra ā bhuvat. The *Gāyatra* is, however, well known. Regarding the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans*, there are three *dohas*; the *Vāmadevya* is to be sung in the *grāma*, and the *Bṛhat* is well known in the verse "mattvām iha vāmaha. The *Saumya* is the *Somavrata*, well known in the verse "sante payāṃsi. The *Raurava* is well known in the verse "punānaḥ soma. The *Rathantara* is well known in the verse "abhi tvā sūrano numaḥ. The *Gavāṃvrata* consists of two *Sāmans* beginning with "tvam anyataḥ prathamam. The *Vikarṇa* is well known in the verse "vibhrāṭ. The *Rakṣoghnā* is well known in the verse "yaśaḥ same bṛhad indrāya."
And to the north of the one belonging to the Atharvans, they should recite the Śāntika and Pauṣṭika [mantras] mentally, taking refuge in the Lord Varuṇa, the gods.
Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the previous day throughout the night,
[one should collect earth] from an elephant, a horse, a road, an anthill, a confluence, a lake, and a cow-pen.
Having brought clay, one should likewise throw it into four pits,
as well as yellow pigment (rocanā), substances of well-known significance, fragrances, and guggulu resin.
A ceremonial bath should be performed for him using the fivefold offerings,
preceded by the great mantras of the performer, having thus acted according to the ritual injunctions.

* Rocanā* is cow-gallstone (*gorocanā*). *Siddhārthas* are white mustard seeds. The five *bhaṅgas* are the tender shoots of the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *vaṭa*, and *cūta*. The mantras for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) are to be found in the *Tulāpuruṣa* [chapter]. The consecration, however, should be performed on the second day:
"May all the deities beginning with Śakra—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—and the gods consecrate you and bestow riches upon you."
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, as well as the all-pervading Saṃkarṣaṇa.
May Pradyumna and Aniruddha always bestow prosperity upon you;
may the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts [grant it as well].
May the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas,
as well as all the rivers, oceans, and mountains, rejoice in you.
The Vedas, the Shastras, the Puranas, Mimamsa, prosody, the Agamas,
the Brihatkatha and other such stories— all these bestow auspiciousness.
May Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Śacī, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Mṛḍānī,
and all the Mothers always be bestowers of boons.
May the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus,
and Saturn— the planets— consecrate you, as well as Rāhu and Ketu, being fully gratified.
May Indra, Vahni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, as well as Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśāna— the guardians of the directions— protect us at all times.
"May the years, the solstices, the months, the lunar days, the weekdays, the nāḍīs,
the muhūrtas, and the constellations, knowing [the difference between] day and night, consecrate [you]. With these words, one should consecrate the performer with the Rudra-pitcher.
Having performed thus the rite according to the rules for fuel-sticks and clarified butter,
then, when the bright dawn has arisen, [he should give] a hundred cows.
It should be given to the Brahmins— either sixty-eight,
or again fifty, or thirty-six, or even twenty-five.
"These cows, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), have been prepared for you as the deities of the ritual limbs; let them go"—with these words, he should give them preceded by water.
Then, when a pure and most auspicious moment has been declared by the years, [he should perform the rite] with the Vedas and Shastras, along with music, song, and various auspicious instruments.
Having adorned a cow with golden ornaments, one should cause it to descend there;
O lord of the people, that cow should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who chants the Sāman hymns.
And this is the mantra for consecration:
"O water, make yourself pure;
may you be ever pure, cleansed, and immortal."
"O Savior, perform the ritual ablution at the sacred ford; cross over the Lokāloka mountain yourself, and cause others to cross as well!"
The sacrificer, clinging to the tip of its tail, should cross over;
and he should encircle the reservoir with a triple-stranded cord. Taking a golden vessel provided with five jewels, [he should proceed].
Then, having cast away the makara and all those fish and other creatures in every way.
And [he saw] a great river filled with water, adorned with curd and unbroken grains of rice, being held by four Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
One should have [the image] placed face down in the middle of the water, facing north; then,
having recited the *Atharvaṇa Sāman*,
the verse beginning with "punar mām," and the mantra "āpo hiṣṭhā," one should cast [it in] and return to the pavilion.

The *Atharvaṇa-sāman* "saṇ no devīr abhiṣṭaye" is well known here as that which is to be sung in the forest (*araṇyageya*), according to its specific basis. One should perform the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) with the thought: "This reservoir of water, being useful for all, is released by me for the sake of all beings.
Having honored the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*), one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) on all sides.
Furthermore, O best of sages, it should be offered into the fire for four more days.
The fourth-day rite must be performed, and there too, O tiger among kings, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's ability, while then recollecting Varuṇa.
Having prepared the sacrificial vessels and the implements for the sacrifice,
and having distributed them equally among the officiating priests, he should then divide the sacrificial pavilion.
One should present a golden vessel and a bed to the officiating priest (sthāpaka). Then, one should feed either a thousand brahmins or likewise eight hundred.
And one should feed fifty or twenty [brahmins] according to one's ability;
in this very manner, the rule for a tank is stated in the Purāṇas.
This same rule is prescribed for all wells and step-wells, as well as for lotus ponds and likewise for their consecrations.
However, there may be a distinction based on the mantra in the case of temples, gardens, and grounds.
And this rule has been seen by the Self-Existent One to depend on one's capacity;
it should be performed by men even with very little wealth, like a single fire-oblation, provided there is no stinginess regarding their resources.
Water standing during the rainy season is considered equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
that which stands during the autumn season bestows the fruits mentioned above.
Water that remains during the winter and the cool season is said to be equal to the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices; that which remains during the spring is equal to the Aśvamedha;
and water that remains in the summer excels even the Rājasūya.
O Great King, he who, with a pure intellect, practices these distinguished dharmas for the sake of the goal,
goes swiftly to the abode of Rudra, purified.
And he rejoices in heaven for many eons.
Having enjoyed the worlds beginning with Mahas and Tapas along with his wives for two parārdhas,
he [attains] that which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
He attains that again by the power of yoga.

Thus, this common procedure for the consecration of ponds and similar works has been described; however, the specific details will be explained later according to the different Vedic branches (*śākhā*). In that regard, when performing the consecration, one should adopt those rites by combining non-conflicting elements from various sources; but where there is a connection with conflicting elements, one must follow what is prescribed in one's own Vedic branch.
Now, in the *Vahni Purāṇa*, the twice-born said:
O Lord, tell me all that regarding the Vāruṇī sacrifice as it was proclaimed by the Self-born One in the Veda, so that no delusion may arise.
Yama said:
On an auspicious day and under a favorable constellation, one should first seat the Brahmins;
having invoked the rice-grains with the Rigveda mantra, "Thou art indeed the Year, the Sacrifice."
"Āvorāja," thus did Atharvan honor this Mehi.
First, one should indeed offer water for the feet with the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and one should cause the guest to receive the respectful offering (argha) with the verse "ā tvā vahantu harayaḥ."
Then [he offers] water for sipping (ācamanīya), a seat with the words "Let there be a seat" (viṣṭaraḥ astu iti),
and honey and clarified butter in a bronze vessel consecrated with the mantra "Thou art the protector of the house" (kukuro 'si).
Having likewise sipped water three times from the mantra "May the waters purify me," he should give [the remainder] to the Sthapati with the verse "The guardian of the assembly."

Then the Brahmins should ask him: "Who has joined you to this rite? Thereupon, having [received the answer], he should begin the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice for subjugation (*vaśya*) according to the ritual of the bird.
For the world is powerful when it places worldly fire at its forefront.
One might as well kill a cow or an ox for a learned Vedic scholar; what would one not do?
Having first offered oblations into the two eyes, one should thereafter offer the Vyāhṛtis.
The two eyes are the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*).

One should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and the full [offering]; then one should perform the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) and so forth. One should also construct five pits and [worship] Varuṇa, who is like water.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should first lead [the fire] to the sacrificial pit (agnikuṇḍa).
With the verse "We choose Agni as the messenger," one should lead [the fire] to the south;
with "Thee, the enjoyer of the oblation," and "Agni the messenger," one should lead it to the west.
"O Agni, come to us from the north and from behind for the feast.
Having thus generated that fire, one should offer the two *vyāhṛti* mantras as oblations for the eyes.
And with the Varuṇa mantras, one should perform five oblations separately in each pit [with the verses]:
"Varuṇa has covered the earth," "This my Varuṇa," and likewise [the others].
With the two verses beginning "ud uttamam" or with "ṛjunītī," they say that the sacrificial porridge (caru) for Varuṇa is indeed to be offered in the east, dedicated to King Soma.
Having offered the oblation and given the final full-offering (pūrṇāhuti), one should place the sacrificial post (yūpa) into that Varuṇa-vessel;
having worshipped it in the Varuṇa-pitcher, one should perform the Śākala-homa.
The verse "brahmaṇo brahma jajñānam" is for Brahmā; "ato devā" is for Viṣṇu; "śambhave sambhavāya" is for Śambhu; and "trātāram" is for Jiṣṇu.
"O Agni, for Rohitāśva, for Yama," thus [the mantra] for me, O twice-born;
"This is for thee, O Nirṛti, and for Varuṇa, the lord of the waters."
Vāta blows for the sake of excessive blowing; how indeed does he act as the lord of the waters?
Listen now to this lord of lords among the planets.
With "ākṛṣṇena" [one offers] to Sūrya; with "imam deva" to Indu;
with "kujāya" to Agni; and with "ūrdhvānta udbuddha" to the Son of the Moon (Budha).
They say "guroḥ" for Jupiter; for Venus, "bṛhaspate"; for Mercury, "annāt pariśrutaḥ"; for Saturn, "śan no vedī"; and for Rāhu, "sīre tu kavāna".

O King, having offered oblations in due order with those mantras— namely "ketuṃ kṛṇvan aketave," "viśvāyuḥ viśvakarmaṇe," "bhūtāya te" for the spirits, and "kṣetrasya" for the lord of the earth— as well as the mantras that destroy demons; [1028]
Having offered one hundred or a hundred thousand sesame seeds individually there, or likewise with sacrificial fuel sticks or barley grains, he should again offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having performed a rite for peace for the sake of all enjoyments and assistance, the best of the twice-born,
as a cook, should prepare the *caru* offering dedicated to Varuṇa, which grants all desires.
One should offer oblations with Vāruṇa mantras and dedicate them to Varuṇa; then, having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the rules in each and every sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
And there one should bow down to Varuṇa, who is accompanied by his aquatic creatures;
there one should release either a hundred cows or even half of that.
But even in the absence of many, one woman adorned with jewels [should be given];
for the sake of the gods, ancestors, and humans, she should offer water with sesame seeds at her tail.
Having given her, adorned with all ornaments, one should afterwards announce her;
first, one should always give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) triple the amount to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and to the preceptor (*guru*).
Then, accompanied by his sons, wife, and friends, he should perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha);
he should bestow sacrificial fees upon them, as well as cows, according to his ability.
O King, he who thus performs the Vāruṇī sacrifice with diligence,
united with his ancestors, attains the supreme Brahman.
Thus have I declared to you that which was spoken by Agni in the past.
Thus ends the Vāruṇī sacrifice,
according to the Bahvṛca-Pariśiṣṭa.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for Varuṇa, the sacrifice of the pond (*vāpīyajña*). On an auspicious lunar day and *karana*, under a favorable asterism, having established oneself toward the eastern direction on ground sloping toward the east or the north, near water, one should kindle the fire, cook a *caru* oblation for Varuṇa, and having performed the rites up to the portioning of the clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), one should offer oblations of clarified butter, reciting the verse beginning with "The ocean is the eldest" (*samudrajyeṣṭhā*) for each verse. Then, one should offer eight oblations of the sacrificial food (*havis*): five with the verses beginning with "I approach you, who are worthy of praise with a sacred prayer" (*tat tvā yāmi brahmaṇā vandamānaḥ*), two with "O Agni, you who know, [protect us] from Varuṇa" (*tvaṃ no agne varuṇasya vidvān*), and the ninth, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, with "Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa" (*imaṃ me varuṇa śrudhi havam*). There are nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the waters are indeed the vital breaths; therefore, one offers with nine [verses]. At the conclusion of the sprinkling (*mārjana*), one should cause a cow to descend [into the water]. While she is descending, one should address her with this mantra: "Make this water pure; may those who are impure become purified and immortal, always contemplating it as consecrated by all holy bathing places (*tīrtha*); crossing over the worlds and the light, it delivers one across. Having himself grasped the tip of the tail while being supported by the teacher (*ācārya*), the sacrificer should emerge and warm himself in the northeast direction (*aparājitāyāṃ diśi*) with the mantra: "May the mothers, the waters, purify us."

"May you be a good milch-cow for the venerable master," [he says]. If she performs [the milking], then he should mutter: "Performing the deeds of the wealthy among the wealthy. He should give that cow—having a cloth around her neck, with golden horns, a copper-colored back, offspring of a bull, silver hooves, and a bronze milking vessel—to a Brāhmaṇa who chants the Sāmans; or else, whatever other gift he is able to afford, he should give as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the teacher. Then he should perform the rite of release (*utsarga*), saying, "May the gods, ancestors, and men be pleased," and having wiped [the cow's feet], Śaunaka says that the sacrificer, having fed the Brāhmaṇas, should have them recite a prayer for well-being (*svastyayana*).
Now, regarding the planting of trees. In that regard, the *Mahābhārata* states:
"Six classes of beings among the stationary (sthāvara) entities are proclaimed:
trees, shrubs, creepers, bark-textured plants, pithy plants, and species of grass."
These, however, are the species of trees; there is merit for me in planting them, as well as fame in the world of men and an auspicious fruit after death.
O Bhārata, the planter of trees shall deliver both his past and future paternal lineages;
therefore, one should plant trees.
O dear one, trees worship the hosts of gods with their flowers, the ancestors with their fruits,
and guests with their shade.
Kinnaras, uragas, rakshasas, gods, gandharvas, and humans,
as well as the great rishis, all take refuge in trees.
Bearing flowers and fruits, they satisfy human beings here;
moreover, those who have planted trees rescue them like sons in the world beyond.
Therefore, those who seek their own welfare should always plant trees by a pond.
And those auspicious sons of yours must be protected like sons, in accordance with the Dharma.

Then Viṣṇu said: "For the planter of trees, the trees become sons in the next world. By their flowers, the trees gratify the gods; by their fruits, they gratify guests; by their shade, those who have arrived; and during the rainy season, by their water, they gratify the ancestors.
(From the Padma Purāṇa).
In this world, trees provide the status of a son to one who has no son;
they grant to those who plant them the merit of visiting sacred fords, performing libations, and other such rites.

The meaning is that they bestow upon the planter the merit arising from the satisfaction [of ancestors] and so forth, which is produced by the libations and other rites performed at the *sattīrtha* established by his son.
O Indra among kings, perform the planting of the *pippala* tree with great effort;
for it alone shall act as the equivalent of a thousand sons.
[1031] The remainder of the sentence is "the duty of those with a thousand sons. Indeed, the *dhana* tree is the *aśvattha*; the *aśoka* is the destroyer of grief;
the *plakṣa* is declared to be the lord of sacrifice; and the *ciñcā* is remembered as the bestower of longevity.
The *jambukī* is said to bestow a daughter, and likewise the *dāḍimī* bestows a wife;
the *karalū* is for the destruction of disease, and the *palāśa* is likewise the giver of Brahman.
A man who plants the *vibhītaka* tree is born as a preta;
by planting the *aṅgula* tree, there shall be an increase in one's lineage, and by the *khadira*, freedom from disease.
The Sun is pleased with one who offers a substitute offering of neem;
Śaṅkara, the god, [is pleased] with the banyan tree; and Pārvatī [is pleased] with the trumpet-flower.
The Apsarases are in the Śiṃśapā tree, the best of Gandharvas in the Kunda;
the group of servants is in the Tintiḍīka, and likewise the Daśyus in the Vakula.
The *śrīvṛkṣa* is the *bilva*; the *tintiḍīka* tree is sour. The *candana* grants virtuous women, as does the *panasa*.
The *campaka* bestows good fortune, while the *karīra* is an adulterer.
The Tāla [breath] causes the destruction of offspring; the Nādīśa [breath] increases the lineage.
The coconut has many wives; the grape is beautiful in every limb;
the *ratipradā* likewise bestows pleasure; the *kelī* is the destroyer of enemies.
The *mocaka* and the *śālmali*,
as well as others such as those mentioned by Yena— they too shall be givers;
those men who plant trees will attain a firm foundation [in the next life].
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
[1032] Five trees are better than ten granaries;
for with their leaves, flowers, fruits, and blossoms, they provide libations to the ancestors.
Indeed, rather than many sons born who are devoid of dharma and wealth,
it is better to have a single tree by the road where people may find rest.
Because of this, she pleases living beings with her branches, bark, and shoots;
she gratifies the gods with her flowers and leaves, the fair-limbed women with her blossoms, and the ancestors with her fruits.
Blessed are those trees whose flowers, leaves, fruits, shade, roots, bark,
and wood do not go to waste for those who seek them.
Just as human sons perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) at the end of the year,
so indeed do trees produce nourishment every day according to their desire.
The fire-sacrifice performed by sons does not accomplish for women that which is accomplished by a tree with dense shade when it is resorted to on the road.
The flower garden, with its beautiful trees and fine blossoms and fine fruit,
follows two paths like a noble woman in the world of her husband.
With hands like *aśoka* sprouts and faces adorned with *tilaka* marks,
the garden grove, like a courtesan, is a source of delight and available for all to enjoy.
He who plants a tree always possesses a wife, always bestows gifts,
and always performs sacrifice.
One *aśvattha*, one half of a *picumarda*, one *nyagrodha*, ten *ciñcikīkas*,
and three, five, and [one] of *kapittha*, *vilva*, and *āmalaka*.
One who plants five mango trees shall not see hell.
Having provided shelter without weariness, and being self-controlled, these two— charity and offspring— yield fruit for one who desires it, serving as causes for the next world.
Having reflected on that, why were trees not planted?
No lotus ponds were dug, nor trees were planted;
what has been accomplished by that son who has stolen his mother’s youth?

Trees provide shade for others while they themselves remain in the heat; they bear fruit for the sake of others and do not focus solely on their own interest. Therefore, trees should always be planted for the fulfillment of all desires.
Thus ends the fruit of planting trees.
Now, the gift of trees. In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He who plants a tree that provides shade, flowers, and fruit..."
On that divine path, a man indeed delivers his ancestors from sin.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"He who gives [a tree] thick with shady branches in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa dwells among his kinsmen in groves of trees and in the gardens and mansions of Mahendra."
Like a god, they pass through ten million aeons while being entertained by throngs of lakes.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, at the beginning of the journey; regarding the word "should give" (*dadyāt*), the word "tree" (*vṛkṣam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
That man who, with the Dharma in mind, should give a fruit-bearing tree, shall go to the abode of Varuṇa, his soul satisfied by all desires.
In the Mahābhārata: "He who gives a fruit-bearing tree to the gods or to the twice-born shall dwell in the world of those who consume nectar, served by women with excellent thighs."
Accompanied by his ancestors, he sports for infinite time like a god;
having given a mango tree, he rejoices together with the kinnaras.
By giving a rose-apple (*jambū*) to a twice-born man, one goes to the same world as Ambikā; by giving a coconut, one attains the world of Varuṇa; and by giving a date palm fruit, one bestows grain.
By the gift of a betel-nut tree, one shall go to the world of Sarasvatī;
by giving a jackfruit tree, one goes to the world that is equal to the moon.
By the gift of a ciñcā fruit, one goes to the beautiful world of the Aśvins;
likewise by giving kapittha, pomegranate, āmrātaka, plantain, and myrobalan trees.
Having given [these], a person enjoys happiness in the worlds of the stars;
furthermore, by the gift of other trees possessing beautiful flowers, fruits, and branches,
a man attains the perfection of supreme sovereignty.
Likewise:
"Whoever offers to a twice-born man a tree that bears flowers or one that bears fruit,"
He indeed obtains a home replete with women, filled with many jewels, and acquired without effort.
[1035] Now follows the gift of the plantain tree (*kadalī*). Baudhāyana says:
One should have a divine plantain tree fashioned, completely covered on all sides with leaves.
Combined with a cluster of fruits, yet possessing the fruit of gold.
One should perform the rite according to one's means, wrapping [the object] with cloth and threads;
one should also feed Brahmins with various kinds of auspicious foods.
And one should have a fire-oblation performed there by a Brahmin as before,
facing the east, with mantras such as "Hiraṇyagarbha" that possess those specific characteristics.

To him— one who is honored, poor, established in good conduct, a knower of the Self, learned in Dharma, and exceedingly self-controlled— the consumer of phlegm should give that plantain tree, preceded by garments and ornaments, with this mantra:
O Hiraṇyagarbha, O Puruṣa, O Supreme beyond the supreme, O you who pervade the universe! By this gift of Rambhā, O Lord of Gods, O Master, bring my decay to an end.
The mantra for the gift:
"The declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) should be performed by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas;
one should partake of a meal together with learned, beloved, and kinsmen."
Now, the gift of the *nyagrodha* tree: likewise, even those wounds that may be caused by weapons or by being scorched by poison in battle, they too heal and grow back, just as was declared by Vāyu.
Whether it be made of gold, silver, copper, or even bell-metal,
weighing two palas, one pala, or even half of that.
One should fashion a banyan tree complete with trunk and branches,
wrap it individually in each section with a pair of cloths,
place it upon a heap of turmeric, and present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
O Lord Kubera, ruler of the northern quarter, whose vehicle is a man,
quickly destroy this sinus ulcer through the gift of a banyan tree.
The mantra for the gift:
Now follows the gift of a horse. In the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
"He whose feet are cracked would [otherwise] destroy the lords of the forest (trees)."
I shall explain the remedy for that through giving, as it has been taught.
One should fashion an Aśvattha tree, complete with trunk and branches, using half of that [measurement], or half of that again, or even half of that once more.
Adorned in the middle of its trunk with rubies, diamonds, and lapis lazuli,
and wrapped in cloth, one should place it everywhere upon a heap of grain.
The preceptor, who is learned in all scriptures, well-established in the treatises on Dharma,
a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and proficient in the performance of sacrificial rites,
being honored with garments, garlands, and other offerings, should worship the auspicious Aśvattha tree.
Accompanied by the mantra "aśvatthe vo niṣadanam," one should immediately perform the fire offering (homa) with the sixteen modes of service (upacāra).

When he intends to offer the medicinal herbs with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, he does so with the mantras containing the word "oṣadhīḥ," with those containing the word "nīr̥tiḥ," and with the three verses beginning with "tāny eva."
Likewise, one should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the mantra beginning "aśvattha";
having offered one hundred and eight, or indeed twenty-eight [oblations].
One should apply the patient's two feet with the *saṃpāta* clarified butter,
together with snake-skin, tortoise, and the powder of *niśā*.
With the mantra "prayātā" and with these fourteen [mantras],
one should, being composed, perform the ritual bath with the water-pot using these very mantras.
Having bathed with the hymns "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," "pratad viṣṇuḥ," and "viṣṇor nu kam" in succession,
as well as with the Oṣadhi-sūkta, he, being pure and wearing white garments, [performs the rite].
Having worshipped the tree, which is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, with perfumes and flowers,
one should devotedly present it to the preceptor while reciting this mantra.
For you alone are indeed like the Pippala tree, the king of trees, containing fire within;
you are the lord of the forest trees because of what was performed in a previous birth.
"Whatever injury has been done and whatever deformity exists in my feet,
you, being thoroughly gratified by this gift, shall quickly and immediately destroy them for me."
The mantra for the gift:
Having thus given the *aśvattha* tree, one should prostrate to it and dismiss it.
Then, having bathed again, one should eat together with Brahmins and kinsmen.
Then Vṛddhagautama said:
"He who cuts down trees in vain shall suffer from a sinus ulcer (*nāḍīvraṇa*).
For the benefit of all people, I shall now describe the remedy for that."
One should have a golden *aśvattha* tree fashioned, adorned with a trunk,
weighing half a *pala*, or half of that, or again half of that;
one should make a silver cord and encircle it with that.
Having placed it upon the rice, one should worship it with ritual offerings, impelled by the mantra:
"In the aśvattha tree is your seat."
The preceptor should be one who knows the treatises on Dharma, has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
is conversant with the Purāṇas, is tranquil, and is well-established in the knowledge of sacrificial rites.
One should personally perform the worship by inviting [the deity] oneself;
one should also perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
The installation of the fire should be carried out according to the method taught in the chapter on mantras.
This which I have proclaimed for the kindling-oblation while seeking vigor:
one should take eight or more oblations of clarified butter, and offerings of sesame seeds accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis*.
The installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) in the northeastern direction should be performed according to the scriptures;
with that [pot], one should perform the consecration using the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
A pacification of the planetary influences (grahaśānti) should be performed by Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
thereafter, the one afflicted with a sinus ulcer (nāḍīvraṇin), having bathed, wearing white garments, and being pure, [should proceed].
Facing north, he should present [the offering] to the preceptor facing east,
according to the rule, after the preceptor has been duly honored with rings and this mantra.
The most excellent among trees, the highly honored form of Viṣṇu,
is to be circumambulated by all and is to be saluted by all embodied beings.
May he, who has increased all his desires and purposes, be delighted by this gift.
By cutting down this useless tree, you have created a wound upon your own vital vein;
destroy it all quickly, for you are indeed the most excellent among trees.
The mantra for the gift:
Having thus given that gift, one becomes happy and free from ulcers in the vessels.
One should also give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability to other Brahmins as well.
Having paid homage to the teacher, one should walk slowly for a hundred paces.
Then, having bathed and being exceedingly joyful, he should feed the Brahmins as well;
with his speech restrained, he himself should eat together with the learned, beloved, and kinsmen.
