Now, the gift of the mango tree. Vṛddhagautama said: "If a man should steal the fruit of a Brāhmaṇa's mango tree, I shall describe the remedy for that once again through gifts, fire-oblations, and other means."
One should fashion an auspicious mango tree using half a *pala*, or half of that, or again half of that; or otherwise, according to one's means.
Likewise, it was glossy, beautiful, and completely covered on all sides by its branches;
it was wrapped in a white cloth and well-adorned with fruits.
Having worshipped it with perfumes and flowers, it is wrapped over rice;
the quantity of that rice is four *droṇas*.
Alternatively, half of that may be accepted by men according to their means;
furthermore, the preceptor should be disciplined and a knower of the true meaning of all the scriptures.

One who knows the Dharma, speaks the truth, is of noble birth, and is esteemed by the world— having summoned such a person with supreme devotion, one should have him perform the worship and other rites.

One should perform the worship and other rites with the verse "vanaspater aśanāya," and the fire-oblation (homa) in the southeastern direction should be performed with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
And the mantras, as seen in the scriptures, should also be recited with the words "may they protect [the child] at birth";
furthermore, there is an oblation of sesame seeds one thousand and eight times accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis*.
Since the oblation of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*) with the Vāyu-mantra is praised,
the pacification of the planets (*grahaśānti*) should also be performed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
Having offered oblations repeatedly, one should cause the remnants to be placed in another vessel;
by that, through the proper offering of clarified butter, may my disease of erysipelas be completely cured.
The installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) should take place in the northern part of the fire;
then, one should perform the consecration for the person seated upon the auspicious throne (bhadrāsana).
Then, wearing white garments and anointed with white perfumes and unguents,
he should present that golden mango tree to one facing the east.
Having worshipped [the tree] with perfumes and garments, the sick person himself, facing north, [should pray]:
"The mango tree was created by Brahmā for the benefit of all living beings."
You are the primordial source of trees and the increaser of the gods' joy.
The deformity resulting from the theft of fruit in a previous birth was [remedied],
and all the deities were gratified by the gift of a golden tree.
May they destroy all abscesses located within the body, whether external or internal, and may they always grant me well-being.
Having thus given that gift to the preceptor with extreme devotion,
one should walk back slowly for a hundred paces, prostrate, and then bid him farewell.
And one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability to other Brahmins as well;
then, having fed the Brahmins, one should eat together with one's kinsmen.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a tree.
In the Nandipurāṇa: "He who constructs a pleasure garden— an orchard abounding in flowers,
provided with water-retreats, well-guarded, and rich in fruit— "
He shall go to the city of Śaṅkara and remain there for three yugas.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*,
Puṣkara said:
"O best of the Bhārgavas, to the north is the auspicious *plakṣa* tree, and to the east is the *vaṭa* tree."
To the south is the Udumbara tree, and to the north is the Aśvattha.
These trees arising from the south and other directions are not desired for ritual acts;
likewise, thorny trees growing nearby are to be avoided.
Likewise, one should construct a beautiful garden on the left side of the left house;
there, in the northwest, one should plant flowering grapevines that have previously been well-tended.
Then, being self-restrained and well-composed, he should plant trees;
having bathed, he should worship the tree, as well as the Brahmins and Śiva.
The five fixed asterisms, Vāyu (Svātī), Hasta, Puṣya, Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇā),
as well as Mūla— these lunar mansions are recommended for planting trees.
O Rāma, when a garden is devoid of water and no longer delightful,
one should cause rivers to be brought into it and have lotus ponds constructed.
One should diligently construct wells for the purpose of purifying the water used for the *udbhid* sacrifice;
the asterisms suitable for this are Hasta, Maghā, Anurādhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Puṣya, and Dhaniṣṭhā.
O Rāma, the three Uttaras, as well as Pūrvā-phalgunī and the constellation Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj),
are auspicious for the commencement of works involving reservoirs of water.
Having worshipped the god Varuṇa, as well as Viṣṇu and Parjanya,
and having made the necessary preparations, O twice-born one, I shall describe the excellent trees:
the ariṣṭa, aśoka, punnāga, śirīṣa, along with the priyaṅgu.
O Rāma, the panasa, aśoka, kadalī, jambū, lakucha, and dāḍima trees,
which are auspicious, should be planted in houses to the east.
Having made many of these, all should be planted within the forest,
with the exception of the *śālmali*, the *kovidāra*, and the *vibhītaka*.
One who possesses discernment should not avoid any of these— damanaka, devadāru, palāśa, or likewise puṣkara— in the celestial garden.
In that regard as well, O best of the twice-born, one should perform many auspicious rites at dawn and dusk, at the conclusion of religious duties, and during the cold season on alternate days.
During the rainy season, when the earth is parched, trees that have been planted should be watered;
the distance between them should be twenty cubits for the best quality, and sixteen for the middling.
The distance between one tree and the next should be twelve *vyāmas*;
trees grown through practice that touch one another from top to bottom,
O twice-born one, become fruitful because they possess a subtle nature mixed with the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
Listen, Rāma, to the treatment for those diseases once they have arisen:
first, one should perform a purification of them, applying some surgical instrument.
One should sprinkle [the tree] with cold water after it has been smeared with a paste of *viḍaṅga* and ghee.

In the event of the loss of fruit, one should always provide water for the sake of flowers and fruit by sprinkling it with water that has been boiled and cooled, mixed with horse gram (*kulattha*), black gram (*māṣa*), milk, sesame, and barley.
One should cause the powder of sheep and goat dung, barley powder, sesame seeds,
beef, and water to be kept together for seven nights.
The irrigation of all trees bestows the growth of fruits, flowers, and so forth;
likewise, a seed nourished by colored water and watered with colored water [yields its fruit].
That becomes the flower of its stage in youth; of this there is no doubt.
By sprinkling fish and ashes, the growth of trees occurs.
Therefore, I shall describe the primary *dohadas* (longings) of trees.
O destroyer of enemies, it is desired that mango trees be sprinkled with cool fish-water; likewise, this same practice should be performed for grapes.
Ripe pomegranate seeds are highly recommended for a long time;
husks should be given for *bhavya* fruits, and liquor for the *vakula* tree.
Moreover, there is a specific quality arising from contact with the face of a passionate woman;
indeed, for those who are bashful, being struck by the feet of a passionate woman is highly praiseworthy.
The flesh of a jackal is beneficial when taken with water;
likewise, water prepared from oranges, liquorice water, and jujube fruits is highly praised.
Molasses-water mixed with beef is recommended for *karakas*;
with milk-ferment (*āsava*), the *saptaparṇa* becomes enchanting.
A sprinkling of flesh, fat, and marrow is beneficial for the *kuruvaka* tree;
likewise, putrid fish and the fruit of the putrid cotton plant are beneficial.
This sprinkling with snake fat is recommended for the *pāṭaka* trees;
one should cause it to be given to the *campaka* trees with jackal flesh and fish.
It is recommended to water fruit-bearing creepers with milk and blood;
one should perform the watering of *kapittha* and *bilva* trees with molasses-water.
The fragrant water of jasmine and *mallikā* flowers is supremely beneficial;
likewise, the flesh of tortoise is recommended for those of an irritable temperament.
Irrigation with salt water is known to promote the growth of date palms, coconuts, bamboos, and plantains.
O best of men, one should provide fish meat mixed with *viḍaṅga* seeds as a pregnancy longing (*dohada*) for all [women] without distinction.
When this is done, the trees will always become beautiful, bearing lovely fruit and fine flowers, fragrant, free from disease, and most delightful.
They are long-lived and endowed with sweet fruits.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "In a marshy place, a watery location, on land, before a deity, or in water,
a wise man should plant a grove according to the ritual prescribed by rule."
In a marshy place that is exceedingly moist, provided with water and containing reservoirs;
[1045] thus, by considering the time, the location, the recipient, the seed, and the ritual procedure for sowing the seed,
it will be planted in such a way as to produce a fruit equal to its cause.
For one whose fruits and flowers are pure, all conditioned things are pure;
otherwise, they are destroyed in the pursuit of achieving dharma, desire, wealth, liberation, and so forth.
O best of gods, when the ritual of seizing the ground (bhūparigraha) is adorned with errors in procedure, seed-syllables, and so forth, the sacrificer perishes along with his lineage and others.

The vessel is for sowing seeds; and the noble procedure for the application of noble seeds is the method of preparing seeds capable of producing sprouts. A deviation from the procedure is the performance of the rite otherwise. One should never cause a grove of mango trees and the like to be made impure in any way, whether it is defiled by contact with the fire of a funeral pyre or contaminated by a cemetery ant-hill.
Having caused a grove of mango trees to be planted, the one who made it goes to the abode of Yama.
O dear one, whether it has already sprouted from the house or has been planted outside,
one who desires his own welfare should counteract it there or cut it down.
Since the *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, *plakṣa*, and other trees, as well as those made of *udumbara* wood situated in the intermediate directions,
bring fear to the world, one should therefore cut them down with a weapon.
One should plant bilva, vīra, āmra, kapittha, kapilā, and arjuna trees,
as well as dāḍimī and bījapūra, to the north and beyond the trees on the eastern side.
Plakṣa trees, along with Kāśana and Dhanvana, should always be planted in the east;
the Kadamba in the northwest; and the Tāla, Bilva, and Aśoka everywhere.

The *vīra* is the *bhallātaka* tree; the *kapilā* is the *śiṃśapā*. The *asana* is the *vījaka*; it should be placed in the northwestern direction (*vāyavya*). [1046] One should establish the *mayandī*, *mādhavī*, *rambhā*, *jātī*, *nepālikā*, *kunda*, *tagara*, *gandha*, and *mallikā* in the place of recreation (*krīḍāsthāna*).
O dear one, these have been declared for the sake of auspiciousness, since they bring fear when applied in reverse.
To the east is Susamārāma, and likewise to the north;
to the west is said to be Dhanada, and in the northwest is Kīrtivardhana.
Those who seek auspicious results should not perform [the rite] in the south, the southwest, or the southeast;
otherwise, the performer incurs quarrels, agitation, or even death.
Therefore, an orchard constructed to the west, north, or east bestows sovereignty, longevity, and auspiciousness, and increases the lineage of sons.
Then Cāmuṇḍā shall pacify the faults committed by the village-born [spirits],
and Mahālakṣmī shall pacify great terror and whatever afflictions caused by the planets have arisen.
The affliction caused by the planets is the work of the planets.
Flowers, leaves, and fruits are equal to the dust of their seeds.
The agent who dwells in the assembly of the gods goes to heaven through proper performance, but to destruction through improper performance.
Likewise: having thus accepted the pure stage as described, which is like a boat and well-composed, [he approached] Śikhidhvaja, who wore a forest garland, according to the prescribed ritual.
Then one should perform the ritual of taking possession of both the *sāman* and the Naga King;
[this applies to] that seed which is devoid of mantra and excluded from the rites of conception and so forth.

If a seed such as that of the *sahakāra* tree is perfumed but devoid of mantra, that which is born from it will lead to harm for the planter; likewise, that which is produced by one who is corrupted [by improper conduct].
With the mantra "śaṅkarāya," one who knows these five mantras thus [proceeds];
O King of kings, the seed-syllable becomes auspicious by means of the Tryambaka mantra.
Those lowest of men who, instead of following the prescribed rule, engage in digging wells, ponds, and the like, or in the planting of mango trees and such,
shall obtain the fruit of those acts in this world, but at the end they will fall into a downward state.
Those who, being impure, perform the planting of trees according to the ritual for the pure, create great uncertainty for themselves, their king, and the world.
O child, by constructing wells, groves, tanks, water-booths, ponds, and shelters— all presided over by the Lord of All— one attains infinite rewards;
indeed, by planting five trees, one reaches the abode of Śiva.
Furthermore, those who are evil and of wicked conduct, who destroy the sacred *śrītara* trees,
are then cooked in the Pācyādina hell for the duration of a day of Brahmā;
though they are dead, on earth they are proclaimed as "slayers of Brahmins" (*brahmaghnas*) even while they are still living.
In that region there is constant fear, the kings are short-lived,
and this world finds no joy where the Śrīvṛkṣa tree is cut down.
Thus ends the planting of groves. Now follows the consecration of trees, as stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.
The sages said:
Tell us in detail and according to rule the procedure for trees there;
by what rite should the wise perform the concluding ceremony (udyāpana) of the tree-planting?
And tell us of those worlds that are remembered [as their reward], or rather, explain their cause to us.
Sūta said:
O Lord of the World, having approached all the requirements according to the rules for constructing a tank, I shall likewise describe the procedure for trees in garden grounds.
The preceptor, likewise, should honor the officiating priests, the sacrificial pavilion,
and the ritual materials, as well as the brahmins, with gold, garments, and unguents.
Having sprinkled the trees with water containing all medicinal herbs, adorned them with ground lac, decorated them with garlands, and wrapped them in garments.

The piercing of the ears of all [the children] should be performed with a golden needle; likewise, collyrium should be applied with a golden probe. One should have seven or eight fruits made of refined gold.
The vessels made of silver should be polished with black powder (*kāladhauta*).
One should consecrate each of all the trees up to the sacrificial altars (*vedi*).
Guggulu resin is the best incense for this rite, and the vessels should be placed upon copper trays.
O Lord of Men, having fashioned pots made from all kinds of grain, and having adorned them with garments, perfumes, and ointments, one should place them in every single spot.

Having made offerings to Indra and the other guardians of the world according to the prescribed ritual and his own capacity, he should present all those [offerings] along with gold as a tribute to the deities.
And the wise twice-born should perform the fire-oblation for the Lord of the Forest.

Then, one should release from the midst of the trees a milch cow facing northward— clad in white garments, adorned with golden ornaments, possessing a bronze milking vessel, and distinguished by her two golden horns.
Then, with the consecration mantra, accompanied by musical instruments,
auspicious songs, and the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as those dedicated to Varuṇa, he was surrounded on all sides.
The eminent brahmins should perform the ceremonial bath with those very jars;
having bathed and wearing white garments, the patron should perform the worship.
With great concentration, he gratified all the officiating priests with cows,
golden threads, bracelets, rings, sacred grass rings, variegated garments, as well as household utensils and sandals.
They should perform the consecration with milk for four days;
likewise, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with ghee, barley, and black sesame seeds.
Palāśa wood fuel-sticks are recommended on the fourth day, as is the festival;
likewise, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given there as well, according to one's ability.
Whatever is most beloved, that one should give without envy;
having given double to the teacher and prostrating, one should dismiss him.
The wise man who should perform the festival of the tree according to this rite, [attains the fruit].
One obtains all desires and attains the infinite state.
And whatever man, O Indra among kings, should establish even a single tree,
he too shall dwell in heaven, O King, for as long as thirty thousand reigns of Indra.
One who is free from passion shall deliver men of the past and those yet to be;
he attains supreme perfection, from which return to worldly existence is difficult to find.
Thus ends the procedure for the consecration of a tree.
Now follows the procedure for the gift of a "tree-son" (*taruputra*). In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"A pond is equal to ten wells; a tree is equal to ten ponds."
A son is equal to ten trees; a tree is equal to ten sons.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"He who performs the rite for a tree-child according to the rules in the presence of the fire,
being liberated from great sins, uplifts three generations of his lineage."
From the hells, a man goes to the auspicious city of Prajāpati.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Having thus heard that her husband was the Lord of the Three Worlds, the devoted wife Bhūmiruhā’s daughter spoke this to Rudra.
O Blessed One, O ocean of the essence of rituals, by what procedure,
O Moon-Adorned One, is a tree made as a substitute for a son?
To the goddess who was thus playfully inquiring about the supreme ritual procedure, the omniscient Mahādeva spoke these words to Mahādevī.
O Goddess, whose thighs are like the trunk of the lord of elephants, who moves with the gait of the lord of elephants,
listen to the procedure by which the son of a merchant is obtained.
The *avanija* tree is the one [to be taken].
Thinking, "I shall take this tree for the sake of my son," Pārvatī said:
"A woman should observe a fast, wearing clean garments and maintaining pure vows."
Then, when the thousand-rayed sun had reached the peak of its setting,
and the stainless moon, resembling a silver mirror, had likewise risen;
At night, she should invite brahmins who are purifiers and exponents of the Vedas;
having invited the brahmins, she, wearing pure garments and observing pure vows, [should proceed].
Having thus passed the night, she should sleep upon the ground strewn with darbha grass while offering salutations, even when the sun has risen.
Taking various kinds of food and drink, one should go to where a tree may be;
then, having bathed it, one should provide it with an umbrella and ornaments.
Having made that tree youthful,
and then having provided those twice-born ones with sacrificial food accompanied by shade,
he should then cause an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be proclaimed, either by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or by himself.
When the Brahmins have indeed been satisfied, you must report this deed of yours,
declaring it accomplished with the highest sincerity.
"Lords, I am childless; I wish to take this tree as a substitute for a son. O most excellent beings, you ought to grant me your permission."
Then, O beloved, with the permission of those gods of the earth, one should indeed accept that tree of youthful form as a son.
In the presence of the gods of the earth and before the Brāhmaṇas,
he who has thus received the "tree-son" according to this rite pours down a stream of honey for his ancestors dwelling in hell.
A son, who is like a tree of auspicious ground, when taken according to this rite, leads to happiness in prosperity; by the opposite method, he brings about suffering.
O lady with full hips and breasts, even a hundred sons are not equal to a single tree;
such a son is considered the best, designated as a true offspring.
Thus was this asked by me, O master of parables, as something desired:
how the son born from the earth is superior to sons born from the womb.

Then the goddess Śokāpahā, radiant and greatly rejoiced, adorned that Aśoka tree with various kinds of ornaments; and before it, she held up a parasol that eclipsed the sun with the brilliance of its pearls.
Girijā covered him with peacock feathers and also with fragrant sandalwood paste of various colors.
From the very root, the goddess bestowed here and there her lotus-like hands,
which were like those made of Jāmbūnada gold and resplendent with jewels.
Pārvatī adorned her beloved Aśoka tree on all sides; she hung strings of pearls upon its branches and twigs.
The cave-dweller bound that Aśoka tree with two garments, so that it shone like the sun among hundreds of stars.
The Mother of the worlds, longing for her son, caused them to dwell there;
then Nameru offered beautiful guggulu and clarified butter.
Then, accompanied by incense and fly-whisks perfumed with incense,
and with the sounding of conchs and the roar of divine musical instruments;
The Brahmins, who were equal to Brahmā himself, were brought by Nandinātha;
having given cows and gold, he had them recite the auspicious day (puṇyāha).
Then, at the conclusion of the proclamation of the auspicious day and the pronouncement of blessings for both,
they took leave of the husband and the queen and gratified the sages.
In the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*,
the Blessed Lord said:
"Henceforth, I shall proclaim the procedure for the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) of a tree."
It pacifies all sins and destroys all that is inauspicious.
O Pārtha, in former times on Mount Mandara, Pārvatī, being childless,
adopted an Aśoka tree as her son to alleviate her grief.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, listen as I describe those rites such as the birth-ceremony and others, which the wise man of that lineage performed according to the Atri-purāṇa.
But that young tree,
with its thick foliage and likewise its tender shoots, must be cultivated so that it may endure cold, wind, and heat.
A grove of thorny trees named after women, containing hollows dug out by insects—
no tree of this kind should be planted, for it is not approved by the learned.
When a well-constructed, auspicious water-trough with four corners has been provided,
one should then have that area cleared and well-smeared.
Thereafter, O Pārtha, the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the trees is highly commended on an auspicious day declared by a Brahmin, marked by a favorable conjunction of planets and constellations.
One should consecrate the tree chosen for the *pātāla* rite on the previous day;
having covered it with red cloths, one should encircle it with a red thread.
Having bathed the tree with [water from] the jars beginning with the *ṣṭā* [mantra], as well as with gold and all medicinal herbs,
the wise practitioner should place the previously prepared jars in the four directions.
Their faces were adorned with sprouts, they were anointed with white sandalwood paste, provided with pairs of white garments and parasols, decorated with garlands, and filled with jewels.
All the trees in its vicinity should be adorned with banners;
they should have water-pots placed at their roots and be encircled with red threads.
There, the fifteen fruits— made of gold and exceedingly beautiful— are adorned with red, yellow, and white streaks.
One should consecrate copper vessels containing seeds along with jewels; then, amidst the sounding of musical instruments and auspicious chants, one should cast offerings in the four directions.
Then, at the clear dawn, the preceptor who knows the mantras, having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with its girdle according to the mantras of Indra and the other world-protectors,
should perform the entire ritual procedure in accordance with the rules for the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña).
Having adorned four or eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas with golden ornaments, one should honor them according to one's ability with garments.
An oblation with sesame seeds and clarified butter shall always bring about satisfaction and nourishment;
having first established the Mothers, one should worship them with flowers and unbroken grains.
Having properly cooked the sacrificial porridge (caru) thoroughly saturated with milk,
one should perform the oblations for all rites beginning with the birth ceremony (jātakarman) and ending with the gift of a cow (godāna).
Having bathed the tree with water from sacred fords accompanied by mantras, one should perform its birth ceremony, naming ceremony, and the first feeding of solid food;
then, according to the prescribed rite, one should pierce its ears with a golden needle.
Then, with a razor of gold, he should perform the tonsure ceremony in due order;
he should bind on a girdle of muñja grass and cause him to put on a garment.
Having performed that [rite] in its entirety, one should perform the auspicious Godāna ceremony;
some, however, desire the marriage of the tree with the Mādhavī creeper.

They know that one may [plant] a *jambū* or a *śālmali* tree together with *mālatī* and *śallakī*. For a tree that has been consecrated by the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should likewise employ a benediction (*āśis*) with the mantra: "This is the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*)."
Then the sacrificer, having bathed, wearing white garments and being pure,
should take a handful of flowers and utter this mantra:
Those trees which are the ornaments upon the crests of mountain peaks,
those which have established their residence in the Nandana and other celestial groves,
and those which grant the desires of gods, humans, serpents, and kinnaras—
May they, by means of this, become the removers of his afflictions from evil.
These twice-born ones have duly offered oblations here into the sacrificial fires;
even this moon, situated within, beholds them.
And you, O tree, are held fast by me through the thought of you being my son.
You must always perform the task that is my son's task.
Having spoken thus and having touched that tree again and again,
one should look at one's own face in a vessel of ghee and pronounce a blessing.
From limb by limb you are produced; from the heart you are born.
You are indeed the self named "son"; live for a hundred autumns.
Then, with joyful minds, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brāhmaṇas;
having given an auspicious cow to the Sthāpaka, one should perform a great festival.
Food was provided without restriction for the poor and the helpless;
however, for others, he, being well-pleased, gave them wine and spirits.
One should eat at will together with one's kinsmen and relatives;
likewise, all laborers should be fed according to one's own means.
This, O Pārtha, has been told to you—the great festival of trees.
One obtains all desires in this world and in the next.
Without sons, men shall not obtain auspicious fruit; likewise, with wicked sons, there is the destruction of both worlds. Having reflected on this, a wise man should protect his trees.
These should be carefully conceptualized through effort according to the Vedic injunctions.

Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a tree. And the gift is completed; may Hemādri, the lord of ritual acts, be victorious—he whose mass of fame encircles the circle of the earth bounded by the oceans.
In the great treatise *Cintāmaṇi* composed by that Hemādri,
the section on gifts (*dānakhaṇḍa*) has reached its complete perfection.
Observing that even those [merits] which are beyond counting cause one who is worthy to attain greatness over the sages,
he makes an effort to practice those acts of giving.
He reached the further shore for Hemādideva.

Thus ends the Section on Gifts (*Dānakhaṇḍa*) in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious sovereign of great kings, the lord of all the faculties of the illustrious Great Queen, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
